en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Great Commentary on the *Paramatthadīpanī Saṅgaha*: The Text.
The Discourse on the Beginning of the Composition [Ka]:
From the rising of which one [sun], whose net of rays is the True Dhamma;
The lotus-born beings awoke in the great lake, the field of birth.
I pay homage to that great hero, the dispeller of the darkness of great delusion.
That mass of darkness which had arisen in my heart has been dispelled.
Many explanations have been praised by the wise of old.
These are explained here in this world, in the *Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha*.
(Gha) Those who are conceited do not find satisfaction in them, even though they seek the essential meaning.
They gathered together and entreated me for an exposition of the ultimate truth (paramattha).
Having extracted jewels from the great ocean, [I shall give them] to the inhabitants of the island.
They may give as much as they wish, yet one cannot say there is any deficiency.
Likewise,
here in this world, those of vast wealth are like jewels in the ocean.
Even if they were to describe them a hundred times, they would not reach the end.
Therefore, having extracted the essence from those descriptions, this description [is composed].
Complete with various essential meanings, its words and phrases are clear;
neither too concise nor too prolix, it awakens those of dull intellect.
"I shall compose this for the sake of the ultimate meaning; let those who possess the treasure of proficiency listen.
This concludes the commentary on the first verse of the *Abhidhammattha-saṅgaha*.
The Elder Anuruddha, desiring to compose the *Abhidhammattha-saṅgaha*, first establishes the purpose for undertaking this compendium.
Demonstrating the fivefold meaning of the "five-fold summary" (*pañcapiṇḍattha*), he spoke the opening verse. The fivefold meanings of the summary are:

homage to the Triple Gem, the subject matter of the work, the type of work, the title of the work, and the purpose of the work. In this context, "homage to the Triple Gem" refers to performing acts of service toward the Three Jewels.
This is expressed by the words: "I pay homage to the peerless Perfectly Enlightened One, together with the supreme Dharma and the supreme Saṅgha."

These meanings are shown by these words. The four subjects of the Abhidhamma, which constitute the primary subject matter expressed throughout the entire treatise, are indicated by the term *abhidhammattha* within the phrase *Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha*.
However, in the *Vibhāvanī*: [1] In the *Vibhāvanī*, however...

Because it was considered that even the state of being "collected" (*saṅgahitabhāva*) is indeed an object of expression (*abhidheyya*), it was stated: "The object of expression is shown by the term *Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha*. That is not correct.
For it is not fitting that this state of being collected—which is a subordinate matter—should be called an "object of expression" in this demonstration of the summarized meaning (*piṇḍattha*).
Furthermore, from here on, whenever the phrase "in the commentary" (*ṭīkāyaṃ*) is used, it refers to the two Sinhalese commentaries (*sīhaḷaṭīkā*) on this *Saṅgaha*.
The *Paṭhamāṭīkā* (First Commentary) is to be understood [in this context]. When "Vibhāvanī" is mentioned, it refers to the second commentary currently well-known.
When "the two commentaries" (*ṭīkāsū*) are mentioned, both are meant. When "the *Mahāṭīkā*" is mentioned, the *Mahāṭīkā* on the *Visuddhimagga* is to be understood.

Furthermore, whatever statement has appeared in the *Vibhāvanī* and has also appeared elsewhere, that too is referred to here specifically as being in the *Vibhāvanī* because of its proximity. This is by way of a compendium of related phenomena (*sabhāgadhamma*).
The "mode of the arrangement of the compendium" (ganthavidhānākāro) refers to the manner of the compendium's composition; this, moreover, is indicated by the word *saṅgaha*.
However, it is stated in the *Vibhāvani* that it is indicated by the phrase "Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha"; that is not correct.
For the term *abhidhammattha* does not indicate the manner of composing a book; rather, it is a designation for the book that follows the meaning [of the Dhamma].
That is shown by the phrase *Abhidhammattha-saṅgaha*.

When the *Saṅgaha* treatise has been composed, the realization of the true nature of phenomena and so forth—which can be obtained without effort through its study, interrogation, and so on—extends up to *anupādā-parinibbāna* (Nirvana without clinging).
The fruit and subsequent fruit of the treatise, as well as its purpose, are also shown by implication through the very term *Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha*.
In the *Vibhāvanī*, however, it is stated that this is indicated by the word *saṅgaha* (compilation). That is not correct.
For, without the term *Abhidhammattha*— which indicates the mere successful accomplishment without effort—

it would not be possible to understand such a distinguished class of people whose ultimate goal is final nibbāna through non-clinging, merely by the word *saṅgaha*, since even those who collect false doctrines (*asaddhamma*) are seen in the world.
2. In this regard, first of all, the homage to the Triple Gem possesses incalculable and immeasurable purpose. As it has been said:
"For one who honors such beings as those, who have attained Nibbāna and are fearless from any quarter, it is not possible for anyone even to calculate the merit therein."
The construction is as follows: "Whatever friendship exists here cannot be reckoned by anyone at all—whether by a human, a deva, or a Brahmā.
The commentators (*ṭīkākārā*) also elaborate extensively on that purpose in various places.
However, the compilers (*saṅgahakārā*), specifically, primarily desire only the warding off of obstacles. By "the compilers," one means the Venerable Buddhaghosa and others.
The masters of the commentaries say:
"For this performance of service toward the Three Jewels that has been performed,"
"For by its power, it dries up obstacles without remainder"—thus it is said. 3.
And how does the homage to the Triple Gem act as a protection against obstacles? It is said: [It is] the homage to the Triple Gem.

Indeed, this great flood of merit, this stream of merit, which consists of the performance of the act of homage occurring seven times, seven times, and many hundreds of thousands of millions of times,
is of great radiance; for it has been cultivated upon the unsurpassed fields of merit such as the Buddha and others,
and has been permeated by the Elder’s own sublime zeal, faith, wisdom, and virtues.
It becomes a preeminent merit that is of great fruit and great benefit.

Standing oneself in the state of perfection of means, having removed external conditions of failure and brought about conditions of success, one effects the nourishment of the eight bodily elements arising from extremely refined temperature, consciousness, and nutriment;
thus, for the karma that produces beauty obtained from the moment of rebirth-linking onwards—
It provides supporting power (*anubala*). It also secures the acquisition of an opportunity for that other merit which had not previously obtained one.

Then, by means of both that merit—consisting of the supporting power thus acquired and the opportunity thus secured—the material and immaterial continuities (*rūpa-arūpa-santati*) produced therefrom proceed within the Elder’s continuum, becoming increasingly powerful like two great twin rivers.
At that time, within that continuum of the Elder, which is densely filled with desirable fruits, [the resultants arise].

Since there is no room for the arising of obstacles such as diseases—which constitute undesirable results—meritorious deeds have already removed from afar those demeritorious karmas that obstruct the continuity of desirable results and produce the continuity of undesirable results.
For indeed, neither meritorious nor demeritorious karmas ripen when there is no opportunity for their own result to arise. Consequently, within that mental continuum...

Dharmas that yield desirable fruits—beginning with long life and beauty and extending up to the completion of the scriptures, or even until the end of one’s lifespan—proceed by remaining on the side of increase. As it is said:
“For one who is habitually respectful and always honors the elders...”
"Four things increase: life-span, beauty, happiness, and strength.

Thus, by that act of homage, there is an obstruction to obstacles. Therefore, when undertaking an act of communal support (*saṅgaha*), the performance of homage to the Triple Gem serves to ensure the completion of the Elder’s own mental act of support without obstacle. And not only this...
For the Elder himself, as well as for the listeners who are receiving this compendium,
the homage to the Triple Gem at the very beginning is for the purpose of accomplishing the task of grasping it without obstacle through its successful completion.
However, in the *Vibhāvanī*:

Among the seven impulsive moments (*javana*), it appears as if the purpose of the salutation is explained by means of the first impulsion alone. For it is stated there: "They are to be experienced in this very life (*diṭṭhadhammavedanīya*).
That is not correct, because here it is specifically the function of support (*upatthambhana-kicca*) that is intended, and that function is found in all seven impulsions.

Just as, of the two functions of nutritive material (*āhāra-rūpa*), the function of generating the eightfold materiality consisting of nutritive essence (*oja*) is limited and insignificant; [so too is the case here].

It exists. For the four peaceful [states], the function of supporting the three [mental] aggregates alone is great and preeminent. Thus, even in the *Paṭṭhāna*, having taken up that very function of supporting, the section on analysis (*vibhaṅga-vāra*) is set forth thus:
"Edible food is a condition for this body by way of the nutriment-condition.
In the same way, here too, the function of producing resultants occurs immediately after the first impulsion.
It is slight and insignificant; it produces merely a rootless resultant (ahetuka-vipāka), as stated in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*).
Its function of supporting the intervening kamma is great and excessive, and this is indeed found even in all seven impulsion moments (*javana*).

However, since the subject matter of the book, the types of the book, and the purpose of the book have been explained at the outset, people will have the enthusiasm to listen to the hearing of the book.
It is born. Therefore, the presentation of the titles and subjects of those books is for the purpose of generating enthusiasm for the books.
The presentation of the designation of the book is for the sake of ease in conventional usage.

This is the summary of the meaning here. 4. Now, as for the meaning of the words: he has awakened perfectly (*sammā*) and he has awakened by himself (*sāma*), thus he is the Perfectly Self-Awakened One (*Sammāsambuddha*). And herein—

The word *sammā* is a particle used in the sense of non-perversion (*aviparīta*). It illuminates the complete and exhaustive nature of the act of awakening with respect to those knowable phenomena that ought to be awakened to.

For it is said in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*) that Paccekabuddhas and others, who abide in partial knowledge, awaken correctly only within their own domain; however, regarding what is not their domain, they are as if entered into darkness. And their domain is...
It is merely trifling when compared to the domain of the Omniscient One, just as the space within a closed fist is trifling when compared to the cloudless sky.
For they are unable to awaken to even a single phenomenon among the factors such as contact in all its aspects.
But for the Omniscient Buddhas, there is nothing that is not their domain, wherein they might perceive anything erroneously. For they...

In the beginningless cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), throughout infinite world-systems, and regarding all phenomena belonging to the three times and the timeless, they awaken having made them equal, as if they were a jewel upon the palm of the hand.
For it is said: "All phenomena in all their aspects enter the gateway of the knowledge of the Buddha, the Blessed One.
In this context, "gateway of knowledge" refers to the Great Life-Continuum (*bhavaṅga*) of the Omniscient One.
For there, at the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), those phenomena remain present at all times through the continuous contemplation of the entire Abhidhamma.

Furthermore, whatever number of phenomena omniscient Buddhas wish to investigate, they set those very same phenomena apart by means of adverting (āvajjanā), and having adverted to them, they investigate them. [Objection: But are not phenomena vast, while the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) is limited?
This need not be questioned, for such is the power of immaterial phenomena when they have reached their highest excellence.

However, the prefix *sam-* is an adjunct (*upasagga*) used here in the sense of "near" (*sāma*). This indicates that the Blessed One had no teacher regarding the states of realization (*paṭivedhadhamma*).
For it has been said: "I have no teacher. [One might ask: But did the Blessed One not possess the third and fourth immaterial attainments?

"Rooted in Āḷāra and Uddaka. This is true. However, because they were merely acquired without being cultivated and were subsequently cast aside, they do not even serve as a foundation for the act of awakening later on.
How much less could they be the Dhamma of penetration? Therefore, they do not establish the Blessed One’s status as a Buddha along with his teachers.
This is the meaning here according to the scripture, as it has been said:
In this regard, what kind of person is a *sammāsambuddha*? Here, a certain person, regarding teachings not heard before, has personally awakened to the truths.
Therein he attains omniscience and mastery over the powers (*bala*).
This person is called a *sammāsambuddha*.
*Tattha* (therein) is the locative case used in the sense of a sign (*nimitta*). *Balesu* (in the powers) refers to the ten powers of knowledge (*ñāṇa*) of the Ten-Powered One.

*Vasibhāvaṃ* means the state of mastery (*issarabhāva*). And here, by the word *pubbe* (previously), etc., he shows the meaning of the prefix *sam-*; and by the words *tattha* and so forth, he shows the meaning of the prefix *sammā*.
[Thus ends the section on the term *Sammāsambuddha*.]
5. Now, the Elder, wishing to make his own act of homage exceedingly powerful, said "incomparable" (*atulam*).

For an act of homage directed toward a field of many qualities becomes more strongly powerful. [An objection: "Is it not the case that even an act of homage directed toward a field of a single quality could be capable of warding off obstacles?
What is the use of a second? [The reply: It is not incapable. However, those of a wise nature act with moderation when praising the virtues of the Teacher.
They were not [monks], and the Elder was one of them; you, however, are of an ignorant nature. Therefore, while acting as their attendant, you reproached them.
Furthermore, it is not only the removal of obstacles that is required for paying homage; rather, proficiency in wisdom and other such qualities must also be desired.
For that too leads to the effortless completion of the texts and to the purification of the scriptures.
"And it is a condition. For the cultivation of the mind regarding the objects of recollection brings about concentration of the mind.

And when there is concentration of the mind, one strikes out having become brave through the sharpening of wisdom. For it is said: "One who is concentrated, monks, understands things as they truly are.
Therefore, for that purpose as well, one must certainly perform one's own salutation with great strength.
In the *Vibhāvani*, however, it is stated:

"Even though the meaning of the words as previously explained applies, because the term *sammāsambuddha* occurs here by way of a conventional designation (*samaññā*) for the Blessed One, it is distinguished by the qualification 'incomparable' (*atula*).
This is not correct. For this term *sammāsambuddha* stands in the midst of the great qualities of the Teacher like the moon among the stars.

In the middle [of the compound]. Therefore, for those who know that conventional language (*sabhāvanirutti*), it is not possible for that which is empty of the meaning of "existence" to be merely the Teacher’s designation (*satthusamaññāmatta*).
However, even if thousands of other words were spoken, they would likewise become merely the Teacher’s designation.
That which is to be weighed, to be measured in comparison with another, is *tulo*. That which is not *tulo* is *atulo*; there is no *tulo* [in this case].
Or, he is called *Atula* because there is no one equal to him (*etassa sadiso*). Thus, the Blessed One (*Bhagavā*). For indeed, there is no one in the world who is equal to the Blessed One himself.
As it is said: "I have no teacher; no one equal to me is found.
In the world together with its devas, there is no rival to me."
It is not surprising that the Great Being possesses incomparable greatness once he has become a Buddha; however, his incomparability was already evident even immediately after his birth.
For at that time, as soon as he was born, the Great Being stood facing the eastern direction.
In that quarter, infinite world-systems became a single open space. The gods and Brahmās stationed within them—
"Great Being, there is no one here equal to you; how could there be anyone superior? Thus they honored him with the highest worship.
In the same way, they did so in all the other directions as well. Then the Great Being, knowing his own preeminence over the entire world, thought:
"I am the foremost in the world, I am the best in the world, I am the eldest in the world; this is the last birth; there is now no further becoming."
"Thus he uttered words free from fear. This too is not surprising, for such is the incomparable nature of one who has reached his final existence.

However, when he, having become Sumedha, received the prophecy of certainty in the presence of Buddha Dīpaṅkara, even then there was no one equal to him in the qualities of the perfections (pāramitā), with the exception of the Perfectly Enlightened One, Dīpaṅkara.
Its non-existence at that time is indeed to be demonstrated by uncommon miracles, such as the shaking of the ten-thousandfold world system and so forth;
for even a hundred thousand *paccekabodhisattas* would not be able to bring these about, let alone *sāvakabodhisattas*.
Therefore, at that time, the knowledge of the discernment of the perfections (*pāramī*) during their manifestation [is] within its own domain.
"It has the nature of the knowledge of omniscience," so it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*.
For from that point onward, even disciples and bodhisattvas are able to know for themselves the requisites of merit (sambhāradhamma) appropriate to their own enlightenment.

From that point on, having become those whose nature is irreversible, they transcend the state of being ordinary worldlings who merely follow the course of conduct and enter the stage of a bodhisattva.
In one sense, they are indeed destined for and culminating in full enlightenment.

At that very moment, when they are in the presence of the Buddhas, they receive the prediction of their certainty. It need not even be mentioned regarding omniscient Bodhisattvas and Pacceka-Bodhisattvas.
However, in the *Vibhāvani*:
It has been stated that this [form] is established by means of either the *yakāra* or the *akāra* in the word *samita*.
That is not correct. For it is not appropriate for the word *atula* to be derived from a verbal root (*dhātu*) and function as a passive noun (*kamma-sādhana*).

Indeed, it is stated in the *Ṭīkā*: "He who is unable to be measured is *atula*; he is immeasurable. By this, it is shown that the word *tula* functions as a passive noun (*kamma-sādhana*). And thus...

Since that purpose is accomplished by the very means of the action (*kamma-sādhana*) itself, what is the point of considering whether the *yya* or the *a* occurs in the sense of "together with" (*samita*)?
If it is argued that this was stated because the application of words follows one's desire to speak, we say no;
for there is no reason to employ a word by imagining something unheard of while abandoning what has been heard and is logical. [The term *atula*]

6. Furthermore, by these two phrases, the Teacher’s threefold perfection (*sampadā*) is analyzed: the perfection of cause (*hetusampadā*), the perfection of fruit (*phalasampadā*), and the perfection of service to beings (*sattupakārasampadā*).
Therein, the Teacher’s possession of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and his accumulation of the requisites for enlightenment (*bodhisambhāra*) are called the perfection of cause.

That which was manifested at the seat of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*)—consisting of twenty-four thousand times ten million *koṭis*—and known as the Great Vajra-knowledge (*mahāvajirāññāṇa*), [is the perfection of fruit].
The great insight of omniscience (*sabbaññu-mahā-vipassanā*) is also included right here, for it is the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) of Great Enlightenment (*mahābodhi*).
Alternatively, it should be understood as being included within the perfection of abandonment (*pahāna-sampadā*) itself. The perfection of fruition (*phala-sampadā*) is fourfold:

the perfection of abandonment, the perfection of knowledge (*ñāṇa*), the perfection of power (*ānubhāva*), and the perfection of the form-body (*rūpakāya*). Among these, the abandonment of the defilements (*kilesa*) together with their underlying tendencies (*vāsanā*)...

"Perfection of abandonment" (pahānasampadā) means the complete fulfillment of abandonment. In terms of its essential meaning, however, it is the Noble Path, or specifically the knowledge of the Supreme Path (aggamaggaññāṇa).
The perfection of knowledge (ñāṇasampadā) consists of the knowledge of omniscience (sabbaññutaññāṇa), the ten powers (dasabala), and so forth.
Furthermore, in the *Vibhāvani*:
Of these two accomplishments, the accomplishment of knowledge (*ñāṇasampadā*) was mentioned first, followed by the accomplishment of abandonment (*pahānasampadā*).
However, it is the accomplishment of abandonment that should have been mentioned first; for that is the precursor to and the condition for the accomplishment of knowledge.
Moreover, in the *Mahāṭīkā*, that very one is mentioned first.
[8] Furthermore, that which was stated regarding the perfection of knowledge—namely, that "the knowledge of the supreme path has omniscience as its proximate cause"—is also not tenable.
For the knowledge of the supreme path ought to be the perfection of abandonment itself; indeed, there is no such thing as a "perfection of abandonment" distinct from the knowledge of the path.
"It exists. And as for what anyone might say—that path-knowledge is both knowledge and abandonment—therefore it is appropriate to state it in both ways;
that too is not tenable. For if that were so, there would be a confusion of categories (*sampadāsaṅkara*). Thus it is stated in the *Vibhāvani*.
Regarding the perfection of knowledge (*ñāṇasampadā*), although omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*) should have been mentioned first of all, it was not mentioned.

That too is not satisfactory. If it is argued: "Is it not the case that in the phrase 'the ten powers and other knowledges rooted therein,' omniscient knowledge is included by the word 'and others' (*ādi*)?"—that also is not tenable.
For it is contrary to logic to indicate the subordinate by its own form and then include the primary, which is manifest, by the word 'and others.'
It is thus: "Possession of majesty" (*ānubhāvasampadā*) is the perfection of psychic powers (*iddhi*) and Dhamma-qualities through virtues and other attributes of inconceivable power.

"Perfection of the form-body" (*rūpakāyasampadā*) is the excellence of the physical body adorned with the primary marks (*lakkhaṇa*) and secondary characteristics (*anubyañjana*). "Perfection of disposition" (*āsayasampadā*) is twofold:
the disposition toward benefiting beings and the purity of application (*payoga*), which consists of the loftiness of aspiration (*ajjhāsaya*) and the purity of bodily and verbal application.

The meaning [of the term *sampadā*] is as follows. In that context, "perfection of intention" (*āsaya-sampadā*) refers to the constant inclination toward the welfare of even hostile beings such as Devadatta and others.

"Perfection of application" (*payoga-sampadā*) refers to the purity of the method of teaching, characterized by a lack of regard for gain, honor, and the like, when teaching the Dhamma to world-renowned kings, royal ministers, wealthy householders, and even the kings of the gods. In that regard:
The two perfections of the knowledge of abandoning are manifested by the term "Perfectly Enlightened One" (*sammāsambuddha*).
Together with the two perfections of the body of essential qualities (*ānubhāva-rūpakāya*), the two perfections of assistance to beings are manifested by the term "Incomparable One" (*atula*).
Furthermore, the perfection of the cause is manifested by implication through both terms, for without such a perfection of the cause, the occurrence of the others is impossible. [Perfections]
7. Furthermore, the Elder, making his own act of homage even more powerful, said, "Together with the supreme community of the True Dhamma" (*sasaddhammaguṇuttama*).

By this, homage is also rendered to the Dhamma and the Saṅgha. For when it is said, "From afar I shall pay homage to the Leader of the World together with the Saṅgha" (*sasaṅghaṃ lokanāyakaṃ*), the inclusion of the act of bowing to the Saṅgha is understood through the word *sa-*. This is how it should be regarded.
In that context, "they will pay homage" means "they paid homage.
Furthermore, it is stated in the *Vibhāvanī*:

"For even though the factors (dhammas) and the community (saṅgha) have become subordinate qualities, their status as objects to be saluted is understood through their association with the primary term."
In this context, it should not be said that there is "the state of being one to be saluted. Rather, it should be said that "the state of having been saluted" means "salutation.
For if this were the case, since the action-inherence intended here is established, the attainment of the act of veneration toward the Elder by the members of the Saṅgha is also established.
Otherwise, because the suffix *-tabba* indicates fitness (*arahattha*), [the meaning would not be properly conveyed].
It might be said that the term "one worthy of salutation" refers to one who possesses a collection of qualities; however, that is not intended here.
Furthermore, it does not accord with his own example [in the verse], where he says, "I have come together with my sons and wife.
Moreover, before composing this work, the Elder already paid homage to the Three Jewels; thus, [the verse]...
It is not impossible to say that he composed this verse while demonstrating his own self-praise in conjunction with the promise of the book;
for it says, "I pay homage," and not "I do not pay homage. This same method applies elsewhere as well.
In that context, [he pays homage] by means of the True Dhamma, the supreme assembly, and himself—who has been fashioned [thereby]—who have become a refuge for the entire world.
"He exists together with" means "possessing the True Dhamma and the supreme assembly. This refers to the Perfectly Enlightened One (*Sammāsambuddha*).

For disciples are not called "possessing the True Dhamma" and "possessing the supreme assembly" merely because they are accompanied by a True Dhamma produced by others and a supreme assembly [of others].
Nor is it fitting to praise Pratyekabuddhas in such a manner as being accompanied by a True Dhamma that has become their own refuge and by a supreme assembly of fellow celibates (*sabrahmacārī*).
"Arahant" means "one who protects"; therefore, this too should be understood as a term for the Teacher’s unique qualities.

In this context, "dhamma" means that which protects. What does it protect? It protects those who practice the Dhamma. For it is said: "The Dhamma indeed protects one who lives according to the Dhamma. And how does it protect?
By preventing one from falling into the four states of misery and the sufferings of saṃsāric existence. And what...

"Retention" (dhāraṇa) means the cutting off, either partially or entirely, of those defilements by virtue of which beings fall into the states of misery or into the suffering of the cycle of existence.
In this sense, the four noble paths and Nibbāna are, in the ultimate sense, called "Dhamma.
For the noble paths, while cutting off the defilements, exist together with Nibbāna.
They cut off [the defilements]; they do not bring them forth. Therefore, these five alone are exclusively called "dhammas" (in the sense of what is to be borne).
The Dhamma of the scriptures, however, is merely the means for bearing [it]. Furthermore, the four fruits of recluseship are themselves the fruits of bearing;
because they proceed by way of the subsiding of the defilements, they proceed in a manner conducive to bearing. Therefore, these five are merely "dhammas" in a figurative sense.

Alternatively, it is called *dhamma* because it is borne (*dhārīyati*). What is meant is that it is worthy of being borne. For that which, when borne, unfailingly liberates one from suffering and establishes one in supreme bliss—it is precisely this, by virtue of being worthy of being borne, that is here termed *dhamma*. And what is that?

Just as there are "duties toward children" (*putta-dhammā*), so too [is this]. Among those, some are [attained] by way of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), some by way of realization (*sacchikiriyā*), and some...
By way of dwelling in happiness in this very life, some [teachings] are retained through grasping and memorization.

When they are thus retained, they liberate the one who retains them from the suffering of the states of misery and the suffering of the round of existence as appropriate, and establish them in the bliss of the highest fruit or the bliss of Nibbāna.
Or, by retaining them, noble persons ensure that they themselves do not fall into the states of misery or the sufferings of the round of existence.

It is called *dhamma* because people carry it by means of it; or, because people—having found their footing, with the island of the *dhamma* as their refuge and the *dhamma* as their resort—abide therein, it is likewise appropriate to call it *dhamma*.
But why is *dhamma* mentioned here as being only tenfold? Should it not be stated as elevenfold, including the *dhamma* of practice (*paṭipatti-dhamma*)?
True. However, that *dhamma* of practice is simply the preliminary path of progress (*pubbabhāga-paṭipadā*) to the [supramundane] Path.

The phrase "it occurs" means that, like prior volition, it is included within the path itself in the context of giving. Therefore, it should be understood that the Dhamma is stated to be tenfold in all instances.

Furthermore, by the same principle that the Dhamma of the scriptures (pariyatti-dhamma) is included here under the category of "Dhamma," it is likewise appropriate that the bearer of those scriptures is included among those worthy of veneration in the Saṅgha.
And by the same principle that the "virtuous worldling" (puthujjana-kalyāṇaka) is included in the Saṅgha among the trainees (sekkha)...
He is included. For that very reason, it should be understood that his practice—which serves as a cause for excellence—and his Dhamma are also included within the Dhammas worthy of veneration.

Although he is still an ordinary person (*puthujjana*), he is included among those in training (*sekha*) who have entered the path for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*) by virtue of being endowed with certain qualities. And those qualities [are found] in the trainees on the path of stream-entry...

"It is not possible to say that he is not included. To this extent, those who say, "I go for refuge to the Saṅgha," [are refuted by the fact that] therein the virtuous worldling (*puthujjana-kalyāṇaka*) is not included in the Saṅgha. For one who goes for refuge to him, the act of going for refuge is not accomplished.
Thus, their position is rejected. However, it should be stated as follows: "Ānanda, whoever by me..."

The Dhamma and the Vinaya have been taught and established; "After my passing, this shall be your teacher"—having thus placed [them] in the position of the Teacher and praised them, the Blessed One included the Dhamma of the scriptures within the refuge in the Dhamma. This is logical.
Furthermore, among those who uphold it, there are some who abide in the practice of the good, and there are some who do not. He who does not abide [in the practice] is not even a refuge for himself.
It does not exist. How could it belong to another? Moreover, he has been censured by the Teacher in many thousands of discourses.
Therefore, he is not included in the refuge of the Saṅgha; only the other [noble ones] are included—this is logical.

The Dhamma that exists within the continuum is the True Dhamma (Saddhamma). It belongs to those who have stilled their defilements, and for that very reason, to the noble persons (sappurisa) who are praised and honored.
The meaning is "the Dhamma of the wise. Furthermore, that which is the Dhamma of the peaceful is itself exclusively peaceful;

thus, it is the "True Dhamma" (Saddhamma) because it is the Dhamma of the peaceful. It means the Dhamma that is praised and honored. Or, it is "true" (sacca). For this [Dhamma] does not deceive one who upholds it, unlike the Dhamma of other sectarians.
For that [other Dhamma], while appearing beneficial to one who upholds it thinking, "This is for my welfare," turns out to be actually harmful.
But for one who maintains it in such a way, this indeed results in welfare. [The Footing of the True Dhamma.
In the world, a "group" (gaṇa) is said to be a collection of those who share the same view and virtue among fellow practitioners of the Dhamma.

Here, however, the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is endowed with supreme qualities such as virtue; thus, in the sense that it is both supreme and a group, it is called the "Supreme Group" (uttamagaṇa).
He is called "the best of the assembly" (*gaṇuttama*) here, just as the best of sages is called the "foremost of sages" (*munivara*).
However, in the *Vibhāvanī*, it is stated:
"The 'best of assemblies' (*gaṇuttama*) means the highest among assemblies, that is, among the multitudes of gods, humans, and so forth. That is not correct.
For when this meaning [of "foremost"] is present, the word *uttama* (foremost) is preeminent;

and since that [term] applies only to a quality (*guṇa*), it is not established that the Noble Saṅgha is what is spoken of here by that [word]. And in this context, "group" (*gaṇa*) is said to be the Saṅgha itself.
That Saṅgha is twofold: the conventional Saṅgha (*sammuti-saṅgha*) and the Saṅgha worthy of offerings (*dakkhiṇeyya-saṅgha*). Therein, that which is performed by a harmonious Saṅgha...

The formal act of full ordination (*upasampadākamma*) is called a "convention" (*sammuti*). The community of monks (*bhikkhusaṅgha*) that stands having reached the stage of full ordination by means of that convention is called the "conventional community" (*sammutisaṅgha*);
this is well-known in the disciplinary procedures (*vinayakamma*). The "community worthy of offerings" (*dakkhiṇeyyasaṅgha*) is the assembly of the eight noble persons (*ariyapuggala*).
Although this [latter] is indeed included within the conventional community, nevertheless, regarding taking refuge, paying homage, and honoring...

It should be understood that the Blessed One described it in such a way—praising it as a supreme field of merit (puññakkhetta) for the purpose of including it among the objects of recollection for offerings and honors—and thus spoke of it separately.

For although the Saṅgha of ordinary worldlings (puthujjana-saṅgha) is likewise a field of merit, it is not a supreme field of merit. Why? Because it is like weeds in a field of fine rice; it is a corruption of the field.

This is because of the presence of the latent tendencies of personality-belief (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*) and doubt (*vicikicchā*). Furthermore, its status as a field of merit (*puññakkhetta*) should be understood according to the method explained in the previous verse on the True Dharma (*saddhamma*).
[The Verse on the Supreme State of the True Dharma and the Assembly] 8. *Abhivādiya*:
Having paid special homage. And here, one who is endowed with qualities such as virtue (*sīla*) is the most excellent and worthy of veneration in this world.
Having thus established such a supreme mind, one who pays homage is said to pay homage preeminently.
Furthermore, homage is threefold, by way of bodily homage and so forth. As it is said:
"Monks, there are these three kinds of homage. What are the three? One pays homage with the body, one pays homage with speech, and one pays homage with the mind."

Therein, having established the most excellent mind and having placed the five limbs—namely, the two knees, the two elbows, and the forehead—upon the ground, one prostrates by way of the body while lying down facing those worthy of veneration.
It is with reference to this that it is stated here and there: "having prostrated with the fivefold contact. And as for that [prostration] performed in places where one should not prostrate...
"An offense occurs for one who pays homage": when one utters words of praise with the voice, one is said to "pay homage with speech.

Such as "Homage to the Buddha," "May there be homage to the Buddha," "Homage to Liberation," "Homage to those who are liberated," and "May there be homage to Vipassī"—in these cases, it is indeed homage by speech.
When one has followed the words of praise and recollects the qualities [of the Buddha], one is said to "pay homage with the mind."

9. *Bhāsissanti*: "I shall speak. Although the Elder, while composing this compendium (*saṅgaha*), will indeed compose it by setting it down in writing, one should understand that the words "he shall speak" and "it was said" are used because the act of writing is well-established among the acts of speech. 10. Regarding the phrase *Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha*:
"The meanings stated in the Abhidhamma are the 'meanings of the Abhidhamma' (*abhidhammattha*). These are what are "collected" (*saṅgayhanti*).

In this regard, by this very [work], the *Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha* is [so called]. "Compendium" (*saṅgaha*) means that it is summarized (*saṅgayhanti*)—that is to say, it is condensed and expounded by the Elder.
Regarding the term "Abhidhamma": here, "abhi" signifies pre-eminence (*atireka*) and distinction (*visesa*), and "dhamma" refers to the Dhamma.
Furthermore, "Dhamma" here denotes the two Piṭakas other than the Vinaya Piṭaka. As it is said: "O Ānanda, the Dhamma and the Vinaya have been taught by me to you..."

For it is said: "It is taught and formulated. And that twofold textual tradition, setting aside the task of discipline (vinaya-kicca) known as the issuing of commands, illuminates only the ultimate phenomena (paramattha-dhamma) such as the wholesome as they actually occur.
When these two categories of phenomena are thus illuminated, that which is superior and distinct from the other is precisely what is called Abhidhamma.
In this way, it is indeed the Dhamma alone. Having established it thus, this tetrad—Dhamma, Abhidhamma, Vinaya, and Abhivinaya—is to be understood.
Regarding these, it is stated in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) that "Dhamma" refers to the Suttanta Piṭaka; "Abhidhamma" refers to the seven treatises (*pakaraṇa*);
"Vinaya" refers to the two Vibhaṅgas; and "Abhivinaya" refers to the Khandhakas and Parivāra. This is because they possess a superior distinction.

And herein, it should be understood that this teaching is established upon pure phenomena (suddha-dhamma) either by way of an exhaustive analysis of the various modes to be taught—such as by way of the wholesome and so forth, the aggregates and so forth, or the categories of inclusion and so forth—or by way of the unfolding of the teaching itself.
For it is only among the devas that the omniscient Buddhas deliver this Abhidhamma teaching; for humans are not capable of such [a teaching].
They are able to receive a discourse-path suitable for continuous practice over three months, from beginning to end, while remaining in a single posture;
yet such a discourse-path following a single *mātikā* cannot be taught to various people at different times.
Furthermore, some [hold that] even according to the Vinaya Piṭaka, there is a specific distinction regarding the *abhiññā* (higher knowledges).

They praise that [work]. However, it does not accord with the *Aṭṭhasālinī*. For in that [work], this specific distinction was investigated only within the midst of two canonical texts (pāḷi) bearing the name "Dhamma.
Furthermore, it is not appropriate to investigate it in such a manner together with the Vinaya, because their functions and domains are different.
For the Vinaya has the function of restraining body and speech, and its domain is transgression (*ajjhācāra*). The Dhamma...
Furthermore, [the Dhamma] has the function of analyzing phenomena and the sphere of the manifestation of phenomena. Some, however, say:

"Even if this is so, the Vinaya alone should be the most senior. For one who disparages the Vinaya incurs an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*), whereas for one who disparages the Dhamma there is only an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
That is not tenable. For the Vinaya is the Wheel of Authority (*āṇā-cakka*), and the Dhamma is the Wheel of Dhamma (*dhamma-cakka*).
In that regard, one who disparages the Vinaya strikes a blow at the wheel of the Teacher’s command. Disrespect toward the Teacher is a great thing.
And for one who has disrespect toward the Teacher, disrespect toward the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, and the three trainings is established as a matter of course.
Therefore, in the disparagement of the Vinaya, the offense is grave. It is not because it is the most senior [of the Pitakas]. Furthermore, what is called "Vinaya" is...
It is the root of the Dispensation. When the Vinaya stands firm, the Dispensation stands firm.
Therefore, for the sake of the long endurance of the Dispensation, a grave offense was prescribed for disparaging the Vinaya.
Thus ends [the commentary] on the *Abhidhammattha-saṅgaha*, titled the *Paramatthadīpanī*.
The Elucidation of the Ultimate Meaning of the first verse of the fourth commentary is finished.
The Elucidation of the Ultimate Meaning of the second verse.
11. Having thus shown the five meanings together with the purpose of the first verse, he now speaks the second verse to show those Abhidhamma meanings by way of summary.
Therein, regarding the phrase "I shall speak therein the compendium of Abhidhamma meanings" (*tattha tattha...

abhidhammatthasaṅgahaṃ bhāsissaṃ*), the Abhidhamma meanings spoken by me in that title "Compendium of Abhidhamma Meanings" (*abhidhammatthasaṅgaha-pade*) are, in every respect, the ultimate reality (*paramattha*).
The construction is "they become fourfold.

Regarding this, first, in the *Ṭīkā*, the meaning of the word *ta-* (in *tatra*)—whether it refers to the treatise *Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha*, the term *abhidhammattha*, or *abhidhamma* itself—is explained. However, in the *Vibhāvanī*, it says "in that Abhidhamma. All of this is not satisfactory.
For it is not tenable to say, "The Abhidhamma topics have been stated by me in the *Abhidhammattha-saṅgaha-pakaraṇa*.
For even this treatise (*pakaraṇa*) is yet to be spoken of further on; it has not [already] been stated. How then could the Abhidhamma topics [be said to have been stated]?
Furthermore, in the commentaries (*saṃvaṇṇanā-pakaraṇa*), there is no instance where the word *taṃ* (that) at the very beginning refers back to subordinate terms. Therefore, in the *Aṭṭhasālinī*...
In this context, the meaning of the word *tatra* (therein) should be understood as it was in the sentence at the beginning:
"In what sense is it called Abhidhamma? For if this were the case, even the construction "stated in all ways in the commentaries (*ṭīkā*)"—as found in [13]—would be rejected.
For that [classification] does not coincide with all the ways mentioned hereafter, such as "all twelve" or "all eighteen," and so forth.
In this context, "in every way" means that even when classified in all their modes—such as the wholesome (*kusala*) and so on—as stated in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*, they are still only fourfold;
and when analyzed in the *Vibhaṅga*, even by all modes such as the aggregates (*khandha*) and so on, they are still only fourfold. This is the meaning. (The Element)
It should also be stated by way of the passage beginning with "What is this that is spoken of? (kathāyaṃ vuttan ti). 12.

"In the ultimate sense" (paramatthato) means from the perspective of ultimate truth (paramattha-saccato). For there are two truths: conventional truth (sammuti-sacca) and ultimate truth (paramattha-sacca).
Among these, designations such as a "being," a "person," a "self," or a "life-principle" do not exist at all by way of intrinsic nature (sabhāvato).

However, in the minds of the masses who lack the knowledge that discerns phenomena (*dhammavavatthānaññāṇa*), even those things that exist only as very great [mental constructions] appear as if they were actually present.
And those masses, being in agreement, grasp their absolute existence and accordingly both express them in speech and accept them.
Therefore, because they are agreed upon and approved by the masses who are in accord, for that very reason...
Because they serve as the basis for the truth of verbal convention and the truth of abstention from falsehood, they are called "conventional truths" (*sammuti-sacca*).
Standing upon that conventional truth and practicing rightly, one accomplishes all worldly success as well as all the qualities that are the requisites for enlightenment (*bodhisambhāra*).
Those who practice wrongly become fillers of the states of misery (*apāya*). Thus, conventional truth is indeed great. As for ultimate truth (*paramattha-sacca*)...
But upon investigation, that is not true at all. For while it is itself non-existent, it causes the great masses of people to grasp it as if it were existent.

Having become the basis for the sixty-two views and the three types of wrong views, the view of a self-body (sakkāyadiṭṭhi) does not allow foolish people to escape from the suffering of the round of existence (vaṭṭa).
Thus is conventional truth (sammutisacca) perverted; thus is it greatly blameworthy.
Ultimate truth (paramatthasacca), moreover, is twofold: truth as intrinsic nature (sabhāvasacca) and noble truth (ariyasacca).
Among these, the wholesome and other phenomena analyzed in the seven treatises beginning with the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī* are called truth as intrinsic nature.
For, because they exist by their own intrinsic nature, they do not deceive one who apprehends them thus: "Wholesome phenomena exist" or "pleasant feeling exists."
But once that Noble Truth is reached, there remains nothing whatsoever that is not true.
For instance, feeling is described as pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant only by way of its specific modes of experience; it is not so because it is pleasant in every respect.
However, in all its hundreds of aspects—such as impermanence, being conditioned, and so forth—all feelings are indeed suffering.
Likewise, even the state of being wholesome (*kusala*)—in the sense of having blameless happiness as its result—is spoken of only in relation to the unwholesome (*akusala*).

For all those states recognized as wholesome within the three planes of existence are indeed blameworthy (*sāvajja*) because they possess taints (*āsava*), are defiled (*saṃkilesika*), and are subject to the floods (*ogha*), the yokes (*yoga*), and the clingings (*upādāna*).
Furthermore, [they are so called] in the sense of generating results that constitute the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*).
They result exclusively in suffering. And the "internal triad" is stated with reference to what is universally recognized as mundane.
For among all phenomena belonging to the four planes of existence, there is absolutely no such thing as a self; how then could there be anything that is "internal"?
They are strictly external, for it is said: "Regard formations as other. This same method applies, as appropriate, to the remaining triads and dyads of phenomena.

It must be understood as follows: what is called the Noble Truth consists in the fact that all phenomena of the three planes are exclusively suffering; that craving is exclusively the origin of suffering;
that Nibbāna alone is the cessation of suffering; and that the Eightfold Path alone is the way leading to the cessation of suffering.
For it is precisely here that the knowledge of the Noble Ones, whose intellects are purified, remains unshakable.
"It is the truth complete in all aspects, the non-figurative truth. Among these, he said "in the ultimate sense" (*paramatthato*) here in order to exclude conventional truth (*sammutisacca*).
Therefore it was said: "in the ultimate sense" means "as ultimate truth" (*paramatthasacca*). In that context, "object" (*attha*) is twofold:
established by intrinsic nature (*sabhāvasiddha*) and established by convention (*parikappasiddha*). Therein, that which exists independently, without reference to anything else...

Having existed as something found by its own characteristic, it is established. That object, such as consciousness and so forth, is called "established by way of its own intrinsic nature" (*sabhāva-siddha*).

On the other hand, that which does not even exist by way of its own characteristic is—having been conceived by the mind based on various modes of occurrence of an existing object, and having been grasped as a conceptual construct—merely made of mind (*cittamaya*) and fashioned by mind (*cittanimmita*).
It is apprehended only in the mind. That object consisting of the "seven persons" and so forth is called "conceptually established" (*parikappasiddha*).

Among these, only that which is established by its own intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) is called "ultimate reality" (*paramattha*). For its meaning is: "In this, existence, becoming, cognition, and words truly exist.

Furthermore, it is "ultimate reality" because it is the supreme (*parama*), having reached the highest excellence, in the sense of being absolutely existent, as opposed to the other [conceptually established]. Moreover, those which...
Having grasped that "this exists" and "it is apprehended," they practice for the sake of directly knowing what is to be directly known,

for the sake of fully understanding what is to be fully understood, for the sake of abandoning what is to be abandoned, for the sake of realizing what is to be realized, and for the sake of developing what is to be developed.
For them, in the accomplishment of those aims, it is supreme and unsurpassed in its quality of being non-deceptive.

"Meaning" (*attha*) refers to the ultimate meaning (*paramattha*). Since the other [meaning] does not exist, for those who practice for the sake of such things as direct knowledge (*abhiññā*), it will only be deceptive in accomplishing that purpose.
Therefore, because it will not accomplish that purpose, it is not fit to be called "ultimate meaning. However, in the *Vibhāvanī*:
[14] In the *Vibhāvanī*, however:
It has also been stated: “The ultimate meaning (paramattha) is the object-sphere (gocara) of the supreme knowledge (parama-ñāṇa). This, however, is not correct.

For the word *parama* is never seen used in reference to knowledge (*ñāṇa*), nor is the word *attha* used in reference to an object-sphere (*gocara*). Furthermore, according to the *Anuṭīkā*: “Truth itself is the real (*saccika*).
That very thing is the ‘meaning of reality’ (*saccikattha*) in the sense of being the objective domain of non-perverted knowledge. Thus it is called *saccikattha*.
It has been stated. That too shows this meaning: that it is an "object" (*attha*) because it is to be approached (*araṇīya*) by means of non-perverted knowledge (*aviparīta-ñāṇa*).
It is not another meaning for the word *parama*. [The term *paramatthapada*]. 13. Regarding "mind" (*citta*):
here, it is called "mind" because it thinks (*cinteti*). And in this context, the act of thinking is always dependent upon an object (*ārammaṇa*).

For that [consciousness] cannot be found without an object. Therefore, it should be understood that here "consideration" (*cintanā*) is simply the apprehension of the object and the acquisition of the object.

For if this were so, the doctrine of those who claim that consciousness proceeds even without an object during the occurrence of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) or during states of unconsciousness would be refuted.
And even when the support (*nissaya*), the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara*), and so forth are present...
It should be understood that since its name cannot be obtained from those [other] conditions, its name is established solely by way of the object-condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*).
It is called "consciousness" (*citta*) because associated states (*sampayutta-dhammā*) think by means of it. For that [consciousness] is the precursor in the function of grasping the object;
thus, when the associated states grasp the object, they do so precisely by way of it. Or, it is simply the act of thinking.
Mind. For all phenomena are merely their respective activities; in them no substance, shape, or structure is found.

They exist dependent upon conditions, and they are not even able to arise by means of their own steadiness, power, mastery, or capability—let alone to think or to touch. And they endure for only a moment.
They exist; they can never be made to function under the control of anything else.
Therefore, it should be understood that among them, no such distinction as "this is the substance," "this is the instrument," or "this is the action" can be found.

And this being the case, among all ultimate terms (*paramattha-padesu*), only one—namely, the abstract noun (*bhāva-sādhana*)—is primarily obtained; the other grammatical factors (*sādhana*) are obtained only figuratively (*pariyāyato*).

This should be understood. Furthermore, in this context, it should be seen that the "figurative discourse" (*pariyāyakathā*) consists in making a distinction by means of conceptual construction (*kappanā*) for the purpose of making known a specific meaning of a non-distinct contemplation based on [the elements such as] earth and so forth.

Just as one speaks of the "body of a stone statue," so too is there an instrumentality belonging to that which is liberated from the phenomena (*dhamma*) designated as various actions—that is, to the agent postulated by others.

This is for the purpose of demonstrating the absolute non-existence of a self (atta), a soul (jīva), a being (satta), or a person (puggala). For if a self and so forth existed, what need would there be for the conceptualization of difference where there is no difference?

However, in the *Vibhāvani*, it appears as if the conceptualization of the unreal as real—like a hare’s horn—is being stated. This is its intended meaning regarding phenomena (dhammas): [the following].

There is no agent (*kattā*) or causer (*kāretā*) whatsoever. However, in the world, an agent is established as one who is primarily characterized by selfhood (*attappadhāna*) and who brings about an action.

Therefore, in order to illustrate that the mind is primarily characterized by selfhood regarding the function of thinking, the state of being an agent is superimposed upon the mind, and it is said: "it thinks" (*cinteti*), thus it is called "mind" (*citta*).

Furthermore, in order to illustrate that through the power of the mind, those factors associated with it also proceed in conformity with it toward that function, the state of being a doer (*karaka*) is [superimposed].
The associated mental states (sampayutta-dhammā) think by attributing the state of being an agent to the mind; thus it is said, "it is called *citta* because they think by means of it.
Furthermore, in this context, the word *citta* should be understood as signifying various meanings. For it is said in the *Saṃyutta Nikāya*:
"Bhikkhus, have you seen what is called 'conduct' (*caraṇa*)? Yes, venerable sir. That too, bhikkhus, is conduct..."
"Mind is indeed thought by mind. And by that very conduct, monks, it is by mind that mind is further distinguished as more mind.
Monks, I do not see even a single other class of beings that possesses such a mind as this—namely, those animals, monks.
Even those animals, monks, are thought of by mind alone.
Monks, even by those animals, the mind alone is more variegated. Therein, "painted" means the mind;

for they wander about demonstrating how, having created various painted works such as celestial mansions (*dibbavimāna*), and performing this and that merit, they are reborn here and there. This refers to that painted chamber.

“Name. “By mind” (*cittena*) is an instrumental case used in the sense of the ablative. “Just as these” (*yathayidaṃ*) means “just as these [beings]. “Variegated by mind” (*cittikatā*): they are made variegated by the mind.
Herein, because of the mind’s variegation, perception is variegated; because of the variegation of perception, craving is variegated; because of the variegation of craving, kamma is variegated;
because of the variegation of kamma, the modes of birth (*yoni*) are variegated; because of the variegation of the modes of birth, their animal...
The diversity of those things that have come to pass should be understood. [The meaning of the terms:
Their respective intrinsic nature is the characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*); the perfection of their function is the flavor (*rasa*);
the mode of being grasped, or the fruit, is designated as the manifestation (*paccupaṭṭhāna*).
That which is the proximate cause is considered its "footing" (*padatthāna*);
these are sufficient for the discernment of phenomena by one who is awakened.
Consciousness has the characteristic of cognizing an object, the function of being the forerunner, the manifestation of continuity, and name-and-form as its footing. [Consciousness]
14. *Cetasikaṃ*: Here, it is called "mental concomitant" (*cetasika*) because it exists in the mind (*cetasi*) due to its dependence upon that [mind] for its occurrence.

It refers to the class of phenomena beginning with contact (*phassa*). Furthermore, "dependence upon that for its occurrence" means its proceeding as if unified with the mind through characteristics such as simultaneous arising (*ekuppāda*).
By this, whatever is the birth of the mind is itself the birth of contact and the rest; whatever is the aging of the mind... what is the aging of the mind... [and so forth].
Death: that which is the object of consciousness and that which is the basis of consciousness is the very same for contact and the other mental factors.

Thus, just as flowers bound together by a single stalk are attached to a single cluster of blossoms, so too are the phenomena of contact and the rest—bound together with consciousness within a single birth and so forth—established here as "mental factors" (*cetasika*). And this being the case, consciousness too [is associated] with those factors such as contact.
If it is argued that since [the process] proceeds in dependence on that very [consciousness], it too should be described as "contactual," "feeling-based," and so forth—[we reply]:
No. Because consciousness alone is the primary factor. For it is said: "Phenomena are preceded by the mind, have the mind as their chief, and are made of the mind.

In this context, "made of the mind" (manomaya) means that they are produced and fashioned by the mind alone; the sense is that they are the activities of consciousness. By this, those factors such as contact and the rest [are shown to be subordinate].
This shows that mental factors (*dhammā*) are not found apart from the mind (*citta*). However, the mind indeed proceeds even without some of those [factors].
For the fivefold sense-consciousness arises without certain [mental factors] such as applied thought (*vitakka*) and so forth;
therefore, it must be said that at that time, the dependence of their existence upon it belongs to those factors themselves, and not to the mind.

[15] In the *Vibhāvani*, however, it is stated that by the mere fact of having a single object (*ekālambanatā*), one should understand that mental factors (*cetasika*) are dependent on that [consciousness]. That is not correct;
for a thing does not become a "mental factor" merely by virtue of having a single object. Furthermore, in this world, various colored elements exist in water...
Having smoothed the surface, they perform various works of painting;
in that surface, the functions of spreading and binding belong to the water alone, not to the pigments. The perception of various forms belongs to the pigments alone, not to the water.
In this context, the object should be regarded as being like the surface, and the mind like the water. The various pigments are like...
"Mental factors" (*cetasika-dhammā*). 15. "Matter" (*rūpa*):

herein, it is called "matter" (*rūpa*) because it is "disfigured" (*ruppati*). It undergoes change by way of an uneven occurrence due to opposing conditions such as cold, heat, and so forth; or the meaning is that it is made to undergo change by them.
As it has been said: "Monks, it is disfigured; therefore it is called 'matter. By what is it disfigured? It is disfigured by cold, and it is disfigured by heat."
"It is disturbed (ruppati). It is disturbed by hunger; it is disturbed by thirst; it is disturbed by contact with gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, heat, serpents, and snakes.
Thus it is said: "It is disturbed" means it is disturbed, it is agitated, it is struck, it is oppressed, it is broken.
This is stated in the *Mahāniddesa*. This is the summarized meaning here: those phenomena which endure for a long time and possess a nature of resistance (*sappaṭigha*).

Only for those [material phenomena] at the moment of their persistence is there what is called "contact with opposing conditions. It is not so for others—namely, for those of limited duration and for those that are non-reactive (appaṭigha) by nature.
For even those subtle material phenomena that are non-reactive by nature have no such thing as contact with external cold and so forth;
how much less so for those of limited duration, which are non-reactive by nature, and for immaterial phenomena?
If it is argued that, in this way, subtle material phenomena might attain the state of being immaterial, it is not so. This is because they share the same destiny as gross material phenomena;
for when those gross phenomena undergo transformation (*ruppati*), these too certainly undergo transformation.

Furthermore, "conjunction" (*samāgama*) here refers only to the great primary elements (*mahābhūta*), which, though gross material phenomena, exist in a state of mutual opposition, consisting in their coming together, their meeting upon impact, and their acting as objects for one another.
It is called mutual impact; for it is said: "it is affected (ruppati), struck (ghaṭṭīyati), and oppressed (pīḷīyati).
This "being affected" is said to be the agitation and breaking up of the elements contained within a group, like the upheaval of a kingdom by the battle of a hostile army. For it is said:
"it is agitated (kuppati) and it breaks up (bhijjati). In this context, "is agitated" means it is disturbed and shaken, and "breaks up" means it undergoes change.
It undergoes change. At the moment they encounter opposing conditions, from that point on they themselves have reached a state of alteration.
The meaning is that they have become the causal basis for the arising of subtle and gross material continua.
Furthermore, in this context, transformation (ruppana) is twofold: increase and decrease. Both of these occur during the dissolution of an eon and the formation of an eon.
It becomes manifest through the revolution of various ages, aeons, years, seasons, months, nights, days, and so forth.
But why is the name "rūpa" established only for those things whose nature is to be affected by impact? Because only those possess a physical form (*saviggaha*).

For material phenomena (*rūpadhammā*) become possessed of a physical form through the attainment of states such as mass and configuration. Therefore, it is only of these that there is "ruppana" (being affected).
It should be understood that the name "matter" (rūpa) is established precisely because it is manifest to the world even when directly perceived.
Non-material phenomena (arūpadhammā), however, are without physical form; thus, their modification is not manifest to the world through direct perception.
That [modification] must be known by the world—except for those who know the minds of others—only after seeing, hearing, or questioning regarding various material modifications. Therefore...
"There is no possibility of their becoming matter.
However, in the *Vibhāvani*, it is stated:
"The undesirable consequence of their becoming matter is averted by the capacity of the mention of 'cold' and so forth. For that which is called conventional usage..."
It cannot be established without recourse to worldly convention (*lokapacāra*). And worldly convention proceeds solely by way of manifest signs (*pākaṭanimitta*).
Therefore, it should be understood that here, even without the explicit mention of cold and so forth, the exclusion of their association is established from the world itself.

Furthermore, because in the Brahma-world the bodily and vocal transformations of the Brahmas proceed as the result of supernormal power (*iddhi-vikuppana*), [they are not subject to those specific conditions].
Furthermore, various transformations of form are indeed seen. And these, in one sense, are simply called "modes of being affected" (*ruppanākāra*);

therefore, it should be understood that by means of these, the "form-ness" (*rūpatā*) of forms is established therein. Or, "form" (*rūpa*) is so called because it manifests itself through its own intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).
For non-form phenomena (*arūpadhammā*) are not manifest through their own intrinsic nature; rather, they become manifest only in dependence upon form.
It should be grasped. This, however, is manifest by its own intrinsic nature and should be grasped even by the five types of sensory consciousness.
Since this is the case, the establishment of the "form-ness" (rūpatā) of forms in the Brahma-world is achieved directly as well.
However, in the *Vibhāvani*:
The establishment of "materiality" (*rūpatā*) therein has been demonstrated by way of the supporting factors such as cold and so forth, and by way of not overstepping its own intrinsic nature.
Furthermore, the statement "neither by cold nor by heat," etc., is merely illustrative, because materialization (*ruppana*) can also occur by way of kamma, consciousness, and nutriment;
for even perception (*saññā*) and consciousness (*viññāṇa*) [are affected] by objects that are forms or tastes.
Thus they are specified in the Pāḷi. For perception does not perceive only visible form, nor does consciousness cognize only taste.
It is understood that the teaching is given merely as an illustration.
Therefore, there is no purpose in demonstrating the establishment of "form-ness" (rūpatā) therein without abandoning the mention of cold and so forth. [Form]
16. Regarding "Nibbāna": herein, it is Nibbāna because all the torments of the suffering of the round (*vaṭṭa-dukkha*) are extinguished (*nibbāyanti*) within it.

"They are extinguished" means that those defilements (*kilesa*) or aggregates (*khandha*) which, for one who has not developed the Path, were situated on the side of being liable to arise in the future, reach the side of being no longer liable to arise for one who has developed the Path. For once they have reached the three moments [of the Path], [they do not arise again].

Past phenomena that have ceased are said to "extinguish" (nibbāyanti). Regarding present phenomena and those that will necessarily arise in the future, there is simply nothing to be said [in this context].

"The torments of the suffering of the round" (vaṭṭadukkhasantāpa) refers to the torments of the suffering of the round of defilements (kilesavaṭṭa), the round of kamma (kammavaṭṭa), and the round of result (vipākavaṭṭa).
For trees and the like, which are devoid of these threefold torments of the suffering of the round, there is no cessation through non-arising.
"Nibbāna exists": here, the locative case is used with respect to this object, as in the expression "birds fly in the sky.
There is no other place for their extinction apart from that [state] which they extinguish themselves in.

Alternatively, it is called *nibbāna* because noble persons (*ariyajanā*) are extinguished (*nibbāyanti*) therein; for it is said: "The wise are extinguished just as this lamp [is extinguished]. Thus, they are called *nibbāyanti*.
The meaning is that it reaches a state where those respective defilements or aggregates will never again undergo rebirth (*appaṭisandhika*).
In the word *ekasmiṃ*, the locative case refers to the object itself; some also connect it by saying "having gone beyond this. Furthermore, in the commentaries (*ṭīkā*), it is stated:
"Craving (*taṇhā*) is called *vāna* because it weaves (*vinanato*) or stitches together (*saṃsibbanato*) existence after existence (*bhavābhava*); that which has emerged from that is *nibbāna*."
[18] However, in the *Vibhāvani*, it is also stated:
"Nibbāna is so called because by means of it the fire of lust and the other defilements is extinguished (*nibbāti*). That is not correct.

For nowhere is the instrumental derivation seen in the case of Nibbāna as it is in the case of the Path (*magga*); nor is Nibbāna a co-operative condition (*sahakāri-paccaya*) for the agent of lust and the rest when the word *nibbūti* is used in the sense of an action. [Nibbāna]
The commentary on the ultimate meaning of the second verse is completed.
17. *Cittasaṅgaha-paramatthadīpanī*:

Now, explaining consciousness (*citta*) first according to the order of the summary, he says "therein, consciousness" and so forth. "Therein" means among those four Abhidhamma topics. "First" means initially. That which has four divisions or modes is "fourfold."
18. *Kāmāvacara*: Here, "kāma" means that which is desired (*kāmīyati*). Alternatively, beings here desire because their passion for sensual pleasure (*kāmarāga*) has not been suppressed;

they delight solely in the pleasure of sense-desires, and not in the pleasure of meditative absorption (*jhāna-rati*) as is the case in the higher planes. Thus it is called "kāma. There are eleven types of sensual planes. [Objection: But are there not those who have attained meditative absorption even in this plane?
[Reply: It is not that there are none. However, even they are never [regarded] as "deities" (*deva*) here.
This is a fault. How can the Avīci hell and the others be desired? And how do beings take delight in sensual pleasure there?

It is by way of attachment to the signs [of those realms] or by way of craving for existence (bhava-nikanti). For at the time of death, the masses of flames of the hell-fire appear as if they were golden in color.
It is said that once a certain Brahmin with wrong view lay upon his deathbed...
It happened that his teacher-brahmins stood near him and said, "O sir, go to the Brahma-world!
But to him, the flames of the Avīci hell appeared. Then he said, "O teachers, the golden-colored ones are appearing!
This, O sirs, is the Brahma-world; go there! Having died, he was reborn in the Avīci hell.
Thus, they are craved for by way of attachment to signs. Furthermore, there is what is called "inclination toward existence" (*bhavanikanti*) even for those [beings] arisen therein.
Moreover, those arisen therein possess unobstructed sensual lust (*kāmarāga*); when there is opportunity, they will surely delight in sensual pleasure.
It "frequent" (*avacara*) that sense-desire, thus it is "belonging to the sense-sphere" (*kāmāvacara*). And here, the word "frequents" (*avacarati*) means "arises" (*uppajjati*).
The meaning should not be accepted, for that meaning does not accord with the text (*pāḷi*) and is moreover fraught with various faults.
For it is stated in the text: "Those which have their range here, which are included here. If that meaning were intended here, then it would have been stated:
"Those which have their range here, which have arisen here. But it is not so stated. Furthermore, the word *pariyāpanna* [is not used in this sense].

It could be said that [the term] has the same meaning as "arisen" (*uppanna*). For supramundane states of consciousness (*lokuttara-citta*), though they have arisen within the three realms of existence (*bhava*), are not included (*pariyāpanna*) therein.
Thus, first of all, it does not accord with the text (*pāḷi*) if that meaning were accepted.
And this being the case, those sublime (*mahaggata*) and supramundane phenomena (*dhamma*) which exist in that sense of "desire" (*kāma*)...

They arise. For those [states], one incurs the fault of reaching the status of being sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) and the fault of losing the status of being fine-material-sphere (*rūpāvacara*) and so forth.

And as for those sense-sphere phenomena that arise in the fine-material and immaterial planes, one incurs the fault of reaching the status of being fine-material or immaterial-sphere and the fault of losing the status of being sense-sphere.
Is it not the case that some things receive their names even by way of their predominant mode of occurrence?

It is like a forest-dweller who is also a combatant. Therefore, even here, since those states arise frequently in their respective planes, there is no fault in their receiving names such as "sense-sphere" (kāmāvacara) and so forth. No;

for if that were the case, one would have to separately state the plane where they mostly arise in order to exclude the supramundane (lokuttara) states from being classified as sense-sphere and so on.
It might be so; however, there is no such plane of existence where those [defilements] arise for the most part.

Since they arise through those [beings], they arise only within the three realms of existence (*bhava*). Therefore, the fault of their falling into the status of belonging to the sense-sphere, fine-material sphere, or immaterial sphere would be difficult to avoid.
Thus, it becomes associated with various faults. Consequently, one should not grasp the meaning in that way; rather, here [the term] refers to those who range within this [realm].
"Included" (pariyāpanna) means that its meaning should be understood according to the method of the Pāḷi as commented upon by the Blessed One;
this is the meaning here. It "moves within the sense-sphere" (kāmāvacara); that is, having plunged into it, it moves and proceeds by way of being included.
And what is called "the state of being included" is the sharing of the same class, lineage, and name with that sense-sphere which serves as its own support.

The state of having entered into—that is, the state of having fallen into—that sensual desire by means of its surrounding portions which have been reckoned [as such]—this is what is meant by "being included within" (*antogadhabhāva*).
And that state of being thus encompassed should be understood as being produced by the grasping craving for sensual pleasures (*pariggāhinī kāmataṇhā*).

To this extent, those phenomena which constitute the continuity of the aggregates of beings in the realms of form and formlessness, though they are not [inherently] mine, are nevertheless grasped by the craving for sensual pleasures as "these are mine."
They are indeed included within the sense-sphere (*kāma*). Thus, it is established that they belong to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*).

This same method should be applied to those belonging to the fine-material and immaterial spheres as well. Among these, however, craving for the fine-material and craving for the immaterial should be understood as the grasping type of craving.
As for those phenomena that are free from the grasp of the three types of craving, even though they have arisen within the three realms of existence, therein—
It should be understood that because they are "unincluded" (apariyāpanna), they are called "supramundane" (lokuttara).

Furthermore, in this *Paṭṭhāna*, it is stated that even within the mental continuum of a being in the formless realm, there is the arising of craving for sense-pleasures (kāmataṇhā)—designated as "lust for sense-pleasures" (kāmacchanda)—dependent upon the hindrance of sensual lust, such as in the passage: "Dependent on the hindrance of sensual lust, there is the hindrance of restlessness," and so forth.
Therefore, [this craving] is the craving that grasps at sense-phenomena (kāmadhamma) arisen in the planes of form and formlessness.
They should also be seen as occurring within the mental continuums of beings belonging to the realms of form and the formless.

In the Pāḷi, the term "hindrance of sensual desire" (*kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa*) is used because it belongs to the class of hindrances; for it is not possible to find hindrances that function exclusively as hindrances on the planes of jhāna.

Herein, the classification of sensual desire (*kāma*) should be stated: there are two kinds of sensual desire—defilement-sensual-desire (*kilesa-kāma*) and object-sensual-desire (*vatthu-kāma*). In this context, excluding attachment to the realms of form and the formless...
All other greed whatsoever is called "defilement-desire" (*kilesa-kāma*) within this fourfold-plane classification.
Furthermore, with the exception of the phenomena belonging to the fine-material and immaterial spheres, all other phenomena arising in the three planes are called "object-desire" (*vatthu-kāma*).
As for the statement in the *Aṭṭhasālinī* that "all phenomena of the three planes are object-desire," that is according to the Suttanta method as explained in the *Mahāniddesa*.
It should be understood that it is "stated. For there are no dhammas of the fine-material or immaterial spheres stated by the name "desire" in the Abhidhamma. [The term *kāmāvacara*: 19.

Regarding the terms *rūpāvacara* (fine-material sphere) and *arūpāvacara* (immaterial sphere), it should be seen that the words *rūpa* and *arūpa* are conventional designations for those respective planes.

Furthermore, there are two planes: the fine-material plane and the immaterial plane. Among these, where there is no *rūpa*—which has the characteristic of being subject to change (*ruppana*)—[that is the immaterial plane].
That is fourfold and is called the immaterial plane (*arūpabhūmi*). The remaining twenty-seven kinds of planes are called the material plane (*rūpabhūmi*).
