Furthermore, it should be understood that among these, the eleven lower planes are designated as the "sense-sphere plane" (*kāmabhūmi*) by way of their distinction from gross sensual desire, while the sixteen higher planes are simply called the "material plane.
However, where there is craving or the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*), [it is the sense-sphere plane].
These have been stated by means of the terms "form" (*rūpa*) and "formless" (*arūpa*).

In that context, the metaphorical designation of the support (*nissaya*) as the supported should be understood as the application of the name of the support to that which is supported. Furthermore, where the terms "sense-sphere" (*kāmāvacara*) and so forth are used, they refer to the planes (*bhūmi*) themselves. In that case, the metaphorical designation of the supported as the support should be understood as the application of the name of the supported to the support.
Whatever needs to be said regarding this has already been explained according to the method set forth under the term *kāmāvacara*.
This is the exposition of the ultimate meaning (paramatthadīpanā) according to the canonical text (pāḷi) within this section on the delimitation of the three planes. As it is said:

"Which phenomena are of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara)? Taking the Avīci hell as the lower limit and the Paranimmitavasavatti devas as the upper limit, whatever aggregates, elements, and bases (khandha-dhātu-āyatana) exist within this interval, belong here, and are included here."
Form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—these states belong to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara). What states belong to the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara)?

Taking the Brahma-world as the lower limit and including the Akaniṭṭha devas above, whatever states exist within this interval, whether they are included therein, whether one has entered them through meditative attainment, whether one has been reborn there, or whether one dwells in happiness in this very life—[these are the states belonging to the fine-material sphere].
Mental states and mental factors—these are the phenomena belonging to the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*). Which phenomena belong to the immaterial sphere (*arūpāvacara*)?

Taking as their lower limit the gods who have reached the sphere of infinite space (*ākāsānañcāyatana*), and taking as their upper limit the gods who have reached the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatana*), whatever exists within this interval—these are the phenomena belonging to the immaterial sphere.

[19] However, in the *Ṭīkās*, they have not adopted the clearly elucidated method of the Pāḷi as it has been stated; rather, the meanings of the words and the determinations (vinicchaya) set forth here are otherwise. All of those should not be accepted as essential. One might ask:
"Are not those meanings and others also stated in the *Aṭṭhasālinī*? True. But having understood the meaning that is actual, clear, and follows the Pāḷi, what is the use of such hesitation?
20. *Lokuttara* (supramundane): Here, "world" (*loka*) refers to the aforementioned phenomena of the three planes in the sense of breaking up and disintegrating.
As it is said: "Monks, it breaks up and disintegrates; therefore it is called the world.

This being so, it might follow that all supramundane phenomena—except for Nibbāna—would also possess the status of being "the world," because they too are subject to breaking up and disintegration. This is not so.

For it is precisely where the great mass of people settles into the false grasp that "it is permanent, stable, and eternal," that this conventional designation of "world" (*loka*) is established in order to prevent that very [grasp].
Therefore, they say that for those who are entirely free from such false grasping, there is no falling into the state of being a "world.
Or rather, the establishment of the state of being a "world" applies only to those for whom the breaking up and disintegration is evident to the great mass of people.

There is no possibility of mundane involvement for those that are supramundane (*lokuttara*). It is called "supramundane" because it transcends the world (*loka*); this refers to the path-consciousness (*maggacitta*).

It is called "supramundane" because it has crossed over from that [world]; this refers to the fruition-consciousness (*phalacitta*). However, Nibbāna is not included here [in this specific definition].

Furthermore, "crossing over" in this context refers specifically to the state of being unconfined within the three worlds through liberation from the grasping of the three types of craving. And that state of being unconfined—
Because it is grasped as if it were the foundation (adhiṭṭhāna) for certain states, the fourth stage is taken separately and named the "plane" (bhūmi).
The *Paramatthadīpanī* on the analysis of the four planes is finished. 21.
Having thus demonstrated that consciousness is fourfold according to the division of planes in the order of the inferior and the superior, [the author] now...

Analyzing the fourfold consciousness according to the order already indicated, he first treats sense-sphere consciousness (*kāmāvacara-citta*). Within that, there is inferior and unattractive consciousness;
and within that, in order to show the most inferior, which is unwholesome consciousness (*akusala-citta*), he says, "accompanied by joy," and so forth.

Here, it should be understood that even for sense-sphere consciousness, the sequence of the rootless and the root-possessing unwholesome types is stated by way of the sequence from the inferior to the superior.
[20] However, it is stated in the *Vibhāvani*:

"In order to facilitate the formation of clear perceptions regarding the many types of consciousness that will be discussed below, [the author] first presents only those that are slight and do not lead to evil. This is not correct;
for the purpose of that [work] is already accomplished by following the sequence of inferior and so forth as previously described.

[21] And as for the statement that "among those various states of existence, because for a being who has taken rebirth-linking, only consciousness-arising accompanied by greed is possible at the very beginning in terms of process-consciousness, therefore those alone are mentioned first"—that too is not tenable.

For, in terms of process-consciousness at the very beginning, it is the adverting of the mind-door (*manodvārāvajjana*) itself that arises absolutely first. Thus it is with regard to the unwholesome [consciousnesses].

However, the mind rooted in greed is both frequent and predominant. It should be understood that because it is associated with two of the roots of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*), it is primary and manifest;
therefore, it was mentioned first. 22.
In this context, "sumano" means "one who has a beautiful mind. It refers to an affectionate state of mind. For beauty does not consist merely in being blameless.
"Here, 'yutta' means 'possessed of. One whose mind (*mano*) is beautiful (*sundara*) is *sumana*. A person endowed with a moistened heart is a *sumana*.
The state of being *sumana* is *somanassa*. This is a name for mental pleasant feeling.

And here, the phrase 'the state of being *sumana*' refers to the cause for the application of the designation 'sumana'—whether to that consciousness, to the person, or to the cognition 'this is a *sumana*'."
Meaning (*attha*). For "state" (*bhāva*) is said to be the cause for the occurrence of both the designation and the cognition. This is because [the word *bhāva*] is understood as:

"that in which designations and cognitions arise (*bhavanti*) or occur (*pavattanti*). And the locative case is used here in the sense of a cause (*nimitta*), just as in the expression, "The elephant is killed by its tusks.
For just as in that case, the act of killing occurs toward the elephant associated with the tusks, having the tusks themselves as the cause.
Thus, here too, the designations and cognitions occur with respect to that sign of feeling, whether in the mind associated with feeling or in the person.
They say it is "existence" (*bhāva*) because by means of this, cognitions and words come into being; others say it is because of this [sign].
"Accompanied by joy" (*somanassasahagata*) means they proceed together with joy as one. The meaning is: "associated with the feeling of joy. "Seeing" (*dassana*).

*Diṭṭhi*. This, moreover, is twofold: by way of right view (*sammā-diṭṭhi*) and wrong view (*micchā-diṭṭhi*). Here, it is associated with wrong view, because the context concerns the unwholesome (*akusala*).
"View itself" is "gone to view" (*diṭṭhigata*), just as one says "gone to excrement" (*gūthagata*) or "gone to urine" (*muttagata*).

That which is associated with "gone to view" in various ways is "associated with gone to view" (*diṭṭhigatasampayutta*). It is associated with "gone to view" through such modes as arising together (*ekuppāda*) and so forth.
"Equal," "unified as it were," and "joined" mean "associated. Regarding the phrase "one is unprompted (asaṅkhārika), one is prompted (sasaṅkhārika)":
here, "prompting" (saṅkhāra) refers to prior prompting. That [prompting] is twofold: application (payoga) and means (upāya).
Among these, "application" is the bodily or verbal effort performed by others, such as through an order, a request, or a threat, saying, "Do this! Furthermore, by means of such orders and so forth...
Others explain various means for the purpose of performing an action;

they show the disadvantage in non-performance and the benefit in performance, or they make a formal agreement, or they impose a penalty, or one recalls and reflects upon those respective reasons oneself.
In such ways, the means are manifold. Both types of this are here termed *saṅkhāra*.

It is called "volitional formation" (*saṅkhāra*) because it prepares and applies the mental continuum—without allowing it to remain as it is by its own nature and unwilling to act—for the purpose of performing various actions.
That collection of conditions which is devoid of such volitional formation is "unprompted" (*asaṅkhāra*). That which is accompanied by it is "prompted" (*sasaṅkhāra*).
For this is said in the Commentary:
"Together with volitional activity" means *sasaṅkhāra*. The meaning is: by that group of conditions which is accompanied by volitional activity, accompanied by application, and accompanied by method.
And here, in the Commentary, the "group of conditions" is stated to be the common group of conditions beginning with the object (*ārammaṇa*). But as for the uncommon [condition]:

In the case of wholesome kamma, a set of conditions beginning with reliance upon a true person (*sappurisa*) is appropriate; in the case of unwholesome kamma, a set of conditions beginning with reliance upon a false person (*asappurisa*) is appropriate—these should be applied with distinction.

Furthermore, when it arouses and fully arouses the mind by itself, without the two kinds of volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*), making the mind not sink down, then it is called "without volitional formation" (*asaṅkhāra*). Moreover, when [it does so] by itself, without that [volitional formation], the mind...

When it is unable to arise or emerge by itself, but is able to do so only after obtaining a volitional formation (*saṅkhāra*) as its companion, then it is called "with volitional effort" (*sasaṅkhāra*).
Thus, the terms "without volitional effort" (*asaṅkhāra*) and "with volitional effort" (*sasaṅkhāra*) are names for the collection of conditions themselves, not for the consciousness.

As for consciousness, that which arises through a pure collection of conditions without volitional effort is "unprompted" (*asaṅkhārika*); [that which arises] through [a collection of conditions] with volitional effort...
That which arises by means of a collection of conditions is "with effort" (*sasaṅkhārika*); for the suffix *-ika* is used here in the sense of "arisen. Indeed, it is stated in the Canon:
"At whatever time an unwholesome consciousness has arisen, accompanied by joy, associated with wrong view, and with effort.
In this context, it should be construed as: "it has arisen by means of a collection of conditions that involve effort."
This is the exposition of the ultimate meaning regarding the terms "unprompted" (*asaṅkhārika*) and "prompted" (*sasaṅkhārika*) here.
However, in the commentaries (*ṭīkā*),
failing to discern this point and taking the mind itself to be unprompted or prompted, they have stated as follows:

“‘It has no volitional formation (saṅkhāra), thus it is without volitional formation (asaṅkhāra). That itself is the state of being without volitional formation (asaṅkhārika). It proceeds together with volitional formation, thus it is with volitional formation (sasaṅkhāra).

That which is with volitional formation is ‘with volitional formation’ (sasaṅkhārika) as well. That which lacks this [volitional formation] is ‘without volitional formation’ (asaṅkhāra). That itself is the state of being without volitional formation (asaṅkhārika).
It is accompanied by volitional formation, thus it is ‘with volitional formation’ (sasaṅkhārika). All of this is simply untenable.”

[23] And that which is to be manifested, the mind prepares by means of a specific embellishment known as sharpness (*tikkhabhāva*). Or, it is called *saṅkhāra* because it is prepared (*saṅkharīyati*) by this according to the aforementioned method; thus it is said. But even that is not correct.
For if that were so, even a volitionally prompted (*sasaṅkhārika*) state of consciousness would have to be called "sharp."
[24] And as for what was stated there:
"Furthermore, it occurs both in one's own mental continuum proceeding in the prior stage and in the mental continuum of another;
thus, it is a specific distinction, characterized by the sharpness of the mind produced, that is here called 'volitional formation' (saṅkhāra). That too—

Having deviated from the literal meanings of the terms *asaṅkhārika* and *sasaṅkhārika*, the subsequent conceptualization of "formation" (*saṅkhāra*) as referring to material form (*rūpa*) is simply not logical. By this—
"The distinction arising from prior application is produced by the mind;
it is a volitional formation (*saṅkhāra*), and by virtue of that, there is here the classification as 'unprompted' (*asaṅkhārika*) and so forth.
Thus, even the supporting verse is rejected.
[26] And as for what is said there:

"Or else, if it is asked whether it is 'with volitional effort' (*sasaṅkhārika*) or 'without volitional effort' (*asaṅkhārika*), this is stated with reference solely to the presence or absence of volitional effort (*saṅkhāra*).
It is not because of the coexistence or non-existence of its simultaneous occurrence. For even in the case of a volitional effort that occurs within a different continuum..."
Because the mind is produced by way of that [volition] existing here, it has volition (*saṅkhāra*) as its factor; thus it is "with volition" (*sasaṅkhārika*).
This is because the word *saha* (with) indicates the sense of "existing," as in the cases of "having hair" (*salomaka*) or "having wings" (*sapakkhaka*).

Its opposite, however, is called "without volition" (*asaṅkhārika*) due to the absence of that [volition], according to the method already stated. That too is the straight and clear meaning established by the Canon and the Commentary.
Because it is stated according to one's own conceptualization, it must not be accepted [as definitive].
And herein, a state of mind that proceeds—whether by command, threat, entreaty, or supplication—of others without one’s own desire, is called "originated by means" (*payoga-samutthita*).
Likewise, [a state of mind] that proceeds of others without one’s own desire, whether out of fear or shame...
That which is set in motion out of reverence, or out of respect for the speaker, or out of fear of punishment, is called "arisen through means.

Alternatively, when one knows one's own mind to be sluggish and sets it in motion by exhorting oneself through various means or by recollecting various means, that mind is called "arisen through means. And this is merely an illustration of the method. [It is] dissociated from views.
It is dissociated from views (*diṭṭhigata*). It is called equanimity (*upekkhā*) because it looks upon the object with a state of neutrality, seeing it in the mode of experiencing it;

or, it is equanimity because it looks upon or sees [the object] by way of its arising or its fitness. For just as joy (*somanassa*) and grief (*domanassa*) see the object with intensity—such that a person who is joyful undergoes a transformation when separated from that object—[equanimity is the opposite].
There is [distress]. Through that object, one who is depressed undergoes a transformation upon contact with it.

This person, however, is not like that; rather, he sees by way of reasoning alone, and thus the object—whether through conjunction or disjunction—does not cause the person to undergo a transformation.
Some, however, say "he sees by way of rebirth and by way of reasoning," but this is not possible here. For what is unwholesome is never called "proper" (yuttarūpa).
They say it "occurs. "Accompanied by equanimity" is a compound.

23. And here, although the states such as contact, applied thought, and delusion are indeed concomitant and associated with this entire eightfold consciousness, they themselves do not possess internal divisions in the same way that feeling does.
Furthermore, there is no such conceptual distinction as "these formations of views exist in some instances of this consciousness and do not exist in others.
Therefore, it should be understood that they are not included here because they do not cause a differentiation within this consciousness.
Greed, however, does differentiate this eightfold [consciousness] from others; likewise, feeling, views, and formations [differentiate it].

It should be understood that only those [factors] which cause mutual dissension among beings are included here. One might object: "But do not joy (*pīti*), conceit (*māna*), sloth-and-torpor (*thinamiddha*), and so forth, also cause dissension?

Therefore, should they not also be included here—joy as 'with-joy' and 'without-joy,' conceit as 'associated with conceit' and 'dissociated from conceit,' and sloth-and-torpor as 'associated with sloth-and-torpor' and 'dissociated from sloth-and-torpor'? No; for among those [factors], it is only in the case of mental pleasure (*somanassa*)...
When that [jhāna factor] is taken up, joy is indeed taken up. The other three, however, are both indeterminate factors and "mere-mention" factors; thus they are not included here.
In the *Vibhāvani*, however, it is said:
"Since phenomena such as contact, applied thought, and delusion are also associated with other minds, they are not [included] by others in this [context]."
They produce a distinction. Therefore, with the intention that "they are not included here," it was asked:
"But why, when other associated states such as contact and so forth are present here, is only the state of being accompanied by joy and so on mentioned?
It is because joy and so on alone are unique (asādhāraṇa) [to this specific type of consciousness]. For some of the factors beginning with contact are common to all consciousness, while others...

“Wholesome states and so forth are common [to all consciousness]. Furthermore, delusion and the rest are common to all wholesome states; therefore, it is not possible to distinguish a particular consciousness by means of them. This must be examined.

For if that were the case, since joy (*somanassa*) and equanimity (*upekkhā*), as well as volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*), are also found in other types of consciousness, they too would not produce a distinction for this [consciousness] from others.

Consequently, those [factors] should also not be included here. 24. In this context, however, the following are the distinguishing features: being reborn with joy (*somanassappaṭisandhikatā*), having a shallow temperament (*agambhīrappakati*), association with desirable objects (*iṭṭhārammaṇasamāyoga*), and freedom from calamity (*byasanamutti*).

It is the cause of joy. Because one who is reborn with joy has a mental continuum constantly permeated by the joy of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), his consciousness, as it arises, for the most part arises accompanied by joy.
Furthermore, one of shallow disposition and inferior inclination considers even the small to be great; he considers even the inferior to be sublime.
Therefore, for that person as well, the mind arising is for the most part accompanied by joy (*somanassa*).

"Association with a desirable object" means association with an object desired by oneself, whether it be inferior or superior. "Liberation from misfortune" means liberation from the misfortune of relatives and so forth.
[The factors are: being reborn with equanimity (*upekkhā*), having a profound nature, association with a neutral object, and liberation from misfortune.
This is the cause for equanimity. In this context, "deep-seated disposition" refers to having great underlying tendencies (*ajjhāsaya*).
For such a person regards even a great thing as small, and regards even a sublime thing as inferior.

The causes for wrong view are: having seen [only] what accords with one's own disposition, associating with persons whose views are corrupted, turning away from the true Dhamma, abundance of wrong thoughts, and emerging from reflection in an improper manner.

In this context, "having a disposition based on what was previously seen" means that, just as in the cases of Kāṇa-Ariṭṭha and Sunakkhatta, because a particular view had come down to them from previous existences as their habitual resort, they possess an inclination toward eternalism or annihilationism even in this present existence.
"Aversion to the True Dhamma" means having lived for a long time without the True Dhamma. "Abundance of wrong thoughts" refers to [thinking] about things that are not within one's own sphere.
In matters within the domain of the Omniscient One, failing to recognize one’s own limits and being full of wrong thoughts due to an obsession with reflection is called "rising up unreasonably.
This refers to rising up [from the depths] by grasping at the reasons for one's own views as essential and true.
By contrast, the reason for being dissociated from such views should be understood. Rebirth produced by unprompted (asaṅkhārika) kamma is "well-formed" (kallakāya).

Mental alertness, abundance of patience, seeing the benefits in manly efforts, being intent on work, and obtaining suitable conditions such as climate and food—this is the cause for spontaneous (asaṅkhārika) action.
In this context, "abundance of patience" means a great capacity for enduring cold, heat, and so forth.
"In manly efforts" refers to tasks to be performed by men. "Being intent on work" means having mastery through habitual practice in various tasks.
The opposite of that should be understood as the cause for the prompted (sasaṅkhārika) type. Furthermore, the method for the arising of these consciousnesses should be taken from the *Visuddhimagga*.

By the word "also" (*pi*), the author includes their manifold variety according to the different types of courses of action (kamma-patha) they may involve, as well as their distinctions in terms of time, continuity, object, and so forth.
The exposition of the states rooted in greed is finished. 25. Regarding the states rooted in hatred (*dosamūlacitta*):

"With a corrupted mind" means having a mind that is corrupted. "A deformed mind" (*virūpaṃ cittaṃ*); or, one whose mind is corrupted is "corrupted-minded" (*dummano*). A person who possesses such a deformed mind is [called] *dummano*.
The state of being corrupted-minded is "mental distress" (*domanassaṃ*). This refers to the feeling of mental suffering.

It is a designation (*adhivacana*). For it is either the cause for the occurrence of the verbal expression "he is dejected" with respect to the consciousness associated with itself, or with respect to the person endowed with it, or it is the cause for the occurrence of the cognition "this is dejection" (*dummanabuddhi*);
thus it is called "dejection" (*domanassa*). The remainder is exactly as explained below.

It is a compound meaning "that which has gone together with dejection" (*domanassena saha gataṃ*). It is "resistance" (*paṭigha*) because it strikes against; it is hatred (*dosa*). For when that [hatred] arises, it also [strikes against] the associated states (*sampayutta-dhamma*).
It strikes back; it makes the rough [object] hot. It strikes even its own cloth; it burns the region of the heart.
It makes that person frown and strikes back at its own object as well. Because it seizes [the object] while causing affliction, it is therefore called "resistance" (paṭigha).
26. Here it might be argued: "Since it is *saṅkhāra* (volitional formation) that effects the dissolution of this consciousness, its inclusion here is appropriate;
however, since feeling (*vedanā*) does not effect dissolution by way of resistance (*paṭigha*), it should not be included here. To this it is said:

First, the inclusion of "mental distress" (*domanassa*) is for the purpose of precluding the possibility that this consciousness might sometimes be associated with other types of feeling. For when kings...
They send for the execution of thieves as if laughing; and when people proclaim their joy at the death of their enemies, they rejoice in that death;
and when foolish people kill deer and birds while laughing—then, would this not indeed be associated with mental pleasure?
There is certainly room for such a conclusion. But in the case of equanimity (*upekkhā*), there is simply nothing to be said.
The inclusion of "dejection" (domanassa) is for the purpose of excluding the possibility of its association with other [mental factors].

Likewise, the inclusion of "aversion" (paṭigha) is for the purpose of excluding its association with other phenomena. For instance, there are those who hold nihilistic views, lack roots of goodness, and maintain the wrong view that action is purposeless;

they hold that there is no such thing as demerit in the killing of living beings. Furthermore, some hold that demerit arises only from the killing of human beings, and not from the killing of animals.

They hold that there is no demerit. And they hold that for those who perform sacrifices after having committed the killing of living beings, there is great merit conducive to rebirth in the divine realms.
Being released from the view of a self-existent body (sakkāyadiṭṭhi), they either kill living beings themselves or send others to do so.
In that case, there is certainly the possibility that this [kamma] would also be associated with that view.
Among those with right view, there are fools who are incompetent; they might sometimes adopt the views of those with wrong view and, while killing a living being, be initially in a state of doubt.
In that case, there would be the undesirable consequence (*pasaṅga*) that this [kamma] could also be associated with doubt for them.
To avoid that consequence, the term "aversion" (*paṭigha*) is included. Otherwise, [the inclusion of aversion is necessary] for the preceding consciousness...

Since its state of being accompanied by greed and its state of being associated with aversion are established by the *Cūḷanigama* [Sutta] alone, the inclusion of those [other factors] would be purposeless.

Furthermore, the non-inclusion of envy, avarice, and worry, as well as sloth and torpor, here should be understood according to the principle applied to conceit and sloth-torpor in the preceding consciousness.
This is the exposition of the ultimate meaning (*paramatthadīpanā*) in this context.
[28] However, in the *Vibhāvani* and the *Mahāṭīkā*, it is stated:

"The mention of mental distress (*domanassa*) is for the purpose of characterizing consciousness by way of its specific, uncommon factor (*asādhāraṇadhamma*). Regarding this, first, the phrase "by way of its specific, uncommon factor" is indeed appropriate.

[29] For even though this [consciousness] is accompanied by joy (*somanassa*) and equanimity (*upekkhā*), it is distinguished from others precisely by way of its mental distress, which is not shared with any other.

"By way of characterization" means because it brings about a specific meaning. For instance, although both this preceding consciousness and this present consciousness are accompanied by delusion (*moha*), the inclusion of "associated with greed" and "associated with aversion" is for the purpose of characterizing them by means of greed and aversion respectively, which are not shared by other [types of consciousness].
Furthermore, it should not be said that it is "for the purpose of characterization."

For if this were so, it would follow that by means of a manifest state of mental grief (*domanassa*), one characterizes other, non-manifest feelings as being present here—as in the expression, "a prince who has obtained his food.
Furthermore, that which was stated in the *Vibhāvani*:
"The mention of the state of association with aversion (*paṭigha*) is said for the purpose of showing the absolute concomitance of both," is also not correct.
The accomplishment of that purpose was achieved by this very small village alone.
27. In this context, the causes of mental distress (*domanassa*) and aversion (*paṭigha*) are:

a disposition toward hatred, a shallow nature, a lack of effort, the presence of a basis for resentment, or the encounter with an undesirable object. Among these, it is due to the abundance of hatred.

The inclination toward hatred (*dosajjhāsayatā*) is to be understood by way of what has occurred [in the past]. The inclination toward the inferior (*hīnajjhāsayatā*) is the state of having a shallow nature.
Furthermore, for one who is of little learning and is beset by the worldly conditions (*lokadhamma*) that are undesirable, there is no such reflective consideration as "how can this be obtained here?
The method for the arising of these two should be taken from the *Visuddhimagga*. The meaning of the word "also" (*pi*) is likewise according to the manner already stated.
The exposition of the ultimate meaning of the mind rooted in hatred is completed. 28.
The word-meanings for doubt and restlessness within the mind rooted in delusion will follow later.
However, because this mind—devoid of other roots—has found an opportunity through delusion alone, which is exceedingly powerful, and by means of [the factors] that creep and distract, [it arises].

It is also associated with doubt and restlessness. Therefore, in this case, since even feeling is unable to experience the object intensely, it is associated only with equanimous feeling (*upekkhā-vedanā*).
Nevertheless, this consciousness arises immediately after those accompanied by joy (*somanassa*) and grief (*domanassa*);
therefore, there is the possibility that it might also be associated with both of those feelings.
The inclusion of equanimity (*upekkhā*) here is for the purpose of excluding its association with that [greed].
The inclusion of doubt (*vicikicchā*) is for the purpose of defining the mind by means of a state that is not shared with any other state of consciousness.

As for restlessness (*uddhacca*), although it is associated with all unwholesome states, it should be understood that it is included specifically here to show that it becomes particularly powerful when it finds an opportunity in this context.

Therefore, in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*, under the section on the enumeration of states (*dhammuddesa*), restlessness (*uddhacca*) is mentioned only as an "occasional" state (*yevāpanaka*), without being extracted by its own specific form from among other evil states of mind. It should be understood that it is only in this final consciousness that it is extracted by its own specific form.
And because these two types of consciousness constitute the natural disposition of beings, they cannot be removed by any application or means whatsoever.
There is nothing that needs to be produced. At all times, it proceeds without shrinking back and without sinking down, occurring without difficulty and without exertion.
Therefore, since it is exclusively spontaneous (*asaṅkhārika*), it should be understood that no classification by way of volitional effort (*saṅkhāra*) is included here.
For this very reason, even in the Canon, the phrase "with volitional effort" (*sasaṅkhārena*) is not used here as it was in the case of the preceding types of consciousness.
"The second section on consciousness is finished. This is the explanation of the ultimate meaning (*paramatthadīpanā*) here.
However, in the *Vibhāvanī*, it is stated:

"These two types of consciousness, because they are extremely confused and extremely restless, are devoid of both lust and hatred in all instances; therefore, they occur only accompanied by equanimity (*upekkhā*). That is not correct.
[32] "Because even for minds rooted in greed that are accompanied by delight, equanimity is seen as their yoke.
And as it is said there in the *Mahāṭīkā*:
"And for this very reason, because they lack natural intensity and the need for exertion, there is also no differentiation of formations among them."
It has been stated. Therein, by the phrase "due to the absence of sharpness of intrinsic nature," he rejects its state of being unprompted (*asaṅkhārika*).
By the phrase "due to the absence of the need for exertion," he rejects its state of being prompted (*sasaṅkhārika*).

Furthermore, by these two [reasons], he shows that this pair of consciousnesses is entirely free from volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*). Even according to the *Aṭṭhakathā*, this does not yet accord with the text.
For in the *Paṭiccasamuppādavibhaṅga-aṭṭhakathā*, only a twofold state of ignorance is mentioned by way of the classification of formations (*saṅkhāra*).
If these two were to be separate from formations, then in this context delusion (*moha*) would also have to be separate from formations;
and since that [delusion] is indeed nothing other than ignorance, a threefold state of ignorance would have to be stated there. Yet it is not so stated. Thus, first of all...
It does not agree with the commentary.

And because here "sharpness" (tikkhabhāva) is said to be the capacity for occurrence by way of the natural condition and the group alone, without any [additional] formation (saṅkhāra), and this consciousness occurs in just that way; therefore, this is sharp by its own nature (sabhāvatikkha).
"It cannot be said that it does not exist.

Because they are thoroughly deluded by delusion (*moha*) which has found an opportunity, what should have been called *mohamūhāni* ("delusions by delusion") is stated as *momūhāni* according to the rules of phonetic euphony (*niruttanaya*).
29. "Thus indeed," etc., is the great conclusion. Therein, *iccevaṃ* means "thus indeed" (*iti evaṃ*). This is a compound of particles (*nipāta*). The latter part...
In this way, the word *evaṃ* expresses the meaning of the preceding word *iti*. Alternatively, *icc’evaṃ* is a single, separate indeclinable particle (*nipāta*).
In every respect, the meaning should be understood as "not" [the number] in the manner described by the phrase "accompanied by joy" (*somanassasahagata*) and so forth.

Furthermore, this [word *dvādasa*] should be understood as a qualifier for the phrase "twelve. "In every respect" means that even according to the method stated in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*, there are exactly twelve.
By the method analyzed in the *Vibhaṅga*, there are exactly twelve. By the method stated in the *Dhātukathā* and other such works, there are exactly twelve.
By the method stated in various Suttantas, there are exactly twelve. Even by the method distinguished by differences of time, place, continuity, and so forth, there are exactly twelve.
How is it that there are exactly twelve? Thus, one should connect [the statement] as "in this way, there are exactly twelve."
[34] In the *Vibhāvani*, however, only the modes such as association (*sampayoga*) mentioned above have been explained. And that is established by this very phrase, "it is precisely thus.
As for "unwholesome consciousnesses" (*akusalacittāni*), these are consciousnesses so named because their intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) is the opposite of the wholesome. And herein—
Faith and the other [mental factors] are exclusively wholesome; delusion and the others are exclusively unwholesome. Consciousness, however, is exactly like contact and the rest;
for the mere cognition of an object is neither exclusively blameworthy like delusion and so forth, nor is it blameless like faith and so forth.
Nevertheless, when it is associated with unwholesome states, it is called "unwholesome."

That which is associated with wholesome states is "wholesome" (*kusala*). Furthermore, the state of opposition between faith and the other [wholesome roots] on one hand, and delusion and the others on the other, should be understood according to their respective roles as that which abandons and that which is to be abandoned. Unwholesome states are weak;
like counterfeit gold, they are mere pith-wood, unfit for cultivation. Even when practiced repeatedly, they remain merely flickering and continue to scatter.
Even those entering the path of certainty (*niyāma*) enter it while still subject to rebirth in the states of misery within a single lifetime.
However, they are not yet able to completely sever the roots of unwholesomeness and place sentient beings under the certainty of the stream of cyclic existence (*vaṭṭasota*).

Rather, their wholesome qualities become powerful; like gold refined through successive births, they become essential, worthy of cultivation, and, when practiced again and again, attain a state of greater stability.
Among mundane states, from the various supernormal powers up to the supramundane paths leading to Arahantship, there are qualities that possess the nature of growth and development.

Those entering the path of certainty (niyāma) completely sever either the stream of the woeful states or the cycle of existence itself, and thereby enter into the state of sharing in Nibbāna without residue.
Therefore, it should be understood that wholesome states alone are called "abandoners," while the others are simply called "things to be abandoned."

Furthermore, even the mere giving of a mouthful of alms-food among wholesome states is prescribed and practiced by the wise for the very purpose of abandoning unwholesome states, just like the administration of medicine in the world;

therefore, those alone are the abandoners. Unwholesome states, however, exist as the natural condition of the entire world, like various types of diseases in the world; thus, they are precisely what must be abandoned.
"Completed" (*samattāni*) means they were taken up and grasped entirely and without remainder on all sides. Furthermore, "completed" means finished or fulfilled.
The verse beginning with "eightfold" (*aṭṭhadhā*) is a summary verse. "Lobha is the root of these" is a compound (*samāsa*).

Regarding the phrase "there may be twelve unwholesome [states]," the word *siyuṃ* should be understood here as a particle; the meaning is that there are twelve unwholesome consciousnesses (*akusala-cittāni*).
Thus ends the Elucidation of the Unwholesome Consciousness within the Fourth Commentary on the *Abhidhammattha-saṅgaha*,
titled the *Paramatthadīpanī*.

31. Having thus summarized all the most inferior unwholesome states, he now summarizes those that are rootless (*ahetuka*). In doing so, in order to first show the most inferior unwholesome result (*akusalavipāka*) among them, he says:

"Accompanied by equanimity" (*upekkhāsahagata*), and so forth. However, in the *Vibhāvani*, it is stated with the intention that because it is an unwholesome result, it was shown first immediately after the unwholesome states.
"Their unwholesome results, though they exist in three ways during the course of a day, must be classified as only unwholesome results immediately following the unwholesome"—this is not correct.
For if that were so, the wholesome results would likewise have to be stated as occurring only immediately following the wholesome. 31.
The meaning of the terms "eye," "ear," and so forth will be explained later. It is called *viññāṇa* (consciousness) because it cognizes (*vijānāti*). As it has been said: "It cognizes."
"Monks, it is called 'consciousness' (viññāṇa) because it cognizes. Consciousness dependent on the eye is eye-consciousness.
Or, consciousness produced by the eye as its condition is eye-consciousness. Or, consciousness brought to the eye by kamma is eye-consciousness.
Or, consciousness born from the eye is eye-consciousness. Or, [consciousness] by way of the eye's faculty..."
Consciousness belonging to one who possesses the eye is eye-consciousness; or, consciousness arisen in the eye is eye-consciousness.
This same method applies to ear-consciousness and the others as well. Furthermore, in the *Mahātaṇhāsaṅkhaya Sutta* of the Pāli Canon it is said:
"Just as, monks, a fire burns dependent on fuel and is reckoned simply as a 'fuel-fire'."
Fire burns dependent on wood shavings; it is reckoned simply as "wood-shavings fire.
Fire burns dependent on grass; it is reckoned simply as "grass fire. Fire burns dependent on cow dung; it is reckoned simply as "cow-dung fire.
Fire burns dependent on chaff; it is reckoned simply as "chaff fire."
Fire burns dependent on rubbish; it is reckoned simply as a "rubbish-fire.
Even so, monks, consciousness arises dependent on the eye and forms; it is reckoned simply as "eye-consciousness.
Consciousness arises dependent on the ear and sounds; it is reckoned simply as "ear-consciousness."
Dependent on the nose and odors, consciousness arises; it is reckoned simply as nose-consciousness.
Dependent on the tongue and tastes, consciousness arises; it is reckoned simply as tongue-consciousness.
Dependent on the body and tangibles, consciousness arises; it is reckoned simply as body-consciousness.
Consciousness arises dependent on the mind and mental objects (*dhamma*). It is said that the mind thus comes to be designated as "consciousness.
By the word "likewise" (*tathā*), the term "accompanied by equanimity" (*upekkhāsahagata*) is drawn forward. It is called "suffering" (*dukkha*) because it causes suffering;
the meaning is that it afflicts or injures the associated states or the person possessing them. Alternatively, it is called "suffering" because, being corrupted, it digs up bodily pleasure.
It is "suffering" (*dukkha*) because it must be endured through what is difficult to do; or it is suffering because the granting of space for it is difficult to perform.
It is simply a name for bodily painful feeling. "It accepts well and faces toward it" is *sampaṭicchana*. "Well" means not letting go. "Facing toward" means not looking elsewhere.
"Accepts" means desires, rejoices in, and receives. For this very reason it is said: "rejoicing."
Regarding this, they have described it as "receiving" (*sampaṭicchana*). It is called "investigating" (*santīraṇa*) because it thoroughly investigates (*tīreti*), weighs, and examines.
In the *Ṭīkā*, it is stated that "it investigates" means "it brings to a conclusion. In the *Vibhāvani*, it is stated that "it investigates" means "it scrutinizes.
32. And herein, there is the non-obstruction of the eye, the acquisition of the support of light, and the coming of visible forms into the range of vision.
He attends to the four conditions as the causes for the arising of eye-consciousness.
He attends to the unimpaired state of the ear, the acquisition of its dependence on space, and the arrival of sounds within its range, as the cause for ear-consciousness.
He attends to the unimpaired state of the nose, the acquisition of its dependence on air, and the arrival of odors within its range, as the cause for nose-consciousness.
The non-interruption of the tongue is the acquisition of the support of water. The arrival of tastes at the [sense-door] and attention are for tongue-consciousness.

The non-interruption of the body is the acquisition of the support of earth; the arrival of any one of the three kinds of tangible objects at the [sense-door] and attention are for body-consciousness. And herein, light, space, and so forth...
The inclusion of the bases [of consciousness] should be understood as being because, without them, there would be no arrival of visible forms and so forth at the sensitive organs (pasāda) even;
for even when light is present, visible forms do not come into the range of the eye if they are not in proximity. This same method applies to the others as well.
As for that which is stated in the Commentary—

Furthermore, even when the eye is unimpaired, visual consciousness does not arise if external visible objects do not come into its range. And it is said that even when they have come into its range, it does not arise if there is no dependence on light.

This [statement] is intended to show the absence of the arising of consciousness without light. However, it should be understood that this is not intended to show that the coming into range [of objects] can occur even in the absence of light.
Otherwise, even in the darkness of night, forms would [be seen] in the eye...
They come about suddenly, thus they are "attained" (*āpajjati*). "Unwholesome results" (*akusalavipākāni*) means the results of the unwholesome.
33. In what sense is it called "result" (*vipāka*) here? In the sense of ripening (*vipaccana*). And what is this ripening?
Just as in the world, when mangoes and other fruits have passed beyond their tender stage and reached the state of maturity, it is called "ripening," so too [is it here].
"Here too, the ripening is to be understood. And this meaning is to be illustrated by means of the four "endowments" (*samaṅgitā*). For the four endowments are:
the endowment of volition (*cetanā*), the endowment of kamma, the endowment of presence (*upaṭṭhāna*), and the endowment of ripening (*vipāka*).
Among these, the endowment of the three moments [of arising, presence, and dissolution] belongs to the wholesome or unwholesome volition at the time of the accumulation of various kamma in the past.
This is called "possessing volition. Furthermore, that volition does not cease by reaching total non-existence when it is ceasing.
Rather, having deposited within that mental continuum a specific activity (*kriyāvisesa*) complete in all its aspects for the manifestation of future fruition, it then ceases.
And that specific activity remains [latent] even for a thousand aeons until it finds an opportunity [to manifest].
He follows that very continuity of existence. With reference to this, it is said in the *Dhammapada*:
"For an evil deed once committed does not simply vanish like fresh milk;
burning, it follows the fool, like fire covered by ashes."
Even this "possession of the state" (*sopana*) does not count as a separate ultimate reality (*paramattha-dhamma*), just like the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) and the elements (*dhātu*).
This is what is called "possession of kamma. When it encounters a condition suitable to itself, it then provides an opportunity for its own ripening.
How does it provide this? It presents itself to a being whose death is imminent.
He manifests either his own sign or the sign of the destination (gatinimitta).
If that being does not let go of it and grasps it, then he gains an opportunity. This is called "possession of the manifestation" (upaṭṭhānasamaṅgitā).

For one who has passed away without letting go of that [sign], immediately after death, there arises a specific activity consisting of kamma, distinct and alone, accompanied by its associated mental factors.
Having become a heap of ultimate phenomena (*paramatthadhamma*), it ripens while fulfilling one existence;

and "fulfilling one existence" means that, for as long as its life-span lasts, it accomplishes the functions of the *bhavaṅga* and, at the six doors, the respective functions of door-pertaining resultants, as well as the function of death at the end.
Among those, the first three types of possession (*samaṅgī*) are called "tender" (*taruṇa*).

They exist. It should be understood that the last [category] refers to those states that have reached maturity while possessing their result (*vipāka*). Thus, "they ripen" (*vipaccanti*) means they become results;
having passed beyond the stage of softness and youth, they attain the state of being fully ripened, which is designated as the stage of maturity (*pariṇata-avasthā*).
This is how the meaning should be understood here. And having done so, even for those things originated by wholesome and unwholesome karma in the Pāḷi...

There is no inclusion of "matter produced by past action" (*kaṭattā-rūpa*) in the category of "resultant" (*vipāka*). For these [types of matter] are established separately from the continuity of kamma;

thus, they are indeed born directly from kamma and are not called "ripened" (*vipakka*). Indeed, the continuity of immaterial phenomena (*arūpa-dhamma*) is one thing, and the continuity of material phenomena (*rūpa-dhamma*) is another.
This is the explanation of the term "resultant" (*vipāka*) in its ultimate sense (*paramattha*) in this context.
Taking only the mere similarity to kamma by way of being immaterial and having an object, they establish that only immaterial phenomena are resultants (*vipāka*).
For them, it follows that the word "resultant" applies to immaterial phenomena by way of conventional usage (*ruḷhi*).
And as for that [analogy] regarding the stalks, leaves, flowers, and fruits produced from a rice seed, [they claim it refers only] to those fruits which resemble the seed.
They offer the simile that it is "accomplished like what is called rice-fruit and rice-ripening," but that too does not apply here.
For even fruits do not receive the name "ripe" at the time they are young; nor is it the case that stalks, leaves, and flowers do not receive the name "ripe" when they have reached maturity.
Even those are then called "the stalk is ripe," "the leaf is ripe," and "the flower is ripe. [The root *pac*] means "to bring happiness."
"Sukha" means that it makes the associated mental states, or the person possessing them, experience pleasure (*sāta*).

Alternatively, it is "sukha" because it thoroughly (*su*) digs away (*khanati*) bodily pain, or because it is to be endured with ease (*sukhena khamitabba*), or because it is easy (*sukara*) to grant space for this [feeling].

The wholesome-resultant rootless consciousnesses (*kusalavipāka-ahetuka-cittāni*) are those resultants of wholesome karma that are dissociated from roots (*hetu-virahita*) due to their association with the feeling of equanimity.

[36] However, in the *Vibhāvani*, it is argued that here the result of maturation (*vipāka*) is considered "with cause" (*sahetuka*) by means of a cause produced by both prior karma and co-nascent [factors]. That is not correct.
For nowhere in the Abhidhamma is the state of being "with cause" or "without cause" for a result of maturation established by means of a cause produced by both prior karma and co-nascent [factors].
There is indeed such a thing as possibility (*sambhava*). Since there is no deviation (*byabhicāra*) when a possibility exists, that undesirable consequence (*pasaṅga*) is pointless.

In this context, "of deviation" means "of the undesirable consequence. Furthermore, in this case, unwholesome resultant states possess a cause because they are themselves indeterminate phenomena (*abyākatadhamma*), and [the wholesome roots] such as non-greed possess a cause because they themselves are unwholesome resultants due to unwholesome causes such as greed, and [the wholesome roots] such as non-hatred possess a cause due to blameless causes (*anavajjahetu*).
There is no possibility [of such a cause]. Since that possibility does not exist, their state of being causeless is indeed invariable;

therefore, the term "causeless" was not applied there. However, for wholesome-resultants (*kusalavipāka*), because they are themselves wholesome-resultants, there is certainly the possibility of being "with cause" (*sahetuka*) through wholesome, indeterminate, and blameless causes such as non-greed (*alobha*). And since that [possibility] exists...

It should be understood that the term "rootless" (*ahetuka*) was included specifically in that context because, in the case of those [other types of consciousness], the state of being rootless is accompanied by deviation.
35. Advertence arisen at the five doors, such as the eye and so forth, is "five-door advertence" (*pañcadvārāvajjana*);
for that advertence arises having apprehended the object impinged upon at the five doors. That which arises at the mind-door, known as the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*),...
Adverting is mind-door adverting. For that occurs by taking up and adverting toward the object as it enters into its range.
And here, "mind-door" should be understood as the entire life-continuum consciousness (*bhavaṅga-citta*).
As for that which is stated in the Commentary:

To that extent, it has been stated: "Regarding 'mind-door' (*manodvāra*): here, the life-continuum consciousness (*bhavaṅgacitta*), which serves as the immediate condition for adverting, is called 'mind. That itself is the 'door,' because it is the gateway for the occurrence of the functional states such as adverting and impulsion.

And what is stated in the *Vibhāvanī*: "'Mind-door' is the life-continuum consciousness which serves as the immediate condition for adverting, because it is the gateway for the occurrence of the functional states"—all of this is indeed untenable.
For if that life-continuum (bhavaṅga) immediately after which the process-thoughts (vīthicitta) arise is,
by necessity, called the "mind-door" because it is the gateway for their occurrence— and not those preceding it— then this being the case,

those very [bases] such as the eye and so forth, through which the process-thoughts beginning with adverting (āvajjana) arise due to the impact of visible forms and other objects, would [also] be [doors].
Because they are exclusively the openings for their occurrence, they are called "doors. This implies that there are no others besides these.
Furthermore, there are no such things as the eye and so forth that are not door-forms.
All of this will be clarified later in the "Compendium of Doors. Laughter (*hasita*) is laughing; it is the manifestation of a joyful expression on the face.

It is called "laughter-arising" (*hasituppāda*) because it arises or produces that [laughter]. Or, it is called "laughter-arising" because by means of it the ones whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*) cause that [laughter] to arise;
or, it is called "laughter-arising" because that [laughter] arises by means of it. This very thing is the "mind" (*citta*); thus it is a compound.

This is the name for that mind by which the ones whose taints are destroyed manifest a smile toward non-obscene objects. For the ones whose taints are destroyed do not [manifest a smile] toward worldly [objects].
They laugh at gross objects of laughter by way of being greatly provocative, delightful, and so forth.
However, in the commentaries (*ṭīkā*), it may be explained as "the arising of laughter" (*hasituppāda*) with reference to the mind.

According to the method stated, these are rootless functional minds (*ahetuka-kriyā-cittāni*), because they are devoid of the functions of ripening (*vipaccana*) and producing result (*vipākuppādana*), and are merely minds consisting of various types of function.

In this context, those consciousnesses outside the cognitive process—the five sense-consciousnesses—occur solely through the mere ripening of kamma, without their own exertion, because their functions are weak;
likewise, the receiving consciousnesses and so forth occur without their own exertion because the bases for their functions are weak.
Therefore, all these are exclusively resultants (*vipāka*). However, those [consciousnesses] that occur through their own exertion because their functions are powerful...
They are accompanied by effort for the purpose of producing a result in the future; these are what are called wholesome and unwholesome states.

However, as for those consciousnesses that proceed solely by their own effort, having transcended the mere process of ripening—among them, the two types of adverting consciousness are somewhat weak because they have obtained conditions from the continuity of the resultant stream, and the others [are weak] because they occur in a continuity devoid of underlying tendencies (*nirānusaya*).
Because they have already occurred, they lack the effort required for the production of any further result; therefore, it should be understood that all of them are termed "functional" (*kriyā*). 36.
Now, the investigation of feeling (*vedanā*) is stated starting from the beginning. To explain, first regarding eye-consciousness and the others:
The bases and the objects are indeed derived matter (*upādārūpa*), and because the mutual impact of derived matter is as weak as that of cotton balls,
these [consciousnesses] are accompanied by equanimity (*upekkhā*) alone toward both desirable and undesirable objects.
However, since the objects of body-consciousness are the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), it is like a cotton ball placed on top of a surface being struck with an iron hammer.
When striking with an iron spike, the impact against the eyeball is more powerful than the impact after it has passed the eyelid.

Likewise, when those same objects become the objective field, the impact against the physical bases of the body (the sense organs) is more powerful than the impact against the physical bodies themselves.
Therefore, body-consciousness arises accompanied by pleasure when the object is desirable, and accompanied by pain when it is undesirable.

Furthermore, because the receiving-consciousness (*sampahaṭṭhanacitta*) arises immediately after all the extremely weak fivefold sense-cognitions (*pañcaviññāṇa*), it is always weak and consequently always accompanied by equanimity (*upekkhā-sahagata*).

However, in the *Vibhāvanī*, this point is explained on the grounds that, although those [fivefold sense-cognitions] have different bases, they provide the necessary conditions for it; whereas the investigating-consciousness (*santīraṇa*), being itself a strong object-base...
It proceeds by depending [on a basis]. Because it has obtained its conditions through a preceding consciousness that serves as a powerful objective basis (*vatthu*), it becomes somewhat strong.
Therefore, that wholesome resultant occurs accompanied by equanimity when the object is desirable, and accompanied by joy when it is undesirable.
As for unwholesome resultants, however, they occur accompanied by equanimity regardless of whether the object is undesirable or very undesirable.

It exists. Why? Because if that [feeling] were connected with a division of feeling by way of an undesirable object, it would have to be associated either with pain (*dukkha*) or with mental grief (*domanassa*).
In this regard, it is first not associated with pain; why? Because pain is exclusively bodily. Nor is it associated with mental grief; why?
Because its state as mental grief arises precisely from being struck by aversion (*paṭigha*).
The feeling of displeasure (*domanassavedanā*) does not arise without resistance (*paṭigha*).

Since displeasure is invariably associated with resistance—which is exclusively unwholesome—it cannot occur among the indeterminate (*abyākata*) states. Furthermore, the two types of adverting consciousness (*āvajjanadvaya*) are somewhat stronger than investigating consciousness (*santīraṇa*);
for resultant consciousnesses possess no inherent power of effort to proceed. However, by those that are powerful...
Those born from conditions such as kamma are called "strong," while those born from weak [conditions] are called "weak.

Even so, these two types of adverting consciousness are always accompanied by equanimity alone, because they arise having emerged both from the power of kamma and from the continuity of the resultant (vipāka). Thus, they are indeed weak.
In the *Vibhāvani*, however,
it is stated that because five-door adverting consciousness occurs for only a single moment upon an object not previously grasped by anyone,

and because mind-door adverting consciousness depends on a different functional process by way of turning the stream of consciousness toward a dissimilar state, it does not experience the flavor of the object to a predominant degree.

It is stated that because one is unable to experience [the object], in all cases it is associated only with neutral feeling (*majjhatta-vedanā*). In this regard, the claim that "it depends on another function" is not tenable.
For the distinction between the strength and weakness of mental states cannot be asserted on the basis of a subsequent state of consciousness;
rather, that [distinction] can only be asserted on the basis of its own conditions. Otherwise, even the investigating consciousness (*santīraṇa*) would depend on another function.
It may be so; for even that [volition] sets another dissimilar mental continuum in motion by means of itself. 37.

It is not the case that these types of consciousness do not arise when their own natural conditions are assembled; therefore, they say they are exclusively *asaṅkhārika* (unprompted). However, in the *Mūlaṭīkā*, regarding the exclusion of resultant states:
because rootless resultants have indistinct functions, even the state of being unprompted (*asaṅkhārikabhāva*) is incompatible with prompted (*sasaṅkhārika*) karma.
There is none. There is also no "prompted" (sasaṅkhārika) kamma that is opposed to "unprompted" (asaṅkhārika) kamma.
Therefore, it is said that their arising through both types of kamma was authorized by the Elder.

By this, the presence or absence of those two states in the three types of functional consciousness (kriyacitta) is also stated; for even those [functional consciousnesses] have functions that are indeed not clearly manifest.
Alternatively: It is established by direct observation that beings do not sometimes hear sounds and so forth by their own desire, but at other times act when urged by others.

In this regard, when they act by their own desire, then all the process-thoughts (vīthi-citta), beginning with the five-door adverting consciousness (pañcadvārāvajjana), are called "unprompted" (asaṅkhārika). When [they act] by others...

They perform [the function] having been incited; at that time, they are called "prompted" (*sasankhārika*). Furthermore, regarding the two door-liberations (*dvāravimutta*), it should be stated that there are two moments of investigation with equanimity (*upekkhā-santīraṇa*), just as in the case of the eight great resultants (*mahāvipāka*).
Thus, all rootless consciousnesses (*ahetuka-citta*) are indeed distinct from one another according to that method of classification by way of formations (*saṅkhāra-bheda*).
Even so, because their functions are not fully manifest, the classification by way of formations does not apply to them.
It should be understood that this is not stated in the Pāḷi.

38. However, because the causes and sources (*hetu-yoni*) are great phenomena, they do not arise in these types of consciousness, which are produced by weak kamma and occupy positions where the function of the basis is weak.
In that regard, all evil kamma is associated with distraction and is itself unstable.
It is weak. Therefore, even though it remains for an aeon (*kappa*), it is unable to produce a result corresponding to its cause at a later time.

Likewise, even though it is a three-rooted (*tihetuka*) kamma, it is unable to produce a result corresponding to its cause when the bases such as the eye are weak, or when the functional spheres such as seeing are weak.
The functions of adverting and laughing are indeed weak functions.
Therefore, it should be understood that all these have arisen devoid of associated causes (*sampayutta-hetu*). 39.
The meaning of the phrase "in every way" (*sabbathāpi*) is to be understood according to the method already stated above.
However, in the *Vibhāvani*:
The statement that "all [eighteen]" refers to the divisions of unwholesome-resultant, wholesome-resultant, and functional [consciousness] is not correct.
For that division is already included by the phrase "and so forth" (icceva). In the summary verse, the unwholesome-resultants are sevenfold according to the distinction of basis and function;
the merit-resultants are eightfold according to the distinction of basis, function, and feeling; and the functional consciousnesses are [divided] according to the distinction of function and door.

The construction is: "Three" refers to the rootless consciousnesses, and there are eighteen [instances] of them. Furthermore, here too, the distinction of feeling (*vedanā*) should be stated for the wholesome and resultant [consciousnesses];

otherwise, there would be no distinction for the investigating consciousness (*santīraṇa*). Likewise, the distinction of the doors (*dvāra*) should be stated for the functional (*kriyā*) [consciousnesses];
otherwise, there would be no distinction for the adverting consciousness (*āvajjana*). However, this is not mentioned in the commentaries (*ṭīkā*).
The Elucidation of Ultimate Reality Concerning Rootless Consciousness. 40.
Now, establishing the name "non-beautiful" for the consciousnesses mentioned below and the name "beautiful" for those to be mentioned above, the author speaks this verse.
For when the beauty of those to be mentioned above has been stated, the non-beauty of those mentioned below is [implied].

"It is established even without being stated. In this context, "freed from the evil and the rootless" means that forty-nine types of consciousness are freed from the unwholesome (*akusala*) and the rootless (*ahetuka*).
Alternatively, the construction is: "even the ninety-one types of consciousness are called beautiful; they are so designated. In this context, "from the evil" means from the unwholesome.
For it is the unwholesome states that, against the will of the beings who possess them, lead them to the states of misery (*apāya*); therefore, they are called "evil."
By this, the undesirable consequence that meritorious deeds (puñña) might also be called "evil" (pāpa) in the sense of leading to a happy destination (sugati) is averted;
for the operation of leading to evil is not evident in the case of those who desire [merit]. Alternatively, they are called "evils" precisely because they are base.
They are called "beautiful" (sobhana) because of their association with beautiful qualities such as faith (saddhā), and because they themselves attain beauty through that very association.
41. Now, showing those beautiful [states] in order from inferior to superior, he says "accompanied by joy" and so forth.

In this context, "knowledge" (*ñāṇa*) means that which knows; the meaning is that it penetrates according to reality. "Associated with knowledge" (*ñāṇasampayutta*) and "dissociated [from knowledge]" (*vippayutta*) are compounds.
"Without volitional formation" (*asaṅkhāra*) means that for it there is no volitional formation (*saṅkhāra*). "With volitional formation" (*sasaṅkhāra*) means that volitional formation exists for it.
The group of natural conditions for the arising of the wholesome, such as association with good persons and so forth,
is called "without volitional effort" (*asaṅkhāra*) when it produces a wholesome consciousness solely by its own power, without the two kinds of volitional effort.

That same group is called "with volitional effort" (*sasaṅkhāra*) when it is unable to produce a wholesome consciousness by its own power and does so only after obtaining the assistance of volitional effort.
It arouses that [feeling]; at that time, it is called "with effort" (*sasaṅkhāra*). That which arises without effort is "without effort" (*asaṅkhārika*);
that which arises with effort is "with effort"—all of this has already been explained below. Furthermore, the causes for the arising of joy and so forth have also been explained below.
Moreover, there is the excellence of faith, the excellence of vision, and the excellence of the gift and the recipient.

Such things as these are causes for joy; their opposites are causes for equanimity. Furthermore, those causes for the enlightenment factor of rapture and the enlightenment factor of equanimity that are mentioned in the commentaries should also be stated in this context.
Wisdom consists in the presence of strong dependence on karma conducive to it, rebirth in a world free from affliction, the maturation of the faculties, and remoteness from the defilements.
The causes for the arising of knowledge are: being reborn with a three-rooted rebirth-linking, having a disposition toward non-delusion, and associating with wise persons.

It is also appropriate to say "devoted to hearing and reflection. Furthermore, those causes for the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena that are mentioned in the commentaries should also be stated here. Conversely, the opposite of these are the causes for dissociation from knowledge. The cause for [the arising of] formations is also [to be understood].

This has already been stated previously. Furthermore, those causes for the energy enlightenment factor (*vīriya-sambojjhaṅga*) and the tranquility enlightenment factor (*passaddhi-sambojjhaṅga*) that are mentioned in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) should also be stated here.
The manner of their arising should likewise be taken from the *Visuddhimagga*.

42. Regarding the word "also" (*pi*) in the phrase "eight also" (*aṭṭha-pi*), the particle has the sense of inclusion (*sampiṇḍana*). By this, [it is implied] that these [factors], apart from the types mentioned here...
This summarizes their manifold variety through various modes. Herein, this is the method:
these eight consciousnesses, when multiplied by the ten bases of meritorious action, become eighty. When those, in turn, are multiplied by the six objects, they become four hundred and eighty.
When those, again, are multiplied by the three types of kamma, they become one thousand four hundred and forty.
When those [three hundred and sixty] are multiplied by the three categories of inferior, medium, and superior, they become four thousand three hundred and twenty.
Taking these as the "pure" (suddhika) states, they should be set down in two places.
Then, taking one of those places and dividing it into two, there are two thousand six hundred associated with knowledge (ñāṇasampayutta). Likewise...
"Disassociated from knowledge": Furthermore, among those [states], the ones associated with knowledge, when multiplied by the four predominances, amount to eight thousand six hundred and forty.

The ones dissociated from knowledge, however, when multiplied by the three predominances—excluding the predominance of investigation—amount to six thousand four hundred and eighty. Again, these two combined together...

Ten thousand, five thousand, one hundred, and twenty. When these are added together with the pure [knowledges] previously set aside separately, they total ten thousand, nine thousand, four hundred, and forty.

Furthermore, as for that which is stated here in the *Ṭīkā*, all [the knowledges]—without separating the pure ones and those dissociated from knowledge according to the method explained here—[are counted as follows...]
It has been stated that when multiplied by the same number of meritorious deeds and so forth, there are seventeen thousand two hundred and eighty.

Furthermore, it has been stated in the *Vibhāvani* that if the "pure" (suddhika) types are not treated separately, but only those dissociated from knowledge (ñāṇavippayutta) are treated separately and multiplied in that manner, there are fifteen thousand two hundred. All of that is incorrect.
If this were so, these sense-sphere wholesome states would always possess a dominant influence and would thus be called "having a fixed dominant influence.
However, unlike the sublime wholesome states and the supramundane states mentioned above, these do not have a fixed dominant influence.
Furthermore, according to the method of the *Ṭīkā*, it would follow that even those states dissociated from knowledge are accompanied by investigation (*vīmaṃsā*). Or else...
In the sense of being produced by skill (*kosalla*), they are "wholesome" (*kusala*);

even those states dissociated from knowledge are indeed called wholesome because they are produced by the supporting knowledge (*upanissaya-ñāṇa*) that occurs through various acts of adverting in the cognitive process (*vīthi*).
Thus, here too, it cannot be said that they are not "dominated by inquiry" (*vīmaṃsādhipateyya*), since they are produced precisely by that [knowledge] which has inquiry as its dominant factor.

It might be thought that for this reason those [types of consciousness] were not made separate. Even so, among those called "wholesome states pertaining to the sense-sphere" (*kāmakusala*), those dominated by the predominance of liberation (*adhipativimutta*) are more numerous.
Therefore, it is impossible for all wholesome states pertaining to the sense-sphere to be rooted in the predominance of investigation (*vīmaṃsādhipatimūlaka*).
43. The analysis (*vigga-ha*) is: "And those wholesome states of the sense-sphere. In that regard, in what sense are they "wholesome" (*kusala*)?
In the sense of health, in the sense of beauty, in the sense of skillfulness, in the sense of blamelessness, and in the sense of having a pleasant result.

For states such as lust and the rest are called "diseases" in the sense that they afflict the mental continuum; they are called "unbeautiful" in the sense of being harmful; they are called "unskillful" in the sense of being unrefined;
they are called "blameworthy" in the sense of being censurable; and they are called "having painful results" in the sense of having undesirable results.
Furthermore, because they have emerged from those [unwholesome states], they are called "wholesome" (*kusala*), which means they are healthy (*aroga*).
And because they are the opposites of those [unwholesome states], they are called beautiful, skillful, blameless, and having a pleasant result.

They are "wholesome" (*kusala*) because they crush, shake, agitate, and destroy the contemptible, evil qualities (*pāpadhamma*). Or alternatively, they are "wholesome" because they dwell within the continuum of beings in a contemptible manner.
They cut, thus they are *kusā*. These are lust and the other defilements. They cut and sever, thus they are *kusalāni*.

Or, "knowledge" (*ñāṇa*) is called *kusa* in the sense of cutting away what is base (*kucchi-tānaṃ*), in the sense of making them thin, or in the sense of bringing them to an end. They are to be reaped with the *kusa*, thus they are *kusalāni*.

Or, they are *kusalāni* because they cut away the side of defilement (*saṃkilesapakkha*) from the region of the hand as if with a *kusa* grass. Furthermore, regarding the base, evil states (*pāpadhamma*):

They are called *kusala* because they ward off (*saranti*) or destroy (*hiṃsanti*) unwholesome states; here, the letter *ra* is changed to *la*. Alternatively, they are called *kusala* in the sense of being produced through skill (*kosalla*). 44.
Regarding the great resultants (*mahāvipāka*), there is nothing to be said from the standpoint of their literal meaning.

Their classification according to feeling must be stated by way of their objects. For these are respectively associated with joy (*somanassa*) and equanimity (*upekkhā*) when their objects are extremely desirable or desirable-neutral, respectively.
The distinction regarding association should be stated by way of karma and by way of impulsion (*javana*).
For those [resultant consciousnesses] produced by powerful karma are associated with knowledge (*ñāṇa-sampayutta*); those produced by weak karma are dissociated from knowledge (*ñāṇa-vippayutta*).

Furthermore, at times when they occur as registration (*tadārammaṇa*), they are generally associated with knowledge when following a three-rooted impulsion; however, when following other types of impulsion, they are dissociated from knowledge.
"Disassociated from knowledge. Regarding the classification of volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*), some teachers have explained them solely by way of karma:

those produced by effortless karma are "effortless" (*asaṅkhārika*), and those produced by effortful karma are "effortful" (*sasaṅkhārika*). However, the author of the *Saṅgaha* has stated this by way of the presence of conditions.
For these [volitions] at the time of death in a previous existence, when one is close to rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), [are influenced] by relatives and others through various means...
Those [consciousnesses] that arise having grasped objects such as kamma that have been presented are called "prompted" (*sasaṅkhārika*).
Those that arise having grasped [objects] that have appeared by the power of kamma itself, without such an effort, are called "unprompted" (*asaṅkhārika*).
At the time of the registration (*tadārammaṇa*), those that follow an unprompted javana are called "unprompted. [The others are] prompted.
"Those accompanied by impulsions are called 'prompted' (*sasaṅkhārika*). Here too, the particle *vi-* has the sense of "collecting.
By this, it collects their manifold divisions according to the sixfold objects, the three grades of inferiority, and [factors] such as time, place, and continuity.
However, these do not arise by making generosity and so forth, bodily action and so forth, or zeal and so forth their primary focus.
Therefore, these do not obtain growth by way of the bases for meritorious action (*puññakriyāvatthu*) or through the predominance of kamma.
However, in the *Vibhāvani*, it is stated:

"Because they lack the production of intimation (*viññatti*), they do not proceed by way of the doors of kamma; and because their nature is non-resultant (*avipāka*), they do not proceed by way of kamma. This must be examined.
In the preceding section on wholesome states, the increase was explained solely by way of the threefold classification of kamma; it was not treated separately by way of the doors of action.
For this threefold classification of kamma is established precisely by way of the three doors of action. [Objection:
But is it not stated in the Commentary that the division of the doors of action, the courses of action, and the bases of meritorious deeds among the sense-sphere wholesome states is not present here?

"Why? Because it is stated [to be so] on account of not producing intimation (*viññatti*), being a non-resultant phenomenon (*avipāka-dhamma*), and because it does not function in that way. This is true.

However, in this context, by "on account of not producing intimation, there is no division of doors of action (*kammadvāra-bheda*)," he states the absence of such a division as "bodily action, verbal action, and mental action" (*kāyakammaṃ vacīkammaṃ manokammaṃ*).
By "on account of being a non-resultant phenomenon, there is no division of courses of action (*kammapatha-bheda*) here," [he means the same].
