By this, he states the absence of the tenfold division of the paths of action (*kamma-patha*).

Here, however, even among the wholesome (*kusala*) actions, without taking up that tenfold division of paths of action, only the triad of kamma—distinguished by the threefold division of doors of action—is taken.

And that [triad] is established precisely by the fact that they do not proceed by way of the three doors of action because they lack the nature of manifesting intimation (*viññatti*) and originating it. And if, as below, even among the wholesome...
It might be said that there is a separate increase [of feeling] by way of the tenfold classification of the courses of kamma.
This being so, it must likewise be stated here that because they lack the nature of maturation, they do not proceed by way of the courses of kamma. 45.

Even in the case of great functional consciousnesses (*mahākriyacitta*), just as in the case of great resultant consciousnesses (*mahāvipāka*), the distinction of feeling occurs solely by way of the object; this will be explained further on by itself.

It will be explained. The distinctions of association with knowledge, dissociation from knowledge, unprompted, and prompted should be understood according to the method stated for the wholesome states (*kusala*), as appropriate.
In the *Vibhāvani*, however—

It has been stated that, likewise, for the functional consciousnesses (*kriyacitta*), when they are wholesome, their association with joy and so forth should be understood according to the method already described;
however, that is not tenable. The meaning of the phrases "thus in every way" has already been explained below.

In the expression "root-cause-endowed sense-sphere wholesome, resultant, and functional consciousnesses," the inclusion of the term "root-cause-endowed" (*sahetu*) serves as a qualifying description in relation to the word "wholesome" (*kusala*).

For that very reason, it has been included in the *Cūḷanigama* among the wholesome consciousnesses (*kusalacitta*). However, in connection with the terms "resultant" (*vipāka*) and "functional" (*kiriya*), it should be understood as a qualifying term used for the purpose of exclusion (*byavacchedaka-viśeṣana*).
In the *Vibhāvani*, however...

It is said that here [in this context], the application [of the terms] follows whatever is available, as in the Sutta passage: "He sees pebbles and gravel, and shoals of fish, whether stationary or moving.
That does not accord [with the intended meaning]. For in that [Sutta], it is appropriate to say that "pebbles and gravel do not move";
however, here it would not be logical to say that "wholesome [kamma] with roots does not exist. Thus, [the previous explanation] is incorrect.

46. In the summary verse (*saṅgahagāthā*), "by way of the division of feeling, knowledge, and formations" means by way of the division of feeling, by way of the division of knowledge, and by way of the division of formations.

Therein, "by way of the division of feeling" refers to the division of consciousness established by the division of feeling; "by way of the division of knowledge" refers to the division of consciousness established by the application of knowledge (*ñāṇayoga*);
and "by way of the division of formations" refers to [the division of consciousness] established by the division of the group of conditions that arise together with, or apart from, the formations.

The meaning is "by way of a distinction in mind. For this is the functional capacity of compound words (*samāsapada*), namely, the ability to illuminate various kinds of well-known word-meanings (*padattha*) with only a few syllables.
By this, it is explained in the *Vibhāvani*.

By this, it is established that there is no room for the objection that [the Suttas] speak of a differentiation of mental formations (saṅkhāras) which are themselves undifferentiated, or that they attribute a differentiating function to consciousness (citta).

Herein, the application is as follows: "With their causes, the sense-sphere wholesome, resultant, and functional [states] are reckoned as six, twelve, and twenty-four respectively, through the differentiation of feeling (vedanā), knowledge (ñāṇa), and formations (saṅkhāra). And here:
"Through the differentiation of feeling, knowledge, and formations, these are eightfold."
It should also be stated that there are twenty-four types of [kamma] through the divisions of meritorious, ripening, and functional.
For when it is thus, the meaning and the classification become clear. This will be explained further on, as it accords with the summary verses (*saṅgahagāthā*) beginning with "pride" (*māna*).

47. The verse beginning with "kāme" is a summary verse for all sense-sphere consciousnesses (*kāmacitta*). In this context, "kāme" means in the sense-sphere plane (*kāmabhūmi*), [referring to] the results (*pākāni*).
All resultant consciousnesses (vipākacitta) are twenty-three, by way of being with root-cause (sahetuka) and without root-cause (ahetuka).

Wholesome and unwholesome consciousnesses (kusalākusalacitta), which are meritorious and demeritorious, are twenty. Furthermore, all functional consciousnesses (kriyacitta), by way of being with root-cause and without root-cause, are eleven.
Thus, in every respect, there are fifty-four; such is the construction. And here, the word "all" (sabbathā) is indicated with the elision of the suffix -thā.

The meaning of this has already been stated above, beginning with: "In every way as described in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*, there are exactly fifty-four; in every way as analyzed in the *Vibhaṅga*, there are exactly fifty-four," and so forth.
By this, it is clarified in the *Vibhāvani*.
The detailed exposition of the meaning of those wholesome states and so forth mentioned here is precluded by virtue of being included within their internal subdivisions.
Furthermore, that which was stated as "in the sense of desire and existence" (*kāme bhava*) must also be investigated.

For the word *bhava* is seen in the Abhidhamma as referring to wholesome and unwholesome kamma, to the materiality produced by kamma, and to the resultant and kamma-produced material phenomena (*vipāka-kaṭattārūpa*).
It does not refer to other mental or physical phenomena (*nāmarūpa-dhamma*). Furthermore, the word *kāma* here is used in the sense of a "plane" (*bhūmi*).
A "plane" is said to be a common locus, a collection of phenomena bound together by faculties and non-faculties; thus, "in the sense of sensual pleasures" means "in the sensual-sphere plane."
This meaning should be understood thus: by way of the Sutta method, "existence" (*bhava*) or "the plane" (*bhūmi*) is so called because beings and mental formations arise (*bhavanti*) therein.
This same method applies to the "other planes" as well.
Thus ends the *Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha*, known as the *Paramatthadīpanī*.
The Elucidation of the Ultimate Meaning (*Paramatthadīpanā*) of the fourth commentary on the mind of sensual desire is finished. 48.
Having thus shown the compendium of the mind of sensual desire, [the author] now, following the sequence, shows the compendium of the mind of form.
He said, "Accompanied by applied thought (vitakka), sustained thought (vicāra), rapture (pīti), happiness (sukha), and one-pointedness (ekaggatā)," and so forth.
"Applied thought and sustained thought, rapture and happiness, and one-pointedness" is a *dvanda* compound. "Accompanied by those" is a [possessive] compound (*samāsa*).

A wholesome consciousness associated with the first jhāna—which is designated as, or comprised of, applied thought, sustained thought, rapture, happiness, and one-pointedness—is "wholesome consciousness of the first jhāna. In that regard, in what sense is it "first," and in what sense...

"Jhāna": because it is to be practiced first, it is "first. It is called *jhāna* because it closely contemplates (*upanijjhāyana*) the characteristics such as impermanence of the object—such as the kasiṇa—and because it burns (*jhāpana*) or consumes (*dayhana*) the opposing states.

In these two senses, one-pointedness (*ekaggatā*) alone should be understood as being associated with it (*sāti*). For that [one-pointedness] is a single, foremost, and supreme portion consisting of a single object.
"Concentration" (*ekaggatā*) is so called because it possesses the quality of sovereignty (*ādhipacca*) in causing the mind—designated as "one-pointedness" in its meaning—to proceed in such a manner.

That very same state, by not allowing the mind to be distracted among various objects and by the distancing of opposing factors, rightly applies (*ādhiyati*) and establishes the mind upon a single object.
Furthermore, by bringing the faculties into equilibrium and thereby ensuring the absence of both dullness (*līna*) and agitation (*uddhacca*) right there, [it performs this function].
It is called "concentration" (*samādhi*) in the sense that it "places together" (*samañ ca ādhiyati*) and "establishes.
And this very same state is defined in the Canon as non-distraction (*avikkhepa*), non-dissipation (*avisāhāra*), stability (*saṇṭhiti*), and steadfastness (*avaṭṭhiti*).

Furthermore, applied thought (*vitakka*) and the other factors are also referred to as "jhāna" because they are exceptionally helpful to it. For instance, applied thought prevents the mind from sinking under the influence of sloth and torpor.
It makes [the mind] firm, directed precisely toward the object. For initial application (vitakka) has the characteristic of directing the mind onto the object;
it is the direct antidote to the hindrance of sloth and torpor. Furthermore, sustained application (vicāra), by not allowing the mind to wander through doubt, makes it firmly adhere to the object.
For sustained application has the characteristic of rubbing against the object and is of the nature of wisdom.
And it is the direct opposite of the hindrance of doubt (*vicikicchā-nīvaraṇa*).

Furthermore, joy (*pīti*) prevents the mind from becoming despondent due to ill-will (*byāpāda*), making it instead fully content with the object; for joy has the characteristic of gladdening the object.
And likewise, it is the direct opposite of the hindrance of ill-will. Similarly, pleasure (*sukha*) prevents that [mind] from being unsettled by restlessness and remorse (*uddhacca-kukkucca*).

It makes that which has found satisfaction in the object further grow. For pleasure (sukha) possesses the characteristic of pervading the whole [body], and it is the direct antidote to the hindrance of restlessness-and-worry (uddhacca-kukkucca-nīvaraṇa).
Equanimity (upekkhā), because its intrinsic nature is peaceful, is included within pleasure itself.

And while performing these functions, those mental factors serve to bring about a state of excellent one-pointedness for that consciousness upon that object. This state of one-pointedness is simply concentration (ekaggatā). And that—
One-pointedness (ekaggatā), being well-supported by those states and becoming very powerful, itself prevents the mind from wandering among various objects due to sensual desire;
instead, it remains motionless upon that object—such as the sign of the kasiṇa—and having approached that object, it contemplates and surveys it.
Therefore, all those states are also [included] in the sense of "contemplating closely" (upanijjhāyana).
"They are called *jhānas*": while these [factors] are thus occurring, the obstructive states (*nīvaraṇadhammā*), being their opposites, find no opportunity and are unable to obsess the mind.
They are indeed "burnt" (*jhāpita*). Therefore, they are called *jhānas* also in the sense of burning away their opposites.
Even so, because [the term] occurs in three contexts—namely, as *jhāna*, as the path (*magga*), and as full enlightenment (*sambodhi*)—...

The harmony of these mental states constitutes the effort. For it is only through the complete integration of the factors that the functions of close contemplation and so forth are accomplished by way of reaching absorption.

And because these states, although performing their own respective functions individually according to the method already described, together accomplish the single function of close contemplation—which is defined as the mind’s unwavering engagement with its object—therefore:
It should be understood that just as the designation "chariot" is established only for the collection of its parts, so too the designation "jhāna" is established only for their collection.
However, others maintain that the respective functions of those five—such as directing toward the object and so forth—are themselves individually called the function of "contemplation" (upanijjhāna);
thus, in the *Paṭṭhāna*, all these [mental factors] are treated separately when they attain the status of a jhāna-condition.
They simply establish the condition for jhāna individually. Therefore, it can be said that they are indeed individual jhānas.

And just as in the case of "fivefold virtue" or "tenfold virtue," where the five factors taken together are the cause for those virtues receiving the designations "fivefold" and so on, but not for their being virtue; for [the mere absence of] killing living beings...
Even a single factor such as abstinence (*veramaṇā*) does not constitute what is called "virtue" (*sīla*).

In the same way, here too, the fivefold aggregates and so forth are the causes for the very state of the first jhāna and so on; they cannot be understood as being the cause for the state of jhāna alone.
Otherwise, it would follow that the jhāna-factors would be the conditions for jhāna, which they are not; thus they say.

To this extent, it is established that although this consciousness is indeed accompanied by contact and the other factors, they are not included here because they lack those specific functions [of the jhāna factors].

A wholesome consciousness associated with the second jhāna—consisting of sustained application (*vicāra*), rapture (*pīti*), pleasure (*sukha*), and one-pointedness (*ekaggatā*)—is called "wholesome consciousness of the second jhāna"; the same applies to the remaining cases.

49. Here it might be asked: "By whom was this differentiation of the factors (*aṅga*) of these meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) made? It was made by way of the inclinations of individuals (*puggalajjhāsaya*).

For instance, one who, being accompanied by initial application (*vitakka*), has produced the five-factored first absorption and attained mastery therein, subsequently becomes disenchanted with initial application.
Having transcended initial application, he attains the four-factored absorption free from initial application (*avitakka*).
The underlying intention (ajjhāsayo) becomes established for the purpose of attaining that [higher state].
Then, having firmly entered that same first jhāna for the sake of making it a basis, and having emerged from it, he applies himself again to further cultivation with that very same intention;
thus, he attains the four-factored jhāna that is without applied thought (avitakka). In that case, although that cultivation is still associated with applied thought, by virtue of that intention—

Because it has been cultivated, it is called the "development of the fading away of applied thought" (*vitakkavirāga-bhāvanā*). By the power of that development, when that jhāna arises, it arises as one without applied thought (*avitakka*) and possessing four factors. This same method applies to the attainment of the remaining jhānas as well.
Thus, it should be understood how the distinction of the factors of these jhānas is made according to the inclination of the individual. And herein, regarding the successive higher jhānas...
In order for a lower jhāna to serve as the basis (*pādaka*) for the attainment of a higher one, the entry into each preceding jhāna must necessarily be intended.
It is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* that each successive lower jhāna, when mastered, becomes the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) for each successive higher jhāna.
However, when a higher jhāna arises through the power of aspiration (*ajjhāsaya*), it does not resemble its basis-jhāna (*pādakajjhāna*).

Indeed, the personal inclination (*puggalajjhāsaya*) is even more powerful than the jhāna based on the foundations (*pādakajjhāna*). Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Monks, the mental aspiration of one who is virtuous succeeds because of its purity.
And this meaning will become clear later upon reaching the supramundane consciousness (*lokuttaracitta*).
50. Here it might be asked: Why is the analysis of formations (*saṅkhārabheda*) not mentioned here? Because it was not stated in the Canon itself (*pāḷi*). And why [was it not stated]?
"As for the statement that this is not mentioned in the *Pāḷi*: it is established by the very mention of the division of the *paṭipadā* (modes of progress).

For when the state of being a pleasant mode of progress (*sukha-paṭipadā*) is established for all mundane and supramundane jhānas, the state of being unprompted (*asaṅkhārika*) is necessarily established.

And when the state of being a painful mode of progress (*dukkha-paṭipadā*) is established, their state of being prompted (*sasaṅkhārika*) is necessarily established. If one asks, "How is this known?"—it is from the observation of the *Aṭṭhakathā*.
For this has been stated in the *Aṭṭhasālinī*:

"He who, from the beginning, suppresses the defilements while experiencing pain, with effort, and with exertion, and thus suppresses them, for him there is the painful way of practice (*dukkhā paṭipadā*).
He who, suppressing the defilements, suppresses them with ease and without fatigue [for him there is the pleasant way of practice]."
"For him there is a pleasant practice" (tassa sukhā paṭipadā hoti).

Likewise, it is stated in the *Visuddhimagga* in the *Sammohavinodanī*: "And here, since in the preceding sentence it was seen as 'with pain, with exertion, and with effort' (dukkhena sasaṅkhārena sappayogena), in the subsequent sentence it is likewise seen as 'not without exertion, not without effort' (sukhe na asaṅkhārena appayogena)."

"Accompanied by volitional effort and application" means by means of the collection of conditions such as the contemplation of the danger in sensual pleasures, together with the application of volitional formations (*saṅkhārappayoga*). By this, it is stated that all jhānas belonging to the painful way of practice (*dukkhappaṭipadā*) are "accompanied by volitional effort.
"Without volitional effort and without application" means by that same collection of conditions, but devoid of the application of volitional formations.
By this, it is stated that all jhānas of the pleasant way of practice (*sukhappaṭipada*) are of the unprompted type (*asaṅkhārika*).

For even in the case of jhānas with quick direct knowledge (*khippābhiññā*), if they possess a painful way of practice (*dukkhappaṭipada*), they are understood to be of the prompted type (*sasaṅkhārika*); likewise, even in the case of jhānas with sluggish direct knowledge (*dandhābhiññā*), if they possess a pleasant way of practice, they are understood to be of the unprompted type.
If this is so, then for those paths devoid of a way of practice—namely, the path-attained (*maggasiddha*) and the birth-attained (*upapattisiddha*) jhānas—[the same principle applies].

How is the differentiation of formations established? Even for those [formations], at the time of their occurrence, there is indeed the possibility of being a path of suffering or a path of happiness, depending on whether the conditions that obstruct attainment are present or absent.

In this context, "jhāna established by the Path" refers to the jhāna established simultaneously with the acquisition of the Path for those who follow pure insight (suddhavipassanāyānika). That is twofold: established by the lower paths and—
"Accomplished through the path of Arahatship. In this regard, the jhāna of the five hundred bhikkhus mentioned in the Mahāsamaya Sutta was accomplished through the lower paths.
The jhāna of the Venerable Ānanda was accomplished through the path of Arahatship.

Furthermore, even that which arises in non-returners who are unaware [of their own state] and die suddenly after being struck by a weapon is included within the destination accomplished through the path.
Having developed the eight attainments (*aṭṭha-samāpatti*), he was reborn in a certain fine-material (*rūpi*) Brahma-world.
There, those attainments remained as they were naturally present for him. This is called "established by rebirth" (*upapatti-siddha*).

For even within a single existence, the jhānas already acquired become associated with various modes of practice (*nānā-paṭipadā*) at the time of their actual employment, depending on the conditions present.
Or, because they are devoid of the method for the arising of jhāna, their inclusion among the "unprompted" (asaṅkhārika) jhānas might be appropriate.
Furthermore, in the *Nettippakaraṇa*, the classification of all mundane and supramundane concentrations according to their prompting is demonstrated by way of their essential nature. As it is said:
"There are two kinds of concentration: prompted concentration and unprompted concentration. And in the Commentary:

It is stated that the absence of volitional effort (*asaṅkhārabhāva*) regarding the two preceding types of concentration—those with sluggish direct knowledge and those with swift direct knowledge—is the "pleasant way of practice" (*sukhappaṭipadā*), whereas the presence of volitional effort (*sasaṅkhārabhāva*) regarding the two preceding types is the "painful way of practice" (*dukkhappaṭipadā*).

Up to this point, it is established that all sublime (*mahaggata*) and supramundane (*lokuttara*) jhāna-consciousnesses are each twofold, according to their being either unprompted (*asaṅkhārika*) or prompted (*sasaṅkhārika*). Furthermore, because this...

The designation "volitional formations" (*saṅkhāra*) is common to both unwholesome states and others. However, the designation "path" (*paṭipadā*) is specifically prominent only in the case of states that are actual practices.
Furthermore, sublime and supramundane states are exclusively states of practice.
Therefore, it should be understood that their classification was stated even in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī* text by way of the "path," rather than by way of "volitional formations."
This is the exposition of the ultimate meaning (*paramatthadīpanā*) here.
51. [47] Furthermore, as for what is explained in the *Vibhāvanī*:
"Without the preliminary volitional formation (*pubbābhisaṅkhāra*) known as the preparation (*parikamma*) for any jhāna whatsoever, solely by the force of the underlying motive (*adhikāra*),..."

It is said: "Because it does not arise [spontaneously], it may be called 'unprompted' (*asaṅkhārika*). And because it does not arise merely through the influence of preliminary work (*parikamma*) without a specific occasion (*adhikāra*), it cannot be called 'prompted' (*sasaṅkhārika*). Regarding this, first of all, the statement "it cannot be called unprompted" is not tenable.
This is because of the phrase beginning with "preliminary work known as... (*parikammasaṅkhāta...*).
For the prior volitional formation known as "preparatory effort" (parikamma) is not itself called a "volitional formation" (saṅkhāra) within this specific classification of formations.

Why? Because it serves as the natural condition for the arising of jhāna. Indeed, in both the world and the Teaching, there is no wholesome or unwholesome kamma whatsoever that arises without its corresponding preparatory effort known as prior volitional formation.

"Even down to the mere giving of a mouthful of alms-food"—this refers to whatever consciousness does not arise without its own corresponding preliminary effort known as *pubba-bhisaṅkhāra*. That [effort] is included within the category of natural conditions (*pakatipaccaya*) for that consciousness.
And all mundane and supramundane jhānas, having come into being, [arise] through their own corresponding preliminary effort known as...

Since there is no such thing as a preliminary-stage development (pubbabhāga-bhāvanā) that arises without volitional effort (abhisaṅkhāra), it is included within the very category of natural conditions (pakati-paccaya-gaṇa) for those [wholesome states].
Otherwise, it would follow that no wholesome or unwholesome kamma whatsoever could be classified as "without volitional effort" (asaṅkhārika).
[48] And as for that which is therein...
It was stated that without a prior qualification (*adhikāra*), it is impossible even to say "it is prompted" (*sasaṅkhārika*) alone; however, that too is not tenable.
For there is no such thing as a mundane absorption (*lokika-jjhāna*) that does not arise without a qualification.

Rather, for one who has previously performed the work of serenity (*samatha-kamma*), the absorption with a pleasant progress (*sukha-paṭipadā*) arises; but for one who has not performed such work, the absorption with a painful progress (*dukkha-paṭipadā*) arises.

Thus it is recorded in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*). For it is said therein: "For one who has not performed the preliminary service (*adhikāra*) regarding serenity (*samatha*), the practice is painful;

for one who has performed the service, it is pleasant. Furthermore, taking into account the service accomplished in a previous existence, even the investigation into the dissolution of formations (*saṅkhārabhedavicāraṇā*) here is entirely appropriate.
Indeed, in the case of the wholesome kamma-jhānas, [the attainment] occurs solely by virtue of the presence of the requisite conditions.
"Reasoning by way of deliberation is appropriate. [49] To this extent,
even the latter alternative beginning with "Or else" (athavā) is effectively rejected.
52. Herein, for one who devotes himself to jhāna, the field prior to the arising of the sign is the field of the way (paṭipadā), and afterwards it is the field of direct knowledge (abhiññā).

Therein, for one who practices while being exhausted by the presence of opposing conditions, the development of the way is called "painful" (dukkhā); for one who is not exhausted, it is "pleasant" (sukhā). And afterwards, [if] slowly...

For one who has attained absorption (*appanā*), the superknowledge of development is called "slow superknowledge" (*dandhābhijñā*); for one who attains it quickly, it is called "swift superknowledge" (*khippābhijñā*).
In this context, jhāna that arises after a painful progress (*dukkhā paṭipadā*)—whether slowly or swiftly—is designated as "painful progress.

That which follows a pleasant progress (*sukhā paṭipadā*) is designated as "pleasant progress. Furthermore, regarding the second jhāna and those that follow, [the same applies] to the preceding jhānas.
The classification of the path according to its difficulty or ease should be understood by way of the suppression of attachment.
Furthermore, if a person— whether a householder or one gone forth— who has not performed meritorious deeds in previous lives, yet is free from obstructive states, established in wholesome practice,
with impediments severed and the mind dedicated, develops jhāna, it is said that his development of jhāna does not succeed.
"One must reach the conclusion that it does not exist. [Wholesome Jhāna] 53.
In the case of resultant jhāna, wholesome kamma that has not reached absorption is weak and pliant;
it ripens even in limited realms, in various functional states, and even in inferior personal existences. Therefore, although it is dissimilar to itself [in its own state],...
It produces a result (vipāka). Furthermore, sublime wholesome consciousness that has reached absorption is sharp and powerful;
it ripens only in the places of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) within a magnificent Brahma-existence. Therefore, it always produces a result that is exactly similar to itself.

For this very reason, he shows that even the result is in every respect identical to the wholesome state, by saying: "accompanied by applied thought, sustained thought, rapture, happiness, and one-pointedness," and so forth.
[50] Some say that because it gives its fruit in the very next existence, it produces a result exactly similar to itself; however, this is not correct.
For if that were so, even a wholesome consciousness of the seventh impulsion in the sense-sphere would produce a result identical to itself.

Furthermore, since it is only wholesome consciousness occurring in a continuum free from underlying tendencies (niranusaya) that is called "functional absorption" (kriya-jhāna), functional consciousness as well— (Note: The provided text ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.)
It shows that it is exactly like the wholesome [consciousness].

54. The summary verse beginning with "In five ways" and so forth. Therein, "by way of the distinction of jhāna" means by way of the distinction of association with the five jhānas, such as the first jhāna and the others.
Consciousness of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara) is fivefold according to the distinction of jhāna: that which belongs to the first jhāna, and so on.
The meaning is that it is fivefold, namely: pertaining to the second jhāna, the third jhāna, the fourth jhāna, and the fifth jhāna.
The construction is that this very same [kamma] becomes fifteenfold through the division into meritorious, ripening, and functional types.
However, in the *Vibhāvanī*:
"By way of the distinction of jhānas" means "by way of the distinction of association with the factors of jhāna. That is not correct.
For the distinction of jhānas is one thing, and the distinction of the factors of jhāna is another. Therein, the distinction of jhānas is such as "the first jhāna," "the second jhāna," and so forth.

The distinction of the factors of jhāna is such as "there are five factors in the first jhāna," "four in the second jhāna," and so forth. Among these, here it is the distinction of jhānas [that is intended].
This is what is intended. It is not by way of a division of jhāna factors that consciousness becomes fivefold; it is not through a division of jhāna factors that consciousness is so classified.
Rather, it is the jhāna itself that is fivefold by way of a division of its constituent factors.
And as for that which is therein...
“It is fivefold: namely, the five-factored, the four-factored, the three-factored, the two-factored, and again the two-factored”—thus it has been stated. That too is not correct;
for it is *jhāna* itself that possesses the five factors and so forth, not the consciousness (*citta*).
This is the ultimate definition of fine-material-sphere consciousness (*rūpāvacara-citta*).
55. Now, in order to explain the immaterial consciousness as it has been reached, [the author] says: "The wholesome consciousness of the base of infinite space," and so forth.
In this context, that which shines (*kāsati*) intensely (*bhuso*) is called "space" (*ākāsa*).

For although it is not perceived by way of its own form, it appears as if it were shining intensely through the light of the moon, the sun, and so on. It does not perish (*nakassati*) by cutting or breaking.
It is called "space" (*ākāsa*) because it is not scratched or marked by anything. They also say that "space" (*ākāsa*) is the same as "open space" (*ākāśa*). That space is fourfold:
unblemished space, delimited space, space revealed by the removal of the *kasiṇa*, and space as the delimitation of a mass of material form.
Here, space revealed by the removal of the *kasiṇa* is intended. For that is, as it were, unified with the infinite unblemished space; and by the yogi, it is regarded as being infinite.

It is extended; therefore, because space is infinite, it is "infinite space" (*ākāsānañca*). It is also called "infinite" because neither its limit of arising nor its limit of passing away is discerned.
That very thing is *ākāsānañca*, since it is established with the letter *ya* added for the sake of the word itself (as a suffix).
Just as the basis for the manifestation of deities is called a "deity-temple" (*devāyatana*), so too here, for one who has attained absorption (*appanā*) therein—
That very same [state] associated with jhāna is also called an "āyatana" in the sense of a basis (*adhiṭṭhāna*).
Thus, because this has the base of infinite space as its āyatana, it is the "base of infinite space" (*ākāsānañcāyatana*).

It is a collection of consciousness and mental factors. For it is said in the *Vibhaṅga*: "The states of consciousness and mental factors belonging to one who has attained the base of infinite space, or one who has been reborn there, or one who dwells in happiness in this very life."

"Wholesome consciousness occurring in the base of infinite space" is *ākāsānañcāyatanakusalacitta*. Regarding "the base of infinite consciousness" (*viññāṇañcāyatana*): here, "consciousness" refers specifically to the consciousness of the base of infinite space.

Although that [consciousness] itself has limits such as arising and so forth, it is called "infinite" because it occurs in space, which is designated as infinite. Furthermore, the word "end" (*anta*) has the sense of a "portion. Of itself—

Because it proceeds by way of a meditation having that as its object (tadārammaṇa-bhāvanā) through pervading the whole, rather than remaining in one part of the factors such as arising (uppāda), it is called "infinite" (ananta).

Furthermore, because it proceeds in space which is itself perceived as infinite, it is called "infinite"; thus, it is called "infinite" because it proceeds by way of a meditation having that as its object.
It is the mode of pervading oneself within space, which is itself perceived as infinite.
It is indeed appropriate to say that it is "infinite" by way of its basis as well. "Infinite consciousness" means the infinity of consciousness (*viññāṇānanta*).

That very same consciousness is called "the base of infinite consciousness" (*viññāṇañcāyatana*) according to the method of grammatical derivation (*niruttinaya*), because it has the base of infinite consciousness as its sphere (*āyatana*). The compound [meaning] is: "a wholesome state of consciousness occurring within the aggregate of mind and mental factors known as the base of infinite consciousness."

Regarding "the base of infinite consciousness" (*viññāṇañcāyatana*): it is stated in the *Vibhaṅga* that it refers to the mental states and mental factors of one who has attained the base of infinite consciousness, or one who has been reborn there, or one who dwells in happiness in this very life.
However, in the *Vibhāvani*, the Great Commentary, it is also stated:
"The second [base] is 'consciousness-infinity' (*viññāṇañca*) because it is to be reached or attained by means of consciousness. This does not accord with the canonical text (*pāḷi*).
"Infinite consciousness": he attends to that very consciousness as touched by knowledge, and it pervades the infinite.
Therefore it is said, "he knows infinite consciousness. By this it is understood that this consciousness is exclusively endowed with the qualification of infinity.
The reading *tameva ākāsaṃ* (that very space) also exists. Regarding "the base of nothingness" (*ākiñcaññāyatana*): here, *kiñci* means "anything" (*kiñcana*).
In meaning, it is one: it is a name for "the infinitesimal. There is nothing whatsoever—indeed, not even so much as a mere fragment—that remains of that first immaterial-sphere consciousness;
thus, it is "nothingness" (*akiñcana*). The state of being nothing is "nothingness" (*ākiñcañña*);
it is the absence of the first immaterial-sphere consciousness. For it receives that name by way of the mental attention, "There is nothing whatsoever."
“Ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ assa” and so forth is exactly as previously explained. Regarding “nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ”:

with reference to gross perception (*oḷārikasaññā*), there is no perception, thus it is “nevasaññaṃ”; with reference to subtle perception (*sukhumasaññā*), there is not a total absence of perception, thus it is “nāsaññaṃ.
It is both “nevasaññaṃ” and “nāsaññaṃ,” hence “nevasaññānāsaññaṃ,” with the long vowel in the middle.

Having formed [the compound], it refers to the aggregates of consciousness and mental factors themselves. For the practitioner, that very state is the "base" (*āyatana*) in the sense of being the foundation for specific types of bliss;
thus it is the "base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception" (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatana*). The compound means "the wholesome consciousness occurring therein.

Alternatively, because of the absence of the function of sharp perception, it is "without perception" (*nevasaññā*); yet, because it exists in a subtle state due to the remainder of formations (*saṅkhāra*), it is "not non-perception" (*nāsaññā*).

Having established that "there is no perception," it is called "neither-perception-nor-non-perception" (*nevasaññānāsaññā*); that itself is the *āyatana*, and the wholesome consciousness associated with it—this is the compound.

And herein, because from the very beginning one has abandoned the coarse factors such as the hindrances and applied thought (*vitakka*), and by the power of meditation has brought the remaining factors to an increasingly subtle state in successive stages...
Those who practice reach this attainment, which is the summit among mundane states in its subtle sense.
Therefore, here the consciousness is neither consciousness nor non-consciousness; likewise, contact is neither contact nor non-contact, and so too are feeling and the other [mental factors].
Thus, it should be understood that the mention of "perception" (*saññā*) here is merely the opening of the teaching. Regarding the resultant states...

Regarding "the base of infinite consciousness" (*viññāṇañcāyatana*): here, "consciousness" refers specifically to the wholesome consciousness of the first immaterial attainment (*pathamāruppa-kusala-viññāṇa*).
That should be understood as having occurred in the immediately preceding past existence. And "the state of nothingness" (*akiñcanabhāva*) is simply the non-existence of that very [consciousness].

Furthermore, among functional consciousnesses (*kriya-citta*), "consciousness" should be known as twofold—the wholesome and the functional—referring to the consciousness of the first immaterial attainment. And the state of nothingness...
"It is simply the non-existence of that same twofold consciousness.

In the summary verse, "by way of the classification of objects" means by way of the classification of the four objects, namely the kasiṇas and the space resulting from the removal [of the kasiṇa], which are to be taken as supports.
For here there are two sets of four objects: the set of four to be transcended and the set of four to be realized.

And the tetrad of what is to be taken as an object. Therein, in the first immaterial attainment, the kasiṇa-sign—which has become the object of the fifth jhāna of the fine-material sphere—is what is called "to be transcended.
Having removed that, the space obtained is what is called "to be taken as an object.

In the second immaterial attainment, the space which has become the object of the first immaterial attainment is what is called "to be transcended. [The object of] the consciousness of the first immaterial attainment—
It is called "to be taken as an object. In the third immaterial state, that first immaterial consciousness is called "to be transcended.
Its non-existence is called "to be taken as an object. In the fourth immaterial state, that non-existence is called "to be transcended.
And the consciousness of the third immaterial state is called "to be taken as an object. In this regard, although this immaterial mind [is the object] of the four...

Although it is fourfold by way of the objects to be transcended, nevertheless, because here only those objects to be taken as supports—namely, the base of infinite space and so forth—are grasped in their specific forms, it should be understood that its division is made manifest by way of those [objects].

The immaterial mind exists in four ways according to the classification of its objects; that same [mind] exists in twelve ways according to the classification of merit, fruition, and functional [states]. Such is the construction [of the meaning].
The Elucidation of Ultimate Reality Concerning Formless Consciousness. 57.
Now, demonstrating the supramundane consciousness as it has been attained, he says, "the consciousness of the path of stream-entry," and so forth.
In this context, a *sota* (stream) is that which flows (*savati*) or moves (*sandati*) by way of proceeding without turning back; it is like the flow of water in the Ganges and other rivers.
It flows, streams, and proceeds from its source all the way to the great ocean without turning back in between;
thus it is called a "stream" (*sota*). As it has been said: "Friend, what is the noble eightfold path?
It is as follows: right view... up to... right concentration. This, friend, is called the stream. For this [path] also, when—

It arises. From that point on, by way of pervading with its majestic power, until the attainment of the Nibbāna-element without residue, it flows, streams, and proceeds without ever turning back. As it has been said:
"Just as, monks, whatever great rivers there are—namely, the Ganges, the Yamunā, the Aciravatī, the Sarabhū..."
“Monks, all these rivers flow toward the ocean, slope toward the ocean, and incline toward the ocean.
Even so, monks, a bhikkhu who develops and cultivates the Noble Eightfold Path flows toward Nibbāna, slopes toward Nibbāna, and inclines toward Nibbāna.

In this context, non-returning should be understood by way of the non-recurrence of defilements abandoned through various paths, and by way of the progressive maturation of the faculties beginning with faith. As it has been said:

“Monks, just as an overturned jar pours out its water and does not pour it back in, even so, monks, one who develops and cultivates the Noble Eightfold Path pours out evil, unwholesome states and does not pour them back in. Thus, as it has been said:
by means of the knowledge of the path of stream-entry, those defilements that have been abandoned are not brought back again.”
"Does not follow, does not return," and so forth.
Just as ordinary worldlings (*puthujjana*) return again to the defilements even after they have been abandoned;

and just as those who possess three roots (*tihetuka*) may again fall into the state of having two roots or being rootless (*ahetuka*), whereby—even though they have been reborn in the higher realms—they are seen again in the states of woe (*apāya*); and likewise even those possessed of virtue (*sīlavantā*).
Furthermore, they may become immoral; even those who were concentrated may again become insane or deranged;
even those who were wise may again become foolish and dull-witted. But it is not so with the Noble Ones. The defilements abandoned by each respective path do not return to them.
They do not revert to the state of an ordinary person (*puthujjana*) nor to the state of a lower noble one. Gradually...
They reach the state of full maturity of the faculties, beginning with faith.

All of this is accomplished solely through the power of the Noble Path; thus, it should be understood that the name "stream-entry" (sotāpatti) is conventionally applied to that very path which is the root and source of that stream.
Reaching the beginning of that stream—that is, arriving at it—is "stream-entry. The path being realized is stream-entry.
The path of stream-entry (*sotāpattimagga*). Alternatively, because it is said that "one who has entered the stream of Dhamma is called a Noble One" (*ariya*),
all the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiyadhammā*) present within the continuum of a Noble One— whether mundane or supramundane—
are called a "stream" (*sota*) in the sense already stated, as they proceed with a non-retrogressive course toward final enlightenment and toward *nibbāna* without residue (*anupādisesa-nibbāna*).
It is called *sotāpatti* because by means of this practice one enters (*pajjanti*) and reaches (*pāpuṇanti*) that stream from the beginning.

It is the "stream-entry path" (*sotāpattimagga*) because it is both stream-entry and the path; it is an "aṅga" (limb) of stream-entry, which is designated as the first path—so it is stated in the commentary using the terms *sotāpatti-aṅga* and *magga-aṅga*.
Furthermore, "path" (*magga*) means a way or a means. It seeks out (*maggeti*) Nibbāna, or it is sought after (*maggīyati*) by those who desire Nibbāna, [and it seeks out] the defilements...
They say that it is called "magga" because one goes while destroying [defilements].
However, in the *Vibhāvanī*, it is stated:
"Sotāpatti is so called because this person (puggala) enters (pajjana) into the stream of the Noble Path from the beginning. That is not correct.
For nowhere is the term "stream-entry" (sotāpatti) seen applied to a person (puggala).
By this, the statement that "his path is the stream-entry path" is also rejected.
Consciousness associated with the stream-entry path is "stream-entry-path consciousness" (sotāpattimagga-citta).
[56] However, in the commentaries (Ṭīkās), it is stated that the path-consciousness obtained through stream-entry is "stream-entry path-consciousness. That is not correct;
for nowhere in the Canon (Pāḷi) is the word "stream-entry" seen in connection with the word "consciousness."
58. One who comes to this world once more by virtue of his character through the mode of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) is a "Once-returner" (*sakadāgāmī*).

He is one who stands at the second fruit. Because he has not yet eradicated the underlying tendency (*anusaya*) of sensual lust, and because the defilements for returning to the sense-sphere world still exist, he is so called due to the recurrence of that nature;
thus, even though he may stand above in the peak of existence (*bhavagga*), he is still naturally disposed to return again to this sense-sphere realm (*kāmadhātu*) by way of rebirth-linking.
"It happens," it is said. For this was stated in the Catukka-nipāta:
"Here, Sāriputta, for a certain person the lower fetters are not abandoned;
he, having attained and dwelling in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception in this very life, passes away while remaining unregressed."

He is reborn into the company of those gods who have reached the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Passing away from there, he is a "returner" (āgāmī) who, having come back, reaches this state of being.
But here, Sāriputta, for a certain person the lower fetters (orambhāgiya-saṃyojana) are abandoned;
he attains final knowledge in this very life... Passing away from there, he is a "non-returner" (anāgāmī) who does not come back to this state of being.
And in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, "this state of being" (*itthatta*) is explained as the existence consisting of the five aggregates of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*).
This meaning is stated by way of the course of defilements (*kilesagati*), not by way of the course of persons (*puggalagati*).
For those who have become Brahmas—namely, stream-enterers and once-returners—do not return even to the lower Brahma-world by way of rebirth-linking; how much less so to the sense-sphere?
...the world. If it is asked how this is known:

in the *Anusaya-yamaka*, after stating that for one who has passed away from the sense-sphere (*kāmadhātu*) and is reborn in the fine-material sphere (*rūpadhātu*) or the immaterial sphere (*arūpadhātu*), seven underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) underlie in some cases, five underlying tendencies underlie in some cases, and three underlying tendencies underlie in some cases—it continues with the fine-material sphere...

"It is understood from what has been stated that for one who passes away from the formless realm (*arūpadhātu*) and is reborn in the sense realm (*kāmadhātu*), seven underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) persist.
Regarding this, it is said that in the first statement, there are seven based on the case of an ordinary person (*puthujjana*);

five based on the cases of the two—stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*) and once-returners (*sakadāgāmī*); and "how many" based on the case of a non-returner (*anāgāmī*). However, in the latter statement, [it concerns] those who have become Brahmās (*brahmabhūta*), stream-enterers...

It is stated that there are only seven [types of persons] by way of the worldling (*puthujjana*) alone, because for the once-returner (*sakadāgāmī*) and non-returner (*anāgāmī*), there is no further going to the sense-sphere world (*kāmaloka*) by way of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*). And in the *Dhammahadayavibhaṅga-aṭṭhakathā*:
"Stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*) and once-returners born in the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*) do not return here again; they attain final Nibbāna right there."

And: "By these [factors], one is called a non-returner through jhāna. And: "For noble disciples reborn in the nine Brahma-worlds, there is rebirth there [in that same plane] and rebirth in a higher plane, but not rebirth in a lower plane.
For worldlings, however, there is rebirth there, rebirth in a higher plane, and also rebirth in a lower plane."
It has been stated. That non-returning was accomplished by the power of jhāna itself, with the Path as its companion; it was not by the power of the Path alone.
In this context, the meaning of the phrase "this world" (*imaṃ lokaṃ*) is explained in two ways in the commentaries: either as "this human world" or as "this sense-sphere world" (*kāmāvacara-loka*).
Regarding these, when the former meaning is taken, [the word] "comes" (*āgacchati*) refers [to coming] from the deva-world.
The meaning is "he comes. However, in the latter case, it means he comes even from the Brahma-world. In the Pāli text, however, it appears as if only the latter sense is expressed.
For this has been stated in the *Puggalapaññatti*: "One who does not come back to this state of existence is to be understood as a Non-returner (anāgāmī).
One who comes back to this state of existence is to be understood as a Stream-enterer (sotāpanna) or a Once-returner (sakadāgāmī). And here, "not coming" [is used].

"By the phrase *itthattaṃ* (this state of being), the meaning is shown as 'one who does not come back to this world of sense-sphere existence (*kāmāvacara-loka*), thus he is a non-returner (*anāgāmī*)'.

By the phrase 'having come back to this state of being' (*āgantvā itthattaṃ*), however, the meaning is shown as 'both the stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*) and the once-returner (*sakadāgāmī*) come back to this world of sense-sphere existence only once more, thus they are once-returners'. Why? Because of the two [terms] standing in the continuous sequence of the sentence: *itthattaṃ*..."
Because various meanings can arise from words. Also, in the *Kaṇṇakatthalasutta* of the *Majjhima Nikāya*, the Blessed One said:
"Great King, that Brahmā who possesses ill will—that Brahmā will come to this state of existence. But that Brahmā who is free from ill will—that Brahmā will not come to this state of existence.
In that context, by the term "possessing ill will" (*sabyāpajjho*), those who have become stream-enterers and once-returners are included along with the worldling (*puthujjana*).

The Brahmās have been seized [by these]. Because they have not abandoned the underlying tendency to aversion (*paṭighānusaya*), the malice (*byāpajjha*) consisting of mental suffering has likewise not been abandoned;

thus, they are called "full of malice" (*sabyāpajjhā*). "One who comes to this state" (*āgantā itthattaṃ*) means one whose nature is to come back again to this sensual world (*kāmaloka*) by way of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*);
the meaning of the latter sentence is the opposite of that.

This is how it should be understood. Furthermore, among those two types of once-returners (*sakadāgāmin*), it should be seen that for the former, the name "stream-enterer" (*sotāpanna*) is established first of all simply by virtue of his retaining [the stream] and by the quality of having entered the stream of the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*).

However, with respect to the destiny of individuals (*puggalagati*), there is no state of being a once-returner here, just as there is no state of being "one who returns seven times at most" (*sattakkhattuparama*) for those residing in the Brahma-world.
Those established in the first and second fruits are also reckoned as non-returners (anāgāmin) therein.

Therefore, regarding the term "once-returner" (sakadāgāmī), it should be understood that for those whose second fruit-status is established solely through the nature of desire (kāmajāti), their "returning once" to the sensual world (kāmaloka) by way of successive births from lower to higher realms is what is stated in the commentaries (aṭṭhakathā). And thus...
Having thus established [the classification], it is stated in the Pāḷi as well: "Here, the culmination for five types is reached:

for one who returns seven times at most, for a family-to-family wanderer, for a single-seed person, for a once-returner, and for one who attains Arahantship in this very life. Furthermore, that [once-returner] is of six kinds:

one who attains Parinibbāna here after reaching this [state], one who attains Parinibbāna there after reaching there, one who attains Parinibbāna there after reaching here, and one who... [reaches there].

"Having reached this [state], he attains final nibbāna here; having reached this [state] and been reborn there, he attains final nibbāna there; having reached there and been reborn here, he attains final nibbāna there.

Regarding these, "having reached this [state], he attains final nibbāna here" means one who, having attained the path of the once-returner (sakadāgāmimagga) here in the human state, attains the path of arhatship (arahattamagga) in that very same human existence and is destined for final nibbāna.

"Having reached that [state], he attains final nibbāna there" means: having reached the path of the once-returner in that deva-world, and having attained the path of arahantship in that very deva-world, he is one whose nature is to attain final nibbāna.
"Having been reborn" means: having arisen by way of taking rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi).
For those, however, for whom the phrase "this world" has the meaning of "this human world," for them that [attainment] is indeed fivefold.
It is not the sixth person who is meant.
And in the *Vibhāvanī*, it is stated: "Among the five types of once-returners, only the fifth is intended here; for he, having gone from here, returns once more to this world."
In the *Mahāparinibbāna-sutta-aṭṭhakathā* and the *Saṃyutta-nikāya-mahāvagga-aṭṭhakathā*,

it is also stated that this sixth type of person is indeed "one who has come" (*āgata*) by virtue of having returned once more. And because even all-knowing Buddhas do not [attain] the higher paths until they have reached them,
they remain as those established in the second fruit (*sakadāgāmiphala*), just like those established in the first fruit who are limited to seven more births.

They remain established in the very nature of returning. Therefore, in this context, no one who stands at the stage of the second fruit is called a "once-returner" (sakadāgāmī) in the primary sense by virtue of returning only once;
rather, all six types of persons here should be understood as being called "once-returners" in the primary sense. The path of the once-returner is the once-returning path. For that—
"Being himself a progenitor, he produces those who are to be produced as once-returners"— here,

the qualification by way of the relationship between the producer and that which is to be produced is indeed established by logical necessity, just as in the cases of "Tissa’s mother" or "Phussa’s mother.
However, in the *Vibhāvanī*:
"It does not mean that he has actually come from Sāñjaya. However, there is a specific purpose [for the designation].

It is stated with this intention: 'Although it is impossible for one possessing the path (maggasamaṅgin) to go in such a way, it is only one established in the fruit who is called a 'once-returner' (sakadāgāmin).
Nevertheless, the path that arose previously and serves as the cause for him is mentioned in order to delimit it from other paths.'"
"It is called the path of once-returning by way of its fruit; likewise for the path of non-returning. That is not tenable.
[The compound] "the consciousness associated with the path of once-returning" is a *samāsa* (compound).

59. Because the fetters belonging to the lower realm (*orambhāgiya-saṃyojana*) have been entirely eradicated, [one does not return] to this sensual world again by way of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).
"One who does not return" (*anāgāmī*) means one who does not come back [to the sense-sphere]. The meaning is that he is exclusively destined for the Brahma-world.

And this is stated solely by way of the power of this specific path. However, when higher-path insight (*vipassanā*) has arrived, he becomes even more so, being destined for the path of *arahantship* in that very same place.
This is the path of the non-returner, who stands in the third fruit.
The analysis of the compound is: "the consciousness associated with that.

(60) One who is worthy of special honor by virtue of possessing the quality of performing deeds of great fruit is an *arahant*. This refers to one who has destroyed the taints (*khīṇāsava*) and stands at the stage of the fourth fruit.
The state of an *arahant* is *arahatta*, which is the fourth fruit. Its path is the *magga*. The etymological definition is: "the consciousness associated with that [path]."
By the word "etc. (*pisa*), the text summarizes the various classifications of paths and consciousnesses as analyzed in the *Pāḷi*.
Therein, first, regarding the five sections on the first path described under the heading of "jhāna" in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*:

in the first section, the "pure mode of progress" (*suddhika-paṭipadā*), there are nine types of consciousness by way of the two methods—the fourfold and the fivefold. Likewise, for the "emptiness mode of progress" (*suññata-paṭipadā*) through pure emptiness...

In the five sections beginning with "the pure, the conceptualized, and the desireless" (*suddhika-kappanidhita-appaṇihita-paṭipadāya*), there are forty-five types of consciousness by way of ten methods.
Likewise, in the one hundred sections stated by twenty names— namely, the nineteen names such as the Path, the Foundations of Mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*),
and so forth, each having five sections— there are two hundred methods.

There are nine hundred types of consciousness. Furthermore, by applying the four predominants to the four hundred rounds as described, there are three thousand six hundred based on the eight hundred methods.
Thus, in the first path, there are four thousand five hundred types of consciousness by way of the thousand methods.
Likewise for the remaining paths; thus, in the four [paths]...
By way of four thousand methods regarding the paths, there are eighteen thousand path-consciousnesses.
However, in the *Saccavibhaṅga* and *Satipaṭṭhānavibhaṅga*, by way of twenty thousand methods, there are ninety thousand path-consciousnesses.
In the *Maggavibhaṅga*, by way of twenty-eight thousand methods, there are one hundred and twenty-six thousand path-consciousnesses.
[They] exist. In the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), only the different methods (*naya*) have been stated, not the different types of consciousness (*citta*).

As for what was stated in the *Vibhāvanī*—that the particle "pi" includes the sixty thousand-fold method found in the *Saccavibhaṅga* (Analysis of the Truths)—that should not be said here in this compendium of the wholesome (*kusalanigama*).
Thus, this method, consisting of sixty thousand divisions, is stated in the Commentary only in the section on the resultant (vipāka).

[59] Furthermore, that which was stated there— without mentioning the divisions of the path (paṭipadā) and merely classifying it as twofold, namely "void" (suññata) and "signless" (appaṇihita)— is not tenable.

For in the Pāḷi, the classification of the way of practice (*paṭipadā*) is presented right at the beginning. And there is no continuous section at the beginning that is analyzed in two ways as "void" (*suññata*) and "aimless" (*appaṇihita*).
Furthermore, regarding what is therein:
one method is "void," one is "aimless," four are distinguished ways of practice that are "void," and four are "aimless."

The statement that "it is thus analyzed tenfold by way of the name 'jhāna' with the intention that there are ten methods" is likewise untenable. For emptiness and the other [characteristics] are not what are called "methods" (*naya*) here.
Rather, among those [methods], two sets of fourfold and fivefold methods each are what are called "methods" here.
By this, everything such as the "Path," the "Foundations of Mindfulness" (*satipaṭṭhāna*), and so forth, is also rejected. [The Path-consciousness]

61. In the phrase "fruit-consciousness" (*phalacitte*), it is the eightfold path that has become the fruition (*vipākabhūta*) which bears fruit; or alternatively, it is the collection of associated states (*sampayuttadhammasamūho*).

It is the fruit attained through stream-entry (*sotāpatti*). Consciousness associated with that [fruit], or consciousness included within that [state], is called "stream-entry fruit-consciousness" (*sotāpatti-phala-citta*).
This same method applies to the second and third fruits as well. Furthermore, it is both "arahantship" (*arahatta*) and "fruit," hence "arahantship-fruit" (*arahattaphala*). By that...
"Associated" or "the mind included therein" is the etymological definition (*nirutti*).
62. In the summary verse, "by way of the distinction of the four paths" means by way of the distinction of the eightfold paths, which are of four kinds because they are to be attained four times.
But why are they to be attained four times? It is said: on the path of stream-entry...
At that stage, the faculties such as faith are still weak; therefore, he is only able to completely eradicate wrong view and doubt.
However, he is not yet able to attenuate sensual lust and ill will. In the second path, those faculties become somewhat more proficient;
therefore, he is able to attenuate sensual lust and ill will, though not yet to eradicate them.
However, he was not yet able [to abandon them]. In the third path, those faculties become more acute; therefore, he is able to completely sever sensual lust and ill will.
Yet, he is still not able to completely sever attachment to the fine-material and immaterial realms, conceit, restlessness, and ignorance.
In the fourth path, however, those faculties become most acute; therefore, he is able to [sever] all those and every other unwholesome state.
It is able to utterly eradicate [the defilements]. Thus, because their tasks are fully accomplished by arising four times, those paths are to be attained four times.
Wholesome consciousness is reckoned as fourfold according to the classification of the four paths.
Its fruition, likewise, is reckoned as fourfold because it is the fruit of that fourfold wholesome [consciousness]. Thus, the unsurpassed...
The construction is: "mind is considered eightfold. It is "unsurpassed" (anuttara) because there is nothing superior to it, nothing higher than itself.
But why is the functional consciousness (kriyacitta) not included here? Because there is no unsurpassed functional state. And why is there no such state?
Because the path-consciousness (magga-citta) lasts for only a single moment of consciousness. For if it were like mundane wholesome consciousness (lokiya-kusala), occurring over various moments—

It would proceed. In that case, having proceeded even within a mental continuum where no underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) exist, the functional [consciousness] (*kriyā*) would be called "supreme" (*uttara*).
But why does it last for only a single moment of consciousness? Because of the great power of the Path (*magga*). And how is it of great power? It is said:
For the Noble Path, upon proceeding but once, renders the defilements (*kilesa*) to be abandoned by it subject to the state of non-arising again.
Having brought it forth, one abandons it. This is its first power.

And having made the fruition [consciousness]—like a wholesome functional (kiriya) impulsion—capable of performing the function of an impulsion and fit for attainment at any time, it generates it starting from immediately after itself.
This is its second power. Therefore, even for the purpose of abandoning defilements, there is a necessity for it to arise again.
It does not exist. Likewise, there is no attainment for the purpose [of fruition]. For even if someone were to perform the preliminary work thinking, "I do not wish to attain the fruit;

I shall attain only the path previously acquired," then, by the power of the volition of the path-consciousness that had arisen once before and ceased, only the fruition-consciousness would arise, not the path-consciousness. Why? Because it cannot be resisted.
This is due to the power of the Path. For this so-called "power of the Path" is indeed impossible for anyone to obstruct by means of desire, influence, inclination, or preliminary preparation. 64.
"Only the twelve unwholesome [states]" and so forth is a classification of all four-plane consciousnesses according to their genus. Thus...
By this aforementioned method, there are twelve unwholesome [cittas]. There are exactly twenty-one wholesome ones. There are exactly thirty-six resultants.

And there are exactly twenty functional cittas—thus it is applied in the Commentary (*Ṭīkā*). However, some have joined the word "exactly" (*eva*) only to the initial and final terms, because of the subsequent increase in the numbers of wholesome and resultant [cittas].
"Fifty-four," and so forth, is a classification by way of plane. In the sense-sphere (*kāmadhātu*), they are fifty.

One may speak of the minds as being set in motion in fifty-four ways: fifteen in the realm of form (rūpa), twelve in the formless realm (arūpa), and likewise eight in the unsurpassed state (anuttara).

This is how the construction [of the verse] should be understood. Here, "unsurpassed" refers to the supramundane plane (lokuttara-bhūmi). That plane, moreover, is twofold: the conditioned plane (saṅkhata-bhūmi) and the unconditioned plane (asaṅkhata-bhūmi). The conditioned [plane] is also fourfold, as it has been said:
At whatever time one develops supramundane *jhāna* for the attainment of the first stage... [and so on]... for the attainment of the second stage... the third stage... and the fourth stage.
In this context, it is stated that "stage" (*bhūmi*) refers to the fruit of recluseship (*sāmaññaphala*).

Alternatively, it is also appropriate to take the pair consisting of the first path and its fruit as the first stage, up to the pair consisting of the fourth path and its fruit as the fourth stage. However, in terms of the actual meaning, it is liberation through the relinquishing of the threefold lust.
It is a specific state of phenomena (dhamma-visesa) associated with a particular condition (avatthā-visesa) defined as being non-included among the phenomena of the three planes.
And that [condition] becomes fourfold according to the specific abandonment of the defilements (kilesa).
Furthermore, in the *Vibhāvani*:
There is no such thing as a "supramundane plane" (lokuttarabhūmi) existing separately from the other planes.
Since the designation "plane" is applied to those [states] by way of the collection of the ninefold supramundane phenomena, what was stated— that “in some instances,

the ‘unsurpassed minds’ are mentioned as being a portion of the collection of the ninefold supramundane phenomena not included [in the mundane], just as branches and so forth are parts of a tree”— is not tenable.
The plane (bhūmi) is twofold: the plane as state (avatthā-bhūmi) and the plane as location (okāsa-bhūmi). Therein, only the plane as state is the plane in the primary sense;
the other is not. For that which is called the plane as location is established only by way of the various specific states of phenomena.
And those various specific states should be understood, according to the method explained above, as specific states such as belonging to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara), and so forth.

Furthermore, even within the thirty-one planes, the inferiority, superiority, grossness, and subtlety of wholesome and unwholesome states are established solely through specific distinctions of state known as *avasthā*. 65.
Having thus briefly indicated the consciousnesses of the four planes, he now indicates them again in detail:
He spoke the verse beginning with "Ittham" (thus). Herein, this is the construction:
Alternatively, having made the ninety-nine-fold mental consciousness into one hundred and twenty-one types in the manner already described, the wise and discerning analyze it.
However, in the commentaries (*ṭīkā*),...

They apply the first half-verse as a conclusion to the preceding verses and treat the second half-verse as an internal elaboration. How does that [explanation] not accord with the statement, "How does the eighty-nine-fold consciousness become one hundred and twenty-one?
Now, in order to show that division into one hundred and twenty-one, he asks, "How... does it become?

and then says, "Accompanied by applied thought, sustained thought, rapture, happiness, and one-pointedness," and so forth. In this context, regarding the phrase "the first-jhāna stream-entry-path-consciousness":
The path of stream-entry associated with the five-factored first jhāna is the "first-jhāna stream-entry path.
The compound [“pathamajjhānasotāpattimaggo”] means the consciousness associated with that [path].
In the commentaries (*ṭīkā*), however...
They connect [the terms] thus: "That first jhāna and that stream-entry path-consciousness. That is not correct.
For jhāna is not consciousness, nor is consciousness jhāna; for jhāna is one thing and consciousness is another.
And as for what is to be explained in the *Vibhāvanī*:
“It is called ‘the first jhāna’ because it resembles the first jhāna by way of its jhāna factors”—this has been said. But that too is not correct.
For it cannot be rightly maintained that the five-factored supramundane jhāna receives the designation ‘first jhāna’ merely in the sense of resembling the first jhāna;
rather, it is the first jhāna in the primary sense precisely because of its own possession of five factors.
"It exists. For this so-called *jhāna*, whether it be mundane (*lokiya*) or supramundane (*lokuttara*), that which possesses five factors is established as the first *jhāna* by its very nature.
That which possesses four factors, three factors, two factors, and again two factors, is established as the fifth *jhāna* by its very nature.
This applies even in the case of the supramundane state of the second *jhāna* and so forth.
It should be understood that it was stated thus because they are not established according to the order of their arising.
Furthermore, in that context,
it is for the purpose of indicating that the designation "jhāna" is established for those five-factored and other types of jhānas in the supramundane solely by virtue of their similarity.

It has been said: “Because each of the four paths resembles a particular jhāna—due to one or another of the factors such as the basis-jhāna, the jhāna of comprehension, or the inclination of the individual—they receive the designation ‘first jhāna’ and so forth through the manifestation of the factors such as initial application (vitakka), and they are thus divided individually into five types. This too is indeed appropriate.
For the paths do not receive the designation of "jhānas," such as the first jhāna and so forth; for the path is one thing and jhāna is another.

Moreover, if the term "jhāna" were applied in the sense of "close contemplation" (*upanijjhāyana*) and in the sense of "burning away the adverse" (*paccanīka-jjhāpana*), then only the supramundane jhānas would truly deserve the name "jhānas" preeminently, and not the others.
For those [mundane jhānas] merely contemplate by approaching the mere signs (*nimitta*) of the kasiṇas and so forth.
They burn away opposing states merely by suppression. However, it is only the supramundane [jhanas] that, having reached Nibbāna—which is exceedingly profound and difficult to see—contemplate it.
And they burn away opposing states by way of completely uprooting them along with their latent tendencies.
In this context, the state of possessing five factors in the jhanas of absorption (*appanā-jhāna*) is indeed their natural characteristic.

Thus, it is established that for the paths and fruits associated with the first jhāna, there is no specific function to be performed by means of a particular condition such as a "foundation-jhāna" (pādakajjhāna).
However, the state of possessing four factors (caturaṅgika) and so forth cannot be accomplished without that specific condition;
for if it were absent, every jhāna would necessarily consist of five factors. In this regard, just as in the case of mundane jhānas at the time of one's initial practice:
The development that constitutes the access stage (*upacāra*) of each respective second jhāna and so forth, although itself still associated with applied thought (*vitakka*) and the rest,

is called "development of the fading away of applied thought" because it is joined with both the knowledge that sees the danger in applied thought and the like, and with a specific underlying intention (*ajjhāsaya*) such as: "Now I shall arouse the jhāna without applied thought," or "Now I shall arouse the jhāna without sustained thought."

There is [this]. Some are called the development of dispassion toward applied thought (*vitakka*); some are called the development of dispassion toward sustained thought (*vicāra*); some are called the development of dispassion toward rapture (*pīti*); some are called the development of dispassion toward pleasure (*sukha*);

and some are called the development of dispassion toward form (*rūpa*). For those who go to the non-percipient realm (*asaññigāmin*), however, it is called the development of dispassion toward perception (*saññā*).
This [development] is capable of making one's respective *jhāna* free from applied thought, or free from sustained thought, or free from rapture, or accompanied by equanimity (*upekkhā*).

At the time when one has attained mastery over the jhānas, one enters whichever jhāna one desires by mere intention alone, even without the knowledge that perceives the dangers (ādīnava-dassana-ñāṇa). In the same way, here too, the development known as insight leading to emergence—
which serves as the access stage for each respective path— though itself associated with applied thought (vitakka) and so forth, [proceeds accordingly].

It is associated with various states of being. Some are called the development of the fading away of applied thought (*vitakka*); some are called the development of the fading away of both applied and sustained thought (*vicāra*);

some are called the development of the fading away of applied thought, sustained thought, and rapture (*pīti*); and some are called the development of the fading away of applied thought, sustained thought, rapture, and pleasure (*sukha*).

In this context, that which is able to cause the fading away of, or to transcend, applied thought is called the development of the fading away of applied thought. This same method applies to the remaining [developments] as well.
66. "That insight is joined with various attainments through the power of Kassapa"—this is said.

One tradition of the Elders (theravāda) says it is "through the power of the foundational jhāna" (*pādakajjhāna*). Another says it is "through the power of the jhāna of comprehension" (*sammasitajjhāna*).

Another says it is "through the power of the individual's inclination" (*puggalajjhāsaya*). In this regard, whichever jhāna is entered into as being proximate to the state of the foundation for that insight, that is called the "foundational jhāna."
If it is the first jhāna, insight remains as it was before. If it is the second jhāna, insight is endowed with the power of the fading away of applied thought (*vitakka*);
it is able to determine a jhāna without applied thought within the path. This same method applies to the remaining foundational jhānas (*pādakajjhāna*).
When a foundational jhāna exists, the jhāna in the path is exactly like it. This is the doctrine of the foundation (*pādakavāda*).
On the path, there is only the first jhāna. The intention is that neither the jhāna being comprehended nor the individual's inclination is able to determine a specific jhāna-factor on the path.
When the foundational jhāna exists, whichever jhāna—whether that same one or another—is comprehended, if it is the first jhāna, then insight remains as it was originally. If it is the second jhāna...
It exists. Insight is joined with the arrow of dispassion for applied thought (*vitakka*). On the path, it is able to determine a jhāna that is without applied thought (*avitakka*).
This same method applies to the remaining jhānas attained through comprehension; this is the doctrine of comprehension (*sammasitavāda*).

The intention is that because they proceed together with insight as their object, the jhānas attained through comprehension are indeed stronger than the foundational jhānas (*pādakajjhāna*) both in terms of aspiration and power.
In the *Vibhāvanī*, however, it is stated in this particular doctrine that there is no jhāna whatsoever that serves as a basis for insight (*vipassanā*). That does not accord with the *Aṭṭhakathā*.
When a foundational jhāna exists, whichever jhāna one desires—whether that [foundational one] itself or another—it succeeds in the path.

Vipassanā also reaches a state of detachment from applied thought (*vitakka*) and so forth in accordance with one's desire; thus, this is the doctrine of the individual's underlying disposition (*puggalajjhāsayavāda*).

Just as in the case of mundane jhānas, a jhāna that has recently emerged serves merely as a support for the cultivation of the access concentration (*upacāra*) of a higher jhāna, yet it is not able to make that higher jhāna identical to itself. It is only through the underlying disposition (*ajjhāsaya*) that [the higher jhāna arises].
It determines the jhāna factor. In the same way, here too, the foundational jhāna (pādakajjhāna) serves as a powerful proximate cause for the sake of making insight (vipassanā) sharp and clear.

The intention is that it is the underlying disposition (ajjhāsaya) alone which, having brought insight to a state free from applied thought (vitakkavirāga) and so forth, determines the jhāna factor within the Path.
As for the insight leading to emergence (vuṭṭhānagāminī-vipassanā) mentioned here, it is precisely this that determines the jhāna factor in the Path.
"It directs" (*niyāmeti*)—this is the position of the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*.

Even there, the meaning should be understood as follows: by the power of a particular inclination of the individual (*puggalajjhāsaya*), it is precisely insight leading to emergence (*vuṭṭhānagāminī vipassanā*) that is endowed with the specific capacity for the fading away of applied thought (*vitakkavirāga*) and so forth.
Although it appears in the *Aṭṭhasālinī* that there is no mutual contradiction among these three Theravāda positions, these views [are nonetheless] mutually...
