They proceed by having been combined. Each supramundane jhāna proceeds having been made complete individually.

Therefore, it is not possible to avoid their mutual contradiction. And herein, for those who have attained jhāna, the practice of insight (vipassanā) with the attainment of the foundational jhāna as its basis has been very well established by the Blessed One himself. For this was said in the Cūḷasuññata Sutta:
Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna.
[He enters and dwells in] the second jhāna, the third jhāna, and the fourth jhāna.
He directs his mind to internal emptiness. If his mind does not leap forward into that internal emptiness...

It does not settle down. Therefore, that bhikkhu should steady his mind right within himself upon that very same original sign of concentration (*samādhinimitta*), should settle it down, make it one-pointed, and concentrate it, and so forth.

In this context, "he attends to emptiness" refers to the work of insight (*vipassanākamma*). "Upon that very same original sign of concentration" means upon the sign of concentration consisting of the foundational jhāna. And in the *Navanipāta*:

"Monks, I say that the destruction of the taints occurs by depending on the first jhāna... [and so on] ...I say that the destruction of the taints occurs by depending on the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception jhāna," it is said.

Now, among these three statements, the one concerning the inclination of the individual (puggalajjhāsayavāda) appears to be the most powerful. For even in the case of mundane jhānas, a "foundation jhāna" (pādakajjhāna) must indeed be desired;
and that [foundation] is required for the development of the access concentration (upacārabhāvanā) for the higher jhānas, which is sharp and clear.

It exists solely for the sake of the state [of the path]. Furthermore, it is through the inclination (*ajjhāsaya*) itself that access development (*upacāra-bhāvanā*) accomplishes the state of the fading away of applied thought (*vitakkavirāga*) and so forth.
It is access development alone that determines the jhāna-factor in the higher jhānas.

In the same way, here too, it is precisely insight leading to emergence (*vuṭṭhānagāminī-vipassanā*), having attained a state of sharpness and clarity by the power of the foundational jhāna, which—through the specific power of the inclination—is endowed with the specific capacity for the fading away of applied thought and so forth.

Having offered [the oblation], one accomplishes various jhānas on the path. However, in the absence of a specific aspiration (*ajjhāsaya*), a commonality of aspiration arises in accordance with each respective foundational jhāna (*pādakajjhāna*).
Therefore, when there is no specific aspiration, the foundational jhāna itself is the measure. But when it exists, that very aspiration is the measure;
this is logical. For it is similar to entering mundane jhānas according to what is desired.
For those who have attained mastery over all jhānas, there is the production of whichever jhāna is desired within the paths.
However, whatever distinction occurs here by way of the foundational jhāna (*pādakajjhāna*) and so forth, all of that serves solely for the purpose of distinguishing insight (*vipassanā*).
This is because it is held that it is the distinction of insight alone that determines the jhāna factors within the path; thus it is stated in the *Aṭṭhasālinī* and the *Visuddhimagga*.

These were stated taking insight (vipassanā) alone as the standard. However, since that entire distinction cannot be accomplished without the foundational jhāna (pādakajjhāna), it should be understood that in the *Maggavibhaṅga*, the *Maggasaṃyutta*, and the *Aṭṭhakathā*, the foundational jhāna itself was taken as the standard when they were stated. For it is said in the Pāḷi:
"Here, householder, secluded from sensual pleasures... [as above] ...a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the first jhāna.
He reflects thus: 'This first jhāna is conditioned and volitionally produced;
and whatever is conditioned and volitionally produced is impermanent and subject to cessation.'"
Standing there, he understands and attains the destruction of the taints (*āsavā*). [He enters and dwells in] the second jhāna, the third jhāna, the fourth jhāna;

the liberation of mind through loving-kindness (*mettā cetovimutti*); the liberation of mind through compassion (*karuṇā*), the liberation of mind through sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and the liberation of mind through equanimity (*upekkhā cetovimutti*);
the base of infinite space (*ākāsānañcāyatana*)... [and so on]... the base of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatana*). He enters and dwells therein. He reflects thus: "This too..."
The attainment of the base of nothingness is conditioned and volitionally produced. And whatever is conditioned... [reaches] destruction.
Thus, in the Ekādasanipāta:
"Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, with applied thought and sustained thought..."
He enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is born of seclusion and possesses rapture and happiness.
Whatever there is therein that pertains to form, feeling, perception, volitional formations, or consciousness, he regards those phenomena as impermanent, suffering, and non-self.
Established therein, he attains the destruction of the taints. If he does not attain the destruction of the taints...

He reaches destruction [of the taints]. By that very lust for the Dhamma, by that delight in the Dhamma, through the complete destruction of the five lower fetters, he becomes one of spontaneous birth (*upapātiko*), attaining final Nibbāna there, not subject to returning from that world.
Thus it is stated in numerous Suttantas such as the Mālukyaputta Sutta and the Anupada Sutta, regarding the eight meditative attainments (*samāpatti*).
It has been stated that after emerging from each attainment, there is only the contemplation of the phenomena of the attainment just emerged;

it is not the contemplation of another jhāna. Therefore, even though practitioners may wish to contemplate another jhāna than the foundational jhāna, it can be understood that the foundational jhāna alone remains the standard.
To this extent, the doctrine of contemplation (sammasitavāda) is entirely weak.
"He becomes accomplished" means: those who, though possessing the eight attainments, produce the path without making jhāna their basis;
or those who, having made the first jhāna itself their basis, produce the path without forming a specific aspiration;

or those who, being possessors of only the first jhāna, produce the path by making that very [first jhāna] their basis; and those who, being dry-insight practitioners (*sukkha-vipassaka*), produce the path.
It should be understood that for them, the path consists of the first jhāna alone. Furthermore, as for those who by their very nature have already attained mastery over the eight attainments—
even without a proximate support (āsannapādaka)— it cannot be said that whichever jhāna they desire does not succeed for them on the paths.
66. Furthermore, in the *Vibhāvanī*:

"If, however, a person lacks such an inclination (*ajjhāsaya*), then having emerged from each successive lower jhāna and having comprehended (*sammasitvā*) the phenomena of the higher jhānas, the path produced—without regard for the foundational jhāna—is similar to the jhāna that was comprehended."
It has been stated [that] it "occurs. That must be examined.
For a jhāna consisting of mere reflection upon an object, even if it is of a higher grade, cannot possibly be stronger than a jhāna that has just emerged from the proximate state;
this is because only that which has just emerged from the proximate state is capable of specifically distinguishing the mental continuum.
For that very reason, the doctrine of "correct comprehension" (*sammasitavāda*) has been placed on the side of only some of the doctrines in all the commentaries.
[Objection: Is it not the case that the doctrine of "inclination toward a person" (*puggalajjhāsayavāda*) has likewise been placed there? [Response: True;
however, because it is consistent with the method for the arising of mundane jhānas, it is indeed more appropriate.
[67] By this, that which was stated there is as follows:
"But having emerged from each successive higher jhāna and having comprehended the factors of each successive lower jhāna, the path produced does not look back at the jhāna thus comprehended;
it is like the preliminary (pākaṭa) jhāna. For, from each successive lower jhāna..."
"The higher jhāna is more powerful"—this too is rejected.
For it is not because the higher jhāna is a "higher" state that it is more powerful; rather, it is more powerful precisely because it is the basis (pādaka). As for what is there...
The determination of feeling (vedanā-niyama) in the path is not established by way of the jhānas that serve as its basis and so forth.
Otherwise, it would follow that insight—which is associated with whatever bodily or mental feeling is present—would have to be conjoined with each specific feeling determined by those [jhānas].
With this intention, it was said: "In all cases, the determination of feeling occurs through the determination of the insight leading to emergence. That too is not tenable.
This is because the fixed association with feeling in insight meditation is established precisely through the basis of the foundational jhānas and so forth.

For instance, when one emerges from various foundational jhānas and practices insight, that insight may initially be accompanied by joy at times, or it may be accompanied by equanimity at other times. However, at the time of emerging from the path, if the foundational jhāna was a jhāna of joy...
It exists. Insight, having been exclusively accompanied by joy, is joined with the Path. For this has been said in the Saḷāyatanavibhaṅga Sutta:
"In this regard, monks, those six kinds of equanimity based on renunciation—relying upon them, depending upon them, those six kinds of equanimity based on renunciation..."
“...these joys. Abandon them! Overcome them! In this way their abandoning occurs; in this way their overcoming occurs.

And in the Commentary it is said that for four monks who have begun insight meditation by taking the first three jhānas and the pure formations as their basis among the eight attainments, the preliminary-stage insight is accompanied by joy (*somanassa*).
...or it is accompanied by equanimity. However, that which leads to emergence is accompanied by joy alone.
For the five bhikkhus who have undertaken insight meditation after making the fourth jhāna and so forth their basis, their preliminary insight is exactly like the previous [insight].
But that which leads to emergence is accompanied by equanimity alone. It is with reference to this that it was said: "Those six who abide in Nekkhamma... and so forth.
"It is said: 'Abandon them. This same method applies even when emerging from the path along with a specific underlying inclination (*ajjhāsaya*).
For at the time of powerful insight (*vipassanā*), that which is called "delight in insight" becomes truly more refined; it proceeds pervading and overflowing the entire body.
As it has been said:
"For a bhikkhu who has entered an empty dwelling, whose mind is peaceful,
there is a superhuman delight as he clearly sees the Dhamma in its true nature.
Therefore, at that time, insight is accompanied by equanimity, whether by way of a specific preliminary jhāna or by way of a specific underlying disposition.
It does not exist. It is exclusively accompanied by joy.

Furthermore, in this regard, for one who has attained mastery over all jhānas, having made any one jhāna the basis, whatever other jhāna they desire at the time of emerging from the path—whether it be that same jhāna or another—one should understand that through the power of their aspiration, there is a transformation of feeling in both insight and the path, corresponding to each respective jhāna.
It should be stated separately that "the restraint of sensation through nutriment" (*āhāra-vedanā-saṃvara*) is indeed a distinct category.

67. Regarding the summary verse, the construction is as follows: the unsurpassed eightfold consciousness is said to be fortyfold by dividing each type fivefold according to the combination of jhāna factors. Now, all the sublime and unsurpassed states of consciousness—
In order to show [the classification] by grouping it into the fivefold factors of jhāna, he says:

"And just as the fine-material-sphere [mind]," and so forth. Just as fine-material-sphere consciousness is included within the divisions of the first and subsequent jhānas—and is thus subsumed under the fivefold division of consciousness beginning with the first-jhāna consciousness—so too is supramundane consciousness included within the divisions of the first and subsequent jhānas.

Because it is associated with the fifth jhāna—characterized by equanimity and one-pointedness—the immaterial-fifth-consciousness is included within the fifth jhāna, specifically among the varieties of consciousness belonging to the fifth jhāna.

Therefore, each individual jhāna, beginning with the first, consisting of the types of jhāna-consciousness starting from the first jhāna, is of eleven kinds. At the end, however, in the final variety of consciousness belonging to the fifth jhāna...
The construction is: "Meditative absorption (jhāna) and consciousness (citta) become twenty-three-fold.
And here, by the word "jhāna," only the consciousness associated with it is meant. For meditative absorption itself does not become eleven-fold or twenty-three-fold.
As for what was stated in the *Vibhāvanī*:

It has been stated: "Because it is said that 'form-sphere consciousness is the first jhāna,' and so forth, even the formless attainment receives the designation of the fifth jhāna. This is not tenable.
For consciousness itself does not become the first jhāna, nor does it receive the designation of the fifth jhāna.
Furthermore, the other interpretation given for this verse is likewise untenable.
Because the phrase "the division of the first jhāna, etc., of the sound" is recited prior [to that].
Thus, when one part of what is to be analyzed has been analyzed, the entire ninety-eightfold consciousness, having been made into one hundred twenty-one, is said to be "analyzed.
Having thus analyzed it, he now speaks the final verse to show its summary: "Merit is thirty-sevenfold."

Thus, the resultant [consciousness] is of fifty-two kinds. Therefore, having made one hundred and twenty-one types of consciousness by totaling the eighty-nine kinds, the wise—the enlightened ones—have spoken and declared them.
When they speak, they analyze [them], for they are said to be discerning.
Thus ends the *Abhidhammattha-saṅgaha*, known as the *Paramatthadīpanī*.
The Elucidation of the Ultimate Meaning (*Paramatthadīpanī*) of the Compendium of Consciousness (*Cittasaṅgaha*) in the fourth commentary is finished.
[Now begins] the Elucidation of the Ultimate Meaning of the Compendium of Mental Factors (*Cetasikasaṅgaha*).

68. Having thus shown the inclusion of the mental factor (citta), he now speaks the first verse in order to show the inclusion of the mental concomitants (cetasika) that have not yet been mentioned, presenting both the etymological meaning and the literal meaning along with the four characteristics of association.
Therein, "arising and ceasing together, having a single object and basis" is the demonstration of the four characteristics of association.
"Yoked to the mind" (ceto-yuttā) is the demonstration of the etymological meaning. It means "joined to the mind" (cetasi-yuttā) or "belonging to the mind" (cetaso-vā).

"Associated mental factors" (*yuttā cetasikā*) is shown by way of their definition; "fifty-two phenomena" (*dvipaññāsa-dhammā*) is the statement of their specific nature; and "mental factors" (*cetasikā*) is the statement of the established term.

In this context, the "arising" (*uppāda*) of phenomena is their passing beyond the prior limit—which is the state of being future—and their manifestation in their own specific form; that is to say, "birth" (*jāti*). For all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhata-dhammā*), the state of being future comes first.
Thus they come to be. Then, having obtained the completeness of conditions, they enter into the state of the present.

Then, having ceased, they enter into the state of the past. Cessation is *nirodha*. Destruction (*bhaṅga*) is the dissolution of their own form; this is what is meant by impermanence (*aniccatā*) and death.
That which is the birth of consciousness is itself [the birth] of contact and the other factors. That which is the aging of consciousness... that which is the [aging] of consciousness.

Death is the object and the basis of the mind. By the method explained below, beginning with "that very [object] is for contact and so forth," those which have a single arising are "co-arising" (*ekuppādā*).
Those which have a single cessation are "co-ceasing" (*ekanirodhā*). Being both co-arising and co-ceasing, they are "co-arising-and-co-ceasing" (*ekuppādanirodhā*).
There is an elision of the word "eka" in the latter member of the compound. The same applies to the following cases as well. Those which have a single object are "single-objected" (*ekālambana*).

They have a single object (*ekālambana*). They have a single basis (*ekavatthuka*) because they possess one and the same physical base. Thus, being both single-object and single-basis, they are called "single-object-and-basis" (*ekālambana-vatthuka*).

Furthermore, although the object here is actually manifold even for a single moment of consciousness, it should be understood that it is spoken of as "a single object" by bringing it into a state of unity.
In the *Vibhāvani*, however, it is stated:
"Those for whom there is both arising and cessation at one [time] are 'simultaneously arisen and ceased' (*ekuppādanirodhā*). This is not correct.

For here, being "simultaneously arisen" is not intended merely by virtue of arising together at a single moment; rather, it is intended precisely according to the method already explained. Indeed, this has been stated in the *Mūlaṭīkā*:
Because the arising and so forth of material phenomena included within a single group occur simultaneously, the arising and other phases of that single group are each one and the same.
Herein, this is the application: those mental factors which are associated with consciousness arise and cease together, and have a single object and a single basis.

These fifty-two phenomena are considered mental factors (*cetasika*). Alternatively, it is appropriate here to take the abstract state as the primary meaning; thus, the ablative case is used for the qualification.

Those phenomena which are associated with the mind by virtue of having a simultaneous arising and cessation, and by virtue of having a single object and basis—those fifty-two phenomena are known and understood as "mental factors.

And herein, when it is said that those which are associated with the mind are "mental factors," this would also include the material phenomena that arise as co-nascent conditions (*sahajāta-paccaya*) of the mind.
Because they exist entirely dependent upon it, these mental factors (cetasika) would be called "associated with mind" (cetoyutta) simply by virtue of being connected to the mind.
Therefore, to exclude them [from being considered associated], it is stated: "arising and ceasing together, and having a single object and basis.
For although these arise simultaneously with the mind from moment to moment, because they belong to a different continuum, the very birth that belongs to the mind does not belong to them. This...
They do not even share the same characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*). For the material continuity (*rūpasantāna*) is one thing, and the immaterial continuity (*arūpasantāna*) is another.

Furthermore, it should be understood that the mention of "one" in relation to cessation and so forth was stated for the purpose of making it known that the mere arising of contact and the rest is not identical with the mind;
rather, their cessation, object (*ālambana*), and basis (*vatthu*) are all entirely one and the same. For it is not thus...
"It is possible to know it thus even without being told. For just as a single ox belonging to many people must still be spoken of individually as "Tissa’s ox" or "Datta’s ox," so too,
although arising and cessation are identical within a single aggregate of material and immaterial phenomena,
they are nonetheless distinguished as "the arising of contact," "the arising of feeling," and "the arising of the earth element."
In the same manner, it should be stated individually for each element, beginning with "the arising of the water element" and so forth. Therefore, in the Suttantas it is said:
"The arising of feeling is discerned; its passing away is discerned; its stability is discerned as change.
[The same applies to] perception, mental formations, and consciousness. ... It is said, "it is discerned. Likewise, monks, regarding the earth element...
Arising is stability, manifestation, and appearance. This is the arising of suffering, the stability of diseases, and the appearance of aging and death.
Monks, whatever there is of the water element; monks, whatever there is of the fire element; monks, whatever there is of the air element; monks, whatever there is of the eye...
[and so on] ...of the mind: this is the arising... [and so on] ...the appearance of aging and death.
It should be understood as "it is said. Otherwise, one would have to state that there is a multiplicity of even the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) and so forth within a single group (*kalāpa*).

For it has been stated: "That which is the life, the persistence, the stability of immaterial phenomena (*arūpadhamma*)," and likewise for the material phenomena of change (*vikārarūpa*), for all derivative material phenomena (*upādārūpa*) such as the eye and so forth, and for the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and the material phenomena derived from them. And [it is said] of the four...

It is said that the "sensitivity" (pasāda) is derived from the great elements (mahābhūta). Furthermore, bodily lightness (kāyalahutā), mental lightness (cittalahutā), and so forth, are stated by dividing them into two types for the purpose of illustrating specific meanings.
And that specific meaning will become clear further on. This is the exposition of the ultimate meaning (paramattha) here.
However, in the *Vibhāvanī*:
Without having considered the intended meaning, it was said:

"If [the term] ‘associated with mind’ (cetoyutta) is intended merely by way of arising together, then material phenomena that arise simultaneously with consciousness would also incur the status of being ‘associated with mind’; therefore, the mention of ‘ceasing together’ (ekanirodha) is included.
Even so, the consequence that the two types of intimation (viññatti), which follow upon the mind, would also be included cannot be avoided. Likewise, from a single..."
For one who conceives that "these have a single arising and a single cessation," there is the grasping of a single object (*ekālambanaggahaṇa*) regarding material phenomena (*rūpadhamma*),
which— though having arisen earlier than consciousness— cease at the moment of its dissolution.

The phrase "the grasping of a single basis" (*ekavatthukaggahaṇa*) is used for the purpose of showing that those things which possess these three characteristics are, by necessity, based on a single foundation (*niyāmato ekavatthukā*).
“Without excessive conceptual proliferation”—all of that is indeed useless. 69.
Having asked, “And how are there fifty-two?”, he first states “How? and so forth, showing the fifty-two in their actual form by dividing them into three groups.
In that context, it touches, thus it is contact (*phassa*); those associated [with it] touch.
It is called *phassa* because by means of it one touches (*phusati*) mental objects (*dhammā*). Or rather, this is simply touching itself; thus it is *phassa*.

Here, "touching" should be understood as the seizing of the object by reaching out to and contacting its desirable or undesirable flavor (*rasa*), from which feeling (*vedanā*) arises as it experiences that [flavor].
For it has been said: "With contact as condition, feeling comes to be. This [contact] has the characteristic of touching. But is this not an immaterial phenomenon (*arūpadhamma*)?
And it is not the case that immaterial phenomena, being non-reactive by nature, touch anything. This is true; however, this "touching" occurs by way of its mode of activity.
And whatever must be accomplished by those things that touch, this [contact] accomplishes that function. Therefore, it is called both "contact" (*phassa*) and "having the characteristic of touching.
What, then, does it accomplish? It brings about a transformation in consciousness corresponding to the flavor of the object.
Or it is the arising of a specific feeling. And this meaning is evident from the production of saliva and so forth in another person upon seeing someone eating sour fruit and the like.
However, in the *Vibhāvani*, it is stated:

"It should be regarded as being like the production of saliva and so forth. This being the case, this [example] might be merely an illustration; for it should be understood that what is intended here is the observation of the occurrence of contact, which is extremely well-known.
70. It is called *vedanā* because it feels (*vedayati*). It experiences the flavor of the object.

The meaning is that it either makes known the flavor of an unknown object, or makes manifest to the associated mental states or to the person possessing them that which was previously unknown. Or, beings find pleasure or pain by means of this;
thus it is *vedanā*. Or, it is simply that which is felt; thus it is *vedanā*. Furthermore, in the Pāḷi:

“Monks, it is called ‘feeling’ (vedanā) because it feels (vedayati), it makes known (vedayati). And what does it feel? It feels pleasure; it feels pain; it feels neither-pain-nor-pleasure—so it has been said. [Objection:
Are not all mental states and mental factors (citta-cetasika-dhammā) likewise characterized by the experiencing of the flavor of the object (ārammaṇa-rasa)?
Should they not also be called ‘feeling’? [Response: They are not so called, for they are occupied with other functions. They are not able to experience the flavor of the object directly.”
While performing their respective functions, [the other mental factors] experience [objects] only in a partial sense.

However, because its function is exclusively experiencing and because it possesses sovereignty through its predominance over the function of experiencing, it is *vedanā* alone that deserves to be called "feeling.
This being so, just as in the case of the enjoyment of the flavors of a king’s meal, the other factors are like the cooks, while *vedanā* alone is like the king.
"Similarity to a king has been stated.
(71) "It perceives" means *saññā*. The meaning is that it again makes a sign (*saññāṇa*) for the purpose of knowing.
For this [consciousness], by means of the sign previously grasped, even at the time of perceiving, again makes a sign precisely for the purpose of knowing. Thus, it repeatedly makes a sign.
Having arisen and attained the state of a stable perception, it establishes for sentient beings the quality of non-forgetfulness throughout their entire lifespan and even across different existences.
Furthermore, by attaining the state of a perception of wrong adherence, it renders these sentient beings incapable of being awakened even by omniscient Buddhas.
For in that way, it creates a sign (*nimitta*) for the purpose of future recognition.
They are said to be like wood-cutters; and because they form a misapprehension based on the sign as it was grasped, they are like blind men who have seen an elephant;
and because they grasp the object as it presents itself, they are like young deer [mistaking] grass-stalks for people.
Furthermore, in the Pāḷi it is said: "It perceives, it perceives, monks; therefore it is called 'perception' (saññā). And what does it perceive? It perceives blue, it perceives yellow," and so forth.
72. It is called volition (*cetanā*) because it wills. It directs associated states toward this or that object or task, and it repeatedly joins them together;
the meaning is that it acts there continuously by way of persistence.
Alternatively, it intends them. It prepares for the attainment of an object or it constructs for the accomplishment of karma.
"Āyūhati" means "it collects. The meaning is that it brings [the mental factors] together upon the object and makes them converge as one.
For it is said that its function (*rasa*) is exertion (*āyūhana*) and its manifestation (*paccupaṭṭhāna*) is arrangement (*saṃvidhāna*).

Indeed, when this [volition] proceeds by way of continuous striving and activity toward that [object], the associated factors also perform their respective functions and proceed in that very same manner toward it.
For that very reason, it is said that she (the volition) is like the chief carpenter and others, as she accomplishes both her own function and the functions of others.
However, in the *Vibhāvanī*,
after stating, "It intends, entering upon activity in the formation of conditioned phenomena," that which was stated for the purpose of establishing that meaning is as follows:
"It is because, while analyzing the aggregate of formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*) in the *Suttantabhājaniya* of the *Vibhaṅga*, it was stated:
'They are called formations (*saṅkhārā*) because they form the conditioned (*saṅkhataṃ abhisaṅkharonti*). That is not tenable.
For it is not said in the *Suttantabhājaniya* of the *Vibhaṅga* that "they are called formations because they form the conditioned. Rather, this was stated in the *Khandhasaṃyutta*.
73. "Ekagga" means that which has a single object (ekatta-ārammaṇa) as its highest part or peak (koṭi).
The state of that [object] is "one-pointedness" (ekaggatā). For an object, even if it is one, possesses various intrinsic natures (sabhāva).

Therefore, the unwavering mode of the mind—which, without falling into distraction amidst those various natures of that single object, proceeds for even a mere moment within a single nature—is one-pointedness.
This exists in that state as the cause for the occurrence of what is termed "one-pointedness" and for one-pointed cognition;
therefore, it should be understood as the stability of the mind, like the steadiness of a lamp’s flame in a windless place.
However, in the *Vibhāvanī*, it is stated:

“It has one object as its peak (*agga*), thus it is ‘one-pointed’ (*ekagga*)”; so it is said. In that context, it is appropriate that the word *agga* (peak) occurs in the sense of a portion (*koṭṭhāsa*) or a limit (*koṭi*). Some, however, say it occurs in the sense of the object (*ārammaṇa*). That is not correct;
for nowhere is the word *agga* seen used as a synonym for the object.
74. It is called *jīvita* because associated states live by means of it. *Inda* means lord (*issara*). But here, the state of being a lord—
It is called *indriya*. It exercises lordship (*issarabhāva*) over its own domain, thus it is an *indriya*. Because it is both life and an *indriya*, it is the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*).
For there is no life for you without me; therefore, as if saying, "In the function of your living, make me your lord," it proceeds by overcoming the co-nascent states (*sahajātadhamma*).
Thus, it is said that it is the dominant factor over the continuity of existence as it proceeds.

And it is said that it is like water that nourishes the lotus. In this context, the continuity of consciousness that proceeds by way of uninterrupted succession until the final Nibbāna of the aggregates is called "pavattasantati" (continuity in process).
"Ādhipateyya" means the state of being predominant. The compound means: that which has predominance within the continuity in process.
For even though the stream of consciousness has ceased again and again, it [arises] by virtue of its power.
Having come to life again and again, it continues to proceed repeatedly until the final nibbāna of the aggregates (*khandha-parinibbāna*).
For among those phenomena devoid of life and not bound by faculties (*anindriya-baddha*), there is no such specific distinction in the continuity of their occurrence. 75.
It is called *manasikāra* (attention) because it makes the object non-empty in the mind, or because it constantly inclines the mind toward the object.

Furthermore, it is threefold: that which introduces the cognitive process (*vīthipaṭipādaka*), that which introduces the impulsion (*javanapaṭipādaka*), and that which introduces the object (*ārammaṇapaṭipādaka*).

Among these, the five-door adverting consciousness (*pañcadvārāvajjana*) is called "that which introduces the cognitive process. For it introduces—that is, joins—the stream of consciousness belonging to the five doors to the object.
The mind-door adverting consciousness (*manodvārāvajjana*) is called "that which introduces the impulsion. That too introduces the stream of impulsion to the object.
Regarding the phrase "it joins": this very pair is stated there as both "wise attention" (*yoniso manasikāra*) and "unwise attention" (*ayoniso manasikāra*).

For, being supported by conditions such as natural habit, inclination, and determination, it causes the continuum of consciousness to incline toward an object either wisely or unwisely. This begins from the moment of rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhicitta*).

The continuity of consciousness (cittasantati), while it is occurring, even though it ceases after relinquishing its object, arises again toward that very same object by the power of a certain state (dhamma), provided there is no specific cause to the contrary. That [state] is called the "object-director" (ārammaṇa-paṭipādaka).
This is what is intended here. For this [state] directs the object toward the mind, or the mind toward the object; it joins them together.

For it is said that this [mindfulness] has the characteristic of recollecting (*sāraṇa-lakkhaṇa*), the function of connecting associated states with their object (*sampayuttānaṃ ārammaṇena saṃpayojana-rasa*), and should be regarded as being like a charioteer for the associated states in the sense of guiding them toward the object.

In this context, "having the characteristic of recollecting" means having the characteristic of causing the associated states—just as a charioteer does for horses—to proceed straight toward the object. Evenly...
They are called "common" (sādhāraṇā) because they are held in common. Being common to all consciousnesses, they are termed "universal mental factors" (sabbacittasādhāraṇā).
76. It is called "initial application" (vitakka) because it applies itself; the meaning is that having conceptualized in such and such a way, it mounts upon the object.
When that [consciousness] mounts upon the object, the associated states also mount upon it; at that time, that [initial application] alone directs them toward the object.
Having established that it is called "directing onto," thought (vitakka) is described as having the characteristic of directing the mind onto an object.
Here, the illustration is the climbing of the royal palace by country-dwellers through the support of a favorite of the king.

For even a thought devoid of initial application (avitakka) is said to be "thoroughly directed" by initial application because of its ascent due to the power of familiarity developed while proceeding together with initial application within a continuum of states characterized by initial application.
Furthermore, even the fivefold sense-consciousness (pañcaviññāṇa), though devoid of applied thought (avitakka), mounts [its object] by way of the impact between the physical base and the object.
And the second jhāna and those following it mount [their objects] by way of access-development (upacāra-bhāvanā). However, in the *Majjhima-aṭṭhakathā*, having asked, "What is the logic in this?
it demonstrates this point: for consciousness (citta) indeed mounts its object as well; yet, attention (manasikāra) is its constant companion.
For if that [attention] were absent, those fivefold sense-cognitions would proceed by seizing whatever object was available, like a boat driven by a helmsmanless steersman.
Thus, the fivefold sense-consciousness mounts its object solely through the power of knowing its own object, having attention as its companion.
However, when unwholesome states are reached, both the consciousness and the greed and other defilements become exceedingly powerful in mounting the object.
For it is said: "The mind delights in evil. The second jhāna consciousness and the others also ascend by way of attention, energy, and mindfulness.
However, applied thought (vitakka), having conceived the object in such and such a manner, makes the factors associated with itself more powerful in ascending upon the object.
Thus, because the other factors possess a more direct and specific functional activity in that task, this [applied thought]—
"It is called 'thought' (vitakka)"—thus it has been said. But one might ask:
Are not other immaterial phenomena (*arūpadhamma*) also of a nature that possesses an object (*sārammaṇa-sabhāva*) and thus ascend to an object? If so, why is this alone called "thought"?

The ascent of others is established only through their connection with other functions; however, for this [thought], there is no function other than this. Therefore, it alone is described in that way.

77. It is called *vicāra* because it investigates (*vicarati*). Alternatively, it is called *vicāra* because it investigates the associated mental states, or because those states investigate by means of it.

Here, "investigation" should be understood as the repeated smoothing over of that very same object, occurring for the purpose of making its specific nature and mode manifest after it has been initially grasped by *vitakka*. In this context, *vitakka* is coarse and acts as the precursor.
And because it is the initial impact of the mind upon the object, it should be regarded as like the striking of a bell.
Sustained application (vicāra) is subtle and follows after; because it is the continued following of the mind upon that very same object, it should be regarded as like the resonance of the bell.
78. Resolution (adhimokkha) is the act of resolving. It is the creeping along [of the mind] occurring in the manner: "Is it thus? Or is it not? with respect to the object.
What is meant is that the mind proceeds by way of overcoming, severing, and releasing one side.

And having done so, it is described as having the characteristic of reaching a definitive conclusion regarding the object, and as being like a city gatepost due to its immovability with respect to the object.
79. *Vīriya* is the state or the action of one who is brave (*vīra*) and skilled in action (*kamma-sūra*). For a person endowed with that [energy] is indeed brave in action.
He regards even great work as small; he regards even what is difficult as easy, and even what is heavy as light. He does not value self-mortification.
His body and mind are constantly exerted for the accomplishment of his task.
Therefore, that state of being is both the cause for that person’s proceeding in such a manner, and it is also the state of that person who is proceeding in such a manner.

It is that which has become the activity of body and mind. It is called *vīriya* because it is to be stirred up and set in motion by means of a method, a way, or a strategy, through prior volitional formations such as, "What undertaking of action will not succeed for one possessed of energy?

Alternatively, it is called *vīriya* because those who possess it move (*īranti*) or exert themselves (*kampanti*) especially for the sake of their own and others' welfare; thus, it is *vīriya*. And herein, energy is the support.
The associated states (sampayutta-dhammā), always remaining steadfast and as if holding their heads high, are constantly filled with enthusiasm for the fulfillment of their respective functions.
When they are thus disposed, the persons possessing them are also constantly engaged in body and mind for the sake of the welfare of themselves or others.
Therefore, it is said that they "move" or "tremble. Likewise...
For it has been said that this [energy] has the characteristic of supporting, the characteristic of exertion, and the characteristic of enthusiasm;
it is like a pillar supporting a house; and when rightly undertaken, it is the root of all success.
It disciplines the body and mind, refreshes them, and produces a state of joy and well-being, like a fully blossomed lotus.
It is called *pīti* because it increases (*vaḍḍheti*). Alternatively, it is called *pīti* because through it those possessed of it become radiant in body and mind like the full moon.
It is fivefold: minor *pīti*, momentary *pīti*, showering *pīti*, uplifting *pīti*, and pervading *pīti*.
81. *Chanda* is desire. It is said to be longing, aspiration, and intention. Furthermore, that is twofold: the desire of craving (*taṇhā-chanda*)...
"Desire is the wish-to-do. Here, desire is intended as the wish-to-do. In this context, one who wishes to do—that is, desires—is "one who wishes to do" (*kattukāmo*).
A person endowed with such desire is a "person possessing desire. The state of that [person] is "wish-to-do" (*kattukamyam*).
That itself is "the wish-to-do," just as the word *deva* (god) is synonymous with *devatā* (divinity). And here, the word *kattu* (to do) encompasses the meanings of all verbal roots (*dhātu*).

It has occurred. Therefore, by the term "desire to act" (*kattukamyatā*), it should be understood that all verbal forms such as "desire to speak," "desire to think," "desire to see," and "desire to hear" are included.
Furthermore, although he desires an object, he does not desire it in the manner of craving—that is, by way of relishing, passion, or attachment—but rather in whatever way he stands in need of it.
He desires things solely through the impulse of wishing to accomplish this or that purpose. Just as the king’s archers, desiring wealth or fame,
desire many arrows even when they are fit to be discarded for the sake of piercing royal enemies,
so too does this person desire to obtain objects for giving— even those unfit to be given away by another— that have not yet been obtained.
"He wishes to protect even those things already obtained. This meaning has indeed been stated in the *Vibhāvanī* as well.
For it is said there:

"Even at the time when he is engaged in the relinquishing of objects for giving, he is one who truly desires that which is to be relinquished; he is like an archer who desires to grasp arrows that have been shot."
In this context, at the moment when the preliminary volition— arising through the search for the object of giving with the thought, "I shall give a gift"—
is included within the act of giving known as the relinquishing of the object of giving, at that same moment,
the time of the occurrence of that preliminary volition should be understood here as the time of its occurrence by way of relinquishing the object of giving. By what is to be relinquished...
It should be given away by one who is fit [to give]. The intention is that he himself has need of it for the purpose of giving to another.
Regarding "the taking of arrows that have been shot": this refers to their taking by way of seeking what has not been obtained, through the act of making what has not yet been made.
In this context, however, some say that even if a hunter has already shot his arrows, if he obtains them, he indeed has need of those arrows; such is the meaning.
Thus it is not appropriate. For if that were the case, it would have been said, "having cast away the arrows.
[The phrase] "as spoken and uttered by the Tathāgata" applies here as well to the statement "it should not be answered in such a way.
Some say the meaning is this: "A marksman who casts arrows is not one who lacks a need for them; rather, being in need, he casts them while desiring some other benefit. This too is not appropriate.

If this were so, then even an archer who shoots arrows when he has need of them would be described as "exceeding" (ativutta), like the aforementioned case. However, in terms of meaning, both of these [interpretations] are indeed to be ridiculed.

And because a consciousness associated with desire (chanda-sampayutta-citta), while grasping its object, grasps it as if it were excessively desiring (ati-icchamāna) by way of desire, as if it were being overwhelmed; therefore, this—
It is said that in the grasping of an object, it is like the stretching out of the mind’s hand.
Here, the phrase "like the stretching out of the hand" should be understood as a figurative expression (abhūtaparikappa). For there is no such thing as a "hand" belonging to the mind.

However, it should be understood that even though it is not real, it was spoken of by treating it as if it were real for the sake of making the specific meaning clear. Furthermore, this so-called "metre" (chanda) has attained its full power.
He becomes more powerful than craving itself. For it is thus that he becomes its sovereign and its very foundation of psychic power (*iddhipāda*).

If he were equal in strength to craving, these beings—standing in the grip of craving and possessed by it—would never be able to escape from the suffering of the round of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*), even if they were to renounce wealth, enjoyments, sovereignty, happiness, or even the attainments of the devas and brahmās.
82. They are called *pakiṇṇa* because they are scattered (*pakiranti*) among beautiful states of mind. Why are they called *pakiṇṇaka*?

Because they are similar to others, or because they are similar to some other [states]. When they are associated with beautiful states of mind, at that time they are similar to others in being non-beautiful;
when they are associated with non-beautiful states of mind, at that time they are similar to others in being beautiful—it is said that they are alike.
The Elucidation of the Ultimate Meaning in the Section on Other Groups. 83.
Now, showing the group of unwholesome states, he says, beginning with "delusion" (*moha*). Therein, it is called delusion because one is deluded;
or, it is delusion because beings are deluded by means of it; or, delusion is merely the state of being deluded. It is like cataracts for the eye, completely obscuring the side of virtue.
It is said that by concealing [the truth], one causes blindness of the mind.
However, it should be understood that when one has fallen into the side of evil, that [blindness] becomes a course of knowledge (*ñāṇagatika*).

For this is called "wrong knowledge" (*micchāñāṇa*) in the Canon (*pāḷi*), and in the Commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) it is stated that wrong knowledge is delusion (*moha*) occurring by way of devising means for unwholesome actions. Furthermore, it is non-practice with regard to ignorance (*avijjā*).
The twofold nature is stated by way of wrong practice (*micchāpaṭipatti*). Herein, "non-practice" refers specifically to ignorance (*aññāṇa*) regarding the side of the wholesome;
"wrong practice" refers specifically to wrong knowledge (*micchāñāṇa*) regarding the side of evil. For when one has reached the side of evil, five factors fall under the category of knowledge:
delusion (*moha*), greed (*lobha*), view (*diṭṭhi*), applied thought (*vitakka*), and sustained thought (*vicāra*). By means of the mind...
However, together with shame (*hirī*), they are sixfold.

By means of these, when evil deeds arise even among those who are by nature wise and accomplished in learning and mastery of the scriptures, they bring about their skill and capability in those matters through the discernment of various means. 84.
*Ahirī* means that which does not feel shame, does not feel modesty, and does not feel disgust regarding bodily misconduct and so forth; it is the opposite of shame (*hirī*).
*Ahirī* is itself *ahirika*. For it functions by not allowing room for shame (*hirī*) when evil deeds are present, but rather by generating a liking for them.
Thus, it is described as having the characteristic of non-disgust toward bodily misconduct and so forth, and the characteristic of lack of shame.

85. *Anottappa* means "lack of dread. The meaning is that one does not fear or tremble because of bodily misconduct and so forth. Alternatively, lack of dread is the opposite of moral dread (*ottappa*).
For this [lack of dread] also proceeds by not allowing an opportunity for moral dread to arise when those [unwholesome states] are present, thereby causing the mind to remain unashamed of them.
Thus, it has the characteristic of being unashamed of bodily misconduct and so forth, and the characteristic of being without trepidation.
And it is said:
"One who is not disgusted, shameless, like a pig in foul excrement;
fearless and without moral dread, like a moth in a flame."
86. It is called *uddhacca* because it "throws up" (*uddharati*). Just as a ball that has been rolled on a stone slab and then released, the mind is scattered among various objects;
the state that serves as the condition for the occurrence of this "throwing-up" mode of the mind is *uddhacca*.
This, moreover, should be regarded as like water tossed by the wind or like a banner and a flag.
87. It is called *lobha* (greed) because it clings (*lubbhati*). It is greed because the associated states cling to it.
Or else, it is greed because it is merely the act of clinging itself. Herein, "clinging" should be understood as the sticking to an object.
Furthermore, in the sense of being stuck to an object, it is like monkey-glue; in the sense of yearning for it, it is like a piece of meat thrown onto a red-hot pan.
In the sense of being unrelinquished, craving should be regarded as like oil and collyrium;

having increased by way of its nature as a flood, it brings beings to states of misery, and thus it is to be seen as like a swift, hot river carrying all dry wood, branches, foliage, grass, and chaff into the great ocean. 88.

*Dassana* (seeing) is *diṭṭhi* (view). Just as there is knowledge and vision regarding the true essential nature of phenomena (*dhammā*), so too [there is a false view] regarding their untrue essential nature.

What is meant is "wrong view. For that [view], having arisen and become firmly established in certain people who imagine themselves wise and are full of wrong thoughts, belongs to the side of non-reality and has as its destination the knowledge of penetration.
Furthermore, it should be seen as characterized by wrong adherence and as the supreme fault.

89. *Maññati* means "to conceive" (*māna*). "I am the one person in the world"—the meaning is that he regards himself with such firm resolve, thinking, "I am not subject to contempt like a piece of wood or a firebrand.
Furthermore, he is supported by his birth, lineage, wealth, possessions, fame, and power, as well as by qualities such as virtue, learning, gain, and honor; thus, he becomes even more [exalted].
Having increased itself, it considers itself like a banner raised high in the midst of people. Therefore, it is described as having the characteristic of inflation and as being like madness. 90.
It hates, thus it is "hatred" (*dosa*). And this, in its sense of ferocity, is like a venomous snake; in its sense of spreading, it is like a lightning strike.
It should be regarded as like a forest fire in the sense of burning its own support; like an enemy who has found an opportunity in the sense of causing harm;
and like fermented urine mixed with poison in the sense of being a mass of absolute disadvantage.
91. *Issā* means "envy. The meaning is that it envies the success of others. For it [envies] the success naturally obtained by others...
Having seen or heard of [another's] success, one cannot endure it; one desires and wishes for the failure of that success.

Even upon hearing, "So-and-so will receive such-and-such," one cannot endure it; one desires and wishes for his lack of gain. Therefore, it is said that its characteristic is envy (*ussūyana*) regarding the successes of others.

92. "Let this collection of qualities or this object belong to me alone; let it not belong to another"—thus, because it proceeds and functions by way of non-expansiveness due to one's own prosperity, it is called *macchara*;
the mind proceeding in that manner is also so called. The state of being *macchara* is *macchariya*.
And this, like envy (*issā*), is twofold: [the stinginess regarding] prosperity already obtained by oneself and [the stinginess regarding] prosperity yet to be obtained.
By way of this. In that regard, first, concerning prosperity already obtained by nature:

having seen, heard, or reflected upon it being taken away by others, or released from being one's own property for any reason whatsoever so as to become the property of others, one becomes pained and dejected.
Also, regarding prosperity that ought to be obtained, [thinking] "in such a place" or "at such a time,"...
Having heard or having thought, "This shall be mine," one desires to obtain that for oneself; one does not desire the gain of others.
Having heard or having thought, "Others will obtain it," one becomes pained and dejected.
Thus, it is said that its characteristic is the concealment of one's own successes—whether already obtained or yet to be obtained. And herein:

Envy (*issā*) is the affliction of the mind that arises from hearing or thinking about someone who does not desire the gain of a prosperity they ought to obtain—whether it be "it is easily obtained" or "they will obtain it.

Stinginess (*macchariya*) is the affliction of the mind that arises from thinking about something one desires to obtain for oneself but which cannot be obtained by oneself. Indeed, these two do not arise simultaneously.
93. *Kukkucca* (remorse): Here, the action performed is what is meant. That which is done badly is *kukata*; the meaning is "a bad action.
What is intended is that it is a particular state of mental activity that is invariably censured by the wise.

In terms of its actual meaning (*attha*), however, it is simply an arising of consciousness associated with remorse (*kukkucca*) that proceeds by way of brooding: "Alas, I have not done what is good; I have done what is evil."
For even while proceeding in such a manner, he is unable to perform again a wholesome deed not previously done, nor is he able to refrain from doing again an evil deed previously committed.

Rather, it leads only to the exhaustion of the mind regarding wholesome states. Therefore, because it is merely a base action, it is called "ill-done" (*kukata*). For this has been said in the *Aṭṭhakathā*:
What is this? *Paṭisāra* is the facing toward what has been done and what has not been done, and toward what is blameworthy and what is blameless.

However, because one does not do what is evil that ought to be done, or does not do what is wholesome that ought not to be done, it is therefore called "bad" (*virūpa*) or "reprehensible" (*kucchita*) *paṭisāra*;
thus it is *vippaṭisāra*. And here, *vippaṭisāra* is simply *kukkucca* (remorse). And regarding *kukkucca*, in the sense of being reprehensible—

When that [remorse] exists, the associated state of consciousness is likewise indeed base. For the very reason that remorse is called "base," for that same reason that state of consciousness is also called "base.
Therefore, it should be understood that this state of consciousness alone is appropriately included under the term *kukata*.
However, in the commentary on the Sudinnaka-vagga, this matter is stated quite straightforwardly.
As it has been said: "Because it consists of reprehensible actions that ought not to be done by the wise, it is called *kukkucca* (remorse).
However, in the *Vibhāvanī*, failing to observe this point, it was stated: "'Kukata' means what has been done in a reprehensible way; 'kata-akata' refers to misconduct and good conduct."
That is simply not tenable. By this, all that was stated there—namely, "For they speak of even what is not done as 'badly done' (*kukata*);

'that which I did not do, that is badly done,' and furthermore, 'here, however, the arising of a state of mind consisting of remorse with respect to what has been done is 'badly done'"—all of that is likewise rejected.
Kukkucca is the state of being the cause for the occurrence of the aforementioned mental states (*cittuppāda*).
Furthermore, in the *Dhātupāṭha* lists, they indeed read the root *kuc* in the senses of contraction (*saṅkocana*) and mental distress (*vilekhana*).

Therefore, it is called *kukkuca* because it contracts or shrinks in a contemptible manner—that is, by way of loathing evil. Or alternatively, it is called *kukkuca* because it contracts or scratches [the mind] in a contemptible manner.
It is called *kukkucca* (worry) because it causes one to extract the thorn of the defilements (*kilesa-sallīkhaṇā-kāraṇā*). It is likewise a collection of states that have arisen in such a manner.
For it contracts by way of a mode of non-approval, thinking: "Alas, I have not done what is good; alas, I have done what is evil.

It does not even allow the mind to incline toward the undertaking of wholesome states. Or else, it carves away the mind. By making thin the essential qualities such as faith and the rest, [it causes remorse].
The mind makes its firmness and strength exhausted in the undertaking of wholesome states; therefore it is called "worry" (*kukkucca*).
Because it is associated with a state that causes one to behave in such a manner, it is termed "worry," taking it to be the state of being worried.
Furthermore, because it functions by way of subsequent remorse concerning what was previously not done that is good, and what was done that is evil—
It also proceeds by way of remorse. Therefore, it is said that its characteristic is subsequent regret and its function is the brooding over what has been done and what has been left undone.

In this context, "characteristic of subsequent regret" means that because one has failed to perform wholesome deeds and has instead performed unwholesome deeds in the past, its characteristic is regret at a later time. By this, it is shown that remorse has exclusively the past as its object.
It is established. And the state of having present or future objects is excluded. Regarding the phrase "its function is not grieving over what has been done and what has not been done":
here, one should conquer both the evil that has been done and the good that has not been done.
For this is said in the *Mahāniddesa*: "In two ways remorse arises: from what has been done and from what has not been done. And how in two ways... [omitted] ...and from what has not been done."
"Bad conduct of body was not practiced by me; good conduct of body was practiced"—thus remorse arises. "Good conduct of speech was not practiced by me...
[and so on] ...bad conduct of mind was practiced"—thus remorse arises. "Abstention from taking life was not practiced by me; taking life was practiced"—thus remorse arises.
... [and so on] ... "Right view was not practiced by me; wrong view was practiced"—thus remorse arises.

By this, however, the twofold nature of remorse is established: on account of the state of not having performed good conduct and on account of the state of having performed evil conduct. For it is said, "in two ways.

And that [remorse] occurs in those who, having previously committed evil, are subsequently terrified by the fear of the states of misery (apāya), as well as in those who, having fallen into the states of misery, recollect the actions they themselves previously performed.
It exists. For it is said: "I have not performed good bodily conduct for others; rather, I have performed misconduct of body.
Just as conceit (*māna*) is twofold—conceit that is according to reality (*yāthāvamāna*) and conceit that is not according to reality (*ayāthāvamāna*)—so too remorse (*kukkucca*) is twofold:
remorse that is according to reality and remorse that is not according to reality. Among these, even the remorse that is not according to reality, when arising, does so in two ways...
"Alas, I have not done what is good; alas, I have done what is evil. But what is that?

It is that which arises subsequently through the mode of remorse, having previously—while regarding wholesome action as evil and holding an evil view—not performed it, and while regarding unwholesome action as wholesome and holding a wholesome view—performed it;
and also that which arises subsequently [through remorse] after having previously performed wholesome action while regarding it as wholesome.
Perceiving evil as evil, one who has not committed it later perceives it as good; this is called remorse that is not according to reality (*ayāthāva-kukkucca*).
This should also be applied in such ways as: perceiving what is blameless as blameworthy, what is permissible as impermissible, and what is non-offense as an offense.
And all of this arises in two ways when it arises; therefore, it is included within those two alone.
It should be understood thus. Furthermore, in the *Mahāniddesa* itself, it is explained that "scrupulousness regarding the hands is scrupulousness;
scrupulousness regarding the feet is scrupulousness; scrupulousness regarding both hands and feet is scrupulousness. This is called the scrupulousness of one who is unrestrained.
However, there is also that which appears in the Vinaya: "The monks, being scrupulous, did not accept [the gift]," and as for what that statement...
It is stated that through being overcome by remorse (*kukkucca*), one falls into the perception of what is allowable as unallowable and the perception of what is unallowable as allowable;
this is called "remorse regarding the discipline" (*vinaya-kukkucca*). That, moreover, is simply a doubt concerning the discipline.

And that is a wholesome arising of consciousness proceeding in the manner of wavering, thinking, "Is this allowable for me or not? within a domain that is not one's own. Now, as for those in whom it arises:
Among them, those who desire to train do not perform that action; with reference to them, it is said, "being anxious, they did not accept.
However, those who indeed do perform it incur an offense even regarding a permissible object.
With reference to them, it is said, "one incurs an offense because of being overcome by anxiety."
94. It is called *thīna* because it makes the mind sluggish and then overwhelms it. For it is defined in the Piṭaka as "sluggishness" (*thiyiyanā*) or "the state of being sluggish" (*thiyitatta*).
95. It is called *middha* because it oppresses the mental factors by making them unworkable.
For when the associated states are proceeding by supporting this or that posture through the expansion [of consciousness] toward the object, [this factor] acts upon them.
Just as if one were striking with a pestle, *thīna* (sloth) overcomes the mind by causing it to shrink away from its object and rendering it incapable even of maintaining its posture.
*Middha* (torpor), however, is a mental factor (*cetasika*).

Regarding the term *vicikicchā*: here, *cikicchā* means "investigation" (*cikicchana*), which signifies a resistance to knowledge (*ñāṇappaṭikkūla*). It is so called because it cannot be cured (*tikicchituṃ*).
It is called *vicikicchā* because it is a state of medical treatment (*cikicchā*) that has departed due to its difficulty;

or, it is *vicikicchā* because by means of it, those investigating the true nature [of things] suffer (*kicchati*) or are exhausted (*kilamanti*); or, it is *vicikicchā* because it proceeds with a state of double-mindedness (*dveḷhaka*).
It is twofold: as an *nīvaraṇa* (hindrance) and as a *paṭirūpaka* (counterfeit). Therein, that which proceeds by way of doubt regarding the eight objects beginning with the Buddha—

They are [hindrances]. Furthermore, all forms of doubt (*vicikicchā*) that arise among those who are not omniscient—consisting of the state of being perplexed regarding various objects of experience, thinking "How is this? "What is it like? or "Is it this?"—are called "counterfeits.

That [doubt], moreover, may be wholesome, unwholesome, or even the functional-inefficient (*kriyābyākatā*) that arises in those whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*). However, in this context, it refers specifically to that which is exclusively unwholesome.
The hindrances and doubt are indeed the obstacles. This concludes the *Paramatthadīpanā* (Exposition of Ultimate Meaning) on the heap of unwholesome states. 97.
It is called *saddhā* because one has faith (*saddahati*). Just as clear, serene, and still water reflects the signs of forms such as the moon, the sun, and so forth...
It burns well within oneself. Thus, the meaning is that this [faith] burns, maintains, and establishes the qualities of the Buddha and so forth well within oneself.
Or, it is called *saddhā* because one has faith (*saddahati*) by means of it; or, it is *saddhā* because it is the mere act of believing itself.
Furthermore, that [faith] intended here is precisely that which occurs as a state of non-turbidity toward objects of faith such as the Buddha; other than that, it is not.
Faith that functions by way of conviction toward such unreliable objects as non-Buddhist teachers (*titthiya*) or the doctrines of non-Buddhists is called "counterfeit faith" (*paṭirūpaka-saddhā*).
In its actual meaning, however, it is simply wrong resolve (*micchā-adhimokkha*).
Just as people, when they lack hands, are unable to grasp jewels even upon seeing them; or when they lack wealth, [are unable to acquire them] for those [jewels].
All enjoyments do not come to fruition. When there is no seed, crops and the like do not come to fruition. Likewise, when there is no faith, the bases for meritorious action do not come to fruition.
Therefore, it is said that this [faith] is like wealth in hand and a seed. 98. It is called *sati* because it remembers (*sarati*).
By way of non-negligence, it remembers the wholesome deeds one has done or ought to do, or the qualities of the Buddha and so forth.
The meaning is "it approaches. That mindfulness (sati) is also twofold: right mindfulness (sammāsati) and wrong mindfulness (micchāsati). Of these, right mindfulness is what is intended here.

The other, however, is not even true mindfulness; it is merely a semblance of mindfulness, a manifestation of unwholesome mental states that occurs through the non-neglect of evil deeds already done or yet to be done.
For this [wrong mindfulness] also [clouds] the mind with all unwholesome phenomena.
It is able to guard [the mind] and to yoke it to wholesome states (*kusaladhamma*). Therefore, it should be regarded as like the king’s chief minister in charge of all affairs.
For it has been said: "Monks, mindfulness, indeed, I declare to be beneficial in every respect.
99. *Hiriyati* means *hiri*. The meaning is that one feels shame, disgust, and aversion toward bodily misconduct and so forth.

100. *Ottappa* is that by which one feels shame (*ottappati*). The meaning is "one is afraid" (*ubbijjati*). Here too, there are those who possess a counterfeit form of moral shame (*hiri*) and moral dread (*ottappa*);
for it is said: "They feel no shame regarding what is shameful, yet they feel shame regarding what is not shameful;
They do not fear what is to be feared, yet they see fear in what is not fearful."

However, because true persons (sappurisa), having generated a sense of shame (*hirī*) toward themselves and a sense of dread (*ottappa*) toward others—such as protective deities and so forth—avoid evil and maintain themselves in purity, these two are called the "world-guarding qualities" (*lokapāladhamma*).

101. Non-greed (*alobha*) is the opposite of greed (*lobha*). For, regarding those objects designated as beneficial to oneself where greed occurs by way of attachment, non-greed dispels that very greed;
it views the success of existence and enjoyments—which serve as the basis for greed—as if they were a heap of excrement.
Having despised and loathed [them], it proceeds by becoming the single element of non-desire (*ekānekkhammadhātu*). 102.
Non-hatred (*adosa*) is the opposite of hatred (*dosa*). For that too, regarding those objects perceived as harmful to oneself, proceeds by way of hating;
yet, having dispelled that very hatred toward those beings seen or unseen, it is a heart full of gentleness (*sommahadaya*), like the full moon.

Having arisen, it proceeds as a single state called the element of non-ill-will (*abyāpādadhātu*). This very state is what is called "loving-kindness" (*mettā*) among the divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*).
Non-delusion (*amoha*) should also be mentioned here. Non-delusion is the opposite of delusion (*moha*).
For that too, having dispelled the delusion regarding those phenomena, objects, or the four noble truths in which delusion proceeds by creating darkness—[it proceeds].
"Even as if causing a thousand moons and suns to rise, it proceeds under the name of 'knowledge' (vijjā).
103. Regarding "equanimity" (tatramajjhattatā): here, "self" (atta) refers to intrinsic nature (sabhāva).

That which has its self proceeding in the middle between the two opposing sides of dullness (līna) and agitation (uddhacca) is "neutral" (majjhatta). The collection of associated states (dhammasamūha) that proceeds with evenness is [the state of] equanimity. Of that...
The state [of mind] is "equanimity" (*majjhattatā*). Equanimity appearing amidst those various associated mental states is "specific neutrality" (*tatramajjhattatā*);
or, specific neutrality is the equanimity of the mind and mental factors toward those various beneficial tasks. For it is thus:
by way of looking on with indifference at the associated states that proceed in balance, it is like a charioteer looking on at well-trained horses proceeding in balance.

It is said that equanimity (*upekkhā*) should be regarded as being like a charioteer who maintains a balanced watchfulness. This very same quality is what is called "equanimity" among the divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*).

104. Regarding the terms "tranquility of body" (*kāyappassaddhi*) and so forth: "body" (*kāya*) refers to the collection of mental factors (*cetasika*), namely the triad of aggregates beginning with feeling (*vedanā*).
"Mind" (*citta*) refers to the beautiful mind (*sobhaṇacitta*). "Tranquility of body" is the tranquility of the body; "tranquility of mind" is the tranquility of the mind—and so on.
This is a compound. *Passaddhi* means calming; the meaning is the state of being peaceful and cool.
Those for whom these two are weak do not concentrate their mental happiness upon meritorious deeds;
rather, their minds leap outward, like a fish placed on a heated stone surface. However, those for whom they are strong, only they [remain] therein.
They find that; their mind becomes like a fish cast into cool water.
105. Lightness is *lahutā*. The meaning is the state of being weightless and unsluggish.
For those whose [minds] are weak in this regard, their mind does not extend toward meritorious deeds but shrinks back; it becomes like a lotus flower cast upon a red-hot stone.
But for those in whom it is strong, their mind extends toward that [object]; it is like a lotus flower cast into cool water. 106.
*Mudubhāva* (the state of being soft) is *mudutā*. For those in whom this is weak, their mind is stiff regarding meritorious deeds;
it is like a great warrior who has gone into the midst of his enemies. But for those in whom it is strong, their mind is soft toward that [object].
It is like a great warrior who has gone into the midst of his enemies. 107.
*Kammañña* means "workable" or "fit for action. That itself is *kammaññatā*.
For those whose [minds] are weak in this respect, it is not possible to place their minds upon meritorious deeds as desired; they scatter, like chaff or dust thrown against the wind.
[It] exists. However, for those in whom [it] is strong, they alone are able to establish it there as they wish;
it does not waver. It is like a mass of gold cast against a headwind. 108.
The state of being proficient (*paguṇa*) is proficiency (*pāguñña*); that itself is proficiency (*pāguññatā*). For those in whom this is weak, their mind...
It wavers and is distressed regarding meritorious deeds; it is like a monkey cast into deep water.
However, those whose [merit] is strong do not waver or become distressed therein; they are like a crocodile cast into deep water.
109. *Uju* means straight; the state of being straight is *ujukatā*. The minds of those for whom this is weak [waver] regarding meritorious deeds.
It becomes irregularly apprehended. At times it is sluggish; at times it is over-exerted; at times it is depressed; at times it is elated.
It is like the progress along a road by one intoxicated by liquor and spirits. However, for those in whom [the factors] are strong, it should be understood as the opposite of what has been described.
110. And here, although mental serenity and so forth are established and have already been mentioned, the separate mention of bodily serenity and so forth is made.

It should be understood that by way of these [qualities], the serenity and so forth of the material body (*rūpakāya*) are also intended to be illustrated. In this regard, after hearing various discourses (*suttanta*), the state of serenity of the material body is evident during such occasions as recovering from illness;
the lightness [of the body] is evident in the supernormal powers (*iddhi*) of those possessing such powers, such as traveling through the air;
and the pliancy [of the body] is evident in the acts of creating emanations by making the body small or large.
It should be understood that when one makes oneself unimpeded while moving about inside the earth or within a mountain, the state of being workable (kammaññabhāva) is evident;
likewise, when one assumes the form of a nāga or a garuḷa and performs such acts as creation, the state of proficiency (paguṇabhāva) is evident;

and in all those cases where the state of long-term persistence occurs according to the manner in which they were fashioned, the state of rectitude (ujukabhāva) is evident. They bear it equally, thus they are common (sādhāraṇā).
"By all beautiful minds" means those beautiful [states] common to them, or "beautiful-common. 111.
Regarding "right speech" (*sammāvācā*), there is a threefold discourse on right speech by way of verbal expression, volition, and abstinence.

Among these, well-spoken words associated with the meaning and the Dhamma are called "right speech as verbal expression. The wholesome volitional consciousness that originates such [speech] is called "right speech as volition" (*cetanā-sammāvācā*).

However, when one undertakes or resolves upon the training precepts such as abstaining from false speech, the mental activity that occurs in the mode of refraining from evil by not transgressing the object encountered—this is *virati*, known as right speech (*sammāvācā*). That is what is intended here.

It is called "right speech" because they speak rightly by means of it. And here, the word "by means of this" (*etāya*) is used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*) and the sense of the cause (*hetu*).

Or, it should be understood as expressing the instrument (karaṇa). In that context, for one who undertakes the training rules (sikkhāpada) by means of speech, the sense of the instrument and the sense of the cause are appropriate with reference to the words of undertaking.

Therefore, those who wander about speaking only blameless words—thinking, "I shall well protect the training rules just as they have been undertaken or just as they have been resolved upon"—[these words]... [are the ones referred to].
Taking this into account, it is only the meaning that is conducive to the function of the instrument (*karaṇa*) which is appropriate here as the cause (*hetu*).
Alternatively, whether they speak in such a way or not, when there are those who do speak, this [right speech] allows them to speak correctly.

Because one does not wish for them to speak incorrectly, it is called "right speech" (*sammā-vācā*). Furthermore, by way of abandoning verbal misconduct, this [right speech] functions as the purification of the door of speech (*vacī-dvāra-suddhi*).
"Thus one speaks rightly" is what is called right speech (*sammāvācā*).
112. Right action (*sammākammanta*) is also threefold, by way of activity (*kriyā*), volition (*cetanā*), and abstinence (*virati*).
In this context, the bodily activity of one performing any blameless action is called the "action-path of activity. The volition that originates that [activity] is the "action-path of volition."

Now, as for right action (*sammākammanta*): it is the mental activity in the mode of abstaining from evil, occurring either when one has undertaken the training rules (*sikkhāpada*) such as refraining from taking life, or when one is resolved upon them, or when one does not transgress the object encountered. This is called "abstinence" (*virati*).
It is "right action" because by means of this they act rightly; that very thing is "right action" (*sammākamma*), and that itself is "right action" (*sammākammanta*) according to the Sutta.
*Vanantoviya*. The rest here is exactly as previously stated. 113.
Right livelihood (*sammā-ājīva*) is also twofold, by way of energy (*vīriya*) and abstinence (*virati*).

Among these, for those who maintain their lives by performing naturally blameless activities such as farming or the practice of alms-gathering, the effort consisting of the power of exertion is called right livelihood as energy (*vīriya-sammā-ājīva*).

However, that mental activity which occurs in the mode of abstaining from evil by those who abandon bodily and verbal misconduct—the causes of their own failure in livelihood and virtue—out of regard for purity of livelihood, is called "abstinence" (*virati*). This is what is intended here as "livelihood.
It is "right livelihood" (*sammā-ājīva*) because by means of it they live rightly, that is, they conduct their lives. The rest here is exactly as explained in the method already stated.
114. Furthermore, abstinence (*virati*) here is threefold: by way of abstinence through encountering, abstinence through undertaking, and abstinence through eradication.

Among these, that abstinence which arises for those who do not transgress an object encountered solely through the power of moral shame (*hiri*) and dread of blame (*ottappa*), whether they have not yet undertaken the training rules (*sikkhāpada*) or even though they have undertaken them, disregarding them—this is called "abstinence through encountering."
That [abstinence] has only the present as its object; for it is said that the five training rules have the present as their object.

However, that which arises in one who is undertaking or resolving upon the training rules, or who thinks, "I shall well guard them just as they were undertaken or resolved upon," or who does not transgress a situation encountered—this is called abstinence by undertaking (*samādāna-virati*).
Furthermore, that [abstention] has either the present as its object or the future as its object.
