For it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* (Commentary) that the five training precepts have the present as their object because they are described by way of abstention from what has been encountered.

At the moment of the Path, however, that which arises through the complete cutting off of the conditions for all misconduct is called "abstention by cutting off" (*samuccheda-virati*). That, moreover, has Nibbāna alone as its object.
The abstinence of fruition (*phalavirati*) is also included right here.

In this regard, it should be understood that mundane abstentions, taking such factors as the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) as their object, abandon the objects to be abstained from, such as killing living beings;
whereas supramundane abstentions, taking Nibbāna as their object, abandon those very same objects to be abstained from.
115. It is called *karuṇā* because it causes heart-weariness (*hadayakheda*) in those who are compassionate when there is suffering in others.

Alternatively, it is *karuṇā* because it scatters (*kirati*) the suffering of others, or because it removes (*vikkhipati*) the suffering of others, or because it destroys (*kiṇāti*) the suffering of others.

Or else, it is *karuṇā* because it extends (*pasārīyati*) toward those who are suffering. Furthermore, *kali-uṇā* means cutting off (*chedo*). *Kali* refers to suffering, as in the expression "born in the *kali*-age."
"Kali" is also called "evil" (*pāpa*) and "defeat" (*parājaya*). For it is said: "In evil, there is kali and defeat.
All of this—whether it be suffering, evil, or defeat from every success—is the very cause of compassion for those who are compassionate.

Thus, because compassionate people protect beings from "kali"—meaning suffering or evil—or from defeat relative to all prosperity, or because they protect beings from being scattered by that [kali], it is called *karuṇā*.
116. They rejoice upon seeing the prosperity of others; thus they are called *muditā* (altruistic joy). There is no measure (*pamāṇa*) for these [beings];
thus they are *appamāṇā* (immeasurable), meaning sentient beings (*sattā*). They exist toward the immeasurable; thus they are *appamaññā* (the immeasurables).

These [mental states] should be practiced only toward so many beings, and not toward others beyond them—since there is no such limitation or measure, even when they are directed toward only a single being, they are nevertheless called "immeasurables" (*appamaññā*).

[77] However, in the commentaries (*ṭīkā*), it is stated: "They are called 'immeasurables' (*appamāṇa*) because they have immeasurable beings as their object; therefore, they are called 'immeasurables' (*appamaññā*). This is not correct. 117. Regarding the "faculty of wisdom" (*paññindriya*): this is simply non-delusion (*amoha*) mentioned below.

For that is called the "faculty of wisdom" because it is "wisdom" (*paññā*) in the sense of understanding (*pajānana*) and a "faculty" (*indriya*) in the sense of being predominant (*adhipati*). Thus it is called the faculty of wisdom.
*Paramatthadīpanī*: An Elucidation of the Ultimate Meaning in the Beautiful Collection. 118. "To this extent," etc., is the summary of the three collections.

Having thus shown the nature of the fifty-two [mental factors], he now states "of these" and so forth, showing the classification of those associated with consciousness (*cetasika*). Following this demonstration of the nature of the mental factors...

The construction is as follows: "the respective association (*sampayoga*) of those mental factors (*cetasika*) that are inseparable from the mind—that is, not dissociated from the mind—with the arising of consciousness (*cittuppāda*) is called 'conformity' (*tathāyoga*).
"In the arising of consciousness" (*cittuppādesu*) means simply "in consciousnesses. They are called "arisings" (*uppāda*) because mental factors arise within them;

thus, by taking "consciousnesses" themselves as the "arisings," they are termed "arising of consciousnesses" (*cittuppāda*). This is because the two sets of fivefold sense-consciousnesses are extremely weak.

Among those, six miscellaneous factors do not arise. Because they have been abandoned by the power of cultivation (*bhāvanābala*), applied thought (*vitakka*) does not arise in the second jhāna and above;
sustained thought (*vicāra*) does not arise in the third jhāna and above; and zest (*pīti*) does not arise in the fourth jhāna and above.

Because its nature is that of decisive resolution (*sanniṭṭhāna*), resolve (*adhimokkha*) does not arise in a mind whose nature is indecisive (*asanniṭṭhāna*), such as doubt (*vicikicchā*). Energy (*vīriya*) [does not arise] because it is the leader of the powers...

It does not arise in the sixteen types of weak consciousness, such as the five-door adverting consciousness. Joy (pīti) does not arise in those accompanied by grief or equanimity, because its intrinsic nature is that of endearment.
Desire (chanda) does not arise in the rootless (ahetuka) states devoid of longing, nor in the utterly deluded consciousnesses (momūha-citta), because its intrinsic nature is that of longing.
Therefore it is said: "But applied thought (vitakka) [arises] in the miscellaneous [types of consciousness], namely, in all consciousnesses except for the utterly deluded ones."
The connection is that those mental arisings, when excluding the miscellaneous factors, are "with miscellaneous factors. 119. Regarding "among the unwholesome":

this refers to the unwholesome mental concomitants (*cetasika*). It is called "common to all unwholesome states. Therefore, the construction is that they are found in all twelve types of unwholesome consciousnesses.
In the *Vibhāvanī*, however...
The intention was that the latter [term] is a qualification for the former;
however, that is not correct. For this section has as its primary purpose the demonstration of the presence [of these factors] within the types of consciousness.
Nevertheless, all unwholesome states of consciousness do not arise without these four; indeed, they do not arise in those who stand having seen the danger in evil.
Nor do they arise in those who are weary of the world out of shame or fear, nor in those who are concentrated in wholesome states (*kusala-dhamma*).

Therefore, they are found in all those [other] instances. Furthermore, because views and conceit proceed by grasping at the aggregates in various ways without relinquishing the gratification (*assāda*) found therein, they arise only in consciousness rooted in greed (*lobha-mūla-citta*). In this regard:
When those aggregates arise, however, view proceeds by firmly grasping at them as a self and then misapprehending that self through such false modes as permanence and so forth.
Pride, on the other hand, proceeds by firmly grasping at the aggregates as "I" and then touching upon that grasped mode through such [false] modes as superiority and so forth.
Therefore, they differ in their manner of touching, and thus their ways of proceeding are dissimilar.

He said, "They exist. Regarding the four views (*diṭṭhi*) among the dissociated states (*vippayutta*): those who hold wrong views (*diṭṭhigatika*) grasp the self exactly as it has been apprehended by their view, thinking "I am this.
Even for them, their view and conceit (*māna*), having reached the mode of contact, function in a dissimilar manner.
For there is no activity on the part of the view in the exalting of the self, as there is in the case of conceit. Nor does the view...

[It is] the conceptualization of a partiality toward phenomena that is not in accordance with reality, as it were, for conceit (*māna*). For this very reason, the conceit consisting in the grasping of "I" (*ahaṃ-gāha*) occurs even in non-returners (*anāgāmin*);
however, the view (*diṭṭhi*) consisting in the grasping of a self (*atta-gāha*) belongs only to worldlings (*puthujjana*).
In the *Vibhāvanī*, however—

Having stated, "Conceit (*māna*) also does not arise in the same moment of consciousness as views (*diṭṭhi*), because it arises in a manner similar to views due to its occurrence by way of the conceit 'I am' (*aham-māna*)," the lion with the mane establishes that point through an illustration.
That is not correct; for similarity of occurrence is indeed a cause for simultaneous occurrence.

However, envy (*macchariya*), although originated by greed that clings to one's own acquisitions, occurs in an absolutely [distinct] manner by way of intolerance toward their being shared with others.
It is said that [the mind] is indeed associated with aversion; this refers to hatred (*dosa*). Regarding "in the minds":

since dullness-and-drowsiness (*thinamiddha*), which has the characteristic of unwieldiness, cannot occur in the five types of unprompted (*asaṅkhārika*) consciousness whose nature is wieldiness, it is said that "dullness-and-drowsiness occurs in the five prompted (*sasaṅkhārika*) minds.
Four [mental factors] are common to all wholesome states. Three are greed, views, and conceit. Four are hatred and the others.
The pair consists of sloth and torpor (*thina-middha*). Regarding the phrase "doubt in the mind," the word *ca* (and) is used for emphasis; the meaning is "only in the mind associated with doubt.
Thus, there are fourteen unwholesome mental factors (*akusala-cetasika*). 120.

Regarding the phrase "in the beautiful [states]," this refers to the beautiful mental factors. In the supramundane Eightfold Path, within the three aggregates, it is included in the aggregate of wisdom (*paññā-khandha*).

Right intention (*sammāsaṅkappo*) is indeed nothing other than the final stage of right view. Therefore, even when that [intention] is absent due to the absence of the foundational jhāna and so forth, the aggregate of wisdom (*paññākkhandha*) does not diminish.
However, among the phenomena of the aggregates of virtue (*sīla*) and concentration (*samādhi*), one does not perform the function of the other.
For this reason, it is said that the supramundane path (*lokuttara-magga*) does not proceed below the level of the seven factors; but as for the abstinences (*viratiyo*)...
"Even the three [factors] are obtained. The construction is: "They are definitely obtained all at once in every respect.
In this context, "definitely" means they are not obtained only occasionally, as is the case with mundane things; rather, they are obtained as being definite at all times. Why?
Because supramundane states always proceed by way of the complete fulfillment of moral conduct (*sīla*). For they are not...
Like worldly states, they sometimes occur by way of giving, sometimes by way of hearing and mastery of the scriptures, and sometimes by way of the development of the kasiṇas and so forth.
"Together" means that, unlike worldly states, they are not found separately; rather, all three are found together as one. Why?
Because their object is non-distinct. For they do not, like worldly states, have objects consisting of things that must be transgressed.
The life-faculty and the others arise by taking various objects as their basis. However, they arise by taking only a single object, Nibbāna.
"In every respect" means that they are not obtained through the partial abandonment found in mundane states;
rather, all three are obtained by way of the complete abandonment of misconduct and wrong livelihood. In mundane states, right speech, once arisen, [abandons] the fourfold...
One is not able to abandon all verbal misconduct at once. Abstinence from false speech is able to abandon only false speech, and not the others.

Even that false speech one is not able to abandon together with its root and its underlying tendency (*anusaya*). Likewise, abstinence from malicious speech is able to abandon only malicious speech, and not the others.
Even that malicious speech [one is not able to abandon] together with its root and its underlying tendency...

He is unable to abandon them. All this should be expanded in detail. However, in the supramundane [paths], right speech, having arisen once, abandons all verbal misconduct together with its roots and underlying tendencies.
Right action, having arisen once, abandons all bodily misconduct together with its roots and underlying tendencies. Right livelihood, having arisen once, abandons all...

One abandons bodily and verbal misconduct together with its roots and underlying tendencies for the sake of right livelihood. Thus, all three [factors] are found in every respect only in the supramundane.
The prefix *vi-* has the sense of a collective whole (*avayava-saṃpiṇḍana*). A single instance of right speech that has arisen once is also found by way of the abandoning of false speech;
and it is not found only by way of that abandonment, but also by way of the abandoning of malicious speech.

Everything should be stated as "it is obtained. Regarding the phrase "here the misconducts are with their roots and with their underlying tendencies (*sānusaya*)," the various types of defilements belonging to the classes of bodily and verbal misconduct—such as the underlying tendency to sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*) and so forth—which are to be abandoned by the higher paths, exist even for those in training (*sekkha*) regarding the formless realm (*arūpa*).

However, there is no need to mention them for those in training regarding the sense-sphere (*kāma*) and the fine-material realm (*rūpa*). Therefore, by way of abandoning these [defilements], the higher path...
The abandoning of misconduct should be understood as occurring in the wholesome states of the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara-kusala*) alone;
the intention is that it does not occur in the resultant or functional consciousnesses of the sense sphere, nor in the sublime consciousnesses (*mahaggata-citta*).

Even among the wholesome states of the sense sphere, it occurs only in those arisen on the sense-sphere plane (*kāmadhātu*), not in those arisen on the fine-material or immaterial planes. For the bodily and verbal misconduct reckoned as the objects from which Brahmās must abstain do not exist there.
They exist. However, worldly abstinences (*virati*) do not occur in relation to persons who lack the objects from which one must abstain.
Furthermore, it is said that they do not occur even among the gods of the six sense-sphere heavens (*kāmāvacara*) above; this has already been examined in the *Kathāvatthu*.
If that is so, it would follow that these [abstinences] also do not occur in the human world for those established in the three lower fruits. For even in their case—
"There are indeed things from which one must abstain, such as the taking of life and so forth. This is true;
however, here the seven classes of offenses (*āpatti-kkhandha*) also stand in the place of things from which one must abstain. Likewise, there are the three bases of hypocrisy (*kuhana-vatthu*).
Some of these are even common to the results of those [offenses]. And for human beings, whatever [actions] have been undertaken by this or that person...

The bases for the training rules (*sikkhāpada*) are indeed the very bases from which one must abstain. Those defilements (*kilesa-jāta*) which cause the agitation of body and speech for those training in the sensual realm (*kāma-sekkha*), and which serve as the bases for the abstinences consisting in total eradication (*samuccheda-virati*), are likewise the bases for their respective abstinences consisting in partial abandonment (*tadaṅga-virati*).
"They may occasionally be seen" means precisely at the time when they occur through one or another of the abstinences perfected by undertaking (*samādāna-sampatta-virati*).
They appear together. Although they appear together in this way, because their objects are distinct, they do not appear as one;
thus it is said, "separately, separately. Even while appearing separately, they appear only by way of abandoning each respective type of misconduct.
It should be understood that this is not like the supramundane [paths], where they appear in every respect.
121. Since it is stated in the *Vibhaṅga* that the sublime states (*appamaññā*) attained in absorption (*appanā*) are exclusively accompanied by joy (*somanassa*), it is said:

"in sublime consciousnesses excluding the fifth jhāna. Because these [sublime states] involve intense activity toward other beings, they do not occur together with the fifth-jhāna equanimity, which is exceedingly subtle and devoid of activity. This refers to those [sublime states] that exist in the preliminary stage (*pubbabhāga*) prior to absorption.
However, it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* that even equanimous feeling (*upekkhā-vedanā*) is indeed admitted as being associated with those [mental states] in the case of "sensual-sphere...
consciousnesses" (*kāmāvacara... cittesu*). "Sometimes" (*kadāci*) means at the time of seeing the misfortune or success of others by one whose nature is compassionate and who is free from envy.
"They arise not being different" (*nānāhutvā jāyanti*) means that at the time of seeing their misfortune, it is precisely compassion (*karuṇā*) that arises by way of sympathy.
*namuditā*. However, at the time of seeing success, it arises specifically as joy (*muditā*) through the act of rejoicing, and not as compassion (*karuṇā*);

such is the meaning of their arising individually. Furthermore, because these are stated in the Suttantas to be the escape from cruelty and discontent that arise from hatred, and because they are precisely mental happiness (*somanassa*) which is the opposite of mental grief (*domanassa*), therefore—
Since some maintain that even those [jhānas] which precede absorption are always associated with joy (*somanassa*), it is said:
"In the case of those accompanied by equanimity (*upekkhā-sahagate*). Regarding the phrase "some say": that doctrine of theirs contradicts even the *Aṭṭhakathā*.
Therefore, because many wise people do not accept that view, the Elder designated that position as the "view of some" (*keci-vāda*).
Furthermore, because the preliminary stage (pubbabhāga-bhāvanā) of all mundane and supramundane jhānas occurs only at the time close to absorption (appanā),

the preliminaries of the jhānas accompanied by joy (somanassa) are themselves accompanied by joy, while the preliminaries of the jhānas accompanied by equanimity (upekkhā) are accompanied by equanimity.
However, when not in close proximity [to absorption], the preliminaries of all of them may sometimes be accompanied by joy.
Sometimes they are accompanied by equanimity (*upekkhā*). Therefore, that doctrine is appropriate only as a partial doctrine.

Furthermore, in this context, all states of mind consisting of the development of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*) would, for the most part, be accompanied by equanimity from the very beginning;
for if they were associated with joy (*somanassa*) from the outset, then these beings [would not experience] those [states] born of joy.
Thinking that "there is no lack of delight in [other] tasks," one should abandon other work and devote oneself exclusively to the task of meditation.
However, it is only at the time when one perceives the specific progress of one's own meditation—both prior and subsequent—that mental joy arises simultaneously with it.

Furthermore, this occurs in the case of the mind engaged in the meditation on foulness (*asubha*) regarding repulsive objects, and in the case of the mind engaged in the meditation on compassion (*karuṇā*) regarding suffering beings.
There is nothing at all that needs to be said [against this]. Furthermore, these two—compassion (*karuṇā*) and appreciative joy (*muditā*)—arise even during ordinary times.
Among them, since appreciative joy has desirable success as its object, it is logical that it is generally conascent with mental joy (*somanassa*).
Compassion, however, has undesirable failure as its object; therefore, it should generally be conascent with equanimity (*upekkhā*). And these...
Because it involves excessive mental activity directed toward other beings, it can be said that [the mind] is indeed incompatible with the feeling of equanimity (*upekkhā-vedanā*).

For that [state], having not yet reached absorption (*appanā*), is called "equanimity of feeling" precisely because it is devoid of activity in the mere experiencing of the flavor of the object, and not in regard to other functions.
Thus, beings even take what is not given with minds accompanied by equanimity, and they also give gifts.
"Teeth, and other such things, also perform great meritorious and demeritorious kamma.
Therefore, it is appropriate to state that for those very states which have attained absorption (appanā), there is a state of opposition with equanimity regarding feeling (vedanupekkhā).
Thus far, as stated in the *Vibhāvanī*:

At the time of developing compassion and gladness, prior to the access stage (*appanā-vīthi*), the preliminary work (*parikamma*) may also be performed with consciousness accompanied by equanimity, by virtue of prior familiarity.
This is just as one who is reciting a well-mastered text might occasionally recite it according to another method;
or as one who is comprehending formations through well-practiced insight might, at times, do so by means of consciousness dissociated from knowledge through the power of that familiarity.

Regarding the statement, "Comprehension (sammasana) is the doctrine that compassion and gladness are impossible among sense-sphere states accompanied by equanimity," this should be understood as having been refuted.
Even though objects such as the kasiṇa-signs are indeed not profound, nevertheless, through the power of the practice of yoga—

"Because of the power of mental concentration (*cittasamādhāna*) and because the defilements (*kilesa*) have been distanced, knowledge (*ñāṇa*) proceeds with absolute certainty toward the jhāna-minds that take those [objects] as their support;

thus he said, 'In all five... minds'. (122) "The three factors of abstinence (*virati*), the pair of the two immeasurables (*appamaññā*), and likewise the beautiful mental concomitants (*sobhana-cetasika*) occur only in the beautiful [states]."

The construction is: "they are associated with the minds in four ways, by four modes. Now, in order to show the distinction between the fixed and non-fixed associations for all those things associated with consciousness (*ceto-yutta*), he says "envy" (*issa*) and so forth.
That which has compassion (*karuṇā*) as its beginning is "compassion-and-the-rest" (*karuṇādi*).
There are two kinds of immeasurables (*appamaññā*). Envy, avarice, worry, the abstinences (*virati*), and compassion and the rest—these are "envy-avarice-worry-abstinence-compassion-and-the-rest."
They arise separately and they also arise together. Pride arises only at certain times; likewise, sloth and torpor arise only at certain times.
However, when they do arise, they arise together with one another. The construction is "not separately.
Here, the separate or occasional conjunction of the immeasurables (appamaññā) and the abstinences (virati) has been stated below and will be stated above. And as for envy and the rest...
He will explain this later. However, conceit (*māna*), restlessness (*thina*), and torpor (*middha*) must be discussed here.

Among these, although conceit is found in the four types of consciousness dissociated from views (*diṭṭhi-vippayutta*), it is found only at the time when they occur in such forms as "I am better than them," and not otherwise.
Although restlessness and torpor are found in the five types of prompted consciousness (*sasaṅkhārika*), they are found only occasionally, by way of their having become sleep.
It is obtained only at the time of its occurrence through unwieldiness (akammaññatā), and not at other times. Furthermore, when it is obtained then, the pair is obtained together, not separately.
However, in the *Vibhāvanī*:

The interpretation stated—that “torpor and drowsiness sometimes arise together with envy, avarice, worry, and conceit, and sometimes they arise separately from those”—is not to be accepted as authoritative.

For its co-existence and separate occurrence with them are not established by way of the opposition or non-opposition between their functions and objects. And as for that which [is stated] in the Commentary...

Conceit (*māna*) and sloth-and-torpor (*thinamiddha*) are never produced separately; the reason has already been stated, and the application (*yojanā*) has also been stated. That [application] too is not elegant. Regarding the phrase "sometimes they arise together":

according to the manner stated in the passage beginning with "the seven are applicable everywhere," the remaining forty-one factors—namely, the rest of the eleven indeterminate factors (*aniyata-yogī*)—are, by that same aforementioned method, associated with themselves...
The construction is: "It should be understood that [these] apply to those types of consciousness that are currently arising for one who is not fixed in their practice.

(123) Having thus shown the method of association by way of delimiting the points of application for mental factors, he now says, "And the inclusion," etc., showing the method of inclusion by way of delimiting the groups of associated states. Now...
The construction is: "I shall explain their inclusion as appropriate. The verse beginning with "Thirty-six," etc., is the summary verse for the method of inclusion.
It is stated that the four immeasurables (*appamaññā*) do not obtain among the objects consisting of the seven conceptualizations (*paññatti*) or Nibbāna;

thus, they are excluded from the immeasurables. Likewise, among the eight types of second-jhāna consciousness, the twelve mental factors common to others—excluding initial application (*vitakka*)—are excluded from the immeasurables.

By means of the word *tathā* (thus), he indicates the method [of enumeration] beginning with: "Thirty-five factors are included, namely the twenty-three beautiful mental factors (*sobhaṇacetasika*) and so forth.

*Teevā* (those very same): those same thirty-three factors, excluding initial application (*vitakka*), sustained application (*vicāra*), zest (*pīti*), and pleasure (*sukha*), when accompanied by equanimity (*upekkhā*).

*Aṭṭhasu* (in eight): here, the expression "eight and eight and eight" is to be understood as a collective singular designation (*ekasesaniddesa*), or alternatively, as a designation involving the elision of repetition (*vicchālopaniddesa*).
"By way of the fivefold jhāna" means by way of the classification of jhāna stated in the Pāḷi according to the fivefold method;
the intention is that, however, when considered by way of the classification of jhāna stated according to the fourfold method, there is a fourfold inclusion.

Between two persons who have attained the first jhāna of the fine-material sphere and are arising the second jhāna, the one with duller applied thought (vitakka) is able to transcend it. For him, [the second jhāna] consists of four factors.
The second jhāna arises. However, one of sharp wisdom is able to transcend both initial application (*vitakka*) and sustained application (*vicāra*) together;
for him, the three-factored second jhāna arises. This is the distinction between these two methods. 124.
Because they are incompatible with their respective functions and objects, the abstinences do not arise in the sublime states; thus it is said, "excluding the triad of abstinences."

For abstinences have the function of purifying bodily and vocal actions, whereas sublime jhānas have the function of purifying the mind through the already well-purified application of body and speech.
Furthermore, abstinences proceed by taking as their object either the things to be transgressed or Nibbāna;
sublime jhānas, however, take as their object either a concept (paññatti) or sublime states.
125. It has been stated that because their functions and objects are mutually opposed, abstinences (*virati*) and the immeasurables (*appamaññā*) cannot both exist within a single consciousness.

Regarding the statement "the immeasurables and abstinences should be combined here," it is said that they are "excluding the abstinences" because abstinences—having as their sole function the abandonment of immorality (*dussilya*)—cannot occur in those mundane indeterminate states (*abyākata*) that lack the function of abandoning such immorality.
For it is stated in the Pāḷi that "the five training precepts (sikkhāpada) are exclusively wholesome.

This, however, should be understood as referring to mundane (lokiya) training precepts. Since the illimitables (appamaññā) have beings and concepts as their objects, and since the great resultants (mahāvipāka) have exclusively limited (paritta) objects, there is no occurrence of those [illimitables] within them;
thus it is said, "excluding the illimitables and the abstinences (virati)."
[Objection: "But surely, since the object consisting of a conceptual designation (paññatti) such as 'seven' is also skilled regarding desire, its result must also have an object similar to it.

[Reply: No, because it is devoid of conceptualization (vikappa). For conceptual designations, being non-existent, and sublime or supramundane states, being subtle and delicate phenomena, are grasped by those performing wholesome and other types of deeds only after they have been conceptually constructed or penetrated in such and such a manner.
Thus they become objects [of consciousness]. However, because the results of sense-sphere kamma (*kāmavipāka*) are themselves exceedingly weak, they are unable to conceptualize or grasp an object;

how much less can they penetrate it? Therefore, it should be understood that these [results] are incapable of taking as their objective support either concepts (*paññatti*) or sublime and supramundane states (*mahaggata-anuttara-dhamma*).
As for the results of sublime kamma (*mahaggata-vipāka*), even though they are devoid of conceptualization, they are [the result of] kamma that has reached absorption (*appanā*).
Because they have arisen together, these specific designations, fashioned by the power of meditation, are able to take [those objects] as their support.
However, in the *Vibhāvani*,

it is stated that because they are produced by karma under the sway of craving for sense-pleasures (*kāmataṇhā*), they are the results of sense-pleasures (*kāmavipāka*) and are indeed sense-sphere phenomena (*kāmadhamma*) that serve as the objects of craving for sense-pleasures.
With the intention that they "are able to take hold [of an object]," it is stated: "Because they are the fruit dependent upon craving for sense-pleasures (kāmataṇhā).
Then, by means of the simile of the slave-girl’s son, he clarifies this point. That must be examined.
For if that were so, even the sublime resultant states would be produced solely by karma dependent upon craving for the fine-material and immaterial realms; thus, those too—
One might think that only sublime phenomena (*mahaggata-dhammā*), which serve as the objects for craving for form and the formless, could be the focal point (*ālambana*).

However, craving for sense-pleasures (*kāmatanha*) also takes only sense-sphere phenomena (*kāmā-dhammā*) as its object; there is no such thing as taking a conceptually designated phenomenon (*paññatti-dhamma*) as its object.

Furthermore, it is not the case that craving which proceeds by way of enjoyment toward designations such as "woman" or "man," or toward [designations] such as hands and feet, is not called craving for sense-pleasures (*kāmatanha*); indeed, it is. Regarding "beautiful" (*subha*):

"Wholesome" (*kusale*). "In the mind" (*mane*) is the locative case used for selection (*niddhāraṇe*). "In beautiful action" (*subhe kriye*) should be understood as the object of selection (*niddhāraṇīya*).

"With cause" (*sahetu*), etc., should be connected by stating that they are included in twelve ways within the mind. "Excluded here" (*vajjitānaṃ saṅgaho*) means those which do not exist here; "here" refers to the beautiful consciousnesses.
"The pair" (*dvayaṃ*) refers to the dyad of abstinences and the dyad of the immeasurables. "In the supramundane" (*anuttare*) is the inclusion of the distinguished [states].

The "jhāna factors" (jhāna-dhammā) are initial application (vitakka) and so forth. In the middling [states], there are the sublime states (mahaggata) and the illimitables (appamaññā), as well as the jhāna factors.

In the limited (paritta) states that beautify the sense-sphere (kāma), the illimitables, the abstinences (virati), knowledge (ñāṇa), and rapture (pīti) are the distinguishing factors; the meaning is that they act as differentiators within the method of inclusion (saṅgaha).
126. The seventeen factors, together with greed (lobha) and views (diṭṭhi), become nineteen and thus enter into inclusion.

The construction (*yojanā*): The twelve mental factors common to other [unwholesome states]—excluding joy—and the four universal unwholesome factors, making sixteen dhammas, together with greed and wrong view, become eighteen and are thus included [in the classification].

As for the statement "envy, avarice, and worry are distinct by way of function and object," these are to be applied [to the respective types of consciousness]. In all instances of unwholesome consciousness-arising...
Associated states (*sampayuttadhammā*) are indeed dissimilar in terms of their intrinsic nature (*dhammata*). However, in terms of number, some are similar to others;
thus it is said there are twelve. Regarding the phrase "they become included":
here, among the five types of spontaneous (*asaṅkhārika*) consciousness, there are nineteen in the first and second, eighteen in the third and fourth, and twenty in the fifth. Among the five...

In the first and second [types of] volitional states (*sasaṅkhārika*), there are twenty-one [factors]. In the third and fourth, twenty. In the fifth, twenty-two. In the two types of deluded states (*momūha*), fifteen.
Thus, there are seven groupings among the unwholesome states. Therefore, he said "nineteen," and so forth. "Common" (*sādhāraṇā*) means common to all wholesome states.
"Shared" (*samānā*) means shared with others. "Others" refers to certain factors, excluding desire (*chanda*), joy (*pīti*), and resolve (*adhimokkha*).
127. *Hasanacitte*: in a mind characterized by laughter. *Voṭṭhabbane*: in the mind-door adverting consciousness. *Sukhasantīraṇe*:
in the investigating consciousness accompanied by joy. *Manodhātuttikāhetukapaṭisandhiyugale*:

in the dyad consisting of the triple mind-element—namely, the five-door adverting consciousness and the two types of receiving consciousness—and the double rootless investigating consciousness accompanied by equanimity.

And in the pair of rebirth-linking [consciousnesses]. In all cases, seven [mental factors] occur with all rootless (ahetuka) consciousnesses; the remaining miscellaneous ones, however, are joined as appropriate.
Thus, the compendium of thirty-three types has been stated by me—this is the construction [of the sentence]. 128.
Now, since this is the "Exposition of Mental Factors" (cetasika-niddesa), the ground and origin of even a single mental factor are [to be explained] just like those of consciousness.
In order to show that the classification [of mental factors] must be explained according to the distinctions of association and so forth, he recites the final verse.

The construction is as follows: "Having thus, in the manner already described, understood the sixteenfold association and the thirty-threefold inclusion of the mental factors dissociated from consciousness, one should point out their respective classifications in accordance with the mind. First, regarding contact (*phassa*):
The meaning is: because they are associated with eighty-nine or one hundred and twenty-one types of consciousness, they are said to be "of eighty-nine kinds" or "of one hundred and twenty-one kinds";
thus, having separately enumerated the fifty-two mental factors (cetasika), one should explain their classification according to their respective planes, classes, associations, and so forth.
Thus ends the Elucidation of Ultimate Meaning (*Paramatthadīpanā*) on the Compendium of Mental Factors (*Cetasikasaṅgaha*),
within the Fourth Commentary on the *Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha* entitled the Elucidation of Ultimate Meaning (*Paramatthadīpanī*).
*Pakiṇṇakasaṅgaha-paramatthadīpanī*, 129.
Having thus shown the exposition of consciousness and mental factors individually, he now says "associated as appropriate," etc., in order to show the exposition of both together once more.
Associated as appropriate, they are thirty-three by way of their intrinsic nature.

Regarding those states of consciousness and mental factors that have been individually pointed out by me: now follows the application [of the text] which demonstrates how the inclusion (*saṅgaha*) of these two is established.
In this context, "own-nature" (*sabhāva*) means the individual essence of each; it is said to be the unique characteristic (*āvenikalakkhaṇa*) of phenomena.
First, consciousness (*citta*), although it is of eighty-nine kinds when divided according to plane, class, association, and so forth, is itself...
By way of its specific characteristic of cognizing an object, it is one alone.

Although contact (phassa) is of eighty-nine types according to the distinctions of plane, class, and association, it is one alone by way of its characteristic of touching; likewise for feeling (vedanā), perception (saññā), and the rest.
Thus, by way of their intrinsic nature (sabhāva), they amount to exactly thirty-five. [The consciousness] proceeds by way of cause, function, door, object, and basis.
"Compendium" (*saṅgaha*) means "connection" (*sambandha*). Therein, "by way of the cause of feeling" (*vedanāhetuto*) means by way of the distinction of the causes for the various types of feeling.
The same applies here to the phrases "by way of function, door, object, and basis. "Only by way of the arising of consciousness" (*cittuppādavaseneva*) connects with "is determined" (*niyyateti*);
by the word "only" (*eva*), it excludes the mental factors (*cetasika*). Up to this point, the Elder has provided the literal meaning of the six miscellaneous compendia right here.

The inclusion of consciousness and mental factors by way of the classification of feeling is the "Inclusion of Feeling" (*vedanā-saṅgaha*); the inclusion of consciousness and mental factors by way of the classification of roots is the "Inclusion of Roots" (*hetu-saṅgaha*), and so forth.
However, in the *Vibhāvani*:

Having included mental concomitants (cetasika-dhammas) under the term "arising of consciousness" (cittuppāda), and seeing no other [category] to exclude, he says, "Nowhere is it without that [mental concomitant]. This is indeed not tenable.

For here, there is not even a single summary-grouping of mental concomitants brought forward by way of such statements as "so many mental concomitants are accompanied by pleasure," "so many are accompanied by pain," and so forth.
Rather, it is stated by way of such [specific instances] as "the wholesome-resultant body-consciousness alone is accompanied by pleasure."

"But it is led away by the mind alone. Since the mind being established implies that the mental concomitants (*cetasika*) are also established, it should be understood that this was stated as "by way of the arising of consciousness" (*cittuppādavasena*) alone. 130.

*Tattha* means among those six groupings (*saṅgaha*). The grouping of feeling is the grouping of the mind and mental concomitants associated with it, according to the classification of feeling (*vedanābhedena*).
In the *Vibhāvani*, however, it is stated:
"The compendium of feeling is the compendium by way of the classification of pleasant and other feelings, as well as the mental states arising together with them.
Therein, by the word "and" (*ca*), it is indicated that this includes both the compendium of feeling and the compendium of the mental states arising together with feeling. In this [context]:
He shows that in the phrase "there is the inclusion of feeling" (*vedanā-saṅgaho*), there is a description by way of "one-remainder" (*ekasesa-niddesa*).
That is not correct. For here, the classification of feelings is stated solely for the purpose of determining the supporting factors (*nissaya-dhamma*) of this inclusion;
it is not for the purpose of showing a separate inclusion of feelings. Why, then, was it said there that "feeling is threefold"? Is it not [stated] in the *Saṃyutta Nikāya*?
It is true that two, three, five, six, eight, eighteen, thirty-six, and even one hundred and eight types of feeling have been taught.
Nevertheless, by way of its characteristic of experiencing, feeling is indeed only threefold.
For whatever beings experience any object whatsoever, they experience it either as pleasant, or as unpleasant, or as neutral; there is no other mode besides these.
"It does not exist. However, other classifications have been stated by various methods.
Among those, two are stated in terms of the bodily and the mental. As it is said: "And what, monks, are the two feelings? Bodily feeling and mental feeling.
Or [they are stated] in terms of pleasure and pain, having included equanimity within pleasure. As it is said: "Two feelings were taught by the Blessed One: pleasant feeling and painful feeling."
"Venerable sir, this feeling which is neither painful nor pleasant was spoken of by the Blessed One as being included within the peaceful and sublime pleasure.

However, it is stated in the *Vibhāvanī* that two [types of equanimity] are mentioned, having grouped together the blameless side of equanimity under "pleasure" and the blameworthy side under "pain. Although this is not found in the canonical text (*pāḷi*), it is indeed appropriate.

There are five by way of the division of faculties (*indriya*). There are six by way of the division of contact (*phassa*). There are eighteen by way of the division of mental explorations (*upavicāra*).
There are six based on the household life and six based on renunciation; thus, by way of the twelve types of joy, grief, and equanimity for each [of these], there are thirty-six.
By way of the three times (*kāla*), those very same [feelings] are said to be one hundred and eight. And whatever [is stated] in some places...
In the Sutta it is stated: "Whatever is felt, all that is included in suffering. That was stated by way of the suffering inherent in formations (*saṅkhāradukkhatā*).

However, since in the preceding "Exposition of Consciousness" (*cittaniddesa*) consciousnesses were classified according to the differentiation of the faculties (*indriya*), here too, in order to include consciousnesses by way of the very same differentiation of faculties, it is further stated: "Happiness... is fivefold."
And here, among those phenomena, those which by way of predominance constitute the faculties of pleasure and pain are twofold—bodily and mental—and thus they are stated as two:
the faculty of physical pleasure (*sukhindriya*), the faculty of mental joy (*somanassindriya*), the faculty of physical pain (*dukkhindriya*), and the faculty of mental grief (*domanassindriya*).
However, the phenomena that occupy the position of predominance for equanimity (*upekkhā*) are exclusively mental.

"They exist" means that they are spoken of as being of one kind, namely, the faculty of equanimity (*upekkhindriya*). Furthermore, even those [faculties] are of two kinds by way of a figurative method (*pariyāya*), because they also exist in dependence upon the physical sensitivity (*pasāda*) of the eye and so forth.
Feeling (*vedanā*), however, is spoken of as being of one kind because it has a single flavor (*ekarasa*).
In the *Vibhāvani*, however...
It has been stated: “Pleasure and pain are said to be twofold, according to the division into bodily and mental, and into pleasant and painful.
In this context, pleasure and pain have, by their very nature, the characteristic of experiencing desirable and undesirable tangibles.

The others [i.e., happiness and suffering] have the characteristic of experiencing the desirable, the undesirable, and the neutral, either by way of their own nature or through conceptualization. The remaining [terms] are as previously described.

Regarding pleasure and pain: all fifty-five types of consciousness—namely, the thirty-two sense-sphere consciousnesses associated with mental grief, the twenty-three five-jhāna consciousnesses, and the remaining [twenty]—are included. "In one" means in a single consciousness.
For the other [feeling] is the feeling of equanimity (*upekkhā-vedanā*).
131. The inclusion of the mind and mental factors associated with those [roots] by way of the classification of the roots is the "inclusion of roots" (*hetusaṅgaha*).
However, in the *Vibhāvani*, it is stated:
"The inclusion of roots is the inclusion by way of the classification of the roots such as greed (*lobha*), etc., and by way of the phenomena associated with them. That is not correct.
The reason has already been stated. The connection is: "The names of the causes (hetu) are sixfold.
In that context, the function of a cause is the accomplishment of the state of firm establishment of associated mental states upon an object.
For just as the roots of a tree, having grown deep within the earth themselves, take up the essence of the earth and the essence of water, [supporting] the tree up to its very top;
They bring [stability]. Just as when a wind or a great flood has come, they remain by firmly uprooting a tree, so too does that tree become grown, developed, vast, and long-enduring;
even so, these mental factors themselves, having attained firmness upon their objects, cause the associated states to become grown, developed, vast, and long-enduring therein.
It should be understood that rootless consciousnesses do not become well-established upon their object, just as rootsless plants cannot take firm hold on the surface of water.
Others, however, say that the function of a cause (*hetu*) is to establish the state of being wholesome and so forth for phenomena.
If this were the case, then for those states which lack a co-nascent cause (*sahajātahetu*), their status as unwholesome or indeterminate would not be possible.
Having stated that those material phenomena which have acquired causes and conditions would also incur the status of being wholesome and so forth, they refute that position as follows:
Just as in the world, what is called "darkness" is not something to be established by any specific condition;
rather, wherever light is absent, it is established there by its own inherent nature (dhammatā). In the same way, among phenomena...

Even delusion-in-the-form-of-darkness (*mohandhakāra*), which consists of the activity of delusion, deserves to be unwholesome by its very nature. For instance, there is such a thing as "desire" (*icchā*).
When it is associated with the activity of delusion and reaches the state of clinging, it is called unwholesome greed (*lobha*).
However, when it is associated with faith (*saddhā*) and reaches the state of desire for the Dhamma (*dhammacchanda*), it is called wholesome desire (*kusalacchanda*).

Likewise, there is that which is called intolerance (*akkhanti*). When this is associated with the activity of delusion (*muyhana*) and reaches the state of aversion (*paṭigha*), it becomes the unwholesome factor known as hatred (*dosa*).

However, when associated with faith (*saddhā*), it reaches the state of opposition toward evil states and evil objects—according to the method of the passage beginning "he does not tolerate an arisen thought of sensual desire"—and thus becomes the wholesome factor known as non-greed (*alobha*). As for the activity of delusion, however, by means of this...
It is not the case that something is called "unwholesome" because it is associated with this or that [factor], nor is it called "wholesome" because it is associated with such-and-such.

Just as the natural sour taste of a mango is inherently sour and devoid of any function of combination with anything else for the sake of sourness, so too these states are of an exclusively unwholesome nature.

Furthermore, that state which is neither wholesome nor unwholesome is "indeterminate" (abyākata); this alone is the reason for establishing the indeterminate status of phenomena. Therefore, regarding rootless consciousnesses...
The fact that both form (*rūpa*) and Nibbāna are indeterminate (*abyākata*) is established by their very nature as phenomena (*dhammatā*).

In this regard, delusion (*moha*) is the root even of the remaining roots; for attachment (*rajjana*) and aversion (*dussana*) are merely the consequences of delusion. Furthermore, the wholesome nature (*kusalabhāva*) of non-greed (*alobha*) and the other [wholesome roots] is established only in conjunction with the underlying tendency of ignorance (*avijjānusaya*).
Moreover, those [unwholesome roots] such as greed (*lobha*) are the specific roots of the states associated with greed and so forth.
For views, conceit, and so forth are the outflows (*nisandāni*) of lust and the like; while faith and the like are the outflows of non-lust and the like.

Furthermore, since the names "cause" (*hetu*) and "source" (*yoni*) refer to the predominant factors among the associated states, it is therefore appropriate to describe the indeterminate nature (*abyākatabhāvo*) of resultant and functional consciousnesses that possess causes by way of their causes as well.
[86] To this extent, it has been stated in the *Vibhāvani*:
"Others, however, say that the cause is the state (*bhāva*) which establishes the wholesomeness and so forth of wholesome states and the rest.

If this were so, another cause would have to be sought to establish the wholesomeness and so forth of those causes themselves. Then, [if one argues that] it is dependent on the causes associated with the remaining [states]...

In that case, the status of those [other factors] as wholesome and so forth would likewise be independent of the cause associated with a deluded (momūha) state of mind, which would then be unwholesome.

Alternatively, if its own intrinsic nature (sabhāva) were to constitute its unwholesome status, then since the remaining causes would also have their status as wholesome and so forth by way of their own intrinsic nature, the status of the associated phenomena (sampayutta-dhamma) would not be dependent on those causes, just as it is for them. And if...

The state of being wholesome and so forth is dependent upon causes. Therefore, it follows that for those states which are rootless (ahetuka), the state of being indeterminate (abyākata) would not be possible;
thus, enough with this excessive scrutiny, and that [objection] is rejected.

And just as among the material and immaterial phenomena that have obtained the condition of jhāna, the jhāna-factors (jhānaṅga) fulfill the sense of "contemplating closely" (upanijjhānaṭṭha) only in the case of immaterial phenomena.
They pervade, but not in material phenomena (*rūpadhamma*). However, because those mental states arise from jhāna, they are said to exist in those things produced by the condition of jhāna.
In the same way, roots (*hetu*) also pervade only non-material phenomena (*arūpadhamma*) with their state of being wholesome and so forth, but not in material phenomena.
Because those [wholesome states] arise from roots, they are said to exist in those things produced by the condition of root; thus, it is not the case for those material phenomena.
"The attainment of the state of being wholesome and so forth should be urged. [87] Furthermore, that which was stated in the *Vibhāvanī*:
"The state of being wholesome and so forth, however, is dependent upon wise and unwise attention (*yoniso ayoniso manasikāra*) toward the wholesome and unwholesome"—that too should be investigated.
For instance, when sunlight arrives during the day, it provides an opportunity for diurnal creatures such as swans;
when the darkness of night arrives, it provides an opportunity for nocturnal creatures such as owls. Yet, that light and darkness do not diminish the distinctions of their color and other qualities;
rather, it is their own respective natures that determine those traits. In this context, right attention (*yonisomanasikāra*) should be regarded as being like the light.
The other [the unwholesome] is like darkness. Wholesome and unwholesome states are like those beings.
The distinction of color and so forth is like the state of being wholesome and so forth. The causes are to be regarded as like the modes of birth (*yoni*).

As for the phrase "but of the indeterminate," everything that is neither wholesome nor unwholesome falls into the category already mentioned as "indeterminate. "Therein" refers to the compendium of causes (*hetusaṅgaha*). Of those with causes...

Even though those [states] that ought to be excluded here for the sake of the happiness of possession (*pariggahasukha*) are themselves rootless (*ahetuka*), they are mentioned first. Therefore he said: "The rest, however... and so on.
[The phrase] "neither with nor without roots" means that even the name "rootless" for them is established separately by virtue of the roots;
thus, their inclusion here is not contradictory. Therefore he said: "The eighteen rootless [states]" and so forth. Their intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).
It is said that even the sixfold causes become ninefold when divided according to the categories of wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate—namely, greed, hatred, and so forth. 132.
The "Compendium of Functions" (*Kiccasangaha*) is the grouping of the mind and mental factors according to the division of their fourteen functions.
However, in the *Vibhāvanī*...

It has been stated: "The compendium of functions is a compendium by way of the classification of functions such as rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) and so forth, and by way of the delimitation of those [factors] possessing such functions.

That is not correct. By whichever single kamma a single existence (*upapattibhava*) is produced, that existence ceases when that [kamma] is exhausted—either through its own inherent force or through being obstructed.
There is thus room for only one kamma. Therefore, from that [kamma], the existence produced...

The function of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) is the manifestation of a new existence, beginning with another birth, by means of a single karma that finds an opportunity without remaining even for a moment after death.

The function of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) is the uninterrupted occurrence of the continuity of the existence at birth (*upapattibhava*), acting as a condition for its persistence until that karma is exhausted.
For when it proceeds in that manner, the continuity of life-force (*āyu*) and the continuity of heat (*uṣmā*) indeed persist;
thus, these three phenomena protect this body so that it does not disintegrate. As it is said:
"When life-force, heat, and consciousness Abandon this body, [it falls]."
Then it lies cast away like a useless log.
"Adverting" (āvajjana) is the turning toward [an object] by the stream of consciousness; or, it adverts, it causes to turn, or it turns itself here, or by means of this—it is therefore "adverting.
Having descended from the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), it proceeds facing toward another object.
This is the meaning. It is called *āvajjanā* because it adverts or directs attention toward another object. Seeing and the other [mental functions] are well known.

*Voṭṭhabbanā* means fixing by isolating [the object] individually; that is to say, fixing it without confusion as "this is blue," or "yellow," or "beautiful," or "ugly"—this is what is meant by "determining" (*niyama*). In terms of its essential meaning, *javana*, *java*, and *vega* are synonymous.
One. The function of impulsion (*javanakicca*) is the occurrence of each individual bile-humor accompanied by speed, like the falling of a stone.

Furthermore, that which is stated in the *Vibhāvanī*—“The function of impulsion is the occurrence of that which is proceeding as if impelling many times or once, by way of accomplishing its respective task upon the object”—is not elegant.
For there is no such thing as a "turning back" of a mind that is impelled even for a single moment.

Indeed, even the path, the penetration-of-knowledge, and the impulsions occur as a continuous stream of impelled mental states proceeding with a single momentum, beginning from the preliminary consciousness of a single adverting moment.
They do not, however, impel by means of an impulse established separately.

[90] And in that context, regarding the phrase "it occurs like one who is running": this means that there is no separate entity called "speed" (*java*)—defined as rapid motion—that exists apart from those momentary phenomena which arise and cease one by one.
Rather, it is due to their occurring many times in succession that they are said to move rapidly, just as a person moving swiftly is described.
It has thus been shown that "impulsion" (javana) refers to the very same mental states [as the preceding moments]. That too is not correct.
For it was stated above that the function of impulsion is the occurrence of each individual consciousness accompanied by speed, like the falling of a thunderbolt.
Indeed, even though the life-continuum consciousness (bhavaṅga-citta) proceeds for a long duration, it is like a dry leaf being carried away in the current of a river.

It is like [a wheel] that has lost its momentum. However, it should be understood that even though each impulsion-consciousness (*javana-citta*) is singular, it proceeds with great velocity, just like a thunderbolt released by Indra. "Having that as its object" means *tadārammaṇa*;
what is grasped by the impulsion is precisely its object—this is what is stated. That which is the object grasped by the impulsion...
For it is said that because that [object] itself has been grasped, it is called "having that as its object" (*tadārammaṇa*). Or, that which is the object of that impulsion (*javana*) is its object;
thus it is "having that as its object. However, here what is intended is the state of having that as its object.

Death (*cuti*) is the release, the falling away, or the passing out of the existence that is being produced. Now, those functions do not proceed without restriction; they proceed only by way of a fixed position.
The different stages (ṭhāna) are mentioned in order to show how [the mind] proceeds. It is called a "stage" (ṭhāna) because the mind, possessing its respective functions, stands and proceeds therein;

it is an occasion (okāsa). What is meant is that it is the respective intervening period. For time (kāla) is also called a "stage," since it is the sphere of activity for those things that possess time.
The stage of rebirth-linking is the "rebirth-linking stage" (paṭisandhiṭṭhāna); the time of rebirth-linking is the "moment of rebirth-linking" (paṭisandhikkhaṇa).
This has been stated. The same applies to the remaining cases as well.
[91] However, in the *Vibhāvanī*, it says:
"The place of rebirth-linking is called the 'place of rebirth-linking' (*paṭisandhiṭṭhāna*); yet, while it is true that a place distinct from rebirth-linking might be called a 'place,'..."

"It does not exist. However, for the purpose of grasping it as 'pleasure,' it should be understood that even though there is no actual difference, a distinction is conceptually constructed—as in the case of [saying] 'the body of a stone statue' and so forth. This should not be accepted.
For time, although non-existent by way of intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), is a single conventional designation (*paññatti-dhamma*) that serves as a distinct object of consciousness.
For it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* that the place of ripening for these eight great resultant consciousnesses (*mahāvipākacitta*) should be understood as follows:
"These ripen in four places—namely, at rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*), death (*cuti*), and the object-receiving (*tadārammaṇa*) moment.
Having stated this, in expanding upon it, it says: "At the time of seizing rebirth-linking, they ripen having become rebirth-linking; even for an incalculable [period of existence]..."
At the time of death, having become the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), it becomes the death-moment (cuti); thus, it is spoken of as "time" alone.
Otherwise, like the functions (kicca), the positions (ṭhāna) would also have to be stated as being fourteenfold.

However, the detailed classification of these positions should be understood according to the method for the occurrence of consciousness in the two subsequent sections on the compendium of occurrence (pavatti-saṅgaha). Since [the life-span] is minimal...
Even though wholesome consciousness with two roots is associated with the mind itself, because it is exceedingly weak, it is unable to provide rebirth-linking accompanied by joy.
Therefore, it is said that "investigation accompanied by joy does not go to the place of rebirth-linking," but rather only the two types of investigation accompanied by equanimity do.
For likewise, in the *Paṭṭhāna*, in the section on "Dependent" within the triad of "accompanied by rapture":
In the context of the "opposite of the cause" (hetupaccanika), these are extracted by way of their point of connection.

Even though mind-door adverting consciousness occurs two or three times upon a limited object or an indistinct object, it remains devoid of the impetus of the impulsion (javana-vega) because it is weak, having obtained its causal status only from the stream of resultants (vipāka-santāna).
Therefore, it is stated that "the two types of adverting [consciousness] are excluded."
In the *Vibhāvani*, however, the reason is stated as: "Because of its existence as the experiencing of the flavor of the object. That is not a valid reason;

for the experiencing of the flavor of the object is neither the cause for the accomplishment of the function of impulsion (*javana*) nor the cause for obtaining the designation "impulsion" (*javana*).

Furthermore, that [resultant consciousness] brings about the fruit through the accomplishment of its function as impulsion (*javana*). However, because the resultant consciousness— even though it lacks the state of repetition (*āsevana*)—
falls upon the object with great speed due to the great power of path-intention (*magga-cetanā*) and because it occurs through the force of preparatory cultivation (*parikamma-bhāvanā*),
it is included among the impulsions (*javana*).
In the *Vibhāvani*, however,
it is stated with the intention that because the path, superknowledge, and impulsion occur only once, the function of impulsion is not fulfilled:
"Even though supramundane states such as the path last for only a single moment of consciousness, they are called 'impulsion' by virtue of possessing that specific nature."
Having said this, he clarifies that point by means of a simile for omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*). That, however, is simply not tenable.

Now, in order to show the types of consciousness grouped according to their common functions, he says "tesu pana" and so forth. The connection is: "the arising of consciousnesses called rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) and so on.
In the *Vibhāvanī*, however...
One might also apply [the classification] by way of the difference in the function of the name (*nāmakicca*).
That is not correct, because there is no separate category to be stated for the difference in names.
Consciousnesses with one function, two functions, three functions, four functions, and five functions are, respectively, sixty-eight, two, and so forth.
The construction is: "nine, eight, and two are indicated. 133.
The "compendium of doors" (dvārasaṅgaha) is the grouping together of consciousness and mental factors according to the distinction of the doors, such as the eye and so forth.
In the *Vibhāvani*, however...
It has been stated: “The ‘compendium of doors’ (dvārasaṅgaha) is the compendium by way of delimitation of both the doors and the consciousnesses occurring at the doors. That is not correct.
A door (dvāra) is so called because two people (dve janā) go (aranti) or move through it; it is the name for that opening through which people inside the city and people outside enter and exit.
Alternatively, it is also a door because two people go or move therein (dvārantipi).
They say this. Furthermore, there are two kinds of openings: the opening of space (*ākāsadvāra*) and the opening of the disk (*maṇḍadvāra*).

Therein, the "opening of space" refers to the aforementioned path of apertures. The "opening of the disk" refers to a light-path made of mirror-plates; that, however, is installed in the houses of those possessed of merit.
And just as it is in those [houses], so too there are only two [kinds of openings] in the bodies of sentient beings as well. Thus, there are nine openings.
For "the great forest" (*mahāvaṇa*) is said to be a gateway of openings (*chiddadvāra*). Indeed, the ninety-nine thousand pores of the body are also gateways of openings.
However, what is intended here is the "polished surface gateway" (*maṇḍadvāra*), which resembles the surface of a mirror.

For that too is called a "gateway" because it is similar to a gateway, insofar as it serves as the path for the exit and entry of objective phenomena (*ārammaṇika-dhamma*) and objective objects (*ārammaṇa-dhamma*).

It is said [thus]. Furthermore, that gateway of the essence of form (*rūpamaṇḍadvāra*) is twofold: the gateway of the essence of form and the gateway of the essence of the formless (*arūpamaṇḍadvāra*).

To show that the gateway of the essence of form is fivefold by way of the specific distinction of its essential state, which is established through the specific great elements (*mahābhūta*) resulting from specific kamma, he says "the eye-gateway" and so forth.
Therein, "the eye itself is the eye-gateway" means that in whichever eye the signs of forms such as the lunar disk and so forth [appear].
They are made known. Those signs, such as the adverting [of consciousness] and so forth, grasp that in which they are made known.
Therefore, the meaning is that this very eye is called the "eye-door" because it serves as the gateway for those two to attain the state of object and subject.
Alternatively, by means of the orb of the eye, external forms such as the lunar orb and so forth are brought within the range of the adverting [consciousness] and the rest.

They come to the state of being objects (visayabhāva). And by means of that [door], the internal processes such as adverting (āvajjana) and so forth come to the state of being the subjects (visayibhāva) of those external forms.
For the reasons stated above, it is called the "eye-door" (cakkhudvāra); this is the meaning. The same applies to the others as well.
However, in the commentaries (ṭīkā):
"It is said that they are 'doors' because they resemble doors in being the means for the occurrence of immaterial phenomena such as adverting (āvajjana) and so forth.
This is not correct, because visible forms and other objects also serve as the means for their occurrence. For it will be stated later: "The occurrence of the sixfold objects.
And here, the occurrences of the objects—visible forms and other sense-objects—which consist in their entering the range of the doors, are called "occurrences of objects" (visayapavatti).
Regarding the term "are called": therein, by the phrase "the eye itself is the eye-door," the meaning that "the door of the eye is the eye-door" is excluded.

Likewise, for the ear and so forth, by the phrase "the ear itself is the ear-door," etc., it is shown that the meaning is not "the door of the minds is the mind-door," but rather "the mind itself is the mind-door. Furthermore, of that [mind-door]...
Since "mind" (*mano*) has many meanings, the text states "the mind-door, however, is called the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*)" in order to show the specific sense intended here.
However, in the *Vibhāvanī*, it is also stated:
"The mind-door is the door for the minds such as adverting (*āvajjana*), etc. That [interpretation] is not correct.
The reason has already been stated. In that context, all ninety-eight types of consciousness are indeed called the "mind-door" (*manodvāra*).
However, here, taking it to mean specifically the door of rebirth (*upapattidvāra*), it is said to be called the "life-continuum" (*bhavaṅga*).
From the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) until the end of one's lifespan, the nineteen-fold life-continuum consciousness flows on like the current of a river.
"Herein, it is called the 'mind-door' (manodvāra); the meaning is that it is spoken of [as such].
However, in the *Vibhāvanī*, it is said:

'Just as what is called the door of a village exists immediately adjacent to the village, so too, in the sense of being the portal for the occurrence of mental states such as adverting (āvajjana) and so forth—'"

Regarding the term "door" (*dvāra*): immediately after the adverting consciousness (*āvajjanā*), there would indeed be the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) itself; it is not the preceding life-continuums that follow from it. With this intention, it was stated:
"The life-continuum is the life-continuum immediately following the adverting [consciousness]. That [statement] should not be accepted.

For if that were the case, those instances of the eye-sensitivity and so forth into which visible forms and other objects do not enter [the range of perception] would also [be doors], because they too [would be followed by] adverting and the rest.
If it were the case that the doors of the occurrence of process-thoughts (*vīthicitta*) did not exist at all, then they [the sense bases] would not be called "doors.
Yet it cannot be said that this is so, because their status as door-forms (*dvāra-rūpa*) is stated in the Canon itself. And here [in this work], he will say:
"The sevenfold door-form, consisting of the sensitive organs and the intimation, is called 'door-form'."
[99] And as for that statement brought forward as a proof— “Whatever there is therein that is an impulsion-moment,
it is called the mind-door”— that too is simply not applicable here.

For that [text] explains the adverting consciousness (*āvajjana*) as belonging to the side of the mind-door (*manodvāra*). However, where it is stated: "Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises;
dependent on the ear... [and so on]... dependent on the mind and mental objects, mind-consciousness (*manoviññāṇa*) arises," there alone is that [adverting consciousness] appropriate.
For in that context, regarding the arising of eye-consciousness, among the four— *Note: The provided source text ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.*
Among the conditions, the eye and visible forms alone are stated by their own nature;
thus, the other two conditions—adverting and the associated aggregates—are included by the word "and" (ca). This is likewise the case for ear-consciousness and the others.

However, in the case of mind-consciousness, in the phrase "mind and [objects]," adverting is taken together with the life-continuum consciousness, while the associated aggregates are included by the word "and."
For this being so, there are four conditions. Indeed, this has been stated in the *Dhātuvibhaṅga-aṭṭhakathā*:
"In instances where the word 'dependent' (*paṭicca*) occurs, advertence (*āvajjana*) should not be treated separately;

it should be understood as being based on the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) itself. Therefore, here "mind" (*mano*) refers to the life-continuum together with advertence, and "mind-consciousness" (*manoviññāṇa*) refers to the impulsion-mind-consciousness (*javana-manoviññāṇa*). And herein:
By the phrase "in the place where [the word] *paṭicca* has come," it is established that elsewhere the adverting consciousness (*āvajjana*) should not be made a member of the door.

Furthermore, because it has come as "*paṭicca*," even the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) must be understood in this text as only two moments of the life-continuum immediately following the adverting consciousness; for only proximate conditions are intended there. However, here...
Because all states that arise are encompassed by their being fit for the status of a door, the term "all" refers to the life-continuum (bhavaṅga).
Indeed, there is no such thing as a life-continuum that would not be fit for the status of the mind-door; this is how the matter should be understood.
In the phrase "therein," the locative case is used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇa*); it connects with "the eye-door" among those six doors.
"According to what is appropriate" means by way of conformity to the object, the plane, the person, the attention, and so forth.
"In every way" refers to the connection with the fifty-four [types of consciousness], by way of all modes—even including those not previously mentioned—counted as forty-six distinct divisions.
Alternatively, "in every way" refers to the various functions such as adverting (*āvajjana*), etc., up to the final registration (*tadārammaṇa*).

"In every respect, they pertain only to the sense-sphere" is the connection. Those functions such as adverting (āvajjana) and so forth, which proceed in dependence upon the modification of the door, are called "door-possessing" (dvārika) in the sense that they are connected to the doors by virtue of possessing those functions.
However, the functions of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi), the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), and death (cuti) are accomplished solely through the power of kamma, without any modification of the door.
Therefore, it is said [in the *Ekūnavīsati-lakkhaṇa*] that they do not possess the status of being "door-possessors" (*dvārika*) because they lack that specific function.

Regarding the phrase "those free from doors": here, "modification of the door" (*dvāra-vikāra*) should be understood as the vibration of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) due to the arrival of objects within its own range, and as the connection with a specific capacity for the arising of consciousness within the eye and the other sense-faculties.
[100] However, in the *Vibhāvani*, it is stated:

"Because they do not proceed through the doors of the eye and so forth, and because they proceed by way of apprehending a different object from the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) known as the mind-door, they are 'door-freed' (dvāravimuttā). This does not even accord with the *Aṭṭhakathā*.
For it is stated there: "By way of rebirth-linking, the life-continuum, and death. By this very principle of function, the doors of the consciousnesses [are established].

The portion [of the mind] released from the doors was shown by the Elder. For it is for this very reason that, even below, in the passage beginning "by way of the five-door adverting consciousness" and so forth, the status of the consciousnesses as belonging to the eye-door and so on is stated precisely by way of their functional roles (*kicca-sīsena*). If it is argued: "Is this not stated for this very purpose by the phrase 'because they do not proceed through the doors of the eye and so forth'? No.
Because that [phrase] lacks the intended meaning and does not serve to exclude the unwarranted application (*apasaṅga-nivattaka*).

The commentary [states] that there is no purpose for the statement [itself]. The intended meaning is as follows: they are "six-door" by way of the functions of investigation (*santīraṇa*) and registration (*tadārammaṇa*);
and they are "door-freed" by way of the functions of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) and so forth.
Thus, those that are five-door and those that are six-door are "five-and-six-door. At times they are exclusively six-door, and at times they are door-freed.
"Those liberated from the six doors. Here, the word "door" (*dvāra*) is applied by way of topical context.
However, in the *Vibhāvani*, it is also stated:
"And those belonging to the six doors, and those liberated from the six doors. That is not correct.

"Because it was not heard thus in the preceding section on the *cuṇṇiya* verses. "Mental states with a single door," etc. "In every way, those free from doors are thirty-six," etc. The construction is: "and in nine ways"—thus he elucidates them as fivefold.
[102] The "Compendium of Objects" (*ārammaṇasaṅgaha*) is the grouping together of consciousness and mental factors according to the distinction of objects such as visible form and so forth.
However, in the commentaries (*ṭīkā*),...

It has been stated: “The compendium of objects (ārammaṇasaṅgaha) is the grouping [of things] by way of their individual nature, their classification, and the consciousness that has them as its domain. This is not correct;
for this is a compendium of only consciousness and mental factors, not of objects. The etymological meaning of form and so forth will be explained below.
It is called an object (ālambana) because it is latched onto (ālambīyati) by consciousness and mental factors, which grasp it without letting go, just as a staff is grasped by a weak man.
[The term] *ālambaṇa*. However, when the word *ārammaṇa* is used, it is called an object (*ārammaṇa*) because consciousness and mental factors come and find delight (*ramanti*) therein.
As for what is stated in the *Vibhāvani*:

“It is called an object (*ālambaṇa*) because it is supported (*ālambīyati*) by consciousness and mental factors, as a stick is by a weak man; or else, because they come and find delight therein,” that is not correct.
For these terms are established separately. "Material form alone" means the sense-sphere of visible form (*vaṇṇāyatana*) alone.
Any kind of mental object (*dhammajāta*), whether existing or non-existing, real or unreal, that is free from the five [physical] objects, is simply a mental-object condition (*dhammārammaṇa*).
However, when that is classified according to its homogeneous components, it is said to be sixfold; thus it is called "mental-object condition."

"But it is comprised in six ways. Regarding the phrase "therein": among those six [bases], beginning with visible form, the eye-door consciousnesses that have arisen following upon a striking visible form are not able to take other objects as their support.
It is said that for eye-door consciousnesses, even visible forms that are not currently striking—namely, those of the past and future—are not able to be taken as supports.

For all [these consciousnesses], visible form alone is the object. That is "present" (*paccuppanna*). This same method applies to those [consciousnesses] connected with the ear-door and so forth as well.
In that context, "present" means arisen in dependence upon this or that cause; the sense is "occurring. "Sixfold" means sixfold by way of visible form and the rest.
"Past" (*atīta*) means that which has gone beyond its state of occurrence; it has gone, it has proceeded. It comes [from the root *i*].
"Has come" (*āgata*) means that which has arrived; this refers to both the present and the past. "Has not come" (*anāgata*) refers to the future.

Conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhata-dhamma*), being subject to arising and birth, fall within the three periods of time. Therefore, it should be understood that the designations for Nibbāna—which are devoid of arising and are unconditioned (*asaṅkhata*)—are called "timeless" (*kālavimutta*).
In the *Vibhāvanī*, however, it is stated:
