"Because of the absence of destruction, and because it cannot be designated by way of time such as the past and so forth, Nibbāna is both a designation and is called 'time-freed' (*kālavimutta*). This should be examined.
For all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhata-dhamma*) are preceded by their future state; therefore, when they [attain] the completeness of conditions...
When they stand on the side of being about to arise after having obtained the necessary conditions, then they are called "future.

When they have arisen after obtaining the completeness of conditions, then they are called "present. When they have ceased, then they are called "past. Thus, for those things whose nature is arising, the threefold temporality rooted in arising is established.
But for those things devoid of arising, even the state of being future does not exist; how much less [the other two]?

"Present and past are the bases. Therefore, the designations for Nibbāna are free from the three periods of time. As for the phrase "due to the absence of destruction," this is a reason specifically for its freedom from the past period;
thus, it should be understood that this does not establish their freedom from the other periods of time.
However, the appropriate classification will follow later in this very work with the words "among these... and so forth. And [the same applies] to those things free from doors.

The connection is: "the object is sixfold as well. However, to show that the objects of the six-door consciousnesses—such as those of adverting (āvajjana) and so forth—are, both in another existence and in this very existence, objects previously grasped by some door in the prior part [of life] as well as ungrasped, whereas it is not so for these [other types of consciousness], it is said:
"grasped by the six doors in another existence. For, regarding the distinction of existences...
Having performed the preliminary work and having made the aspiration, for those reborn there, that object is indeed apprehended by some door even in another existence.
However, in the *Vibhāvanī*, it is stated:

"But in order to show that this object of theirs does not become a range of experience without being apprehended by any [door]—as is the case with adverting—the phrase 'apprehended by the six doors' was said. That is not tenable.
For even in the case of the mind-door, the object of advertence may indeed have been previously apprehended by some other door, or it may not have been so apprehended at all.

For instance, that which was previously apprehended with the thought, "I shall obtain this," "I shall eat this," or "I shall see this," does not fail to become the object of advertence later on. Furthermore, within a single cognitive process (*ekāvajjana-vīthi*), [it is not the case that] by some previous consciousness...
"Non-grasped state" (*agahitabhāva*) here means "the criterion" (*pamāṇa*).

And just as the object of the five-door consciousnesses is exclusively present, and just as the object of mind-door consciousnesses belongs to the three times or is timeless (*kālavimutta*), it is not so for these;
thus it is said: "present, past, or conceptualized" (*paññattibhūta*). And just as...
The object of the sixfold-door consciousnesses may be either one that conforms to conventional usage established by scripture or one that is free from such usage.
To show that it is not so in these [three types of kamma], it is said: "Kamma, the sign of kamma, and the sign of destiny are so designated.
However, in the *Vibhāvanī*:

It has been stated: “Nor is it the case that their object—because it is proximate to death—is devoid of the conventional designations established by tradition, such as ‘kamma,’ ‘kamma-nimitta,’ and so forth, as is the case with the preceding javanas; thus he said, ‘Kamma... is agreed upon (sammatan). That too is not satisfactory.

For even in the period prior to the proximity of death, beings [perceive] either the kamma they themselves have performed, or shrines (cetiya) and the like as ‘kamma,’ or various ritual manuals (pakaraṇa).

They indeed take it as their object. For even then, the action is simply action, and the requisites for the action are simply the signs of the action (*kamma-nimitta*), because they are the sign and cause for the accomplishment of the action; thus they are called "signs of action. They also say that the sign of action is the object (*ārammaṇa*) of the action.
And like King Ajātasattu, there are also signs of destiny (*gati-nimitta*) by way of seeing dreams and so forth.
It simply takes that as its object. For the king kills his father in two types of existence;
and from the very moment he has been killed, the signs of the destination (gatinimitta) appear to him even while he is sleeping.

In this context, "according to what is possible" means in accordance with the object that arises through the six doors, such as the door of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi), and so forth. This is the analysis according to what is possible.

However, it will arise later at the moment of death. "For the most part" (*yebhuyyena*) means by way of frequency. "In another existence" (*bhavantare*) refers to the immediately preceding past existence, specifically at the time near death therein.
"Seized by the six doors" (*chadvāra-gahita*) means seized by the death-proximate mental moments (*javana*) through the six sense-doors.
And here, by the phrase "for the most part," the non-universality of this rule—that it is "seized by the six doors in another existence"—is indicated.

He qualifies [the object]. Why? Because it is possible even for that which has not been grasped. For that which is recognized as the kamma, the kamma-sign, or the sign of the destination for those who have passed away from the non-percipient realm (*asaññibhava*), and that which is recognized as the sign of the destination for those who have passed away from the formless realm (*arūpabhava*)—namely, the object of the rebirth-linking, life-continuum, and death-moments in the sense-sphere existence—that very thing remains ungrasped by any door whatsoever in the subsequent existence. And here, because in the *Paṭṭhāna*...

In the formless realm (arūpabhava), both types of prenascence condition (purejātapaccaya) are prohibited. Furthermore, in the Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathā), it is stated that for those who have passed away from there, the object of the present sign of the destination (gatinimitta) serves as the objective support (ārammaṇa) for rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) in the sense-sphere realm (kāmadhātu).
And they explain that what is called the "sign of the destination" is indeed an object consisting of form (rūpārammaṇa).
Therefore, even in the case of sense-sphere rebirth-linking, the sign of the destination recognized by them has not been apprehended through any door whatsoever in another existence.

It should be understood that this occurs. Furthermore, the appearance of kamma and so forth through the power of kamma at the time near death generally happens only for those who die with a confused mind.

However, for others, it may also occur through the power of another’s effort or through the power of recollecting things they have habitually practiced themselves, as in the case of righteous lay devotees (*dhammika-upāsaka*) and others [who are brought from the deva-world].
It happens even through the supernatural power (*ānubhāva*) of the devas who come and seize them; the hell-wardens (*nirayapāla*) themselves also come from hell and seize them.

In this regard, the *Revatī-vimāna* should be cited. For two hell-wardens seized him, first led him to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, and afterwards led him back to hell. This was because they were of the nature of *yakkhas* and belonged to the retinue of Vessavaṇa.
They are indeed able to go even to the realm of the Thirty-three. For it is stated in the Pāḷi: "Yama’s messengers are two yakkhas.
Some also say that here, the messengers of Vessavaṇa are referred to as "Yama’s messengers.

Therefore, for those who have well cultivated the signs of serenity such as the kasiṇas and the *asubha* (foulness) objects, and having stood in access concentration (*upacāra-jjhāna*), die while grasping those very same signs—for them too, there is rebirth-linking with the sense-sphere (*kāma*).

The object may not have been grasped by any of the sense doors in another existence. This same method applies even to those who arise here from the Brahma-world solely through the power of access concentration (*upacāra-jjhāna*).
As for what is stated in the *Vibhāvanī*:

It is said: "By the power of kamma alone, for those who have passed away from the non-percipient realm (asaññibhava), an object such as the sign of kamma (kamma-nimitta) and so forth appears at the moment of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi).
Herein, regarding the phrase "the sign of kamma and so forth," the word "and so forth" (ādi) must certainly include kamma itself;
for there is no reason not to include it. Furthermore, all of these [objects] are merely [manifestations] of the kamma that produces rebirth-linking.

It should be understood that [the sign] appears at the moment of rebirth-linking by its very influence alone. However, when a future sign appears, it must be the sign of the destination (gatinimitta) itself;
there is no separate function for it to perform. Since the present sign of the destination is established, it is already established [for the future];
thus it is said: "The past is a designation for the present, as if it were real."
In the *Vibhāvani*, however, the following reason is stated:

"That which is called 'future' has not been experienced like the past, nor has it come into range like the sign of a present destination (*gatinimitta*). That is not a valid reason, because the objection remains unrefuted.
For indeed, the so-called "sign of a destination" is not something that has been experienced even though it is present; that too—

It has come into range solely through the power of karma. This being so, the contingency that even the future [object] would likewise come into range solely through the power of karma remains exactly as it was before.
"Among those" refers to the aforementioned objective consciousnesses (*ārammaṇika-citta*). The compound means:
"those for which each one of the five [objects], beginning with visible form, is the object. The analysis (*viggaha*) is: "that for which the five objects, beginning with visible form, belong."

"The rest" refers to the investigating consciousnesses (*santīraṇa*) and the great resultants (*mahāvipāka*), remaining after the five sense-consciousnesses and the two types of receiving consciousness (*sampaticchana*).

"In every way, they have only sense-sphere objects" means that in all their modes—whether occurring as rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) and so forth through various functions upon various objects such as visible forms—they have exclusively sense-sphere objects.
For even when these arise in Omniscient Buddhas...

Because they lack the power of volitional determination (*vikappa*), they are unable to take as their object those phenomena that are non-existent, nor those that are subtle, exalted, or supramundane (*lokuttara*) even though they are designated phenomena (*paññatti-dhamma*).
In this context, first, the three types of investigation (*santīraṇa*) operate upon the five objects such as visible form by way of the function of investigating.
However, all eleven types of resultant consciousness (*vipāka*) [operate] by way of having those [five] as their object and so forth.
“They occur with respect to the six limited objects.
However, in the *Vibhāvani*, it is stated:

“First, as regards the resultant [consciousness], they occur with respect to the five objects such as visible form, by way of investigation (*santīraṇa*) and so forth. In that context, the phrase “by way of investigation and so forth” should not be said; rather, it should be said simply as “by way of investigation.”
Furthermore, the analysis of how consciousness functions with respect to its objects should be taken from the *Aṭṭhakathākaṇḍa*.
It has been stated that supramundane states (*lokuttaradhammā*) are the domain of knowledge alone because of their extreme profundity. Regarding "all objects, excluding the supramundane":
therein, for those who have attained meditative absorption (*samāpatti*), these [supramundane] objects become sublime objects (*mahaggatārammaṇāni*) at the very moment they arise.
And among those, the two types of consciousness rooted in hatred (*dosa*) should be understood as arising at the time when jhāna has been lost.
It is said that "knowledge" (*ñāṇa*) is unable to take as its object those supramundane states not yet attained; thus it is called "associated with knowledge.

Regarding the phrase "having abandoned all objects," therein, when the wholesome sense-sphere consciousnesses associated with knowledge arise in worldlings who have attained internal heat (*ajjhāna*).

Together with the designations (paññatti), these have sense-sphere objects. Prior to the moment of change-of-lineage (gotrabhū) from the stream-entry path, those same [objects] have Nibbāna as their object for worldlings.
For those who have attained jhāna, those same [objects], as well as those of the higher realms, have the super-knowledges (abhiññā) and skillful states as their objects.
It should be understood that for those established in the lower fruits, they have as their objects the path, fruit, and Nibbāna attained by themselves.

Just as here the Noble Ones are able to take only the paths and fruits they themselves have attained as their object, so too it should be understood that those who have attained jhāna are able to take only the jhānas they themselves have attained as their object. Here it might be asked:
"Those who aspire for jhānas, those who perform the preliminary work for jhāna, and those who comment upon the suttas on jhāna—do they not fail to attain them?"
Are they able to take sublime meditations (*mahaggata-jjhāna*) as their object, or not? They are not able. For those so-called jhānas possess such great power and such great benefits;

having heard this, or by means of the knowledge that discerns the mode [of attainment] established through the power of what has been heard and mastered (*sutapariyatti*), they aspire to them merely by way of inference. They even perform the preliminary work (*parikamma*).
"They also comment upon the suttas": otherwise, even worldlings (puthujjana) would aspire toward supramundane states (lokuttara-dhamma) and perform the preliminary work for the path;
since they discuss and comment upon the terms "path," "fruit," and "Nibbāna," those [terms] would likewise become mere objects of their [worldly] consciousness.
However, it should be understood that their minds experience only the qualities of the conceptual designations (paññatti-guṇa) of the jhānas and so forth.

For even the designations for sublime states are themselves of a sublime nature. Indeed, one who possesses great psychic power and knows the minds of others—such as Māra, the son of a god—perceives only the form-sphere jhāna-citta that is dependent on the round of existence (*vaṭṭanissita*);
he does not perceive that which is dependent on the turning away from existence (*vivaṭṭanissita*).
Furthermore, he does not perceive even the formless-sphere jhāna-citta when it is dependent on the round; this is stated in the commentary to the *Aṅguttara Nikāya*, in the *Navanipāta*.

It has been stated: "However, for those who penetrate the supreme path and fruit (aggamaggaphala), it is not the case that their arisen functional javanas associated with ñāṇa (uppannāniññāṇasampayuttakāmakriyajavanāni) and the functional direct-knowledge javana (kriyābhiññājavana) are unable to take any object among the phenomena of the four planes together with a concept (paññatti) according to the individual's capacity.
Likewise, their preceding mind-door adverting consciousness (manodvārāvajjana) [is also capable]. Thus it was said in the *Ṭhāṇasampayutta*.
"In every way, all objects. Herein, "in every way" means by way of all sense-sphere, all sublime, all supramundane, all conceptualized, and all present and so forth.

And this is said with reference to those [knowledges] that have arisen in Omniscient Buddhas. As for others, even those that have arisen in Paccekabuddhas are only "partial-all-objects" (padesa-sabbārammaṇa).
[They] exist. For even all [of them together] are unable to know a single earth element in its entirety in every respect.
Among the formless attainments (*ārūpya*), the second and fourth are sublime because their objects are the consciousnesses of the first and third formless attainments.
"The rest" refers to all twenty-one types remaining after the two kinds of direct knowledge (*abhiññā*) and the second and fourth formless attainments.
"Exalted states of consciousness" means that their objects are designated as the kasiṇas and so forth.
"Twenty-five" is said with reference to the five-door adverting consciousness, the twenty-three sense-sphere resultant consciousnesses, and the smiling consciousness.
"In the limited" means only in the objective sphere of the sense-world (kāmāvacara). For that [consciousness], due to its weak power, is obstructed and cut off on all sides by obstructive factors.
That which is "inferior" (paritta) is said to be so because it possesses a state of lack of splendor (nittejabhāva). 135.

The "compendium of bases" (vatthusaṅgaha) is the grouping together of the mind and mental factors that have those bases as their support, according to the classification of the bases such as the eye and so forth.
However, in the *Vibhāvani*, it is stated:
It has been stated: "The 'compendium of bases' (vatthusaṅgaha) is the compendium by way of the classification of bases and by way of the delimitation of the consciousness that has those as its basis.

That is not correct. [The term] *vatthūni* means "bases" because consciousness and mental factors dwell (*vasanti*) and are established (*patiṭṭhahanti*) upon them; thus, the construction is "the eye-base," and so on, up to "the body-base" and "the heart-base.
The eye itself is the eye-base, and likewise the ear and so forth are the ear-base and so on. For this reading is a contraction of the sentence.

It is appropriate to call this either the "method of enumeration" (*peyyālanaya*) or the "method of internal indication" (*antadīpaknaya*). However, some consider it a *dvanda* compound; for them, the word "and" (*ca*) is not appropriate.
Others say that the word "basis" (*vatthu*) and the word "and" (*ca*) should be supplied to the preceding terms.

For them, the compound term "heart-basis" (*hadayavatthu*) is not appropriate. Still others say it is a designation without case-endings (*avibhattikaniddesa*). These [bases] exist in the sense-sphere world (*kāmaloka*).

"All are obtainable" means that because the fullness of the sense faculties (*indriya*) occurs only in those personal existences (*attabhāva*) produced by karma rooted in craving for sensual pleasures (*kāmataṇhā*), all six of these bases (*vatthu*) are obtainable only in the sense-sphere world (*kāmaloka*).

For it is when the physical bases such as the eye exist that the enjoyment of visible forms and so forth becomes possible. Therefore, those who delight in the bases of sensual pleasure, such as visible forms and the rest—
Sensual craving always desires the excellence of the five bases, such as the eye and so forth.
Just as a minister who performs all duties always carries out every royal task while fulfilling the King’s very wishes,
even so, sense-sphere karma, while always fulfilling the desire of sensual craving, results in the perfection of the sense faculties.

It produces a personal existence (*attabhāva*). Therefore, beings in the sense-sphere realm (*kāmasatta*), produced by karma under the influence of craving for sensual pleasures (*kāmataṇhā*), possess complete faculties.

Furthermore, while the eye and ear—which consist of the unsurpassed excellence of seeing and hearing—are conducive to the purification of beings through the sight of the Buddha and the hearing of the Dhamma, the triad beginning with the nose is not so. However, that [triad]...
It exists solely for the purpose of enjoying sense pleasures. Therefore, it is said that the cultivation of dispassion toward sense pleasures is not found in the Brahma-bodies produced by kamma;
thus, it is stated that the triad of nose and so forth does not exist in the fine-material world (rūpaloka).

This was said with reference to the three sensitive material phenomena (pasāda-rūpa). However, the physical structures of the nose, tongue, and body, along with their constituent parts, are indeed fully developed and complete.
"They exist. Even in the formless world (*arūpaloka*), none of these [material phenomena] are found;

thus, due to the complete absence of the occurrence of matter—both internally and externally within the continuity produced by karma—in that world which is the result of the cultivation of dispassion toward form (*rūpavirāga-bhāvanā*), beings born there remain as mere continuities of consciousness upon a pure expanse of space.
In this compendium (*saṅgaha*), however, in order to include the consciousnesses by way of the seven elements of consciousness (*viññāṇadhātu*), it is said therein:

"The five elements of sense-consciousness," and so forth. "Therein" means among those six bases. The analysis (*viggaha*) is: the five consciousnesses themselves are called "elements" in the sense of being devoid of a sentient being or a life-principle (*nisattanijīva*).
The same applies to the rest. Because it lacks the function of cognizing, but is merely the act of reflecting (*manana*), it is the "mind-element" (*manodhātu*). At the five doors...
For the functions of mere adverting and mere receiving do not possess the function of discerning distinctions.
However, the five sense-consciousnesses possess to some extent the function of discerning distinctions by way of direct seeing and so forth.

But the remaining [mental states], such as investigating consciousness and the rest, are not mind-elements (*manodhātu*), because they are endowed with the function of discerning superior distinctions by way of examining the specific nature of the object.
They are not merely mentalizing like the [other] mind-element, nor are they merely cognizing like the five sense-consciousness-elements.
Rather, because it is "mind" (manas) in the sense of mentalizing and "consciousness" (viññāṇa) in the sense of cognizing, it is called the mind-consciousness-element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*).

The meaning is: "the element that cognizes with an exceeding distinction. For in a descriptive compound (*visesana-samāsa*), the sense of excess is understood from synonymous terms, just as in the term *padaṭṭhāna* ("basis of the word").
In the *Vibhāvanī*, however, it is stated:

“Either ‘mind itself is consciousness’ is *manoviññāṇa*, or ‘the consciousness of the mind’ is *manoviññāṇa*. Regarding this, first of all, the interpretation “mind itself is consciousness” (*manoyeva viññāṇaṃ*) is not tenable.

For nowhere is a restrictive analysis (*avadhāraṇa-viggaha*) seen or found to be appropriate in a descriptive determinative compound (*visesanappakara-samāsa*)—such as in the case of *padaṭṭhāna* and so forth—which indicates that two terms are co-referential (*abhi-ekaṭṭha*) by distinguishing one from the other.
[111] That "consciousness is of the mind" (mano-viññāṇa) is likewise untenable.

For "mind" (mano) refers to the mind consisting of the triad of the mind-element (manodhātu). Therein, the two types of receiving consciousness (sampaṭicchana) serve as the condition for the subsequent stream of mind-consciousness beginning with investigation (santīraṇa).
However, five-door adverting consciousness (pañcadvārāvajjana) [is the condition] for the next door.

Considering that what is occurring is the conditionally arisen state of that very stream of mental consciousness (*manoviññāṇa*), the meaning is "the consciousness connected to the mind"—that is, to the mind which was the condition at the beginning and which has become the conditionally arisen state within another door at the end.
Alternatively, all consciousnesses excluding the fivefold sense-consciousness are called "mind" (*mano*) because their function is to cognize (*manana*). Regarding the object...
However, since the five sense-consciousnesses consist merely in the striking [of the object] and do not possess the function of reflecting (*manana*), they are called "seeing" and so forth.

Furthermore, although the five-door adverting consciousness (*pañcadvārāvajjana*) arises from the mind, it is not a condition for the mind; rather, it is a condition for seeing and the other [sense-cognitions].
And although the two types of receiving consciousness (*sampaṭicchana*) are conditions for the mind, they do not arise from the mind; they arise precisely from seeing and the others.

It has arisen. However, since the investigating consciousness (*santīraṇa*) and the others arise in the midst of two successive moments of mind—those occurring before and after themselves—they are "consciousness related to the mind" in the sense that they are related to the mind which serves as their own condition and the resultant of that condition.
This being so, even the fivefold sensory consciousness is [called "related to the mind"] because it occurs between two moments of the mind-element (*manodhātu*).
It must indeed be said that the consciousness which is related to that which has arisen by way of condition is "mind-consciousness" (*manoviññāṇa*).
However, in the *Ṭīkā*, it is also stated that it is "consciousness born from the mind" (*manato jātaṃ viññāṇam*); this too is entirely appropriate according to the method already explained.

The construction is as follows: furthermore, the remaining thirty factors—consisting of the mental-consciousness-element (manoviññāṇadhātu) including the investigating consciousnesses (santīraṇa), etc., and the fifteen fine-material-sphere (rūpāvacara) states—occur depending solely upon the heart-base.
Here, the word "and" (ca) implies that the remaining seventy-six factors also possess the nature of the mental-consciousness-element.
In the *Vibhāvani*, however, having taken up the sense of a collective summary, it is stated: “It is not only the mind-element (*manodhātu*) alone. This is not tenable;
for if that were the case, one would have to state that the remaining [elements] are also comprised within the mind-consciousness-element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*).

[114] As for the commentaries, the application is that those occurring by way of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*)—namely, the *santīraṇa* (investigating consciousness) and the *la* (the five-door adverting consciousness)—and the remaining thirty states reckoned as the mind-consciousness element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*), are what is meant. That too is not excellent, because it is unclear regarding the course of the meaning.
In that regard, why do they occur only in dependence on those [bases]? Because they do not arise in the immaterial realms (*ārūppa*).

And why is it said that those [consciousnesses] do not arise there? First, the investigating consciousnesses and the great resultant consciousnesses do not arise there because of the absence of the five sense-doors and their respective functions.

The two types of consciousness accompanied by aversion (*paṭigha*) also do not arise, because aversion is absent in a state free from hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), and because states of hindrance are impossible on the planes of meditative absorption (*jhānabhūmi*).
In this context, however, if there were no resentment existing in a state free from hindrances,

then the statement in the *Pāḷi* regarding the complete cessation of the faculty of displeasure (*domanassindriya*) in the second jhāna itself, as well as the statement in the Commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) regarding the possibility of its arising in the preliminary stage (*upacāra*) of the second jhāna,
would be contradictory. Therefore, [resentment] exists in the planes of jhāna as a coarse sensual lust (*kāmarāga*) that serves as its own concomitant condition.
Some say it is logical that the two types of repulsive consciousness do not arise there because of their absence.

However, the authors of the *Ṭīkā*, regarding the statement that their arising is possible in the preliminary stage (*upacāra*) of the second jhāna as being merely hypothetical, maintain the former reason alone.
If this were merely hypothetical, then the canonical text (*pāḷi*) itself would also have to be merely hypothetical.
It might be so. Therefore, it is our view that the final [moment] alone is appropriate as the "conflict" (raṇa).

A mind of laughter does not arise either, because for those who are formless (arūpin), there is an absence of the function of laughing. It is also logical [to say this] because of the absence of the body.

A stream-entry path-consciousness (sotāpatti-magga-citta) also does not arise, because in the absence of the voice of another, there is no realization of the Dhamma for an ordinary person (puthujjana) arising therein.

This is because Buddhas and Paccekabuddhas do not arise there. For that very reason, an ordinary person (*puthujjana*) who is born there is said to be situated among the eight inopportune births (*akhaṇa*).

Furthermore, fine-material-sphere consciousnesses (*rūpāvacara-citta*) also do not arise there, because those states have transcended the objective supports consisting of the signs of form (*rūpa-nimitta-ārammaṇa*) through the cultivation of dispassion toward form (*rūpa-virāga-bhāvanā*).

The construction is as follows: the remaining forty-two states, comprised of the mind-consciousness element (manoviññāṇadhātu) according to their classification as wholesome, unwholesome, functional, and supramundane, proceed either depending upon or not depending upon the heart-base (hadaya).
The intention is that those depending [on the heart-base] exist in the five-aggregate plane (pañcavokāra), while those not depending [on it] exist in the four-aggregate plane (catuvokāra).
The compound analysis (*viggaha*) is: "the wholesome and the unwholesome, and the functional and the supramundane."
In this context, "wholesome" refers to the twelve mundane wholesome consciousnesses remaining after excluding the five types of wholesome [resultant] materiality.

"Unwholesome" refers to the ten unwholesome consciousnesses remaining after excluding the two types of consciousness accompanied by aversion. "Functional" refers to the thirteen functional consciousnesses remaining after excluding the five-door adverting, smiling, and the five types of functional materiality.
"Supramundane" refers to the seven supramundane consciousnesses remaining after excluding the first path-consciousness.

The application [of the terms] is as follows: in the sense-sphere (kāma), seven elements are considered to be based on six bases; in the fine-material sphere (rūpa), four kinds of elements are considered to be based on three bases;
and in the immaterial sphere (ārūpa), one element is considered to be based on no base at all.

The phrase "forty-three" is said with reference to the thirty states beginning with investigating consciousness (santīraṇa), together with the fivefold sense-consciousnesses and the triad of mind-elements (manodhātu).
Thus ends the Elucidation of the Ultimate Meaning (*Paramatthadīpanā*) of the Section on Miscellaneous Subjects (*Pakiṇṇakasaṅgaha*),
within the Fourth Commentary on the *Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha* entitled the Elucidation of the Ultimate Meaning (*Paramatthadīpanī*).
The Elucidation of Ultimate Reality: A Compendium of the Path of Consciousness (Vīthi-saṅgaha-paramatthadīpanī).

136. Having thus demonstrated the compendium of the classification of consciousness, the compendium of the classification of mental factors, and the compendium of the combined classification of both consciousness and mental factors within the "Compendium of the Body," [the author] now presents the compendium of the occurrence of consciousness in the cognitive process (*vīthicitta*) and that which is outside the cognitive process (*vīthimutta*).

The inclusion of the occurrence of consciousness (*cittappavatti-saṅgaha*) consists of those two very same modes of inclusion of occurrence; in order to show these, he said, "of mental arisings" (*cittuppādānam*), and so forth.
Therein, they arise, thus they are "arisings" (*uppādā*). They arise therein.

Since there is no other [term] because of its identity with consciousness, it is simply understood as "in consciousness. Thus, "consciousness and the arisings in consciousness" (*cittuppādā*) means "consciousness and mental factors" (*citta-cetasika*). Of those mental arisings.
"In this very way" refers to the manner described from the beginning onwards. "The supreme compendium" refers to the exposition of birth (*jāti-niddesa*).

The connection is: "having made three divisions of the supreme and the highest compendium. "By way of the distinction of planes and persons" is an instrumental expression used in the sense of accompaniment (*sahatthe karaṇavacana*);

the meaning is: together with the distinction of planes such as the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) and so forth, and the distinction of persons (*puggala*) such as those possessing two roots (*duhetuka*) and so forth. It is "determined by what precedes and follows."

The process beginning with adverting and so forth—consisting of eye-consciousness and the rest—is determined and fixed by the successive order of preceding and succeeding moments of consciousness. The term "pavattisaṅgaha" (compendium of occurrence) is also merely a designation for a class.
Thus, the meaning is that there are two such compendia of occurrence under these names. In the phrase "paṭisandhipavattiyaṃ," it refers to the rebirth-linking and the occurrences [of consciousness].

This is a reversal of the word order; the meaning is "at the time of rebirth-linking and at the time of occurrence. [It includes] both the compendium of rebirth-linking and the compendium of occurrence.
The meaning is: "I shall explain two types of inclusion—namely, the inclusion of the process during the time of occurrence (pavatti) and the inclusion of the process itself.
This meaning is evident from the verse concerning the subsequent inclusion. However, some say that the locative case here is used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇa*).
If that were so, the inclusion mentioned above would be called the "inclusion of rebirth-linking" (*paṭisandhi-saṅgaha*), and not the "inclusion of the process" (*pavatti-saṅgaha*). And thus...

This does not agree with the statement: "Now, regarding the section on the inclusion of continuity (*pavatti-saṅgaha*) within the verse concerning the inclusion of what is outside the path (*vīthimutta-saṅgaha*), it will be explained.
However, in the commentaries (*ṭīkā*),...
It was stated: “The ‘superior’ [section] is so called because it is superior due to the analysis of the inclusion of feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth. This must be examined;
for if that were the case, it would follow that only the miscellaneous inclusion (*pakiṇṇaka-saṅgaha*) is intended here by the word “inclusion.
However, since this transitional verse (*anusandhigāthā*) occurs situated between the three and the two types of analytical inclusions (*pabhedasaṅgaha*), therefore, as before—
It should be understood that those two types of classification (pabhedasaṅgaha) are also appropriate to be included here by the term "classification" (saṅgaha).
However, since this "classification of occurrence" (pavattisaṅgaha) has been well-stated when combined with the bases, doors, and objects, these three sets of six have been set forth again here.
In the *Vibhāvani*, however...

It has been said: "The inclusion of bases, doors, and objects was already explained below, but it is set forth again here in order to show the inclusion of the process [of consciousness] in its completeness.

This is not correct; for it is not the case that the entire inclusion of bases, doors, and objects is presented here. The occurrence of objects within the doors is "object-occurrence" (*visaya-pavatti*).
And here, "occurrence" refers specifically to the mere arrival at the threshold of the sense-doors. For he will say later: "In a single moment of consciousness..."
"Past" and so forth. That [consciousness], moreover, is of six kinds: the very swift, the swift, the swifter, the swift, the slow, and the slower, and the slowest.
The manifestation of the doors of the objects such as kamma is the "occurrence of the object," which is its arrival at the threshold.
For it will be said: "By the power of kamma, either kamma, or the sign of kamma, or the sign of destiny..."
"It presents itself at one of the doors.
However, in the *Vibhāvani*, it is also stated:
"The occurrence of consciousnesses toward objects is 'occurrence toward objects' (*visayappavatti*). That is not correct.
For if this were so, it would follow that the occurrence of an object within an extremely limited range of focus is untenable.
"Therein" means among those six groups. Having reached the analysis of elements, the diversity of elements is taken as the measure;

thus, having separated it from the act of thinking and cognizing, the mind-element (*manodhātu*) is stated separately. However, having reached the analysis of consciousness, whatever thinking occurs is included within the act of cognizing.

"Only intense" is said [of] eye-consciousness... "As for the 'cognitive series' (chavīññāṇāni)," the connection is that the cognitive series proceeding through the doors should be applied to the cognitive series proceeding through the skin-door.
A "series proceeding through the eye-door" (cakkhudvāravīthi) is a stream of consciousness that proceeds dependent upon a modification of the eye-door;
such is the meaning. It is the same for the others. By means of the uncommon [cause].

A cognitive process characterized by eye-consciousness is an "eye-consciousness process" (*cakkhuviññāṇavīthi*). A pure continuity of mind-consciousness, however, is a "mind-consciousness process" (*manoviññāṇavīthi*).

In the *Vibhāvani*, it is stated: "A process connected with eye-consciousness is an 'eye-consciousness process' because of its state of co-occurrence with it, due to having the same object and the same door."

"Door-occurrence" (*dvārappavattā*) means arisen at a door. The meaning is: arisen in dependence upon this or that modification of a door. "Occurrence of consciousness" (*cittappavattiyo*) refers to the continuity of consciousness.
"Exceedingly great" (*atimahanta*) is a nominative case used in the sense of a genitive.

Thus, there is the occurrence of an exceedingly great fivefold object, and so forth, up to the occurrence of an exceedingly small fivefold object; thus it is fourfold at the five doors. At the mind-door (*manodvāre*), [it is likewise].

The construction [of the sentence] should be understood as follows: "the occurrence of the six objects when they are distinct and the occurrence of the six objects when they are not distinct" constitutes the twofold sixfold occurrence of the objective field.

Furthermore, in this context, the state of being "excessively large" and so forth should be understood either by way of conditions such as light, or by way of the physical basis (vatthu) being excessively large and so forth.
Among these, even that which is subtle and delicate, or distant, [is included within] visible forms and the other [objects].
Regarding the basis for resolution (*adhiṭṭhānavatthu*), when there is the perfection of conditions such as light and so forth, it is indeed too vast. For instance,
during the time of the Blessed Buddha’s first emergence [from meditation] and at the time of performing the miracle of opening the world,
those standing right here see subtle and delicate forms, as well as distant ones— even in the Avīci hell, in the Akaniṭṭha heaven, and in other world-systems— as if they were standing right there.
For at that time, a magnificent radiance appeared. By its power, even the entire earth, Mount Sineru, the Cakkavāḷa mountains, and all other mountain ranges became like masses of pure crystal.
It is said: "A great, magnificent radiance appeared, surpassing the divine majesty of the gods.
Furthermore, it was due to the arising of radiance in those who serve as the basis for the serene confidence of the gods of rebirth, the Brahmās, and others.

The earth, mountains, and so forth are unable to create an interval between the eye and visible forms. Likewise, even when distant, forms such as mountains are called "very large" because their physical basis is extremely vast;
and forms such as the moon, sun, and stars are called "very large" because their objective bases are vast and because they possess a natural radiance.
However, this does not apply to conditions such as light, nor to the bases for the resolution of the mind.
One should state the progression from weak to weaker to weakest, and so on, up to the state of being "great" and beyond.

Furthermore, those five objects that come into range after one mind-moment has passed are called "exceedingly great objects. Those that come after two or three mind-moments have passed are "great objects.
Those that come after four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, or ten mind-moments have passed—
"Having passed beyond" means having gone beyond those objects that are merely limited (*paritta*).
However, those which come into range after passing ten, eleven, twelve, thirteen, fourteen, or fifteen mind-moments (*cittakkhaṇa*) are "exceedingly limited objects" (*atiparittārammaṇāni*).
Regarding the phrase "on the other hand, those past by even a single mind-moment," and so forth: "manifest" (*vibhūta*) means evident; "unmanifest" (*avibhūta*) means not evident. Thus...
Having demonstrated the six sextads according to their individual nature, he now asks, "How?

and, in order to explain in detail the occurrence of consciousness in the cognitive process by combining all of them together, he says, beginning with "Arising and presence," etc., in order to show the delimitation of time for both the material and immaterial realms.
In this context, "how" means: in what manner does the occurrence of consciousness in the cognitive process take place?
In the *Vibhāvani*, however, it is stated: "Having asked, 'How?

In what manner does the determination of the object occur by way of being too great and so forth?', [the text] begins with 'arising and presence' (*uppādaṭṭhiti*) and so on in order to explain that by way of mind-moments (*cittakkhaṇa*). This does not appear to be correct.
For if that were the case, there would be no room for the first five sets of six [factors]. Nor is it the case that "arising and presence... is the life-span of material phenomena."
It can be understood that this is stated solely for the purpose of defining the objective sphere (*visaya*). Arising (*uppāda*) means coming into being;
the meaning is the acquisition of intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*). Abiding (*ṭhiti*) means staying; the meaning is the non-retrogression of that which has acquired its intrinsic nature.
Dissolution (*bhaṅga*) means breaking up; the meaning is its disappearance after having declined. "A single moment of consciousness" (*ekacittakkhaṇaṃ*) means of one consciousness...

This is called a "moment" (*khaṇa*). Furthermore, that moment should be understood as being a hundred-thousand-fold part of a billionth of the time it takes for a snap of the fingers or the blinking of an eye.
For it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "In the time of a snap of the fingers, feelings numbering many hundreds of thousands of koṭis arise.
However, according to the opinion of the teacher Ācariya Ānanda Thera, there is [only] arising and dissolution here.

It should be said that two moments of subsistence constitute what is called a single moment of consciousness. For just as in the world, that which is called lightning grows and immediately thereafter breaks;
no separate "duration" is perceived between its growing and its breaking.
And just as a clod of earth thrown straight upward falls after having flown up; no [separate duration] is perceived between its flying up and its falling.
And yet, a separate "duration" (ṭhiti) is seen [as a distinct phase]. So too is consciousness (citta). For that too falls into the phase of fall (vaya) immediately after the phase of rise (udaya).
However, unlike material phenomena (rūpadhammā), no separate, countable portion called "duration" is found existing between those two phases.
And this being so, in the dyads, only the arising and dissolution of consciousness [are mentioned].
These have been stated here and there. Specifically, however, in the *Cittayamaka* (The Pairs on Consciousness), it is said: "Arising" (*uppanna*) and "arising" (*uppajjamāna*).
At the moment of dissolution (*bhaṅgakkhaṇa*), it is "arisen" but not "arising. At the moment of origination (*uppādakkhaṇa*), it is both "arisen" and "arising," and so forth;

thus, only dissolution and origination are predicated of consciousness. Furthermore, in the *Kathāvatthu*, it is asked: "Does one consciousness last for a day? [The opponent] says: "Yes. [The questioner asks: "For half a day..."
[If you say: "The moment of arising (*uppādakkhaṇa*) lasts for half a day, and the moment of passing away (*vayakkhaṇa*) lasts for [the other] half a day," that should not be said.
[If you agree that] "one consciousness lasts for two days," then it should not be said that "one day is the moment of arising and one day is the moment of passing away.
[If you agree that] "one consciousness lasts for four days," then [it follows that] two days are the moment of arising and two days... [are the moment of passing away].
"One should not say, 'It is momentary' (vaya-kkhaṇo). For [it is said]: 'For a month,' 'for two months,' 'for four months,' ...
'for a year,' 'for two years,' 'for four years,' ... 'for an aeon' (kappa), 'for two aeons,' 'for four aeons,' and so forth.

By such statements, only two portions—the arising and the passing away—of the mind are mentioned, but not the portion of its duration (ṭhiti-bhāga). [This would be so] if that [portion of duration] were perceived separately.

"It is admitted that one consciousness lasts for a day. [If this is so,] the first part of the day would be the moment of arising (*uppādakkhaṇa*), the second the moment of presence (*ṭhitikkhaṇa*), and the third the moment of dissolution (*vayakkhaṇa*)—thus it might have been analyzed by the Great Elder (*Mahāthera*).
[In that case,] three days, three months, three years, and even three eons (*kappa*) would likewise have to be considered faultless. Herein, it might be argued:
But surely it is said in the Suttantas: "Monks, there are these three conditioned characteristics of the conditioned.
What are the three? Arising is discerned; passing away is discerned; change while persisting is discerned.
Likewise, for feeling, arising is discerned; passing away is discerned; change while persisting is discerned. And so for perception.

It is said: "The arising of volitional formations... and of consciousness is discerned. Therefore, one might think that a third portion of the duration of consciousness is indeed perceived separately.
This is not so; for it is stated there [in the *Paṭṭhāna*] solely with reference to the duration of the continuous stream (*pabandha*).

If it is asked how this is known, it is because after first mentioning arising and passing away, it is subsequently stated again that "the duration of what is separate is discerned" in order to indicate its distinctness.
"Because this has been stated": otherwise, it would have to be said that "arising is discerned; the alteration of what stands is discerned; passing away is discerned. [Objection:

Is it not the case that so-called "continuity-stability" (*pabandha-ṭhiti*) is a mere designation (*paññatti*), and that while it is unconditioned (*asaṅkhata*), the discourses (*suttanta*) deal with the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṅkhata-lakkhaṇa*)? Therefore, it is impossible for that continuity-stability to be spoken of therein.
If it is asked, "Is it not understood? It is not that it cannot be understood.
For even in the Abhidhamma, in the descriptions of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhata-dhamma*), descriptions are seen by way of collections, configurations, continuities, and concepts (*paññatti*).

Thus, in the descriptions of the visible-object base (*rūpāyatana*) and so forth, there are [terms such as] long, short, fine, coarse, round, circular, square, hexagonal, octagonal, and sixteen-sided.

By such passages as "The lowlands become dry land," and by the Vibhaṅga’s presentation of the categories beginning with "Head-hairs, body-hairs, nails, teeth," conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhata-dhammā*) are pointed out.
In the Suttantas, there is nothing at all that needs to be said [regarding this].

For in such instances, even though the teaching proceeds by way of a designation (*paññatti*), it stands in direct contact with conditioned phenomena themselves. Therefore, just as for each of the two—arising and dissolution—there is a single [corresponding] factor...
"A moment for the mind is obtained; it does not remain [long] in that way. This is the intention of the teacher Ānandatthera.
And this statement appears in the *Saṃyutta-aṭṭhakathā* itself; however, it was rejected by the compiler (the author of the *Visuddhimagga*).
For it is said there: "But others say: 'It is impossible to designate a so-called "moment of aging" for immaterial phenomena. Correctly...
When the Fully Enlightened One says, "The arising of feeling is discerned; its passing away is discerned;

its alteration while it persists is discerned," he is thereby describing the three characteristics of immaterial phenomena as well. Having stated that these are obtained by taking the moment of existence as the basis, he says:
"The existence of all phenomena is what is called 'persistence' (ṭhiti)."
"The breaking up of that very [existence] is death; at all times, for all living beings.
With this verse of the Teacher, they establish that point. Alternatively, they say that "abiding" should be understood by way of the continuity of the stream (*santati*).
However, in this sutta there is no such distinction. Therefore, without contradicting the sutta, the verse of the Teacher [is applied].

"The Sutta alone must be made the authority. In this context, "the moment of aging" (*jarākhaṇa*) refers to the moment of stability (*ṭhitikkhaṇa*), which is a distinct field for aging situated between the moment of arising (*uppādakkhaṇa*) and the moment of dissolution (*bhaṅgakkhaṇa*). "Alteration" (*aññathatta*) is simply aging itself. "The moment of existence" (*atthikkhaṇa*) consists of those two moments [of arising and dissolution] alone.
Furthermore, although this position has been rejected, it is nonetheless perfectly consistent with the *Kathāvatthu* Pāḷi.
Furthermore, just as there is a cessation of the upward flight of a stone that has been thrown upwards, there is likewise a cessation of the mind’s growth, which is termed its "arising" (*udaya*).
For as long as arising does not cease, decay (*vaya*) cannot occur.
This very cessation, which is merely the limit of arising, can here be called by the synonym "stability" (*ṭhiti*); however, it is not to be counted as a separate [momentary phase].
Considering that there is no such thing as a single moment, only two moments of consciousness are mentioned in the Abhidhamma.

However, setting aside the initial limit of the phase of arising (*udaya-bhāga*) and the final limit of the phase of fall (*vaya-bhāga*), the characteristic of aging (*jarā*)—which consists in the process of maturation dependent upon the middle portion of the two phases—is indeed found even in formless phenomena (*arūpa-dhamma*).
With reference to this, it should be understood that in the *Dhātukathā*, it is stated that aging is included within the two aggregates of formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*).
[119] As for what is stated in the *Vibhāvani*:

“A state distinct from the phases of arising and dissolution, which faces toward dissolution, must also be admitted; that is named ‘stability’ (*ṭhiti*). This does not accord with the *Kathāvatthu-pāḷi*.
Half a day is the moment of arising (*uppādakkhaṇa*); half a day is the moment of dissolution (*vayakkhaṇa*). The first day is the moment of arising.
For one who investigates the phrase "the second momentary state," since the states of arising and dissolution are distinct,
a third state is indeed rejected in that textual passage.
By this, whatever [was stated] therein...
"But in the Pāḷi, that [distinction] was not stated by way of showing the method (naya) out of deference to the inclinations of those to be converted (veneyya).

For even an over-elaborate teaching of the Dhamma sometimes proceeds out of deference to the inclinations of those to be converted; for example, the arising of matter (rūpa) was taught by dividing it into two ways—as production (uppāda), accumulation (upacaya), and continuity (santati). This too is rejected. For regarding a Dhamma that deserves to be analyzed...
The term "making a division" (vibhāgakaraṇa) is appropriate both in terms of those to be trained (veneyya) and in terms of the Dhamma.
However, it is not logical to say that the reason the Abhidhamma does not speak of things separately when they do exist is because of those to be trained.
[121] As for what is there...
“Monks, there are these three conditioned characteristics of the conditioned found in the Sutta. Which three?
Arising is discerned; passing away is discerned; change while persisting is discerned.

Since arising and the others are stated thus for the purpose of showing the characteristics of conditioned phenomena alone, it is not possible [to apply them] to a continuum (pabandha) which has the nature of a conceptual designation (paññatti).”
"It was said: 'The stability of the unconditioned (asaṅkhata) is stated therein'—this too should not be accepted.

For even in the Abhidhamma, according to the method explained below, it is seen that there is a description of conditioned phenomena (saṅkhata-dhammā) under the heading of conceptual designation (paññatti).
[122] As for what is also stated therein:
It has been said: “Because a prefix functions only within the meaning of a verbal root, ‘is made known’ (paññāyati) has the sense of ‘is understood’ (viññāyati).
This too is not correct. For a sutta is a teaching that follows the proper sequence. Therefore, in this context, what is intended is simply the thorough making known for those to be trained.

That which is formless (arūpa) is subject to rapid transformation because its intrinsic nature is immaterial; matter (rūpa), however, is subject to slow transformation precisely because it is a material phenomenon.
It is stated in the *Paṭṭhāna-aṭṭhakathā*: "They are called 'forms' (rūpa) because they are deceptive (māyā).
However, in the *Vibhāvanī*, the reason given is:
"Because the state of being the grasper and the grasped is produced according to each respective moment. That is not a valid reason.

For it cannot be said that the immaterial apprehending [consciousness] transforms quickly or transforms slowly for the sake of the successful completion of the grasping of the material object to be grasped.
The construction is as follows: those seventeen moments of the seventeen types of consciousness are the life-span of material phenomena; they have a measure equal to seventeen consciousness-moments.
"Moments" refers to the life-span of material phenomena (rūpa-dhamma) that are excluded from the characteristics of matter (*rūpalakkhaṇa*) and from intimation (*viññatti*).
However, in terms of mere moments, according to the method of the *Aṭṭhakathā*, there are fifty-one moments; according to the method of the *Mūlaṭīkā*, there are thirty-two moments.
Among these, the two initial moments consist of only one: the moment of arising (*uppādakkhaṇa*). The two final moments consist of only one: the moment of dissolution (*bhaṅgakkhaṇa*).
It should be understood that among those [twenty-eight moments], twenty-eight moments in the middle constitute a single moment of presence (*ṭhitikkhaṇa*).

For the arising and dissolution of material phenomena that mature slowly cannot possibly be as swift as those of consciousness. In this context, the two types of intimation (*viññatti*) last for only a single thought-moment;
the continuity of accumulation (*upacaya-santati*) consists merely of arising, while impermanence (*aniccatā*) consists merely of dissolution; and the materiality of decay (*jaratā-rūpa*)...
They should be understood as lasting for only the moment of the stability (*ṭhitikkhaṇa*) of phenomena.
However, according to the method of the *Mūlaṭīkā*, it should be stated here that those sixteen mind-moments (*cittakkhaṇa*) constitute the lifespan of material phenomena (*rūpadhamma*).

For the commentator (*ṭīkācariya*), while establishing the words of the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā* found in the *Paṭiccasamuppādavibhaṅga*, acknowledges the state of having a lifespan of sixteen mind-moments; nevertheless, this is [stated] specifically in the *Khandhavibhaṅga*.
Since the proponent of the Great Commentary (Mahā-aṭṭhakathā) on the method of the arising and ceasing of forms has been refuted by the compiler for contradicting the Yamaka-pāḷi,
it is impossible to establish that position. For when that doctrine is refuted,
the theories of "sixteen-year life-span" and "more than sixteen-year life-span" mentioned therein are likewise refuted.
[124] As for that which is stated in the *Vibhāvani*, having rejected it as being without substance because it contradicts the method of the *Ṭīkā*, one who wishes to explain its meaning should say:
"The material form co-arisen with the rebirth-linking consciousness ceases together with the seventeenth [consciousness] from that point onward. Of the rebirth-linking consciousness..."

"The reason stated [by some]—namely, that 'the matter arisen at the moment of subsistence (thitikkhaṇa) ceases at the eighteenth moment of arising,' and so forth, because seventeen thought-moments are mentioned in the Commentary itself"—is not sound.

For the commentator has already examined the statement by the author of the *Saṅgaha* regarding the "seventeenfold association" (sattarasāyuka). Having demonstrated that very point, the method of the commentary [is as follows]:...
"Rejected" means it is not appropriate [to say they are simultaneous]. A "single mind-moment" (*ekacittakkhaṇa*) is like a moment of a single consciousness.

Although this moment is non-different in its actual meaning, it is treated as if it were different by way of conceptual designation, thinking "this is of the mind" and "this is of the material phenomena.
Those for whom a single mind-moment has passed are "those for whom a single mind-moment has elapsed" (*ekacittakkhaṇātītāni*). These are the five objects that have become exceedingly vast.
In the *Vibhāvani*, however, it is also stated:
"Are these [past aggregates] those that have passed away from a single moment of consciousness? This is not correct.
For the term "past" refers to phenomena that have ceased; it does not denote present material forms that have arrived after having transcended something.
It can be said that they "illuminate. Those for which many mind-moments have passed are called "those for whom many mind-moments have elapsed" (*bahucittakkhaṇātītāni*).

The great elements and so forth are the five objects. However, regarding material phenomena, a degree of strength must be admitted in their arrival within the range of other material phenomena themselves.
And these [material phenomena], having obtained complete conditions, exist only at the moment of their duration (*ṭhitikkhaṇe*).
It is stated that they "become powerful" only when they have reached their station (*ṭhiti*). By the word "only" (*eva*), the author of the *Ṭīkā* refutes the position of another;
for he maintains that material form (*rūpa*) strikes the sensitive organs (*pasāda*) at the very moment it arises.

Regarding the statement, "The five objects enter the range of the five doors," here the objects of visible form and sound do so by way of not having arrived (*asampatta*), while the others do so by way of having arrived (*sampatta*).
They come within the range [of the senses]. And this distinction is to be understood by way of the striking of the specific object (*visesa-ghaṭṭana*).
For the first two strike only by way of the sign (*nimitta*), not by way of the physical basis (*vatthu*). But the latter three strike by way of the physical basis, not merely by way of the sign.

Furthermore, "striking of the sign" (*nimitta-ghaṭṭana*) refers only to those who have not yet reached [the object], not to those who have reached it. "Striking of the physical basis" (*vatthu-ghaṭṭana*)...
But it occurs only when [the objects] have arrived; it does not occur when they have not arrived. "Nam" means:

just as the reflections of bodies are seen in the water of a lotus pond by those walking along the bank, yet those same reflections are no longer seen there by those who descend into that water—exactly so, the objects of form and sound do not strike [the sense-faculties] once they have arrived. Why? Because [they have passed] between the object and the subject.
Because of the absence of light and space, there is no room for a sign;
therefore, they do not strike [the body] without having reached it, but rather strike by way of establishing their own signs. Why? Because the space for the sign has been obtained.
However, the other three strike according to the very location where they are produced. Therefore, they strike only when they have reached [the object], not without having reached it.
In that regard, those [signs] which strike while still remaining unattained do so because they strike the sign from a distance by way of absorption;

therefore, even though they are large and numerous—appearing as the moon’s disk, the sun’s disk, and so forth, or as the sound of thunder, the sound of a ram, and so forth—they indeed come into range within each individual sense-faculty. As for the others, however...
"Only those that have reached [the sense base] strike it"—this should be understood to mean that at each sensitive part (*pasāda*), only one object at a time enters the range of impact.
And this has been stated by way of the five doors. However, in the case of the mind door, all objects enter the range of impact even without having reached it.
Furthermore, the phrase "at the five doors" here is stated by way of showing the specific (non-common) doors.
When those five objects strike their respective doors, they do not fail to enter the mind-door as well.
For it is stated in the Aṭṭhakathā: "Each single object enters the range [of consciousness] at two or two doors.
Therefore, when one sees the moon, the sun, a mountain, a tree, or whatever else, then in each case—
In the case of the eye-sensitivity, many [images] such as the moon’s disk appear simultaneously at the mind-door one by one;

it should be understood that the same applies to the remaining objects. Herein, "striking" (apāta) should be understood as when sealers, having placed a sealing block upon a palm leaf, strike it with a mallet, causing the sealing block to strike the palm leaf and thereby produce the appearance of the characters.
It should be viewed as being like that, since a transformation of the doors occurs.
Furthermore, regarding what is stated in the *Vibhāvanī*:
"In accordance with the mental application (*ābhoga*), groups of many [objects] come into range"—in this context, the phrase "in accordance with the mental application" must be investigated.
For however many objects there may be situated within the range of the eye and the other sense-doors, accompanied by light and so forth— all of them, even while one is sleeping,
unconscious, or otherwise occupied, and even while one is entering any jhāna, fruition-attainment, or the attainment of cessation,
come into the impact of their respective doors without any conscious effort on one's part. Not only that...
It occurs in the doors of the [other] sense-faculties themselves, and also in the mind-door (*manodvāra*).
It is not only in the life-continuum mind-door; rather, it indeed enters into the range of even the four-plane process-consciousnesses, such as adverting consciousness (*āvajjana*) and so forth.
For it is stated in the *Dvārakathā* (Discourse on the Doors): "One cannot say that this mind is not the mind-door. And this meaning applies to the sound of the first jhāna.

This should be illustrated by the reading "thorn" (*kaṇṭaka*). For when one has attained the first jhāna, a sound, having struck the ear, enters the range of the mind-door, which is termed the consciousness of jhāna.
At that time, the continuity of the jhāna-consciousness wavers and is interrupted.

One emerges from the jhāna; there is a lapse into the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*). Then, a process-consciousness (*vīthicitta*) occurs with that sound as its object. This applies to the second jhāna and the others as well.
But when entering [the attainment], one does not emerge with a slight sound; rather, one emerges only with an intense sound.
For those [form-sphere jhānas] are not called "unshakable" (āneñjappatta); it is only the formless jhānas that are called "unshakable.
Therefore, when entering them, one does not emerge even with an intense sound. Now, when these have thus come into range:

It should not be said that the process-consciousnesses (vīthicitta) proceed with those [five objects] as their sole object. They proceed only when the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) series or the impulsion (javana) series has been interrupted;

they do not proceed when it is uninterrupted. Even while proceeding, they proceed toward each respective object individually, having obtained specific conditions by way of intensity of the object and so forth.
It should be understood that they do not proceed toward all five objects simultaneously in a single moment.

And here, having understood that "transformation" (*pariṇāma*) refers to the modification of the case endings for the sake of meaning, one should connect the terms as follows: "passed over by one mind-moment" (*ekacittakkhaṇātīta*) refers to the five objects that have reached the state of presence (*ṭhitippatta*) within one mind-moment;

"passed over by many mind-moments" (*bahucittakkhaṇātīta*) refers to those [objects] within the five doors that have reached the state of presence after many mind-moments have passed. However, in the *Vibhāvanī*: [The text continues:
"In the *Vibhāvanī*, however... (as per the provided fragment).
It is said: "But those [five] clarities arise together with the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) which serves as their immediate condition for the vibration of the life-continuum.

If this were the case, it would follow that even five objects that have passed through many moments of consciousness could enter the range of the five doors at the same time as an object that has passed through only a single moment of consciousness.
However, in reality, only bases and objects that arise simultaneously within a single moment [can so enter].
They maintain that there is a mutual impact. Whether they have already arisen or have not yet arisen, it is our preference that their state of intensity alone serves as the measure.
Everything should be accepted after due consideration.
As for what is stated in the *Vibhāvanī*:
It has been stated: “Others say they arise together with adverting. That is not tenable;

for if that were so, it would entail a contradictory conclusion, namely, that the basis for the arrival of the five objects at the threshold is one thing, while the physical bases for the five consciousnesses are another. Thus, regarding the functioning of the objects in the five doors:

Having shown the initial characteristic, he now says "Therefore," etc., in order to show the complete analysis of the functioning of the sense objects and the occurrence of the process-thoughts (*vīthicitta*).

"Therefore" means because of the condition of the object coming into the range of the eye. It is said that "the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) vibrates twice" because it vibrates at the very same moment the object comes into the range of the eye;
for the life-continuum indeed comes into the range [of perception] simultaneously with the object's arrival. And here, "vibration" (calana) refers to...

It should be understood that the occurrence of a modification in the continuum of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) is like one who, having released the previously grasped object such as a kamma-object, now generates an effort to grasp a new object as it enters the field of perception.

And herein, the coming of the eye into the field of perception is the cause for the arising of visual consciousness alone, not for the arising of the adverting consciousness (*āvajjana*). This is because of the life-continuum.
It should be understood that the very arrival at the range of presentation (*āpātāgamana*) is also the cause for the arising of adverting consciousness (*āvajjana*).

However, in the *Vibhāvanī*, it is stated that even in the mind-door (*manodvāra*), the arrival at the range of presentation does not occur separately; rather, it is the striking against the eye and other sense organs by visible forms and so forth, which consists in their being situated in a suitable location.
And because that very [impact] is also the cause for the cutting off of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), it was said:

"For when the object is struck by the five sensitive organs through their presence in a suitable location, the continuity of the life-continuum is cut off by the power of that impact on the sensitive organs," and so forth.
That should not be viewed in that way.
For it cannot be said that "impact" (*ghaṭṭana*) is merely the standing in a suitable place.

Rather, it should be understood that when the lightning bolt—having stood in a suitable place—strikes the sign by way of impact and by way of striking the object, there occurs a conflict within the translucent elements (*pasāda*), which is called "churning," "agitating," "impacting," and "coming into contact. And this meaning has already been explained above.

And here, considering that this too is simply one fixed order of phenomena (*dhammaniyāma*), it should be understood that at each of the various pairs of doors, there is a simultaneous arrival at the threshold [of consciousness].
When the sense-faculties are struck by visible forms and so forth, there may be a movement of the fivefold consciousnesses supported by them. But why should one not raise the objection:
"How then can there be such movement for the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) which is supported by the heart-basis? This is not to be questioned.
[130] However, in the *Vibhāvani*, having raised that very same objection and seeking to resolve it, it says: "Because of being a single unit by way of continuity," and so forth.
In this context, it should not be said "by way of continuity" (*santativasena*); rather, it should be said "by way of configuration" (*saṇṭhānavasena*). And all of this...
It should not be accepted [as] essential.
Why? Because such a gradual progression has been firmly rejected in the Commentary itself. For it is stated there:
"Each individual object enters the range of two doors at a time. Indeed, a visible-object object [enters] the eye-sensitivity...
Having struck [the object], it enters the range of perception at the mind-door at that very moment. The meaning is that it becomes a condition for the vibration of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*).
This same principle applies to sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles as well.
For just as a bird, having come through the air and alighting on the top of a tree, strikes a branch of the tree, so too its shadow is cast against the ground.
The striking of the branch and the spreading of the shadow occur neither before nor after, but at one and the same moment.

Likewise, the striking of the eye-sensitivity by present visible forms and so forth, and the capacity to vibrate the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) such that it arrives at the "door of arrival" (āpāta) at the mind-door, occur neither before nor after, but at one and the same moment.
Thus, according to the simile of the bird, it is said to occur at that very instant and neither before nor after.

Having said "at that very same moment," because it has been firmly penetrated, one should understand that—without considering gradual movement—it is a simultaneous movement by way of the fixed order of phenomena (*dhammaniyāma*).
"Having cut off the stream of the life-continuum" means having completely severed the flow of the life-continuum.
"Adverting" means adverting [the mind] while not yet seeing, thinking, "What is this? "Seeing" means [seeing for oneself].
"Making manifest" means making it directly present. "Receiving" means grasping back the form exactly as it was seen, without letting it go.
"Examining" means thoroughly examining and investigating. "Defining" means establishing it clearly without confusion;
the meaning is that one observes it. "Having obtained conditions" means that by which conditions such as appropriate attention (*yoniso-manasikāra*) have been acquired.
The connection is: "Whatever impulsion it may be, it impels.
Furthermore, that impulsion impels either six times or five times—at a time when the object is weak, or at times such as fainting or near death; thus it is said "mostly" (*yebhuyyena*).

It "impels" (*javati*) because it proceeds with a speed like the falling of a thunderbolt. In that context, the first impulsion is so called because it has not yet attained the state of repetition (*sevana*).
It is the weakest of all. Then the second is stronger; then the third; then the fourth.
But this fifth is the strongest of all, being the "crown-peta" (muddhapatta). From this point on, it proceeds by gradually diminishing in strength.

It should be understood that when the seventh round has passed, its impetus (java) is completely exhausted. Regarding the phrase "impulsions follow one another," it is as if [running] against a current.
Just as water follows and pursues a moving boat, so too do the [subsequent] javanas follow [the object].
"Two resultants with that same object" means that two resultant consciousnesses perform the function of registering (tadārammaṇa) twice.
"As appropriate" refers to the javanas and the object according to the nature of the beings. "Lapse into the life-continuum" occurs when the object has passed beyond this [registering stage].
From the moment of adverting, or indeed from the very movement of the first bhavaṅga, the stream of consciousness that has arisen and emerged continues until the fourth javana;
from the fifth javana onwards, it has truly fallen away.
Even so, because the momentum of what has emerged is not entirely exhausted, it is not said to have "fallen" [until then]. From the second tadārammaṇa...
However, because the momentum that had arisen has been completely exhausted, that mental continuum is said to have "fallen" at that very moment.

Therefore, "falling" (pāta) means falling back. The "falling into the life-continuum" (bhavaṅgapāta) refers to the falling of the mental continuum into the state of the life-continuum; it should be understood as meaning "falling by becoming the life-continuum. It is a falling into the function of the life-continuum, into the position of the life-continuum, and into the object of the life-continuum.
"Or falling back into the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*). At this point, the similes of the gatekeeper, the villager, and the mango tree should be told;
all of these are to be found in the *Aṭṭhakathā*. The connection is that "up to this point, the seventeen moments of consciousness are fulfilled.
And here, the application of the six sextets (*chachakka*) should be stated. For wherever the eye-stuff (*rūpaṃ*) strikes the object (*ārammaṇaṃ*), that is the eye-base (*cakkhu-vatthu*).
Depending on that [heart-base], eye-consciousness arises taking a visible object that has impinged there as its object.

However, the other types of mental consciousness, such as adverting and so forth, arise depending on the heart-base—which arose simultaneously with each respective preceding consciousness—and taking that same object. The eye-door and the mind-door serve as the doors for all process-thoughts (vīthi-citta).

They accomplish the function of the door. And because this process arises at the eye-door, it is called the "eye-door process" (*cakkhudvāra-vīthī*). Because it is characterized by eye-consciousness, it is also called the "eye-consciousness process" (*cakkhuviññāṇa-vīthī*).

Because it arises in relation to an extremely powerful object capable of striking [the consciousness] after one mind-moment has passed, it is called the "process with a very great object" (*atimahanta-ārammaṇa-vīthī*). And herein, as many...
Visual objects, having arisen within the range of the eye, reach the state of presence.
It cannot be said that they do not strike against any one of the forty-nine units of visual sensitivity (cakkhu-pasāda) existing in succession during that period of presence.
However, among those, it is only a single unit of the eye that, according to its suitability, serves as the basis and the door for this cognitive process.

It accomplishes [its task]. And wherever this cognitive process (vīthi) proceeds, taking as its object the form that has been struck, that alone is called the "accomplishment of the function" (kicca-sādhana).
Regarding this, they speak of the "medium lifespan"; however, the others are called "vain bases" (mogha-vatthu), which they refer to as "short lifespan" and "long lifespan.
These, moreover, are of two kinds: those preceding and those following the accomplishment of the aforementioned function.
Both of these [bases and objects] should be understood as numbering forty-eight, being obtained by way of their presence at the moment of the arising of eye-consciousness.

However, the remaining factors—those preceding it and those following it, even though they have attained contact—are not included here because their status as fulfilling the functions of the base and the door is not to be expected. Herein, it might be asked: by this...
At the moment of arising in the cognitive process (*vīthi*), does that person know, "I am seeing this," or not? He does not know. But when does he know?
When the process of observation (*sallakkhaṇa-vīthi*) is occurring. For it is thus: first of all, the visual-door process (*cakkhu-dvāra-vīthi*) occurs;
after that, the mind-door process that follows it; after that, the process grasping the whole; and after that, the observation of color.
Then there is the grasping of the object; then the observation of the object; then the grasping of the name; then the observation of the name.
Therein, while the observation of color is occurring, one observes the color by thinking, "I see a blue color," and so forth.
By the observation of the object, one observes the shape. By the observation of the name, one observes the name.
