Thus, it is precisely while each respective process of specific-characteristic apprehension (*sallakkhaṇa-vīthi*) is occurring that one knows, "I am seeing this or that.

And herein, the third mind-door process, which apprehends the collection of forms repeatedly apprehended by the two preceding processes—like the apprehension of a circle of fire (*alātacakka*)—is called the "collective-apprehending" (*samudāya-gāhikā*).
For without the apprehension of the collective, there can be no clear apprehension of color-form (*vaṇṇa*).

"It is possible. However, "not sufficient to reach the arising of the registration [consciousness]" means that it has passed away after two cycles of three mind-moments—having become insufficient to proceed until the arising of the registration consciousness.
For that [kamma] for which two or three mind-moments have already passed is not sufficient, nor is it able, to proceed until the arising of the registration consciousness. Thus it is "insufficient."
"Having been offered" means it has passed away. "Has come into the range" means it has entered the range of the eye-door and the mind-door.

Regarding the phrase "there is no arising of registration": for one whose three thought-moments have already passed, since the object—which has a lifespan of fourteen thought-moments—has ceased together with the seventh impulsion (*javana*), there is no arising of registration with respect to that object.

This is appropriate. For the commentators of the Aṭṭhakathās do not maintain that within a single adverting-cognitive series (*ekāvajjana-vīthi*), the consciousnesses have different objects by way of time, as they do by way of mental state (*dhamma*).

If it is argued: "But for one whose two mind-moments have passed, while there remains only one mind-moment of life-span in the object, a registration consciousness (*tadārammaṇa*) must arise from that seventh impulsion (*javana*) onwards"—this is not so.
For such a perception of cessation cannot serve as an object for the arising of registration even once.

Indeed, in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*, within the enumeration of the occurrence of consciousness under the section on fruition (*vipāka*), only two instances of registration are mentioned: "two [instances] of registration."
As for what is stated in the *Vibhāvani*: "The arising of that object was restricted in the *Pāḷi* to exactly two occasions"— therein,
by "the *Pāḷi*" it should be understood that he is referring to the lineage of the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā-tanti*), for there is no such *Pāḷi* (scriptural text) where [the arising] occurs twice.
Thus, the arising of registration (tadārammaṇa) is determined.
However, the Majjhimabhāṇakas maintain that even a single instance of registration occurs;

since this has been refuted by the author of the *Saṅgaha*, it should be understood here as well that this [position] was rejected by the Thera. If that is so, why [does it appear] in the *Paramatthavinicchaya*?
"Once or twice they take that as their object," it is said because it was spoken by the Elder. This should be understood as being according to the opinion of the Majjhima reciters (*bhāṇaka*).
However, the teacher, the Elder Ānanda, maintains that even one [moment] occurs.

For just as the adventitious life-continuum (*āgantuka-bhavanga*) occurs once, it cannot be said that the registration consciousness (*tadārammaṇa*) likewise does not occur even once. And as for that which, in the reckoning of the occurrence of consciousness...
Thus it is said, "two [moments] have that as their object. That too is stated by way of the highest limit; it cannot be said that it is not so.
The connection is: "it is past, having been unable to proceed even until the arising of the impulsion (javana).
For that object for which four, five, six, seven, eight, or nine thought-moments (cittakkhaṇa) have passed—that [object], until the arising of the impulsion...
It is not able to proceed. The meaning of "having thus been unable" is that it has passed away.

"Even without the arising of impulsion" means because of the non-arising of impulsion as well. For this suffix *tvā* should be understood only in the sense of a state (*bhāva*), not in the sense of an agent (*kattṛ*).
Why? Because there is an absence of a common agent with its own primary action.
In the *Vibhāvani*, however, it is stated:
"And here, the suffix *tvā* occurs in the sense of cause (*hetu*). That is not correct.
For the meaning of cause, being an external referent, does not fall within the scope of the *kitaka* suffixes. Therefore, in this context, it is used solely in the sense of state (*bhāva*).
The suffix *tvā* [is used here]. From that, it should be understood that the nominative case ending occurs in the sense of a cause (*hetu*).
By this, even the occurrence of the suffixes *mhi*, *ca*, *māna*, and *anta* in the sense of a characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*) or a cause, which is stated in some places, is also excluded;
for external objects consisting of characteristics or causes do not fall within their scope. And herein, nine thought-moments have passed for whichever object.

Since the remaining eight consciousness-moments of that [person] have ceased along with the second determining (voṭṭhabbana) consciousness, it is logical that impulsion (javana) does not arise in him either;
the reason has already been stated. As for one whose four...

[or] eight consciousness-moments have passed—if it is argued that in his case impulsion must arise—no; for even one whose life-span consists of the remaining six consciousness-moments [does not experience it].
Indeed, an object cannot serve as a condition for the arising of javana.
For javana arises only when there is an object sufficient for it to proceed for seven turns; this is because, according to its natural law, the maximum duration of javana is seven moments.
In this context, however, just as in the case of the loss of consciousness, fainting, and the time of death, [the heart-base remains]—of the physical base...
Due to its lack of clarity and weakness, even the impulsion (javana) occurs for only five or six moments.
Likewise, even at the time of the natural (pakatika) process, if the object is weak, it occurs for only five or six moments. "Two or three times" means either twice or thrice;
for thus it is said in the Commentary: "Standing upon the determining (voṭṭhabbana), one or two consciousnesses occur."
It is said that "having obtained repetition from that, it stands at the stage of impulsion (javana) and then descends again into the life-continuum (bhavaṅga).
Here, by the phrase "having obtained repetition from that, it stands at the stage of impulsion," he demonstrates the occurrence of the third determining consciousness (voṭṭhabbana).
Otherwise, only one or two moments of consciousness would occur. Therefore, it is said: "Then it descends into the life-continuum."
"Could be" (*siyā*): however, "once" (*ekaṃvā*) should be regarded as merely a smooth turn of phrase, as in the expression "two nights or three nights" (*dirattatirattaṃ*).

Alternatively, "from that" (*tato*) means from one consciousness or from two consciousnesses; therein, by the first [alternative] the arising of the determining consciousness (*voṭṭhabbana*) twice is stated, and by the second, three times.
"Having obtained repetition" (*āsevanaṃ labhitvā*), moreover, is merely a figurative expression.
It should be understood that the *paṭṭhāna* does not state that there is repetition (*āsevanatā*) for determining (*voṭṭhabbanā*).

However, the Elder Ācariya Ānanda maintains here that the section on limited objects (*parittārammaṇa-vāra*) refers specifically to the arising of four or five impulsion moments (*javana*) when four or five consciousness-moments remain after determining, and not by way of the conclusion of determining. According to the *paṭṭhāna*, the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*)...

It is stated only that adverting (āvajjanā) is a condition for [the first impulsion] by way of the proximity-condition (anantara-paccaya). However, it is not stated that adverting is a condition for the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) by way of the proximity-condition.

And just as six or five impulsion-moments (javana-vāra) are required at the time of death through fainting due to the weakness of the physical basis (vatthu), so too here, it cannot be said that [only one impulsion is possible] due to the weakness of the object (ārammaṇa). And in this context, from the investigating consciousness (santīraṇa)...

It would be logical that there is one determining consciousness (*voṭṭhabbana*) when one moment of consciousness remains of the object, two when two moments remain, and three when more than that remain.
However, nowadays they have combined [the views] such that there are six limited-object cognitive series with two determining consciousnesses, and five with three determining consciousnesses.
This being so, in what kind of limited-object [series] are there two determining consciousnesses, and in what kind are there three?

"They should be investigated. However, as for an object that is insufficient to produce two or three acts of adverting (*voṭṭhabbana*), it does not even serve as a condition for the attainment of adverting;

thus it is said that in such a case there is only the vibration of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*). "There is no arising of process-thoughts" means that there is merely the vibration of the life-continuum twice.

"Thus, in this way, at the eye-door": in this manner, if a visible object that has passed away in a single moment of consciousness comes within the range of the eye, then according to the method described starting with those words, the occurrence of the object should be understood as fourfold by way of the four modes at the eye-door;
the same application should be made for the ear-door and so forth. "In every respect it should be understood as fourfold"—this is the connection.

Even an extremely limited object becomes an "object" for the first section merely by having come into the range of perception; it is not so by way of being made an intentional object (*ārammaṇakaraṇa*).
However, the other [objects] become objects for the remaining sections in both ways. Thus it is said that they are the objects of the four sections respectively.

In the *Vibhāvanī*, however, regarding the phrase "having become an object," the meaning stated as "having become a condition" refers to a very limited object; for it is said that wisdom is a condition for the section on Futility (*Moghavāra*).

There are exactly seven types of process-consciousness in the five sense doors according to their respective functions. "Arising of consciousnesses" (*cittuppāda*) is by way of the moment of the arising of those consciousnesses.
"Fourteen": the connection is that from the detailed enumeration according to the nature of consciousness, there are fifty-four. "Therein" refers to the limited (paritta) impulsion (javana) process.
However, in the mind-door (manodvāra), objects (ārammaṇa-dhammā)—whether they belong to the limited moment, the past, the future, or are timeless—indeed come into range.
Therefore, in that case, whether they have passed for one moment of consciousness or for many moments of consciousness, they must have reached their state of presence (ṭhitippatta).

Regarding the statement, "There is no such rule as 'it comes within range'": this refers to the mind-door (*manodvāra*). For while in the case of the eye-door and so forth, [an object] comes within range only upon contact (*ghaṭṭana*), that is called a "mixed door.

Here, however, only the pure [mind-door] is intended. Thus, even if a manifest object (*vibhūta-ālambana*) comes within range at the mind-door, there is no fixed rule that it must necessarily be apprehended.

Therefore, it was said: "There is no such rule. In that context, "at the mind-door" means at the pure mind-door. For where [an object] comes within range simultaneously with the impact in the eye-doors and so forth, that is called a mixed door; but here, only the pure one is meant.
That [resultant consciousness] is also twofold: that which follows upon the five doors and that which is established independently.

In this regard, just as when a bell is struck once with a stick, the groups of material phenomena (*rūpa-kalāpa*) constituting the body of the bell continue for a long time, striking one another and producing a succession of reverberating sounds;
so too, when the five sense-doors are struck once by an object, the five [sense-consciousnesses]...

Even though the avenue of the door has been interrupted, the past fivefold object, having returned as it were to its original state, causes many thousands of mind-door process-thoughts (manodvārika-vīthicitta) to proceed in a stream.
The life-continuum (bhavaṅga) stream that serves as the door for these is called the "consequent" (anubandhaka).
And those thoughts are known as "consequent process-thoughts" (anubandhaka-vīthicitta).

[Such states] exist. However, where the impact on the five sense-doors occurs without being followed by [subsequent mental processes], and objects of the six types simply enter the field of awareness in their respective ways, that is called "established separately.
But how do objects of the mind enter the field of awareness in that separately established mind-door?
It is said: from what has been seen, through the connection with what has been seen; from what has been heard, through the connection with what has been heard.

They come into range through such causes as: by means of faith, by preference, by reflection on modes, by approval resulting from meditation on views, by the power of various kamma, by the power of various psychic abilities (*iddhi*), by way of the flow of the elements, by way of the intervention of deities, by way of recollection, and by way of penetration.
In this context, "the seen" refers to the five objects previously apprehended through the five sense-doors.
That too, when the conditions are met at a later time, certainly enters the range [of consciousness] at the pure mind-door.

"Connected by what was seen" means that which is similar to what was seen. For when one, having previously seen something, infers another thing—whether it be unseen, past, future, or present—that which is similar to it certainly enters the range [of consciousness] in great abundance. "Hearing" (suta) means...
That which is grasped after hearing from another consists of the six objects of cognition (*chaḷārammaṇa*). However, that has a vast range of scope;
for having heard the teaching of the Omniscient One, there is nothing whatsoever that is without an object. That which is called "connected with what is heard" is similar to what is heard.

Faith (*saddhā*) is the act of believing in another. Inclination (*ruci*) is one's own opinion. Discernment of modes (*ākāraparivitakka*) is [the examination of] the shadow of the meaning and the shadow of the phrasing.
And "reflection" is the pondering in various ways by relying on the shadow of a cause.

"Adherence to views" (*diṭṭhinijjhānakkhanti*) is the grasping [of an object] after one has repeatedly examined it through wisdom, or through one's own tenets, and having reached a conclusion that "it is exactly thus.
The rest is self-evident. And herein, the state of being a proximate decisive support condition (*anantarūpanissaya-paccaya*) involves a great expansion of the mental continuum.

It occurs. Even after an object has been thoroughly cultivated and has ceased, for a hundred years, a thousand years, or even in another existence, that object remains a condition for the vibration of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*).
Furthermore, consciousness—when developed by the aforementioned causes such as what has been seen and so forth—becomes greatly expansive. Having obtained some sign, in one [moment]...
It proceeds by pervading even thousands of objects seen and so forth within a single moment.

Because of those causes, the mental continuum, though constantly being urged on, becomes inclined toward emerging from the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) at all times whenever there is no cause for weakness of mind, such as physical exhaustion.
For indeed, the mind does not delight in an object that has not become manifest.

One delights only in what has become manifest. Therefore, the attention associated with the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) repeatedly stirs the life-continuum and directs the process of adverting (āvajjana) again and again toward those objects for which conditions have been obtained.
At that time, those objects come within the range of the life-continuum consciousness, which is functioning in a manner directed toward them through its association with that attention.
For it cannot be said that there is no "turning toward" (abhininnāhāra) another object for a consciousness that is already proceeding by having grasped one object.
The statement that "resultants with that as their object proceed" is made with reference to beings in the sense-sphere (kāmadhātu).
However, for beings in the fine-material and immaterial spheres, there is simply no arising of resultants with that as their object even when the object is clear. And as it is here...
Thus, even in the case of the five doors, there is no arising of registration consciousness (*tadārammaṇa*) when the objects of the presence of forms are too vast.

However, it should be understood that the statement "when the object is not manifest, there is only a lapse into the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) at the conclusion of the impulsion" is made by way of the maximum limit.
In the *Ñāṇavibhaṅga-aṭṭhakathā*, however, it is stated by way of the occurrence of determining consciousness (*voṭṭhabbana*) two or three times.
Even when the object is not extensive, the stage of determining (voṭṭhabbana) has been introduced.

Furthermore, that which was called the fourth stage—the so-called "vain stage" (moghavāra)—consisting merely of the vibration of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) at the five doors, is also appropriate to be included here.

For even in the pure mind-door, when an object enters the field of perception, if the process-consciousness (vīthicitta) does not arise and the life-continuum vibrates twice, there occurs the stage of turning back (nivattanaka).
There will certainly be no limit; for when an object has entered the field of perception and the *bhavaṅga* has vibrated, it is not the case that the "occurrence of the object" does not take place.

Thus, in this mind-door as well, the occurrence of the object—which serves as the cause for the four stages known as the registration (*tadārammaṇa*), impulsion (*javana*), determining (*voṭṭhabbana*), and the futile (*mogha*)—should be understood as being fourfold according to their respective order. In that regard:
The objects of the registration phase (*tadārammaṇa-vāra*) are called "very clear" (*abhivibhūta*); those of the impulsion phase (*javana-vāra*) are called "clear" (*vibhūta*);

those of the determining phase (*voṭṭhabbana-vāra*) are called "unclear" (*avibhūta*); and those that are the objects of the futile phase (*mogha-vāra*) are to be understood as "extremely unclear" (*ati-avibhūta*).
In this context, "very clarity" should be understood as the extreme strength of either the object or the consciousness. Even when [the consciousness] is weak...
For when the mind is extremely powerful, an object such as earth or mountains becomes what is called "overly vivid.
And when the mind is extremely powerful, even Nibbāna, though exceedingly subtle, becomes what is called "overly vivid. The same applies to the remaining [bases].

Furthermore, in this context, the classification of the turnings (vāra) is twofold: that which is consecutive (*anubandhaka*) and that which is established independently (*visuṃ siddha*). Therein, the consecutive [turning] occurs by way of being consecutive to the eye-door and so forth.

It is fivefold. In each of these, there are four sections: the section on the past, the section on the aggregate, the section on the basis, and the section on the name. Among those, the sections on the object-of-result (tadārammaṇa) and so forth should be applied as appropriate. Furthermore, there are the following distinct sections:

the section on what is seen, the section on what is connected with what is seen, the section on what is heard, the section on what is connected with what is heard, and the section on what is cognized.

The section on what has been cognized (*viññāta-sambandha-vāra*) is sixfold. Here, it should be understood that the sections occurring by way of faith (*saddhā*), inclination (*ruci*), mode (*ākāra*), reflection (*parivitakka*), and so forth, are stated as the "section on what has been cognized" and the "section on what is connected to what has been cognized.
However, in the *Aṭṭhasālinī*, the object grasped by way of faith, inclination, and so forth, exists both as it is and otherwise; therefore, in the commentary...
It is said that it is not apprehended. Let it be so or otherwise; when there is the occurrence of process-thoughts (*vīthicitta*), it must necessarily be apprehended.
In this regard, for each single occasion, there are four occasions by way of the occasion of the object-repetition (*tadārammaṇa*) and so forth.

And within those, the objective phenomena (*ārammaṇadhammā*) exist by way of the classification of the sense-sphere, the sublime, and the supramundane, as well as by way of the present, past, future, and the timeless.
"They should be applied as appropriate. However, nowadays they establish a distinction of turns based on the past life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) and the registration consciousness (*tadārammaṇa*).
In that regard, establishing a distinction of turns based on the past life-continuum is useless;

for in the mind-door, unlike in the five doors, there is no possibility of the objects being strong or weak by way of their momentary duration. This is because [the objects] are non-existent at that time.
"...and because of the arrival [of consciousness] at those [objects], whether past, future, or liberated from time. Here it might be asked:
the masters of the Aṭṭhakathās maintain that for a single adverting-cognitive series (*ekāvajjana-vīthi*), the object is indeed non-different from them in both its nature and its time.
Yet these beings, having observed various modes of appearance, certainly know one another's minds. Furthermore, there are those who possess the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittavidū*).

The deities know even without the observation of external signs. In that regard, when knowing another's present mind, does one cultivate adverting (āvajjana) and thus know that other's mind as co-arising with one's own, or does one advert to it?

Or rather, do they know it as co-arising with various impulsive moments (javana) from another? And as for the impulsive moments, do they know that which is co-arising with the adverting, or that which is co-arising with the subsequent impulsions?

"Or it arises simultaneously with itself individually. What does this mean? If, first of all, that which arises simultaneously with the adverting consciousness adverts and knows, then in that case it is non-different from the mental state (*dhamma*) but different in time.

For that [subsequent] consciousness is present relative to the adverting consciousness, whereas it is past relative to the impulsion moments (*javana*). Alternatively, it adverts to that which arises simultaneously with itself individually.
And they know it. This being so, there is non-difference in terms of time; however, there is indeed difference in terms of the phenomenon (*dhamma*).
Furthermore, whatever they know as having arisen simultaneously with the adverting consciousness (*āvajjana*), that very thing is what is adverted to. Even in this way, there is indeed difference.

Herein, in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, having stated that there is non-difference in terms of the phenomenon by saying, "They know that very thing which has arisen simultaneously with the adverting consciousness, and that very thing is what is adverted to,"...
It has been determined that even though that consciousness has ceased, by way of its duration and its continuity, it is still considered "present" for the impulsion moments;

this is the established conclusion. However, according to the opinion of Ācariya Ānanda, at the time when one perceives various aspects in another person and understands their respective intentions, the advertings and impulsions each advert to the consciousness that has arisen simultaneously with themselves.
And they know it. Furthermore, there is nothing here that is distinct from the object either by way of its intrinsic nature (*dhammata*) or by way of time.
For the object of all [consciousnesses] is indeed the mind itself, and it is present. Nor are the impulsion moments (*javana*) called "without adverting" (*nirāvajjana*).
For even by means of adverting, it is the mind itself that adverts; and the impulsion moments know the mind itself. But if, in the case of adverting...
When "mind" is adverted to, the impulsion-moments know it as "form"; or when "form" is adverted to, they know it as "mind";
or when "blue" is adverted to, they know it as "yellow. This being so, the impulsion-moments are technically termed "without adverting" (nirāvajjana) with respect to the object (dhamma).
Likewise, when "past" is adverted to, they know it as "present. And this being so, they are technically termed "without adverting" with respect to time (kāla).

"They exist. And because it is stated in the *Paṭṭhāna* that a past state is a condition for a present state by way of the "immediate condition" (*anantara-paccaya*), it is therefore appropriate here to speak of the "present" solely by way of the moment (*khaṇa*).

It is not by way of the period (*addhā*) or the continuity (*santati*). Otherwise, even in all the sections on process-thoughts (*vīthi-citta*), the pastness and so forth of objects would have to be defined solely by way of the period and the continuity.
"It may be said": in the verse, "only three" refers to the three by way of function (*kicca*).

"Ten impulsions are stated" refers to ten being stated by way of the moments of consciousness-arising (*cittuppādakkhaṇa*). "In detail" means by way of the detailed exposition of the nature of consciousness. "Therein" means in the mind-door (*manodvāra*).

"Forty-one" refers to forty-one [types of consciousness] by way of the sense-sphere consciousnesses (*kāmāvacara-citta*), excluding the fivefold sensory consciousnesses and the mind-element (*manodhātu*). "Therein" [refers to the same].
In the occasion of limited javanas (*parittajavana-vāra*). [The Section on the Limited] 138.
The intention is that there is no distinction between the manifest (*vibhūta*) and the unmanifest (*avibhūta*); only the manifest is obtained.
For absorption (*appanā*) cannot occur with an unmanifest object. Likewise, there is no arising of the registration consciousness (*tadārammaṇa*), for it does not arise from what is too distant.
"The javana of absorption follows that object. In this context, the connection is: "among the twenty-six sublime and supramundane javanas, whichever javana enters the process of absorption.

It is stated that "of the eight sense-sphere javanas associated with knowledge," because a two-rooted javana devoid of knowledge lacks the nature of stability, it does not serve as the immediate decisive support (anantarūpanissaya) for absorption.
Regarding the phrase "by means of the preliminary (parikamma), access (upacāra), conformity (anuloma), and change-of-lineage (gotrabhū)":

here, *parikamma* is so called because by means of this, absorption (*appanā*) is performed—that is, prepared—through proximate factors such as the balancing of the faculties. It is called *upacāra* because it moves toward (*upecca carati*) absorption;
the meaning is "movement in proximity. Furthermore, this movement in proximity should be understood as being capable of bringing about absorption in the immediate future. Of which... [text continues]
"Immediately upon its occurrence, absorption arises. "Conformable" (anuloma) means that which is favorable to absorption by dispelling opposing states through the process of absorption;
it is established for the sake of absorption, and the meaning is simply that absorption flows forth.
It is so called because "by means of this, one goes toward [the goal] or awakens to the meaning. Thus, it is both a designation and awakening.
It is called *gotra* because it protects (*tāyati*) and guards (*rakkhati*) that twofold lineage (*gava*). A lineage (*jāti*) is a synonym for a clan (*anvaya*).
It is called *gotrabhū* because the lineage is overcome (*abhibhuyyati*) and cut off (*chijjati*) therein.
And here, all four types of impulsion are indeed called "preliminary impulsion," "access impulsion," or "conformity impulsion"; however, the term *gotrabhū* applies only to the last one.

This is the name. However, here, for the purpose of including all four stages of the name, it should be understood that "preliminary work" (*parikamma*) is spoken of by way of the names *parikamma*, *upacāra-anuloma*, and *gotrabhū*.
And having done so, there is no room for such an objection as: "Why is it called 'preliminary work' only at the beginning?
Do not the others also prepare for absorption (*appanā*)? Thus it is said: "Four times or indeed three times."
Either four times or three times. Therein, by the first word "eva" (only/just), the fifth [moment], the arising of the lineage (*gotrabhu*), is excluded.
For at that time, the impulsion (*javana*) is said to have fallen; it quivers and trembles.
It is unable to become a condition for advancing beyond the realm of sense-desire (*kāmagotta*) and reaching the higher plane. By the second [word], the second...

The arising of the change-of-lineage (*gotrabhu*) is excluded. For at that time, the conformity (*anuloma*) thought, having not yet attained sufficient repetition, is unable to bring its immediately succeeding consciousness to the state of change-of-lineage.
By this very fact, it is established that there can be no attainment (*appanā*) beyond the fifth [moment] nor before the fourth.
However, by the word "or" (*vā*), it is indicated that for one of dull wisdom, it occurs only four times.
"Not three times" means that for one of sharp wisdom, it occurs exactly three times. This shows that it does not occur four times.
However, in the *Aṭṭhasālinī*, having divided [wisdom] into three types—sluggish, medium, and great—it appears as if the arising of five preliminary and impulsion moments is permitted.
But since this has been thoroughly investigated and rejected in the other commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), [the former view is not accepted].
"It should not be grasped.
As for what is stated in the *Vibhāvani*:
"Because it is close to the sixth and seventh moments of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*), like a person near a precipice, it is unable to become established by way of absorption (*appanā*)."
In this context, "by way of being near to the life-continuum" (bhavaṅga) means by way of being near to the state of the life-continuum.
For from the fifth impulsion onwards, the stream of impulsions gradually becomes exhausted in its momentum.

It thus transforms itself for the sake of the state of the life-continuum. And by doing so, the simile of a person near a precipice also becomes applicable. "Immediately after it has ceased" means when [the consciousness] has ceased.
The word division is *anantarameva* (immediately after). To the question "Immediately after what?", since nothing else has been heard, the meaning "after that which has ceased" is already obtained.
For absorption (*appanā*), when it arises, does so starting from the fourth or the fifth [jhāna];
it does not arise from the sixth or the seventh. Even when one has attained mastery, its arising occurs only in the fourth or fifth.
If it does not obtain [the object], it simply does not arise at all. But if it does obtain it, it continues to proceed uninterruptedly even for a whole day.
Therefore, it should be understood that the statement "the fourth or the fifth" is said merely to define the initial limit. For this very reason, he will later say:
"it enters the path of absorption," and "after that, at the conclusion of absorption, there is only the falling back into the life-continuum (bhavaṅga)."
If, however, from the fifth [impulsion] onwards, the javana is said to have "fallen," then why is it that from that point on, appanā-javana occurs within the field of falling?
It is replied: when a clod of earth is placed in the hand, its "field of falling" begins the very moment it is released from the hand.
Even so, the clod thrown by the strength of the hand still travels a great distance.
And here, the speed of the clod is rooted in the speed of the hand; the speed of the hand, in turn, is rooted in the strength of the body.
In this context, the absorption-javana should be regarded as like the clod. The period subsequent to the fourth [moment] is like the field where the clod falls.
The change-of-lineage (gotrabhu) javana is like the speed of the hand. The preceding preparation (parikamma) and access (upacāra) javanas are like the strength of the body.
Strength must be observed. The strength of the impulsions (*kāmajavana*) in the cognitive process of a beginner is like the strength of a young infant lying on its back.
The strength of the impulsions in the cognitive process of one who has attained development is like the strength of a grown man.
And just as a clod of earth thrown by a young infant falls even at the mere moment it is released from the hand, so too in the cognitive process of a beginner...

The appanā-javana falls after having impelled [the mind] once. Just as a stone thrown by one who has attained strength goes even further and further, without falling within the area where it would normally fall, so too in the cognitive process of attainment (*samāpatti-vīthi*), the appanā-javana proceeds for a long time, even for a very long time.
However, in the *Mūlaṭīkā*, it is stated that the appanā-javana, even while proceeding in the "falling area," reaches another plane.
It is said that as long as one has not attained another object, it is not called "fallen. Here, one might ask:
why is it stated that the impulsion (javana) falls starting from the fifth [moment]?

Is it not the case that precisely because it does not fall, the seventh impulsion-consciousness—due to its state of being very powerful—is both a giver of result quickly in the immediately following existence and an action of immediate retribution (ānantariya-kamma)? As for the five consciousnesses in between...

Likewise, due to the absence of strength, they yield their result only after a long time in subsequent existences such as the third birth, and they do not attain the status of an *ānantariya* (immediate) karma.

However, this should not be viewed in that way; for if it were called "strong" simply because it yields its result quickly, then the first volition would have to be called the strongest of all, since it yields its result in this very existence.
"...it gives. This, however, is the definitive conclusion here: the transformation of the first volition should be understood as being like that of grass and trees living for one year;
that of the seventh volition as being like that of those living for two years; and that of the intermediate volitions as being like that of great sal trees.
In this context, grass and trees living for one year are pithless; and because they are pithless, they are weak and lack endurance.
They do not remain for long. Therefore, their transformation occurs more rapidly;
for they grow more quickly, reaching increase and full development. They flower and bear fruit more swiftly, and they fall and vanish more quickly.
They are unable to survive even one summer season; they do not reach a second year. And here, the summer season is like the time of death.
This is to be understood. However, those that live for two years possess a small degree of core-essence (*sāra*).

Because they possess this core-essence, they are somewhat strong and long-lasting. For this very reason, their transformation takes a long time. Indeed, in their first year they sprout and attain growth and increase;
yet they are not able to flower or bear fruit. It is only in the second year that they flower and bear fruit.
They fall away and disappear. However, they are unable to survive beyond the second summer;
they do not reach a third rainy season. But the great *sāla* trees possess all essential qualities; they are strong and long-enduring.
Therefore, they undergo transformation only very slowly. For even after one or two years, they remain only a span or a cubit in height.
They do not attain growth or increase; they are unable to flower or bear fruit. Moreover, they remain for only a very short time;

having endured for only five or six hundred years, they fall away. In the same way, the first impulsion-consciousness (pathamajavana-cetanā), because it has received no prior repetition, is without substance and weak.
It is unable to produce a single separate existence by itself, nor a single instance of death.
It is not able to transcend [this state]. Having ripened in this very existence, or even without ripening, it is exhausted.
However, the seventh impulsion-consciousness (javana-cetanā), due to its repeated practice, becomes somewhat substantial. It is capable of producing a single separate existence (bhava).
Precisely because of its substantiality, it undergoes transformation slowly; it is unable to ripen in this present existence.
It is not able [to ripen] here. It ripens only after reaching another existence.

However, among the "fallen" (patita) javanas, because of the weakness of their final state as javanas, they are unable to survive past the second moment of death. Having ripened or not ripening within that very second existence, they are exhausted.
As for the remaining five types of intermediate volitions (*majjhima-cetanā*) that have been well-practiced, [they ripen in subsequent existences].
The gradual process of transformation should be understood according to the method already described.
Furthermore, this matter should be illustrated not only by the similes of the grass and the tree, but also by the simile of living beings.
Whatever beings born from a womb are short-lived by nature, they dwell in the womb more briefly and are born more quickly; and their various limbs...
They become more firmly established more quickly. The faculties also reach maturity more quickly; they arise and depart on that very same day.
They seize their respective objects and attain consciousness of their own respective spheres more quickly.
They grow old and die more quickly. However, for those born with a long life-span, [the stages] such as dwelling in the womb...
"All [these] are accomplished only gradually. In this context, it should be understood that the sublime wholesome states remain in the seventh impulsion-moment.
For the preliminary impulsions, in terms of their long duration, are like well-cooked rice grains;
the absorption impulsions, in terms of their short duration, are like well-cooked rice porridge—thus they too are of very brief duration.
They exist. Having ripened or not having ripened in the second existence, they are exhausted.
Even in this present existence, when obstructed by even a slight adverse state such as sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*), they reach a state of total non-ripening.
Therefore, in that sense, they are called "weak."
And because the certainty of the ripening of the fruits of deeds of immediate retribution (ānantariya-kamma) is not possible without a restriction of time;
and because this restriction of time applies exclusively to the seventh javana, and not to the intermediate javanas—
for there is no such rule for them that they must ripen only in a specific existence— therefore, regarding these two kinds of certainty...
Because it is established [as such], the fact that the volition of the seventh impulsion (javana) is an immediate-retribution action (ānantariya-kamma) is thereby proven.
One should conclude here that this is not due to its being more powerful. However, in the *Mūlaṭīkā*, having raised the objection:

"But surely, because the volition of the seventh impulsion is powerful, it possesses both the state of being experienced upon rebirth (upapajjavedanīya) and the quality of being an immediate-retribution action," the following intention is expressed therein:

It may be so. Because the final javana-cetanā is well-conditioned by way of being the proximate condition for the resultant continuum that exists as the proximate condition for rebirth-linking, that seventh javana-cetanā becomes both "to-be-experienced-in-the-next-birth" (upapajjavedanīya) and "of immediate retribution" (ānantariya).
He replies that it is not because of its strength, as is the case with a javana-cetanā that has not fallen [into the resultant stream]. That [reply] does not seem correct.

It is seen. For if this were so, it would have to be said that the first impulsion-cetanā is called "to-be-experienced-in-this-life" (diṭṭhadhammavedanīya) because it is well-conditioned by way of being the immediate condition (anantarapaccaya) for [the subsequent moments].

However, in the *Mahāṭīkā*, it is stated that even the final impulsion-cetanā, though weak, is "to-be-experienced-after-rebirth" (upapajjavedanīya) because it is endowed with the specific function of determination (sanniṭṭhānakicca) and thus possesses a specific capacity for the ripening of the fruit.
And it is said that this [state] is one of immediate retribution (*ānantariya*). "As appropriate" means according to the specific individual.

"By way of the direction of the application" means in accordance with the directing of the mind toward either the sign of the *kasiṇa* during the development of the preliminary stage, or toward the characteristics such as impermanence.
"The path of absorption" refers to a continuous series of absorptions. And this occurs many times.
This was stated for the purpose of including the javanas of absorption (appanā). For this very reason, it was said immediately after that:
"At the conclusion of absorption, there is only a lapse into the life-continuum (bhavaṅga). In this context, "from there" means from the fourth or the fifth [javana].

If this were the case, it would follow that the lapse into the life-continuum occurs invariably at the fifth or the sixth [javana]. Therefore, it was further stated: "At the conclusion of absorption, there is only a lapse into the life-continuum. Thus it is said.
The intended meaning is that there is no arising of the registration consciousness (*tadārammaṇa*).
However, it is stated in the *Vibhāvanī*:

"The doctrine of other schools, who claim that even at the conclusion of absorption there is the occurrence of sense-sphere javanas for the sake of completing the seven javanas in certain sections on absorption, is here excluded by the word 'only' (*eva*)."

"In that" means in that series of appanā-javana moments. It is said that for javanas occurring in immediate succession, there is no such thing as "different feeling," hence the phrase "immediately following a javana accompanied by joy," and so forth.
However, in the *Vibhāvani*, the reason is stated:
"Because it has not been asserted that those with different feelings serve as mutual object-predominance conditions (*āsevanapaccaya*) for one another. That is not correct.
For here, the state of being a condition through repetition (*āsevanapaccaya*) is not the criterion. Why?

Because it must be admitted that even for the fruition and impulsion moments—which are opposed to repetition—there is a non-differentiation of feeling from the preliminary and impulsion moments, and between each other. "To be expected" (*pāṭikaṅkhitabbā*) means necessarily to be admitted.
However, in the *Vibhāvani*:
It is said, "They are to be praised. That is not correct, for no such basis for commendation is seen [in the texts].

Even though this sequential order occurs in the cognitive process of the path to Arahantship immediately after the path-kusala [consciousness], this rule of priority and sequence applies only to the absorption-javanas together with the preliminary (parikamma) and impulsion (java) javanas.
It is stated that after the functional javana (kriya-javana), the fruit of Arahatship (arahattaphala) occurs as well.

Following a wholesome (puñña) javana accompanied by pleasure (sukha), thirty-two absorption javanas (appanā-javana) can arise. Following a wholesome javana accompanied by equanimity (upekkhā), twelve arise;

following a functional javana accompanied by pleasure, eight arise. The construction is that following a functional javana accompanied by equanimity, six absorption javanas arise. In this context, "thirty-two" refers to...

There are thirty-two [types of consciousness] by way of the four wholesome consciousnesses of the form realm excluding the fifth jhāna of the fruit of arahantship, the sixteen wholesome consciousnesses of the path, and the twelve lower fruits.
There are twelve by way of the wholesome consciousnesses of the path of the form and formless realms belonging to the fifth jhāna and the lower fruits.
There are eight by way of the four functional consciousnesses of the form realm excluding the fifth jhāna.

There are eight [types of absorption] by way of the four fruits of arahantship. There are six by way of the five fine-material and immaterial functional states belonging to the fifth jhāna, and the fruit of arahantship.
For worldlings and those in training (sekkhā), forty-four absorptions are possible beyond the three-rooted sense-sphere wholesome states.
For detached arahants, [there are those] beyond the three-rooted sense-sphere functional states...
The construction is: "fourteen types of absorption arise.
(139) "In every way" means even by all modes, such as being excessively large and so forth. "Therein" refers to these aforementioned five doors and the mind door.
Furthermore, the reading "sabbatthāpi" (in all places) is also found; for that very reason, it is stated in the commentaries: "sabbatthāpi" [refers] to the five doors.
It is said, "also at the mind-door. "Desirable" means what is wished for (*iṭṭha*). By whom is it wished for? By the worldly masses.
And therein, excluding those who are extremely exalted and those who are extremely destitute, it is by the middle class of people.
For when this is so, there is a proper definition of the desirable and the undesirable; thus it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*. In whatever object wholesome...
When a resultant state arises, that very object is called "agreeable" (*iṭṭha*); but when an unwholesome resultant arises, that very object is called "disagreeable" (*aniṭṭha*).
For it is not possible for a resultant consciousness to be deceived regarding an object as being either agreeable or disagreeable.

Furthermore, it has been stated that the quality of being agreeable or disagreeable should also be understood by way of the sense doors. Therefore, [this applies] to those states occurring within a continuum bound by faculties and non-faculties.
In a certain group of material phenomena (*rūpa-kalāpa*), among the visible forms and other qualities, some are desirable and some are undesirable.
Sometimes they are desirable, sometimes they are undesirable; therein, some are desirable and some are undesirable.
For example, in a certain flower, the color is desirable, but the odor is undesirable, the taste is undesirable, and the tactile quality—the rough contact—is undesirable.
In some instances, the color is desirable, the fragrance is desirable, while the taste and so forth are undesirable.
Likewise, even in a single group of material elements within the Buddha’s body, the color is desirable, but the fragrance is undesirable.
Even in the bloated corpse of a dead black dog, the color is desirable, but the fragrance is undesirable; for that color would be desirable if it belonged to a cloth worn or draped over one.
"That cloth is of great value" means: sometimes it is desirable, sometimes it is undesirable.

Fire, for instance, is desirable in winter as a condition for a pleasant result, but in summer it is undesirable as a condition for a painful result. Cold water is desirable in summer, but in winter it is undesirable.
Likewise, a cloth with a pleasant touch is desirable to the natural body, but when it comes upon a wound—
"Unpleasant" (*aniṭṭha*). Or rather, for one who touches [an object] gently it is pleasant, but for one who touches it firmly it is unpleasant.

"Not pleasant" means unpleasant; in that unpleasant [object]. "Pleasant" refers to the pleasant and the neutral; the connection is with the fivefold sense-consciousnesses, the receiving consciousness, the investigating consciousness, and the registration consciousness, which are the wholesome-resultants.
And here, the investigating and registration consciousnesses are associated exclusively with equanimity (*upekkhā*).

These things are to be understood. For this very reason, he said: "Exceedingly desirable," and so forth. Therein, "exceedingly desirable" refers to the six objects of sense—such as the colors of gold, silver, and gems;
the color of the palmyra tree; the color of silk cloth; and the appearance of celestial nymphs—which are intensely desired by the great masses of worldly people.
And because, in this context, it is only when there is contact with undesirable objects that unwholesome karma has the opportunity to ripen.

[Association with] a desirable object belongs only to wholesome kamma; therefore, in the case of an undesirable [object], there are only unwholesome results, and in the case of a desirable [object], there are only wholesome results—this rule is established.

However, the restriction regarding feeling is due to the extreme weakness of those results produced by the power of kamma alone, without the force of its own initiative, like the reflection of a face in a mirror.
It should be understood that by thus imagining and fashioning [the object], the apprehension is established as being directed toward the object itself according to its nature.

And this applies not only to resultant states; rather, it is stated with the intention that even in the mental continuum of one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava), which is free from perversion, the association with feeling in the functional javanas of the sense-sphere occurs in accordance with the object itself—there too, it is accompanied by joy.
"At the conclusion of functional (kriya) impulsion," and so forth. "There too" means even among those resultant [consciousnesses].

"At the conclusion of functional impulsions accompanied by joy" refers to the end of functional impulsions accompanied by joy that have occurred in relation to a very desirable object, such as the praise of the Buddha.
"At the conclusion of functional impulsions accompanied by equanimity" refers to those occurring in relation to an undesirable, a desirable-neutral, or [neutral] object.

At the conclusion of functional javanas accompanied by equanimity. Furthermore, this rule regarding registration (tadārammaṇa) at the end of functional javanas is indeed stated in the Aṭṭhakathā as well.

For it is said there: "The pair of sense-sphere functional [consciousnesses] accompanied by joy and associated with three roots is a condition by way of immediate antecedent for the five resultants accompanied by joy, by way of registration," and so forth. And this...
This was stated with reference to functional javanas that proceed by way of their natural flow.

Likewise, however, for functional javanas that proceed through the influence of matter or mental volition (cittātisaṅkhāra), there is indeed an association with equanimous feeling even toward the desirable, and an association with joyful feeling even toward the undesirable. As it is said:
"And how, Ānanda, is one noble with developed faculties? Here, Ānanda, when a bhikkhu has seen a form with the eye..."
The agreeable arises; the disagreeable arises; the both agreeable and disagreeable arises. If he so desires:
"May I dwell perceiving the non-disagreeable in the disagreeable," he dwells there perceiving the non-disagreeable. If he so desires:
"May I dwell perceiving the disagreeable in the non-disagreeable," he dwells there perceiving the disagreeable.
The entire *Indriyabhāvanā-sutta* from the *Uparipaṇṇāsa* should be cited here. In that context, it says:
"The agreeable arises; the disagreeable arises; the both-agreeable-and-disagreeable arises.

By this, it is shown that for those whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*), there is a connection with joy (*somanassa*) toward the desirable through the natural mode of functional impulsion (*kāmakriya-javana*), and a connection with equanimity (*upekkhā*) toward the undesirable. If he so desires...

"One should dwell perceiving the repulsive in the non-repulsive. However, by the passage beginning "He dwells there perceiving the non-repulsive," it is stated that when such a mental formation exists, there is an application of equanimity even toward the desirable, and an application of joy even toward the undesirable.
Furthermore, in the *Satatavihāra-sutta* regarding those whose taints are destroyed, it is said here: "When a bhikkhu, having seen a form..."
"He is neither elated nor dejected; he dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending"—by such passages, the rejection of mental joy (*somanassa*) at the six sense-doors is stated.
That too should be understood as being said with reference to the abundance of such formations of body and mind in those [beings].

Or rather, because even those whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*) [experience joy] upon seeing the form of the Buddha, or upon seeing the establishment of a posture appropriate for striving, and so forth...

And they indeed become joyful. Therefore, it is also appropriate to say that this was stated with reference only to desirable and undesirable visible objects and so forth, which serve as the basis for lust and other defilements.
And herein: How does one dwell perceiving the unrepulsive in the repulsive?
One pervades an undesirable object with loving-kindness (*mettā*), or one brings it to mind by way of its elements (*dhātu*). Thus one dwells perceiving the unrepulsive in the repulsive.

He dwells. How does he dwell perceiving the repulsive in the non-repulsive? He pervades a desirable object with the meditation on the foul (*asubhā*), or he contemplates it as impermanent (*anicca*). In this way, "he dwells perceiving the repulsive in the non-repulsive," and so forth;
according to the method of the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*, such mental volition (*cittābhisaṅkhāra*) should be understood here. However, others...

It is said that when those whose taints are destroyed encounter an extremely desirable object, such as the beauty of a celestial nymph, they then direct their attention toward it as foul or contemplate its impermanence.

In this case, either the undesirable characteristic of foulness or the characteristic of impermanence becomes the object for the functional javanas of equanimity; it does not remain an extremely desirable object.
Such as the appearance of celestial nymphs (*devaccharā*) and so forth.

Likewise, when an extremely unattractive object—such as the body of a leper or a cripple—comes into range, they then pervade it with loving-kindness (*mettā*), or they resolve it in terms of the elements (*dhātu*).
In that context, even what is considered desirable possesses only the characteristics of being free from enmity, harmlessness, and so on.
It becomes the object of impulsion-moments associated with joy (*somanassa-kriyā-javana*). It is not something extremely undesirable, such as a body afflicted by leprosy or similar conditions.

Therefore, it is argued that these impulsion-moments—just like the resultant consciousnesses of the sense-sphere (*kāmavipāka*)—are always associated with a feeling that corresponds exactly to the object. That is not tenable;
for those characteristics (the *lakkhaṇas*) cannot be found separately from the beauty of celestial nymphs and so forth. By means of them...

However, they are obtained together with [the other feelings]. Therefore, just as it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* that the arising of joy (*somanassa*) occurs even toward extremely undesirable objects such as a bloated corpse (*uddhumātaka*), by means of seeing the benefits (*ānisamsa*) and by means of seeing the progressive distinctions in the development of meditation (*bhāvanā*);

and just as in the case of the Elder Mahāmoggallāna, who—by seeing the excellence of the Buddha and his perfect enlightenment, and by seeing his own attainment—[experienced joy] even toward what was undesirable...
The arising of joy in relation to the form of a skeleton-like *petā* is stated in the Canon (*pāḷi*).
And just as the arising of joy even toward putrid sour gruel— though undesirable— obtained from the hand of a leper by the Elder Mahākassapa through such a mental volition (*cittābhisaṅkhāra*),
is stated in the Commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), so too here the mental volition consisting of the pervasion of the foul (*asubha*) and so forth [is required].
It should be understood that what is extremely desirable is a condition for the arising of javanas of equanimity, while what is extremely undesirable is a condition for the arising of javanas of joy.
For this so-called "desirability" or "undesirability" of objects is established merely by the whim of worldly people;
it is shallow and serves as the basis for the defilements that consist of the perversions. As it is said therein:
What is inferior form? That form which is despised and held in contempt by this or that being, and so forth.
Herein, by the phrase "by this or that being," he shows that the status of objects as desirable or undesirable is established by the conventional consensus of worldly people.
Therefore, even that which has the appearance of a celestial nymph for worldly people whose perversions have not been abandoned...

The apprehension of things that are extremely desirable as being extremely undesirable, and the apprehension of things such as the praise of the Buddha—which are extremely desirable—as being undesirable:

both of these occur only through the influence of perversion (*vipallāsa*). However, when wise disciples of the Buddha perceive celestial nymphs and the like as undesirable, and perceive the praise of the Buddha and the like as extremely desirable, [this is not so].
It should be understood that both of these occur through the power of wisdom alone.

As for what is stated in the *Vibhāvani*: "However, because wholesome and unwholesome states proceed within mental continua where the perversions have not been abandoned, there is a grasping of even the desirable as having the aspect of the desirable, the intermediate, or the undesirable; and likewise, there is a grasping of even the undesirable as having the aspect of the desirable, the intermediate, or the desirable."
And as for what was stated there—
"Even functional javanas proceed in accordance with the object alone due to the absence of cognitive distortions (*cittavipallāsa*) in those whose taints (*āsava*) are exhausted"—

that indeed must be investigated. For those phenomena which are devoid of the eye, they follow the influence of the mind and follow the influence of the object precisely by way of cognitive distortion.
"They are wholesome" means that wholesome states for the most part proceed according to their object, but not so the functional impulsions (*kriya-javana*).

For those whose taints are destroyed do not follow after objects or follow after the mind with respect to things—whether desirable or undesirable—that are conventionally regarded as such by worldly people. As it has been said:
"Forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and delightful tangibles..."
"The wise do not tremble at desirable or undesirable phenomena.

Therefore, even after a functional (kiriya) javana of joy, the registration (tadārammaṇa) moments must likewise be associated with the feelings of joy or equanimity. The same applies after a functional javana of equanimity.
However, in the *Mūlaṭīkā*, regarding this point, it is stated that in the *Paṭṭhāna* [the rule is] for wholesome and unwholesome [states].

When the [kamma] has ceased, the result arises by taking that as its object; thus, it is stated that the "taking-as-object" (tadārammaṇa) occurs only immediately after wholesome or unwholesome [states].
It is not stated to occur after the indeterminate (abyākata), nor is any instance found where it is stated to occur after functional (kiriya) states.

And since it does exist [after those], there is no reason for it not to be mentioned. Furthermore, this life-continuum (bhavaṅga) is like a river current, which can only be crossed by a boat going against the stream.

It is logical that such a javana follows immediately after a state of wide diffusion. However, for one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) and who possesses the sixfold equanimity, there is no javana characterized by peaceful conduct.
Therefore, it is stated that the occurrence of a registration consciousness (tadārammaṇa) following a functional javana (kriya-javana) must be examined.

In the *Paṭṭhāna*, however, within the question-section of the "Wholesome Triplet" (kusalattika), specifically in the analysis of the object-condition (ārammaṇapaccaya-vibhaṅga), this is discussed in the three sections concerning the indeterminate states (abyākata).
For both trainees (*sekkha*) and worldlings (*puthujjana*), the predominance is precisely that [resultant] object.

It is not the wholesome [consciousness] that is the wholesome impulsion. Therefore, in both sections, after stating that "the trainee or the worldling contemplates the wholesome as impermanent and relishes the wholesome," it is further stated:
"When the wholesome has ceased and the unwholesome has ceased, the resultant arises with that as its object."

For an Arahant, however, even the impulsion (javana) and the registration (tadārammaṇa) are merely predominant. Therefore, it is said that an Arahant contemplates the wholesome as impermanent, suffering, and non-self;
but it is not said that when functional or inoperative states have ceased, a resultant state arises as registration.
If this were stated, then registration alone would be considered predominant.
It may be so. By the phrase "one contemplates even when that [resultant consciousness] has not arisen," the object-referent (tadārammaṇa) is already included.
Therefore, it was stated in the *Paṭṭhāna* that "the wholesome... arises" immediately after the wholesome and unwholesome, but not immediately after the indeterminate;
and it was further stated that there is no reason for not mentioning it when it actually exists. That...

This is indeed not logical. However, in the *Anantarapaccayavibhaṅga* (Analysis of the Condition of Immediate Succession), it is stated: "Wholesome aggregates that are subject to ripening are a condition for emergence;

unwholesome aggregates that are subject to ripening are a condition for emergence; functional aggregates that are subject to ripening are a condition for emergence; and aggregates that are neither resultant nor subject to ripening are a condition for emergence.

By such statements, [it is shown that] following a functional impulsion (*kriyajavana*), there occurs both the registration consciousness (*tadārammaṇa*) together with the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*).

The place where it is stated by the name "emergence" (vuṭṭhāna) is indeed seen. Therefore, that which was said—that nowhere is the place for the registration (tadārammaṇa) following an action seen—is also not tenable.

Furthermore, even for one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava), the peaceful dwelling is not merely the six-factored equanimity; the functional javana (kriya-javana) is not without its expansion. [This applies] to the wholesome javana (kusala-javana).
"Because, like that [other consciousness], it too is originated by a gross bodily or verbal application.

However, in the *Vibhāvanī*, while stating a rebuttal to the opinion of the *Ṭīkā*, it is said: "If an indeterminate [consciousness] were also called 'that-object' (tadārammaṇa) immediately after [the impulsion]," and so forth.
"Thinking that the votthabbanā might continue its occurrence even after a limited object, the object [of the javana] was not stated immediately following the functional javanas.
This is not correct. For in this Paṭṭhāna, there is nothing unstated such that one might think, "This or that [state] would be conceived [to follow]. Nor is it the case that an Arahant...

In the passages stated according to the practice of insight (*vipassanā*)—such as "one contemplates the wholesome as impermanent, suffering, and non-self"—there is the possibility of limited objects (*parittārammaṇa*) pertaining to the five doors.
[The jhānas] are accompanied only by equanimity (*upekkhā*), not by joy (*somanassa*). Why? Because joy and displeasure (*domanassa*) are mutually contradictory.
For this very reason, their mutual immediate conditionality (*anantarapaccaya*) is not mentioned in the *Paṭṭhāna*.

Here, by showing that the registration (*tadārammaṇa*) is restricted to the functional and grief javanas (*domanassajavana*) alone, the Elder indicates that no such restriction exists for other wholesome or unwholesome javanas. Therefore, of the eight...

Immediately after eighteen types of impulsion—eight unwholesome (akusala) associated with greed, two rooted in hatred, and eight wholesome (kusala) associated with desire—there arise, in accordance with the object, either registration (tadārammaṇa) consciousnesses or life-continuum (bhavaṅga) consciousnesses. However, for the most part, following an unwholesome impulsion, the registration is rootless (ahetuka);
following an impulsion with two roots, it possesses two roots; and following an impulsion with three roots, it possesses three roots.
The general rule is that immediately after a javana with three roots (tihetuka), there occurs only a javana with three roots.

However, for one in whom wholesome javanas with two roots or three roots frequently manifest, when unwholesome javanas occasionally arise, then even following those unwholesome javanas, javanas with two roots or three roots may occur having those same objects. This applies to one for whom unwholesome javanas...

They frequently occur. Sometimes, when two-rooted or three-rooted wholesome impulsion-moments have impelled, even immediately after a wholesome [impulsion], rootless "object-identical" (tadārammaṇa) moments arise.
For this is stated in the Paṭṭhāna: "In relation to rootless aggregates as impermanent...
sorrow arises. When the wholesome or unwholesome has ceased, the resultant with roots arises as object-identical."
It arises. Resultant [consciousness] without root-cause arises as the registration (tadārammaṇa).
For indeed, although those called registration-moments are produced by a single kamma that generates rebirth-linking, they appear in various ways within different cognitive processes (vīthi).

However, there is no need for further explanation regarding those produced by various kammic acts that generate resultants during the course of existence (pavatti). Therefore—because immediately after [the feeling of] mental grief...

There is no arising of joy; therefore [it is said]. "Of one whose rebirth-linking has joy" means of a being who has taken rebirth-linking by means of any one of the four great resultant states accompanied by joy.

"The occurrence of an object at that time" means the cause for the arising of registration (*tadārammaṇa*), or simply the arising of registration itself. "Whatever" refers to any visible-object base or other objects, whether desirable or undesirable.
"Whatever": "formerly familiarized" means that in this very existence, it has been familiarized by way of frequent grasping at moments prior to the present moment;

the meaning is that it has been repeatedly practiced. "Limited object" means an object consisting of limited phenomena (*parittadhamma*). "Taking as an object" means having made it the focal point (*ālambitvā*).
"Investigation accompanied by equanimity" refers to the two types of investigation accompanied by equanimity.

In the case of a desirable object, there is wholesome-resultant investigating consciousness accompanied by equanimity; in the case of an undesirable object, there is unwholesome-resultant investigating consciousness accompanied by equanimity.

However, for those in whom the other four types of resultant consciousness accompanied by equanimity generally occur by nature, it cannot be said that even those [other four] do not become adventitious *bhavaṅga*. But in the Commentary, according to the opinion of the Elder Mahādhammarakkhita—

Because it falls within the scope of the "majority-rule" principle (*yebhuyyaniyama*), only two types of rootless investigating consciousness accompanied by equanimity (*upekkhā-santīraṇa*) are mentioned, corresponding to unwholesome javanas.

For this very reason, later on—in the section examining the Theravāda—the fact that the position of those Theravādins is incomplete is demonstrated by pointing out that they teach only rootless registration (*tadārammaṇa*) following an unwholesome javana. When...

It is stated in the Aṭṭhakathā that when unwholesome [consciousness] flashes between wholesome javanas, then at the conclusion of the wholesome, it is appropriate for there to be a tadārammaṇa (registration) with a root-cause, similar to what was habitual; this is likewise appropriate even when the tadārammaṇa is without a root-cause.
Therefore, all six types of resultant consciousness accompanied by equanimity indeed become the adventitious bhavaṅga.

It should be understood as follows. Herein, for one whose rebirth-linking was accompanied by equanimity, even when very powerful and clear desirable objects such as the Buddha’s virtues arise, there is no possibility of an object-receiving consciousness (*tadārammaṇa*) because grief arises;
thus, immediately after the impulsion of grief, there is a lapse into the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*).
However, for one whose rebirth-linking was accompanied by joy, in all cases—whether the objects are desirable or undesirable—[the process continues].

When one arouses mental distress (*domanassa*) toward the six objects—whether they be great or obscure—there is no possibility of that [distress] becoming the object of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*).

Nor, considering that the root-life-continuum cannot arise [in such a state], does one of the six resultant states accompanied by equanimity (*upekkhā-sahagata-vipāka*) arise as an adventitious life-continuum immediately after the mental distress, according to the circumstances.
The same applies when that very person [arouses distress] regarding the praises of the Buddha and so forth.

"Of one who arouses mental distress toward objects that are excessively desired, excessively great, or excessively manifest—whether these be the six sense-objects or sublime concepts (*mahaggata-paññatti*).
And here, because it is stated in the *Dhātuvibhaṅga* of the Abhidhamma:
"But, friend, the first application of attention is toward all phenomena"; and also in the *Mahāhatthipadopama Sutta*: "And internally, friend..."
The eye is unimpaired, external forms come into its range, and yet there is no corresponding act of attention;
as long as this is so, there is no manifestation of the corresponding portion of consciousness.
But when, friends, the internal eye is unimpaired, external forms come into its range, and there is the corresponding act of attention—then [the corresponding portion of consciousness arises].
In this way, there is the manifestation of the corresponding portion of consciousness. Friends, when the internal ear...

[and so on] ...the nose... the tongue... the body... and the mind are unimpaired, and external phenomena come into its range, yet there is no corresponding act of attention, then there is as yet no manifestation of the corresponding portion of consciousness. But when—

"Friends, when the internal mind is unimpaired and external phenomena come into its range, and there is the corresponding act of attention, then the manifestation of the corresponding portion of consciousness occurs. Thus it is said.

Therefore, the so-called "process-thoughts" (vīthicitta) do not arise without preliminary adverting (āvajjana). If, by way of the nature of things or by way of time, [the conditions] are met through adverting...
Whatever object has been determined and adverted to, that very object they seize; even those [preceding moments] seize it as well.
If something has been adverted to without being determined, they too seize whatever was adverted to, provided it is of a similar nature.

However, within a single cognitive process (*ekāvajjana-vīthi*), all the process-moments do not have different objects—whether by way of the adverting consciousness, or by way of mutual exclusion, or by way of their intrinsic nature, or by way of time.
"It should be understood that they exist.

Here, it might be argued: "If that adventitious life-continuum (bhavaṅga) arises by taking as its object some other limited (paritta) object previously familiarized, rather than the object presented at the beginning of a single cognitive process (vīthi) by the adverting consciousness (āvajjana), then [the following would occur]."

If this were so, it would follow that there is such a thing as "non-adverting" (nirāvajjana). Furthermore, it would follow that [the consciousness] could have an object different from that of the adverting consciousness and the others, both in terms of its intrinsic nature (dhamma) and its time.

This is true; however, just as in the cognitive process of the path (maggavīthi) the change-of-lineage (gotrabhu) and the purification (vodāna) moments, and in the process of the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti) the fruition-consciousness (phalacitta), and for one emerging from cessation (nirodha), these are indeed non-adverting and have a different object.
Thus, for this [access consciousness] as well, there is no fault regarding its lack of non-interruption (*nirāvajjanatā*) or its having a different object (*bhinnārammaṇatā*).

Furthermore, as for that which has been stated in various places—that in a single existence the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) is identical to the rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) in terms of both its intrinsic nature (*dhammatā*) and its object (*ārammaṇa*)—that was said with reference to the fundamental life-continuum (*mūlabhavaṅga*). This, however, is the adventitious life-continuum (*āgantukabhavaṅga*), so there is no fault.
"Having intervened" means having made that incoming bhavaṅga its immediately preceding condition (*anantara-paccaya*). Thus say the teachers.

However, the intention is that this procedure does not exist in the Pāḷi or in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā. They maintain that the registration consciousness (*tadārammaṇa*) occurs only at the conclusion of sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) javanas, and not at the conclusion of sublime (*mahaggata*) or supramundane (*anuttara*) javanas.
If one asks why, it is because [the registration consciousness] belongs to the sense-sphere.
This is because the javanas alone possess vibration, whereas the others do not.
However, in the *Vibhāvanī*, the reason given is:
"Because it is produced by kamma which has craving for sense-pleasures as its source. That is not a valid reason.
Furthermore, the sublime and supramundane javanas—excluding those of direct knowledge (abhiññā)—have non-limited objects.
However, since their registration (tadārammaṇa) moments have only limited objects, there is no possibility for registration to arise at the conclusion of these.
As for some of the javanas of direct knowledge, although they may have limited objects, they are more peaceful; thus, there is likewise no arising of registration at the conclusion of these either.
[137] By this, [the arguments] such as "because it is not a producer" and "because it lacks the state of being equal to a producer" are also refuted.

They maintain that only beings of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) have that [state] as their object, not beings of the fine-material or immaterial spheres. For [that state] does not arise in those [beings].
At the conclusion of sense-sphere javanas that have limited objects, there is the arising of registration (tadārammaṇa).

This is because there is no sense-sphere life-continuum (bhavaṅga) capable of serving as the support for such registration, and because the sublime life-continuum is too tranquil to perform the function of registration.
However, eye-consciousness and ear-consciousness [arise] through the eye and ear faculties of beings possessing form.
Due to the influence of the process of occurrence (*pavatti*), and because the determination of consciousness is established according to the specific doors and cognitive series (*vīthi*),

the receiving (*sampaṭicchana*) and investigating (*santīraṇa*) consciousnesses occur only with respect to the seven classes of material phenomena (*rūpa*). They maintain that the "registration" (*tadārammaṇa*) occurs only when sense-sphere phenomena (*kāmāvacara-dhamma*) serve as the object,

and not with respect to sublime (*mahaggata*) or supramundane (*anuttara*) conceptualized phenomena (*paññatti-dhamma*), because registration consciousnesses have exclusively limited objects (*paritta-ārammaṇa*).
Furthermore, the reason why those [objects] are exclusively limited in their capacity as objects has already been stated below.
In the *Vibhāvanī*, however, the reason "because they are unfamiliar" (*aparicitattā*) is given; that is not the reason.

For indeed, the mind— whether by the power of conceptualization (*vikappa*) or through a specific practice of meditation that has reached absorption (*appanā*)— proceeds toward even an unfamiliar object, just as it does toward Nibbāna.
[139] And as for the reason stated in the *Vibhāvanī*— "because it is produced by kamma dependent on craving for sense-pleasures"— that too has already been refuted above.
For it is precisely for this reason that, in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, after stating, "What is the use of this investigation of logic?", all the reasons stated in the *Vibhāvanī* are rejected.

[The phrase] "In the sense-sphere, impulsion is restricted to sentient beings as its object" means that among the impulsions included within the sense-sphere plane, [it is restricted] to sentient beings...
When there is a threefold restriction by way of the objects [of consciousness], it is stated that "the registration [consciousness] occurs when the object is clear or very great.
By this, the restriction is shown as follows: the so-called registration [consciousness] occurs only when the object is clear (*vibhūta*) or when the object is very great (*atimahanta*);
however, it does not occur wherever registration might otherwise occur. This very [object] is what is called "clear" (*vibhūta*).

And there is a rule that [the object] is indeed "very great" (*atimahanta*).
