Therefore, it should be understood that for the material-brahma beings (*rūpabrahmā*)—who are produced by sublime kamma and possess very clear physical bases—the cognitive processes (*vīthi*) that arise generally have manifest objects (*vibhūtārammaṇa*), and their objects are indeed very great.

However, some, failing to observe this point, [claim that] in the realms of both the fine-material and the immaterial, there are cognitive processes with manifest objects and cognitive processes with very great objects.
They say that [the registration consciousness] is not obtained. [The Rule for the Object. 140.
Regarding the phrase "in the case of the impulsion consciousnesses," the word *ca* has the sense of *pana*. They impel exactly six times. The intention is:
"even during the normal state, when the object is weak. For in the Commentary as well, during the normal state, the weakness of the object...

It is stated that the sense-sphere impulsions (kāmāvacara-javana) occur six times at the very moment of death. However, some consider that the phrase "six times" is stated with reference to the period of fainting.
Regarding "weak occurrence": at the time near death, because the objective base has been passed over by many mind-moments, it is weak;
furthermore, even at other times, due to its extremely soft nature, its being afflicted by something, or its being overwhelmed, [the consciousness occurs weakly].
At the time when [the mind] proceeds by way of the slackened momentum of the impulsive consciousnesses (javana) which depend upon that [object], due to the weakness of the physical basis (vatthu).
"At the time of death, etc. means: at the time near death, at the time of fainting, at the time of becoming unconscious, and at the time of extreme youth.
Therein, "the time of fainting" refers to those who are overwhelmed by unbearable forms and painful phenomena, and for whom the coarse physical body (karaja-kāya) is excessively [afflicted].

The time of being afflicted is when one has reached a state of distress. The time of being unconscious is the period when natural consciousness has vanished due to the force of rapture, or because of being overcome by sleep, or by possession by a *yakkha*, or by means of intoxicants such as liquor and wine.

The time of extreme infancy is the period during which the internal bases of a child—whether still in the womb or just born—are exceedingly tender. For in such times, the pathways of the six sense-doors [are intermittently obstructed].
Even when occurring, they generally do not proceed through a full series of impulsion moments (*javana*).
Rather, they proceed as either two or three registration moments (*voṭṭhabbana*) or four or five impulsion moments.

In this context, the series of two or three registration moments is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, while the series of four or five impulsion moments is stated in the *Mūlaṭīkā*. As for the phrase "only five times," this refers to [the case of] death...
This was stated by way of the time when one is dying (sannakāla). It is not by way of the time of falling down, etc.

And that [is] only with reference to ordinary beings (pākatika-sattā). However, for those who pass away immediately after jhāna, or immediately after reviewing (paccavekkhaṇa), or immediately after direct knowledge (abhiññā), or who attain final nibbāna (parinibbāyanti), their jhānas and so forth—whether fivefold, more, or less—are called "death-impulsion" (maraṇāsanna-javana).
It should be understood that they "exist. And this meaning will become clear later in the section on the arising of death.

Regarding the phrase "at the time of the Blessed One’s Twin Miracle and so forth," it should be understood that by the word "and so forth" (ādi), the swift occurrence of such [powers] by others, such as the Elder Mahāmoggallāna, is also included. For it is said in the *Visuddhimagga*: "But this..."
Mastery up to the head [of the body] was attained by the Blessed One during the Twin Miracle (*yamakapāṭihāriya*).

Or, at such times as these, it occurs for others as well. However, according to the entire statement, with the exception of a time when a light occurrence similar to the Twin Miracle takes place, even for the Blessed One, at other times, the seven types of reviewing consciousnesses (*paccavekkhaṇacitta*) arise in a coarse manner. But for others, it is simply a matter of speaking.
He shows that [it] does not exist. Regarding the statement "there are four or five reviewing consciousnesses," it is also logical to interpret the meaning as follows:
even for the Blessed One, there are five reviewing consciousnesses when his mental activity is slow, and four when his mental activity is swifter.
In the *Vibhāvanī*, however,
it is stated that for the Blessed One there are four [powers], while for others there appear to be five or even six. In that context,
when performing the Twin Miracle (*yamakapāṭihāriya*), the Blessed One [emanated] pairs of things, such as masses of fire and streams of water.
For the purpose of manifesting the miracles, he first attained the foundational jhāna upon the fire-kasina.
Then, he reviewed two of the jhāna factors. Thereafter, he resolved: "Let a mass of fire proceed from my upper body.
Then, he attained direct knowledge (abhiññā) upon that very kasina. By means of that direct knowledge, a mass of fire proceeded from his upper body.
Then he entered the foundational jhāna upon the water-kasiṇa. Then he reviewed two jhāna factors. Then he resolved: "Let streams of water flow from my lower body.
Then, by means of that very kasiṇa, he attained direct knowledge (*abhiññā*).
By way of direct knowledge, streams of water flowed from his lower body. This same method applies to the remaining elements as well. And herein, due to the lightness of its occurrence—
Because they are desired, there are two rounds of reviewing for each [of the three miracles], consisting of four or five impulsion-moments (*javana*).
Between two rounds of impulsion, there are exactly two life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) moments. And these two appear to those watching the two miracles as if they were occurring simultaneously.
However, nowadays, some [also maintain this] regarding the reviewing of jhāna by a beginner.
They say there are four or five impulsion-moments (*javana*). "For the beginner" means for one engaged at the very beginning of the accomplishment of the work of yoga.

"The first arising absorption" is the first conceptualization (*kappanā*); the meaning is "in that first conceptualization," which refers to the cognitive process (*vīthi*) of the beginner’s absorption.
For at that time, all sublime (*mahaggata*) impulsions are exceedingly weak because they lack further repetition (*āsevana*).
"They impel only once" refers to the impulsions of direct knowledge (*abhiññājavana*), such as the transformations of psychic power (*iddhivikubbanādi*).

Because they are employed solely for the accomplishment of a task, and because there is nothing further to be done after that accomplishment—whether at the time of a beginner or at the time of mastery—it is said that "the impulsions of direct knowledge also always impel only once.
And just as it is with the impulsions of direct knowledge and so forth, so too it is with the impulsions of the Path (*maggajavana*).

It is said that "but four... are of a single thought-moment" because they flow only once, as there is nothing further to be done after the accomplishment of the task of abandoning the respective defilements.

Alternatively, because the fruit is immediate to the volition of the path, the opportunity for the fruit to occur is exhausted as soon as the path has arisen; thus, there is no occasion for the path-consciousness to arise again.
It is said: "But four... and so on, up to "...occur in a single moment of consciousness.

Because the arising of javanas is by nature limited to a maximum of seven moments, two fruition-consciousnesses arise after the fifth [moment] following the path that has arisen for one of dull faculty. For one of sharp faculty, three [fruition-consciousnesses] arise after the fourth [moment] following the path that has arisen;
thus it is said, "...after that... and so on, up to "...arise. At the time of the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti)...
However, because such a preparatory effort (*payogābhisaṅkhāra*) was performed in the prior stage, there is no further occurrence of consciousness beyond two moments;
thus it is said that [the mind] "ceases" (*nirodha*). Regarding this, the phrase "twice" is stated by way of the maximum description.
For it is also said that one becomes "without consciousness" after having passed over one or two mental moments.

The fourth immaterial javana refers to the javana of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatana*), which is of the nature of wholesome for a non-returner (*anāgāmin*) and of the nature of functional (*kriya*) for an arahant.
It is stated that "at the time of emergence" and so forth because it occurs only once, being merely the outflow (*nisanda*) of cessation at the moment of emerging from it.
In that context, "the fruit of non-returning or the fruit of arahantship" means either the fruit of non-returning or [the fruit of] arahantship.
"Or the fruit of arahantship. This is the nominative case used to characterize one state by another state. Therefore he said, "ceased.

In all instances, "in the cognitive process of attainment" means throughout the entire process of attainment, by way of both meditative absorption (jhāna-samāpatti) and the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti).
The statement that "there is no process-series like the stream of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga)" is said with reference to the time when mastery has been attained.

However, for one who has not yet performed the preliminary work (*adhikāra*), the javanas of jhāna proceed by gradually increasing from two, three, four, and so forth, starting from the beginning of the attainment.
But for those great beings (*mahāpurisa*) who have performed the preliminary work, these [javana moments] become mastered from the very moment they are attained.
Likewise, the fruition-javanas constitute the "fruit-state" for all.
It should be understood. As for the word *pi* (also/even) in the phrase *bahūni pi*, it has the sense of inclusion (*sampiṇḍana*).
By this, it includes the occurrence of the remaining types of consciousness even on the basis of a single instance during the time of the first action and so forth.
[The Rule for Knowing. 141. Having thus shown the occurrence of process-consciousnesses by way of the rule of sequence, now [it will be shown] by way of the classification of individuals.
Showing their occurrence according to the distinction of planes, he said, "Those with two roots," and so forth.

Those that have two roots associated with the rebirth-linking consciousness are "those with two roots" (*duhetuka*). These are those who have taken rebirth-linking by means of the four great resultant [consciousnesses] dissociated from knowledge.
However, there are no "rootless" (*ahetuka*) ones who have taken rebirth-linking by means of the two rootless resultants; for these do not have a root for rebirth-linking.
Because both of these [types of persons] possess the obstruction of karmic result (*vipākāvaraṇa*), even the sublime jhānas do not arise for them;

how much less the supramundane ones? Furthermore, since functional impulsions (*kriya-javana*) are unique to those whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*), it is said that neither functional impulsions nor absorption impulsions (*appanā-javana*) are obtained by them.
In this context, the "obstruction of karmic result" refers to being reborn with a rootless rebirth-linking consciousness (*ahetuka-paṭisandhi*).

And [the state of] having a twofold root-cause at rebirth-linking. Likewise, the great resultant states associated with knowledge do not obtain for those included within a happy destination (*sugati*)—this is the meaning of "likewise, the great resultant states associated with knowledge do not obtain in a happy destination.
Here, by the phrase "in a happy destination," one excludes individuals with no root-causes who are included within an unhappy destination; for such individuals [do not possess them].

In this statement, it should be understood that for others, even those dissociated from knowledge and resultant states are admitted; therefore he said, "But as for the miserable destinies," and so forth.

Therein, the complete construction should be seen as follows: among those included within the miserable destinies, neither the rootless states associated with knowledge, nor those dissociated from knowledge, nor the great resultants are found. Herein—

It may be so. But why is it stated here that among those included in the happy destinies (*sugati*), the four rootless resultant consciousnesses associated with knowledge (*ñāṇasampayutta-vipāka*) are not obtained, and among those included in the miserable destinies (*duggati*), even the eight root-cause-accompanied great resultants (*sahetuka-mahāvipāka*) are not obtained?
Is it not stated in the *Paṭṭhāna* that a root-cause-accompanied life-continuum (*sahetuka-bhavanga*) is a condition for a rootless life-continuum by way of proximity-condition (*anantarapaccaya*)?

For here, since there is no distinction in the occurrence of the root life-continuum (mūla-bhavanga) such that for a single being in one existence the life-continuum is sometimes with root-cause and sometimes without root-cause,
it is understood that the statement "the life-continuum is with root-cause" refers to the adventitious life-continuum known as the registration (tadārammaṇa). And [it is] with root-cause...
Because it is a general term, it should be understood that both the two-rooted and the three-rooted [consciousness] take that as their object (*tadārammaṇa*).

Regarding the phrase "of the rootless life-continuum (*ahetuka-bhavanga*)," however, what is intended here is specifically the primary life-continuum (*mūla-bhavanga*) that arises immediately after that object-taking consciousness.
Here too, because it is a general term, any one of the two types of rootless life-continuums may be taken.
Therefore, even for the two types of rootless [consciousness], the eight types of root-possessing registration-minds (*tadārammaṇa*) must indeed be obtainable.

However, there is nothing at all that needs to be said regarding those with two roots. To this it is replied: first, in all the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), the occurrence of root-possessing registration-minds for those included in the miserable destinies (*duggati*) among the rootless is rejected.
Therefore, the phrase "of the rootless life-continuum" (*ahetukassa bhavaṅgassa*) refers to that which is the result of wholesome kamma (*kusalavipāka*).

It is appropriate to say that this was stated with reference to the rootless life-continuum (ahetuka-bhavanga), for such is the principle (dhammatā) in the *Paṭṭhāna*: namely, that [the term] is taken according to what is available.

Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with all the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*). Furthermore, just as for wholesome states, because they are accomplished through application (*yoga*), there is "application-knowledge" (*ñāṇayoga*) even during their occurrence due to the operation of application;
it is not so for resultant states. This is because those [resultants] are accomplished without application (*ayoga-sādhanīya*).
In the course of occurrence, the application of knowledge (*ñāṇayoga*) is not possible without the knowledge of decisive support (*upanissayaññāṇa*),

which is termed "life-continuum knowledge" (*bhavaṅgañāṇa*). Therefore, since it is appropriate here as well to take only that "root-conditioned life-continuum" (*sahetukaṃ bhavaṅgaṃ*) which is dissociated from knowledge and has a root-conditioned object,
the Elder rejected the knowledge-associated object-moment for those with two roots and for those without roots.

Regarding the word "katā" (how many): the Elder Ācariya Buddhadatta, however, states that the object of registration (*tadārammaṇa*) for those [beings] can be either similar to or inferior to the resultant consciousness by which they take rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*); it cannot be superior.
Having thus excluded the eight great resultants of both types of rootless consciousness, he speaks of the attainment of thirty-seven types of consciousness. That, moreover, is...

This contradicts the Paṭṭhāna-pāḷi as it has been stated. However, others say that just as for those born of no-root-cause (ahetuka) who are included in a happy destination, there is an object-condition (tadārammaṇa) with two root-causes, so too for those with two root-causes, an object-condition with three root-causes is possible.
This appears reasonable; for in some parts of the Aṭṭhakathā, both of these [cases] are mentioned without distinction.

The occurrence of the eight great results has been explained. Those which possess three roots (*tihetuka*) are those accompanied by the three roots associated with rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhi-viññāṇa*).

These, moreover, are threefold according to the sense-sphere, fine-material, and immaterial realms. They are ninefold when divided into the worldling (*puthujjana*) and the eight noble ones (*ariya*).

Among them, neither wholesome nor unwholesome impulsion (*javana*) cittas are found in those whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*), because they have abandoned all underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) in every respect.

Because the wholesome and unwholesome states have ceased together, their state [of being] is bound to the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*). The word "likewise" (*tathā*) has the sense of an alternative position.
The seven Noble Ones (*ariya*) who possess the habit of training because they have not yet completed the task of training are called "trainers" (*sekkha*).

Here, however, the three who stand at the level of the lower fruits are intended. For in them, by the very path of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-magga*), views and doubt [are abandoned from the beginning].

Because it has been abandoned, the five impulsion moments associated with it are not obtained. Furthermore, for non-returner (anāgāmin) individuals, impulsion moments of aversion are also not obtained, because they have been abandoned by the path of non-returning.

However, since a single path consists of only one moment of consciousness, only the respective impulsion moments of the path itself are obtained for each of the four stages of the path. And as for the higher fruits...

Because they have not yet arrived at the lower persons, and because the lower [factors] do not arise among the higher classes of persons, it is said that for each of the four stages of fruition (*phalaṭṭhāna*), only their respective fruition-impulsions (*phalajavana*) are obtained; thus it is said, "they arise supramundane" (*lokuttara*).
And here, when the higher path has been reached, this is by way of the complete subsiding of the influence of the lower paths.
It should be understood that the distinction between the higher types of persons (*puggalantara*) is established here.
Now, in order to show the process-consciousnesses (*vīthicitta*) obtainable for each of those respective persons by way of elimination (*pārisesato*), he recited this verse:

"Those who have no further duty to train because their training-tasks are fully accomplished are the *asekkhas* (those beyond training). They are those whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*). For them, [there are] twenty-three resultant consciousnesses of the sense-sphere and twenty functional consciousnesses, by way of the fruit of Arahantship."
One should enumerate the forty-four types of process-thoughts (vīthicitta) according to their possible occurrence.

One should enumerate fifty-six process-thoughts according to their possible occurrence by way of the seven [thoughts] of those in training (sekkha), the seven unwholesome thoughts excluding those with wrong view and doubt, the twenty-one wholesome thoughts, the twenty-three sense-sphere resultant thoughts, the three lower fruits, and the two kinds of adverting consciousness. As for the remaining four...

The construction [of the sentence] is as follows: "One should enumerate the fifty-four process-thoughts (vīthicitta) that can arise for worldlings (puthujjana) by way of the two types of mundane wholesome and unwholesome adverting consciousnesses, which are the results of sensual desire.
The "distinction of persons" (puggalabheda) refers to the distinction of process-thoughts according to the difference between individuals.
(142) All process-thoughts are found only here, because it is in this very place that their complete arising occurs for both individuals and sense-doors.
"According to what is appropriate" means in accordance with the specific stages and individuals for whom they are suitable to arise.

Regarding the sixteen types of consciousness in the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara) that are to be excluded, it is stated that those excluding the javanas of repulsion and their registration are meant, because six of those types of consciousness will be mentioned later in the subsequent section.

In the immaterial sphere (arūpāvacara), those excluding the first path-consciousness, the fine-material-sphere smiling-consciousness, and the lower immaterial-sphere consciousnesses [are to be understood].
The construction is as follows: "the javanas of aversion and the path-of-consciousness moments, excluding those with that same object (tadārammaṇa), are obtained.
Here too, among the thirty-eight path-of-consciousness moments to be excluded, it should be understood that sixteen types of consciousness are mentioned subsequently.

"In all cases" means in all planes, both the fine-material and immaterial realms. For those devoid of this or that sensitive faculty, the path-of-consciousness moments pertaining to those respective doors are simply not obtained.

First, regarding the fine-material-sphere plane (*rūpāvacara-bhūmi*), since the triad of nose and so forth does not exist there, the six process-consciousnesses that operate through the doors of the nose, tongue, and body cannot occur at all for the material Brahmās who are devoid of the sensitivity of the nose, tongue, and body.
It was with reference to these that it was stated previously: "because they will be mentioned later in the section on the six types of consciousness.
Furthermore, in the immaterial-sphere plane (*arūpa-bhūmi*), even the five types of sensitivity do not exist.

The sixteen types of process-consciousness belonging to the five doors—consisting of the two sets of fivefold sense-cognitions, the mind-door adverting consciousness, the three types of reception, and the three types of investigation—are simply not obtained [in the case of those lacking certain faculties].
It is with reference to these that it was said: "above the sixteen types of consciousness.

However, in the sensual plane, one must consider those who lack this or that specific sensitive faculty, such as those born blind and so forth. In the sensual realm, there are eighty types of process-consciousness.

“They obtain what is appropriate; they obtain it accordingly. “In the fine-material sphere (rūpa), sixty-four [results] are obtained accordingly; in the immaterial sphere (arūpa), forty-two are obtained accordingly”—this is the construction.
And herein, in the Brahma-world or in the six higher sense-sphere heavens (kāmāvacara), there are no such things as undesirable objects.
Therefore, on the fine-material plane, of the four unwholesome-resultant [consciousnesses]...
The statement regarding their "availability" (labbhamānatā) should be understood either with reference to those [beings] staying there or those coming here who encounter undesirable forms and sounds.
However, some maintain that for Brahmās who have come here, there is no contact with undesirable objects;
thus, the four bases do not exist as "obtained" (laddhāni) in the fine-material plane (rūpabhūmi). Therefore, there are only sixty process-minds (vīthicitta) there.

They say this, but it is not tenable. For even those [defilements] that arise in those who have come here must be said to have arisen in the Brahma-world, because they arose in a Brahma-existence; and even while remaining there, they do not fail to grasp what is undesirable here.
This is because Brahmas are capable of grasping an object even when it is far away.
[140] And that which was stated for the purpose of refuting that doctrine— namely, "Furthermore, even for those standing there who see this world,
it is impossible to say that an undesirable object does not exist"— by that, [it is shown that] for those standing there who see this world...
Those four types of consciousness that have arisen there are indeed called "arisen there.
It is admitted that those which have arisen here for those who have come here are called "arisen here.

However, that is not logical, because it is established that those very [consciousnesses] which have arisen in the mental continuum of a being included within a particular plane are simply "arisen" in that particular plane.

"Thus, etc. refers to the great conclusion (*mahānigamana*). "According to possibility" (*yathāsambhava*) means in accordance with what is possible regarding the respective planes, persons, doors, and objects.
"Interrupted by the life-continuum" (*bhavaṅgantarita*) means separated by the life-continuum.

"For as long as the lifespan lasts" (*yāvatāyuka*) means for as long a time as the continuity of life proceeds in that particular existence, starting from the cognitive process (*vīthi*); this is the meaning.
The intention is that it proceeds uninterrupted [except] during the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
Thus ends the fourth commentary, the Compendium of the Cognitive Process (*vīthisaṅgaha*),
within the *Abhidhammattha-saṅgaha* titled *Paramatthadīpanī*.
The *Paramatthadīpanī* is completed.

143. Having thus shown the summary of occurrence during the period of the course of existence (*pavatti*), [the author] now shows the summary of occurrence at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).

He spoke the opening verse in order to demonstrate this. Thus, by the method already stated, what is called the "Compendium of Occurrence" (*pavattisaṅgaha*) has been declared and explained with reference to process-thoughts (*vīthicitta*).

Now, the construction is as follows: the "Compendium of Occurrence" regarding the linking of rebirth (*sandhi*) will be stated with reference to thought-moments outside of the cognitive process (*vīthimutta-citta*).
And here, since the occurrence of consciousness and mental factors during rebirth-linking has already been discussed, following that, at the time of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*),...
Since their occurrence at the time of death has already been explained, it is stated simply as "at the moment of rebirth-linking" (*sandhiyam*).
However, in the *Vibhāvanī*,
having first shown the death-moment in the arising of death that follows, the rebirth-linking in the immediately subsequent moment will be explained later.

The statement, "By the inclusion of the 'junction' (*sandhi*) here, the death-moment immediately preceding [the next life] must also be understood," which was said with the intention that "because of its proximity,
it is included by the very mention of that [birth]," is indeed untenable.

For the occurrence of objects for those [consciousnesses] outside the cognitive process (*vīthimutta*) is established only at the moment of death in the existence immediately preceding [the next life].

In order to demonstrate the occurrence of those process-freed consciousnesses—headed by rebirth-linking—along with the arrival of the sense objects within a single existence, the Elder has shown the manner of the arising of death together with that immediately preceding past death-consciousness.
They are called "planes" (*bhūmi*) because beings and formations exist (*bhavanti*) within them. "Growth" (*aya*) means increase. As for the meaning:

Happiness, the cause of happiness, and the conditions for happiness are to be understood [as such]. Because beings are mostly born here having departed from that [state], it is called an *apāya* (a state of loss).
That itself is the ground, thus it is the "ground of loss" (*apāyabhūmi*). It is called *kāma* because it is desired through coarse sensual lust.
It is called a *gati* (destination) because it is to be gone to and approached; or else, it is a *gati* because beings go there. Of manifold excellences...
A *sugati* is a beautiful destination (*sobhaṇā gati*) by virtue of its foundation (*adhiṭṭhānatāya*). It is a compound meaning "a pleasant (*sukha*) and good (*gati*) destination.

A *niraya* is that in which there is no such "gain" (*ayo*) as previously described. Alternatively, it is a *niraya* because beings who have fallen into suffering constantly (*niccaṃ*) "rush about" (*rayanti*), tremble, and quiver there.

They are called *tiracchāna* because, unlike humans, they do not exist upright (*uddhaṃ uccā*), but are bent across (*tiro añcitā*) and stretched out (*āyata*). They "yoke" (*yuvaṃti*) themselves to various [tasks].
It is called *yoni* because by means of it beings, though identical in color and shape, become as if unified through belonging to the same class (*samānajātitā*). It is birth (*jāti*).
In the *Vibhāvani*, however, it is stated that it is a specific mode of manifestation of the aggregates (*khandha*).

The womb of animals is the "animal realm" (*tiracchānayoni*). "Pettas" (departed ones) are those who have passed away, gone, and departed; the meaning is that they have moved away from here, having fallen away and gone to another existence.
This refers to anyone who has died. For in the world, even those who have gone to heaven are called "departed ones" (*petā*) when they have passed away.
However, in this context, the meaning is that they have passed away from a happy abode and have gone to a remote, distant exile, remaining so until they are liberated from that state.
The third class of beings, those subject to the states of misery (apāyika), who are constantly afflicted by suffering and mentioned in such texts as the *Lakkhaṇa-saṃyutta*, is intended here.

A "group of spirits" (*petti*) refers to a collection of *petas*. The "domain of the spirits" (*pettivisaya*) is the sphere of the *petas*; and "domain" (*visaya*) is said to mean the place where they move about.

Regarding the term "the host of *asuras*": here, *surās* are called the higher deities; they "rejoice" (*suranti*) through their special supernormal powers, or they "delight" (*dibbanti*). Or [it means] "well" (*suvā*).
They are called *asura* because they do not rejoice (*na suranti*), having made it their practice to experience the pleasure of sensual desires.
With reference to Vepacitti, Pahārāda, and others, the meaning is that they are the adversaries of the *suras* (gods) and resemble *suras*.

With reference to the mothers of the *viyaṅkara* (demigods), such as Uttaramātā and others, who belong to the *vini-pātika* class, the meaning is that they are minor *suras* or small *suras*. With reference to Yamarāja and others, the *vemānika-petas* (ghosts of the intermediate realm)...

The meaning is that they are "somewhat like asuras" in certain respects. For even *vemānika-petas* (ghosts of the celestial realms) are occasionally referred to as belonging to the "asura host" (*asurakāya*).
With reference to those in the *lokantarika* (inter-world) hells, the meaning is that they are entirely devoid of asura qualities.
Indeed, they too are called the "asura host" in the *Buddhavaṃsa-nidāna-aṭṭhakathā* and in the exposition on the suffering of birth. Likewise, with reference to the *kālakañcika-petas*, entirely...
The meaning is "devoid of the state of being a *surā* (a celestial being). Thus, the analysis of the meaning should be understood by way of the five types of *asuras*.

Regarding the scriptural passage, "Alas, the hosts of *devas* will diminish; the hosts of *asuras* will increase," the *Aṭṭhakathā* explains that all four states of misery (*apāya*) are included under the term "hosts of *asuras*."

In that regard, first, the asuras such as Vepacitti and Pahārāda are included among the Thirty-three gods (*tāvatiṃsa*). The asuras who dwell in the states of misery (*vinipātika*) are among the gods of the Four Great Kings (*cātumahārājika*).

The same applies to the asuras who are ghosts dwelling in various abodes (*vemānika-peta*). For it is stated in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) that these [latter] asuras, like those in the states of misery, may possess three roots (*tihetuka*), two roots (*duhetuka*), or no roots at all (*ahetuka*). As for the kings of Death (*yamarāja*), they are called Vessavaṇa and so forth.
"King Petti, Soma, Yama, and King Vessavaṇa"—thus it is stated in the *Kathāvatthu-pāḷi*.

Although Vessabhū and the others were themselves possessed of great psychic power and majesty as kings of the *vemānika* petas, out of compassion for beings in the hell realms, they continued to exercise sovereignty even in the lower worlds of hell.
For this very reason, all the peta-worlds and the hell-worlds [are under their jurisdiction].

They are called both *yamalokā* and *yamaviṣayā*. Furthermore, those who belong to the retinue of the Four Great Kings, who have evil inclinations and perform cruel deeds, are known as *yakkhas* when they appear in the Revatī-vimāna; they are known as *rakkhasas* when they appear in the Saṅkicca-jātaka.
These beings, called *yakkhas* and *rakkhasas*, go from here and wander about in the Ussada hells, inflicting various tortures upon the denizens of hell. Of them too...
By names such as Kāla and Upakāla, the command of the Overlord (Uparimarāja) is indeed exercised over the hell-wardens who appear in the Nāradajātakas.
The *lokantarika* spirits are included within hell. However, here it is specifically the *peta*-asuras, such as the Kālakafñcikās, that are intended.
The "asura-body" (*asurakāya*) is the collection or multitude of those asuras. And herein, there is what is called the "hell-ground" (*nirayabhūmi*).
It should be understood that they are situated within the earth by way of the eight great hells, each surrounded by sixteen secondary hells (*ussada-niraya*).
There are indeed various hell-grounds even in forests, mountains, oceans, islands, and so forth;
therefore, because such distinct and established locations exist, they are simply called "hells. As for the others, however—

Because such a place does not exist within the three planes of misery (*apāyabhūmi*), the terms "womb" (*yoni*), "object" (*visaya*), and "body" (*kāya*) are applied [to them], and thus they are understood as either "masses" (*khandha*) or "locations where the aggregates arise" (*khandhappavatti-padesa*). [The Plane of Misery.
Those whose minds (*manas*) are elevated, uplifted, or exalted are "human beings" (*manussa*). Among those infinite world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*), even compared to those belonging to other planes...

The minds of beings there are sharper, more courageous, and more diverse. It is precisely here that the fulfillment of wholesome and unwholesome courses of action, as well as the immediate (ānantariya) karmas, occurs.
Among those [beings], however, it is the inhabitants of Jambudīpa alone who possess especially exalted minds;
the others, because they share the same physical appearance and so forth with them, are merely called "human beings. In this [regard]...
As for the world-system (*cakkavāḷa*), however, there is nothing at all that needs to be said; as it has been said:
"Monks, by three things do the people of Jambudīpa surpass the people of Uttarakuru and even the gods of the Thirty-three. By which three things?
By being brave, by possessing mindfulness, and by living the holy life here. But the etymologists say that *manu* refers to King Mahāsammata.

It is said thus. These people, abiding by the laws of boundaries established by him, become his "sons" (puttaṭṭhāniya). Therefore, because they are the offspring (apacca) of Manu, they are called *manussa*.

However, here, taking it as a synonym for the earth (*bhūmi*), it should be understood that the feminine gender and the singular number have been employed in the word *manussā*. The same applies to the remaining cases. But in those [verses] where the Four Great Kings...
They exercise sovereignty. These are the gods of the Four Great Kings (*cātumahārājikā*). Therein, Dhatarattha is the king of the *gandhabbas*; Virulhaka, of the *kumbhaṇḍas*;

Virūpakkha, of the *nāgas*; and Kuvera, of the *yakkhas*. Therein, they are called *gandhabbas* because they descend upon and approach the *gandha-rukkhas* (fragrant trees) by way of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*);
that is, the deities residing in the fragrant trees. They [experience pleasure] by means of the scent of roots and so forth.
They appear in the Canon in ten ways. *Kumbhaṇḍas* are a type of *dānava* or *rakkhasa*. *Nāgas* and *yakkhas* are well known.

For the most part, they all possess evil dispositions and perform cruel deeds. Therefore, the Four Great Kings appointed various kings or various generals among them in order to prevent one another from harassing human beings.

The Āṭānāṭiya Sutta should be discussed here. For in that [sutta], four classes of non-humans (*amanussa*)—namely, *yakkha*, *yakkhinī*, *gandhabba*, *gandhabbī*, *kumbhaṇḍa*, *kumbhaṇḍī*, *nāga*, and *nāgī*—are mentioned as those who have come under subjugation.
Among them, a non-human endowed with the excellence of bodily radiance and beauty is called a *yakkha*, a *deva*, or a *devatā*. One devoid of the excellence of bodily radiance and beauty...
A non-human spirit (*amanussa*) who has a form that is invisible is called a *yakkha*. One born in a tree-dwelling celestial mansion (*rukkhaṭṭhakavimāna*) is named a tree deity (*rukkhadevatā*).
One born within a tree is named a fragrance-lover (*gandhabbapriya*), who is what is called a "wood-yakkha" (*kaṭṭhayakkha*) in the world.
Due to inferior karma performed in the past, some fragrance-lovers are even born inside the bodies of human women; they are known as *yoginīs* in the Vedic texts.

In the world, they are called *yoginīs*. On particularly distinguished nights, at the time when they are intent upon their range [of activity], they are called *juṇhā* (full moons) in the sense of radiance.
There are also *kubbhaṇḍas*, great-bellied *rakkhasas* with wide eyes, who in the world are called "protectors of wealth.
For they guard the *maṇi-ratana* on Mount Vepulla. Within the Himavat, inside the *ambā* tree—

They guard [them]. Thus, having guarded their places of treasure—whether they be forest trees, celestial medicinal trees, celestial fragrant trees, or lakes—they dwell there and consume [their offerings];
therefore, they are called *rakkhasa* (demons). Regarding the terms *nāga* and *nāgī*:
here, those born within mountains or within the earth, belonging to the class of *vasundhara* deities and *yakṣas*, are also called *nāgas* in this context.

They are called [earth-deities]. In the *Mahāparinibbāna Sutta*, in the passage on the earthquake, she who is called "the earth-deity" is mentioned—she by whose playfulness an earthquake sometimes occurs.

Furthermore, regarding those for whom the mantra-words, the *vatthu-vidyā* (science of objects), and the *bhūmi-vidyā* (science of the earth) were spoken in the *Brahmajāla Sutta*, there are among them various beings possessing psychic powers, obstructors, those delighting in evil, and performers of sinful deeds.
Whether as troops greedy for sport or as troops greedy for fodder, they roam about harassing beings— whether by their natural color or by the color of crows,
vultures, and other such creatures— in the realms of ghosts and in the hells. All of this should be understood by the wise from the Suttantas, the Jātakas, or the Vedaga texts.
Thirty-three meritorious beings were born here together with the chief person named Māgha; thus they are called the "Thirty-three" (*tettiṃsā*).

By way of linguistic derivation, this very term becomes *Tāvatiṃsā*. Indeed, in all world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*), according to the method found in the *Janavasabha-sutta*, this second deva-world consists of thirty-three [deities] such as Sakka, Pajāpati, Varuṇa, Īsāna, and so forth.
Cough is the affliction of the kings of the gods. For it is stated in the *Aṅguttara Nikāya*: "There are a thousand [deities] of the Cātumahārājika realm; a thousand of the Tāvatiṃsa realm.
However, those who were formerly human beings (*māghapurisa*) are reborn among them when those positions of the kings of the gods become available.
Furthermore, they are still living at present; therefore, it should be understood that this etymological explanation is formulated according to their status. Others say...
However, just as [the gods] have the luster of the color of the *indagopaka* insect, they are seen for "thirty" (*tāvatiṃsa*).
In this *Vidhura-jātaka*, the word *tāva* is merely an adjunct to the word *tiṃsa*. Considering that it is the same here as well, it would be appropriate to say:
"The *Tāvatiṃsa* are so called because they are the dwelling place of the thirty or so royal families of the devas who occupy Sakka’s position. Yet, in the commentaries, it is stated as follows:

Some, having established a method of etymological interpretation (*niruttinaya*), claim that in various places within the *Māgha-vatthu* verses, the number of Sakkas is stated as exactly thirty-three.
That is not tenable, because it is stated in the Canon itself:
"Brahmā Aṅkumāra, having manifested thirty-three bodies, sat upon the couches of the Tāvatiṃsa devas. [The word] *yāma* refers to that...
In the world of the gods (devaloka), there is the realm named Issara-devakula; likewise, there is Suyāma.
Because they are associated with that [realm], both that world of the gods and the gods reborn therein are called simply "Yāmas.

They are called Tusita because they are constantly satisfied due to being endowed with abundant glory and prosperity, and because their faces are exceedingly joyful and glad. Regarding the enjoyments as they desire—
They are called *Nimmānarati* because they take delight there after having repeatedly created [objects] by themselves.
They are called *Paranimmitavasavatti* because they exercise mastery over enjoyments created by others according to their own wish.
They are called *Brahmā* because they expand and increase, attaining growth, development, and abundance through exceedingly sublime qualities such as *jhāna*. They are great.
Where it should have been said "Brahmās, Great Brahmās," there is an elision of the word *mahā*.
Those who exist in an assembly (*parisati*) are *pārisajjā*; or, those born among assemblies are *pārisajjā*, meaning "attendants.

The attendants of the Great Brahmās are *brahmapārisajjā*. They stand and place themselves in a high position in front [of others], thus they are *purohitā* (chaplain-priests). [Of] the Great Brahmās...
"Brahmā’s Ministers" (purohitāti brahmapurohitā) refers to those who are ministers to Brahmā. "Great Brahmās" (mahābrahmāno) refers to the great Brahmās.
"Thousand-Brahmās," "Two-Thousand-Brahmās," "Three-Thousand-Brahmās," and so forth—these are the sovereign Brahmās mentioned in the *Saṅkhārupapatti Sutta*; this is the meaning.
In that context, a "Thousand-Brahmā" is the lord over a thousand world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*), while a "Two-Thousand" is [the lord] over two thousand world-systems.
The meaning is "the Lord" (*issara*). These three also dwell on the same level. In this regard, the people of the world each separately attend upon their own family deities (*kuladevatā*);
some attend upon the one named Mahādeva, some upon the one named Vāsudeva, some upon the one named Maheśvara, and some upon the one named Parameśvara.
There are also household deities, village deities, tree deities, and so forth, belonging to those great king-deities.
They indeed become attendants. In that regard, the Great Brahmas should be seen as being like the Great Devas;
the Brahma-purohitas should be seen as being like the household deities and so forth; and the Brahma-parisajjas should be seen as being like human beings.

Furthermore, among them, the household deities and others attend upon the Great Devas and the Great Brahmas even without seeing them. And both the humans and those [other deities] attend upon them even without seeing them.
In the same way, the Brahmapurohitas do not see the Mahābrahmās, nor do they know the dwelling place of the Mahābrahmās.
The Brahmapārisajjas likewise do not see them, nor do they know the dwelling places of either.
However, when [the Mahābrahmās] manifest themselves by creating a gross form, only then are they seen. This same method applies to the higher planes as well.
As for what is stated in the commentary on the *Brahmanimantanika Sutta*— namely, that the natural form of a Brahmā does not come within the range of anyone’s sight—
that was said with reference to the fact that the natural forms of the higher Brahmās, such as those of the Brahmā-purohitas and so forth, do not come within the range of sight of anyone,
whether they be a member of the Brahmā assembly (*brahmapārisajja*) or any other deity or human being. This does not apply to the lower [Brahmās].
However, their natural form will indeed come within the range of vision of those above.

For this very reason, it is stated in the *Janavasabha Sutta-aṭṭhakathā* that the lower and lower deities are able to see the bodies of the higher deities as they have been fashioned, having made them grosser [for the purpose of being seen].
Therein, on the second plane, the Parittābhā are the Brahmapārisajja themselves. The Appamāṇābhā...
They are indeed the Brahmapurohitas. "The Ābhassaras" refers specifically to the Mahābrahmās; the meaning is that they are the Brahmās who are lords over that level.
However, it should be understood that their name is taken from their radiance (*ābhā*) for the purpose of distinguishing them from the lower level.

In this context, those who possess limited radiance are the Parittābhās (Limited Radiance); those who possess immeasurable radiance are the Appamāṇābhās (Immeasurable Radiance). They are called "Ābhassarā" (Radiant Ones).
They emit light from these [abodes], thus they are called *Ābhassara* (Radiant). On the third plane, the *Parittasubha* (Limited-Beauty) are none other than the *Brahmapārisajja* (Retinue of Brahmā).

The *Appamāṇasubha* (Immeasurable-Beauty) are none other than the *Brahmapurohita* (Ministers of Brahmā). The *Subhakiṇṇa* (Wholly Beautiful) are none other than the *Mahābrahmā* (Great Brahmās). The meaning is that these are the presiding Brahmās on that plane.
In this context, "beauty" (*subhā*) refers specifically to light that is dense, solid, and immovably established. Those who possess limited beauty are the *Parittasubha*.
"Parittasubhā" means those who possess limited beauty. "Appamāṇasubhā" means those for whom beauty is immeasurable. "Subhakiṇṇā" means strewn with beauty; they are also read as "Subhakiṇhā.
In these two readings, the vowel *ā* should be seen as short, and the final letter *ṇa* should be understood as *ha*.
In these two planes, however, the natural radiance of the body is preeminent; therefore, by way of that [radiance], they are called "Parittābhā" (Limited Radiance) and so forth.
The name is established as such; it is not [derived] from "birth among the Brahmas" (*brahmapārisajjāti*) and so forth.

And having done so, in the *Verañja Sutta*, those dwelling on the first level arrive as the "Brahmakāyika devas"; those dwelling on the second level as the "Ābhā devas"; those dwelling on the third level as the "Subhā devas";

and those on the fourth level are called "Vehapphalā" because they possess abundant fruit (*vipula-phala*). Alternatively, [they are so called] because of their jhānas of joy (*somanassa-jjhāna*), which are of a nature subject to movement (*iñjana-jātika*).

For those born on the three lower levels, there is a meritorious fruit characterized by movement—due to obstacles such as the conflagration and so forth—that lasts until the end of the aeon together with the earth-plane.
Regarding these, that which is stated to be sixty-four aeons for the Subhakiṇṇa devas is said in reference to those who were the first inhabitants of that level; for those of the later generations...

However, the fruit of merit produced by the immovable-born (*āneñja*) equanimity-jhāna is not subject to such movement as sixty-three aeons, sixty-two aeons, sixty-one aeons, and so forth; rather, it is a fruit of merit that is withdrawn from such movement.
Therefore, it is specifically sought after and increased in accordance with the power of the jhāna.
They are called *vehapphalā* because the fruit of merit (*puññaphala*) exists there.

They are called *asañña* because the four immaterial aggregates (*arūpakkhandha*), which are grasped by way of perception (*saññā*), do not exist in them. Being both *asañña* and *satta*, they are *asaññasattā*.
However, due to the absence of mind and mental factors (*cittace tasika*), the possibility arises that they might be considered non-beings (*asatta*).
It should be understood that the term "seven" is used inclusively. These two [classes] also dwell on the same level.

Here too, because there exists a distinction in the inferior, middling, and superior quality of the jhāna that produces rebirth, a corresponding distinction among the Brahmās—such as being a member of the assembly (pārisajja), a chaplain (purohita), or a Great Brahmā (mahābrahmā)—is indeed possible.
However, due to differences in lifespan and the fact that they do not see one another, etc., [further distinctions are not perceived].
It should be understood that there is no division of planes by way of assembly and so forth due to their non-existence. The same applies to the Aviha and other realms.

Because they are the dwellings only of pure Non-returners and Arahants, owing to the absence of the latent tendencies for sensual lust and ill will which are coarse, they are called "Pure Abodes" (Suddhāvāsa).
Among them, those dwelling in the first plane do not abandon their own station for a long time; thus they are "Aviha" (Non-abandoning). Alternatively, [the explanation continues...]
Because the five gross fetters have been abandoned, there is no vexation of the mind;
because they have attained non-distraction regarding the states of serenity and insight, they are called the Avihas.

Because those dwelling on the second plane are not tormented by any mental fever, they are called the Atappas. Because those dwelling on the third plane possess the pure eye of faith, the divine eye, and the Dhamma-eye...
They are "beautiful to behold" (*sudassā*) because they see clearly due to being endowed with the eye of wisdom (*paññā-cakkhu*).

However, those dwelling on the fourth plane are "exceedingly beautiful to behold" (*sudassino*) because they possess an even more excellent quality of clear vision; for here the vowel *ī* has the sense of intensification (*atisaya*).
As for those dwelling on the fifth plane, there is no other material-brahma (*rūpi-brahma*) existing in a higher plane.
They are called Akaniṭṭha because among the beings possessing form (*rūpin*), they are the youngest (*kaniṭṭha*) by virtue of some quality.

Regarding the phrase "the plane of the base of infinite space" (*ākāsānañcāyatanabhūmi*): here, to whatever extent a spatial region (*ākāsapadesa*) is pervaded such that the four aggregates known as the base of infinite space (*ākāsānañcāyatana*) arise, that spatial region together with those aggregates is the "plane of the base of infinite space. Thus...

Regarding the remaining [realms]: the construction is that neither ordinary persons (puthujjana), nor stream-enterers (sotāpanna), nor once-returners (sakadāgāmin) are found in the Pure Abodes (suddhāvāsa) in any way whatsoever or by any means.
And here, by the exclusion of once-returners, the exclusion of those standing on the path of non-returning (anāgāmi-maggaṭṭha) is also established;
thus, by this verse, it is shown that only the three higher noble ones (ariya) attain rebirth there.
It should be understood that it is "stated. "In the remaining places" means in the twenty-one places other than the five Pure Abodes and the non-percipient realm;
"noble ones" refers to worldlings (*puthujjana*). [The Fourfold Scheme of Planes] 144.
"At the moment of descent" means at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*); for by means of rebirth-linking, there is a descending or entering into another existence.
"Entering" is said in the sense of descending [into the womb]. The construction is: "after that, having become the life-continuum (bhavaṅga).
Some, however, read "at the conclusion of the life-continuum"; that is not tenable. "Born blind" means blind from birth (*jaccandha*).
By the word "etcetera," it includes those born deaf, born noseless, born mute, born dumb, born insane, the impotent, the hermaphrodite, the neuter, those with mammas, and so forth.
In this context, one who has received rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) through kamma incapable of producing the eye is called "born blind.

This same method applies to the others as well. Therein, one devoid of the translucent medium of the ear is called "born deaf. One devoid of the translucent medium of the nose is called "born noseless.
There is no such thing as being "born tongueless. One devoid of speech is called "born mute. Even the mere distinction between the cardinal and intermediate directions—
One who cannot be persuaded is called *jātieḷa*. One whose mind is perpetually deranged is called *jaccummattaka*.
One who has reached a state of deformity due to sensual desire, such as being drenched [in semen] and so forth, is called *paṇḍaka*.
One endowed with both sexual organs is called *ubhatovyañjanaka*. One devoid of the two sexual characteristics is called *napuṃsaka*. Even in ordinary speech, each individual syllable...
The term *mamman* refers to that which produces [the eye] with great effort (*mahussāhena*), having the sense of "striving.

Here, at the time of the process (*pavatti*) for one who has obtained rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) through a karma capable of producing the eye, either that same karma or another karma produces the eye.

However, for one who has obtained rebirth-linking through a karma incapable [of producing the eye] and whose physical basis (*vatthu*) is defective, even another [karma]—during the time of the process—[cannot produce it].

It is not the case that kamma produces the eye. Therefore, it should be understood that even for those born in the womb, the state of being blind from birth is established at the very moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).
This same method applies to the rest, such as those who are deaf from birth and so forth.

Because it is stated that "the acquisition of the sense bases (*āyatana*) is birth," the time when the eye is ready to arise is called the "time of the eye's birth. At that time, the eye has not yet arisen.
"Of those born blind" means that the time of birth for each respective sense base should be understood according to the time when it is due to arise for each individual.
For if this were not so, they would say that those born deaf and so forth would also have been reborn [with those faculties].
Thus, this meaning has been clarified in the *Vibhāvani*.
[142] Furthermore, regarding what is stated in the *Vibhāvani*:
"Others, however, say that 'blind from birth' means blind by very nature; the meaning is that he was born having been blind within his mother's womb.
By this, it is established that for those with two or three root-conditions (*duhetuka-tihetuka*), the eye-faculty does not fail while in the mother's womb."
That which was stated is not tenable;

for in the world, it is observed that even in the case of some who are born blind while still in the mother’s womb, there exists a distinctness of wisdom regarding various crafts and branches of knowledge.
Indeed, setting aside the Great Bodhisattvas and others in their final existence, [such cases are seen].

For the remaining beings—whether they possess two roots or three roots—even when their eyes or ears arise through external violence, or through the mother’s improper conduct, or through various diseases, there is no such thing as a "deficiency" (vipatti) of those faculties; thus, it is not possible to establish a fixed rule.
And regarding the phrase "those who dwell on the earth and the Asuras fallen into the lower realms": herein, those born upon the earth are called *bhummā*. Those connected with the earth...
The terrestrial deities (bhummadeva) such as Āḷavaka, Sātāgira, Hemavata, and others— who possess great psychic power (mahiddhika) and are reborn in tree-dwellings,
mountain-dwellings, and celestial mansions— are also called "yakkhas" in the world in the sense of being worthy of worship through the offering of oblations.
However, although they belong to the class of terrestrial deities, some lead a life of hardship due to the absence of any wealth or pleasure produced by their own merit.

They wander about for the duration of an eon. Because they are included among the successive retinues of those powerful earth-deities, they are called "earth-dwellers" (bhummassitā) in the sense that they are dependent on and supported by the earth-deities. There is also a reading *bhummisitā*.
Due to the absence of a dwelling place produced by merit, they reside in secluded places such as trees, thickets, caves, grottoes, and charnel grounds.
The meaning is that they dwell depending on specific locations on the earth. Because they exist in a deformed state and fall into other states of existence, they are called *vinipātikā*.
And because they are *vinipātikā* and, in the sense mentioned below, are *asura*s, they are *vinipātika-asura*s.
They live near villages or within villages in secluded places, consuming rice-grains, cakes, snacks, fish, meat, and so forth, which have been discarded by the village-dwellers.

"Having searched for them and not finding them, or having afflicted children or the sick, they are able to maintain their lives by threatening and afflicting other people as well"—this refers to those *vinipātika-asuras*.
The intended meaning is "some of them," for it cannot be said that all those called *vinipātika-asuras* are without cause; for there are also those with two roots and three roots.

Because of their actual existence. And having accepted this, it should be understood that even for some among them—such as Piyaṅkaramātā, Uttaramātā, Dhammaguttā, Phussamittā, and others—the realization of the Dhamma is mentioned in the Commentaries.

Furthermore, it should be seen that certain beings belonging to the class of *yakkhas*, the class of *rakkhasas*, *vemānika* ghosts, and ghosts who subsist on the gifts of others are also included here.

"Among them" means among those persons endowed with the aforementioned rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*). For the determination of the life-span occurs by way of a specific measure of duration that holds for all beings without exception who are included within a single plane (*ekabhūmi*).
There is no such specific measure of duration for those in the states of misery (*apāya*), humans, or the deities of the earth.
This is because those included within the entire world-system (*cakravāḷa*) do not belong to a single plane.
All hells have a single limit to their lifespan. This same principle applies to the animal realm and so forth. Therefore, it is said: "Of the four states of misery," and so on.

There is no fixed rule regarding the calculation of the measure of the lifespan for individuals in the four states of misery, because there, for the most part, the lifespan is determined by the measure of the karma [that led to that birth]. Among those, in the ten hells beginning with Abbuda:
It should be understood that even the limit of the lifespan mentioned by the Blessed One in various places is established solely by the karma that causes rebirth in those respective states.
Regarding the phrase "of humans," they say this is stated with reference to those dwelling in Jambudīpa;

for only among them is there an increase and decrease of the life-span, not among the inhabitants of the other continents. Among those [other continents], for the inhabitants of Uttarakuru, it is fixed.
It lasts for a thousand years; they say that for the other two, it is five hundred years each.

This being the case, it follows that even for the beings of the first eon (*ādikappika*) on those islands, that same duration applies. However, for the inhabitants of Jambudīpa, there are successes and failures regarding climate and food, which are rooted in the irregular and regular movements of the moon, sun, constellations, and so forth, and which result from their own conduct—both even and uneven. For them as well...
They are indeed common [to all]. Therefore, it should not be said that even for them there is no ascending or descending of the limits of their lifespan.
However, it may be said that because they are merely a secondary result (*nissanda*), they do not share the same destiny as those destined for Jambudīpa.

For thus it is stated in the Pāḷi: "The humans of Uttarakuru are without 'mine-ness' and without possessions; they have a fixed lifespan, while others have a remaining lifespan. In this context, "remaining lifespan" means:
The meaning is: "by remaining motionless for a thousand years after descending from the incalculable [heavens].
As for the phrase "the Asuras fallen into the states of misery," this should be regarded as a mere illustration;

for here, all terrestrial deities—both those of great power and those of little power—as well as the *vemānika* ghosts (*peta*s) and so forth, are intended. For indeed, for all of them, it is karma alone [that determines their state].
"Measure": the phrase "of the gods belonging to the Four Great Kings" is said with reference to those in the upper realm of the Four Great Kings.
"Divine" means established in that world of the gods. "Five hundred years"—this should be understood as stated by way of the majority.
For it is because the sons of gods who were stream-enterers (sotāpanna) and disciples of the Buddha Kassapa [lived] in the sky-dwelling [realms].
It is stated in the *Jātakaṭṭhakathā* that those reborn in celestial mansions (*vimāna*) remain there even until the time of King Nimi.

Therefore, it should be understood that for certain space-dwelling deities (*ākāsathakadeva*), the limit of their existence is determined by their karma. Furthermore, one should not consider them being reborn there again and again;
for once the stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*) have reached the seventh [existence], there is no further rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) in the sense-sphere realm (*kāmabhava*).
There is. And even if one were to be reborn in that heavenly world a thousand times, one would not be able to reach the end of such a duration of time.
"By human calculation" means by the reckoning of human years. For in the human world, fifty years constitute a single divine night and day for the Cātumahārājika devas.
Thirty such nights and days make a single divine month. Twelve months...
One divine year. By that divine year, their five hundred years amount to ninety million human years.
"From that" means from the measure of the lifespan of the Cātumahārājika devas.
"Fourfold" means multiplied by four—that is, increased—by way of both the doubling of the measure of the lifespan and the doubling of the divine day and night.
This is the meaning. This method of calculation applies to the remaining [heavens] as well.

In this context, "doubling the increase of the lifespan measure" means that the lifespan measure of the higher deities increases twofold compared to the lifespan measure of the lower deities. By this, one divine thousand years is for the Tāvatiṃsa [gods];
two thousand years for the Yāma; four [thousand] for the Tusita; and [eight thousand] for the Nimmānarati.
Eight. It is established that the lifespan of the Vasavatti gods is sixteen thousand celestial years.
Regarding the doubling of the celestial day and night: there is a doubling of the day and night of the higher gods compared to the day and night of the lower gods.
By this reckoning, one hundred human years constitute one celestial day and night in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.
Two hundred years in the Yāma realm; four [thousand] in the Tusita; eight [thousand] in the Nimmānaratī;

and one thousand six hundred years in the Vasavatti realm—this is established as one divine night and day. Since the doubling of the nights and days is thus established, the doubling of the months and years is likewise established.
This being so, the aforementioned [lifespans] for the Tāvatiṃsa and the other realms...
It is established that even the [lifespans] of a thousand celestial years and so forth should be understood as being, for each respective realm, merely a single night and day, month, and year.
This being the case, it is established that the lifespans of those in the higher realms are four times the lifespans of those in the lower realms.
Therefore it was said: "Four times that is for the Tāvatiṃsa devas; four times that is for the Yāma devas," and so forth.
And since this is established by divine reckoning, it is likewise established that, even by human reckoning, there is a fourfold increase from one stage to the next.

Therefore, taking the lower figures—such as nine million years and so forth—and multiplying each successively by four, the higher figures amount to three hundred and sixty million years and so on; thus, all of these are shown from beginning to end.
Explaining by way of this, he spoke the verse beginning with "nine hundred. The construction is as follows:
nine hundred thousand years, twenty-one koṭis, and likewise sixty-six hundred thousand years is the measure of the lifespan among the Vasavatti devas.
This is because the jhāna consisting of vicāra alone, through the surmounting of gross vitakka, [arises] from the first jhāna.

It is very strong; yet, for that very reason, it is not excessively weak even compared to the third jhāna. Therefore, it is said that by combining with the third jhāna, it yields its result within the same level of the plane;
thus, both the result of the second jhāna and the result of the third jhāna are said to belong to the plane of the second jhāna.
For this very reason, the established order of the planes is also determined by way of the fourth jhāna.
However, the Elder has already explained the jhānas below by way of the fivefold method (pañcakanaya).

Therefore, here too, having taken the resultant states according to that same method, it is said: "The result of the fourth jhāna on the plane of the third jhāna," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "among those":
this refers to those who have received rebirth-linking by means of those six [resultants]. The word "of an aeon" (kappassa) refers to an incalculable aeon (asaṅkhyeyyakappa).

It has been stated. For there are four kinds of aeons (*kappa*): the great aeon (*mahākappa*), the incalculable aeon (*asaṅkhyeyyakappa*), the intermediate aeon (*antarakappa*), and the life-span aeon (*āyukappa*).
Among these, the "life-span aeon" refers to the specific limit of the lifespan of various beings.

The "intermediate aeon" refers to the sixty-four divisions seen as the intervals occurring through the decrease and increase of the human life-span within one incalculable aeon of the world’s expansion and duration.
They are called *cūḷakappā* (minor eons). Some say there are eighty types; others, fourteen types, according to those learned in the Vedas.
These are what are called "eons of a Manu" (*manvantarakappa*) in the world. What is meant is that they are intermediate eons characterized by each great king named Manu.
However, some [say] that during one period of the world’s expansion (*vivaṭṭaṭṭhāyi*), while the Great King Mahāsammata [reigned]...
They maintain that there is only one [great aeon]. However, sixty-four intermediate aeons (*antarakappa*) constitute what is called one incalculable aeon (*asaṅkhyeyakappa*). That is fourfold:

the aeon of dissolution (*saṃvaṭṭa*), the aeon remaining in dissolution (*saṃvaṭṭaṭṭhāyī*), the aeon of evolution (*vivaṭṭa*), and the aeon remaining in evolution (*vivaṭṭaṭṭhāyī*). Among these, the aeon while it is perishing is the aeon of dissolution;
the aeon remaining as it has perished is the aeon remaining in dissolution. The aeon while it is increasing is the aeon of evolution; as for how...
The aeon remaining during the period of expansion (*vivaṭṭa*) should be understood as the "aeon abiding in expansion" (*vivaṭṭaṭṭhāyī*).

Those four incalculable aeons (*asaṅkhyeyya-kappa*) constitute one great aeon (*mahā-kappa*). Furthermore, even if a heap of white mustard seeds equal in size to the world-system were depleted by removing a single seed every hundred years, one great aeon would not yet reach exhaustion.
Thus, the great aeon should be understood as being of such immense duration.
In this regard, since it is stated in the Commentary that "when the eon dissolves by fire, everything below the Ābhassara realm is consumed by flames;
when it dissolves by water, everything below the Subhakiṇha realm is dissolved by water;
and when it dissolves by wind, everything below the Vehapphala realm is scattered away by the wind," this world [is destroyed] continuously for seven...
In the first seven cycles it is destroyed by fire; in the eighth cycle it is destroyed by water. Again, for seven [cycles] it is destroyed by fire; in the eighth it is destroyed by water.
Thus, by way of eight sets of eight, in sixty-four cycles, at the final water-cycle, having abandoned water, there occurs a wind-cycle—this meaning is established.
How so? Regarding what was stated: "for the Ābhassara [deities], eight eons."
By this, it is established that in the eighth cycle there is a dissolution by water; and that in the intervals between every seven cycles there are dissolutions by fire.
Furthermore, regarding what was said concerning "sixty-four eons strewn with the Subha heavens": by this, it is established that in each sixty-fourth cycle there is a dissolution by wind;
and that in the intervening sixty-three cycles there are dissolutions by fire and dissolutions by water.
"It is established. Regarding this, the ancients said:
"By fire it is radiant below, by water from being overspread with beauty;
by wind from the Vehapphala realm—thus does the world perish."
There are seven turns of the seven fires, and on every eighth turn there is water;
when sixty-four [turns] are thus completed, there shall be one turn of wind.
And when the world has perished in this way, even within a single aeon (*kappa*), there is no ground for the first jhāna that has not been destroyed. Therefore...
The lifespan of the gods of the Retinue of Brahmā (Brahmapārisajja) is one-third of an eon (kappa); that of the Ministers of Brahmā (Brahmapurohita) is half an eon;
and that of the Great Brahmās (Mahābrahmā) is one full eon. In this context, it is the incalculable eon (asaṅkhyeyya-kappa) that is intended. This is not a "great eon" (mahākappa).
Therefore, when it is said "of an eon," this is stated with reference to the incalculable eon. It may also be stated with reference to a lifespan-eon (āyukappa).
This is indeed logical. For during the aeons of destruction by fire, the surface of the first jhāna is the very first to evolve when evolving, and it is the very last to dissolve when dissolving.

Therefore, taking one aeon of evolution, duration, and dissolution—consisting of the latter half of the evolving period together with the former half of the dissolving period—there are two incalculable aeons.
It can be said that on that plane there is one life-span of a *āyukappa*. However, starting from the second plane, only a *mahākappa* should be taken.

Considering that what is slightly deficient or excessive does not count toward the total number, it is stated that "for the Ābhassara devas there are eight *kappas," referring to seven *kappas* together with half a *kappa*. Thus, [it totals] sixty-four *kappas*.
"Even here" means: those who approach the state of the base of infinite space are "those approaching the base of infinite space" (*ākāsānañcāyatanupagā*);
[the text refers to] them. That which has a single object-field as its objective support is "single-object-field" (*ekavisaya*). "Of one kind" (*ekajātiya*) means within a single existence.

[The Tetrad of Rebirth-linking. 145. It generates, thus it is "generative" (*janaka*); it supports, thus it is "supportive" (*upatthambhaka*); it oppresses, thus it is "oppressive" (*upapīḷaka*); it destroys, thus it is...

[It is] obstructive. Therein, "productive" refers to wholesome and unwholesome volition (*cetanā*) which brings about the arising of resultant aggregates and the matter produced by karma (*kaṭattārūpa*) during both rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) and the course of existence (*pavatti*).
Among these, that which produces rebirth-linking should be understood as having reached the level of a path of action (*kammapatha*).
However, that which produces the course of existence may or may not have reached the level of a path of action; it includes even the impulsion volitions (*javana-cetanā*) of the five sense doors.

In the dream state, there are both wholesome and unwholesome volitions (*cetanā*). What is called "supporting" refers to all wholesome and unwholesome volitions that have either not yet found an opportunity to ripen or have already ripened their result (*vipāka*).

For although such volition is indeed generative, it proceeds by supporting—either before or after its own phase of ripening—another kamma-factor that constitutes a constituent part, or the continuity of the aggregates produced by that kamma.
As in the case of the volition of paying homage to the Triple Gem at the commencement of a book. Furthermore, as for what is stated in the *Visuddhimagga*:
"But it is not able to produce a supporting resultant," that should be understood as referring to a stage where the resultant has not yet been obtained;
for when the completeness of conditions exists, there is no kamma whatsoever that does not produce at least a process-resultant.
"It exists. In this context, "supporting of another karma" means making room for another productive karma that has not yet found an opportunity.
This, however, becomes manifest at the time near death. For when a wholesome state flashes forth, another wholesome karma capable of producing rebirth finds an opportunity;
and when an unwholesome state flashes forth, another unwholesome karma does so. For this has been said in the Itivuttaka:
And at this very moment, if a person were to pass away,
they would be reborn in heaven, for their mind has been purified.
And at this very moment, if a person were to pass away...
"He would be reborn in hell, for his mind is corrupted.
This [corruption] is indeed frequently found even during the course of existence (*pavatti*).

"Supporting" the continuity of aggregates produced by karma means that the continuity of aggregates produced by either wholesome or unwholesome karma, which has obtained an opportunity through another [condition].
Having removed obstacles to life and having procured the requisites for living, one brings about a longer duration of existence. As it is said:
"For one who is habitually respectful and constantly honors the elders, four things increase: longevity, beauty, happiness, and strength."
In this context, however, it should not be stated that there is no wholesome [state] that supports the continuity of aggregates produced by unwholesome karma,
nor that there is no unwholesome [state] that supports the continuity of aggregates produced by wholesome karma. For even in the case of powerful beings such as nāgas and supaṇṇas,

whose continuity of aggregates is produced by unwholesome karma, at the time of the occurrence of that continuity, previously performed wholesome karma acts as a nourishment in the manner already described.

It indeed acts [as a support]. Likewise, even for certain beings born from wholesome karma—such as those in the states of ruin (vinipātika) or the asuras—it is past unwholesome karma that causes the continuity of their aggregates to persist for a much longer duration.
Furthermore, the types of kamma known as "oppressive" (upapīḷaka) and "destructive" (upaghātaka) are likewise only wholesome and unwholesome volitions of the aforementioned kinds.
For although these are also "productive" (janaka), they [function] from their own category of result...
Whether before or after, at the time of grasping the fruition-phase, or while making another karma or the continuity of the aggregates produced by karma weaker,
it proceeds by either obstructing them or cutting them off entirely. In that context, regarding the "oppressive" (upapīḷaka) [kamma],
what is called "obstructing another karma" means making another productive karma weak.
For indeed, even a kamma that is powerful at the time of its accumulation may later have its potency destroyed when it is countered by another intervening kamma that acts as a direct opposite.
Thus, although it is capable of producing rebirth in a higher plane, it produces rebirth in a lower plane;
and although it is capable of producing rebirth among those of great influence and great psychic power, it produces rebirth among those of little influence.
Likewise, that which produces rebirth in high families may produce rebirth in low families; that which produces rebirth among those of long life may produce rebirth among those of short life;
that which produces rebirth among the wealthy may produce rebirth among the poor. Even while producing the state of masculinity, it may produce the state of femininity or the state of neutrality.
That which produces excellence of physical appearance may produce ugliness; and that which produces excellence of the faculties—
Whether it be blindness, deafness, or any deficiency of the sense faculties; even that which produces the perfection of limbs and members may produce a deficiency of limbs such as hands and feet.

Likewise, unwholesome karma that would cause rebirth in the great hells at the time of its accumulation may, when obstructed by subsequently arisen powerful wholesome karma, cause rebirth among the *ussada* (extraordinary) hells or among the hungry ghosts (*petas*). King Ajātasattu is an example of this.
This is the illustration. It should be stated in full that [kamma] produces rebirth among the *ussadas*, or among the *petas*, or among the animals, and so forth.

Its supportive function (*upatthambhaka*) should likewise be understood by way of its opposite. For indeed, although kamma is weak at the time it is performed, when it is supported by a subsequent similar state (*sabhāga*)—whether wholesome or unwholesome—it becomes very strong.
The "obstructing" of the continuity of aggregates produced by karma means that, for a being born through another [past] karma,
one creates various obstacles in the body at any time from the moment of taking rebirth-linking onwards; or, having brought about the ruin of their status,
