fields, lands, cattle, buffaloes, wealth, grain, enjoyments, and prosperity, as well as the misfortune of their children, wives, kinsmen, and friends.
It is the cause for the arising of suffering. For the fruit of karma is indeed twofold: the fruition-fruit (*vipākaphala*) and the outflow-fruit (*nisandaphala*).
Among these, the fruition-fruit belongs only to the one who performed the karma, and not to anyone else. However, the outflow-fruit is common even to others.
The story of the merchant Ānanda in the *Dhammapada* should be cited here. Furthermore, regarding the eye and so forth, which are the specific types of matter born of karma (*kammaja-rūpa*):
By whatever karma even one, two, or three [faculties] are entirely broken—as in the case of Cakkhupāla and others—that karma is rightly included among the "destructive" (*upaghātaka*).
Furthermore, "destructive" (*upaghātaka*) and "interrupting" (*upacchedaka*) are identical in meaning;
for thus, in the *Majjhima-aṭṭhakathā*, having first mentioned it by the name "interrupting," it is also called "destructive."

It is said, "of this very [kamma] it is the name. In the *Aṅguttara-aṭṭhakathā*, having first mentioned it by the name "destructive" (*upaghātaka*), it is further stated that "cutting off" (*upacchedaka*) is also its name.
In the *Visuddhimagga*, in the exposition on mindfulness of death (*maraṇassati-niddesa*), it is likewise stated that "this is the kamma that cuts off kamma.
And here [in the present work], he will later say, "by the cutting-off kamma."
The interruption of other kamma is also evident at the time of death.
For then, when signs of an unhappy destination first appear through the power of evil kamma, wholesome kamma again obstructs that, displays signs of a happy destination, and causes rebirth in heaven.
Likewise, when signs of a happy destination appear through the power of wholesome kamma, evil kamma again [obstructs that].
Having warded off [the wholesome], it shows the sign of an unhappy destination and causes rebirth in the states of deprivation (*apāya*).

The cases of King Duṭṭhagāmaṇi and the father of Thera Soṇa should be told here. However, in the *Aṅguttara-aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated that even the path-action which exhausts both wholesome and unwholesome karma is called "that which cuts off other karma," as in the case of Thera Aṅgulimāla and others. In this...
In a given existence, there are acquired sublime (*mahaggata*) kamma-formations by which one may decline through unwholesome (*akusala*) states.
It is logical to include such [unwholesome states] within that which interrupts other kamma, as in the case of Devadatta.

However, the interruption of the continuity of aggregates produced by kamma occurs through the power of some transgressive kamma that has found an opportunity, even while the life-span and kamma of that particular existence still exist.
This should be understood by way of those who die prematurely due to some disease, fear, or external assault from the time of the *kalala* stage onwards.
And herein, with reference to the support provided by another karma or the continuity of the aggregates produced by karma,
the wholesome or unwholesome nature of these four types of karma is explained in the *Visuddhimagga* and in the *Aṅguttara-aṭṭhakathā*.

[This] was stated [in the *Visuddhimagga*]. However, in the *Majjhima-aṭṭhakathā*, in accordance with the suttas to be commented upon, it is stated that the wholesome nature of the supporting [kamma] refers specifically to its providing support for the continuity of the aggregates produced by that kamma, while the unwholesome nature of the obstructing and harming [kammas] is likewise stated.
Yet, in the *Majjhima-ṭīkā* and the *Aṅguttara-ṭīkā*, this appears to have been stated as if it were not acceptable; however, in the *Mahā-ṭīkā*...

However, some [alternative] arguments have been made. In this regard, because they were stated in accordance with the suttas that are to be commented upon, they should be understood as a separate scriptural method (*pāḷinaya*).

Yet, no further arguments need be made. For in the sutta, it was stated by way of the harmful act of taking life—namely, "this is the practice of the young man that leads to a short lifespan, namely, being a killer of living beings"—that there is both what causes oppression and what causes affliction.
This way of practice, young man, leads to affliction, namely, being of a nature to harass living beings;
thus it is stated by way of violence and so forth. And that which is supportive leads to long life, young man;
this way of practice, namely, having abandoned the taking of life, one abstains from the taking of life; thus it is stated by way of the abstinence from the taking of life and so forth.
This is stated by way of [the person]. All of this, moreover, is according to the being who has attained human status; thus should the method of the Pāḷi be understood separately.

However, in the *Mahāṭīkā* and the *Aṅguttaraṭīkā*, it is said: "By those who do not accept the support of other kamma and so forth, the state of being a progenitor (*janaka*) and so on must be accepted as the result (*vipāka*).
It is not 'not-kamma' [that produces it], for it is logical that only the result itself can be subject to impairment."
"It appears as if" is what was stated.
"By way of function" means by way of the four functions: producing, supporting, oppressing, and cutting off.
Therein, a single volition of killing accomplishes these four functions; for it continues until it ripens.
It does not find an opportunity [to ripen]. Until then, it performs whichever among the three functions—supporting and so forth—for which it has obtained the requisite conditions.
When it finally finds an opportunity to ripen, then by means of that single volition, there is only a single rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).
Thus, according to the method explained in the Sāketa Question, it produces one existence in the woeful states (*apāyabhava*). Beyond that, however, the function of producing rebirth-linking...
There is none. Even in a hundred thousand existences or a hundred thousand aeons, the process of existence accomplishes the other three functions along with the production of its own result.
The story of Queen Dhammadinnā, the consort of King Uggasena, should be told here.
However, when—prior to her own fruition stage—she was either a noble one, an ordinary person, or possessed of a virtuous mind...
It effects an interruption. Having thus interrupted it, it creates an opportunity for the course of action during the very same watch; it does not itself produce its own result.
However, when it interrupts the continuum of the aggregates belonging to one possessed of an evil mind, it produces its own result immediately upon that interruption.
From the moment the rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) has been obtained once, throughout many successive existences...
Even in the case of hundreds of thousands [of lives], it performs only such acts as cutting off [the breath] and so forth.
Herein, the stories of the Elder Mahāmoggallāna, Sāmāvatī, the monks from the banks of the Vaggumudā River, Dussimāra, and King Kalābu should be told.
Furthermore, because this so-called "cutting-off karma" is frequently found among animals, it is therefore well—
It should not be said that a powerful unwholesome kamma does not act as a cutter-off of either a weaker unwholesome kamma or the continuity of aggregates produced by an unwholesome kamma.
For it is precisely for this reason that the *Madhyama-aṭṭhakathā* states:
"When much unwholesome kamma has been accumulated, the powerful kamma, having warded off the result of the weak kamma, [brings about] its own result..."
It is said that "he makes space. Furthermore,
even during the course of existence, without interrupting the continuum of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) produced by other kamma,
[the mind] occurs in relation to one of the five "summits of the stream" (santati-sīsa), namely those comprised within the decads of eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body.
It is appropriate to say that even the total cutting off [of the continuity] is the function of this [kamma] alone.
As for what was stated in the *Mahāṭīkā* and the *Aṅguttara-ṭīkā*—namely, "The obstructive [kamma] cuts off the fruition of another;
it does not itself produce its own fruition"—that was said having observed the commentary’s statement: "It oppresses pleasure and pain, and does not allow them to proceed for a duration."
It may be so. Regarding the phrase "it cries out to proceed for a duration," the meaning is simply that it cries out for the continuity of either happiness or suffering to proceed for a long time.
However, it does not cut off the ripening of another karma along with the stream of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) as if it were something destructive.
[143] As for what is stated in the *Vibhāvanī*:

“The productive [kamma] generates its result without interrupting the continuity of other results; the obstructive [kamma], however, is preceded by an interruption”—this, it is said, is the definitive conclusion in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*).
That is not correct, because within the commentaries themselves there are accounts of those who, having died due to an obstructive kamma performed in a previous life, were reborn in heaven.

[144] Furthermore, regarding the statement "And as for that which therein... other teachers say," etc., the use of the abstract noun (*bhāvavacana*) is stated because it is the harmful action itself that produces its own result. That too is not correct;

for it is recorded in the *Aṭṭhakathās* that for those such as Dussimāra and Kalāburāja who were reborn in the woeful states by that very same karma, that karma functioned as the "interrupting karma" (*upacchedaka-kamma*). [The Tetrad of Productive Karma]
146. "Weighty" (*garuka*) refers to a sublime wholesome deed on the side of the wholesome that cannot be obstructed by any other karma;
and on the side of the unwholesome, it refers to the five deeds of immediate retribution (*ānantariya-kamma*) together with fixed wrong view. Here, one might ask:

why is "sublime deed" mentioned? For that [sublime state] may be lost either through negligence, or through the occurrence of the factors of hindrance (*nīvaraṇa*), or through the power of craving (*nikanti*).

"It does not give its result when being obstructed. Likewise, when many deeds of immediate retribution (*ānantariya-kamma*) have been committed by one person, while one is ripening, the others do not ripen.

It is said: setting aside for the moment sublime karma (*mahaggata-kamma*), in the sense of being unobstructable by another meritorious deed, [it is stronger] than the states of negligence, the states of hindrance (*nīvaraṇa-dhamma*), the states of attachment (*nikanti-dhamma*), and other more powerful sublime karmic intervals belonging to oneself.

It is called "weighty" (*garuka*). However, setting aside the deeds of immediate retribution (*ānantariya-kamma*), one's own stronger deed of immediate retribution is "weighty" in the sense that it cannot be obstructed by any other phenomenon;
thus, their weightiness should be understood according to what is appropriate.

"Proximate" (*āsanna*) refers to what is recollected at the time of death and what is performed at that time. In this context, "performed at that time" means [what occurs] from the final cognitive process (*javana-vīthi*)...
Any wholesome or unwholesome kamma performed in the proximate past during the preliminary stage [is included].

However, it should be understood that kamma of wrong view occurring through insight meditation (*vipassanā*) and so forth, as well as kamma of right view, is also included even if performed in the final twenty thought-moments (*javana*). As it is said:
"At the time of death, he may have a wrong view or a right view that has been fully undertaken and adopted. By this, from that kamma of wrong view...
It is established that another action occurring in the final cognitive process (*javana-vīthi*) is incapable of producing rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).
"Habitual" (*āciṇṇa*) means performed repeatedly over a long period; even after performing it once, it subsequently produces either joy or distress through being done again and again.
"Kamma by way of having been done" (*kaṭattā-kamma*) means "kamma because it has been made"—thus, it is so called by reason of its having been performed.
"Kamma" means that which is to be called "kamma. The meaning is that there is no kamma to be designated by way of being heavy (*garuka*) and so forth.
Among those, the first three are precisely *upapajjavedanīya* (to-be-experienced-in-the-next-birth) kamma performed in this present existence.

However, *kaṭattā-ūpaga* (stored) kamma consists of what was performed in this existence—lacking the qualities of being heavy, habitual, or cultivated—along with *aparāpariyāyavedanīya* (to-be-experienced-in-a-later-life) kamma performed in past existences.
Any kamma that has reached the path of action and is to be experienced upon rebirth (*upapajjavedanīya-kamma*).
However, in the *Mahāṭīkā*, "kamma already performed" (*kaṭattā-kamma*) is taken to mean only that which was done in previous births; this does not accord with the *Aṭṭhakathā*.

For it is said: "But that which is free from these three [types of kamma] and has been repeatedly practiced is called 'kamma already performed' (*kaṭattāva-kamma*). And this does not refer to past existences.

Even such actions as matricide and the like—karmas of subsequent retribution—cannot be distinguished by these three [criteria] as being either "freed from" or "not freed from," or as being "repeatedly practiced" or "not repeatedly practiced.
For at that time, they proceed within a continuum of grave karma; they also proceed within a continuum of proximate habitual karma.
And in the *Aṅguttara-aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated: "But action performed by means of ignorance, other than these three [types], is called *kaṭattā-vā* (stored) karma.

It is not possible to qualify those [other actions] as being "performed by means of ignorance," for they may have been performed by means of ignorance in previous existences, or they may have been performed by means of knowledge.
However, those qualifications apply to this present existence.

It should be understood that those actions performed in previous births— along with those seven impulsive moments of karma described as being "done" by way of the three types such as the heavy (*garuka*) and so forth—
are called "karma by way of having been done" (*kaṭattā-kamma*). And having established this,
wherever the phrase "that previously done karma" (*taṃ-pubba-kataṃ kammaṃ*) occurs, it refers to that [karma] either in this present existence or in past existences.

The meaning should be understood as "performed in a previous time. Now, among these four types of kamma that exist, it is the weighty (*garuka*) alone that provides rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) in the immediately following existence.

In the absence of a weighty kamma, it is the proximate (*āsanna*). In the absence of a proximate, it is the habitual (*āciṇṇa*). In the absence of a habitual, it is the kamma performed (*kaṭattā-kamma*).
Therefore he said, "by way of the sequence of giving the result" (*pākadāna-pariyāyena*); the meaning is "by way of the section on the giving of results. Here, one might ask:
Why is that which is near mentioned first here because of its habitual practice? Is it not the case that in the Pāḷi, that which is near is indeed mentioned first because of its habitual practice?

As it is said: "That which is heavy, that which is frequent, that which is near, and then karma performed (kaṭattā-vā kammaṃ). Furthermore, in the Aṭṭhakathās, the section on the giving of results is arranged according to that very same sequence.
It is replied: in the Pāḷi, [the order] follows the sequence of strength and weakness according to their intrinsic nature (sabhāva).

The "habitual" (*āciṇṇa*) was mentioned first. However, since that sequence can sometimes also occur in the order of maturation (*pāka*), the section on the giving of results (*pākadānavāra*) has been arranged in that same sequence in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*).
For even a proximate mental state, being unable to satisfy or distress [the mind], is weak and cannot turn back a strong habitual tendency. Because...
Furthermore, in the Mahākammavibhaṅga Sutta it is said: "Either previously he has performed wholesome karma to be experienced as pleasant;
or afterwards he has performed wholesome karma to be experienced as pleasant; or at the time of death he possesses right view that is fully undertaken and adopted.
Thus, even for one who has habitually practiced misconduct, by means of a wholesome deed performed proximately to death—

Going to heaven has been described. Likewise, it has been stated that even for one who has practiced good conduct, there may be rebirth in a state of misery due to a proximate evil deed—such as the performance of a past evil karma to be experienced as suffering, up to the point of having fully adopted wrong view.
For when both [the good conduct and the evil deed] possess strength, it is the proximate one alone that becomes effective.
It is appropriate [to say this]. Therefore, it should be understood that here the Elder spoke first of that which was nearest [in time].
Furthermore, in this context, the statement "it was previously done by him" should be understood as being said with reference to the most recently recollected deed.
Here, the stories of the executioner named Tambadāṭhika and the lay follower named Mahāvātakāla should be told.

[145] However, in the *Vibhāvani* commentary, after presenting the simile of the old ox, it is stated categorically that "it gives its first result precisely to that which is nearest. This is not correct.

For it is not stated categorically in this way in the *Aṭṭhakathā*. Furthermore, even if he were unable to stand up, that old ox would not necessarily emerge sooner simply because he was standing near the gate. [The Tetrad of Weightiness]

147. "Diṭṭhadhamma" refers to the present personal existence (attabhāva) that has become manifest to direct perception. "Vedanīya" means that which is to be experienced or felt; it refers to the fruit (phala). That which has its fruit to be experienced in the present life is "diṭṭhadhammavedanīya.
However, in the *Vibhāvani*, it is stated:
"'Diṭṭhadhammavedanīya' means that which is to be experienced in the present life by way of the experiencing of the result (vipāka). This is not correct.
"For one experiences the result in this very life" (diṭṭheva dhamme vipākaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti) is what is stated in the Pāḷi.
Here, by the phrase "experiences the result," it is shown that the word *vedanīya* has the sense of "kamma" (the action) and refers to that which transcends the result (*vipākātideyya*).

This being the case, here only a *aññapadatthasamāsa* (compound with a different referent) is possible; it is not an *uttarapadatthasamāsa* (compound where the meaning resides in the final member). Having approached the seen state (*diṭṭhadhammaṃ upecca*).
It is called *upapajjavedanīya* because its fruit is to be experienced after having been reborn (*pajjitvā*) immediately following that [existence].
For this very reason, when explaining the meaning of the word *upapajja* in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), it is stated as "having been reborn" (*upapajjitvā*).
However, in the textual passages of the Suttas, the reading *upapajjeva* is seen. Therefore, it is to be reborn in the immediate next [existence] close to the present life (*diṭṭhadhamma*).

"Upapajja" means "having been reborn. Regarding the term *upapajjavedanīya*: its meaning should be understood according to the reading as "that which has a fruit to be experienced upon being reborn (*upapajje*), because it belongs to a second personal existence (*attabhāva*) that arises at rebirth.
Alternatively, *upapajja* is a single indeclinable particle occurring in the sense of the immediately subsequent existence, just as in the word *paccā*. However, in the *Vibhāvani*, it is stated:
[147] In the *Vibhāvani*, however: [text follows]
It has been stated: “To be experienced after having been reborn immediately following the present life (diṭṭhadhamma) is ‘to be experienced upon rebirth’ (upavajja-vedanīya).
That is not correct. For it is stated in the Pāḷi: “Having been reborn, one experiences the result. “Pariyāya” means that which comes again and again.
Since it is another (apara) such occasion (pariyāya), it is called “another occasion” (aparapariyāya). [This refers to] existences other than the present life and those immediately following.

There is another sense of the transformation of the personal existence (*attabhāvapariyatto*). For neither in the *Mahāṭīkā* nor in the *Aṅguttaraṭīkā* is it stated that "transformation of the personal existence" refers to a sequence of personal existences other than those of the present life, the immediately following life, and future lives.
However, in the sūtra passages, two readings are observed: *apare vā pariyāyena* and *aparāpare vā pariyāyena*.
In that regard, according to the latter reading, one should understand that here in the middle there is the elision of one of the two words "apara.

However, in the *Saṅgaha-poṭṭhaka* manuscripts, the word "aparāpariya" is seen in the middle with a long vowel and the meaning of "yā" (going). That [reading] does not exist in many commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) and does not accord with the Canon (*pāḷi*).
[148] Regarding that which was stated in the *Vibhāvanī*:

“Other [kamma] is ‘to-be-experienced-in-a-subsequent-birth’ (*aparāpariya-vedanīya*), which is to be experienced in some other state of existence (*attabhāva*) anywhere else than the present life (*diṭṭhadhamma*)”—in this regard, the term “present life” (*diṭṭhadhammato*) is indeed not appropriate.
For it is not logical that, having excluded the intermediate state of rebirth (*upapajjabhava*), only the first [state], the present life, should be added here as the third term.
[149] However, in terms of both meaning (*attha*) and phrasing (*byañjana*), it does not entirely agree with the canonical text (*pāḷi*).
For in the text it is stated: "He experiences the result (*vipāka*) either in another way (*aparena vā pariyāyena*) or in yet another way (*aparāparena vā pariyāyena*).
"Non-existent action" (*ahosikamma*) is action that has been; it is non-existent action. There is future action (*bhavissatikamma*), existing action (*atthikamma*), and there is no... [text ends]
By way of the textual passage stating "it is a result" (*vipāka*), what has been thus designated by the teachers as "kamma" refers to that which has not obtained any stage of result at all.

In this context, among the seven wholesome and unwholesome impulsion consciousnesses (*javana*), the volition of the first impulsion is called "to be experienced in the present life" (*diṭṭhadhammavedanīya*).
For, due to its lack of repetition and its extreme weakness, it is short-lived and yields very little result.
Having obtained a condition, it gives its fruit—which is merely rootless—within this very life (diṭṭhadhamme) and then passes away.
It is not able to follow along the continuum even beyond a single moment of death. However, when failing to obtain a condition, it is called "non-existent" (ahosika).

A "condition" (paccaya), moreover, is that which provides the opportunity for the arising of its own fruit, consisting of desirable or undesirable objects encountered during various postures (iriyāpatha).

Any condition whatsoever, such as "going" (gamana) and so forth, is indeed applicable. However, in the commentaries (*ṭīkā*), the condition is described as being "great" by way of its state of not being overcome by opposites and so on.
This should be understood as having been stated with reference to the yielding of more manifest results, like those of the *kākavaliya* and other such [strong] deeds.
For even the volition of the first impulsion (*pathama-javana-cetanā*) occurring within the continuum of the path-of-action impulsion (*kammapatha-javana-santāna*) does not [yield such results].
There are indeed conditions obtained through the conjunction of the desirable and the undesirable that do not yield any fruit corresponding to their own power.
Nor can it be asserted that every fruit being given by such [conditions] must necessarily be manifest either to the general public or to the agent alone.
However, as for that which is mentioned in the *Ñāṇavibhaṅga-aṭṭhakathā* as "one [kamma] to be experienced in this very life" (*diṭṭhadhammavedanīya*)...

"It gives a result. It is stated that "the remaining ones are without result" (*avipāka*). This should be understood as being said with reference to those remaining [volitions] that have not obtained their conditions;
for it is impossible to understand that a single present life constitutes the opportunity for only one [volition] that is to be experienced in the present life.
However, the final javana-volition, which accomplishes the purpose and brings about a definitive conclusion, is called "to be experienced upon rebirth" (*upapajja-vedanīya*).
For that [volition], because it has been repeatedly practiced, becomes somewhat substantial; thus, like the first volition, it is unable to ripen more quickly.

And because it is powerful, it is able to produce one existence (*bhava*). However, among those whose speed has declined, because it is the final impulsion (*antimajavana*), it does not endure for long—like intermediate volitions—and therefore, having obtained the necessary conditions, it brings about either rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) in the immediately following existence, or...

Having given its fruit either during the course of existence (*pavatti*) or immediately upon arising, it ceases. However, if it fails to obtain that fruit, it remains merely as "kamma that has been" (*ahosikamma*).

It is not capable of persisting beyond the moment of death. As for the statement in the *Ñāṇavibhaṅga-aṭṭhakathā* that one [type of] kamma to be experienced upon rebirth (*upapajjavedanīya*) draws forth the rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), while the others are without fruition—that too was said with reference to the fruition of the rebirth-linking itself.

It should be understood that this has been stated. For even the remaining [karmas], until the second death arrives, continue to give their result during the course of existence as long as they have obtained the necessary conditions.

Here, having performed mixed karmas and experiencing the fruit of those mixed karmas in the immediately following existence, there are the *Vemānika-peta* stories and others who, having performed various specific karmas, attain a happy destination (*sugati*) in that very next existence.
Regarding this, hundreds of instances must be told here of those experiencing misfortune that is the result of such [actions],
or those experiencing prosperity that is the result thereof, within the miserable destinies (*duggati*).
Furthermore, as for what is to be elucidated in the *Vibhāvanī*:

“It is said: ‘And that [kamma] gives its result as a process-result only after it has already given rebirth-linking; there is no case where it gives a process-result without having first given rebirth-linking.
This is not tenable, because it contradicts the aforementioned instances.
And as for what was stated therein:
“The reason stated—that ‘the opportunity for [kamma] to be experienced upon rebirth exists immediately after death’—is also not a valid reason.
For the opportunity remains possible from the moment immediately following birth all the way until the end of life.
And as for that which is therein...”
"But once rebirth-linking has been given, it gives the result of the process-of-becoming even in a hundred births"— this too should not be accepted, because it would lead to a confusion of kamma.

And in the *Aṅguttara-aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated that there is no transference between those [types of kamma]— namely, that to be experienced in the present life (*diṭṭhadhammavedanīya*), that to be experienced upon rebirth (*upapajjavedanīya*),
and that to be experienced in a subsequent period (*aparapariyāyavedanīya*)— but rather they remain established in their respective places.

Nor can it be said here that this was stated solely with reference to rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), because there is neither a passage from the *Aṭṭhakathā* nor a logical justification (*yutti*) to prove that point.
However, the five javana volitions in the middle are called "to-be-experienced in a subsequent state" (*aparapariyāya-vedanīya*).
For these are very powerful and substantial; thus, they are unable to ripen quickly and persist for a long duration.
However, they do exist. Therefore, from the third existence onwards, when they find an opportunity, they grant rebirth-linking five times;
thereafter, as long as the process of saṃsāra continues, they grant results of the course-of-existence even for a hundred thousand aeons.
Furthermore, these same three types of kamma, when they fail to obtain any result whatsoever within their own respective fields, are called "ineffective kamma" (ahosikamma).

Their "field" (khetta) should be understood as follows: for the first, it is delimited by death in the present life (diṭṭhadhammacuti); for the second, by death immediately preceding a future existence;
and for the third, by the death of final Nibbāna (parinibbānacuti). [The Tetrad on the Present Life] 148.
"By way of the place of ripening" means by way of the place where [the result] ripens, such as the states of deprivation (apāya) and so forth; thus there are four types of kamma.

The construction is: "they exist. "Therein" means among those four types of karma, beginning with the unwholesome. "By way of the doors of action" means by way of the doors of action such as the body, which serve as the instrumental factors for the accomplishment of karma.
"Pāṇātipāta" (killing) is so called because by means of it they cause the destruction of living beings (*pāṇa*).

Here, "destruction" (*atipātana*) should be understood as causing them to fall prematurely through the force of an application, rather than allowing them to fall by their own nature. They take what is not given (*adinnam ādiyanti*).

By this [it is meant] taking what is not given (*adinnādāna*). By this one practices wrongly among sensual objects (*kāma*) which are reckoned as things that should not be approached; thus it is sexual misconduct (*kāmesumicchācāra*).

Therein, the volition of killing—which originates the bodily and vocal exertion that cuts off the continuity of the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) of another living being while perceiving them as a living being—is called the destruction of life (*pāṇātipāta*). One’s own life-faculty...

For one who is killing, there is no such thing as taking life. Taking what is not given (*adinnādāna*) is the volition of stealing that originates the bodily or verbal effort intended to deprive another of their property when that property belongs to another and one perceives it as belonging to another.

Sexual misconduct (*kāmesumicchācāra*) is the volition of gratification that originates the bodily effort of one who leads another onto an improper path among those things that should not be approached.
Some, however, desire the reading "even here some perceive it as an object not to be approached. That does not agree with the Aṭṭhakathā; for it is stated there:

"The mind that indulges in that [act] is a mind directed toward an object not to be approached. By this, it is established that when there is an object not to be approached, whether one perceives it as an object to be approached or perceives it as an object not to be approached, there is indeed a course of kamma for one who indulges in it.
Otherwise, it would have to be said that there is a path-intention regarding an object that is not to be approached,
yet which is perceived as such. However, others say that even when one has personally made the effort and experiences pleasure from the insertion of the organ by another person into oneself,
there is no breach of the course of action (*kammappatha*), because of the absence of personal effort (*payoga*).

Some say that when there is a mind of repeated practice (*sevanacitta*), the preliminary effort (*payoga*) is not a factor. If this were so, it would follow that sexual misconduct (*micchācāra*) consists of only three factors, not four.
However, others hold that in the *Aṭṭhakathā* it is stated that it consists of four factors including the preliminary effort of repeated practice.
Yet, the preliminary effort of repeated practice is mentioned only because it is generally found; it is not because it is an absolute factor.
Otherwise, they say that since women for the most part have no need for sexual activity, sexual misconduct would be rare among them;
furthermore, the violation of a bhikkhunī is included here as well, for she is included among those who are protected.

However, in the commentaries (*ṭīkā*), it is said that she is not even protected by the Dhamma—how much less by her mother and others? For here, "Dhamma" refers specifically to the religious systems of the heretics.
They say it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*. But even the Dhamma of the Dispensation does not support this.
For one’s fellow celibates, such as the preceptor and so forth, are indeed regarded as mother and so on by her. For thus it is said in the *Sikkhāpadavibhaṅga-aṭṭhakathā*:
"Even sexual misconduct [is an offense] for a shameless female novice, a female probationer, a female bhikkhunī who is a worldling, a female stream-enterer, or a female once-returner... and so on.
It is said that for a non-returner (*anāgāminī*), a transgression is a great offense; however, for one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*), it is an absolute great offense.
Why, then, was the drinking of fermented liquor (*surāpāna*) not included here? For that too has been stated to lead to the states of misery (*apāya*). As it is said:
"Monks, the drinking of fermented and distilled liquors, when practiced, cultivated, and frequently indulged in, leads to hell, leads to rebirth as an animal..."
It leads to the realm of hungry ghosts (*pettivisaya*). And whatever is the lightest ripening of drinking fermented liquor and spirits, that leads to madness for one who has become a human being.
Furthermore, it is stated in the Commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) that, by way of their constituent parts, all five courses of action beginning with killing are indeed courses of action (*kammapatha*).
It is said: first, in the *Mūlaṭīkā*, because of its similarity to it and because of its assistance in sexual misconduct...
It is stated that [these] are included within all ten courses of action (*kamma-patha*).

Regarding this, some, taking the point of similarity, say that drinking intoxicants is also subsumed under this very category because it constitutes misconduct (*micchā-cāra*) with respect to sensual pleasures consisting of flavors;

this is stated [in the *Visuddhimagga*]. Taking the point of being contributory factors, the *Paṭisambhidāmagga-ṭīkā* states that both wholesome and unwholesome [actions] are indeed those that produce rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).

They are called "paths of action" (kammappatha). Regarding the commentary on the statement that those remaining [factors] beyond what has been mentioned are not called paths of action because they are manifold in producing rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*):
"those remaining beyond what has been mentioned" refers to drinking intoxicants and so forth, as well as abstaining from them and so forth.

For drinking intoxicants is a condition for intoxication (*mada*); intoxication is a path of demerit (*apuññappatha*). Abstaining from it, however, leads to non-intoxication; and that, moreover, is a path of merit (*puññappatha*).

It is said that those [karmic paths], by virtue of being the decisive support (upanissaya) for the path of action, can also produce rebirth-linking (sandhi) through the power of proximate karma (*tadāsanna-kamma*).

In this context, "by virtue of proximate karma" means by way of non-meritorious or meritorious karmas rooted in that [act] which occurred in proximity to either the drinking of liquor or the abstention from drinking liquor. This is what is meant: whoever...

If, after drinking liquor, one commits any action such as taking life for the sake of intoxication, that drinking of liquor serves as a powerful supporting condition (*upanissaya*) for that action and occupies the place of the prior volition (*pubba-cetanā*).
That [drinking] alone produces a separate rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), and not the other [action].
For just as both the preceding and succeeding volitions are merely the accompaniments of an action that has reached the state of a full course of action (*kammapatha*).

They produce rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), not the others. This case is likewise. For it cannot be restricted by saying that only those courses of action (*kammapatha*) mentioned explicitly in the Suttas produce rebirth-linking, while the others do not.

Rather, only those courses of action which possess the inherent capacity to produce rebirth-linking are stated explicitly there; whereas those which are inconclusive regarding the production of rebirth-linking are not.
It can be understood that these [factors] were not mentioned there because they do not possess that specific nature.
For instance, in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga-aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated that only those wholesome and unwholesome [kamma] which produce rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) are "paths of action" (*kammapatha*).

It is further stated that the remaining factors are not called "paths of action" because they are not determinative (*anekantika*) in producing rebirth-linking. Therefore, this [category] also, due to its indeterminacy in producing rebirth-linking...
In that context, it has not been stated explicitly by way of its own specific form (*sarūpato*).

That which was previously stated as "producing rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) by means of a latent action (*sannakamma*) at that time"—it can be said that this is included among those latent actions stated explicitly in that context.
Its function, moreover, is twofold: the production of rebirth-linking and the production of [subsequent] karma. Among these, because it produces rebirth-linking...
Considering that his production of kamma alone is great and of vast diffusion, Sakka, the lord of the devas,
said in the *Kumbha Jātaka*: "Those who, having secluded themselves,
practice misconduct by body, speech, and mind..."
"Having practiced misconduct, they go to hell;
buy this full jar of hers!
Thus, by means of the very karma that was near at hand, his going to a state of misery was stated. Taking both of those as his task, however—
It should be understood that it is stated in the *Aṅguttara Nikāya*: "Monks, the drinking of fermented and distilled liquors, when indulged in... leads [to such states].

For this is the established nature (*dhammatā*) in these sections of the Suttas: namely, that wherever the term "leads to" (*saṃvattanika*) is used, the construction is according to what is available.

Thus, in the *Mūlaṭīkā*, regarding the reading "it leads to renewed existence" (*punabbhavaṃ deti*), it is explained: "it leads to renewed existence" means it leads to renewed existence together with the karma.
It is said that, acting as companions to kamma but not co-nascent with it, they lead to renewed existence.
However, some, failing to consider this point, imagine from this passage that it possesses the status of an independent path of action (*kammapatha*).

As for the commentary’s statement, "From the perspective of its constituent parts, all five are indeed paths of action," there, by the word "indeed" (*eva*), [it is indicated] because they possess the nature of volition (*cetanā*).
This precludes [the view that it] belongs to the category of jhāna and so forth.

For volition—whether it has reached the status of a course of action (*kammappatha*) or not—is, by its very nature as a constituent part, exclusively "belonging to the category of a course of action. For this very reason, the *Mūlaṭīkā* states: "They are courses of action" means "exclusively belonging to the category of a course of action.
And the *Anuṭīkā* states: "Exclusively belonging to the category of a course of action; not belonging to the category of jhāna and so forth. However, some...
Failing to observe this point, they claim that by this statement [the Buddha] asserts its status as a distinct course of kamma (*kammappatha*).
However, in the *Khuddakapāṭha-aṭṭhakathā*, its status as a course of kamma is rejected in its entirety;

for there, after having separately stated that the preceding four possess the nature of bodily action (*kāyakamma*) and so forth as well as the status of being courses of kamma, upon reaching the drinking of fermented liquor (*surāpāna*), it is said:
It is stated that it is "only bodily action. By this, both its status as verbal action and its status as a course of action (kamma-patha) are rejected.
This is what is rejected in the *Dhātusaṃyutta-aṭṭhakathā*. As it says: "The third was spoken according to the inclination of those who awaken by way of the five courses of action;
the fourth, by way of the seven courses of action; and the fifth, by way of the ten courses of action."
For in that context, regarding the third [course of action], it is stated specifically as "by way of the five courses of action" because of the inclusion of drinking intoxicants;

it is not stated "by way of the five paths of action. Furthermore, regarding these [courses of action], one cannot say that the agent is excluded from producing rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) as being manifold;
for if that were so, all the canonical texts, commentaries, and sub-commentaries would be brought into harmony. As for "bodily action" (*kāyakamma*), here the body is threefold.
"The body with its equipment," "the body of clarity," and "the body of intimation. Here, it is stated that "the body of intimation" is intended by the phrase "reckoned as bodily intimation.
For the body of intimation is sometimes performed by means of a limb of the body for the purpose of making one's own intention known to another;
thus, it is called "bodily intimation. And that very [intimation] is so called because it is the gateway for the occurrence of kamma.

"Door" means the body-door (*kāyadvāra*). For when that [door] proceeds with its respective preparatory function, the functions such as the cutting off of the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) are accomplished;
thus, the volitional state (*cetanādhamma*) that produces it receives the designation "bodily action" (*kāyakamma*) due to its function of instigation (*āyūhana*) and its production.
In that body-door: and herein, because all actions are preceded by this associated [volition], [it is the forerunner].
They do not succeed without it. For it has been said: "States have mind as their precursor; mind is their chief; they are mind-made.
Here, "states" refers to states of good conduct and bad conduct. Therefore, because the mind-door is common to all kamma, it is unable to distinguish between specific types of kamma.
However, the body and speech, being unique (asādhāraṇa), are able to do so. And because—
The first seven types of karma are not accomplished by the mind alone; rather, they are accomplished only through the bodily and verbal applications originating from it.
Therefore, it is said that these [applications] themselves constitute the "door" for the occurrence of those karmas, as expressed by the term "bodily door" (kāyadvāra).
The subsequent term is likewise "verbal door" (vacīdvāra).

However, if it were stated merely that "it is called bodily action because it is performed at the door of the body" and "it is called verbal action because it is performed at the door of speech," then the definition of actions by way of their doors would not be established—namely, that the three beginning with the destruction of life are bodily action, and the four beginning with false speech are verbal action. How so? For when those first two...

By way of command, they are broken at the door of speech with even a slight [effort]. At that time, they would have to abandon the name "bodily action" (*kāyakamma*) and come to be reckoned as "verbal action" (*vacīkamma*).
Why? Because it is stated that they are called "verbal action" due to their occurrence at the door of speech.
Or else, they would have two names, because they are seen manifesting at both doors. However, when the four intermediate [factors]...
By means of small things such as the clenching of a fist, they are accomplished at the door of the body (*kāyadvāra*).
In that case, even those [actions] would have to abandon the name "verbal action" (*vacīkamma*) and come to be reckoned as "bodily action" (*kāyakamma*). Why?

Because it is stated that they are called "bodily action" due to their occurrence at the door of the body. Or else, they would have two names, since they are seen to manifest at both doors. And this being so—
If it were stated that "taking life... and wrong conduct are called bodily action," this definition would indeed be pointless.
Likewise, if it were stated later that "false speech... and idle chatter are called verbal action.

However, when it is said "by way of frequent occurrence," one excludes each of those six kinds of faults by means of the word "frequent" (bāhulla) and [classifies them] according to the door as previously described.
The determination of action (*kamma*) is thus established.
Just as one who roams the forest is called a "forest-roamer" (*vanacāraka*), so too, mental actions, even when occurring through other doors, are merely "roaming.
The other doors are not factors for the establishment of those actions. Therefore, it should be understood that they are treated separately. Furthermore, because...
The name "body" (kāya) for the body-door (kāyadvāra) is established and evident by itself throughout many thousands of suttas.

Likewise, the name "speech" (vācā) applies to the speech-door (vacīdvāra). And the name "mind" (mano) applies to the mind-door (manodvāra), which consists of wholesome and unwholesome impulsion-consciousness (javana-citta).
Therefore, in all cases where the body-door, speech-door, or mind-door are mentioned, [the door is designated] by means of its function (kamma).

There is no separate function called "determination" (*vavatthāna*). However, it should be understood that wherever the doors of bodily action, verbal action, and mental action are mentioned—specifically in the *Dvārakathā* (Discourse on the Doors) and other such sections—the determination of the door by way of the action must also be stated separately.
By this, that which was stated in the *Vibhāvanī*...
“The statement that ‘the bodily door is so called because it is the gateway for the occurrence of bodily action’ is refuted. Furthermore, as for what was said there:

‘Likewise, when one performs lying and so forth by means of a bodily gesture, verbal action occurs at the bodily door; thus, the definition of a door by way of the action would not be possible’—that too is not tenable.”

For verbal action performed by means of a bodily modification, even though it occurs at the door of the body, is unable either to subvert the name of that door or to give its own name to it; this is because the name of that door is established by its own intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).

By this very principle, it should be understood that which was stated there: "In that case, bodily action alone occurs for the most part at the door of the body, not the others. Therefore, of bodily action... [155]

"Because it occurs for the most part in this very place, its status as the door of bodily action (kāyakammadvāra) is established—just as the status of being a 'brahmin village' and so forth is established for places like brahmin villages. This too is rejected;
for there is no such term as "door of bodily action" mentioned here. [Bodily Action]
149. *Musā* is a particle used in the sense of "unreal. That by which they speak what is unreal is *musāvāda* (false speech).

It is *pisuṇā* (slanderous speech) because by means of it one crushes, breaks apart, and creates mutual division among others—that is, the essence of harmony known as their mutual state of friendliness.

Or, according to the method of etymology (*nirutti*), it is *pisuṇā* because by means of it one makes oneself beloved and causes the absence of friendship in others. They speak by means of these [words], thus they are called *vācā*.
It is speech; and because that speech is malicious, it is malicious speech (*pisuṇavācā*). It scorches and burns the heart of the one by whom it is heard as it pervades it;
thus it is harsh. And because that speech is harsh, it is harsh speech (*pharusavācā*).

It bears fruit, scatters, and destroys the happiness and welfare to be attained by virtuous people, and it breaks the path to welfare and happiness; thus it is frivolous chatter (*sampha*). Or else, it bears fruit [in that way].

It is called *sampha* because it is broken by this. This is the name for speech that consists merely of a subject matter, arising from a mind of inspired eloquence devoid of meaning and Dhamma—such as [tales of] the Bhārata war or the abduction of Sītā—in which there is no word pertaining to the Dhamma, Vinaya, or benefit, whether for the present life (*diṭṭhadhamma*) or for the future life (*samparāyika*), that illuminates a skillful means.
It is so called in the sense of "prattling nonsense" (*samphaṃ palapanti*).
They speak with this, thus it is "frivolous talk" (*sapphappalāpa*).

In that context, lying (*musāvāda*) is the unwholesome volition (*akusalacetanā*) that originates from bodily and verbal application, having as its primary aim the speaking of poison to another. That which is exclusively destructive to the welfare of another constitutes a course of action (*kammappatha*);
the other is merely an action (*kamma*). And here, "course of action" refers to the gateway or path for the emergence of those actions that produce rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).

It is so called because, just as the place where kings arise is called a "royal road" (*rājapatha*), so too, among the activities of the body, speech, and mind that are visible in the world, it is through those activities that the kamma producing rebirth arises;
or rather, it is in those activities that they arise and proceed. These are the activities of the formation of body, speech, and mind.

They are called "paths of action" because they are the primary gateway for the arising of those karmas that produce rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*). But what are they? They are the ten types of actions:
in the unwholesome [category], the acts such as killing living beings and so forth; and in the wholesome [category], the acts of abstaining from those and so forth.
These very actions [lead to] happy and miserable destinies, as well as the pleasure and pain that arise therein.
They also say that they are called "paths of action" because they serve as paths.
Malicious speech (*pisuṇāvācā*) is defiled volition originating from bodily or vocal effort directed toward the destruction of another with the intent to cause division.

That too constitutes a breach of the path of action only when others have been divided; if they are not divided, it is merely an action (*kamma*). [The same applies to] bodily [action] that cuts the vital parts of another...
Harsh speech is corrupt volition that originates through verbal effort. It is called a *mamma* because beings die here, or undergo suffering amounting to death, when this [speech] strikes it;
thus it is a "corrupt sore. That which cuts, pierces, and strikes the *mamma* is a *mammacchedaka*, meaning the act of striking a sore.
However, in this context, it is called *mamma* because it is like a *mamma*. [This applies] to birth and so forth.

"Among the ten bases of abuse, it is any one of them. "A 'lacerator of the vitals' (*mammacchedaka*)" refers to harsh physical or verbal conduct that proceeds by way of striking at [another's] birth and so forth.
This meaning should be understood according to the *Sīlakkhandha-ṭīkā*. Alternatively: "It belongs to me" (*mamāyati*) thus it is "mine" (*mama*).
"Mine" (*mitta*) is a friend. The state of being "mine" is "vitality" (*mamma*); it is a mind of loving-kindness (*mettā-citta*). That which cuts this vitality is a "lacerator of the vitals."
Some say that this [path of action] regarding one who is to be reviled occurs only in their presence; others say it occurs even in their absence.

However, the authors of the *Dīgha-aṭṭhakathā-ṭīkā* and *Majjhima-aṭṭhakathā-ṭīkā* maintain that just as the act of asking for forgiveness succeeds even when the other person is standing at a distance or is dead—provided one asks for forgiveness after having reviled them—so too does the act of reviling succeed. This is with the intention of reviling.

They say that even when one curses another in such a manner as, "May a fierce she-buffalo pursue you," or "May thieves cut you into pieces," or "May your head split into seven parts," there is indeed a breach of the course of action (kamma-patha).
Idle chatter (samphappalāpa) is the evil volition that gives rise to bodily and vocal exertions intended to convey what is harmful. This [is illustrated by] the Battle of the Bhāratas...

In cases such as the abduction of Sītā, even when the mind is engaged in creative imagination (*paṭibhāṇa*), the breach of the path of action (*kammappatha*) occurs only when there is the mere basis of speech.
However, that [path of action] exists only for one who truly grasps that harmful matter; for one who does not grasp it, there is only the kamma itself.

Likewise, in the case of talk about kings and so forth, as well as among the thirty-two divisions of frivolous talk (*tiracchānakathā*), there is only kamma; and that too exists only for one who speaks with a sense of relishing it.
It should be understood that for one who speaks while relying upon the Dhamma and Vinaya for the sake of the goal (attha), everything is indeed the Teacher’s own work.

Regarding the term "verbal action" (vacīkamma): here, "speech" (vacī) refers simply to vocal expression. That is fourfold: vocal sound (saddavācā), vocal abstention (virativācā), vocal volition (cetanāvācā), and vocal intimation (copanavācā).
However, in this context, what is intended is vocal intimation (copanavācā), which is accompanied by sound and designated as vocal manifestation (vacīviññatti).

It is said that it is "reckoned as vocal intimation. For the speech of instigation (*copanavācā*) is sometimes performed by means of the vocal faculty for the purpose of making one's own intention known to another;
thus, it is called "vocal intimation" (*vacīviññatti*). And because it is the very opening through which kamma proceeds, it is the "vocal door" (*vacīdvāra*).
For it is only when that [speech] proceeds by way of its function as various vocal applications that functions such as deception are accomplished.

And there is the acquisition of the name "verbal action" (vacīkamma), which consists in the activity of accumulating and the production [of the result] by the volitional state (cetanā-dhamma) that originates it.
Regarding that door of speech: whatever needs to be said here has already been stated in the section on bodily action (kāyakamma). [Verbal Action] 150.
They covet (abhijjhāyanti): not remaining satisfied with mere enjoyment, they excessively [desire] another's property by way of appropriating it for themselves.

*Abhijjhā* (covetousness) means that by means of this, one *jhāyati* (broods) and *nijjhāyati* (contemplates) upon [what belongs to others]. *Byāpāda* (ill will) means that by means of this, one *byāpādenti* (harms)—that is, one thinks with the intent to bring about the destruction of other beings.
Regarding *micchā-diṭṭhi* (wrong view): here, *micchā* is a particle used in the sense of "perverse" (*viparīta*).

It refers to the opposite of the entire path of the true person (*sappurisa*) and what is prescribed by the true person, which proceeds in such a manner as "there is giving," etc.; it is the opposite of that, proceeding in the manner of "there is no giving," etc.

"Wrong view" (*micchā-diṭṭhi*) means that one sees by means of this [view]. In that regard, when one sees what belongs to another and does not remain merely in states of gratification, delight, and passion, but instead—thinking "O, may this be mine!"—appropriates it for oneself and transfers it to one's own mind, there occurs the transgression of the path of action consisting of covetousness (*abhijjhā-kamma-patha*).
However, if one leaves the state of it being another's property as it is, thinking, "How fortunate these people are! Those who enjoy such things; oh, may I too... [there is no such transgression].

"It would be for a limited time," "I will enjoy it after asking for it or buying it," or "I might obtain something else like this"—for one who consoles oneself in this way, it is merely an action (*kamma*).

For this has been stated in the commentaries: "Even when greed arises with another's goods as its object, there is no breach of the path of action (*kammapatha*) so long as one does not appropriate it for oneself by thinking, 'Oh, if only this were mine!'"
Even with respect to something as small as a gadfly or a mosquito, thinking, "May these perish, may they be destroyed; oh, that they might perish, that they might be destroyed!

May they not prosper, or may they not endure for long; when indeed will they perish and be destroyed?"—such is ill-will (vyāpāda) in one who contemplates the destruction of the aggregates and life of another being.
The other [type of ill-will] is simply karma. For this has been said regarding the basis of another being: [text follows].

For even when anger has arisen, there is as yet no breach of the path of action (*kammappatha*), so long as one does not contemplate its destruction, thinking, "Alas, may this person be cut off, may they perish!

It is only through a definite wrong view (*niyata-micchādiṭṭhi*)—which is threefold by way of being a nihilist who utterly rejects the outflow of action (*kammassava*) and the outflow of the result of action (*kammavipākassava*)—that there is a breach of the path of action. This refers to the wrong view based on ten grounds.

However, they are indeed varieties of views such as nihilism (*natthika-diṭṭhi*). They maintain that even the views of Ariṭṭha, Kaṇṭaka, and others—which arose after they had rejected the teaching of the Omniscient One—are indeed courses of action (*kamma-patha*).
Furthermore, the twenty-based view of a self-identity (*sakkāya-diṭṭhi*) or the sixty-two types of speculative views (*diṭṭhigata*) are themselves kamma.

And in this context, "fixed" (*niyata*) refers to how, having seen the three characteristics to whatever extent, one reaches a definitive conclusion through conviction and resolution (*saddhā-adhimokkha*).
The arising of consciousness in one who is proceeding becomes fixed by the necessity of yielding its fruit immediately following itself.
One who perceives to that extent is said to "enter upon the certainty (niyāma) regarding wholesome states.

Similarly, for one who reaches a definitive conclusion through wrong resolve after seeing things that are merely the semblances of reasons for the bases of views, the arising of consciousness becomes fixed by the necessity of yielding its fruit immediately following death.
He becomes fixed. Having seen only that much, he reaches a conclusion and enters upon the certainty regarding unwholesome states;

he is called "incurable. However, without seeing it thus, but merely through a false conviction, having reached the conclusion "it will be exactly so," he stands upholding his own teacher's tradition and doctrine.
It is not called "incurable. Why? Because there is no fixed necessity for the giving of its fruit. And this meaning should be illustrated by the triad of wrongness (*micchattattika*).

For in that context, it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* that both the states of rightness and wrongness receive the designation "fixed" solely by way of the fixed necessity for the giving of their fruits.
However, in the commentaries on the Suttas, [the designation is applied] also by way of the fixed necessity of their inclusion.
"Its state of being certain has been stated.
"Even apart from intimation" means even without the two types of intimation; the meaning is "even without having produced the two types of intimation.
By the word "even," however, it is shown that [the action occurs] even together with the two types of intimation. For these three types of action, when [performed by] the body-limbs...
Without moving the limbs, these succeed in the mind alone;
at that time, they proceed even without intimation (*viññatti*). But when, having moved them, they succeed through the doors of body and speech, then they proceed together with intimation.
By this, he illustrates their activity in all three doors. Even so, these [mental formations] mostly proceed in the mind-door (*manodvāra*) alone.

However, it is said that [these consciousnesses] occur only to a small extent at the doors of body and speech; therefore, it is stated that they "occur predominantly in the mind alone" (*manasmiṃyeva bāhullavutti*).
In this context, "in the mind alone" means precisely in the mind-door (*manodvāra*), which is comprised of wholesome and unwholesome impulsion-consciousnesses (*javana-citta*).

By this, the application of the word "alone" (*eva*) to the preceding locations—the body-door and the speech-door—is also indicated. For when this is the case, [the predominance] is also [determined] by way of the door there.

"The determination of action (*kammavavatthāna*) is established even more clearly. Otherwise, there might even be the contingency of it being something else, by way of mere characterization (*upalakkhaṇa*) and so forth.

Furthermore, here the word *eva* also indicates this specific meaning: for in cases such as the taking of life, the volitional act (*cetayita-kiriyā*) proceeding in the manner of an intention—such as 'I shall kill him' or 'I shall steal it'—is what is primary."
And that [kamma] cannot be accomplished without bodily and verbal exertion. Therefore, among these, bodily and verbal exertion constitute one factor for the accomplishment of kamma.
Furthermore, covetousness and the like, which are co-nascent with it, fall outside the scope of [the definition of] kamma because they belong to the side of volition (*cetanā*).
However, in cases such as coveting another's property, covetousness and the like—which have the self as their primary basis—[operate] through the doors of body and speech.
Even for those [actions] that have already occurred, they become mere factors for the accomplishment of the action through the application of body and speech.

Likewise, because the accomplishment of the action therein occurs by the mere occurrence of thought (*cintā*), it should be understood that the inclusion of the word "only" (*eva*)—in the phrase "only in the mind"—is made here specifically to exclude the status of being a factor in every respect for the doors of body and speech among these actions. However, regarding the mere occurrence within those doors...
The term *bāhulla* (abundance) is also included here with reference to its actual existence (*sabbhāva*).
However, what is stated in the *Vibhāvani*— namely, that "here,
covetousness and so forth associated with the consciousness that originates intimation belong to the side of volition (*cetanā*)"— is not tenable in this context.

For even though covetousness and the like, when associated with the consciousness that originates intimation (*viññatti*), are mental actions (*manokamma*) by virtue of their specific function, they do not belong to the category of volition (*cetanā*). Rather, it is volition alone that belongs to the category of covetousness and the rest. [Regarding Mental Action:

151. Furthermore, it is stated in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga-ṭīkā* that, among these ten courses of action (*kammappatha*), the preceding and succeeding volitions are of an indeterminate nature regarding the drawing forth of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*). Therefore, those too [do not necessarily lead to rebirth for this being].

When strong conditions—such as "I shall kill this person" or "I shall take what is not given"—arise from the very beginning, they draw forth rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) once those conditions are obtained;
it is logical that they do not draw it forth when they are not obtained.

However, those wholesome and unwholesome states that have not reached the level of a course of action (kammapatha), even while manifesting at the door of the body, are called bodily actions (kāyakamma).
It should be understood that those appearing at the door of speech are called verbal actions (*vacīkamma*), and those appearing at the pure door of mind are called mental actions (*manokamma*).
Regarding the phrase "by a root of hatred": there are two meanings—namely, by a root designated as hatred, or by a mind rooted in hatred.
Of these, the former applies to the [two courses of action] excluding ill-will (*vyāpāda*), while the latter applies to all three. Regarding the phrase "by a root of greed" (*lobhamūlena*): here...
This is the method of exposition. Herein, the former [formula] corresponds to two [roots], excluding covetousness; the latter corresponds to three.
"By two roots" means that they arise sometimes from the root of hatred and sometimes from the root of greed; thus they occur by way of two roots.
However, delusion is not included here because, being common to all, it does not serve as a specific differentiator.
[157] Furthermore, regarding what is stated in the *Vibhāvanī*:
"For the purpose of suppressing the wicked, kings and brahmins who take away the property of others do so according to the measure of a treasure-finder;
all this was given by the kings to the brahmins. However, because they are the weakest of all, others enjoy it."

It has been stated: "By saying such things as 'The Brahmins consume only what belongs to themselves,' [one denies] the connection between action and its fruit for those who take whatever they please under the perception that it is their own, and for those who deny such a connection through the root of delusion. That [explanation] is not applicable here.
For what is intended here is the co-nascent root (*sahajātamūla*), which is unique [to each individual]. And as for the taking away by those who take in that manner—
At the time of seizing [the property], it occurs sometimes with the root of discord and sometimes with the root of greed; thus, it arises through these two roots alone.

However, setting aside the ancient treatises on hidden treasures (*nidhisattha*) that were current during the time of righteous kings such as Mahāsaṃmata, [this applies] to the majority of unrighteous treatises on treasure (*dhanmasattha*) that arose subsequently during the time of unrighteous kings, which are generally characterized by delusion (*moha*).
It arose among kings who perceived themselves as righteous according to the legal treatises known as the *Nidhipāṭhas*.

And it arose among those brahmins who, based on the statement that "grass, wood, and water [given] to ascetics and brahmins at the time of a king’s consecration" implies that all this has been given by kings to the brahmins, held such a perception. And there is no well-performed...
The view of those who hold the opinion that "the fruit and result of unwholesome deeds" has arisen for those who propound a connection between action and its fruit.
This is all known as "underlying-delusion" (*upanissaya-moha*), but it is not what is intended here. Otherwise, it would contradict the statement: "Greed is the source for the arising of actions;
hatred is the source for the arising of actions; delusion is the source for the arising of actions."
From the perspective of verbal expression, all unwholesome courses of action (*akusala-kammapatha*) should indeed be mentioned here as being rooted [in greed, hatred, and delusion].

Furthermore, it might be argued here as follows: for those people who have arisen doubts regarding both actions and the fruits of action, when they perform the four actions such as taking what is not given (*adinnādāna*) and so forth with a mind possessed by those very doubts, those actions—being performed with a pure [intention]—[would result in a different outcome].
"They arise with delusion as their root. This being so, it follows that doubt is also included among the volitions that produce rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).

[Unwholesome Karma. 152. Regarding "wholesome karma of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) occurring at the door of the body is bodily action," two methods of interpretation (*pariyāya*) should be understood here.

How so? For among the bases of meritorious action that will be explained, bodily action (*kāyakamma*) is that which proceeds by employing some basis of meritorious action through the medium of the body; vocal action (*vacīkamma*) is that which proceeds by employing the medium of speech;
and mental action (*manokamma*) is that which proceeds solely within the mind-door without employing the media of body or speech—this is one method of classification. This...
Furthermore, loving-kindness of bodily action is established toward his fellow practitioners both openly and in private;

loving-kindness of verbal action is established toward his fellow practitioners both openly and in private; and loving-kindness of mental action is established toward his fellow practitioners both openly and in private.
All his bodily actions are preceded by knowledge and follow after knowledge.
All verbal action is preceded by knowledge and follows after knowledge; all mental action is preceded by knowledge and follows after knowledge.
Righteous is bodily action, righteous is vocal action.
It occurs in such scriptural passages as: "Wholesome mental action" (*padakkhiṇaṃ manokammaṃ*) and "in the case of wholesome [actions] directed toward a goal" (*paṇīhite padakkhiṇe*).
Furthermore, this meaning should be illustrated by the entire discussion on the doors of new work (*navakamma-dvāra-kathā*) in the *Aṭṭhasālinī*.
For therein, even that which consists of giving (*dānamaya*) is analyzed into three types according to bodily, verbal, and mental action.

Likewise, there is that consisting of virtue and that consisting of meditation. However, when unvirtuous conduct (*dussīlya*) occurs, the body becomes impure and bodily restraint (*kāyasaṃvara*) is broken.

But when wholesome states (*kusala*) occur, they proceed by abandoning that unvirtuous conduct through methods such as abandonment by substitution of opposites (*tadaṅgappahāna*), thereby purifying the door of the body and fulfilling bodily restraint. That...

Even though it is devoid of physical movement, because it performs the function of restraining the members of the body, it is called "bodily action" (*kāyakamma*) by way of its function as it occurs at the bodily door.

It is also called "good bodily conduct. And herein, the phrase "having abandoned that immorality" refers to the state of not allowing that consciousness to arise in which bodily immorality—such as the killing of living beings—would otherwise arise. By way of preventing the arising of that consciousness...
Having abandoned that bodily misconduct. "Cleansing the door of the body" means: when a certain misconduct arises, the limb of the body becomes impure;
thus, it refers to cleansing the door of the body by way of not allowing such [misconduct] to arise.
"Fulfilling bodily restraint" means: fulfilling bodily restraint by personally accomplishing the function of restraining the limbs of the body.
This is the meaning. The same method applies to verbal action as well.

However, all wholesome action, even when proceeding through all three doors, proceeds while purifying the mind-door alone and fulfilling the restraint of the mind alone; thus, it is called "mental action" (*manokamma*) when proceeding in the mind-door.
It is also called "mental good conduct" (*manosucarita*). This is one way of explaining it. Furthermore, among the many hundreds...
It is found in the *Kammapathasuttas*. Furthermore, in the *Aṭṭhasālinī*, this meaning should be illustrated by means of the entire "Discourse on the Doors" (*Dvārakathā*).

Now, regarding these two methods, it should be understood that in the Teacher’s dispensation, the fulfillment of wholesome qualities (*kalyāṇadhamma*) exists solely for the purpose of abandoning unwholesome qualities (*pāpadhamma*);
therefore, the latter alone is the primary [method]. That by which something is given is "giving" (*dāna*). It is the volition (*cetanā*) of relinquishing the object.
It is called *sīla* because it cools (*sīlayati*). By restraining blameworthy bodily and verbal actions and making blameless ones well-composed, it thoroughly heats [the mind] and establishes it;
it also supports the higher wholesome states. The meaning is that, acting as their foundation, it sustains them.
It is called *bhāvanā* because they are developed (*bhāventi*) by means of it. It causes wholesome states that have not yet arisen to arise, and those already arisen to increase.
The meaning is "increasing. It is called *apacāyana* because one honors (*apacāyanti*) by means of it; the meaning is that they worship with body and speech, demonstrating a humble disposition.
It is called *veyyāvacca* because it is the state or the action of those who are especially engaged (*byāvaṭānaṃ*), exerting themselves with zeal.

It is called *patti* because one has attained (*pajjittha*); it is a name for a portion of merit obtained within oneself. Alternatively, it is called *patti* because one attains (*pāpīyati*) [merit] through others who offer expressions of appreciation (*anumodana*).
This is the name for the outflow of merit that is to be obtained. It is called *pattidāna* because by means of it, they give the attainment [of merit].

They rejoice in that very same [merit] when given by others. It is called *pattānumodanā* because by means of it, they give a cry of "well done. It is called *dhammasavana* because by means of it, they hear the Dhamma.
It is called *dhammadesanā* because by means of it, they teach the Dhamma. There is what has been given; there is...

"Right view with ten bases" (*diṭṭhijukamma*) refers to that by which one straightens right view through such statements as: "There is sacrifice; there is offering; there is fruit and result of deeds well done and ill done.

"Merits" (*puññāni*) are so called because all of them purify and cleanse the continuum of consciousness (*cittasantāna*). They are also called "merits" because they produce a state worthy of honor (*pūjanīyabhāva*). These very [actions]...
They are called "bases of meritorious action" (*puññakriyavatthu*) because they are bases (*vatthu*) in the sense of being the foundation for specific types of happiness;
they are called "meritorious actions" (*puññakriyā*) in the sense of being actions that must necessarily be performed. Herein, each one is threefold: inferior, middling, and superior.
Regarding giving (*dāna*), first, the act of relinquishing to a recipient is called the middling [inferior] form. From that...
First, the wholesome volition (kusala-cetanā) that arises through the three doors, beginning from the time one produces the requisite conditions with the thought, "By means of this condition,
I shall perform merit consisting of giving," directed toward the gift and having the gift as its object, is called "prior. Subsequently, however,
it is the volition that arises for one who repeatedly generates a joyful mind (attamana-citta) with respect to the gift already given by oneself.
Wholesome volition is called the "last. All of this, according to the method explained for the unwholesome, gives rebirth-linking when it has obtained a strong condition;
it should be understood that when it has not obtained one, it does not give it.
Furthermore, it is threefold by way of being inferior, medium, and superior. Among these, [it is] by means of inferior desire, thought, and energy...
That which is set in motion by investigation is inferior; that set in motion by middling zeal and so forth is middling; that set in motion by sublime [zeal] is sublime.
Alternatively, that set in motion out of a desire for fame is inferior; that set in motion out of a desire for the fruit of merit is middling;
and that set in motion based on the noble state, knowing what ought to be done, is sublime. [It is not so] through self-exaltation, disparagement of others, and the like.
That which is defiled is inferior. That which is undefiled and proceeds by way of sharing in worldly happiness is middling.
That which proceeds by way of sharing in the happiness of the path and its fruits is sublime. Alternatively, that which proceeds by way of craving for the sake of existence and enjoyment is inferior.
That which proceeds for the sake of one’s own liberation is middling. That which proceeds for the sake of the liberation of all beings is sublime.
The meaning that "the perfection of giving is sublime" should be understood by consulting the Description of Virtue (*sīlaniddesa*) in the *Visuddhimagga*.
And just as it is here, so too in the remaining [perfections], the three dyads and triads should be explained by dividing them according to what is applicable.
In this context, "virtue" (*sīla*) is fourfold: the virtue of a bhikkhu, the virtue of a bhikkhunī, the virtue of a male novice (*sāmaṇera*), and the virtue of a householder.
It exists. In that regard, the function of undertaking for the first two [categories] is accomplished by means of the formal ritual (kammavācā).
However, through the commission of a final offense or through the renunciation of the training, when the ritual has been broken, the entire undertaking is broken.

At that time, all the precepts of one who is fully ordained (upasampanna) are broken; such a person, though remaining without having abandoned the claim to being a bhikkhu, is called "immoral" (dussīla).
...exists. However, for one who transgresses other training rules—excluding the final matter—the breach of restraint occurs only with respect to that which is transgressed;
it is not a breach of the formal undertaking itself. For there is no need to undertake that [undertaking] again through a formal act of proclamation (*kammavācā*).
But for one who performs the act of restoration (*paṭikamma*), the restraint becomes as it was before. Even for one who transgresses intentionally...
One who does not perform amends is called "shameless. The same principle applies to the virtue of a novice (sāmaṇera).

In that case, however, the undertaking [of the precepts] is accomplished by the mere act of going for refuge. When the going for refuge—which constitutes the factor of adopting the emblem—is broken, the entire undertaking is broken.
Regarding the other [precepts], it should be understood that the breach of restraint occurs only in respect to whichever one is transgressed.
