Regarding the moral training for householders (*gahaṭṭhasīla*), however, the undertaking is established by way of the householders' own natural grasping [of the precepts].
Therefore, when one undertakes them as a single group, all are undertaken; and when one is broken, all are broken.
All must be undertaken again. But when one undertakes them individually, only that which one transgresses is broken.
"That very same [precept] must be undertaken again. However, when the time limit has expired, the entire undertaking is indeed brought to an end.
In this context, the state of being immoral (*dussīlabhāva*) should be understood through the breach of the five perpetual precepts (*niccasīla*).
Among those that are perpetual and non-perpetual, only what is perpetual is appropriate. What is non-perpetual is not fitting and becomes blameworthy. That is the perpetual precept.

[This is] the name [of that]. However, that which is permissible even when permanent results in a great outflow of merit. That which is permissible even when impermanent and is not blameworthy is called "impermanent virtue" (*aniccasīla*).
In this regard, for one established in the state of a bhikkhu, there is the virtue of a bhikkhu; for one established in the state of a sāmaṇera, there is the virtue of a sāmaṇera;
for those who are ordinary householders, there is the fivefold virtue; and for those included among the ordained, [there is the respective training].
For lay followers (*upāsakas*) and ascetics (*tāpasa*) or wanderers (*paribbājaka*), the ten precepts (*dasasīla*) are known as the "constant precept" (*niccasīla*).
For them, it is necessary to constantly maintain and protect their respective precepts, making them pure.

For those who do not protect them, their status as monks (*bhikkhu*) and so forth becomes blameworthy and impure. Why? Because of the failure of conduct appropriate to oneself. However, for ordinary householders...

The eightfold Uposatha precept is called the "occasional precept" (*aniccasīla*). For them, it is appropriate both as a regular (*nicca*) practice and as an occasional one, according to the method already described.
The same applies to the ten precepts; for these are indeed occasional precepts for laypeople by their very nature.
They become regular precepts only for those who have entered the order by abandoning the dress of a householder and donning the saffron robes. Just as it is with ordinary people...
The five precepts—whether formally undertaken or not—must always be observed; it is not fitting to transgress them.
Likewise, for those who wear the robes of one gone forth, the ten precepts—whether formally undertaken or not—must always be observed;
it is not fitting to transgress them. This is because they are established simultaneously with the wearing of the robes.
The two-fold development (bhāvanā) mentioned above—consisting of serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā)—is what is termed "development.

Here, however, it is intended as that which has not yet reached absorption (appanā). Included within this very category is the volition involved in cultivating proficiency in the Dhamma and Vinaya, as well as in blameless crafts, sciences, and fields of knowledge.
Furthermore, [this includes] [cultivation] toward the Triple Gem, one’s parents, and the elders of the family.
"Veneration" (*apacāyanā*) refers to all such acts as rising from one's seat, bowing, joining the palms in salutation, performing respectful greetings,
and attending to the duties and counter-duties toward teachers, righteous recluses and brahmins, and others who are virtuous, advanced in age, or elders, as is appropriate.
It also includes attending to the needs and obligations of those very same persons, as well as others— such as newcomers, those departing, travelers on the road, the sick, and the elderly.

*Veyyāvacca* (service) is the exertion of body and speech by means of a pure mind that radiates benevolence toward fellow practitioners (*sabrahmacārī*) in matters such as robe-making and other various meritorious deeds of others, just as one would exert oneself in one’s own duties.

*Pattidāna* (the giving of merit) is the act of sharing with others whatever merit has been performed by oneself. *Anumodanā* (rejoicing) is the expression of appreciation for the merit given by others.

Rejoicing that has reached the state of mental gladness is called *pattānumodanā* (rejoicing in what has been attained). However, rejoicing in merit that has not been attained is merely *anumodanā* (rejoicing);
it is not *pattānumodanā*, because there is an absence of anything actually attained. Furthermore, that which is attained is twofold: specified (*uddisikā*) and unspecified (*anuddisikā*).
In this regard, it should be understood that for one who rejoices in merit specifically directed toward oneself, the result becomes experienced in the present life (*diṭṭhadhammavedanīya*).
Furthermore, this pair is especially evident in the case of meritorious acts of giving.

For when a gift is dedicated to deities, or to *petas* who subsist on what is given by others, or to *vemānika-petas*, or to *asuras* fallen into the lower realms, and it is then rejoiced over, that [merit] becomes experienced in the present life (*diṭṭhadhammavedanīya*) for them at that very moment.
This is so through a discourse on the Dhamma connected with welfare and benefit.
Hearing and speaking while established in wise attention (yoniso manasikāra) is called "hearing the Dhamma" and "teaching the Dhamma.
Herein, the volition of hearing and speaking regarding blameless actions, crafts, and sciences is also included.

This refers either to the ten-based wrong view proceeding in such a manner as "there is no giving, there is no sacrifice," and so forth, or to views such as that of creation by a Supreme Lord (issaranimmāna).
"Rectification of views" (diṭṭhujukamma) is the purification of the right view known as "knowledge of the ownership of one's actions" (kamma-sakata),
which has been rendered pure either by means of views such as "seeing what is auspicious" (diṭṭhamaṅgala) and so forth, or by means of various grounds, logical arguments, or reasons. However,

in those instances where only the three bases for meritorious action (puññakriyavatthu) are mentioned, there the acts of dedication (pattidāna) and rejoicing (anumodanā) are included within the category of giving (dāna).
Because it has that as its intrinsic nature by way of being the opposite of envy and avarice. Reverence and service are included within virtue (*sīla*), because their practice is virtuous.
The remaining three are included within that consisting in development (*bhāvanāmaya*), because they have that as their intrinsic nature.

For it has been said: "There is no state whatsoever that is not a meditation subject. And the straightening of views is simply the increase of knowledge; thus, this [straightening of views] is included within those three alone.
It is included. It is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* that the act of rectifying wrong view (*diṭṭhujukamma*) is the defining characteristic for all [three types of action].

For it is mindfulness itself that accomplishes the three—giving and so forth—when there is knowledge of one’s own ownership of action (*kamma-sakata-ñāṇa*). "Only mental action" means that because the function of the course of action is accomplished within the mind alone, it is called mental action.
In the *Vibhāvani*, however, it is stated:
"Because it originates intimation, it does not function as a state within the doors of body and so forth. That is not correct.

For even when a master of higher knowledge (*abhiññākusala*) who originates intimation is functioning within the doors of body and so forth, that [knowledge] is not reckoned as bodily or vocal action.

It proceeds because it is impossible for the paths of action (kamma-patha) of body and speech to constitute its constituent factors. And that [wholesome state] consists of cultivation (bhāvanāmaya), since it does not operate by way of giving or virtue.
Because it is exclusively a specific type of kamma consisting of cultivation, that sublime wholesome state is indeed only the kamma of cultivation.

Furthermore, regarding the Path of Discrimination (paṭisambhidā-magga): by means of the first jhāna, the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) are abandoned; by the second, applied thought and sustained thought (vitakka-vicāra).
By the third [jhāna], there is rapture (*pīti*). By the fourth, the abandoning of pleasure and pain is virtue (*sīla*);

it is virtue as abstinence (*veramaṇi*), virtue as volition (*cetanā*), virtue as restraint (*saṃvara*), and virtue as non-transgression (*avītikkama*). It should be understood that this was stated by way of a figurative description (*pariyāya*).
It has reached absorption (*appanā*) because it proceeds by entering into the object through the power of meditation and by way of an unshakable state of stability.
The action has reached absorption (appanā).
However, in the *Vibhāvani*, the reason given is:
"Because they belong to the sense-sphere state occurring in the preliminary stage (pubbabhāga). That is not correct.

For it is not merely their status as belonging to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) that is the cause for reaching absorption (*appanā*); thus it is said, "by way of the distinction of jhāna-factors" (*jhānaṅgabhedena*).

However, it should rather be stated as "by way of the distinction of jhānas" (*jhānabhedena*). The meaning of "by way of the distinction of jhāna-factors" is "by way of the distinction of the collection of jhāna-factors";
what is intended is simply "by way of the distinction of jhānas. [This refers to] wholesome kamma.
153. “In this” means in this tetrad of manifest states (*pākaṭṭhāna*). “Free from restlessness” means excluding volition accompanied by restlessness (*uddhacca-sahagata-cetanā*).
But why is volition accompanied by restlessness excluded here? Because it does not draw forth rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*). How is this known?

From its absence among those things to be abandoned by vision (*dassana-pahātabba*) as shown in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*, and because it is mentioned only among those things to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-pahātabba*).
As it has been said: "The four types of consciousness-arising associated with views, the consciousness-arising accompanied by doubt—these states are to be abandoned by vision;
the consciousness-arising accompanied by restlessness—these states are to be abandoned by cultivation;
and the remaining four types of consciousness-arising dissociated from views, as well as the two types of consciousness-arising associated with aversion."
It is stated therein that [unwholesome states] may be abandoned by vision (*dassana*) and may be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā*). How is this known?
Because any unwholesome state (*akusaladhamma*) not mentioned among those to be abandoned by vision does not project rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).

This is because, in the *Paṭṭhāna*, the asynchronous kamma-condition (*nānākkhaṇika-kammapaccaya*) is extracted only in the context of states to be abandoned by vision; therefore, it does not apply elsewhere.

"Because it has not been extracted. As it has been said: "Volition to be abandoned by seeing, when co-nascent, is a condition by way of kamma-condition for its associated states and for mind-originated matter;
and volition to be abandoned by seeing, when asynchronous, is a condition by way of kamma-condition for resultant aggregates and for kamma-produced matter. Thus [it is] co-nascent.

Volition associated with states to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is a condition, by way of kamma-condition (*kammapaccaya*), for mental phenomena and for non-mentally-produced material phenomena.
And there is no such thing as the production of a result (*vipāka*) without the efficacy of the asynchronous kamma-condition.

If it is argued that, in this case, it could be said that it does not produce even a result pertaining to the course of existence (*pavatti-vipāka*), [the answer is] no; for it is stated in the *Paṭisambhidā-vibhaṅga*:
Because that result has been extracted. As it is said: "Which phenomena are unwholesome?
At whatever time an unwholesome consciousness has arisen, accompanied by equanimity, associated with restlessness, having visible form as its object...

these phenomena are unwholesome. Knowledge regarding these phenomena is the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dhamma-paṭisambhidā). Knowledge regarding their result is the analytical knowledge of meaning (attha-paṭisambhidā)."
Therefore he said: "But in the course of existence (pavatti), all twelve kinds...
and so forth. [160] As for what was stated in the *Vibhāvani*:

"Even that which is entirely weak due to being devoid of resolve (adhimokkha) draws in rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) when accompanied by doubt; whereas even that which is stronger than that, being accompanied by restlessness (uddhacca), does not draw it in because of its association with resolve"—that is not correct.
For it cannot be said that the state accompanied by doubt is entirely weak merely because it lacks resolution (*adhimokkha*),
nor can it be said that the state accompanied by restlessness is stronger than that merely because it possesses resolution. This is because doubt—
as described in the passage beginning "He is uncertain about the Teacher, he is uncertain about the Dhamma"— is more powerful in its own domain than even a great tusker elephant.
"And because it is exceedingly black in nature. For it is stated as being preeminent among those [defilements] to be abandoned solely by seeing.
And for that very reason, its drawing forth of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) should also be understood.

Furthermore, because it is diametrically opposed to its own intrinsic nature, it is logical that it is accompanied by doubt and devoid of resolve (adhimokkha). Therefore, it is only associated with restlessness (uddhacca).
It should be understood as "weakest of all. "In all cases" means in every instance, by way of both happy and miserable destinies (*sugati-duggati*).

"As appropriate" means in accordance with the bases and doors obtained within those worlds. "It ripens" (*vipaccati*) means it causes [the result] to ripen; it brings about the state of having ripened.
Alternatively, the meaning is that all twelvefold unwholesome karma ripens for sentient beings by becoming wholesome results; it goes to the state of having ripened.
Because wholesome kamma, even in the woeful planes, produces great prosperity during the course of existence;
it creates its own opportunity for fruition within the mental continuum of powerful beings such as nāgas and supaṇṇas, thereby generating a pleasant result.
Furthermore, even for other beings in the woeful states, when there is a conjunction with desirable objects through various causes, [it produces its own result].
Having obtained an opportunity, they produce a pleasant result. Therefore, he did not say "and in such a course of existence," and so forth.
For those [results] cannot possibly be pleasant results that are the maturation of unwholesome karma. Indeed, this was stated in the Vibhaṅga:
"It is impossible, it is out of the question, that a desirable, lovely, and agreeable result should arise from bodily misconduct," and so forth.

In that regard, it is said that the eight great resultants (*mahāvipāka*)—which are rootless (*ahetuka*)—ripen in the happy destinies of the sense-sphere world (*kāmaloka*), and all of them ripen throughout the entire sense-sphere world.
Furthermore, among those, the five pairs consisting of eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, receiving consciousness, and investigating consciousness ripen in the fine-material sphere (*rūpaloka*).

As for the wholesome fine-material-sphere kamma, while it generates material phenomena produced by kamma (*kamma-samuṭṭhāna-rūpa*), it itself ripens accordingly as follows: [The wholesome fine-material-sphere kamma] while generating material phenomena produced by kamma, itself ripens...
On another object, it does not ripen as a result belonging to a different plane.

However, due to the specific nature of the karma that has reached absorption through the cultivation of dispassion toward sense-desires, it ripens as a material-resultant state alone—having attained a sublime state that is in every respect similar to itself—upon a sign-object that is no longer within the domain of craving for sense-desires.
Therefore, even in the fine-material world (*rūpaloka*), those [karmas]...
It should be understood that the five results of maturation belong exclusively to wholesome kamma of the sense-sphere. Of the two places where kamma ripens, rebirth-linking is the primary place.
Therefore, when kamma ripens at that time, it is able to produce a result that is not too inferior, corresponding to its own capacity.
However, during the course of existence, it ripens in various ways through various functions in diverse locations.
Therefore, at that time, the karma is unable to ripen according to its own inherent power.
When it ripens in limited (paritta) states such as the fivefold sensory consciousnesses, it ripens in accordance with the nature of those states.

When ripening in the state of registration (tadārammaṇa), it generally ripens in accordance with the impulsion (javana). Therefore, the sixteenfold path, the twelvefold path, and the rootless (ahetuka) path are called "the wood."
Thus, in order to show the classification of the fruition of each individual kamma as it occurs, he said, "Therein also," and so forth.
Wholesome kamma is twofold: that performed with full awareness (*sampajānakata*) and that performed without full awareness (*asampajānakata*).

Among these, that which is performed by thoroughly applying even the aforementioned knowledge of straightening the course of kamma at the time of exerting the kamma is called "performed with full awareness. As it is said: "And kamma..."
Action performed with full awareness (*sampajañña*) is that which is done after having faith in the fruit of action (*kammaphala*).

That which is done without applying even a measure of knowledge regarding the straightness of view (*diṭṭhujjukatā*) is called "done without full awareness. As it has been said: "Action performed without knowing either the action or the fruit of the action is called 'done without full awareness.
In this context, what is done with full awareness is accompanied by three roots (*tihetuka*), while what is done without full awareness is accompanied by two roots (*duhetuka*).
As it has been said: "Full awareness occurs through association with the four kinds of knowledge; lack of full awareness occurs through dissociation from the four kinds of knowledge.
In that context, each one is twofold: superior and inferior.
Therein, at the moment of a wholesome state, having thoroughly cleansed either the hindering states (*nīvaraṇa-dhamma*) or the evil states such as self-exaltation and disparagement of others—

That which is done after having purified [the offering] is called "superior" (*ukkaṭṭha*). That which is done without purifying it, being mixed with those same [impurities], is called "inferior" (*omaka*). Furthermore, that which is performed repeatedly with such rejoicing as:
"Having done this, what a gain for me! Indeed, it is not a loss for me. What a blessing for me!
Indeed, it is not a misfortune for me. Such merit has accrued to me!"—that is superior. That which is done after having performed [the act]... [and so forth].
Remorse arises because one thinks, "I have done something wicked for some reason. That is weak.
Having thus analyzed and shown the fourfold division of the resultant portion by way of the fourfold karma, he said "Nevertheless," and so forth.
In that context, "even there" means even in that sense-sphere wholesome [kamma]. "Three-rooted and superior" means that which has become superior, that which has become sublime.
The three-rooted [consciousness] is fourfold. Regarding "three-rooted rebirth-linking": this refers to the four types of three-rooted rebirth-linking kamma-result.

Herein, a single volition produces only a single rebirth-linking. However, as for the result during the course of existence (*pavatti*), it indeed produces results even throughout incalculable existences.
Here, it might be asked:
"For it is said: 'Having offered a single flower, for ten million billion aeons, among gods and humans, one attains final Nibbāna by means of the remainder.

Therefore, the claim that a single volition (cetanā) bestows only a single rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) is not tenable. "It is not untenable. [This is so] because of preceding and succeeding volitions..."
This is because it must be stated as being equal in measure to ten million billion aeons (*sahassakappa-koṭi*).

Indeed, the mind arises even in a single moment of a finger-snap (*ekaccharakkhaṇa*) numbering many hundreds of thousands of millions; therefore, there is no time that can be described as even slightly longer than that.

Furthermore, in the *Nettippakaraṇa-aṭṭhakathā*, "ten million billion aeons" (*sahassakappakoṭi*) is explained as ten million billion aeons of lifespan and ten million billion aeons of individual existences (*attabhāva*).
It has been said. Furthermore, the fact that volitions occurring earlier and later can grant rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) should be illustrated by the *Kosalasaṃyutta*.
For in the case of a single gift of alms-food, a single volition does not grant two rebirth-linkings.

Indeed, it is stated in the *Saṃyutta-aṭṭhakathā*: "By way of the preceding and succeeding volitions, he was reborn seven times in heaven and seven times in the family of a wealthy merchant. This applies even to a [kamma] possessing three roots (*tihetuka*).
Kamma that is being overwhelmed by its opposites has its potency destroyed and is unable to produce a three-rooted (tihetuka) result.
Nor does it—though being exceedingly weak—produce a rootless (ahetuka) result accompanied by such calamities as congenital blindness, which arise from extremely confused conditions;
for it is associated with the wisdom known as skillfulness (kosalla). Thus it is said: "the minimum of a three-rooted [result]," and so forth.
"Twelve resultants ripen. This refers to the twelvefold path, which ripens as only rootless resultants (*ahetuka-vipāka*). This is what is called "the group of eight rootless [resultants].

Having thus shown the occurrence of resultants according to the doctrine of the Elder Cūḷanāga of the Tipiṭaka, he now spoke this verse to show the doctrine of the Elder Mahādatta, the resident of Moravāpi. For that elder [held that] of the resultants...
Although the states of being effortless (*asaṅkhārikatā*) and being with effort (*sasaṅkhārikatā*) are established by way of the kamma itself,
it is said that an effortless kamma does not ripen as results with effort, nor does a kamma with effort ripen as results without effort.
Just as the reflection of a face remains still when the face is still, and moves when it moves, so it is by way of the application (*payoga*).

The distinction between the sharpness and dullness of results that cannot be remedied is a differentiation of formations (*saṅkhāra*) that must be explained solely by way of karma, not by way of application.
Otherwise, for those [formations] produced as sharp or dull through a specific karma, their dullness or sharpness would result merely from the presence of conditions.
However, because those without cause or with weak results are extremely feeble, they are simply indistinct.
The phrase "the distinction of sharpness and dullness" means that both types of karma produce [results]; this is the intended meaning.

Furthermore, their state of being "with effort" (*sasaṅkhāra*) or "without effort" (*asaṅkhāra*) is appropriately described either by way of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) or by way of the object of that [rebirth-linking], depending on the presence or absence of a specific condition known as prior application (*pubbapayoga*) at the time of arising. It is not described by way of the arrival of the karma itself;
for in the existence of karma (*kammabhava*), there is no "effort" (*saṅkhāra*) in another becoming (*bhavantare*).
It is appropriate [to say] that one is intent on distinguishing the results (vipāka). Therefore, making this doctrine known as the "Some-Doctrine" (Kecivāda), he said "some.

In this Some-Doctrine, having excluded the results of prompted (sasaṅkhārika) karma from unprompted (asaṅkhārika) karma, and the results of unprompted karma from prompted karma, the results in the two unprompted [moments] among the four triplets of wholesome (tukaṭṭha) karmas [arise] at rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi).

Two [types of consciousness arise] in the process [of existence], and twelve in the course of existence. In the two types of prompted (sasaṅkhārika) kamma, there are two in rebirth-linking and twelve in the course of existence.
In the four types of weak double-rooted kamma, there are two in rebirth-linking and ten in the course of existence for the two unprompted (asaṅkhārika) types;
for the two prompted types, there are two in rebirth-linking and ten in the course of existence. The same applies to the four types of strong double-rooted kamma.

However, among the four types of consciousness with two roots, there is one resultant consciousness without root in the rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) stage and eight without root in the course of existence (pavatti).
Thus, for resultants, there are two sets of twelvefold groups, four sets of tenfold groups, and one set of eightfold groups without root.
To show all of this together in summary, he recited the verse beginning with "tesaṃ."
"Tesam" means "of some elders," according to their doctrine. However, in the *Aṭṭhasālinī*, the following view of the Elder Mahādhammarakkhita is also recorded:
"By means of karma accompanied by three roots, rebirth-linking is necessarily accompanied by three roots; it is neither accompanied by two roots nor rootless.
By means of karma accompanied by two roots, rebirth-linking may be accompanied by two roots or it may be rootless, but it is never accompanied by three roots. In that regard:

Just as a rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) devoid of roots (ahetuka) must necessarily be admitted when the karma is inferior and devoid of roots, so too, when the karma is inferior even though it possesses three roots (tihetuka), a rebirth-linking with two roots (duhetuka) must necessarily be admitted.

Having taken this into account, it should be understood that this doctrine was not accepted by the Elder here. However, in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*, regarding the attainment of a fortunate destination (gatisampatti):
Rebirth occurs by way of the condition of eight roots in association with knowledge (*ñāṇasampayutta*). At the moment of impulsion (*javana*) of wholesome kamma, three roots are wholesome.
At the moment of attachment (*nikanti*), two roots are wholesome. At the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), three roots are indeterminate (*abyākata*).
Thus, rebirth occurs by way of the condition of six roots in dissociation from knowledge (*ñāṇavippayutta*) for the attainment of a destination. Of the wholesome...

At the moment of impulsion (*javana*) of a kamma, two roots are wholesome; at the moment of attachment (*nikanti*), two roots are unwholesome; and at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), two roots are indeterminate (*abyākata*).
Thus, it is said that when the kamma possesses three roots, the rebirth-linking itself possesses three roots; when the kamma possesses two roots, the rebirth-linking possesses two roots.
However, this does not mean that the seven roots are conditions for the attainment of a happy destination (*gatisampatti*) in a state dissociated from knowledge (*ñāṇavippayutta*), and so forth.

It has been stated that a two-rooted rebirth-linking arises from a three-rooted kamma. Nor does it follow from the passage beginning "there is no condition for four roots" that a two-rooted kamma produces a rootless rebirth-linking.
In this context, however, throughout the three moments [of the cognitive process], this method of teaching is based solely on the roots by way of conascence-cause (*sahajāta-hetu*).
Because there was no opportunity [to discuss it], the rootless rebirth-linking (*ahetuka-paṭisandhi*) was not mentioned there; it was not because it is impossible to obtain.
However, it can be understood that the two-rooted rebirth-linking (*duhetuka-paṭisandhi*) is likewise not mentioned simply because it is not obtained, as it has no opportunity at all.
Therefore, considering that the canonical text (*pāḷi*) itself is more authoritative than mere reasoning, the doctrine of the Elder Mahādhammarakkhita alone accords with the canonical text.

This is stated in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga-aṭṭhakathā*. However, the commentators maintain that the Great Elder (Buddhaghosa) spoke with the text left incomplete for the purpose of showing the correspondence between the action and its result.
This being the case, even in the *Aṭṭhasālinī*, it is stated that the doctrine of the Elder Tipiṭaka-Cūḷanāga alone is the authoritative standard.

In the *Vibhāvani*, regarding the statement that "by a single volition there are twelve resultant [factors]," the reading found here—including both the tenfold set and the eightfold set without roots—is attributed to the Venerable Mahādhammarakkhita Thera, resident of Moravāpi;
however, it should rather be attributed to the Venerable Mahādatta Thera, resident of Moravāpi.
Furthermore, the doctrine of the Venerable Mahādhammarakkhita Thera is indeed included here in part. For even in his view, non-provoked (asaṅkhārika) karma results only in a non-provoked resultant.
It gives [its result]. It does not give the result of the unprompted (*asaṅkhārika*). Prompted (*sasaṅkhārika*) karma gives only the result of prompted karma;
it does not give the result of the unprompted—this is exactly as it has been handed down.
[Sensuous-Sphere Karma] 154. Regarding form-sphere karma, "limited" (*paritta*) is twofold: limited by way of lack of proficiency (*apaguṇatā*) or limited by way of inferiority (*hīnatā*). Therein—
That which, though endowed with excellent zeal and so forth, remains undeveloped and is merely acquired, is called "limited" (paritta) due to its lack of proficiency.

With reference to this, it is stated in the *Aṭṭhasālinī*: "That which is unproficient and is unable to serve as a condition for the higher jhānas—this is what is called 'limited'. However, that which, even while being well-developed...
It is endowed with inferior desire and so forth. Because of that inferiority, it is called "limited" (*paritta*). With reference to this, it is stated in that very same place:
"At the moment of its accumulation, if desire is inferior, or energy, or mind, or investigation is inferior, that is called 'inferior'.
Intermediate [kamma] is also twofold. Therein, with reference to that which is intermediate by way of not being highly proficient, it is said: "not well cultivated is intermediate."

It is stated in the *Visuddhimagga*: "With reference to the 'middling'—because it is endowed with middling zeal and so forth—at the moment of application (*āyūhana-kkhaṇa*), those factors are middling;
that is called 'middling. This is stated in the *Aṭṭhasālinī*. The 'excellent' (*paṇīta*) is also twofold.
Therein, with reference to the excellent because of its extreme proficiency, it is said in the *Visuddhimagga*: 'Well-developed, having reached mastery—that is the excellent.'"
It has been said. However, with reference to that which is "excellent" (*paṇīta*) by virtue of being endowed with excellent zeal (*chanda*) and so forth, it is stated in the *Aṭṭhasālinī*:
"That for which those states are excellent at the moment of their exertion—that is 'excellent'.

In this context, those [states] described as "limited" (*paritta*) and so forth by way of being unskilled (*apaguṇa*) and the like are not intended here. Rather, it refers to those [states] associated with inferior or excellent zeal and the rest.
The *paritta* (protection) and other recitations were taught for the sake of being "yoked" (*yuttatāya*); these alone are intended here.

For it is these very [recitations] that accomplish the threefold distinction of rebirth as a Brahmā across the three planes. Furthermore, the fact that even women who have attained mastery over the *jhānas* do not arise among the Mahābrahmās due to the inferiority of their desire (*chanda*) and other factors is proof of this point. And for this very reason, in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, by way of desire and so forth...
Having classified the accomplished [deeds]—inferior, middling, and superior—into eighteen divisions, it is said:

"These are called the eighteen doors of action (kammadvāra). Because they are manifested by these, one should understand that by way of these there are eighteen Kṣatriyas, eighteen Brāhmaṇas, eighteen Vaiśyas, eighteen Śūdras, and forty-eight clans and lineages. By this...
For even among the gods and even among the Brahmās, one observes a difference in rebirth according to what is obtained.
However, in the *Vibhāvani*, it is stated:
"In the Commentary, it is said without distinction that 'the limited' (*paritta*) is merely what has been acquired but not cultivated. Likewise, 'not so'..."

"‘Well-developed’ refers to the middling [state] which possesses mastery that is mostly complete; ‘exceedingly well-developed,’ however, refers to the sublime [state] which possesses mastery that is entirely complete"—this has been said. None of that is applicable here.

For that was said with reference to whether [the concentration] is capable or incapable of becoming a condition for the higher jhānas, or with reference to specific qualities such as being subject to decline (*hānabhāgiyatā*), and so forth; it was not said with reference to the specific quality that produces differences in rebirth.
[162] And as for that which is stated therein:
"In this context, it appears that even a slight degree of practice, provided it has been attained, is intended by the Teacher. For likewise, in the *Nāmarūpapariccheda*:
'When a similar practice has been attained, and the Great Powers are present...'"
"Because it has not obtained such repetition (āsevana), the higher knowledge (abhiññā) does not ripen.

This was said after stating that sublime states (mahaggata-dhamma) give rise to fruition (vipāka) due to their strength through the acquisition of repetition within the same plane; however, because that [repetition] is absent, it was stated that higher knowledge does not ripen. That too must indeed be examined.

For just as the volition of the Noble Path (ariyamagga-cetanā), although equal to the impulsion (javana) of its own plane, gives rise to fruition even without obtaining repetition—so too [should this case be considered].

"It does not give" means that it is not the case [that it does not give]. Likewise, even sublime volition—which occurs only once in a process of action (kammavīthi) and is not present at all in the processes of meditative attainments (samāpatti)—does not give a result because it is weak, having failed to acquire the habituation (āsena) from dharmas of its own plane.
Thus, it is not impossible to understand that "it does not give. Herein, it might be argued: of that very same fine-material-sphere [volition]...
It is said that "due to having performed and accumulated wholesome karma, one enters and dwells in the first jhāna as its result.

Yet, that volition (cetanā) is not what is called "accumulated," because it has not received repeated practice (*āsevana*) among the factors belonging to the same plane. This is not so; for otherwise, even the volition of the supramundane path would incur the status of being non-resultant.
For that [path-volition] is likewise [of the same plane] as that very wholesome supramundane jhāna.
Because it has been performed and cultivated, it is a result. It is said that "one enters and dwells in the first jhāna.
And yet, even this [resultant consciousness] does not possess the quality of having been practiced (*laddhāsevana*) by way of factors belonging to its own plane.

However, because it has arrived here after being accumulated and cultivated starting from the very first act of attention (*pathamasamannāhāra*) in both cases, it possesses the state of having been practiced even by way of impulsions (*javana*) belonging to a different plane.
It can be said that "accumulation" and "development" are mentioned in reference to [kamma] dependent [on these].

Therefore, even though a sublime volition (mahaggata-cetanā) may have been the initial act of kamma, it should not be said that it does not yield its result because it was obtained near the time of death and has become a proximate kamma.

Furthermore, the volition of direct knowledge (abhiññā-cetanā), due to having been more thoroughly cultivated by various adverting and impulsion processes within its own plane, is of a sharper nature.
How could they be weak? For that very reason, this position is rejected in the *Anuṭīkā*. For it is said there:
"Some, however, hold that because they possess the same plane (*samānabhūmaka*) and obtain through repetition (*āsevana*), the jhānas are strong and thus yield fruition (*vipāka*).

But the supernormal powers (*abhiññā*), although they too have the nature of jhāna, are weak because they lack that [repetition] and because they are merely adventitious (*āgantuka*) with respect to each respective object."
Therefore, they say that it does not yield a result (vipāka). That is not the reason. For mastery over even the higher knowledges (abhiññā) is possible through repeated preliminary work (parikamma).
However, the volition of the higher knowledges, which constitutes the benefit of the fourth jhāna concentration, stands in the place of the fruit and is similar to its fruit;
therefore, the commentators maintain that it does not yield a result.
Furthermore, the function of supernormal power (*iddhi*), such as transformation (*vikubbana*) and so forth, is even greater than the function of ripening (*vipaccana*).
Moreover, for one who accomplishes the function of transformation and so forth in every way, even the power of ripening comes to exhaustion along with that power.
Therefore, it is indeed logical that it does not yield further result (*vipāka*). "The fifth jhāna" refers to its state as a direct knowledge (*abhiññā*).
The fifth jhāna is threefold, distinguished as "not-yet-attained" (*apatta*), "limited" (*paritta*), and so forth. "That very same" refers to the fifth jhāna itself.

"Having developed the fading away of perception" (*saññāvirāgaṃ bhāvetvā*): when the mind exists, there are attachment, aversion, and delusion; when that [mind] is absent, one is said to have attained Nibbāna in this very life (*diṭṭhadhammanibbānappatta*).
Thus, having seen the danger in the mind itself, for some—accompanied by the aspiration for a state of non-mindfulness—there is [the attainment] through the wind-kasiṇa.
Having developed the fading away of perception as in the space-kasiṇa delimited by their own view, they arise among the non-percipient beings.

By whichever posture they die here, by that very same posture they arise there; this is the intention [of the text], namely, that it refers only to those heretics who maintain the doctrine of the inefficacy of karma.
For indeed, for those who deny the efficacy of karma, there can be no such thing as the cultivation of jhāna. But as for the non-returners...
"They arise in the Suddhāvāsa [Pure Abode] realms" means that only non-returners (anāgāmin) arise in the Suddhāvāsa realms;

others, such as once-returners (sakadāgāmin) and so forth, do not. By this, it is shown that the arising of non-returners in other Brahma-worlds is not prohibited. Furthermore, among the non-returners, one who is preeminent in faith arises in the Aviha realm;
one preeminent in energy arises in the Atappa realm; one preeminent in mindfulness arises in the Sudassa realm; and one preeminent in concentration...

"In the Sudassīs; in the Akaniṭṭhas, one preeminent in wisdom. The construction is: "Having developed [the jhānas] in their respective order, they arise in the formless realms (arūpa) in their respective order.

And here, the entire passage beginning with "having developed the first jhāna to a limited degree" is stated according to the determination of the specific plane of fruition for each respective jhāna.
However, as for ordinary persons (puthujjana) and stream-enterers (sotāpanna) who have attained these meditative absorptions (samāpatti)...
Once-returners are reborn in a desired plane among the planes where the meditative attainments they have personally acquired ripen.
Among them, the worldling (puthujjana) is reborn even in the sense-sphere world (kāmaloka) if there is attachment.

The others, however, are reborn even in the sense-sphere world provided that their jhānas have not degenerated. Furthermore, if the jhānas have not degenerated, those who possess attachment are reborn in the sense-sphere existence (kāmabhava).
"It is not possible for them" means that they are reborn there only after having fallen away from jhāna.

However, in the *Vibhāvani*, it is stated by one who maintains that even those stream-enterers and once-returners are reborn in the sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*) through the influence of craving: "In that way..."
"Even in the realm of sensual existence (kāmabhava), it succeeds through the power of sense-sphere karma (kāmāvacara-kamma).
For it is said: 'Monks, the mental aspiration of one who is virtuous succeeds because of its purity. This statement is not tenable.
When those jhānas have not been lost, they lead exclusively to rebirth in the Brahma-world; therefore, they are called "jhānas of the non-returner" (anāgāmi-jhāna).
...are so called. And their loss of jhāna occurs only by way of those respective hindrances (*palibodha*), not by way of sensual lust (*kāmarāga*) and so forth.
Why? Because it has been thoroughly suppressed by jhāna, which is the companion of the path. For this has been said in the *Aṅguttara Nikāya*:
"Monks, with the mere arising of vision, three fetters (*saṃyojana*) are destroyed for the noble disciple... He, quite secluded... [attains] the first..."
He dwells having attained that jhāna. And if, monks, at that time a noble disciple should pass away, there is no fetter by which that noble disciple, being fettered, would return again to this world.
And here, by the phrase "if at that time," etc., it is meant that if he passes away without losing the jhāna he has obtained, [he will certainly...]
"He will go precisely to the Brahma-world. This, however, shows that for one who lets [the attainment] fall away, that fetter remains manifest.

And in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga-aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated: "But for those who have attained jhāna and for non-returners (anāgāmī), because rebirth-linking occurs only in the Brahma-world, there is no [further] condition [for rebirth in the sense-sphere realms].
In that context, "those who have attained jhāna" refers to stream-enterers (sotāpanna) who have attained sublime jhāna.

Regarding once-returners (*sakadāgāmin*): "There is no attachment" means that their craving for insight (*vipassanā-nikanti*) does not exist as a craving for rebirth in a happy destination (*kāmasugati*).

Therefore, it should be understood that even for these two types of trainees (*sekkha*), though they possess the qualities liable to relapse, there is no such thing as attachment to sensual existence (*kāmabhava*) when jhāna is present.
However, in the case of a non-returner (*anāgāmi*), even while he is merely sleeping, [if] his neck were cut by a sword...
Even for one being killed, there is no passing away without having attained *jhāna*; for he is said to be "one who fulfills concentration.

However, even women who have attained the eight meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) and are reborn in the next existence in the Akaniṭṭha heaven do not arise among the Mahābrahmās who possess sovereign power;
because of their inferior disposition, they arise only among the chaplains and courtiers.

They are reborn. For instance, in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), regarding the meaning of the Sutta passage stating, "It is impossible for a woman to attain the state of a Brahmā," the term "state of a Brahmā" (*brahmatta*) is intended to mean the state of a Great Brahmā (*mahābrahmatta*).

Furthermore, in this context, a woman who has developed meditative absorption (*jhāna*) and passed away is reborn in the company of the Brahma’s Retinue (*brahmapārisajja*), but not as a Great Brahmā.
It has been said. Furthermore, it should be understood that the term *brahmapārisajjānaṃ* (of the retinue of Brahmā) here includes the *brahmapurohitānaṃ* (the ministers of Brahmā) as well;
for they constitute the assembly (*parisa*) of Brahmā. Indeed, this is stated in the *Saṃyutta Nikāya*:

"Then, monks, the Blessed One Sikhī addressed the monk Abhitu: 'May it occur to you, O Brāhmaṇa, to deliver a discourse on the Dhamma concerning Brahmā, the assembly of Brahmā, and the retinue of Brahmā.'"
"And when there is an assembly, those born within assemblies also exist. In this context, "by Brahmā" means by Mahābrahmā.

"Of the Brahmā assembly" means of the host of the Brahmapurohitas; such is the meaning. If it is argued that since they are mentioned as "the Brahmā-pārisajjas," it is more appropriate for their inclusion to be right here [in that category] rather than under Mahābrahmā—no, that is not so. For it is said:
"Whatever woman might exercise the power of Sakka, or might exercise the power of Māra..."

"One might become the state of Brahmā; such a possibility does not exist"—this is because [the text] speaks here of the denial of lordship (*adhipati*) in relation to Sakka and others who have attained that status, as it is only in this context that such a denial is possible.
For this very reason, it is stated in the *Netti*: "That a woman could be a Great Brahmā (*Mahābrahmā*); such a possibility does not exist.

Up to this point, [the discussion has covered] the Brahmās who serve as chaplains (*purohita*) and members of the assembly (*pārisajja*) even in the higher Brahma-worlds, such as the Vehapphala realm.

Thus, their existence is established. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Saṃyutta-aṭṭhakathā* that among the Brahmās there are indeed those called "Brahmā attendants," just as among elders there are young novices who act as storekeepers.
However, in the *Vibhāvani*, it is said:

"Furthermore, it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: 'Noble women as well as non-noble women who have attained the eight meditative attainments (*aṭṭhasamāpatti*) are reborn only among the Retinue of Brahmā (*brahmapārisajja*).

In this context, 'only among the Retinue of Brahmā' means that even those being reborn in Akaniṭṭha are reborn only among the attendant deities of the Great Brahmās (*mahābrahmā*), and not among the Great Brahmās themselves; such is the meaning to be understood.
However, in the *Maṇimañjūsā*..."
It has been stated that they are reborn only among the *Brahmapārisajja* [retinue of Brahmā], and not among the *Brahmapurohita* and so forth; however, that should not be accepted.
Furthermore, the account given there regarding Sāmāvati and others being reborn first among the *Brahmapārisajja* does not accord with the *Aṭṭhakathā*.
However, because they realized the fruits of the Noble Ones (ariyaphala) in this present existence, those non-returners (anāgāminī) were reborn in the Suddhāvāsa [heavens].
As for the others, some were reborn among the Tāvatiṃsa [devas] and some among the Paranimmitavasavatti [devas];
thus it is stated in the Udāna-aṭṭhakathā. Furthermore, in this context, [the heavens] are the Vehapphala, the Akaniṭṭha, and the fourth Āruppa.
Noble ones reborn in the three highest realms of existence (*bhavagga*) do not arise elsewhere. Those reborn in the remaining Brahma-worlds do not arise in the lower planes.
[The Tetrad of Kamma. 155.
Death by the exhaustion of the life-span, death by the exhaustion of kamma, and so forth, should be applied accordingly. In that regard, while [the kamma] is still unexhausted...

Death by the exhaustion of the life-span (*āyukkhayamaraṇa*) is death occurring through the complete depletion of the specific measure of life that was determined for a particular class of beings according to the power of their karma.
Death by the exhaustion of merit (*puññakkhayamaraṇa*) is death occurring prematurely while the measure of life is not yet exhausted,
solely due to the depletion of the "arrow" of karma for a being born in a particular existence with weak karma.
Death by the exhaustion of karma is called *kammakkhaya-maraṇa*. Death through the simultaneous exhaustion of both is called *ubhayakkhaya-maraṇa*.

Even while both [karma and life-span] still remain, death occurs when a harmful karma committed in previous existences or in this very existence gives rise to obstacles to life—both internal and external—such as various diseases and afflictions, or entry into the earth, or being struck by lightning.
The death of a being whose continuum of aggregates has been interrupted midway—like that of Dussīma, Kalāburāja, and others—is called "death by interruption" (*upacchedaka-maraṇa*).
Now, one might ask: since for all those who die, the karma that produces their respective existence is indeed exhausted, why then are the other types of death also mentioned?
It is said in reply: it is solely through the inherent power (*sarasavasena*) of the karma that its efficacy [is determined].
Here, "destruction" (khaya) is intended as the destruction of karma (*kammakkhaya*).

Furthermore, those various modes of lifespan—ranging from ten years, twenty years, up to incalculable eons—that are established for various classes of beings and are common to all people, consist of temperature, nutriment, and name (*nāma*) produced internally and externally within those beings.
These [factors] constitute that respective lifespan-period.
They are of three kinds: those that cause stability, those that cause increase, and those that cause decrease.
Among them, when the unwholesome roots (akusalamūla) are increasing, those that cause decrease increase; when the wholesome roots (kusalamūla) are increasing, those that cause increase increase;
and when both sets of roots are established equally, those that cause stability proceed equally. By virtue of these, the lifespan of beings in some places—
It is always a portion of stability. In some cases, at certain times, it is a portion of decline and at other times a portion of growth.
Furthermore, these three—stability and the others—proceed by overwhelming the respective classes of beings and delimiting their lifespan;
thus, there is karma conducive to an incalculable lifespan and karma conducive to the prosperity of a wheel-turning monarch during a ten-year [famine].
When it ripens in due time, it bestows corresponding wealth and power and is exhausted by way of the ten [modes].

The material phenomena (rūpadhamma) that constitute the continuity of beings included within various classes of sentient beings— even those that constitute the continuity of the aggregates of omniscient Buddhas—
evolve as being of that same nature and following that same course, except in the case of those produced through supernormal power (iddhimaya).
"One who knows the life-formations through the method of the elixir consisting of clear knowledge. For this is said in the *Mahāpadāna-sutta-aṭṭhakathā*:

"All omniscient Buddhas have an incalculable lifespan (*asaṅkhyeyya-āyuka*). Why did they not live for an entire incalculable aeon? Because of a failure in climate and food. For it is by way of climate and food that the lifespan decreases or increases.
Therefore, while the two types of material phenomena (*rūpa-dhamma*) arising from those [four] bases of striving undergo transformation according to each respective world-cycle of the lifespan..."
Even a very great deed, when it is being exhausted, is simply worn away due to the absence of its own basis for ripening (*vipākādhiṭṭhāna*).
Its exhaustion does not occur through its own inherent power (*sarasena*), but rather occurs precisely through the failure of the life-formations (*āyusaṅkhāra*);

thus, here the "exhaustion of life" is mentioned separately. This same principle should be applied to "cutting-off death" (*upacchedakamaraṇa*) as well. In that context, "cutting-off death" refers to...
Untimely death is what is meant. That occurs either through the karma that interrupts the life-process, or through many thousands of other causes.
These, however, have been summarized in the Canon according to their primary divisions and stated as being eightfold.
What are they? There are afflictions arising from wind; there are those arising from bile; there are those arising from phlegm...

Origination: There are those arising from a combination [of humors], there are those arising from the seasons, there are those born from improper conduct, there are those caused by external injury, and there are diseases born as the result of kamma.
Among these, some born as the result of kamma are produced by obstructive kamma, while others are produced by interrupting kamma.
Furthermore, wind becomes deranged due to ten causes, such as cold, heat, and so forth.
And among those, only one type of disease is born of kamma-vipāka; the rest, however, are not born of kamma-vipāka, as stated in the *Milindapañha*.

Furthermore, since even diseases born of kamma-vipāka do not arise without the provocation of wind (*vāta*) and so forth when they manifest, it should be understood that some diseases originating from wind and the other humors are indeed born of kamma-vipāka.
In this context, "arising from a combination" (*sannipātika*) refers to those [diseases] that occur due to the convergence of two or three factors, such as wind (*vāta*) and the others.

Furthermore, those various dangers and calamities in the world that arise spontaneously for beings without being caused by their own deliberate actions should be understood as included among those "originating from temperature" (*utusamuṭṭhāna*).
Those "born from the neglect of what is uneven" (*visama-parihāra-jāta*) refer to those who, through lack of circumspection, place themselves in many kinds of uneven states of misfortune.
Those that arise through falling or stumbling here and there while one is being struck;

those that are "self-inflicted" (*opakkamikā*) arise by way of applications (*payoga*) made by oneself or by others—such as kings, thieves, enemies, non-human beings (*amanussa*), wild beasts, *yakkhas*, deities, or predatory animals.
For when a deity is provoked, it may [destroy] an entire kingdom, a country, or an island.
They destroy them entirely and without remainder all at once, as in the cases of the Daṇḍaka country, the Majjha country, the Kaliṅga country, and the Mātaṅga country.
They release many thousands of fierce *yakkhas*, as in Vesālī; or they release *rakkhasas*, as in Suvaṇṇabhūmi.
For it is said in the *Aṅguttara Nikāya*: "The *yakkhas* release fierce non-human beings (*amanussā*). By that..."

"Many people are dying. In the *Aṭṭhakathā* it is said: "Yakkhas" refers to the lords of the yakkhas. "They release wild non-human beings" means they dispatch fierce yakkhas onto the paths frequented by humans.
It is stated that, having found their opportunity, they bring the great multitude to the end of life.
In that context, "they release" means that upon seeing many people abounding in immoral conduct, their faith is shattered.

The meaning is that the yakkha generals do not provide protection for human beings as they did before. There is no need to mention [the calamities] regarding countries, cities, market towns, and villages, nor regarding this or that individual.
The eons of weapons, famine, and disease mentioned in the *Aṅguttara Nikāya* should also be mentioned here.
[The phrase] "born of the ripening of kamma" refers to the process of maturation of those karmas that cause oppression and destruction.
The meaning is: "afflictions have arisen. Thus, untimely death occurs through obstructive karma (*upacchedaka-kamma*) or through many thousands of other causes—whatever is seen in the world.

Whether they be life-taking, destroyers of vitality, various diseases, various afflictions, various fears, various punishments, various calamities, or various secondary complications—all of these arise solely from one's own karma.
There is nothing that is not shared by oneself. Even that which arises from the actions of others is indeed shared by oneself.
Even that which arises from one’s own actions is indeed shared by others. Even that which arises from any source whatsoever, independent of karma, is indeed shared by oneself or by others.
Regarding those things arising from karma that is common to all, there is simply nothing to be said. As it is said in the *Visuddhimagga*:
Just as when a target is set at a crossroads, arrows, spears, javelins, stones, and so forth, coming from all directions, fall upon it; even so, all calamities fall upon the body.

And those [calamities] arise in certain kingdoms and countries. In those places, the people are neither skilled in means (*upāyakusala*), nor skilled in remedy (*paṭikārakusala*), nor skilled in prevention (*parihārakusala*). Furthermore, their karma is weak. Thus, the misfortune arises.
Or by force. Even without an interrupting kamma, they are not released from that [result]. They certainly encounter death or suffering amounting to death.

For even a wholesome kamma is unable to ward off a disease, an affliction, fear, punishment, misfortune, or calamity arising from any source whatsoever that is stronger than itself. Diseases and the like—indeed, these alone...

They proceed casting it off. For just as water is not able to resist a fire that is stronger than itself, and it is the fire alone that proceeds casting the water away—so too should this be understood.
Furthermore, the natural weakness of karma in these beings is established in the *Mahāniddesa* by the "Jarā-sutta-niddesa" and in the *Visuddhimagga*.
In the exposition of the mindfulness of death (*maraṇassati*), it should not be explained under the phrase "the frailty of life" (*āyu-dubbalatā*).

As it has been said: "Life is called this because it is weak and fragile. For the life of beings is bound up with inhalation and exhalation, bound up with the postures (*iriyāpatha*), bound up with cold and heat, bound up with the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), and bound up with nutriment," and so forth.
Likewise, it is also evident in the exposition of these phrases: "because the body is common to many" and "because it is signless. [This applies] to that which is produced by kamma.

For when the fragility of life is stated in the Pāḷi and the Aṭṭhakathā to be like a drop of dew on the tip of a blade of grass, the same fragility of kamma is thereby established. This must be accepted;
otherwise, it would become the view that everything is caused by past actions (*pubbekatahetu*). As it has been said:

In this regard, a certain ascetic or brahmin holds such a doctrine and such a view: "Whatever this person experiences—whether pleasure, pain, or neither-pain-nor-pleasure—all that is caused by what was done in the past.
This point has been explained in detail in three places in the *Milindapañha*.

Furthermore, it should be understood that even death occurring through the many thousands of causes already mentioned is included here under "death by interruption" (upacchedaka-maraṇa), due to its commonality with untimely death (*akāla-maraṇa*).
In the *Vibhāvani*, it is stated: "But this [benefit] does not exist for those in the hells, for the inhabitants of Uttarakuru, or for certain devas.
However, as stated in the *Mahāṭīkā*, when certain hungry ghosts (petas) rejoice in the merit transferred by their relatives here [in the human world], [they receive a benefit].
It is stated that for those who, at that very moment, pass away and are reborn in a happy destination, their wholesome state constitutes a "cutting-off" death. Likewise,
it cannot be said that there is no such thing as "cutting-off death" even for certain inhabitants of hell who, while being interrogated by King Yama and the like,
recollect the merit they themselves have performed and, at that very moment, pass away and are reborn in a happy destination.
For certain gods, such as those of the Tāvatiṃsa realm, that death is indeed a "cutting-off" death (*upacchedaka-maraṇa*).

For instance, it is stated in the *Saṃyutta-ṭṭhakathā* (Commentary on the Saṃyutta Nikāya) regarding the Subrahma-devaputta: "Then, having climbed the tree, they died all at once due to the power of their cutting-off karma and so forth, and were reborn in Avīci. In this context, "the tree" refers to the Pāricchattaka tree in the Tāvatiṃsa realm.
"Abhiruḷhā" means they have ascended; [this refers to] the five hundred celestial nymphs (*devaccharā*).

The death of the gods who die from mental corruption (*manopadosika*) or from the corruption of food (*khittapadosika*), and the death of Great Bodhisattvas who, having been reborn in a long-lived heavenly world or the Brahma-world, pass away through the exercise of their own resolve (*adhimutti-kālaṅkiriyā*), as well as the death of those like the Elder Channa and the Elder Godhika who attain final Nibbāna by themselves taking up a weapon—[all these are included].
It should be understood that it is included right here. "In that manner" means by those aforementioned modes. The connection is:

"it manifests at one of the six doors of those who are dying. "At the time of death" means at the moment proximate to death. "As appropriate" means according to what is fitting for those going to a happy destination or a miserable destination.
As for those whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*), they do not arise anywhere; among them, regarding those who are dry-insight practitioners (*sukkha-vipassaka*):
By nature, name-and-form as it has been established is the object of the final impulsion moments.
However, for those who attain meditative absorption (jhāna) and pass away immediately after the jhāna, the object is the sign of the kasiṇa and so forth;

for those who pass away immediately after the reviewing [of the jhāna], the factors of the jhāna; and for those who pass away immediately after the direct knowledges (abhiññā), their own physical body (karajarūpa).
However, for those who attain final Nibbāna at the very moment their life-span is exhausted, immediately following the review of the Supreme Path (agga-magga),

the objects of the final impulsion moments— such as the path factors and so forth— become the object of consciousness. But it should be understood that for all [beings], the death-consciousness of final Nibbāna has as its object only one among the kamma and other factors exactly as they were grasped at the time of their respective rebirth-linking at the beginning of existence.

Having seen this scriptural passage, "The Sage, having conquered the fear of Māra, passed away without remainder," they claim that Nibbāna alone was the object of the Blessed One’s final passing away (parinibbāna-cuti).
By doing so, they demonstrate their own lack of proficiency regarding the objects of consciousness within the Abhidhamma’s triplets of objects. As it is said:

Which states have limited objects? All resultant and functional states of the sense-sphere, the functional mind-element, and the functional mind-consciousness-element accompanied by joy—these states have limited objects.

Furthermore, because that which is called "parinibbāna" truly exists as peace, and because one’s aspiration is exclusively inclined toward that peace, therefore the scriptural passage "seeking peace" (*santiṃ ārabbha*) was spoken. For it is said in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "seeking peace..."

It is stated [in the *Theragāthā-aṭṭhakathā*] that this is said "with reference to" (*ārabbha*) and "dependent upon" (*paṭicca*) Nibbāna without residue (*anupādisesa*), but it is not stated that it is "having taken as a basis," "having made an object," or "having made an objective support" (*ālambitvā*, *ārammaṇaṃ katvā*). However, in the *Theragāthā-aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated:
"With reference to peace" (*santiṃ ārabbha*) means "having made peace, which is Nibbāna without residue, an object. That does not accord with the *Mahāparinibbāna-sutta* or its commentary.

For it is stated that among those [three immediate antecedents], the Blessed One’s final passing away (parinibbāna) occurred immediately after his reviewing of the factors of jhāna (*jhānaṅga-paccavekkhaṇa*).

Here, the first two immediate antecedents are mentioned in the commentaries on the *Parinibbāna Sutta*. The one immediately following the higher knowledge (*abhiññā*) is found in the commentary on the *Udāna* and elsewhere. As it is said:
"Having emerged, he passed away" means having emerged from the consciousness of supernormal power (*iddhicitta*).

"One who attains final nibbāna with the life-continuum consciousness" (bhavaṅgacittena parinibbāyī) is mentioned in the *Puggalapaññatti-aṭṭhakathā* and other commentaries as occurring immediately after the reviewing of the highest path (*aggamagga*).
As it is said: "Having established himself in the nineteen knowledges of reviewing, he descends into the life-continuum and attains final nibbāna.
However, in the *Saṃyutta-aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated that after the path of arahantship comes the fruit, and after the fruit, [the mind] proceeds from the life-continuum.
After emerging, there is reviewing. That reviewing may be complete or incomplete.
It is said that even if one's head were being cut off with a sharp sword, one or two acts of reviewing would still certainly arise.
However, in the *Vibhāvanī*:

Without making such a distinction, it has been stated: "In some cases, for one whose taints are exhausted (khīṇāsava) and in whom [defilements] do not arise, only the phenomena of name-and-form as they appear—beginning with the mind and so forth—become the objects of the final moments of death;
it is not karma, nor the kamma-mitta, and so on. This is not correct.
For it is not the case that his death-consciousness does not take as its object karma, the sign of karma, and so forth.
Nor is it true that for all beings, the karma and other factors grasped at the moment of death do not come into existence for the sake of another becoming.
"Manifested" means it has presented itself by making room for itself without giving opportunity to any other karma. Or, "karma manifests" [means the same].

The connection [is as follows]. The phrase "previously perceived" is said with reference to the objects of that karma, namely, the gifts such as cloth and so forth, as well as other living beings and the like.

The phrase "serving as an instrument" is said with reference to those things serving as instruments for the accomplishment of the karma and those serving as its accessories, such as recipients and so forth, as well as weapons, goods, and the like. And because of the characteristic...
In the *Aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated that in the *Saṃyutta Nikāya*, cows and other animals, having been slaughtered and piled up, appear as kamma-signs (*kamma-nimitta*) such as heaps of bones.
Therefore, it should be understood that whatever objects or sense-bases (*ārammaṇa*) are connected with kamma are included here under the category of "requisites" (*upakaraṇa*).
The term "to be apprehended" (*upalabhitabba*) refers to the sign of an unhappy rebirth (*duggati-nimitta*).

It has been said. "That which has become an object of enjoyment" means a sign of a happy destination (*sugati*). Alternatively, whatever is to be obtained by being bound to the body is called "that which is to be apprehended" (*upalabhitabba*).

That which is to be obtained not by being bound [to the body], but solely for the purpose of experiencing pleasure and pain, is called "that which has become an object of enjoyment" (*upabhogabhūta*).
And in this context, [the examples include] the flames of fire, the iron cauldrons, the hell-wardens, and the fierce dogs of hell.
It is a sign of hell. For some people, it appears as if in their own dwelling place;
for others, it appears as if coming from here and there, surrounding them on all sides. As it is said:
"To him who has lain down upon his sickbed, hell appears. From the foot of Mount Soṇa, great dogs come, as if desiring to devour him."

"They were surrounded. Likewise with the divine signs. As it is said: "They appeared as if they stood surrounding Nandavana, Cittalatāvana, Missakavana, Phārusakavana, the celestial palaces (vimāna), and the divine dancers.
For some, however, it appears as if seen by them personally upon reaching those various places. The color of the mother’s womb is like a woolen rug (kambala).
The sign of humans. The foothills of mountains, groves of forest, precipices, and so forth, are the signs of animals.
"By the power of kamma" means by the influence of the kamma that has arisen now to produce rebirth-linking.

And this is stated according to the general rule; for [the object] may be something naturally habitual, or something experienced previously, or something done at that very moment, or something caused to be remembered by another.

It should be understood that [the object] presents itself either by one’s own recollection, or by producing, as its very nature, either remorse or gladness, or by a deed already established, or by the sign of that [deed], or by the force of some other cause.

And the phrase "taking that very object which has presented itself from there" is stated by way of the majority of cases; for in some instances, it may first present itself through the power of karma alone.

Alternatively, when unwholesome factors arise, they appear later when wholesome factors manifest—either for those who, like the wicked village headman [Duṭṭhagāmaṇi], recollect their previously performed powerful merit;
or for those who, like the Elder Soṇa, perform at that very moment merit that generates confidence; or likewise for some others at first.
When those on the side of the wholesome attend upon one, just as they did for King Dhammāsoka,
those on the side of evil attend upon those who, later on, due to some cause, give rise to mental distress and create an opportunity for unwholesome action.
"In accordance with the ripening karma" means that for one whose ripening karma is wholesome, their continuum of consciousness is pure and wholesome.
It occurs constantly. For one who possesses that unwholesome state, the defiled continuum of unwholesome consciousness occurs constantly;

this is the meaning. For likewise, in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, it is said: "For those going to a happy destination, a sublime object—which serves as the cause for the arising of the wholesome—comes into range;
and for those going to a miserable destination, an inferior object—which serves as the cause for the arising of the unwholesome [comes into range]."

It is said that "it arrives at the moment of death. In both the *Mūlaṭīkā* and the *Mahāṭīkā*, it is stated that unwholesome kamma is the decisive support (*upanissaya*) for rebirth-linking in an unhappy destination, while wholesome kamma is the decisive support for rebirth-linking in a happy destination when one is near [death]. Here, it might be asked:
when signs of heaven such as celestial nymphs appear, how can that be so for one who is passing away while still finding gratification in them through craving?
It is said: "His mind is indeed defiled; therefore, they say that an unhappy destination (duggati) is to be expected for him.

However, since in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga* it is stated that such craving serves as a concomitant cause (*sahakāri-kāraṇa*) for wholesome karma—just as it is said, "At the moment of attachment, two causes are unwholesome"—therefore, even in the production of a happy destination (*sugati*), [craving acts as a condition].

Since this craving is, in every respect, a decisive and cooperative condition for wholesome karma, it must—when one is passing away while still relishing those celestial nymphs or the signs of wholesome karma—necessarily serve as a support for that [wholesome state].
It cannot be understood as something that obstructs it; for even one who is attached to the gratification of the sign...
“Monks, consciousness persists as it persists when it is attached to the gratification of secondary characteristics (*anubyañjana*).
Monks, if one were to pass away at that time, it is possible that one would go to one of two destinations: either hell or the animal realm;
this was stated in the *Āditta-pariyāya* (The Discourse on Being Aflame). That [attachment] occurs in relation to one’s own or others’ hands, feet, and so forth.”
This was said with reference to craving that has become intensified (*gāḷha*). "It can be said not regarding karma and so forth" means it is possible to speak thus.
"In accordance with the existence to be experienced" means: if the existence to be experienced is a happy rebirth (*sugati-bhava*), then [craving arises] in the mode of relishing it;
if it is an unhappy rebirth (*duggati-bhava*), then [it arises] in the mode of not relishing it—in this way, it is in accordance with the existence to be experienced. "Bending toward that" means...

When that object has thus been established, [the mind] inclines toward it. For it is said in the *Bālapaṇḍita Sutta*: "At that time, those [karmas] of his hang down, hang down completely, and hang down all over.
Therein, "those of his" (*tānissa*) refers to the meritorious and demeritorious karmas of that person.
Under the heading of "karma," the signs of karma (*kammanimitta*) and the signs of destiny (*gatinimitta*) are also included. "Hang down" (*olambanti*) means...
Having caused his own mental continuum to incline, lean toward, and turn towards itself alone, they hang down and dangle.
The meaning is that they appear as if binding and pulling it back.
But when they are thus hanging down in that manner, that mental continuum becomes inclined, leaning, and bent towards them; hence it is said: "the inclination towards that."
For thus it is said in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "Having heard that [consciousness] is driven by the power of the defilements, it proceeds in such a way;
because craving and ignorance have not been abandoned, craving inclines toward that object whose dangers are concealed by ignorance, while the co-nascent formations propel it.
In this context, "it" (*taṃ*) refers to consciousness (*viññāṇa*); the meaning is simply the mental continuum (*cittasantāna*). "Toward that object" (*tasmiṃ visaye*)...

“Upon the object consisting of karma and so forth. “It inclines toward craving” means that craving, being the root of the round of existence, causes one to lean toward and directs one toward that [object].
In the *Vibhāvani*, however, it is stated:
“*Tatthoṇataṃ vā* means either ‘leaning as if toward’ or simply ‘leaning toward’ that state of existence in which one is to be reborn. This does not accord with the *Aṭṭhakathā*.
"Constantly" (*abhiṇhaṃ*) means without interruption. However, such a mode of occurrence is found only in those who die slowly; it is stated that it is not found in those who die by a sudden death.

Regarding the phrase "by way of the majority" (*bāhullena*), what was said in the *Vibhāvanī*—"The intended meaning here of 'by way of the majority' is to be understood according to the method stated in the passage 'for the most part in another existence'"—is not tenable.
For there is no possibility of the frequent arising of the mental continuum for those non-percipient beings mentioned therein, because they lack a mental continuum altogether.
Now, in order to show the establishment of action (*kamma*) by another method, it is said:
"But furthermore... it reaches the door. Therein, "reaching the door" means by way of performing [the action] anew.
The meaning is: it "appears" (hoti) by not producing a recognition based on what was done previously, but rather producing the mode of performing [the action] at that very moment;
having made oneself as if new, it appears manifested at the mind-door through the occurrence of a javana similar to that [object].
For just as in this present existence, some manifest karma performed at a certain time is recognized as "this was done by me at such-and-such a time."

Even after generating such a perception of what was done in the past, it still appears [to the mind]. However, it does not appear in the same way as that which occurred in another existence and is concealed by existence (*bhava*), nor as that which occurs in this present existence and is unmanifest.
Furthermore, here some people have habitually practiced giving, worship, and so forth toward the three objects beginning with the Buddha.
When they reach a state of despondency due to the power of a terminal illness at the time of death, they do not recognize any suffering.

In the intervals between [the moments of fruition], those giving alms to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, venerating the cetiya, and making offerings, remain with minds serene and joyful, just as they did before.
Conversely, it should be understood that even those burdened by much evil karma are likewise [to be described]. This too is merely the arrival at the door.
All of this should be illustrated by the *Lakkhaṇa-saṃyutta-ṭīkā*. Therein:
Regarding those such as the horse-lickers and the skinless ones, the very fact that he had his sword raised was the cause;
the very fact that he was pierced by a spear was the cause; the very fact that he was pierced by an arrow was the cause;
and the very fact that he was pierced by the needle of a goad was the cause. As for the pain of being goaded by needles, [it was likewise caused].
Having made karma itself the sign in order to experience [the result], he was born as a "Needle-hair Ghost" (Sūciloma-peta). Thus, the manifestation of karma has been described by way of many doors.
For in that case, his very state of having a raised sword was the sign;
after he had been cooked in hell and was again near death, that karma then produced in him the perception of a raised sword.
The meaning is that the sign (nimitta) arose by way of reaching the door. This same method applies to the remaining cases as well.

And that form which has reached the door is indeed a constituent part of the kamma. Since there is nothing whatsoever hidden from that being, its capacity for grasping rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) has arisen.
"Of one whose death is imminent" means of one who is again near to death by way of the occurrence of the final impulsion (javana).

"At the conclusion of the process-thoughts" means: at the end of those process-thoughts belonging to the sense-sphere that arise within the sense-sphere itself after passing away from the sense-sphere existence—whether they conclude with the impulsion (javana) or conclude with the registration (tadārammaṇa).

However, for others, it means at the end of only those process-thoughts that conclude with the impulsion. This meaning has indeed been stated in the Commentary as well; as it says: "Referring to that..."
