Immediately after the pure cognitive series (suddhāya-vīthi), which begins with the arising [of the object] and concludes with the registration (tadārammaṇa), the death-consciousness (cuticitta) arises.
However, in the *Vibhāvani*, it is stated:

"In that regard, for those who pass away from the sense-sphere existence (kāmabhava) and are reborn in that very same place, the series conclude with registration; for the rest, they conclude with the impulsion (javana). This is not correct.
For in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, it is said that when [the process] has been described in its entirety, what need is there for an incomplete account according to the Dhamma?

"At the very exhaustion of the *bhavaṅga*" means "at the very end of the *bhavaṅga*. If, after the two types of resultant consciousness (*pīthicitta*), the materiality of the physical base (*vatthurūpa*) remains for two mind-moments in the five-aggregate realm, or the mental continuum remains for two mind-moments in the four-aggregate realm, then [it is said] "at the end of one *bhavaṅga*."

This has been stated. Herein, for one who is reborn with a mind of mental joy (*somanassa*) and passes away with a mind of mental grief (*domanassa*), there is the occurrence of an adventitious *bhavaṅga*.
When that occurs, the occurrence of other *bhavaṅgas* is also not precluded; thus, it is well said: "at the exhaustion of the *bhavaṅga*.
"At the conclusion of its cessation" means when that [consciousness] has ceased, at the end of that which has ceased. As for those in the world who [speak of] death...
Between the moments of rebirth-linking, there exists what is called the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
A being arisen therein is capable of traveling instantly to the desired place, like one possessing the divine eye or supernormal powers.
Some beings, having passed away from here and arisen there, remain for seven days or more than seven days while waiting for the union of their mother and father.
They grasp that [wrong] view. To refute that for them, it is stated immediately after that [view]. "With a basis" means in the five-aggregate realm;
"without a basis" means in the four-aggregate realm. "As appropriate" means according to the suitability of the formation, whether it be wholesome or unwholesome.
The latent tendencies of ignorance and craving are [present] in the sense of being unabandoned in the case of the wholesome, but in the case of the unwholesome...

The meaning is that they exist as both companions and as a foundation by way of being co-nascent. They are "conformable" because they are not in contradiction with the continuum of wholesome or indeterminate consciousness, even before reaching the stage of active manifestation (*pariyuṭṭhāna*).
It is called an *anusaya* because it lies down following along (*anubandhamāno vā seti*), or because it lies down continuously and without interruption (*anuanuvā nirantaram setīti*).

One who is enveloped by ignorance which has become an underlying tendency is "enveloped by the underlying tendency of ignorance" (*avijjānusayaparikkhitto*). [Likewise for] the underlying tendency of craving (*taṇhānusayo*).
"Rooted in the underlying tendency to craving" (*taṇhānusaya-mūlaka*) means that this [craving] has its root in the underlying tendency to craving.

However, it is even more appropriate when it is stated as "surrounded by the underlying tendency to craving, which is rooted in the underlying tendency to ignorance" (*avijjānusaya-mūlakena taṇhānusaya-parikkhitena*). For ignorance is indeed the root of craving as well;

for craving can only arise with respect to an object whose dangers have been concealed by that [ignorance]. Furthermore, craving acts as a cooperative cause (*sahakāri-kāraṇa*) for each respective [state].
It proceeds by enjoining volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*); thus, it becomes a powerful and close associate that serves as an attendant to volitional formations.

Furthermore, in this context, because they are similar in nature to underlying tendencies (*anusaya*), [ignorance and craving] are associated with unwholesome kamma, or with attachment to kamma and attachment to signs, or with remorse, or with the impulsion (*javana*) occurring at the moment of death.

The arising of conventional usage (*vohāra*) should be understood as being due to the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*). Furthermore, in the production of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), the underlying tendencies also serve as powerful auxiliaries even for wholesome formations (*kusalasaṅkhāra*).

Therefore, since here only those things that are exclusively underlying tendencies are intended by the term "pervasion" (*pariyatti*), what is the point of including [factors] that arise simultaneously with them?
For this very reason, it is stated in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*) as well: "Because craving and ignorance have not been abandoned"—thus, by means of the word "not abandoned" (*appahīna*).

Only the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) are grasped as being absolute. "By formations" (*saṅkhārena*) means by the formation of volition (*cetanā-saṅkhāra*), which is designated as the karma that produces rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*);

or alternatively, by the collection of phenomena such as contact (*phassa*) that are co-nascent with it. For even that [volition] does not produce rebirth-linking when it exists merely as a decisive support (*upanissaya*).
Or else, "by formations" refers to the formation of volition co-nascent with the impulsion consciousness (*javana-viññāṇa*) at the moment of death. That [volition] is co-nascent...

Or rather, it is by means of the collection of phenomena such as contact (*phassa*). For both of these, by way of being formations (*saṅkhāra*) that project toward objects such as karma, produce rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).

Thus, it is said in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "Because craving (*taṇhā*) and ignorance (*avijjā*) have not been abandoned, craving impels one toward that object whose dangers are concealed by ignorance; the co-nascent formations (*sahajātasaṅkhāra*) then project."

And in the *Mūlaṭīkā*, it is stated that "concomitant formations" (*sahajātasaṅkhārā*) refers to the volition (*cetanā*) concomitant with the impulsion-consciousness (*javana-viññāṇa*) immediately preceding death; or alternatively, it refers to all [mental factors] beginning with contact (*phassa*).

However, by the entire statement, it is meant that ignorance (*avijjā*), karma, and so forth—which have not been abandoned by the supreme path—conceal the danger (*ādīnava*) either within the object or in the next existence;
likewise, craving (*taṇhā*) [conceals danger] regarding form (*rūpa*) alone, while both together [conceal it] within the continuum of consciousness (*cittasantāna*).
"Name": it is the aforementioned formations that project it there. This shows that they bring about the manifestation of that new consciousness.
"Being grasped by the associated [factors]" means being surrounded and taken up by the associated mental states such as contact (phassa) and so forth.

"Co-nascent" means of the phenomena of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). "By way of being a foundation" means by way of being a support. "Having become the precursor" means having become the primary factor.
With these two phrases, he demonstrates the exceedingly great power of the element of consciousness (*vijānanadhātu*).
For just as in the world, when a certain distinguished person of great power is born, the people who are his retinue and those born together with him [are likewise affected].
Just as palaces, wish-fulfilling trees (*kapparukkha*), and so forth—which serve as objects of enjoyment and utility—arise together with it, so too should this be understood.
"By way of linking to another existence" means by way of the linking of another existence immediately following [the cessation] when one existence has ceased;
it is established at the very moment of arising, not in the previous existence.
The intended meaning is that, having arisen and not yet ceased, it proceeds by way of its state of persistence and establishes itself in another existence.
For indeed, there are no phenomena (*dhammā*) that, even during their natural time of arising, are said to have moved to another location or another moment;
how much less so at the time of death could they move to another existence? And as it is said: "Bhikkhus, this saṃsāra is without discoverable beginning; its prior limit is not known."
It has been said that "beings hindered by ignorance and fettered by craving run on and wander through the cycle of existence.

That too is said by way of a figurative expression (*pariyāya*). For it is through ignorance, craving, and volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*) that rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) manifests in another existence.
And that continuum (*santāna*) in which these previously occurred, it is that which runs on to another existence by way of the connection between cause and fruit.
"It is said that it 'wanders' (saṃsarati). And for this very reason, it is established that this rebirth-linking does not arise without causes existing during the course of the previous existence.
In this context, echoes, lamps, seals, and so forth serve as illustrations. "In this context" means at the place of death and rebirth.
"Of feeble occurrence" is due to the weakness of the karma and the weakness of the physical basis (vatthu).
Having become sluggish, they proceed slowly. Therefore, the connection is: "the present object is obtained.

"While they are persisting" means while they are actually remaining. "Of the rebirth-linking and the life-continuum as well" means of the rebirth-linking and of several life-continuum moments as well.
"By this reason" refers to the phrase "iti katvā. And here, although in the Aṭṭhakathā it is called the "sign of the destination" (gatinimitta) in the place where one is to be reborn...
Having stated that "only one color appears," in all sections concerning the signs of rebirth (*gatinimitta*),
it is shown that only the color-base (*vaṇṇāyatana*) is apprehended by the mind-door (*manodvāra*), and that it is exclusively present. Nevertheless, for those such as the lay follower Dhammika,
Duṭṭhagāmaṇi, and King Abhaya, who were passing away after making the divine chariot itself the sign of rebirth upon their arrival from the six celestial worlds into their own presence—
By way of this [object], that [object]—like a kamma-nimitta—is sixfold and apprehended by the six doors; it may be either present or past.
With this intention, having treated it as indistinguishable from a kamma-nimitta, it is stated: "It is obtained for the rebirth-linking of the sense-sphere realm (*kāmāvacara-paṭisandhi*).
For likewise, at the moment of death, even one of divine form, through the power of the deities, [is seen] by the eye...
It is indeed seen. The sound of a divine chariot, the sound of musical instruments, or the sound of speech is indeed heard with the ear.

A divine fragrance is indeed smelled with the nose. And [the suffering] of Devadatta, Nanda the Yakkha, Nanda the Māṇava, Vakā, and others, whose bodies are being burned by flames of fire rising from hell as they pass away; and of Mittavindaka and others, who are being struck by the razor-wheels.
By way of that [object], even a tangible object can indeed arise. The properties of taste (rasa-dhamma) should also be applied according to what is possible. And it is said in the *Saccasaṅkhepa*:
"In the five doors there may be a junction, even without karma, when two objects are present.
This same meaning was also stated in the *Mahāṭīkā*. However, at the stage prior to the final impulsion-series (*javana-vīthi*), as it has arisen...
The sign of the destination (*gatinimitta*) becomes the object of the final impulsion (*antimajavana*). At that time, it is indeed past.
However, in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, its presentness is stated by way of its continuity (*santati*).

Likewise, it should be understood that its status as an object of color and its being grasped by the mind-door are generally stated [in this manner]. Otherwise, even the sign of kamma (*kammanimitta*) would have to be considered present.

It might be argued that since [the object] is shown in the *Aṭṭhakathā* as belonging to the five doors alone, it cannot possibly be something included within the mind-door (*manodvāra*) that is present, nor can it be one of the five sense-objects or a mental object (*dhammārammaṇa*).
However, it is not possible to state this. Why? Because [the object] has been described in the *Paṭṭhāna* as being one of the six objects in such passages as:
"one who contemplates the eye as impermanent, suffering, and non-self," and so forth.

Because it is also accepted that even the death-proximate impulsion (javana) occurring in the mind-door is a pre-arisen condition (*purejāta-paccaya*), for that very reason, rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) which follows upon it can also come to pass.
However, in the *Vibhāvanī*: [168] But in the *Vibhāvanī*:

Likewise, that which was stated without investigation—namely, "in the case of present objects that have entered [the cognitive range], by way of the sign of destiny in the mind-door, and by way of the sign of kamma in the five doors"—is not sound.

Furthermore, what was said there—"That which is apprehended by the six doors: the sign of kamma is apprehended by the six doors, and the sign of destiny is apprehended by the sixth door; this should be applied according to possibility"—that too is not tenable.

If this were so, then the Elder might have spoken of the sign of the destination (*gatinimitta*) as being broken [by the mind-door], just as he did for kamma. And it is not the case that such a thing is impossible, given that it can be apprehended by the five doors according to the method already stated.

Furthermore, regarding what was stated there in the *Aṭṭhakathā* and in the *Mūlaṭīkā* and other works—having not yet analyzed that incomplete reading which was stated there by way of general rule: "In the *Aṭṭhakathā*... [170]

However, because it is stated that the sign of the destination (gatinimitta) enters the range of the mind-door (manodvāra), and because rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) via the five doors has not been shown to have that as its object,
and because it is determined and stated in the *Mūlaṭīkā* and other works that— even for one seeing a dream—
the visible sphere (vaṇṇāyatana) presented by the power of karma becomes the objective domain of the mind-door alone, just as it is for the divine eye— therefore, for those [beings],...
It is said: “The teachers do not accept our statement. Even there, there is no other reason for their non-acceptance than their failure to investigate.
Regarding the phrase “the present and the past”:
here, it refers to one whose death occurs during a five-door cognitive process that concludes with impulsion (*javana*).

For one whose death occurs with a mind-door process that has a present object and concludes with registration (tadārammaṇa), the present state of being an object is found for the rebirth-linking and two life-continuum moments.
For one whose death occurs with a mind-door process concluding with registration, it is found for the rebirth-linking alone.

However, for one whose death occurs with a mind-door process having a present object and concluding with impulsion (javana), it is found for the rebirth-linking and six life-continuum moments. For one...

However, it should be understood that in this context, even for beings in the sense-sphere, if the physical basis (*vatthu*) is weak, the cognitive process (*vīthi*) ends with the impulsion (*javana*), even though the object is long-lasting and powerful;
this is because in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, [the process] is applied as ending specifically with the registration (*tadārammaṇa*). Thus, regarding the mind-door (*manodvāra*):
After rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi), it is stated that for the four life-continuum (bhavaṅga) moments and at the five sense doors, the object is present, just as it is for rebirth-linking itself.

However, because it is stated that "the cognitive process (vīthi) consists of either ending with the registration (tadārammaṇa) or being pure (suddha)," it should be understood that here [in this context], the process is also formulated as ending with the impulsion (javana).
In the *Vibhāvani*, however...

Thus, what was stated without such investigation—namely, that "in the mind-door, the state of having a present object is obtained for the four bhavaṅgas following rebirth-linking, and likewise for the rebirth-linking itself in the five doors," and so forth—is untenable.
For here, it is intended that the "kamma-sign" (kammanimitta) is either the object or the instrument of the very same kamma that produces rebirth-linking.
And kamma pertaining to the five doors does not produce rebirth-linking. Therefore, at that time, [the object] is that which produces rebirth-linking...
Kamma is established by way of the mind-door (manodvāra) at the very beginning [of the cognitive process].
And that which serves as its object, or which serves as its instrument, is exclusively called the "kamma-sign" (kammanimitta).

However, that which becomes the object of the final impulsion (javana) of the five-sense doors is also called a "kamma-sign" because it is not distinct in substance from the object that had ceased previously, or because it resembles it.

It is said thus. For it is stated in the *Mūlaṭīkā*: "In the five sense-doors, that which comes into range—the present *kamma-nimitta* (sign of the deed), the object of a deed recently performed, and that which resembles it—should be seen as having arisen within the continuity (*santati*).

In this context, it refers to those objects of giving such as robes and so forth, or shrines (*cetiyas*) and so forth, or by means of which deeds such as the Teacher’s [gift] were previously accomplished.
With reference to their existing in direct perception (*paccakkha*), it is said: "arisen in a continuity" (*santati*).

With reference to the existence of similar bases (*vatthu*) along with those [beings], it is said: "and similar to them. For even similar bases are indeed causes for karma to find an opportunity [to ripen].
Just as, for example, in the case of those reborn in the neighboring regions of the *Ussada* hell due to a small evil deed committed here.
Just as those who, having heard the sound or seen the appearance of the flames of hell-fire— which resemble the signs they perceived at the time of performing meritorious deeds in the past—
recall their merit and, upon passing away, are reborn in heaven, [they appear] like those very flames.
However, in the *Vibhāvani*:
Without examining the reading of the *Mūlaṭīkā* and having seen a reading similar to it that omits the letter "ca," it was stated:

"Because it is identical with that which serves as the object for mind-door impulsion, that which falls within the same continuity—even though it is grasped by the death-proximate impulsion—is also called 'present' in the sense of being a kamma-sign, such as color-form and so forth. That is simply untenable.
Furthermore, in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, it is said that at the time of another’s death, relatives might say, "Dear one, this worship of the Buddha is being performed for your sake;

please gladden your heart. They may then present an object of form (*rūpārammaṇa*) by way of flower garlands, banners, flags, and so forth; or an object of sound (*saddārammaṇa*) by way of listening to the Dhamma or musical offerings;
or an object of smell (*gandhārammaṇa*) by way of incense, perfumes, and the like; or they might say, "Please taste this... [and offer an object of taste].
It is said that they present [objects] at the five sense doors, saying: "This is a gift to be given for your sake," while presenting an object of taste such as honey or molasses;
or, saying: "This is a gift to be given for your sake," while presenting an object of touch such as a Chinese cloth or a Somāra cloth.
Among these, the objects of visible form, sound, and smell—
In this commentary, it is stated that [the object] arises within the continuity (*santati*).
It is stated that "and similar to that" with reference to the objects of taste and touch; for those which were first tasted or touched are one thing, while those subsequently given are another.
And herein, these form-objects and so forth, thus brought together, are first apprehended by the five doors.

It should be understood that for those passing away after having previously failed to attend to [the object] but later thinking, "Now there are such things as these," and thus grasping them through the pure mind-door, those objects grasped by the mind-door are present-become kamma-signs (*kammanimitta*).

Regarding the designation of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) in the first and third immaterial realms, it is "become" (*bhūta*); regarding the rebirth-linking in the second and fourth immaterial realms, it is "lofty-become" (*mahaggatabhūta*).
"It is stated as appropriate. For those formless beings born in the higher planes among the formless realms, the lower jhānas subside;
yet they do not exert effort toward them again. Therefore it is said that "the lower formless states are excluded.
Having fallen into negligence and abandoned the jhānas, they are dragged back down by the fetters belonging to the lower plane which have not been abandoned.

Regarding those mental [kamma-formations] arising in the sensual existence (*kāmabhava*), it is said that—setting aside the preparatory-jhāna volition associated with the three roots which has become the "cock's stand" (*kukkuṭṭhabhūta*)—no other weak kamma finds an opportunity;
thus it is stated: "likewise, [those] with the three roots in the sensual realm. For indeed, in the *Aṅguttara-aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated:
"For there is no kamma whatsoever more powerful than that preparatory jhāna. And in the *Ṭīkā*:

For it is stated that by the phrase "it does not exist for him," it is shown that for those passing away from there, only access-jhāna (*upacārajjhāna*) is the karma that produces rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhijanaka*).
However, for them, there is no rebirth-linking in the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*) at all.

And having established this, in the *Yamaka*, regarding one who passes away from the immaterial sphere and is being reborn in the immaterial sphere, or one who passes away from the immaterial sphere and [is reborn] in the sense-sphere...

It has been stated [in the context] of one being reborn; however, it has not been stated [specifically] of one passing away from the formless realm (*arūpadhātu*) and being reborn in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Yet, it should not be said that for those passing away from the world of form (*rūpaloka*), no other weak kamma finds an opportunity [to ripen].

Even so, because their mental continuum (*cittasantāna*) has been well-cultivated by means of the specific meditative attainments (*jhāna*) reached through absorption (*appanā*), their hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) have been thoroughly suppressed.
Even a weak, two-rooted kamma that produces such misfortunes as being born blind finds no opportunity; how much less so, then, kamma leading to the states of misery?

Thus it is said: "They may be devoid of roots. However, in the *Vibhāvanī*: [173] It is stated: "Even a weak, two-rooted kamma that produces such misfortunes as being born blind finds no opportunity; how much less so, then, kamma leading to the states of misery? Thus it is said: 'They may be devoid of roots. However, in the *Vibhāvanī*:
It has been stated: “By the power of access concentration (upacāra-jjhāna) alone, rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) may be double-rooted (duhetuka) or triple-rooted (tihetuka). This must be examined.
For if that statement were made with reference to the giving of rebirth-linking, a double-rooted rebirth-linking would not be logical.
Indeed, access concentration—which occurs in the process of absorption (appanā-vīthi) when the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) have been thoroughly suppressed—is not even called "weak triple-rooted."

"It is possible. Now, if it were said with reference to the support of another karma, there would be no reason why, even though it is itself stronger, it should not grant rebirth-linking but instead support another weaker karma.
For in the case of the form-brahmas, wholesome deeds of body, speech, and mind other than access-concentration do indeed arise.
And some of those very [mental states] are minor states with three roots, while others are even minor states with two roots.
However, because the gross hindrances have been thoroughly suppressed, those minor states with two roots that produce failure and restoration do not arise for them.
Furthermore, such states belonging to subsequent lives find no opportunity to arise for them. And this applies to various objects as well.

For them, desire or attachment continues to operate; by means of this, even various karmas find the opportunity to ripen, and by means of this, they pass away from there through the doors of the eye and the ear.

Therefore, it should be understood that rather than citing access concentration as the cause here, it is appropriate to state the cause according to the method already described. [This refers to] passing away from a state caused by the three roots of sensual desire.

However, all twenty types of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) may occur. The construction is as follows: the others—those with two roots and those without roots—may occur as ten types of rebirth-linking only within the sense-sphere existences (*kāma-bhava*) following death.

Having thus shown the mode of occurrence of the path-of-vision-transcending consciousnesses (*vīthimutta-citta*) together with the presentation of objects at the moment of rebirth-linking, [the author] now shows it for the period of the life-continuum and in successive existences.
He said, "Thus, etc. "Immediately after the cessation of rebirth-linking" means from the time immediately following the cessation—that is, the dissolution—of the rebirth-linking consciousness.
"That very same consciousness" should be understood as a designation for what is similar to it, just as one says, "those very same medicines.
"Up to the arising of the death-consciousness": here, by the mention of "death," the inclusion of the proximate process-consciousnesses at that time should also be understood.
"When there is no arising of process-thoughts" means when there is no arising of process-thoughts at intervals.
"By way of being a factor of existence" means by way of being the cause for the non-interruption of rebirth-existence (*upapatti-bhava*).

"In that [absence]" means that because material phenomena, which lack the condition of post-nascence (*pacchājāta-paccaya*), reach a state of withering—just like young crops deprived of rainwater—the rebirth-existence [would perish].
"It ceases" means: having become the death-consciousness (*cuticitta*), that very consciousness ceases; this is the connection.
"Proceeding by revolving in due order" means they proceed by revolving in due order until the death-moment of final Nibbāna (*parinibbāna*).
The meaning is that they do not, like in other systems, ever reach a cessation anywhere.

In the *Vibhāvanī*, however, it is stated: “As long as the root of the round has not been completely cut off. The complete cutting off of the root of the round refers to the path of Arahantship. Even beyond that, they continue to proceed until the final Nirvana of the aggregates (*khandhaparinibbāna*).
“Iha” means in this existence. “Iccayaṃ” means “this is thus. The word “iti” has the sense of “beginning with” (*ādiattha*). Just as here, there is rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*)...
The life-continuum (bhavaṅga), adverting (āvajjana), and so forth, as well as the cognitive process (vīthi) and the death-consciousness (cuti)—this is the continuity of consciousness that proceeds.
Likewise, in another existence, this continuity of consciousness revolves, beginning with the rebirth-linking life-continuum; the meaning is that it proceeds while thus revolving.
Now, for the sake of insight, the path, the fruit, and Nibbāna, [there follows] the analysis, the proceeding, and the synthesis of consciousness and mental factors.

They are established. To demonstrate that meaning, he spoke this verse. Therein, "having reflected" (*paṭisaṅkhāya*) means having known again and again by means of insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*), which is termed reflection. "This" (*etaṃ*) refers to the aforementioned method of the differentiation and occurrence of mind and mental factors.
"Unstable" (*adhuvam*) means impermanent. "Having attained" (*adhigantvā*) means having acquired by means of the knowledge of the four paths, which is termed attainment.
"Having realized. "The state" (*pada*) refers to *nibbāna* with residue remaining. "Awakened ones" (*budhā*) means the wise.

Because they have thoroughly severed the bond known as the "affection of craving"—which adheres to the aforementioned mind and mental factors—leaving not even a trace of underlying tendency (*anusaya*) behind along with all residual defilements, they are called "those who have completely severed the bond of affection. "Tranquil" (*sama*) means they are pacified.

"Samā" means equal [to all] because of this [realization] regarding the heat of the suffering of saṃsāra. "Anupādisesa-nibbānaṃ" refers to Nibbāna without residue. "Essanti" means they will go. "Cirāya" means for a long time.
"Subbatā" means those whose vows consist of the virtues known as the *dhutaṅgas*, which bring about the attainment of what is beautiful;

the meaning is that their conduct is characterized by perfectly purified virtue and effacement (*sallekha*). Having reflected upon this instability, the wise ones have been well-vowed for a long time.
The construction is: "Having attained the deathless state, with the bonds of affection completely severed, they will go to the state of equality.
Thus ends the fourth commentary on the *Abhidhammattha-saṅgaha*, titled the *Paramatthadīpanī*, concerning the section on those who follow the path outside the regular course (*vīthimutta*).
The *Paramatthadīpanī* is completed.
156. Having thus shown the mind and mental factors through two modes of classification, [the author] now treats matter (*rūpa*) as it has been encountered.

He spoke the first verse in order to show this. In that context, "ettāvaṃ" means "that which has this measure. [The phrase] "tena ettavatā" means "by that much. Or rather, this is an indeclinable particle (*nipātapada*).

The word *hi* is used for the purpose of completing the metrical line. "Pabheda" (classification) and "pavatti" (occurrence) are "pabhedappavattiyo. Those things which exist together with these are "sappabhedappavattikā" (possessing classification and occurrence).
By that much, I have [described] the mental states and mental factors (*cittacetasikadhammā*) together with their classifications and occurrences.
The construction is: "Now, matter (rūpa) is being explained. Briefly stating is "enumeration" (samuddesa).
The further analysis of that matter already enumerated is "classification" (vibhāga). That by which matter originates is "origin" (samuṭṭhāna);
[this refers to] kamma and so forth. Parts are called "kalās"; that wherein they come together and enter is a "kalāpa," meaning a collection (piṇḍī).

"By way of the order of their occurrence" means by way of the order of their arising. They are called "great elements" (*mahābhūtāni*) because they exist and manifest as great both in terms of their specific characteristics and their constituent parts.
For these [elements] manifest having taken up the derivative forms (*upādārūpa*), being great indeed even by virtue of their own intrinsic nature.
In the *Vibhāvani* and the *Mahāṭīkā*, however, it is stated:
"By way of the elements together with their constituent materials (*sasambhāra-dhātu-vasena*). That is untenable.

For it cannot be said that this designation for them occurs solely by way of the physical bases together with their constituent materials; nor can it be said [that it occurs] by way of their specific characteristics (*salakkhaṇa*).
Without "greatness" (*mahatta*), their so-called "greatness" could not arise from their constituent parts (*sasambhāra*).

Therefore, that greatness which exists in their continua—whether bound by faculties (*indriya*) or non-faculties (*anindriya*)—in the form of earth and mountains, or in the ocean in the form of fish and turtles, due to their constituent parts, should be understood as being rooted solely in the greatness of their specific characteristics (*salakkhaṇa-mahatta*).
Or, in common parlance, they are called "great elements" (*mahābhūta*) in the sense of being non-deceptive, like a master illusionist.
In the sense of being an inconceivable place for those entering their grasp, they are called *yakkhas* and so forth; or, in the sense of being deceptive, they are called *yakkhinīs*.
Precisely in that sense, because these [great elements] are similar to them, they are "possessed by great beings" (*mahābhūtāvi*), and thus they are "great elements" (*mahābhūtāni*).
Furthermore, the derivation is equally appropriate in both cases: "in these there are great things that have come into being" (*mahantāni abhūtāni*) or "great wonders" (*mahantāni abbhutāni*).
In the *Vibhāvanī*, however, after treating the *yakkhinī* separately as a mere simile, it is stated:

"Because they deceive beings by means of seeing the forms of attractive men and women and so forth—just like *yakkhinīs* and the like who deceive beings with their charming colors and shapes—therefore, great unrealities exist within these. [176]
It has been stated, “the great elements (mahābhūtāni). That does not agree with the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā).

For in the Commentary, in the detailed explanation of the phrase “because of the commonality of the great elements,” it is said that three great elements—the illusionist, the male spirit (yakkha), and the female spirit (yakkhinī)—are mentioned.
In the expression “of the four great elements,” the genitive case is used in the sense of the accusative. “Derived from” (upādāya):
"Depending on the firm"—this is the remainder of the reading (*pāṭhaseso*). Or rather, the compound word should be understood as "derived matter" (*upādāya-rūpaṃ*).
However, in the *Vibhāvani*, it is stated:
"Matter that arises depending [on the primary elements] is derived matter. That [definition] is not appropriate here.
Indeed, in this reading, no instance of the absence of the letter *y* is seen anywhere. For thus it is stated in the *Mūlaṭīkā*:

"It takes hold of (*upādāyati*) and depends upon (*nissayati*), therefore it is *upādāyaṃ*. It is also said that it is 'form' (*rūpaṃ*) itself. "It makes manifest (*pathayati*), therefore it is *pathavī*. The meaning is:

"It stands forth (*pakkhāyati*) and presents itself (*upaṭṭhāti*) by way of being the foundation for co-nascent forms. It is also called *pathavī* because it arises (*jāyati*) as something broad and great (*puthu mahantī*).
It is praised in various ways because it serves as the foundation for all the constituent parts of material form.

It is called *pathavī* (earth) because it is praised through various descriptive terms of its qualities, such as "this is their foundation (*adhiṭṭhāna*), their support (*patiṭṭhāna*), the site (*vatthu*), the earth (*bhūmi*), the element (*bhūta*)," and so forth.

That very same thing, in the sense of being devoid of a sentient being or a soul (*nisatta-nijīva*), is an *dhātu* (element); thus it is the earth-element (*pathavī-dhātu*). It pervades (*āpeti*) the co-nascent material phenomena by spreading throughout them.
It remains, it nourishes, and it thoroughly develops and increases them; thus it is *āpo*.
Or, having prevented them from being scattered, it protects them intensely (*bhuso*); or, as if drinking and savoring them, it gathers and consolidates them;
thus it is *āpo*. That very element is the *āpodhātu*. Among co-nascent phenomena, it shines forth as if with a state of sharpness.
It illuminates, or it sharpens and strengthens; or it ripens and heats—that is *tejo*.

That itself is the element (*dhātu*), thus it is the fire element (*tejodhātu*). It blows or moves, causing the aggregate of primary elements (*bhūtasaṅghāṭa*) to go to another location by way of being the cause for its arising in that other place—that is *vāyo*.
Or, it is called *vāyo* because it carries the co-nascent phenomena (*sahajātadhamma*), keeping them from falling.
The element of motion (*vāyodhātu*) is what is called "space" (*soeva dhātu*). In this context, earth has the characteristic of hardness;
water has the characteristic of cohesion; fire has the characteristic of heat; and wind has the characteristic of distension. Here it might be asked:
Why is earth said to have the characteristic of hardness? Is it not also sometimes soft? True, it is; however, even when it is soft, it is so only in relation to the other three elements.
It is only as "hard" that it comes to be reckoned. However, it is only by depending upon one another that there arises the notion, "this is soft" and "this is hard.
For this very reason, softness and hardness lack any fixed status, just like length and shortness.
For even that which has become soft, having reached a state even softer than before, is called "hard"; and even that which is hard, having reached a state even harder, is called "soft."
"Born. Water is said to have the characteristic of cohesion (*ābandhana*). If it is asked:

"Since that [cohesion] is excessive in natural water, would it follow that natural water is merely bound and solidified? No; because it is very weak there in relation to the earth that is to be cohered.
However, wherever earth is powerful, there it coheres more strongly. It has the characteristic of heat (*uṇhatta*).
It is called "heat" (*tejo*). If it is argued that, this being so, coldness itself could not be heat, we say: no.
That which heats, burns, ripens, and brings about a state of transformation is what is called "warmth. And coldness likewise heats, ripens, and brings about that very state of transformation.
As it is said in the *Mūlaṭīkā*: "Coldness is indeed heat; for it is seen to ripen coldness during times such as the onset of snowfall."

Thus it is said. Wind is defined as having the characteristic of distension (*vitthambhana*). If it is argued that this [characteristic] is not found in solid and rigid things such as stone pillars, it is not so;
for there, the earth element, having obtained the distension provided by the wind co-arisen with itself, proceeds having attained strength and greater stability.
It is called "eye" (*cakkhu*) because it sees (*cakkhati*); it makes known (*ācikkhati*) the even and the uneven.
Because it is rooted in that [ignorance] for one who does not know the even and the uneven. Or, it relishes form (*rūpa*), because it does not reject the forms that come into its range;
the meaning is that it discerns them. It hears, thus it is the ear (*sota*). They hear or are heard by means of this, thus it is the ear. It smells, thus it is the nose (*ghāna*).
They smell or are smelled by means of this, thus it is the nose. Taste is called "life" (*jīvita*) because it is the sign of life.

It is called the *jivhā* because it hankers after that [taste] due to its inclination toward it. Alternatively, it is the *jivhā* because it carries (*vahati*) life, or because they carry and maintain it by providing the sustenance for life.
"Life" (*jīvi*) refers to either victory or defeat; it is the *jivhā* because it carries or conveys both of these by means of it.
This is the tongue together with its constituent parts. As it has been said:
"For when a man is born, a sharp sword is born in his mouth, with which he cuts himself by uttering ill-spoken words.

Here, however, because it functions as their companion, it is called the "tongue" as a representative of sensitive matter (*pasāda-rūpa*). It is also [the seat] of the loathsome things such as hair and so forth, and of evil states.

The body (*kāya*) is so called because it is the source of arising (*āyo-uppattiṭṭhāna*). It is the "body with its constituent parts" (*sasambhārakāya*). However, in this context, what is intended is specifically the sensitive matter (*pasāda-kāya*) that accompanies it.

They are called "sensitive" (*pasāda*) because they are clear (*pasīdanti*). Alternatively, they are called "sensitive" because the signs of objects, such as the lunar disk and so forth, become clearly visible in their own form there, as if sinking into them;
thus they are like the surface of a perfectly polished mirror.

These are born of karma (*kammaja-maṇḍā*). However, these five—the sensitive matter of the primary elements (*bhūta-pasāda*) originating from karma based on causes such as the desire to see—should be understood as the sensitivity of the eye and so forth, characterized by their capacity to strike against visible forms and other objects.

Among these, the eye first resides within a very small opening, the size of a louse’s head, in the center of the black circle (*kaṇhamaṇḍala*) which is itself surrounded by a white circle (*setamaṇḍala*).

The body [of the eye] arises and remains pervading the seven layers of skin and the seven layers of the eyeball, like oil spread over the area of the visible mandala that serves as its physical basis.
The ear remains pervading the area within the ear canal, which is thickened with fine, thin, tawny hair and shaped like a finger-ring.
The nose remains pervading the area within the nostrils, shaped like a goat’s hoof.
It remains. The tongue, together with its constituent parts, remains covering the area in the middle of the tongue that has the shape of the tip of a lotus petal.
As for the body, it is like a large cotton pad filled with oil and placed upon a heating element;
it consists of the tips of the hair, the openings of the pores, the tips of the nails, the dry skin, and the rest of the entire physical frame.
"Remaining pervading" means that those five [elements], according to their respective roles, establish themselves as the bases and doors for the consciousnesses of the five sense-bases.
Furthermore, among them, each one assists the others through four functions: supporting, binding, maturing, and moving.
This is just as a prince has four nurses whose duties are holding, bathing, dressing, and playing with him.
"By means of bathing, adorning, and fanning"—thus the temperature, consciousness, and nutriment support it, just as the father, elder brother, and elder sister do for a prince.
And vitality protects it well, just as a world-renowned physician, honored by the king, does for that same prince.
Furthermore, beauty and the other [qualities] attend upon it, just as [attendants do] for him.
The ministers’ sons were like co-born companions to the khattiya prince. However, because the mind of sentient beings is diverse, their perception is diverse due to the diversity of the mind;
perception is diverse due to the diversity of craving; karma is diverse due to the diversity of craving;
the primary elements produced by karma are diverse due to the diversity of karma; and due to the diversity of the primary elements...

These sensitivities are diverse; they are dissimilar to one another. Although all are equally the essence of sensitivity, some are capable of receiving only the impact of visible forms, not of sounds and so forth;
others are capable of receiving only sounds and so forth, not of visible forms.
Therefore, their unmixed nature—both in relation to one another and in relation to other types of matter—should be understood by way of their specific characteristics.
It is called *rūpa* because it manifests (*rūpayati*). Having attained a particular color, it makes manifest the state that has entered the heart;

or alternatively, the meaning is that it manifests whatever is even or uneven by its very nature. It is called *sadda* because it flows (*sappati*), that is, it becomes something cognizable by the ear-consciousness.
Or it is called *sadda* because it sounds (*saddayati*); the meaning is that it declares various meanings or its own basis. Or it is *sadati*.

It is called *sadda* (sound) because it is forgotten (*vissarati*) and spreads (*vippharati*) in this or that direction or place in an instant. It is called *gandha* (odor) because it causes one to smell (*gandhayati*); the meaning is that it makes itself known through its own substratum.
It is called *go* (wind) because it goes (*gacchati*). It is called *gandha* because it is borne by that [wind].

It is called *rasa* (taste) because it is tasted (*rasīyati*) or relished (*assādīyati*). Or, it is called *rasa* because they taste it or relish it. It is called *phoṭṭhabba* (the tangible) because it is touched (*phusīyati*). And here, "touching" refers to...
It should be understood that there is both friction together with *pasāda* [sensory sensitivity] and resistance with those things belonging to other groups.
Since neither of these two exists in the water element (*āpo-dhātu*), it is said to be "devoid of the water element. But why does it not exist in that [element]?
Is it not the case that coldness or fluidity is perceived through touch? It is replied: Coldness is indeed fire (*tejo*), not water. If...

For it would then be water itself. Even in molten, heated liquid metal, coolness would have to be found; for that liquid is composed of water. But this is not possible. Therefore, it is indeed fire and not water.
Furthermore, it is understood from the fact that cold and heat do not occur together in a single aggregate, and from their instability, like the near and far shores.
For heat does not occur together with a mass of cold, nor does cold occur together with a mass of heat.
In whatever location the perception of cold was previously established, when something colder than that arrives later, the perception of heat is established in that very same place again.

The same principle applies to the previous perception of heat as well. Likewise, when the heat is weak, the perception of cold is established; when the cold is weak, the perception of heat is established.

Furthermore, water, having become liquid in nature, is apprehended through contact; even in cases such as a lump of iron, that which acts as a binder would likewise be apprehended only through contact.

This being so, just as the other three elements among them serve as objects for bodily pleasure and pain individually, without depending on one another, so too would this [element] serve as an object for bodily pleasure and pain individually, without the others.
It may indeed be the object itself; however, it does not [arise] as such.

For when bodily pleasure or pain arises for those who touch those iron balls and so forth, it arises either by way of their smoothness or hardness, or by way of coldness or heat, or by way of the internal support being weak or firm—and not otherwise.
Therefore, in the preceding section, there are three...

Just as one might perceive the shape—long, short, and so forth—of various holes or gaps after first touching the primary elements or seeing their color, with a subsequently purified mental consciousness-stream; or just as one perceives a fire-brand wheel at night;

so too, having first touched the earth itself—the three elements that are accompanied by fluidity, melted, and soft—or indeed the earth alone, with a subsequently purified mental consciousness-stream.
They know the state of being separate and the state of not being moistened. Even so, those who know by touching it think only "this," for they are knowers without distinction.
*Gocara* is the place where cattle frequently roam; here it is called *gocara* because it resembles such a place.
Or, "go" here refers to the sense-faculties, such as the eye; these, having been presided over by consciousness—
They move within these; they move, proceed, and strike against them, thus they are called "objects" (*gocara*).

It is precisely these that are spoken of here as "the form of the object" (*gocararūpa*) by bringing them together into a unity. Furthermore, these five—form and so forth—should be understood as having the characteristic of resistance (*paṭighana-lakkhaṇa*) respectively in the case of the eye and the other [senses].
"Female" (*itthī*) refers to the pentad of aggregates (*khandhapañcaka*) established in a feminine form.

That phenomenon (*dhamma*) by whose power it is so established and proceeds is "femininity" (*itthabhāva*); this is "femaleness" (*itthatta*). "Male" (*purisa*) refers to the pentad of aggregates established in a masculine form.
The rest is exactly as previously stated. In that context, there is the female characteristic (*liṅga*), the female sign (*nimitta*), and the female nature (*kutta*).
Femininity (*itthatta*) is the characteristic that constitutes the causal state for feminine appearance, feminine marks, feminine gestures, and feminine deportment.

Masculinity (*purisatta*) is the characteristic that constitutes the causal state for masculine marks, masculine signs, masculine gestures, and masculine deportment. In this context, "mark" (*liṅga*) refers to the primary constituent, the general configuration;

"sign" (*nimitta*) refers to the secondary constituents, the minor details of configuration; "gesture" (*kutta*) refers to specific activities such as playfulness and grace; and "deportment" (*ākappa*) refers to—
The modification of form consists of such things as walking and so forth. All these are merely specific modes of activity within the five aggregates (*pañcakkhandha*).

It is these that are called "gender" (*liṅga*) in the treatises on grammar. And it is by virtue of these that people perceive: "This is indeed a woman, not a man," or "This is indeed a man, not a woman.
For in this context, the very state of being indistinct in shape and so forth is, in its actual meaning, what constitutes femininity and masculinity.

There is also the state of being devoid of both [sexes], which is neuterhood (*napuṃsakatā*). And this is indeed seen accordingly in words designated as syllables and phrases, as well as in the meanings of those words.

Therefore, it should be understood that the establishment of femininity, masculinity, and neuterhood occurs even by way of figurative application (*pariyāya*) in places devoid of sense faculties, such as trees, and in the meanings of words such as "tree."
[178] As for what is stated in the *Vibhāvani*,
"The female organ is the female characteristic (*itthiliṅga*)," that is not correct.
For nowhere in the Canon (*pāḷi*) or the Commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) is the word *liṅga* seen to be commonly used for the sexual organ in the same way as the word *nimitta*.
[179] And as for that which is stated there, namely, "the female shape and the female appearance," that too is not correct.
For the word *ākappa* (appearance) is not as commonly seen or well-known in the sense of "shape" (*saṇṭhāna*) as the word *liṅga* (gender/sign). As for the rest stated there:
Whatever does not agree with the commentary is nevertheless consistent through that particular method.

It is called *bhāva* because sounds and cognitions such as "this is a woman" or "this is a man" arise (*bhavanti*) or proceed (*pavattanti*) in the continuum of aggregates associated with that [gender];

or because gender-marks and so forth become manifest (*bhavanti*) or appear (*pātubhavanti*) in the continuum of aggregates associated with that; or because it exists (*bhāvo*) when this [gender] is present.
"Of such a form" (*evaṃrūpaṃ*) means its essential nature (*bhāvarūpaṃ*). It is called "heart" (*hadayaṃ*) because by means of it sentient beings accomplish this or that purpose or non-purpose.

Or else, it is called "heart" because from it sentient beings discharge or release various kinds of [mental] states. Or else, it is called "heart" because sentient beings carry it about and cherish it like their own life, protecting it with care.
They dwell and reside within it; [it is the locus of] mind and mental factors...
The "basis" (*vatthu*) is that wherein the mental phenomena (*dhammā*) reside. That which is both the heart and the basis is the "heart-basis" (*hadayavatthu*).

The materiality of the basis (*vatthurūpa*) has the characteristic of being the support for the two elements [of cohesion and heat]. It should be understood that it exists within the interior of the heart-enclosure, pervading a measure of half a *pasata* of blood.
However, in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*, this was not mentioned for the sake of preserving the diversity of the teaching; rather, it is found only in the *Paṭṭhāna*.
It has been said: "The physical basis (vatthu) is a condition for wholesome aggregates by way of the support-condition (nissaya-paccaya).
The physical basis is a condition for unwholesome aggregates by way of the support-condition," and so forth. In this context, there is no other thing called a "basis" apart from these six bases.
Furthermore, among those [six], the first five are not even supports for the wholesome and so forth. Therefore, by virtue of their being supports...
In that regard, it is established that what is called "base" (*vatthu*) is simply one distinct base-form (*vatthurūpa*).

However, in the *Vibhāvanī*, because the reading "that form depending upon which... was cited, there arises the possibility of a confusion with the general category of "form" (*rūpasāmañña*); therefore, in order to clarify this:

It is called "yutti" (reasoning). However, in the *Paṭṭhāna*, because it is stated by distinguishing [the term] with the name "vatthu" (basis) in many instances that are not shared with others, it should be understood that the prefix [“sa-”] is indeed absent.

That by which co-nascent phenomena live is "jīvita" (life-faculty). By virtue of its sovereignty (*ādhipacca*) over their living, it is the "indriya" (faculty), meaning the lord (*issara*) among them.
It is called a faculty (*indriya*) because it exercises mastery (*karoti*). Because it is both life and a faculty, it is the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*).
The life-faculty has the characteristic of maintaining those things that have arisen together with it.

For just as water-lilies and other plants produced from seeds continue to live for a long time even after the seed has perished, being maintained by water; even so, the material phenomena born of karma (*kammajarūpa*), though produced by karma, persist even when that karma has ceased.
Sustained by the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*), they continue in their continuity for a hundred years, a thousand years, an eon (*kappa*), or even sixteen thousand eons;

for material phenomena devoid of the life-faculty cannot be said to "live. Indeed, these [mental states] arise through a single moment of consciousness, or through temperature (*utu*), or through nutriment (*āhāra*).
When that [cause] ceases, they cease; they do not persist for even a mere moment beyond that.

They are unable to connect the continuity. For among these, the present continuity of mind-born material phenomena is delimited by a single cognitive series, a single impulsion-moment, or a single attainment-moment.
Furthermore, that of temperature-born and nutriment-born material phenomena is delimited by a single similar temperature or nutriment.
However, for kamma-born material phenomena, there is no such thing as a separate present continuity.
For them, the present exists only as a duration delimited by a single existence (*ekabhava*). If this is so, how is it with immaterial phenomena (*arūpadhamma*)?

They exist only as living beings through their connection with life-force (*jīvita*). Even though this is the case, their continuity-present (*santatipaccuppanna*) is nevertheless perceived. It is said:
among immaterial phenomena, first, those that are results (*vipāka*) are similar to matter born of karma (*kammajarūpa*). For even these, when absent—
In the arising of a cognitive process (*vīthicitta*), they will indeed continue to proceed by way of a single continuity (*ekasantati*) even for the duration of one’s life.

However, as for the others, they arise because a particular object has come into range; once that object has ceased, even in its absence, many mental continuities with that same object (*tadārammaṇa*) continue to proceed through the power of pervading the course of life.
Moreover, this continues until the final Nibbāna of the aggregates (*khandha-parinibbāna*).
This same point may also be stated by way of the mental continuity proceeding without interruption through the connection of immediate condition (*anantarapaccaya*).
For it has been said: "Ignorance is the head of the defilements; the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) is the head of the process.
Furthermore, in the *Vibhāvani*:
For nutriment-born and other types of phenomena, nutriment and the rest are the cause both for their arising and for their persistence. Why? Because they exist at that very moment.
However, for karma-born phenomena, karma is the cause only for their arising, not for their persistence. Why? Because it is absent at that moment.
But because they are sustained by the life-faculty (jīvita), the persistence of those phenomena during that moment is established; it is with this intention that it was said:
“[It is argued: ‘For [kamma] is the sustainer by way of being the cause for the occurrence of conascent states that each abide for only a moment.
For their stability does not have kamma alone as its cause; just as nutriment and so forth are for those things born of nutriment and so forth, kamma is absent at that very moment.
This is not tenable. This is not correct.

For the so-called "momentary duration" (*khaṇaṭṭhiti*) of phenomena depends solely upon the co-nascent conditions (*sahajātapaccaya*) contained within a single group (*ekakalāpa*); it does not depend upon the producing conditions (*janakapaccaya*) contained within various groups.

Otherwise, just as the accumulations (*upacaya*) and continuities (*santati*) found at the moment of arising are stated in the Canon to have a specific origin, the aging (*jaratā*) found at the moment of duration would likewise have to be stated in the Canon to have some origin. Furthermore, momentary duration is established by its very nature (*sabhāvasiddha*).
For it is not the case that arisen phenomena, failing to remain fully established in their own moments due to a deficiency of conditions, break up prematurely;
nor is it the case that they persist for longer than their natural duration due to an abundance of conditions.
Therefore, although nutriment and the rest provide support for the stability of the moment, and life-force maintains it, the subsequent continuity of matter remains powerful.
They support and preserve [the continuity] solely for the sake of its ongoing occurrence. "Not for the sake of momentary persistence" means:
by this much it is established that for all things, what is called "momentary persistence" does not depend on the body of living beings or on life itself.
However, if it were said with reference to the continuity of the stream (*santati-pavatti*) alone, then it would be appropriate. This is also stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*.

Even though there are procedures characterized by preservation and so forth, the statement that "it preserves those three properties at the very moment they exist" implies that it persists according to its own continuity (*santati*).
Having reflected thus, it should be understood. Furthermore, this [heat] remains pervading the entire appropriated body along with the digestive fire (*pācaka-aggi*).
That which is made into a mouthful is "edible food" (*kabaḷīkāra*); it is so called because it is brought in (eaten).
It is called *āhāra* because it is swallowed (*ajjhoharīyati*). Since it is both "morsel-like" (*kabaḷīkāra*) and "nutriment" (*āhāra*), it is "edible nutriment" (*kabaḷīkārāhāra*).
There is also a reading: "morsel-like nutriment" (*kabaḷīkāro āhāro*). This should be understood as a term that includes its basis.

Alternatively, it is called *āhāra* because it carries (*harati*) the personal existence (*attabhāva*) of beings who subsist on edible nutriment, bringing them through the course of life. [This refers to] things to be chewed, eaten, and so forth, which constitute the morsel-like.

Because it depends on that and is designated as a synonym for that, it is called "edible food" (*kabaḷīkārāhāra*). When this meaning is present, only the nutritive essence (*ojā*) produced [thereby] is obtained.
However, in terms of its actual nature (*atthato*), the nutriment-form (*āhārarūpa*) here is the essence of the nutrient fluid that follows through every limb and member;
it is the support and the producer of strength, dependent upon the primary elements (*bhūta*), and is the most subtle, oily moisture. Therein, that which follows through every limb and member...

"Flavor" (*rasa*) means that the food constituents, having been swallowed and established in the stomach, are separated by the heat of digestion and undergo a fivefold division into flavor and so forth.
Among these, the refined, smooth, light, and oily portion is called "flavor" (*rasa*);

it is what is known in the world as the "flavor element" (*rasadhātu*). By the power of the digestive heat, it rises up from there and follows along the network of flavor-carrying channels (*dhamani-jālā*).
Because it follows and permeates every limb and member throughout the entire body, both below and above, it is called "limb-permeating" (*aṅgamaṅgānusārī*).
Because it provides support and strength as its essential substance, it is called "support-strength-maker" (*upatthambhabalakāro*).
For, merely by being established in the stomach, it generates the supporting strength within the elements of the entire body.
In the *Vibhāvani*, however, the reading is:
“It is called the nutrient-transporting system because it flows from limb to limb. That is a faulty reading.

But that nutriment-form (*āhāra-rūpa*) has the characteristic of supporting the body together with its sense faculties, or else it has the characteristic of nutritive essence (*ojā*). Therein, it arises.

It is called *ojā* because it "produces" (*pasavati*). Alternatively, the prefix *ava-* has the sense of "protecting" (*rakkhaṇa*); and here, protection means specifically "supporting" (*upatthambhana*).

Thus, it is *ojā* because it "protects" (*avati*) and "produces" (*janeti*). What does it protect? Its own supporting basis (*nissayavatthu*). And what does it produce? Matter originated by nutriment (*āhārasamuṭṭhānarūpa*).

Some also say it is *ojā* because it produces matter immediately after its own arising. It is [also defined] by its own nature (*bhāva*), such as hardness and so forth, devoid of any other designation.
Established form (*siddha-rūpa*) is form that possesses its own intrinsic nature (*sabhāva-rūpa*).

Form accompanied by the characteristics of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhata-lakkhaṇa*), such as arising and impermanence, is form with characteristics (*salakkhaṇa-rūpa*). Form produced by conditions such as karma through a direct process is produced form (*nipphanna-rūpa*).

Form endowed with the characteristic of being subject to change (*ruppana-lakkhaṇa*) in its primary sense is actual form (*rūpa-rūpa*), just as "suffering-as-suffering" (*dukkha-dukkha*) is "internal-as-internal" (*ajjhatta-ajjhatta*).

Having applied the three characteristics beginning with impermanence by means of that which is associated with the characteristics of the conditioned, matter that is fit for contemplation is "contemplative matter" (*sammasana-rūpa*).
It is called "space" (*ākāsa*) because it manifests (*ākāsati*) and makes manifest (*pakāsati*) various collections of substances or groups of matter individually and abundantly.
In the sense of being devoid of a sentient being and devoid of a soul, it is an "element" (*dhātu*). An element reckoned as space is thus "the space-element" (*ākāsadhātu*). [It is] all around.

It is a "delimitation" (*pariccheda*) because it cuts away from all sides those things that have become part of a cluster, making them unmixed with other clusters and preventing them from attaining unity.
Or else, it is delimited by those very things; or it is placed separately in the middle without being joined to itself or others;
or it is merely a gap or opening between them. It is not a single, independent phenomenon possessing its own intrinsic nature (*sabhāva-dhamma*) accompanied by arising.

Nor is it a member of any material group; this is the delimitation. For the material phenomena characterized by change, although they are non-essential (asabhāva) states, are nonetheless members of their respective material groups because they are manifest within them.
This [phenomenon], however, being entirely released from those material groups and existing externally to them, is not a member of any material group whatsoever.
"It does not exist. Furthermore, because it is a non-substantial phenomenon (*asabhāva-dhamma*), it lacks entirely even the figurative sense of being touched by any form;
thus, it is stated in the Canon that "it is untouched by the four great elements.

However, in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), regarding the bases of dense masses and lumps, there is a mutual touching among the elements belonging to various groups, which possess the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of resistance and tangibility.

Having accepted that "it exists," it is said that the "unblemished space" (*ajaṭākāsa*) is "unimpeded by the four great elements" (*asaṃphuṭṭhaṃ catūhi mahābhūtehi*), meaning it is not touched by these [elements].
However, in the *Ṭīkā*, this description is not a description of unblemished space, but rather a description of the delimiting form (*paricchedarūpa*).
And that [delimiting form] should be understood as a solid mass within the very basis [of the body]; and among those [bases], there is no such thing as non-impediment by the elements.
Therefore, the non-pervasion of primary elements (bhūta) by one another is precisely their failure to attain unity.
With the intention that "in this context, non-contact would be appropriate," it is said that "non-pervasion is non-contact.

In terms of meaning, however, the characteristic of delimitation (pariccheda-rūpa) is the property of spatial boundary (antarāla-dhamma), which consists in the limitation of primary elements belonging to distinct groups. It is the characteristic of the delimitation of matter.
However, that which, by means of a moving bodily action, makes known and clearly demonstrates to people standing before one both oneself and the intention of the person possessing that body—
that very action is understood by those people through that bodily action— is called *kāyaviññatti* (bodily intimation). That which,
by means of the sound of a vocal organ being uttered, [makes known] oneself and the person possessing that [organ]...
It makes known the intention of a person to people standing within the range of hearing, and it is itself understood by those people through that vocal factor;

this is called *vacīviññatti* (vocal intimation). Alternatively, it is called *viññatti* because by means of it people make themselves known, or because the minds of people are mutually made known to one another.
It occurs in the body, which consists of the primary elements and the limbs and parts derived from them.
Intimation is bodily intimation. Or, the body—consisting of the act of touching—is itself the intimation; thus it is bodily intimation.
Intimation that occurs through speech, which is defined as sound born of mind, is vocal intimation. Or, speech—consisting of the act of touching—is itself the intimation; thus it is vocal intimation.
In this context, for one who performs any movement of a limb by means of the mind, that respective limb becomes steady and sustained.
Moving the various limbs, the groups of mental-velocity aggregates (cittajavātakalāpa), which are known to follow each limb, arise filling that respective limb.

As they arise, whether in this way or that, they do not arise without having arisen; rather, by the power of the co-nascent wind-body (copanakāya) associated with those mental-velocity aggregates, all those aggregates arise directed precisely toward the intended direction.
This alteration of form, known as the collection of bodily movements, is called "bodily intimation" (*kāyaviññatti*).
Indeed, this bodily intimation is like a helmsman, and the body is like a ship.

For just as a helmsman, standing at the stern of a ship and firmly grasping a large rudder, steers it through the river current and directs the entire great vessel toward the desired direction—whether upstream or downstream—so too does this bodily intimation direct the body.
Or it allows one to go in that direction. This should be understood in the same way.

For intimation (*viññatti*), lasting for only a single moment of consciousness, is obtained precisely at the base of those [great elements]; by acting thus, it directs them toward the intended direction, and so it is like a pilot.
And in this regard, as for what is stated in the Commentary: "In a single impulsive cognitive series (*javana-vīthi*), among the seven..."
Among the javanas, the air element produced by the first javana is able to stiffen and sustain the material body co-nascent with itself, but it is not able to move it from one place to another.
The same principle applies to the second and subsequent javanas as well.
However, the air element produced by the seventh consciousness [of the javana series] [is able to move] the air element produced by the six preceding consciousnesses.

It is said that having obtained the condition of support (*upatthambhana-paccaya*), one is able to stiffen, sustain, move, and cause the physical body (*rūpakāya*)—which is co-nascent with oneself—to advance. Regarding the phrase "I am advancing":
when thousands of impulsion moments (*javana*) are occurring as one exerts the body, it is at whichever moment the reaching of another location—which is termed "movement"—arises, that [moment]...
This was said with intentional meaning (*sandhāya*). For movement does not arise through a few moments of cognitive speed (*javana*).

If it were to arise [in that way], then a speed greater than that of all others would be perceived, just like the travel by supernormal power (*iddhi*) of those possessing such powers. Why? Because even within the duration of a single moment of consciousness (*ekaccharakkhaṇe*), there occurs the arising of many hundreds of thousands of millions of moments.
And this point will be explained further on in the investigation into the arising of syllables (*akkharuppatti*).
"It will become manifest. Therefore, it should be understood that in the preceding sections, only stiffening and supporting occur.
Furthermore, the simile of the seven pairs of oxen-carts mentioned here is also appropriate for the successive propelling of the air-elements arising in the various cognitive series (*javana-vīthi*).
For instance, in the continuity of material phenomena born of a moving consciousness:
Even the aggregates of temperature-born materiality that have come into being proceed as if accompanied by intimation, possessing those very shapes, with momentum and expansion.
Therefore, even during the moments of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) in between various successions of impulsion (javana), movement such as advancing and so forth certainly occurs.
And these material phenomena produced from the four origins (catusamuṭṭhānika) proceed as a single, continuous stream.
It should be understood that within the domain of one [material group], the others follow it entirely as if they were co-originated;

thus, when the mind-born [group] moves, the others move as well. Here, "movement" refers to the successive arising of each subsequent aggregate of material groups in another location from the location where the preceding ones arose, in the manner of their established arrangement.

This should be understood. For there is no movement of material or immaterial phenomena from one location to another, even by the measure of a hair-tip, without ceasing at the place where they have arisen.
Otherwise, their momentary nature, their inactive nature, and their lack of mastery over themselves would not exist.
This applies to whatever vocal expression one makes, within the acquired earth element located in the throat and other such places.

Through the conjunction of the earth element born of mind—which resides in the regions of the moving throat and so forth—and what is termed the "act of articulation" (*ṭhānakaraṇasannipāta*), there arises a sound born of mind termed "verbal utterance.

By means of the modification of form co-arising with that [sound], it assumes various specific phonetic qualities according to the speaker's intention; and by means of this, it makes manifest the respective meanings for those who hear it.
A specific combination of syllables, consisting of words and phonemes, is perceived. This modification of form, designated as vocal speech, is called *vacīviññatti* (vocal intimation).

However, in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated that "vocal intimation" refers to a certain modification of form which serves as the condition for the impact of the derived matter (*upādinnarūpa*) of the earth element produced by consciousness. In this regard:

"Being the condition for the striking of what is clung-to" means that it is the condition for the occurrence of a specific sound in dependence upon the striking together with the earth-element that is clung-to, which is either born of karma or consists of the fourfold primary elements.

Furthermore, the condition for the striking itself must be a particular part of the body that constitutes a modification, such as a moving region of the throat and so forth. And these two modifications are unmixed.
"It should be understood by making [the contact]. Herein, the function of the mind-born earth elements is to strike together with the appropriated earth elements.

However, the method of striking in such a way that the desired syllable is produced—whether by striking them exactly as they are or otherwise—is the function of bodily intimation (*kāyaviññatti*). This refers to the sounds that arise simultaneously with that striking.
The function of vocal intimation (*vacī-viññatti*) is simply the manifestation of various colors.
The earth element derived from kamma (*upādinnaka-pathavī*) is like the surface of a water-pot; the mind-born earth element (*cittaja-pathavī*) is like the hand holding the weapon;
bodily intimation (*kāya-viññatti*) is like the movement of the hand; vocal intimation is like the modification of sound; and it is like the various distinctions of sound produced by the water-pot.
Regarding "the distinction of various colors": here, the mind that arises thinking, "I shall speak this" or "I shall speak that," produces eight types of material phenomena (*rūpa*).
Within those, the earth element produced by the mind arises while actually striking the clung-to (*upādinnaka*) matter.
Simultaneously with that striking of the elements, sound arises; thus [it is said] that it is produced by the preceding mind.
It was stated that this [mental state] does not even have the function of providing support (*upatthambhana*).
That statement should be understood as referring to the specific occasion among hundreds of successive impulsion-moments (*javana*) when a clearly manifest syllable occurs.

For it is for this very reason that the *Mūla-ṭīkā* states: "There is no function of support, because the striking [of the object] is powerful by means of the mind itself through acquired habituation."

It has been said. Here, by the phrase "having obtained practice" (*laddhāsevana*), he shows that in the prior stage there was an attainment of practice through various sequences of impulsion-moments (*javana-vīthi*).

This is because it is intended that even the first impulsion-moment possesses the quality of having obtained practice. Furthermore, it cannot be understood that a single syllable becomes fully manifest through a mere single instance of impulsion.
Why? Because that [single instance] lasts for only one or two moments of time (*acchara-khaṇa*).

Because it must be spoken at the proper time, and because it is possible for many hundreds of thousands of impulsion-sequences (*javana-vīthi*) to occur within the duration of a single finger-snap. And it has been said:
"A short vowel is measured by one *matta*; a long vowel is pronounced with two *mattas*;
a protracted (*gīta*) vowel should be known as three *mattas*; and consonants are half a *matta* each."
And in the *Milindapañha*, it is demonstrated that even the seeds of rice in more than seven hundred cartloads do not approach even a fraction of a single moment of consciousness that has arisen;
they do not approach even a part of a fraction. Furthermore, while one is pronouncing a single syllable, the activity of the pronouncing consciousness is indeed discernible for that entire duration.
And yet, in the ultimate sense, one does not think, "I am pronouncing this very same sound."

One can utter the words "I hear" only after having determined [the object]; likewise, even for one who determines it thus, the utterance and hearing of sounds occur as a succession of many hundreds of thousands [of moments].

However, the conceit that there is "only one" [sound] should be understood as arising because [the process] is concealed by the density of the collection (*samūhaghana*) and the density of the continuity (*santatighana*).
The rest here is as stated regarding bodily intimation (*kāyaviññatti*).

"By which [it] should be understood according to what is possible. And here, in such instances as "he makes known by body" or "he makes known by speech," the word *viññatti* has the sense of making known (*bodhana*).
In such instances as "Sudinna made his request three times" (*tikkhattuṃ viññāpeti*), it has the sense of proceeding (*pavattana*). But here, both meanings are appropriate.
For this being so, in all those cases—whether they involve the movement of a limb of the body or a limb of speech—the desire to make another understand is present.
It should be understood that it is obtained through the intimation that sets [the action] in motion.

However, in the *Mūlaṭīkā*, it is stated that even without the performance of approaching and so forth, that mental concomitant modification intimates the intention by the desire to inform another, and because it is itself known, it is "intimation" in both ways;
therein, between the two types of intimation—informing and setting in motion—the former...
Bodily intimation is perceived by the visual consciousness process as the appearance of a moving limb or member,
and subsequently by the pure mind-door impulsion after the moving limb or member has been grasped by the body-consciousness process; likewise,
subsequent verbal intimation is perceived by the ear-consciousness process as the sound being uttered, and subsequently by the pure mind-door impulsion alone.
It is known by the mind-door javana, not by the five-door javana. For that [knowledge] makes known the mind of another person who possesses it only when one knows oneself;
it does not do so when one does not know oneself. Indeed, a "making-known cause" (ñāpaka-hetu) makes known what is to be made known only when it itself knows, not when it does not know.
