And this being the case, having seen or touched a movement of a limb of the body...
For those who, upon hearing a sound, understand the various intentions of others—even for animals—the cognition of intimation (*viññatti*) is established.
This is because it is impossible to know an intention without knowing that intimation.
Furthermore, for those who cognize intimation, the knowledge of intention is impossible without knowing the relationship established by prior convention.
They maintain that it is not possible [to grasp the relationship] through a separate prior convention in the interim;

rather, having seen another person moving forward by means of the visual consciousness-process (*cakkhu-viññāṇa-vīthi*) during two successive acts of intimation (*viññatti*), they know both the intimation of moving forward and the thought of moving forward by means of the mental consciousness-process (*mano-viññāṇa-vīthi*).
This same method applies to retreating and so forth. Likewise, regarding another person...

How is it that, having heard through the process of ear-consciousness (*sotaviññāṇa-vīthi*), they know both the intimation of speech (*kathana-viññatti*) and the thought of speaking (*kathana-citta*) by means of the process of mind-consciousness (*manoviññāṇa-vīthi*)?
Having seen another person moving a limb with a lustful mind, they know both the intimation of movement (*calana-viññatti*) and the mind of lust (*rāga-citta*).
Having heard the speech of one who is lustful, they know both the intimation of speech and the mind of lust. This is the method.
"In all bodily and vocal actions": lightness is the state of being light;
malleability is the state of being malleable. "Fit for action" means *kammañña*; the meaning is "suitable for action. The state of being fit for action is adaptability (*kammaññatā*).

The characteristic of matter as lightness is the absence of sluggishness; the characteristic of matter as malleability is the absence of rigidity; the characteristic of matter as adaptability is the state of fitness for action that conforms to bodily activity.
The wieldiness of material form. Although these elements do not abandon one another, they should be understood as unmixed by way of their adverse conditions and their favorable conditions.

For instance, when those who indulge in a temperature, food, or mental activity that is adverse to their own bodies, the elements within the body sometimes disturb the entire body or a portion of the body, particularly...
The water element, known as the "putrid-mouthed serpent," having become fully manifest, makes the body heavy and burdensome, like an unbearable load.
It produces suffering characterized by bodily heaviness during the shifting of postures.

Consequently, the lightness (*lahutā*) of that material form does not function. Furthermore, for those who resort to a temperature or food suitable to their own body, or to mental activity, [the lightness arises].
Thus the disturbance of the elements is stilled; the body becomes light. When changing postures, there is no pain characterized by heaviness in the body.
At that time, that [lightness] occurs. This same method applies to the remaining [elements] as well.
However, by way of distinction, here one should effect the "earth-obsession" known as the "wood-mouthed snake," making the body rigid like dry wood.

They produce hardness. It should be said that they generate a painful state characterized by rigidity and hardness, reaching the point where the various limbs break and shatter during the shifting of postures.

Regarding adaptability (*kammaññatā*), the wind known as the "sword-mouthed snake" becomes an obsession; having rendered the wind unbalanced, it is like a bordering kingdom beset by murderous bandits and thieves.
They cause the body to turn away [from its natural state]; it should be said that there is no such thing as pleasure in any of the postures.
However, it should be understood that the fire element is the root of all of these.
These [elements], moreover, are like the healthy state of one who is free from disease, like the softness of well-polished leather, or like the pliability of well-refined gold.

Because specific characteristics are evident in the transformation of the material body through its change of postures by way of lightness and so forth, it is called "transformative matter" (*vikāra-rūpa*). Accumulation (*caya*) means piling up;
the meaning is that it is produced as a mass. Accumulation from the beginning and further accumulation are "growth" (*upacaya*); the meaning is initial production and subsequent increase.

For this prefix *upa* has the sense of "first," as in the expressions *upaññatta* (proclaimed) and so forth, and it also has the sense of "above" (*upari*), as in *upasitta* (sprinkled above) and so forth.
And it is stated in the *Mūlaṭīkā*: "The prefix *upa* has both the sense of 'first' and the sense of 'above'. Precisely for that reason, it is said in the Pāḷi:

"That which is the accumulation (*ācaya*) of the bases (*āyatana*), that is the accumulation of matter (*rūpa*). That which is the accumulation of matter, that is the continuity (*santati*) of matter."
It has been said. *Tati* means stretching out or expansion. Alternatively, *tati* means continuity (*santati*), which is a continuous succession.
The meaning is: the occurrence of the sense bases (*āyatana*) as they proceed, by way of filling the course of time.

In that context, for beings born from a womb, the arising of material phenomena at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) is called "accumulation" (*upacaya*) in the sense of being the first production. From that...
Furthermore, from the very first arising of the eye, ear, nose, and tongue until that point, the arising of material phenomena is called "accumulation" (*upacaya*) in the sense of upward growth.
Thereafter, for as long as life lasts, the arising of the fourfold continuity of matter is called "continuity" (*santati*).
For this has been stated in the Commentary: "It is like the time when water rises in a well dug on a riverbank."

Accumulation (*ācaya*) is arising (*nibbatti*). Accumulation is growth (*vaḍḍhi*), like the time when [the body] is fully developed. Continuity (*santati*) is the process of proceeding after having overspread [the body], like the time of walking.
In the *Vibhāvani*, however, it is stated:

"From the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) until the arising of the decads of the eye and so forth—within this interval, the production of material form is called accumulation; from then on, it is called continuity. That too is indeed consistent with that method of explanation.

However, for moisture-born and temperature-born beings, the arising of material phenomena at the moment of rebirth-linking is called "origination" (*bhinibbatti*) in the sense of first appearance, and "accumulation" (*upacaya*) in the sense of full development;
the arising of material phenomena after that is called "continuity" (*santati*).
Furthermore, even for material phenomena originating from the three [causes], there exists a distinct "present continuity" for each one. And of each of these...
There are three stages each, according to arising (*nibbatti*), growth (*vaḍḍhi*), and occurrence (*pavatti*).

Among these, in each individual continuity (*santati*), the very first arising of the material phenomena that are the head of the continuity is called "arising. The arising of the material phenomena that follow in growth thereafter is called "growth.
When growth has reached its limit and no further increase occurs, the arising that proceeds by way of continuous persistence and maintenance is called "occurrence."
In this context, "accumulation" (*upacaya*) refers to the growth of what has been produced; it is called "continuity in occurrence" (*pavattasantati*).

In brief, however, within all occurrences of material form bound to the faculties and non-faculties in the world, one should understand accumulation and continuity by observing the distinctions in states characterized as being born, growing, and occurring.
Herein is the method: just as branches [grow] from trees, grass, and so forth...

Just as leaves, flowers, fruits, and so forth arise at the beginning, having arisen they grow; when their growth is complete, instead of growing further, they proceed by way of continuity and then break up.
Decay (*jarā*) is that by which things age—that is, they undergo the state of being worn out—and thus it is called decay.
That very thing is "the state of decaying" (*jaratā*). That which does not move or shake because of arising, decay, and dissolution is permanent (*nicca*) and unconditioned (*asaṅkhata*).
Dhamma. It is not permanent; it is impermanent, a conditioned dhamma. The state of being impermanent is impermanence (aniccatā), which is disintegration.
However, in the *Vibhāvanī*, it is stated:
"It is 'impermanent' because it should not be pursued as having the nature of permanence and stability. That is not correct.
For the word *nicca* (permanent) is well-known both in the Dispensation and in the world. Here, that very same word is joined with the letter *na* and is thus spoken of as *anicca* (impermanent).

*Lakkhaṇaṃ* (characteristic) means that by which phenomena (*dhammā*) are marked, observed, and determined as "these are conditioned" (*saṅkhata*). The meaning is: it is the sign for knowing the state of being conditioned.
As it is said in the *Aṅguttara Nikāya*: "Bhikkhus, there are these three characteristics of the conditioned in the conditioned. Which three?"
"Three [characteristics] are discerned: arising is discerned, passing away is discerned, and the alteration of that which stands is discerned.

Is it not the case that "birth" (*jāti*) is mentioned in the Canon? Therefore, it was said: "Only the materiality of birth," and so forth, [to address the objection] that it should also be mentioned here.

"Here" refers to the summary of materiality. Birth is the act of being born, the manifestation [of matter]. Or, it is called "birth" because things are born by means of it; it is designated by the names "accumulation" (*upacaya*) and "continuity" (*santati*).

The intended meaning is that it is so because of its connection with the differentiation of states despite being of a single birth. For she (the kamma) first brings about the manifestation of the rebirth-linking material phenomena;
then she fulfills the sense bases that were previously incomplete; and having fulfilled them, she causes them to proceed and continue uninterruptedly for a long duration.
"Even though it is one, it is tenfold" means by way of bringing about a unity through the state of the great elements and so forth.

[It is] one [type], though it has eleven divisions. Having asked, "How does it become twenty-eightfold by way of its own nature (sarūpa)?"—one should understand that the demonstration of the elevenfold [nature] itself by way of its own nature, through the passage beginning with "the primary elements, the sensitive organs, and the objects," is clearly evident because the internal subdivisions have already been stated previously. Therefore he said: "eighteenfold."
The four primary elements, the five sensitive organs, and—by including what was not previously mentioned—the four sense objects as their respective domains;

these constitute the sixteenfold materiality. There are two kinds of existence (bhāva) and one heart-base. Thus, this sixteenfold materiality, together with the materiality of life-faculty and nutriment, becomes eighteenfold;

likewise, there is one delimitation (pariccheda). There are two kinds of intimation (viññatti) and three kinds of transformation (vikāra)—these being included by way of what was not previously mentioned—and fourfold [space].
Regarding the characteristic: the construction is that matter, by its own nature, consists of twenty-eight kinds, including the ten that are "unproduced" (*anipphanna*).

Herein, the latter ten kinds of matter are called "unproduced" because they are not produced by conditions, as they are not found to exist as independent entities by way of their own intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).
Furthermore, these are specifically enumerated and explained separately in the Abhidhamma.
It cannot be said that these [conditioned phenomena] are unapprehendable by way of their own-nature (*sabhāva*) or non-existent from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramattha*),
because they are apprehended through the characteristic of ultimate reality established by the mode of pure phenomena, transcending the mere existence established by conventional usage (*vohāra*).
Otherwise, even unconditioned *nibbāna*, which is devoid of the characteristic of arising, would [likewise be non-existent].
It might be argued that something which is not being apprehended could still exist in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*).

Therefore, it would be more logical to say that these are "unproduced" (*anipphanna*) precisely because they lack the characteristic of arising, rather than because they are not apprehended by way of their own intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).

[The Enumeration of Matter] 157. Furthermore, all this twenty-eight-fold matter that has been enumerated according to its classification is, in the sense of being rootless (*ahetuka*), [to be understood as follows...]
It is of only one kind. It is not twofold according to the distinction between "with cause" and "without cause.

Likewise, it is of only one kind in the sense of being "conditioned," and not twofold according to the distinction between "conditioned" and "unconditioned. Thus, the passage beginning with "And all... was commenced in order to first demonstrate this method of the single kind as it occurs.
In the *Vibhāvani*, however, it is stated:

"Since even the singlefold method (*ekavidhanaya*) is merely an analysis of matter (*rūpavibhāga*), the passage beginning with ‘And all this... was spoken for the purpose of showing the singlefold and other methods regarding the kinds of matter as they were enumerated. This does not accord [with the truth].
For he will say later:—
"They classify [it] according to its internal and other divisions as is appropriate.
By this, it is understood that the classification of matter (*rūpa*) consists precisely of its internal and other such divisions.
In that regard, all matter is indeed rootless (*ahetuka*) by way of its association with roots; not even a single thing is possessed of roots. Something...

The intention is that there is such a classification as "without cause" (ahetuka). The reading "with cause, with taints, conditioned, mundane" (sappaccayaṃ sāsavaṃ saṅkhataṃ lokiyanti) is [incorrect];

rather, "with cause, conditioned, mundane, with taints" (sappaccayaṃ saṅkhataṃ lokiyaṃ sāsavanti) is appropriate, because it is seen so in the Canon (Pāḷi) and because it allows for the occurrence of corresponding pairs.
However, the others, although not following the order of the Canon, do form corresponding pairs.
They are indeed appropriate according to their respective portions. In this context, it is "with conditions" (*sapaccaya*) because it proceeds together with its own producing condition.

It is "conditioned" (*saṅkhata*) because it is produced by coming together through conditions. It is "mundane" (*lokiya*) because it is included within the world itself, which is designated as the five aggregates of clinging.
It is "with taints" (*sāsava*) because it proceeds together with the taints that arise directed toward a self. [This applies to] the continuum of the Akaniṭṭha Brahmā.
Even though form (*rūpa*) is real, it is included in the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) because sensual craving craves it by way of its being an object.
It is "without an object" (*anārammaṇa*) because there is no object whatsoever that has been grasped by itself.

A phenomenon (*dhamma*) which, even if abandoned by another means, remains unabandoned when there is no abandonment of its origin (*samudaya*), because it is certain to arise again—though not yet abandoned.

When that [cause] exists, it is indeed abandoned, because it does not arise again. A phenomenon of such a nature is called "not to be abandoned" because it is not a proper object for the effort of abandonment.
Matter (*rūpa*) is exactly like this; therefore it is said to be "only not to be abandoned.

The meaning is that, because it is not a proper object, it does not admit the effort of abandonment. Alternatively, the meaning is that it cannot be abandoned without the abandonment of its origin (*samudaya*).

"If, monks, form is not yours, abandon it. When it is abandoned by you, that will lead to your welfare, benefit, and happiness for a long time"—how is this to be understood? This too should be seen as spoken with reference to the abandoning of the lust (*rāga*) directed toward its object. As it has been said:

“Rādha, whatever desire, whatever lust, whatever delight, whatever craving there is for form—that you should abandon. In this way, that form will be abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and subject to non-arising in the future.
This method should be understood to apply to other [factors] as well, such as the wholesome and so forth, which are not to be abandoned.

Here, the word “evaṃ” (thus) should be construed with the preceding words as well. The word “iti” has the sense of “beginning” or the sense of “manner. By this, [the list] beginning with “not a cause, dissociated from cause,” as it appears in the Pāli, is included.
It comprises [them]. The collection of phenomena included within the personal existence (*attabhāva*) of each respective individual is called "internal" (*ajjhatta*).
Furthermore, among those, that wherein craving (*taṇhā*) has an especially firm grasp is the sixfold phenomenon—beginning with the eye—along with the mind;
this is called "internal. This is because it is known and made manifest within the internal self. For it is thus:

It is also called "internal-of-the-internal. However, the other things—namely, visible forms and so forth, as well as contact and so forth—are called "external" because the craving that grasps them is weak.

For example, in the world, it is as if a jewel, gold, or silver were placed and stored outside the house, while a mat, a winnowing basket, a jar, or a saucer were placed inside the house. Among these, the latter...

Even after discarding the former ones, they protect the latter; therefore, because of the firmness of their grasp by craving, those very [latter] are called "internal enjoyment," while the subsequent ones are called "external enjoyment" alone. This should be understood as being exactly like that.
For here too, if it were possible, even after discarding all [objects] such as visible forms and [faculties] such as contact, only the sixfold set beginning with the eye would remain.
"They will certainly protect it. Thus, the internal and external nature of these two is stated solely by way of the strength or weakness of craving's appropriation;
it should be understood that this is not by way of the location where they occur. As for what is stated in the *Vibhāvanī*:
“Internal material form (ajjhattika-rūpa) is so called because it occurs with reference to, or directed toward, the self (attā) designated as the state of being (atthabhāva).
Granted that there are other things produced internally, yet by way of conventional usage (ruḷhī), only the eye and so forth are called ‘internal’”—this has been said. That is not correct.
And as for what is therein...
“The mind, having made itself its own object, occurs by way of being its door; thus it is ‘internal. That very [mind] is what is called ‘internal’”—this too is not satisfactory.

For if that were the meaning, the internality of the mind would not be established. Furthermore, it would result in there being no distinction between internal phenomena (*ajjhattadhamma*) and internal bases (*ajjhattikāyatana*).
As for what was stated therein...

Alternatively, it is said that they are specifically "internal" because they are exceptionally beneficial to the personal existence (*attabhāva*), just like the eye and so forth—speaking as if to say, "If we did not exist, you would be like a wooden pillar.
This is more appropriate; for it is precisely due to their exceptional benefit that beings' sense of ownership (*pariggaha*) toward them is firm.

These seven types are called "gate-forms" (*dvāra-rūpa*), because they are, respectively, the gateways for the occurrence of consciousness-continua (*vīthi-citta*) and of kamma such as killing living beings.
In that context, the fivefold sensitive matter is called the "door of rebirth," and the two types of intimation are called the "door of action.
Gross matter is so called because its intrinsic nature is coarse and because its own function, termed "impact," is gross.
Neighboring matter is so called because it is suitable to be grasped by knowledge more quickly than that which exists at a distance. And there is also impinging matter.

Here, *paṭigha* means "striking against" (*paṭihanana*). It is twofold: the striking against between the sense object and the sense faculty, and the mutual striking against among the great primary elements (*mahābhūta*).

Among these, that striking against by which the sensitivity of the sense doors and the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) undergoes modification is called the striking against between the sense object and the sense faculty.
That [striking against] by which [the primary elements] characterized by the nature of being struck...
In material phenomena, there occur deformation, agitation, impact, oppression, breaking, and so forth. This is called the mutual resistance of the great elements (*mahābhūta*).
That which exists together with resistance (*paṭigha*) is "with resistance" (*sappaṭigha*).
Furthermore, in the *Vibhāvani*:

"That which is the state of being face-to-face with one another—the mutual falling toward each other—of those [elements] that have come together by way of dependence, is called *paṭigha* because it is like a striking (*paṭighāta*).

For just as when there is a striking, there is a movement in the weak [object], so too, when there is this state of being face-to-face, there is a movement of the weak life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) due to its immaterial nature. Thus is the impact of the great primary elements.
Having made a mere comparison, only the impact between the object and the subject was taken [as the definition].

That is untenable; for if that were so, then those impacts which are seen in the world within the internal and external continua—by virtue of which there occur among material phenomena mutual clinging, binding, stiffening, supporting, moving, and so forth, as well as growth—[would not be accounted for].
Waning, cutting, splitting, dissolving, scattering, and so forth also occur; these might not be included here.

Yet, it is impossible for them to exist in any other way than as types of impact (*ghaṭṭana*) characterized by conjunction (*sannipāta*), which occurs through the modes of assistance (*anuggaha*) and injury (*upaghāta*).
The other sixteenfold subtle form exists by way of being the opposite of what has been stated.
There is distant form and non-reacting form. "Clung-to form" (upādinnarūpa) is, in some contexts, said to be any form that sustains the body.
In other contexts, both of these [types of form] are called "clung-to" because they are grasped and adhered to by craving and views;
however, in the primary sense, only that which is originated by kamma is called "clung-to. Why is that? [Because it is only that which is the result of kamma that is truly clung-to.]

It is called "matter derived from clinging" (*upādinnarūpa*) because it is excessively and intensely grasped, seized, and clung to by way of its constant occurrence within the continuum of a sentient being;
thus it is said: "matter born of karma that is derived from clinging. It is "clung to" (*upādinnam*) because it is intensely grasped by craving and views through such thoughts as "this is mine.
In the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), however, it is explained that it is "grasped" or "seized" as one's own fruit by means of karma accompanied by craving and views.

This shows the meaning. "With demonstration" (*sanidassana*) means together with a demonstration. "Demonstration" (*nidassana*) refers to the state of being visible by means of eye-consciousness (*cakkhuviññāṇa*).
Although that [state] is not different from the phenomenon (*dhamma*) itself, it is used metaphorically as if it were something else.

For when this is so, there is an understanding of a specific distinction in meaning. Alternatively, "demonstration" refers to the function of eye-consciousness. That which exists together with that is also called "with demonstration."
This indeed is logical. The pair beginning with the eye grasps its object by way of non-arrival; the triad beginning with the nose grasps its object by way of arrival.
Thus, the application is that all five are "matter that grasps its object.

In this context, an object that arises having attached itself to and adhered upon the sensitive matter (*pasāda*) is called "arrived" (*sampatta*); one that arises even a hair’s breadth away from it is called "not arrived" (*asampatta*).

But why, in this context, does the dyad beginning with the eye grasp [its object] only when it has not reached it, while the triad beginning with the nose grasps [its object] only when it has reached it?
It is due to the distinction in their conditions. For light is the condition for the eye in the apprehension of visible form, and space is the condition for the ear in the apprehension of sound.
Furthermore, when the eye and the visible form arise in mutual contact, there is no room for the surrounding light; likewise [for the other cases].

And in the case of sounds heard by the ear, there is the accompaniment of space. However, air, water, and earth serve as conditions for the apprehension of odors and so forth by the triad of the nose and the other [senses].
In that context, "air" refers specifically to the nasal breath which draws in odors; and that is a condition only for what has come into contact [with the sense organ].
"Water" refers to the moisture that moistens the tongue; that too is a condition only for what has come into contact. For flavor is not [apprehended] by a dry tongue.
"It reaches. Earth is a condition for the purpose of impact; for light or dust falling into the air does not strike the sensitive material (pasāda) when it is supported by weak earth.
Thus, due to the difference in conditions, there is a distinction in their apprehension according to whether they reach [the object] or do not reach it.
In this regard, the non-reaching apprehension of the eye is evident; for that [eye] is near.

One does not see the color of the eye or the root of the eyebrow; yet one sees distant and large colors such as the lunar disk, or colors concealed by crystal and the like, and the determination of direction and location is discerned for it. But how is this so for the ear?
For in that case, a sound heard from afar is perceived after a long time, and even a sound produced in the western direction is [heard] after a long interval.
When a shrine or similar object is obstructed, the sound is heard either from the right side or from the left side; or it may not be heard at all.
It is said in response: the arisen collection of sounds, for those standing nearby, becomes manifest in sequence from the beginning until the end.
The impact and friction are powerful, and the thought "I hear" arises.

The paths of observation proceed more rapidly and as if continuously. However, for those standing at a distance, the impact of the resistance is weaker; it is not manifest from the beginning, but becomes manifest through the synthesis of the middle or the end. The paths of observation proceed slowly over a long duration. Therefore, there arises the conceit that "I heard [the sound] quickly" or "I heard it after a long time. Furthermore, [The text continues: ...Moreover, [the Master said: "If one does not understand the meaning of the words 'quickly' and 'after a long time,' one might think: 'When a sound is struck by a hand, the sound is produced immediately; thus, the path of observation proceeds quickly. But when a sound is struck by a drum, the sound is produced after a delay; thus, the path of observation proceeds slowly. This is not so. For even in the case of a hand, the sound is produced after a moment's delay. And even in the case of a drum, the sound is produced immediately. Therefore, the distinction between 'quick' and 'slow' is merely a matter of the strength of the impact, not of the speed of the cognitive process. Thus he spoke. Furthermore, [the Master said: "If one does not understand the meaning of the words 'quickly' and 'after a long time,' one might think: 'When a sound is struck by a hand, the sound is produced immediately; thus, the path of observation proceeds quickly. But when a sound is struck by a drum, the sound is produced after a delay; thus, the path of observation proceeds slowly. This is not so. For even in the case of a hand, the sound is produced after a moment's delay. And even in the case of a drum, the sound is produced immediately. Therefore, the distinction between 'quick' and 'slow' is merely a matter of the strength of the impact, not of the speed of the cognitive process. Thus he spoke. But when a sound is struck by a drum, the sound is produced after a delay; thus, the path of observation proceeds slowly. This is not so. But when a sound is struck by a drum, the sound is produced after a delay; thus, the path of observation proceeds slowly. This is not so. For even in the case of a hand, the sound is produced after a moment's delay. And even in the case of a drum, the sound is produced immediately. Therefore, the distinction between 'quick' and 'slow' is merely a matter of the strength of the impact, not of the speed of the cognitive process. Thus he spoke. Furthermore, [the Master said: "If one does not understand the meaning of the words 'quickly' and 'after a long time,' one might think: 'When a sound is struck by a hand, the sound is produced immediately; thus, the path of observation proceeds quickly. But when a sound is struck by a drum, the sound is produced after a delay; thus, the path of observation proceeds slowly. This is not so. For even in the case of a hand, the sound is produced after a moment's delay. And even in the case of a drum, the sound is produced immediately. Therefore, the distinction between 'quick' and 'slow' is merely a matter of the strength of the impact, not of the speed of the cognitive process. Thus he spoke. Sound, proceeding by way of a succession of supporting elements (*nissaya-dhātu*), indeed travels even to a distant place.
And as it travels, it strikes the ears of thousands of people standing within earshot, but only at the very spot where it has already reached.
However, when there is an obstruction such as a large stupa, from whichever side the space is directly open—whether from the right side or the left side—it proceeds from that direction.
It strikes against the ear-hole from the place where it has already passed. However, the sound becomes so faint that it is no longer audible.
Thus, while moving, as long as it has not arisen after reaching the ear-hole, it is "not yet arrived.
But that which arises after having reached [the ear-hole] is called "arrived. That [sound] is not heard. If, however, the ear were to have its object only when it has been reached—
It might be so. Just as a scent within the womb is not smelled outside, so too a sound within the womb would not be heard outside.
Like the scent, there might be a diffusion [of sound] with a determination of direction and location.
However, in the *Vibhāvanī*: [188]

“If it is argued that [the eye] goes to the region of the object and grasps it after pervading it, then its range of operation (*adhiṭṭhāna-vidhā*) would also have to be its objective field (*gocara*). This has been examined in three ways, but it is not correct.

For there is no possibility of the pair of eyes and so forth going to the external region of the object. "Grasping the objective field" means that which grasps the objective field. The meaning is that, because it is like the essence of the sensitive materiality (*pasāda*), it receives the sign of the object (*ārammaṇa-nimitta*) as soon as it comes into range.
However, in the *Vibhāvani*:
It is said that [the object] is determined by consciousness because it has the nature of grasping its respective range of experience (*gocara*).
"Color" (*vaṇṇa*) is a name for the objective field of visible form (*rūpārammaṇa*). "Nutriments" (*ojā*) refers to nutriment-form (*āhāra-rūpa*).

"Analysis" (*vinibbhoga*) means that which is analyzed apart. The meaning is that it is defined separately according to its location, its place, and its cause of arising. "Non-analysis" (*avinibbhoga*) is the opposite.
"Indivisible" (*avinibbhoga*). That which is itself form is "indivisible form" (*avinibbhogarūpa*).

Although the Elder Ācariya Ānanda states that odour, flavour, and nutritive essence are seen to be separated from it in some instances, he maintains that there are only five kinds of indivisible form.
This will be explained further below. [The Analysis of Form.]

158. "Kamma" refers to volition (*cetanā*) alone. For it is that very same [volition] which is stated in the *Paṭṭhāna* as having the status of a "kamma-condition" (*kammapaccaya*) in the case of asynchronous [relations].

As it is said: "Wholesome and unwholesome volitions belonging to different moments are a condition, by way of kamma-condition, for resultant aggregates and for [matter] produced by kamma (*kaṭattā-rūpa*).
However, in the *Paṭṭhāna*, "consciousness" (*citta*) is intended to include its associated states (*sampayutta-dhamma*).
This is because mental states (*cetasika-dhamma*) are also described as having the nature of originating matter. As it is said:
"Roots are a condition by way of root-condition for those states associated with roots and for the matter originated by them," and so forth. "Temperature" (*utu*) is simply heat.

For it maintains the world-system (*loka*) in its entirety as a single world-period (*kappa*) through its stabilizing function, and it also maintains various bodily forms within one's own [continuum].

"Lam" [means] that it causes the body composed of form, the world of sentient beings, and even the entire world of formations—including various trees, grasses, and so forth, as well as clouds, rain, water, fire, wind, and the rest—to be established, produced, generated, and increased.
Therefore, it is called "utu" (season/climate). They also say it is called "utu" because it moves about and proceeds. "Āhāra" (nutriment) is simply *ojā* (vital essence).

It is said that there are twenty-five kinds [of materiality], because the immaterial wholesome [kamma]—which consists in the cultivation of dispassion toward form—does not produce matter born of kamma.
"Excessively conditioned" (*atisaṅkhata*) means it has been well-made by distinguishing it as producing matter in the past and likewise in other intervals of time.

It is stated as "in the internal continuum" (*ajjhattasantāne*), but it should rather be said "in the internal continuum" (*ajjhattasantāne*); or, "internal" (*ajjhatta*) itself is the same as "internal-adjacent" (*ajjhattika*).
The meaning of the word *ika* should be understood. "Starting from rebirth-linking" means starting from the moment of arising of the rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhicitta*).
"In each and every moment" means in the three moments of each individual consciousness.

However, the Venerable Ācariya Ānanda Thera maintains that for all material phenomena produced by the four causes, there is arising only at the moment of arising of each consciousness, and dissolution only at the moment of its dissolution.

And he speaks of cessation. But my intended meaning here is this: all material phenomena (rūpa) arising from the four causes arise only at the moment of the mind's arising, not at the moment of its dissolution. As it is said:
"In one for whom the truth of the origin ceases, the truth of suffering arises. Thus it is said.
Likewise, those [material phenomena] cease only at the moment of the mind's dissolution, not at the moment of its arising.
As it is said: "When wholesome states or unwholesome states arise for someone, indeterminate states cease for him. This is not so.

These two pairs of propositions were stated with reference to the immaterial existence (*arūpabhava*). However, material phenomena arise even at the moment of the mind's dissolution and cease even at the moment of its arising. If this is argued, it is not so; for if that were the case—

Furthermore, for whomsoever the truth of origination ceases, does the truth of suffering arise for them? In the formless realm, at the moment of the cessation of craving, the truth of origination ceases for them, but the truth of suffering does not arise for them.
In the five-aggregate realm, at the moment of the cessation of craving, both the truth of origination ceases and the truth of suffering arises for them.
In other cases,
during the moment of arising of wholesome states in the formless realm, wholesome phenomena arise for them, but indeterminate phenomena do not cease for them.
During the moment of arising of wholesome states in the five-aggregate realm, both wholesome phenomena arise for them.
"Indeterminate phenomena cease as well"—thus, these questions would have been stated in their full form. However, only a negation (*no*) was stated.

Therefore, it cannot be said that this was spoken with reference to the immaterial existence (*arūpabhava*). If it is argued that it was spoken with reference to mind-born matter (*cittajarūpa*), [the response follows].

That too is not so. For there is no contradiction in the inclusion of matter born of kamma (*kammaja-rūpa*), nor is there a *Yamaka* (Pairs) variant reading; rather, it exists only in the forward order (*anuloma*). As it has been said:
"In whomsoever, wherever, the mind-faculty (*manindriya*) does not arise, in him, there, the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) does not arise.
In the case of non-percipient beings (*asaññasatta*), the mind-faculty does not arise in them there, yet it is not the case that the life-faculty does not arise in them there.

For all those passing away, and at the moment of the dissolution of consciousness during the course of existence (*pavatta*), neither the mind-faculty (*manindriya*) nor the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) arises therein.
Here, by the phrase "of non-percipient beings" (*asaññasattānaṃ*), only the material life-faculty (*rūpa-jīvitindriya*) is intended.

And if that [material life-faculty] were to arise even at the moment of the dissolution of consciousness, then in the preceding section—at the moment of the dissolution of consciousness during the course of existence for non-percipient beings—[the same would apply].
It might be said that for them the life-faculty does not arise; it might also be said that this applies to all those passing away in the final section.
If it is argued that, in the final section, this was stated with reference to the immaterial-sphere life-faculty, we say no.
This is because there is no variant reading in the *Yamaka* for the purpose of such an interpretation, and because the canonical texts (pāḷiyo) stand as the domain of the Omniscient One.
Having reconciled [the views], one must stand by the powerful scriptural tradition (*pāḷi*).

And because material phenomena (*rūpadhammā*) proceed slowly, while immaterial phenomena (*arūpadhammā*) proceed rapidly, and their moment of duration (*ṭhitikkhaṇa*) does not admit of a separate calculation, therefore the continuity of moments for material phenomena is one thing, and that for immaterial phenomena is another. In this regard, all material phenomena...
Measured by a single moment of consciousness—that is, conjoined with its own moment of arising—they arise continuously from moment to moment.

Furthermore, because they have arisen together from the moment of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) onwards, their arising and so forth, as well as their cessation, occur simultaneously throughout the entire life;
such is his intention. However, the *Yamaka* texts differ both in meaning and in phrasing.
The Teacher’s intention is profound; therefore, it must be thoroughly investigated and discerned.

However, it is not the nature of the *Yamaka* that every instance of the *Yamaka*-text seen by one who stands by their own intention can be joined simply according to whatever happens to be available—that is, by means of "joining according to what is found" (*yathālābhayojanā*).
[This is so because] it is a specific state consisting in the cultivation of dispassion toward form (*rūpavirāgabhāvanāvisesa*).
In that world, wholesome immaterial states do not produce rebirth-linking accompanied by matter; they produce only pure immateriality.
Therefore, because there is a total absence of the beginning of a material continuity, all forty-six types of consciousness arising there are not incapable of producing matter.
However, as for immaterial-resultants, since they arise there according to a fixed rule, it is only the immaterial resultants [that are so].
This has been established; for that very reason, it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* that many other [mental states] arising in the formless realm do not produce matter due to lack of space.
In this context, "lack of space" (anokāsata) should be understood as the mere absence of the head of the material continuity (*rūpasantati*) that has arisen from the beginning.
In the *Vibhāvani*, however, the reason is stated as: "Because the cause is the production of the development of dispassion toward form (*rūpavirāgabhāvanā*), and because it is opposed to that.

That is not a valid reason, because it shows the capacity to produce form when there is a basis for form (*rūpokāsa*) in the supramundane resultant (*lokuttaravipāka*) produced by the path consisting of the development of dispassion toward both form and the formless (*rūpārūpavirāgabhāvanā*).

Because they lack the factors of jhāna (jhānaṅga), even though their constituent parts are weak, they do not produce material form; thus, the inclusion of the two sets of fivefold sense-consciousnesses was made.

Furthermore, the fifteen types of rebirth-linking consciousnesses of the sense-sphere and fine-material sphere, as well as the death-consciousness of those whose taints are exhausted (khīṇāsava) at the moment of final Nibbāna—these consciousnesses do not generate material form at all. Nevertheless, all of them [function] during the period of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga).
And since it arises at the time of death for those whose taints (*āsava*) are not yet exhausted, their non-inclusion here should be understood.
However, in the *Vibhāvanī*, it is stated:

"But the rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhicitta*) and the death-consciousness (*cuticitta*) do not constitute a different state of consciousness because they are included within the nineteen moments of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*); therefore, no 'adverting' (*vajjana*) is performed for them. In this regard, it should not be said that they are "included within the nineteen moments of the life-continuum."
Because the immaterial resultant [consciousness] is excluded by its very nature.
But why do the fifteen types of rebirth-linking consciousness mentioned above not produce matter at the moment of rebirth-linking? Because they are extremely weak.
For consciousness indeed becomes powerful only when it has obtained a complete condition at the very moment of its arising, whereas matter [becomes powerful] only at the moment of its presence.
Therefore, because they arise depending on a weak basis at a moment when their own strength is arising, they themselves become very weak;

thus, all of them do not then produce material form. And herein, some [teachers] maintain that conditions such as contiguity and repetition exercise their influence only at the moment of the mind's arising, whereas those that serve as supports for material form [exercise theirs] at the moment of its presence.
Since temperature and nutriment, as well as states that are postnascent conditions, exercise their influence only at the moment of presence,
it should be understood that they obtain their full complement of conditions respectively at the moment of arising and at the moment of presence.
However, in the *Vibhāvanī*...
"However, because it occurs dependent on a weak physical basis that lacks the postnascent condition (*pacchājāta-paccaya*) and is not supported by nutriment and so forth,
and because it occupies the place of mind-originated material phenomena through both its own adventitious nature and the materiality born of kamma," such is the reason stated.
In this regard, the phrase "lacking the postnascent condition" must be investigated.

Because it will be explained that even for the father, who lacks the postnascent condition (*pacchājāta-paccaya*) at the moment of the subsistence of the rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhi-citta*), there exists the state of being a producer of material form.

For a subsequent consciousness that does not exist by itself cannot be the postnascent condition for any material form existing at the moment of the preceding consciousness. This is because that [postnascent] condition is but one part of the "existence" (*atthi*) condition.

However, the death-consciousness (*cuticitta*) of those whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*) is more peaceful because it occurs within a continuum where the root of the round has naturally subsided.
Furthermore, because it depends upon a physical basis that is weaker and at its final limit due to the exhaustion of the life-formations (*āyusaṅkhāra*), it is even weaker;
thus, it does not arouse that [rebirth] matter. But the Venerable Ācariya Ānanda Thera [says] that for all beings...
He maintains that the death-consciousness does not produce matter. This is stated by specifying "the death-consciousness of those whose taints are exhausted" (khīṇāsavānaṃ cuticittaṃ).

[This refers to] at the moment of arising of the final consciousness of those belonging to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara), which is immediately followed by the arising of another sense-sphere final consciousness;

and for those belonging to the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara) and the immaterial sphere (arūpāvacara) who are in their final existence, as well as for those who will arise in the fine-material sphere.

From the statement: "For those who will attain final Nibbāna after being reborn in the formless realm (arūpāvacara), at the moment of their death, their verbal formation (vacī-saṅkhāra) will cease, but their bodily formation (kāya-saṅkhāra) does not cease," it is understood that the death-consciousness (cuti-citta) of others also does not produce matter. For [the death-consciousness] is not a producer of matter...
In the absence of the mind’s entry into a womb and so forth, there is no production of bodily formations;
yet it is not logical that [bodily formations] should still proceed from the mind even after death. Furthermore, there is no canonical text stating that the death-consciousness produces matter.
However, in the *Anuṭīkā*...
In that passage, the statement "for those passing away, the bodily formation does not cease" demonstrates not only the absence of the production of matter by the death-consciousness alone,
but also establishes the absence of the production of matter by all the preceding consciousnesses close to death; for it is in the death-consciousness that the bodily formation ceases.
From that point prior to the prohibition up until the seventeenth consciousness, its arising is likewise prohibited.
All of this must be investigated.

For "bodily formation" (*kāyasaṅkhāra*) refers to inhalation and exhalation; and since that is a very coarse material phenomenon (*rūpadhamma*), by the statement that there is no cessation of it at the death-consciousness (*cuticitta*), one can also maintain that other subtle material phenomena do not produce the death-consciousness.

[192] Furthermore, as for what was stated there—that because of the absence of a connection to entering the womb and so forth, there is no non-arousing of bodily formations by the consciousness that originates matter—that too is not tenable.

For those very factors, such as entering the womb and so forth, ought to be the means of establishing this point: that even a consciousness which does not originate gross bodily formations nevertheless certainly originates other subtle matter.
[193] As for what was stated there—
that it is not logical to say that mind-originated materiality continues to proceed even after death— that too is without foundation.
For there is no contradiction whatsoever to the proceeding of mind-born materiality for even a few moments beyond the moment of death.

As for what was said—that there is a textual passage stating, "And therein, the death-consciousness does not produce matter"—even there, it cannot be said that "the death-consciousness does not produce matter" is not the case, except in the instance of bodily formations (*kāyasaṅkhāra*).
However, this would be more appropriate: just as material phenomena, from the very beginning at the moment of rebirth-linking, [arise] for the duration of a single consciousness-moment...
They are weak either because their conditions are limited or because they proceed slowly;
likewise, it can be said that at the end, at the time of death, they are indeed extremely weak because their conditions are being exhausted or because they are close to cessation.
Therefore, the rebirth-linking consciousness and the death-consciousness, which depend on the beginning and the end of the physical basis respectively, are equally weak.
"It can be understood that they exist. However, in the *Vibhāvani* and the *Abhidhammatthavikāsini*,

[the author]— considering [those views] to be in contradiction with the Canon (pāḷi)— has proceeded by merely expanding upon the method stated in the commentaries (*ṭīkā*) without investigating even the slightest point.
"Starting from the first *bhavaṅga*" means beginning from the moment of the arising of the first *bhavaṅga*-consciousness.
"Only as it is being born" means only as it is arising at each moment of its arising, not while it is persisting; nor is it [the consciousness] that is dissolving—this is the meaning.
The reason has already been stated. "Therein" refers to within those seventy-five kinds of consciousness. "Appanā-javana" refers to that which excludes the two types of direct knowledge (*abhiññā*).
The absorption impulsion consciousness is of twenty-six kinds. "Posture" refers to the three postures excluding walking.
However, in the *Vibhāvani*, it is stated as "walking and so forth"; that is not tenable.
For not even the mere movement or trembling of the limbs and members of the body is accomplished without intimation (viññatti); how much less, then, walking?
Furthermore, the aforementioned absorption-impulsion (appanājavana) is not capable of producing intimation.
By the word "api" (also/even), he shows that it is not merely a producer of material form. "Sannāmeti" means "it sustains"; this is indeed the reading.
It may be that it sustains and supports the posture as it occurs, conditioned by the minds to be described hereafter, so that it does not fall or become unsteady;

this is the meaning. And in this context, "supporting" should be understood merely as the preservation of the posture as it occurs, not as its being projected forward like a boat being pushed off. Otherwise, there would be [the fault of] intimation through stiffening.
"An occasion might arise": here, while the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) consciousness is proceeding in uninterrupted succession, whether one is sitting or standing, the limbs sag and fall.

It is not so when these twenty-six kinds of wakefulness-consciousness (*jāgaraṇacitta*) about to be described, or the thirty-two kinds of wakefulness-consciousness, are proceeding; for when those are proceeding, the limbs are firm.
They do not sink; they do not fall. It should be understood that they proceed exactly as they were previously established.
However, in the *Vibhāvani*, the reading is:
"Not even among these thirty-two types, nor among the twenty-six wakefulness-minds that will be mentioned, do they proceed."
The reading "when these aforementioned twenty-six types of wakeful consciousnesses, or the thirty-two types [of consciousness], are occurring" is appropriate.
"Adverting" (voṭṭhabbana) refers to the adverting of the mind-door; for even the impulsion-consciousnesses belonging to the five doors do not originate intimation.
By the word "or" (pi), the mere stabilization of the postures is also included.
It should be understood that by mentioning "resolution" (*voṭṭhabbana*) and so forth, the five-door processes are also included.
Herein, "posture" (*iriyāpatha*) refers specifically to material phenomena (*rūpadhamma*) occurring through various particular states such as walking and so on.

Even though this is so, some consciousness produces only the commonality of matter and nothing beyond that; some [consciousness], however, [produces matter] according to the posture as it occurs under the influence of another consciousness.
It is able to maintain [the state] itself, but it is not able to initiate an unarisen posture (*iriyāpatha*).
However, having produced some intimation (*viññatti*), it is able to initiate an unarisen posture. It is also able to produce other bodily and vocal modifications.
And those consciousnesses that are capable of producing a subsequent function (*uttarakicca*) [are able to produce] the preceding, lower function.
It should be understood that this analysis was made for the purpose of showing that [the mind] is indeed capable of producing [intimation].
However, what is stated in the *Vibhāvani*—
"That consciousness which generates intimation invariably stiffens the postures, because there is an inseparable connection between the posture and intimation"— is not tenable.
For here, by "supporting the postures," only that which is devoid of intimation (viññatti) is intended, not that which is accompanied by intimation.
Otherwise, it would follow that even the javanas of absorption (appanā) produce intimation. There are thirteen joyous (somanassa) javanas:
four from each of the great wholesome, the great unwholesome, and the great functional (kriya), together with the smile-producing (hasituppāda).

There are thirteen javanas accompanied by joy (*somanassa*). Among these, the wholesome ones are for the eight types of worldlings (*puthujjana*) from the perspective of wholesomeness; those dissociated from views are for the six types of trainees (*sekha*) from the perspective of wholesome-ness;
and those of the functional type are for the five types of those whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*)—this is how it should be understood.

Because of the statement, "All bodily, verbal, and mental action is preceded by knowledge and follows after knowledge," the smile-producing consciousness (*hasituppāda*), which is devoid of the function of investigation (*vicāraṇa*), belongs to the Omniscient Buddhas.
The doctrine that [laughter] does not arise is indeed rejected in the *Aṭṭhakathā*.
For if that doctrine were held, it would follow that other rootless consciousnesses (*ahetuka-citta*), as well as the great functional javanas dissociated from knowledge, could not occur in Buddhas.
Therefore, regarding the act of smiling (*sitakamma*) that occurs through a smile-producing consciousness (*hasituppāda-citta*), [one must consider] its preceding and succeeding occurrences...
By way of knowledge, it should be understood that there is precedence by knowledge and conformity to knowledge.
"Known as 'cold' and 'heat'" means that these are well-defined and known by all ordinary people in the world as "this is cold" and "this is heat.

"Having reached their own state" (ṭhitippattā) means having reached their own condition or moment of stability; the meaning is not that they are merely born like the mind. The reason has already been stated.
[197] As for what is stated in the *Vibhāvani*:

“Because it receives support from conditions such as the postnascent condition (*pacchājāta-paccaya*), the temperature and the fire element possess a state of strength precisely at the moment of their presence; thus, the fire element has reached its station,” and so forth—therein, the mention of the postnascent condition has already been examined above.
Furthermore, if the strength of the temperature and its production of matter were dependent upon the postnascent condition, then...

Thus, at the moment of the subsistence (*ṭhitikkhaṇa*) of the rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhicitta*), it would not produce matter, because at that time there would be an absence of the postnascent condition (*pacchājātapaccaya*).

As it will be stated: "They are temperature-originated (*utusamuṭṭhāna*) starting from the period of subsistence. And here, "the period of subsistence" refers to the period of subsistence of the rebirth-linking consciousness.
Therefore, having examined the statement regarding the postnascent condition, it should be accepted [as follows].

"Nutriment reckoned as nutritive essence (*ojā*) is fourfold by way of being produced by kamma and so forth when it has entered the internal continuity, and fourfold by way of what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted;
and there is also a twofold nutriment reckoned as nutritive essence that has entered external continuity.
Since both of these, having obtained support through contact, produce such [matter], it is said: 'at the time of ingestion. And herein:
It is stated in all the commentaries that just as there is the production of internal materiality by means of the nutritive essence produced externally—

similar to the production of the fourfold-originated internal nutritive essences by the external temperature— so too is it for the nutritive essence produced externally. As it is said in the *Majjhima-aṭṭhakathā*:

First, edible food (kabaḷīkāra-āhāra), by the mere act of being placed in the mouth, produces eight types of material phenomena. However, once it has been chewed by the teeth and swallowed, each morsel produces eight types of material phenomena.

But the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla states: "If nutritive essence produced externally were to produce material phenomena, then just as temperature produced externally produces material phenomena both internally and externally, so too [would this be the case]."
It might produce material form externally, but it does not. Therefore, even when it reaches the internal [body], it certainly does not produce material form;
rather, it produces exclusively the internal nutritive essence (*ojā*).
However, with the intention that it serves merely as a supporting condition for that [essence], it is sufficient merely to place it in the mouth, not to chew it.
Even by that much, it certainly becomes a condition for what is internal; why, then, does the *Majjhima-ṭīkā* say, "it produces eight material qualities each"?
It is because the temperature (*utu*) and the nutritive essence (*ojā*) known as "clung-to" (*upādinnaka*) are extremely refined material qualities;
therefore, even external nutritive essence, having reached the interior and being thoroughly heated by that temperature and thoroughly [assimilated] by that nutritive essence...
It is logical that the supporting [nutriments], by way of the accumulation of fat and moisture in the body, indeed give rise to material form.
The phrase "at the time of ingestion" is stated with reference to the period when this [food] has reached a state of full potency.
However, in the *Visuddhimagga*, it is said that even food consumed by the mother gives rise to material form by pervading the child’s body. In the body...
It is said that even when smeared, it produces material form; and it was stated previously that as soon as it is placed in the mouth, it produces the eight types of material form.
"Having reached its place" means having reached its own moment of existence.
And here, among the four modes of origination, it alone is great, possesses great power, and has great extension; for it [extends] outside the entire world of space.
He is the originator and destroyer of the world of formations (*saṅkhāra-loka*). He alone is the great internal constituent of the world of beings (*satta-loka*).
As for the other three, they merely serve as his retinue.
The heart and the sense-faculties are born only of kamma, not of mind and so forth. If that is so, friend, these are indeed serene...
“Sāriputta, the faculties... By means of what dwelling do you now dwell? Why was this said?
Because the attainment of the colors produced by the mind—which are the equipment of the faculties—is approached by way of their clarity and serenity.
For when the four primary elements proceed as a single continuous unit, if one is serene, all of them are indeed serene.
"Milāte ca milātāneva" means "withered and withering. It should be understood that temperature, consciousness, and nutriment are the supporting conditions for those nine [material phenomena].
In this context, kamma-born material phenomena are to be seen as being like the blue and red lotuses; kamma is like their seed;
and temperature, nutriment, and so forth, are like the mud and water. The two modes of intimation are born of consciousness alone; for it is thus:
The Blessed One has pointed out those phenomena that coexist with the mind and follow along with the mind.

Why, then, is it said: "Sound, mind, and heat"? Is it not stated in the *Nidhikaṇḍa Sutta* that by means of such a specific type of kamma, there is what is called the perfection of sound—namely, excellence of gold, excellence of voice, excellence of shape, excellence of form, and so forth?
True; however, by means of a specific type of kamma, just as [there is] clarity...

An exceedingly sweet sound arises; likewise, there is the well-proportioned state and the lack of obstruction by wind, phlegm, and so forth in the appropriated bodies of those who have reached the [appropriate] places and organs of articulation.
Therefore, the excellence of the sound rooted in that [physical condition] is included among the fruits of karma and is called "sweet-voiced.
It should not be understood, however, that sound is produced by karma in an absolute sense.
Why is it said that the triad beginning with lightness (lahutā) arises from temperature, consciousness, and nutriment?
Is it not stated: "O youth, this practice leads to freedom from illness, namely, non-violence"?
And yet, this triad of materiality arises from conditions conducive to freedom from illness; for slowness and so forth arise from the presence of opposing conditions that disturb the elements.

Regarding the statement "it is said of this": it is explained that the material phenomena born of kamma (kammaja-rūpa), like hundred-times-boiled oil placed in water, naturally become light, soft, and wieldy in accordance with the kamma. Therefore, there is no separate transformation such as "lightness" and so forth for them;
because in a single existence, only a single time-period—the present—is obtained for them. And thus:

Having established this, even in the case of the Yamakas (the Twin Suttas), the temporal distinction of those [factors] is understood as being grasped solely by the present time, which is delimited by the occurrence of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).

For consciousness, indeed, is endowed with various states at various moments, either by way of the different types of hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), or by way of pleasure, pain, rapture, tranquility, faith, wisdom, and so forth. Likewise, temperature and nutriment are also suitable [conditions].

By way of the distinction of suitability. Therefore, the material phenomena arising from those three [roots] possess various modifications at different moments by way of being heavy, light, and so forth;
hence, a temporal distinction is obtained for them according to their continuity (santati).

And this being the case, even in the *Yamaka*, for non-kamma-born phenomena during the time of their occurrence, a temporal distinction is understood by way of both the moment (khaṇa) and the continuity (santati).

[Objection: But was it not stated that "diseases are born of the ripening of kamma"? If there is a disease-form derived from kamma, then the qualities such as lightness (*lahutā*) born of kamma—which constitute the emergence [of the body] from that [disease]—should also be obtainable separately. [Reply: No.

For those [karmic forces] by virtue of which diseases called "born of the ripening of kamma" arise in this body—namely, those karmas that are *upapīḷaka* (tormenting), *upaghātaka* (injuring), or *gati-kāla-payoga* (pertaining to destiny, time, and application)—[it is these that are meant].

When they undergo misfortune, the elements of the body—earth and so forth, as well as the temperature-originated elements such as wind and bile—become disturbed and give rise to various diseases. When the temperature-originated elements are disturbed, the others necessarily follow suit.
For this very reason, one is afflicted by cold, afflicted by heat, afflicted by hunger, and afflicted by thirst.

By the statement beginning with "it is afflicted" (*ruppati*), it is shown that temperature alone is the condition for the affliction (*ruppana*) of material phenomena. Therefore, there is no such thing as a disease produced solely by kamma;
for if there were, the aforementioned qualities born of kamma, such as lightness (*lahutā*) and so forth, would have to be found separately [from the affliction].
However, because beings are produced by non-harming kamma, they remain at a great distance from those karmas that cause oppression and the like.
Because the bodily constituents possess a dense, moist, and stable configuration, they are not subject to the arising of suffering within the rebirth-process existence;

therefore, with reference to that fact, it was said: "This way of practice for a young man, namely non-violence, leads to being free from illness," and not because the triad of lightness and so forth—which are the causes of freedom from illness—are produced by kamma.

Having understood it thus, it should be seen that this triad of matter is demonstrated only among those material phenomena that constitute the "ownership of action" (kammassakaṭṭha) in the section on matter (rūpakaṇḍa).
Indeed, various kinds of material groups (rūpakalāpa) occur even within a single atom.
Therefore, when fourfold material groups occur in a dense state, the space element (ākāsadhātu), which constitutes another group, is likewise perceived.
Having established this, their inclusion among the four [types of derived matter] was made.
Granted that all non-derived matter (anipphanna-rūpa) is produced by some condition or other, among them, the characteristic matters (lakkhaṇa-rūpa) are not so;

for unlike the others, they do not possess visible distinctions manifested through specific conditions such as consciousness and so forth. Thus it is said that "characteristic matters are not born from anything. [This refers to] being born and so forth.

"Of forms" means of the aggregates of form that are being born, decaying, and perishing. "Because they consist merely of their own nature" means because they consist merely of the nature of the characteristics defined as birth, aging, and death.
Furthermore, in this section on matter (*rūpakaṇḍa*), there is no mention of "temperature-originated" or "nutriment-originated"; it is stated only in the *Paṭṭhāna*. Here one might object:
"Aging and impermanence are not said anywhere in the Canon to be originated from anything; therefore, here too—"

It is not appropriate to include them among those [material phenomena] that arise from no source whatsoever. However, the continuities of accumulation (*upacaya-santati*) are indeed mentioned in the Canon as arising from various sources.

In the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*) as well, twenty material phenomena born of kamma, seventeen born of mind (*citta*), fourteen born of temperature (*utu*), and thirteen born of nutriment (*āhāra*) are mentioned alongside them.
Therefore, in this context, it is not the case that they arise from no source at all.

"It should not be said [that they arise from nutriment]. It is replied: The generative activity of those factors that produce matter exerts its influence only at the very moment of arising (*uppādakkhaṇa*) of the matter produced by themselves;

it does not continue beyond that. Therefore, it is only the continuities of accumulation (*upacaya-santati*) existing at that moment which deserve the designation "born from something," and not aging or impermanence.
This being so, both the Canon and the Commentary refer only to those [continuities].
In some instances, [the term] "arising" (samuṭṭhāna) has been employed. Furthermore, phenomena (*dhamma*) that have not yet arisen arise when conditions (*paccaya*) exist;
they do not arise when they do not exist—this is "existence" (*atthi*). Once arisen, however, phenomena decay and perish when conditions exist;
they do not decay or perish when they do not exist—this is "non-existence" (*natthi*). Therefore, the occurrence of these two preceding factors is entirely dependent upon conditions.
It exists. However, the occurrence of the final two [factors] is entirely independent of conditions;
it is by this method that their inclusion or non-inclusion among those [twenty-two factors] is to be understood.
As for what is stated in the Sutta passages: "Monks, aging-and-death is conditioned and dependently arisen," that pair is only known when birth exists.
It should be understood that this was stated by way of the method: "When [the cause] is absent, [the effect] is not manifest.

However, here, according to the method previously explained, these four—just like the other unproduced forms (anipphanna-rūpa)—do not possess any manifest distinction due to specific conditions such as consciousness;
thus, it is stated that none of the four are born from anything. Even so, one who runs too far ahead of the essential method of the Pāḷi—
"It is as if they were" means that the three types of accumulation are included within some origin; thus it is "better. [The Method of the Arising of Matter] 159.
Those which have a single arising—reckoned as birth—are "co-arising" (*ekuppāda*). Those which have a single cessation—reckoned as impermanence—are "co-ceasing" (*ekanirodha*).
Here, the word "single" (*eka*) functions in the sense of enumeration. Therefore, by that [word], those material phenomena which [share] a single...
They arise through birth; they cease through a single impermanence. This shows that their aggregate here is called a "material cluster" (*rūpakalāpa*).

However, for those who imagine that there are multiple [factors] such as birth and so forth even within a single cluster according to the enumeration of material clusters, this does not accord with the *Mūlaṭīkā*.
Nor is it logical. For it is stated therein: "Of those things included within each individual cluster..."

Since the occurrence of arising and so forth happens simultaneously with the material phenomena themselves, the arising and other characteristics of each individual group (kalāpa) are unique to that group.

Just as the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) is called "derived matter" (*upādāyarūpa*) because it sustains the groups of matter, so too birth and the other characteristics—which possess the nature of arising and so forth for each group—are called derived matter.
In this same way, the matter of change and the matter of delimitation are also to be applied accordingly.

Furthermore, because it is stated that "whatever is the accumulation (*ācaya*) of the sense-bases (*āyatana*), that is the growth (*upacaya*) of matter; and whatever is the growth of matter, that is the continuity (*santati*) of matter," those characteristic-forms (*lakkhaṇa-rūpa*) such as birth and so forth would have to be called the characteristics of matter individually, rather than [characteristics] of a single material aggregate (*kalāpa*).
This is because [the Sutta] states: "Derived from the four great elements, the sensitive faculty is the life-force of material phenomena," and so on.
Otherwise, it would follow that the eye-faculty and so forth, as well as the life-faculty and so forth, would each be multiple within a single group (kalāpa).

Therefore, without conceiving them in such a way, one must conclude that just like the other derived material phenomena (upādārūpa), the characteristic material phenomena (lakkhaṇarūpa) are also each single within a single group.
"Having a single support" (ekanissaya) means those which have a support designated as the "great elements" (mahābhūta) that is common (eka) to them. Here, the word *eka* has the sense of "common."
It is "associated" because it arises in dependence upon the four primary elements (*bhūta*).

And since those [factors] which are associated with characteristics such as simultaneous arising (*ekuppāda*) and so forth are necessarily co-existent, it is said that they are "co-existent" (*sahavutti*).

A collection of ten in measure is a "decad" (*dasaka*); or, a group of ten is a decad. A decad characterized by the eye is the "eye-decad" (*cakkhu-dasaka*), or rather, that which has the eye as its preeminent factor.
The eye-decad consists of the eye together with the [other] nine. This same method applies to the remaining [decads] as well.

However, since sound born of mind does not occur without a modification of intimation (*viññatti-vikāra*), and a modification of intimation does not occur without that sound, it is with the underlying intention that there can be no nonad consisting of sound born of mind, nor a nonad consisting of vocal intimation; rather, [the nonad] exists within the sound of vocal intimation.

For it has been stated that vocal intimation consists of ten [material qualities]. Herein, it is indeed logical that intimation is a modification which does not occur without sound. For it has been said:
"That which, by means of speech, is the intimating, the making known, the state of being made known—that material quality is vocal intimation.
However, there is a ninefold set of mind-born sounds that is devoid of the modification of intimation.
This is indeed found in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*). As it is said in the expositions on dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda-niddesa*):
"From the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) onwards, there is the sound-nonad consisting of both the physical heat and the consciousness.

According to the method of the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*, that which is called the "sound of the diffusion of applied thought" (*vitakka-vipphāra-sadda*), produced by consciousness and devoid of intimation (*viññatti*), is cognizable by the mind and not by the ear.
Sound is obtained [as a mental object]. However, that has been rejected by the compiler [of the Paṭṭhāna]. As he said:
"In the Paṭṭhāna as well, it is stated that sound-originated sound-base is a condition for ear-consciousness by way of the object-condition (ārammaṇapaccaya).

Therefore, there is no such thing as a 'sound produced by the diffusion of applied thought' (vitakkavipphārasadda) that arises without the impact of intimation (viññatti) and is cognizable by the ear. (Visuddhimagga, on breathing)
The ninefold group of sound born of mind (*cittaja*) in inhalation and exhalation has been stated. As it was said: "In the parts of inhalation and exhalation born of mind, there are nine:
the octad of nutritive essence (*ojatthamaka*) and sound. When the ninefold group of sound arrives, the twelvefold group beginning with lightness (*lahutā*) also necessarily arrives.

Therefore, there is the pure octad, the ninefold group of sound, the tenfold group of bodily intimation (*kāyaviññatti*), the tenfold group of verbal intimation (*vacīviññatti*), and the single [group] beginning with lightness.
The tenfold group, the twelvefold group beginning with the lightness of sound, the twelvefold group beginning with the lightness of bodily intimation,
and the thirteenfold group beginning with the lightness of vocal intimation and sound— these eight mind-born groups (cittaja-kalāpa) are to be understood.
However, in the *Saccasaṅkhepa*, seven mind-born groups are mentioned, as the twelvefold group beginning with the lightness of sound is not taken separately.
In the commentaries (*ṭīkā*), however, according to the method of the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā* in the *Porāṇa-ṭīkā*,

after showing the "ninefold sound" (*saddanavaka*) regarding the sound produced by the diffusion of thought (*vitakka-vipphāra-sadda*)— which is devoid of intimation (*viññatti*) and cognizable without the ear—
the author presents another position. Furthermore, [he states that] in the case of a great assembly of people, from a distance, the meaning of the syllables, words, and phrases is not discerned.
They say that sound produced by the mind (*cittasamuṭṭhānanighosasadda*) is indeed non-intimating (*aviññattika*).

Likewise, it is stated that there exists a sound produced by the mind that is non-intimating for wild animals, birds, and others such as the blind and the Damilas, who do not understand one another’s speech.
In that regard, the *Aṭṭhasālinī* rejects the notion of a sound devoid of intimation (*viññatti*), which is cognizable by the ear and is merely the diffusion of applied thought (*vitakkavipphāra*).

Even the sound of a voice arising from the mind in a great assembly of people is indeed communicative (*saviññattika*) for those standing nearby, as its words, phrases, syllables, and meanings are discernible.
Otherwise, all sounds produced by the mind would be indiscernible in their words, phrases, and syllables for those standing at a great distance;
thus, they would all be devoid of communication (*viññatti*). Furthermore, [this is not the case] for animals, birds, and so forth...
Sound born of mind is devoid of intimation (*viññatti*). This is because it makes known the intended meaning of others who belong to the same class [of beings].
However, in the later commentary (*pacchima-ṭīkā*), it is stated:

"In this context, the 'nine sounds' (*saddanavaka*) consist only of the eight [sounds] together with the sound produced by the clapping of hands, the snapping of fingers, and so forth. That too is not correct.

For such a sound is a condition for consciousness and is produced solely by temperature (*utu-samuṭṭhāna*). Therefore, according to the method explained in the *Visuddhimagga*, this group of nine sounds—consisting of inhalation and exhalation (which are sometimes accompanied by consciousness), as well as the sounds of speaking, coughing, spitting, vomiting, and discarding—should be understood.
Why, among the groups produced by temperature, are even the last two not found externally?
[Objection: But are not lightness, heaviness, softness, hardness, and wieldiness seen even in external forms? [Reply: True;
