however, it should be understood that these occur through the deficiency or predominance of the primary elements (*bhūta*), and not by way of the triad of lightness and so forth.
Why, then, is it said "of the groups" (*kalāpānaṃ*) and so on, stating that the space element and the characteristic-forms are not included within the material groups?
Because they consist merely of the delimitation of groups of space-elements, they do not become constituent parts— that is, members—
of any group of material phenomena. Furthermore, because the characteristic-materials consist merely of the characteristics such as arising and so forth common to all groups,
like the changeable-materials, they do not become constituent parts that differentiate the groups or serve as the cause for the designation of specific groups.

Therefore, he shows that those [factors] are not included among them. By this, it is demonstrated that the previously stated rule—beginning with "arising together" (ekuppāda)—applies only to produced material phenomena (nipphanna-rūpa) and not to unproduced material phenomena (anipphanna-rūpa).
Furthermore, it clarifies that the very act of causing the dissolution of a group (kalāpa) constitutes the "breaking up of the group" (kalāpabhedakaraṇa).

And having established this, even for the two types of intimation (viññatti), which lack the factor of simultaneous cessation, they are nonetheless included because they cause the dissolution of the group.
It should be understood that among these, the inclusion is well-established. [Kalāpayojanā] 160.

"As appropriate" means according to the nature of the states and according to the suitability for those whose faculties are either complete or incomplete. "Not deficient" means complete. For this name-and-form is not found lacking during the course of existence in the sense-sphere world;
thus, it "exists. [198] However, in the *Vibhāvani*:
It has been stated, "‘As appropriate’ means according to the suitability of those whose sense bases are complete with their constituent parts," but that is not correct;
for the term ‘not deficient’ is not a qualification based on the individual (puggala). Regarding the phrase ‘of moisture-born and spontaneously born beings,’ it is said in the Mahāsīhanāda Sutta:
“Sāriputta, there are these four modes of birth (yoni). Which four? The egg-born mode of birth, the womb-born mode of birth, the moisture-born mode of birth... [and so forth].

"Spontaneous birth as a mode of origin. Sāriputta, those beings who are born by repeatedly breaking out from an eggshell—this, Sāriputta, is called the egg-born mode of origin. Sāriputta, those beings who are born by repeatedly breaking out from a womb-sheath—this, Sāriputta, is called the womb-born mode of origin. Those who... [are born by repeatedly breaking out from a moisture-sheath—this, Sāriputta, is called the moisture-born mode of origin. Spontaneous birth as a mode of origin: Sāriputta, those beings who appear all at once with all their faculties complete and unimpaired, whether they are gods, hell-beings, or certain types of humans and animals—this, Sāriputta, is called the spontaneous mode of origin. These, Sāriputta, are the four modes of origin. Regarding these four modes of origin, there are three destinations for beings: hell, the animal realm, and the sphere of afflicted spirits. There are two destinations for beings: heaven and the human world. There is one destination for beings: Nirvana. What do you think, Sāriputta? Is it fitting for a noble disciple who possesses right view to regard hell as his final destination? "No indeed, venerable sir. "Is it fitting for him to regard the animal realm as his final destination? "No indeed, venerable sir. "Is it fitting for him to regard the sphere of afflicted spirits as his final destination? "No indeed, venerable sir. "What do you think, Sāriputta? Is it fitting for a noble disciple who possesses right view to regard heaven as his final destination?

"No indeed, venerable sir. "Is it fitting for him to regard the human world as his final destination? "No indeed, venerable sir. "What do you think, Sāriputta? Is it fitting for a noble disciple who possesses right view to regard Nirvana as his final destination? "Yes, venerable sir. "It is in this way, Sāriputta, that a noble disciple who possesses right view has transcended all destinations."
They are born from a rotten fish, or they are born from rotten filth, or from rotten gruel, or from a cesspool, or from stagnant water;

this, Sāriputta, is called the moisture-born womb. Devas, denizens of hell, certain humans, and certain beings in the states of deprivation—this, Sāriputta, is called the spontaneously born womb. Thus it was said.
In the *Aṭṭhakathā*, it is said: those born from an egg are "egg-born" (*aṇḍaja*); those born from a womb are "womb-born" (*jalābuja*); those born from moisture are "moisture-born" (*saṃsedaja*).
Those who arise and are produced without these causes, as if by spontaneous appearance, are "spontaneously born" (*opapātika*).

"Born having burst forth" (*abhinibbhijja jāyanti*) means they are born by way of emerging after breaking through [the covering]. By terms such as "putrid" and "corpse," only undesirable places are indicated.
[The various modes of birth] have been shown. It is said that beings are born among desirable things such as ghee, oil, honey, and molasses.
Here, according to the method of the Pāli, "egg" (*aṇḍa*) refers to the eggshell (*aṇḍakosa*), and "womb" (*jalābu*) refers to the amnion (*vatthikosa*).
From these they are born, produced, and emerged; thus they are to be understood as "egg-born" (*aṇḍaja*) and "womb-born" (*jalābuja*). In that context, *jara* means decay (*jīraṇa*).
"It undergoes division" and "it enters"—thus it is called *jalābu* according to the Saddanīti. "Jala" refers to the *kalala* (the embryo in its first stage).

It is called *jalābu* because it envelops (*āvunāti*), conceals (*avati*), or protects (*rakkhati*) that; it is the membrane surrounding the fetus. "Saṃseda" means that things sink or dissolve therein.
[Examples include] putrid fish and the like, ghee, oil and the like, the interior of a lotus, the interior of a bamboo, the hollow of a tree, flowers, fruits, and so forth.

With the entire surface of his body moistened by perspiration. Because they are born with all their limbs and minor members complete at the very moment of rebirth, as if leaping up from here and there, they are called *opapātika* (spontaneously born).
However, in the *Vibhāvani*:

Thinking that even those born from eggs and so forth are indeed called "falling" (uppatantā) when they descend into the eggshell and such, and thus fearing the undesirable consequence that they too would be classified as *opapātika* (spontaneously born),
[the author] says they are *opapātika* because "there is a falling (*upapāto*) for them. Furthermore, in this context,
a distinguished kind of spontaneous birth is intended by way of delimiting the highest possible state (the *ukkaṃsagati*), just as one might say, "A maiden should be given to one who is handsome."
"By way of the highest degree" means by way of excellence, which is defined as the state of having complete sense bases (*āyatana*).
Among these, those born spontaneously (*opapātika*) are born with a selfhood (*attabhāva*) that is entirely complete, including all major and minor limbs.

Furthermore, they have no need for further growth. In the case of moisture-born beings (*saṃsedaja*), however, only the sense bases are complete; the major and minor limbs become complete only after further growth.
It should be understood that these have "arisen. "By way of inferiority" means by way of deficiency.
It is said that they are never found in those born blind, deaf from birth, or lacking [the sense organs], because such states are possible for them; this is the support [for the argument].
In that regard, all of these are sometimes not found among those born in happy or miserable destinies who are born without roots (ahetuka) or by moisture (saṃsedaja). In a happy destiny...
However, the state of being spontaneously born (*opapātika*)—which is the acquisition of a superior personal existence—is not obtained through any inferior kamma.
Therefore, among those of noble rebirth who are spontaneously born, there is no deficiency of sense faculties, except for the beings of the first eon who were devoid of [certain] elements.
Even among those of miserable rebirth, they occasionally possess the nature of eyes and ears.

It should be stated as a deficiency [of the nose] itself; it is not a deficiency of the nose-faculty (*ghāna-vekallatā*). For it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* that "there is no spontaneously born being (*opapātika*) in the sense-sphere realm (*kāmadhātu*) who is without a nose.
It should be understood that a deficiency of the tongue-faculty (*jivhā-vekallatā*) does not exist for anyone at all.
Thus, it is said in the *Dhammahadayavibhaṅga*:

It is said: "At the moment of rebirth in the sense-sphere realm (*kāmadhātu*), for some eleven bases (*āyatana*) become manifest; for some ten; for others another ten; for some nine; and for some seven bases become manifest.

Therein, "in the sense-sphere realm" means in the world of desire (*kāmāvacara*). "At the moment of rebirth" means at the moment of the arising of the rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhicitta*).
Regarding the four statements beginning with "for some eleven bases," moisture-born and spontaneously born beings are described. "For some seven bases" refers to...

Here, however, only those born from a womb (*gabbhaseyyaka*) are mentioned. In that regard, since what is called the "sevenfold base" (*sattāyatana*) is not found at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), but is found only during the course of existence (*pavatti*), it is therefore stated as "eleven bases.
For some, there are ten due to the deficiency of the eye; for others, another ten due to the deficiency of the ear; and for others, nine due to the deficiency of both the eye and the ear.

This was stated by way of the deficiency of two [faculties]. And if there were such a thing as a "spontaneously born" (opapātika) being who lacked a nose, then three sets of ten would have been stated together with those of pure birth who lack a nose;
likewise, three sets of nine and one set of eight would have been stated by way of the three impaired faculties—namely, those born blind, those born deaf, and those lacking a nose. Thus...
However, because it is not stated [in that context], it is not understood that there is any instance of a spontaneously born (*opapātika*) being who lacks a nose.

Furthermore, since in the *Indriya-vāra* section of that same *Vibhaṅga* it says "spontaneously born beings who are neuter" (*napuṃsakānaṃ opapātikānaṃ*), and because it does not mention those who lack sexual organs—excluding only those of the first cosmic age—it follows that there is indeed no spontaneously born being who lacks sexual organs.

Nevertheless, although it is not explicitly stated in the Canon (*pāḷi*), the specific types of deficiencies in the eye and other faculties among moisture-born beings (*saṃsedaja*) as described [in the Vibhaṅga] are established by way of the Commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*).
This should be understood. As it has been said: "At most, there are seventy material phenomena in the moisture-born and spontaneously born modes of birth; or, at least, there are thirty.
In this context, "thirty" refers to the thirty material phenomena by way of the three decads—the tongue-decad, the body-decad, and the heart-base-decad.
Indeed, it is stated in the *Mahāṭīkā* that this statement was made with reference to moisture-born beings. [Thus spoke] the teacher, the Elder Nanda.

However, since in the *Yamaka* (Book of Pairs) the mutual inseparable occurrence (*avinābhāvavutti*) of the nose and tongue faculties is stated, it is intended that there is no deficiency of the nose faculty just as there is no deficiency of the tongue faculty. But in the *Indriya-yamaka*:
"Or, for whomsoever the female faculty arises, does the nose faculty arise for him? [The answer is: "For those who are noseless..."
For females being reborn, the female faculty arises, but the nose faculty does not arise for them.
Or, conversely, for whomsoever the male faculty arises, the nose faculty arises for them;
however, it is stated that for males being reborn who are noseless, the male faculty arises, but the nose faculty does not arise for them.
Therefore, it is logical that there is also a deficiency of the nose (*ghāna-vekallatā*), according to the method stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*.
However, in the *Vibhāvani*, it is said:
"In the *Yamaka*, the coexistence of the nose and tongue is mentioned; therefore, since [a being] without a tongue is impossible, [it follows that] one without a nose is also [impossible]."

They describe it precisely as non-existence. Even there, just as the eye and ear function in the fine-material realm (rūpabhava) without the nose and tongue, the nose and tongue do not function without each other.

Because both fail to arise in the fine-material realm, their concomitance is stated by way of their individual non-occurrence in the sense-sphere realm (kāmabhava); thus, it cannot be said that this is impossible. That [explanation] is logical.

For in the section on "abodes" (*okāsa-vāra*), absolute concomitance was stated; however, it is not possible to state such absolute concomitance regarding persons (*puggala*) merely by what has been said.

Those who lie in the womb, that is, in the mother’s belly, are called "womb-dwellers" (*gabbhaseyyaka*). They are called "beings" (*satta*) because they settle upon and cling to the aggregates (*khandha*) such as form and so forth.
As it is said: "Rādha, whatever desire, whatever lust, whatever delight, and whatever craving there is for form—that is where one is stuck."
"Attached to that, therefore it is called a 'being' (satta)," and so forth. "And those beings who dwell in the womb" is a compound.
Both the egg-born and the womb-born. Three sets of ten [factors] appear; those which are called the *kalala*.
The intention is that the "tenfold set of factors" (*bhāvadasaka*) is sometimes not obtained for a neuter being. Having done so, in the *Dhammahadayavibhaṅga* regarding those born from a womb...
It is stated that for beings who are without roots and are neuter, four faculties manifest at the moment of rebirth:
the body faculty, the mind faculty, the life faculty, and the equanimity faculty. "Thereafter" means after the moment of conception for those born from a womb.
"At the time of the course of existence" refers to the eleventh week; for thus it is said in the *Kathāvatthu-aṭṭhakathā*: "The remaining..."

It is said that four [faculties] arise on the seventy-seventh night. Therein, "the remaining ones" refers to the four sense bases—eye, ear, nose, and tongue—remaining after the body base and the mind base.
"On the seventy-seventh night" means on the night marking the conclusion of the eleventh week.
This meaning should be illustrated by the *Yamakaṭīkā*, for it is stated therein:

For one who is to have their final existence as a womb-born being at the moment of rebirth, the visible base (*rūpāyatana*) will not arise eleven months and seven days prior [to birth], yet the eye base (*cakkhāyatana*) will not fail to arise.
Furthermore, for whomsoever, wherever the visible base has arisen, the nose base (*ghānāyatana*) arises there.
This applies to those passing away from the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) who are without a nose, and to those being reborn in the sense-sphere or the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*).
In that context, the base of visible form (*rūpāyatana*) had arisen. Regarding the statement, "But for them, the base of the nose (*ghānāyatana*) does not arise there," it is said:
"for those who are reborn in the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) without a nose.
This refers to those beings who will die before the eleventh week [of gestation]; for them, by the karma that produces the base of the nose...

And it is stated by way of those who have already taken rebirth-linking. Furthermore, in this context, although the ear and tongue are not explicitly mentioned when the eye and nose are mentioned, they are nonetheless established by implication.
As for what is stated in the *Vibhāvani*:
It is stated: “At the time of the occurrence, on the seventh day. That should not be accepted, because it contradicts the *Aṭṭhakathā*.
And in such instances, the *Aṭṭhakathā* is the authority.
[200] And as for that which is therein...
“It is said, ‘According to the opinion of the author of the *Ṭīkā*, on the eleventh day. That too is not correct.
For it is impossible to claim that a determination stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* is the opinion of the author of the *Ṭīkā*. And as for what is there...”
“As for the statement: ‘The eye-decad appears first; after the passing of seven days, the ear-decad [appears]; after the passing of another seven days, the nose-decad;
after the passing of another seven days, the tongue-decad—thus it is said to appear in succession,’ that too is not to be accepted.
For it contradicts the aforementioned commentary.”
[202] As for what was stated there—"For this meaning is also shown in the Aṭṭhakathā"—that too is not correct.
For there is no such Aṭṭhakathā in which such a sequence of arising (uppattikkama) could be shown. Is it not the case that [this is found] in the Paṭiccasamuppāda-aṭṭhakathās?
Alternatively, the preceding cycle of existence was stated by way of the womb-born (*gabbhaseyyaka*). If it is argued that this was stated "to illustrate the sequential occurrence," we say no;

for that was stated with reference to the five-worded formula found in the Canon, which proceeds according to the sequence of the relationship between cause and effect among the five factors beginning with consciousness. However, in the commentaries on the *Āyatana-niddesa*, that [explanation] is indeed rejected.
Nor can it be said that the sequence of arising, which is rejected in the *Aṭṭhakathās*, is shown here by the Elder through this reading, "by way of order.
Therefore, even here, "by way of order" means "by way of the order of teaching. Furthermore, the connection [of the phrase] "they were taught" should be understood.
However, in the *Saccasaṅkhepa-ṭīkā*:

Having passed the stage of *sākhāvaṭṭha*, afterwards, in the seventh week, the sets of eye, ear, nose, tongue, and teeth arise. However, it is stated that the author of the *Ṭīkā* says they arise in the eleventh week; that too is indeed not incorrect.
And here, the sequence of the arising of the *kalala* and so forth is stated in the *Saṃyutta Nikāya*.
As it is said: "First there is the *kalala*; from the *kalala* comes the *abbuda*."
"From the *abbuda* the *pesī* arises; from the *pesī* the *ghana* is produced;
from the *ghana* the limbs arise, as do the head-hairs, body-hairs, and nails.
This is stated in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*). In that context, "first" means by the first rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhiviññāṇa*), such as [the consciousness of] Tissa.
There is no name such as "Phussa" [at this stage]. Rather, there is a *kalala* (embryonic mass) the size of a drop of oil resting on the tip of a thread made from three fibers of *jātiuṇṇa* wool.
With reference to this, it was said:
"Just as a drop of sesame oil, or a pure essence of ghee."
Thus, that which resembles color is called *kalala*.

From the *kalala* comes the *abbuda*; therefore, after the lapse of seven days from the *kalala*, there arises what is named the *abbuda*, which has the appearance of water used for washing meat, and the name "kalala" disappears. For it is said:
"For seven days it is the *kalala*, a mass that is fully developed."
As it turns over, that state becomes what is called the *abbuda*.
From that *abbuda*, the *pesi* is born; thus, after the lapse of another seven days, from that *abbuda* there arises what is called the *pesi*, which resembles melted tin.
This should be illustrated by the example of black pepper and molasses. For village boys, having taken well-ripened black peppers, place them inside a cloth...
Having made it into a bundle and squeezed it, they take the essence, place it in a potsherd, and set it out in the sun.
As it dries and continues to dry, it exudes from all sides. Such is the *pesi*; the name "*abbuda*" disappears. And this has been said:
"For seven days it is an *abbuda*, a mass that is fully matured."
"Transforming into that state, it produces what is called the *pesi*.

From the *pesi*, the *ghana* is produced: after seven days from the *pesi*, there arises by means of that what is called the *ghana*, a mass of flesh shaped like a hen's egg. The name "pesi" disappears. And this has also been said:
"For seven days it is the *pesi*; when fully matured, it becomes the *samūhaka*."
"As it turns over, that state called 'solidity' (ghana) arises;
just as a hen’s egg is perfectly round all over,
so too is the shape of the solid mass produced through the condition of kamma."
"Thick branches arise" means that on the fifth week, five swellings (*piḷaka*) arise for the sake of the two hands, the two feet, and the head.
It is with reference to this that it was said: "Monks, on the fifth week, five swellings arise.
"The karma becomes compacted" means that on the forty-second week, these—hair of the head, body hair, and nails—are produced.
And here, the sixth, seventh, and subsequent weeks are the times when the limbs and minor members—the supports for the faculties—have gradually increased and reached maturity.
However, it should be understood that on the final day of the eleventh week, the eye and the other [faculties] arise simultaneously.
As for what follows regarding "like a drop of sesame oil," etc.:

The color and shape of the *kalala* have been described. That was stated with reference to it having increased slightly; it does not refer to its state at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).
For at that time, no such natural color or shape would be discernible by the physical eye.
However, it should be understood through inference as follows: one-seventh of a louse is called a nit (*likkhā*).
The thirty-sixth part of a *likkhā* is called a *rathareṇu*. The thirty-sixth part of a *rathareṇu* is called a *tajjārī*.
The thirty-sixth part of a *tajjārī* is called an *aṇu*. The thirty-sixth part of an *aṇu* is called a *paramāṇu*.

Furthermore, that [paramāṇu] occupies a portion of space and does not come within the range of the fleshly eye; it comes only within the range of the divine eye—so it is said in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*).

It has been stated. Regarding their size, it is said that the atom (aṇu) appears as a series of spheres revolving within the rays of the sun that have entered through a tiny hole or a palm-leaf opening.

However, at the moment of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi), the entire [body]—being merely the measure of three clusters (kalāpa)—would be even more minute than an atom. For it proceeds by way of a continuous succession (santāna).
Since it consists of nothing but a collection of massed material groups accumulated moment by moment, at its minimum limit it would amount to forty-nine such groups.
For if there were fewer than that, the continuity of the stream would be impossible.
As for what is stated in the *Mahāṭīkā*—that "those groups are the size of an atom"—that is merely said in accordance with the mode of attention directed toward the atoms of the elements.

"It is said" should be understood [as follows]. "The second consciousness" refers to the first *bhavaṅga* consciousness. "At the time of its duration" means the period during which the rebirth-linking consciousness persists.

"Depending on the diffusion of nutritive essence" (*ojāpharaṇa*) means that, for those born from a womb, at the time when the state of the embryo has reached the stages of the *abbuda*, *pesi*, *ghana*, and so forth, the nutritive essence—which has become a lubricant—derived from the food swallowed by the mother and residing in her stomach, [flows] through the umbilical cord.
According to the sequence, starting from the time of the pervasion of the physical basis,
as it is said: "Whatever food, drink, and nourishment his mother eats,
by that he sustains himself there, being within the mother's womb."
And in the *Aṭṭhakathā* it says, "By that he sustains himself there. For the *nāḷi* (tube) that has arisen from his navel is connected as one with the membrane of the mother’s womb;
it is hollow like the stalk of a lotus. Through it, the essence of food flows and produces the matter originated by food (*āhārasamuṭṭhānarūpa*).
In this way, he sustains himself for ten months. "Entered into the mother’s womb" means entered into the mother’s womb through her [side].

The meaning is stated as "having entered within the mother’s womb. In that context, however, it should be understood that the phrase "the tube has not yet arisen" refers to the time when the umbilical cord has not yet emerged;
for at the stage of the *abbuda* (the oval stage) and so forth, no such thing called a "tube" could have arisen.
But in the case of moisture-born (*saṃsedaja*) and spontaneously born (*upapātika*) beings, at the time of swallowing whatever they have obtained or even their own saliva...
Based on the pervasion by nutritive essence (*ojā*). Therefore it was said: "based on the pervasion by nutritive essence, [they are] born of nutriment.
"Of the seventeenth consciousness above the death-consciousness" means of the seventeenth *bhavaṅga* consciousness in the period prior to the death-consciousness.
Kamma-born material phenomena do not arise because they have simply not arisen from that point onward; therefore, the seventeenth...

There is what is called "death-consciousness" (*cuticitta*). "Nothing else" means that the phrase "prior to that" is said with reference specifically to the moment of arising of that seventeenth consciousness.
"After that" means in the moment following the death-consciousness, measured by sixteen moments of consciousness.

Both "consciousness-born matter" and "nutriment-born matter"—that is, the continuity of consciousness-born matter and the continuity of nutriment-born matter—are cut off within the continuity of non-clung-to matter.
Because their arising is impossible [there]. Whatever needs to be said regarding this has already been stated in the section on the origination of matter (*rūpasamuṭṭhāna*).

As for the "decad of existence" (*bhāvadasaka*), it is originated by kamma rooted in sensual lust; therefore, its non-attainment is stated in the fine-material world (*rūpaloka*), which is produced by kamma consisting in the cultivation of detachment from that [lust].

Furthermore, nutritive groups (*āhāraja-kalāpa*) are not found there, because food that has been swallowed does not exist in a state of being "existence" (*bhāva*); and for that very reason, [they are absent] in what pertains to the body.
This is because even internal nutriment has the nature of originating matter.
However, the Venerable Ācariya Ānanda Thera describes the absence of odors, tastes, and nutritive essence (*ojā*) even within the material groups found therein.
At the moment of rebirth in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), the five sense bases (*āyatana*) appear: the eye base, the visible-form base, the ear base, and the mind base.
Regarding the "base of mental phenomena" (dhammāyatana), five elements manifest: the eye-element, the form-element, the ear-element, the mind-consciousness-element, and the mental-phenomena-element;
and three nutriments manifest: the nutriment of contact, the nutriment of mental volition, and the nutriment of consciousness—since this is stated in the Vibhaṅga.
And here, although tangible objects are excluded from the world of form in the Pāḷi text...
Because other functions exist there, the presence of the great primary elements (*mahābhūta*) is not prohibited.
However, odors and so forth have no other function by which they might persist even in the state of being mere phenomena (*dhammamatta*);
therefore, the Master’s intention is that their non-mention indicates their absence there. Likewise, the tetrad of primary elements is present there.
It certainly exists, as it has been said: "In the case of non-percipient beings, depending on one great primary element (mahābhūta), there are three great primary elements," and so forth.
However, the tangible base (phoṭṭhabbāyatana) and the tangible element (phoṭṭhabbadhātu) are excluded therein.

Therefore, although all phenomena (dhammas) are equal in their status as phenomena because they possess intrinsic nature (sabhāva), it is by virtue of a specific functional activity (kiccavisesa) that they are called "odor," "taste," "the tangible," and "edible nutriment" (kabaḷīkārāhāra). Of that—
Because they do not exist, they are not found there under those names; with this in mind, their negation is stated everywhere—in the *Vibhaṅga*, the *Kathāvatthu*, and the *Yamaka*.

However, it is said that since these [derived phenomena] exist as mere states (dhamma) which are the outflow (*nisanda*) of the great primary elements (*mahābhūta*), it would be logical for them to be included within the base of mental objects (*dhammāyatana*) and the element of mental objects (*dhammadhātu*). Thus, there are three decads.

Regarding the phrase "the life-nonad" (*jīvitanavaka*): according to the opinion of Ācariya Ānanda, one should state that there are three heptads—the eye-heptad, the ear-heptad, and the base-heptad—and a hexad of life.

"He desires" means that when [something] is not obtainable, having first excluded it, it remains by virtue of being obtainable therein; the sense is that it is "in excess. And here, in the world of form (*rūpaloka*)...
Why is the "vital nonad" (*jīvitanavaka*) not mentioned separately in the sense-sphere world (*kāmaloka*) as it is?

However, in the fine-material sphere (*rūpaloka*), because there is no other life-force that sustains the nutriment and pervades the entire body to protect it, this [vital nonad] alone stands in the place of both and protects the whole body;
thus, it is clearly stated there as a separate "vital nonad. In the sense-sphere world...
However, there are many other supporting and protective factors that are well-known. Therefore, because the life-nonad (*jīvita-navaka*) is not prominent, it was not mentioned separately.

Furthermore, even in the sense-sphere world (*kāmaloka*), this [heat] exists by way of its power to digest what is eaten and so forth, and by way of the bodily fire known as heat (*uṣman*), which protects the entire body and constitutes its very source of vitality.
This is quite evident. With reference to this, it is said:
"When life, heat, and consciousness leave this body, then it lies cast away like a useless log."
In this context, "life" (*āyu*) refers specifically to the life-force established upon those two fires. "Heat" (*usmā*) refers to those two fires.
When these become unbalanced through excess or deficiency, various ailments arise in the body. As it is said:
"He is subject to many afflictions, subject to many calamities; he is possessed of a digestive fire that is irregular in its digestion—being either excessively hot or excessively cold."
But when the elements are in equilibrium, beings are free from affliction. As it is said: "He is free from illness; he is free from disease; he possesses a digestive heat that is well-balanced;
it is neither too cold nor too hot, but moderate and fit for striving. Some, however, think this refers only to the fire that digests what is eaten and so forth.
But the Elder [Buddhaghosa], in the *Pariccheda* on Name-and-Form, stated that the "vital nonad" may exist separately in the form-world (*rūpaloka*).

In the *Visuddhimagga*, however, it is stated that among the remaining fourfold-originated [material phenomena], thirty-three material qualities each are evident: namely, the eight life-nonads and the three nutritive-nonads. Therein, "in the eight" refers to the eight [bases]:
the three fire-elements excluding the digestive fire and the breaths, and the five air-elements. Thus, even in the sense-sphere world (*kāmaloka*), [these are present].
Because it is found in the elements of fire and air that pervade the entire body, this [cessation] should be understood as occurring in the whole body itself.
Here it might be asked: "Why, then, is the sequence of the cessation of material aggregates not stated for the realm of form (rūpaloka) as it is for the realm of desire (kāmaloika)?
It is because there is no difference; for even in the realm of form, at the time of death, the death-consciousness (cuti-citta) lasts for the duration of seventeen moments of consciousness.
The sequence of cessation beginning with "no material qualities born of kamma arise" is exactly the same as in the case of the sense-sphere world (*kāmaloka*).
However, here there is no such thing as the cessation of nutriment-born matter, nor the casting off of the physical body.
Therefore, even in that case, after the death-consciousness (*cuticitta*), the continuity of mind-born matter is severed in a single moment measured by sixteen consciousness-moments.
It is logical that thereafter the succession of temperature-born material phenomena (utu-samuṭṭhāna-rūpa) continues for only the duration of one or two finger-snap moments and then ceases.
Yet, even though the stream of matter persists for such a brief time, it is not possible to perceive what is called a "corpse" during that interval;
for to those who look, the disappearance of the body appears as if occurring in a single moment.
And just as it is in the fine-material world (rūpaloka), so too in the sense-sphere world (kāmaloka) for the gods born there and for other beings of spontaneous birth (opapātika).

For their bodies, because they are produced at the very moment of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) with a completely perfected body born of kamma, are filled solid with kamma-born material phenomena (kammajarūpa) and are light in their burden.
Other types of material phenomena arise only after being established upon those kamma-born material phenomena.
Therefore, at the time of their death, when the material phenomena born of karma have ceased, those three bases are unable to sustain the continuity for long.
After proceeding for a short while, they cease entirely. It should be understood that there is no such thing as the "laying down of a body" for them.
[203] As for what is stated in the *Vibhāvani*:

“At the time of death, however, because there is no laying down of a body for the Brahmās, for all of them the threefold-originated and twofold-originated [formations] cease simultaneously,” that is not correct.
For if that were so, it would follow that the death-proximate consciousnesses of all material Brahmās do not produce form.
For it cannot be said that the material phenomena arising from the consciousness at the moment of death cease simultaneously with the material phenomena born of kamma;

rather, just as those kamma-born material phenomena continue to exist for a short while after their cessation, so too it is not impossible to understand that the temperature-born material phenomena also continue to exist for a short while after the cessation of the consciousness-born material phenomena. And it is not by that much alone...
Even when these [deities] are active during their time, it is possible for them to perform the laying down of the body.

However, because the Brahmas possess the class of hindrances such as sloth and torpor (*thina-middha*), a transformation of lightness, heaviness, and so forth—corresponding to those [hindrances]—is possible in both the mind-born material phenomena (*cittaja-rūpa*) and the temperature-born material phenomena (*utu-ja-rūpa*) that follow them;
thus, including the triad of lightness and the rest, it was stated [as follows].
"Twenty-three material phenomena": this means that twenty-three material phenomena exist when the triad beginning with the nose and the two types of non-existence are excluded.
Those same [twenty-three], excluding the eye, ear, base, and the two modes of intimation, constitute the seventeen material phenomena of non-percipient beings; such is the construction.

Furthermore, the specific characteristics of non-percipient beings, such as heaviness and lightness, need not be considered here, for there is no alteration through being affected (ruppana) among material phenomena.

"Because it is of great service": "In rebirth" means at the moment of arising (*uppādakkhaṇa*) of the rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) of those in the sense-sphere, fine-material, and immaterial realms. For it is precisely the moment of arising that is invariably called the "moment of rebirth.

"But in the course of existence" means that from the moment of the duration (*ṭhitikkhaṇa*) of the rebirth-linking onwards, throughout the entire period of the course of existence (*pavatti*), nothing whatsoever is not obtained;
rather, everything is indeed obtained—this is the intended meaning. For this is not the case... [end of fragment].
"Matter is not obtained during the course of existence (pavatta); it is obtained only at rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi). Thus it 'exists'. [The Sequence of the Course of Matter] 161.

Having thus made a compendium of consciousness, mental factors, and matter, he now speaks the passage beginning with "Nibbāna, moreover," making a compendium of Nibbāna as it has not yet been reached.
The connection is: "Nibbāna, however, is called 'Nibbāna'"; it is reckoned as supramundane (lokuttara).
"Supramundane" is what was spoken by the Blessed One; as he said: "Which phenomena are supramundane?
The four noble paths, the four fruits of recluseship, and the unconditioned element—these phenomena are supramundane.
By this, he excludes the possibility that *nibbāna* is a mere conceptual designation (*paññatti-matta*). For a designation established through worldly convention cannot be called "supramundane."

"Is to be realized. "To be realized by the knowledge of the four paths" means it is to be seen directly by the noble ones who have attained the knowledge of the four paths with their eyes, just as one with sight sees the lunar disk;
the meaning is that it is to be penetrated. In this context, by the phrase "by the knowledge of the four paths," [it refers to] from the path of practice for such a one...
This shows that for those face-averse blind worldlings, it is outside their range of perception, just as the lunar disk is for those born blind.
Yet, the lunar disk does not truly cease to exist simply because it is not perceived by the eyes of the born blind.
By the term "to be realized," he shows its existence in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*). For whatever...
In the ultimate sense, that which exists does not exist [as a self]. To whom, then, could it possibly be directly perceived in its own form?
By both of these points, he demonstrates that for wise, virtuous worldlings (*kalyāṇaka-puthujjana*), it is established through inference;
for indeed, there can be no effort toward the realization of that which is unestablished and unmanifest even to one's own intellect through inference. By means of which [inference], realization...
It attains accomplishment (*siddhi*). Having thus shown that Nibbāna exists in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*), it is now stated that it is not merely existent;
rather, it is to show that it possesses great majesty (*mahātejavanta*) and great power (*mahojavanta*), it is said to be the objective support (*ālambana*) for the paths and fruits.
By this, he shows that without this Nibbāna, the paths and fruits cannot fulfill their function. Therefore, its great majesty...
This illustrates its great power. For instance, there was once a king of great psychic power.

In his kingdom, in a certain large village, there lived a village headman and a chief bandit with a large following; these two were constantly plotting against one another for the sake of killing each other.
Thereupon, the village headman went to the city and attended upon the king.
Thus, before long, he became a favorite of the king and received a great decree from the king.
Hearing this, the chief of the bandits thought, "Now there is no life for me living here," and entered the forest together with his own retinue.
But the village headman, refusing to release him even though he had entered the forest, seized him and executed him. Such is the present situation.
It should be understood thus: Nibbāna is like a king of great power; knowledge (ñāṇa) is like a village headman; delusion (moha) is like a chief thief;

the remaining defilements are like the thieves who accompany him. Just as the village headman was [negligent] when he did not attend upon the king previously, so is the knowledge of an ordinary person (puthujjana).
But at the time of attending upon him, it is like the knowledge of the Path (maggañāṇa), just as the village headman is [diligent]. While craving (taṇhā) is active...
It proceeds by becoming entangled among the phenomena such as the aggregates, distinguished as internal, external, and so forth. As it has been said:
"Tangle within, tangle without; beings are entangled in a tangle.
Therefore, like a bamboo branch in a bamboo thicket, it receives the designation "weaving" (vāna) in the sense of weaving together or in the sense of binding.

"Or from craving, which is called 'desire' (vāna). "Because it has gone out" (nikkhantattā) means because it has escaped. The meaning is: because it stands having transcended the state of being an object for that [craving].
By this, he shows the meaning: "Nirvana is so called because it has gone out from desire. "By its own nature" (sabhāvato) means by way of its characteristic of peace (santi).
It is in the sense of the extinguishing of the threefold burning of the cycle of existence (vaṭṭa) that has arisen within. Of those...
The meaning is: "in the sense of absolute non-existence. As for the phrase "even of one kind":

although consciousness is of one kind by way of its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), it is nevertheless differentiated by way of its object through distinctions such as birth, plane, association, and so forth, as well as by distinctions of time, direction, place, and person.
Nibbāna is not like that. Rather, this [Nibbāna] is of one kind, being undifferentiated both by way of its intrinsic nature and by way of its object.

It is so. For this [consciousness] is one and the same for all those who have attained final nibbāna—whether Buddhas, Pacceka-buddhas, or disciples of the Buddha—throughout the past, present, and future of this beginningless saṃsāra. Why? Because it is a dhamma that cannot be pointed out.
For the Blessed One has said: "Consciousness is non-manifesting, infinite, and luminous on every side. In that context, "consciousness" refers to...
Because it is established as the state of the destruction and cessation of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhata-dhamma*),
this must be understood by making it clearly manifest through that very nature. It is "incomparable" (*anidassana*) because, being a signless phenomenon (*animitta-dhamma*),

it cannot be demonstrated by any sign that is an object of perception for foolish worldlings (*bāla-puthujjana*), nor by distinctions of time, direction, place, individual continuity, or qualities such as inferior or superior.
The meaning is that it cannot be demonstrated by making [the parts] distinct. "Endless" (*ananta*) means devoid of a prior or subsequent limit.

"Radiating light in every direction" (*sabbatopabha*) means shining forth from all sides with infinite rays of virtue established as the antidote to the suffering of cyclic existence (*vaṭṭa-dukkha*).

Furthermore, because its nature cannot be pointed out, even throughout the beginningless cycle of rebirth (*anamatagga-saṃsāra*) and in all directions, [it cannot be said to be] "in such-and-such a place..."
It cannot be said that "in such-and-such a time, in such-and-such a direction, [this] does not exist. Why?
Because it is obtainable at all times and in all places by virtue of its necessity to be attained by one developing the Noble Path, whenever and wherever that may be.
For this has been stated in the Vinaya, in the Aṅguttara Nikāya, and in the Udāna:
“Just as, monks, whatever rivers in the world flow into the great ocean,
and whatever showers of rain fall from the sky, the great ocean is not perceived to be either diminished or filled by them;
even so, monks, though many monks attain final nibbāna through the element of nibbāna without residue, it is not thereby [diminished].”
"Is there any deficiency or fullness perceived in the element of Nibbāna?
In the commentaries it is also said: "Neither deficiency nor fullness is perceived in the element of Nibbāna by that [fact];
even if Buddhas do not arise for incalculable great aeons, not even a single being is unable to attain final Nibbāna. Even then, it remains empty..."
It cannot be said that the element of Nibbāna (nibbāna-dhātu) is full. However, during the time of a Buddha, even at each single assembly, incalculable beings attain the Deathless (amata).
Even then, it cannot be said that the element of Nibbāna is full; thus it has been stated.

And in the *Brahmanimantanika Sutta*, consciousness is described as "invisible, infinite, and all-pervading" (viññāṇaṃ anidassanaṃ anantaṃ sabbatopabhaṃ). Furthermore, in the commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), regarding the phrase "all-pervading":
"Endowed with radiance on all sides. For there is no other state (dhamma) whatsoever more luminous, more brilliant, more pure, or more white than Nibbāna.

Or, it is "abundant on all sides" (sabbatopabhu-taṃ). It is said that one cannot say, "Nibbāna does not exist in such-and-such a direction," regarding the eastern direction and so forth; thus it is called "abundant on all sides" (sabbatopataṃ).

Even though this is so, it is said "with a residue remaining" (*saupādisesa*), etc., because although this [Nibbāna] is known by relying on phenomena that have ceased in the three times, it is possible to apply the designation [of "residue"] by making a distinction based on the cessation of those phenomena. In that context, "residue" (*upādi*) means that which is grasped—that is, intensely seized—by craving and views;
it refers to the pentad of aggregates that are clung to (*upādinnakhandha*). That very [pentad], either partially or without remainder...

"Upādisesa" means that which remains by virtue of the kamma-defilements having been abandoned. That state of existence in which an "upādisesa" exists within that continuum at the time it is attained is "saupādisesa.
"Nibbānadhātu" is the state of being extinguished (nibbuti). The compound "saupādisesanibbānadhātu" is thus [the state of] the element of extinction with a remainder.
That state of existence in which no "upādisesa" exists within that continuum at the time it is attained is "anupādisesa"; and [the state of] being without a remainder...
The analysis of the compound is: "that which is the element of Nibbāna" (*sā nibbānadhātu*). For this has been stated in the *Itivuttaka*: "Monks, there are two elements of Nibbāna. Which two?

The element of Nibbāna with residue remaining (*saupādisesa*) and the element of Nibbāna without residue remaining (*anupādisesa*)," and so forth. Therein, the former is called the Nibbāna of the defilements (*kilesa-nibbāna*);
the latter is called the Nibbāna of the aggregates (*khandha-nibbāna*). Alternatively, the former is called the Nibbāna pertaining to the present life (*diṭṭhadhammika-nibbāna*).

The latter is called *nibbāna* pertaining to the future life (*samparāyika*). As it is said: "For there is one element here pertaining to the present life (*diṭṭhadhammika*), which is with remainder (*saupādisesa*) and is the conduit to becoming;

but that which is without remainder (*anupādisesa*) pertains to the future life. Furthermore, in the *Aṅguttara Nikāya*, in the *Sattaka Nipāta*, regarding those liberated in both ways (*ubhatobhāgavimutta*)—the two types of *khīṇāsava* who are liberated by wisdom—it is stated that they are distinguished by way of the aggregates with remainder as "body-witness" (*kāyasakkhin*) and "attainer through vision" (*diṭṭhippatto*).

In that same [text], in the ninth chapter, the state of having a residue remaining (saupādisesa) and the state of having no residue remaining (anupādisesa) are taught for four types of trainees (sekkha)—namely, those known as the faith-liberated (saddhāvimutta) and the Dhamma-follower (dhammānusārī)—as well as for the noble ordinary person (kalyāṇaputhujjana) who has initiated insight (vipassanā), with respect to the defilements (kilesa). In that very same place, it is said:

"one who attains Parinibbāna in the interval (antarāparinibbāyī), one who attains Parinibbāna upon landing (upahaccaparinibbāyī), one who attains Parinibbāna without exertion (asaṅkhāraparinibbāyī), one who attains Parinibbāna with exertion (sasaṅkhāraparinibbāyī), and one who goes upstream to the Akaniṭṭha realm (uddhaṃsota-akaniṭṭhagāmī)."

The state of having a residue remaining (saupādisesa) is stated for the nine trainee persons (sekkhapuggala)—namely, the five non-returners, the once-returner, and the three stream-enterers—by way of the remaining substrate of defilements (kilesupādisesa).
However, in the *Nettippakaraṇa*, even the fruit of arhatship is called "nirvana with a residue remaining. That [definition] is not intended here.

In this context, at the moment of the path (*magga-khaṇa*), the destruction of the defilements (*kilesa*) is called "with residue" (*saupādisesa*). The non-arising of the aggregates (*khandha*) immediately after death is called "without residue" (*anupādisesa*).

Since the bonds of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi-bandha*) arise only when defilements exist and do not arise when they do not, these [bonds] are also destroyed together with the destruction of the defilements.
The continuity of the present aggregates (*paccuppanna-khandha-santāna*) that persists until death—

However, even for one whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*), there exists—arising from the overflow of the results of kamma and defilements active in previous existences—a natural law established for all beings.
Therefore, even though his defilements are exhausted, that [natural law] continues to function until death.

At the moment of death, its cessation is likewise merely the cessation according to the nature of things (*dhammatā-nirodha*). As for the non-arising of renewed existence immediately thereafter, that is...
It is established simultaneously with the destruction of the defilements (*kilesakkhaya*). It is not only that there is no further existence immediately thereafter;
even beyond that, the non-arising of the succession of existences throughout the beginningless cycle of rebirth (*anamatagga-saṃsāra*) is also established by that very same [destruction].

All of this is indeed one and the same *nibbāna*. Nevertheless, because there remains a residue of the aggregates (*khandhāvasesa*), this distinction is stated by way of that residual trace of existence.
"It is said to be twofold by way of cause" means that it is twofold from the perspective of the reason for its designation.
For conditioned phenomena (saṅkhata-dhammā), because they are states accompanied by obstacles, constantly afflict people with various hindrances;
they cry out that the bliss of peace (santa-sukha) cannot be attained. And because of the nature of the defilements (kilesa) and of aging, death, and so forth, they possess signs (sanimitto).

They serve as the basis and the ground for all misfortunes. And because they possess a specific intention (*sapaṇihita-dhammatā*), they constantly generate what is called the suffering of hope (*āsā-dukkha*), which is the root of all suffering.
Therefore, in order to demonstrate its threefold division by means of the distinct qualities established as its opposite, he said "emptiness" (*suññatā*) and so forth.
In that context, it is "emptiness" because it is secluded from all impediments (*palibodha*).
For when personality-belief exists, all the obstacles of evil kamma and the obstacles of suffering in the states of loss that appear to fools,
as well as all the obstacles of wholesome kamma that appear to the wise for the purpose of protecting themselves from it—
all these obstacles rooted in personality-belief are brought to cessation by the very cessation of personality-belief itself.
It is capable [of doing so]. There is no other way apart from that. Therefore, its cessation is secluded from those obstacles (*palibodha*);
likewise, the destruction of lust (*rāgakkhaya*) alone is capable of ceasing the obstacles rooted in lust. There is no other way apart from that.

The same applies to the destruction of hatred (*dosakkhaya*) regarding obstacles rooted in hatred, and the destruction of delusion (*mohakkhaya*) regarding obstacles rooted in delusion, and so forth. Thus, Nibbāna is [secluded] from all obstacles.
Seclusion is called emptiness (*suññatā*).
A "sign" (*nimitta*) refers to a gross aspect rooted in arising and occurrence;
that which is possessed by conditioned phenomena makes them the basis and the ground for all defilements, aging, and death, as well as for all Māras.
They serve as the basis and the ground for all enmities and all harmful conditions such as diseases;

therefore, they are called "the realm of Māra" and "the realm of Death. They undergo differentiation according to distinctions such as time, direction, location, and continuity, as well as according to distinctions such as inferior and superior.
Nibbāna, however, exists by way of the destruction and cessation of all conditioned phenomena characterized by signs (*nimitta*).
Because it is established, there is no [further need for proof]. "In that sign" means the signless (*animitta*).
For, having destroyed the sign-phenomena which serve as the basis for all disadvantages such as the defilements, it remains eternally, establishing the non-existence of those disadvantages.
And it is not differentiated by differences in time. This [was taught] in the past, in such-and-such an eon, by such-and-such a Buddha...

Nirvana is not differentiated by time, such that one might say, "This is in the future" or "This is now. Nor is it differentiated by difference of direction, such that one might say, "This is the nirvana in the direction named so-and-so among the ten directions," or "This is in the direction named so-and-so.

Nor is it differentiated by difference of location or difference of continuity, such that one might say, "This is in the human world," "This is in the deva world," "This is in the Brahma world," or "This is for humans," and so forth.
This Brahma-sphere of the devas extends infinitely. Likewise, it is not divided by distinctions such as "superior" and so forth. [One does not think: "This belongs to the omniscient Buddhas;
this belongs to the Paccekabuddhas; this belongs to the disciples of the Buddha.
*Paṇihita*, *paṇidhāna*, *paṇidhi*, *patthanā*, *āsā*, *jighacchā*, and *pipāsā* are one in meaning.
Even though conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhata-dhammā*) are obtainable, because they are subject to disintegration, the hope to obtain them again and again is indeed called suffering.
There is no end to the suffering of hope. Furthermore, all suffering has its root in hope; there is no source of suffering like hope.
Nibbāna, however, because it is by its very nature the cessation of thirst, is designated as "hope."
There is no such thing as "it proceeds" while one is removing or dispelling every aspiration of craving (*taṇhā-panidhi*) or aspiration of desire (*chanda-panidhi*).

That which is directed toward that [state] is "undirected" (*appaṇihita*). Furthermore, here there are two kinds of happiness: the happiness of feeling (*vedayita-sukha*) and the happiness of peace (*santi-sukha*).
Among these, it refers to the joy and gladness (*pīti-somanassa*) that occurs by way of experiencing the attainments of humans, devas, and Brahmas.
What is called "pleasure felt" (vedayita-sukha) is indeed pleasure; however, it is by nature subject to breaking moment by moment like a flash of lightning.
Prosperities, too, are impermanent by nature. All of them merely increase one's boundless suffering of hope.
Therefore, all that is called "pleasure felt" is exclusively suffering because it gives rise to the suffering of hope. As it has been said: "Whatever..."

"Whatever is felt, all that is included within suffering. And when the General of the Dhamma was asked by [the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita], "Friend Sāriputta, what is that bliss in Nibbāna where there is no feeling?", he replied, "In this case, friend, that very absence of feeling is the bliss in Nibbāna.
This so-called "bliss of peace" refers to the non-arising of defilements that have already arisen within oneself or their not arising at all.

It is the happiness of liberation based on one’s own right application toward the defilements and so forth that have presented themselves, as well as the suffering of the states of misery and so forth.
This alone is the absolute happiness and the unshakable happiness here.

For in its absence, even for worldlings experiencing human, divine, or Brahmā success, the terrors of the Avīci hell and so forth remain ever-present in the sense that they are inevitably to be encountered.
Therefore, this term "wishless" (*appaṇihita*), which illuminates the happiness of peace for all suffering rooted in the pleasure of feeling, is one great quality-term for Nibbāna.
"By way of distinction of aspect" means by way of the distinction of the threefold categories of qualities, such as emptiness (*suññatā*) and so forth. And herein, that which...

The cessation and exhaustion of the defilements—which have lain latent within and followed one along throughout the beginningless cycle of existence—occurring right here within at the moment of the Path, is reckoned as the element of exhaustion (*khayadhātu*) and the element of cessation (*nirodhadhātu*).

This is one base of phenomena (*dhammāyatana*), one element of phenomena (*dhammadhātu*), and one ultimate phenomenon (*paramatthadhamma*). It is so by way of its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) in the sense of exhaustion and in the sense of cessation.

Because it exists, for that [Nibbāna] is not a conceptually designated form (*paññatti-rūpa*). Since it is apprehended as a real entity (*sarūpato*) both in the body and through knowledge—given that the realization of Nibbāna is twofold, namely realization by the body (*kāya-sacchikaraṇa*) and realization by knowledge (*ñāṇa-sacchikaraṇa*)—it is as he said:

"One who has conceived desire exerts himself; having exerted himself, he investigates; having investigated, he strives. Being one whose self is resolute, he realizes the ultimate truth (*paramattha-sacca*) by means of the body itself."

He realizes it. And by means of wisdom, he penetrates and sees it. In this context, "realization by the body" (*kāyasacchikaraṇa*) refers to the cessation and extinction right within oneself of those defilements that have come down through the beginningless cycle of existence, having constantly tormented and scorched the internal [mind].
Having thus realized it by the body, one who reviews it again [sees] within oneself...
One sees that cessation directly through knowledge. One knows, "My defilements have ceased"—this is what is called realization by knowledge (*ñāṇasacchikaraṇa*).
Among these two, realization by the body exhausts the endless and immeasurable suffering of the round of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*).

Realization by knowledge produces no small measure of rapture and mental joy. Regarding the phenomena of conceptual designation (*paññattidhamma*), there is indeed no such thing as realization by the body.
Furthermore, because that cessation is a state of emptiness (*suññatā*), a dull-witted person forms the perception of it as void or as useless.
Because it is a signless (*animitta*) state, they form the perception of it as mere non-existence or as something ultimately non-existent.
Because it is a wishless (*appaṇihita*) state, people who are enslaved by craving imagine that there is no such thing as happiness in it.

Furthermore, that which is called Nibbāna is not merely the cessation through exhaustion as previously described. For that [mere cessation] is a mere non-existence, a conceptual designation (*paññatti-rūpa*).
Moreover, Nibbāna is the locus of infinite qualities such as profundity and so forth; a mere non-existence cannot possibly serve as the locus for these.
It is said that "Nibbāna is the supreme happiness," and in a mere non-existence, there is nothing whatsoever.

That which is called "happiness" is indeed obtainable by all. Therefore, they maintain that whatever is the condition for that cessation through destruction (khayanirodha), and by whose power that cessation through destruction is accomplished—that alone is what is called Nibbāna.
Even for them, no purpose beyond the stilling of the suffering of saṃsāra can be found. Furthermore, the qualities of Nibbāna are infinite, as are the phenomena of saṃsāra.

They are established by way of their opposites, and not otherwise. Therefore, however many terms for non-virtues (aguṇa) are found among the phenomena of saṃsāra, that many terms for virtues (guṇa) become infinite and are established upon the destruction and cessation of those [non-virtues].
Even this very destruction and cessation is profound and difficult to comprehend as a distinct state of existence; for it is a mere absence (abhāvamatta).
They imagine it to be a conceptual form (*paññatti-rūpa*). However, there is nothing at all to be said regarding the profundity of its constituent qualities (*guṇa-pada*).
What is called the "bliss of peace" (*santi-sukha*) is simply the subsiding of the sufferings of saṃsāra. For it has been said: "The subsiding of those [sufferings] is bliss.
And this subsiding is precisely their total destruction and cessation; thus, for all feelings of pleasure included within the suffering of saṃsāra—
Thus, the supreme bliss of that cessation through destruction is established as reaching its ultimate excellence.
Regarding its existence in the ultimate sense, first there is this sutta:
"Bhikkhus, there is, O bhikkhus, that which is unborn, unbecome, unmade, and unconditioned. If, bhikkhus, that unborn..."
If there were not the unarisen, the unbecome, the unmade, and the unconditioned, then an escape from what is arisen, become, made,
and conditioned would not be discerned. But because, monks, there exists the unarisen, the unbecome, the unmade, and the unconditioned,
therefore an escape from what is arisen, become, made, and conditioned is discerned.
In this context, "not born" (*ajāta*) means non-knowing; the meaning is the destruction of birth (*jātikkhaya*). "Not become" (*abhūta*) means non-becoming;

the meaning is non-existence (*abhāva*). "Not made" (*akata*) means non-doing. "Unconditioned" (*asaṅkhata*) means non-conditioning. The meaning is the absence of the suffering of formations (*saṅkhāradukkha*), whether in terms of arising or in terms of proceeding.
Alternatively, "the destruction of birth" is a distinct single element of phenomena (*dhammadhātu*). Therefore, with reference to its status as a distinct phenomenon:
The expression “there is no being born here” (*ajātaṃ*) is indeed appropriate. This is what is meant: conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhata-dhammā*) arise when there are conditions;
they do not arise when conditions are absent. Thus, even that which is unarisen exists for them as if it were arisen. The meaning is that it exists in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*).
If there were no such thing as the unarisen, then only the arisen would exist. Such being the case, [it follows] regarding the self (*attani*).
Even for those who practice correctly for the sake of the non-arising of defilements, all defiled phenomena would still have arisen; they would not be unarisen.

Why? Because that which is "unarisen" simply does not exist. This same principle applies to all forms of misconduct, to the suffering of the woeful states and the suffering of the cycle of existence, and to all diseases, afflictions, fears, and calamities in this present life. And this being so, all human efforts in the world...
It was said, "Bhikkhus, [if it were not so], human strength and human exertion would indeed be useless," with reference to this meaning.

However, since that which is unarisen (*ajāta*) exists absolutely, therefore for those who practice correctly for the sake of the unarisen state within themselves, those [defilements] do not arise absolutely. This being so, all human efforts and human strengths...
It is with reference to the meaning that "the sword is indeed the manly exertion of a person" that the passage beginning with "But because, monks...

was spoken. Up to this point, it has been stated: "From the cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of volitional formations; from the cessation of volitional formations comes the cessation of consciousness...
[and so on]... there is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering. Thus, the existence of this cessation as something ultimately real is established.
It shows this because the word *atthi* (is) expresses the sense of existence. In that context, cessation (*nirodha*) is twofold:

cessation of what has arisen and cessation of what has not yet arisen. Therein, cessation after having arisen is called "cessation of the born" (*jātanirodha*). "The end of death" (*maccu-anta*) and "the end of dying" (*maraṇa-anta*) are synonyms for this very thing.
Furthermore, the absolute non-existence of the arising of defilements and so forth included within the internal [person] is "cessation of the unborn" (*ajāta-nirodha*).
Cessation (nirodha): that which is called the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna.
This is what is intended here; for it is precisely this that is called "emptiness" (suññatā) because of its voidness of all impediments.

It is called "signless" (animitta) because of the absence of any sign that serves as the basis for defilements, aging, death, and so forth. [It is the absence] of that which is the source of all suffering...
Because of the absence of the suffering of hope, it is called "the wishless" (*appaṇihita*). Therefore it was said: "Emptiness, the signless, and the wishless—thus it is threefold.
The words beginning with "footprint" (*pada*) are synonyms for Nibbāna. For that is a single ultimate reality (*paramattha-dhamma*) found as distinct, unmixed, and absolute;
thus it is called a "footprint," since the word *pada* has the sense of a "portion" (*koṭṭhāsa*). Just as [one studies] the Dhamma "by footprints" (*padaso*).
"Should recite": It is *accuta* (undecaying) because it is devoid of falling away (*cavana*). It is *accanta* (ultimate) because it proceeds having transcended both the past and future limits.
It is *asaṅkhata* (unconditioned) because it is free from the function of conditioning (*saṅkharaṇa*). It is *anuttara* (unsurpassed) because there exists no phenomenon superior to itself.

Those who are liberated from craving (*vāna*) are *vimutta* (liberated); those who have sought and attained the great phenomena such as the aggregate of virtue (*sīlakkhandha*) and so forth are *mahesiyo*, the Buddhas.
Thus ends the Elucidation of Ultimate Meaning (*Paramatthadīpanā*) for the Compendium of Matter and Nibbāna within the Fourth Commentary on the *Abhidhammattha-saṅgaha*,
titled the Elucidation of Ultimate Meaning.
*Samuccaya-saṅgaha-paramatthadīpanī* 162.

Having thus shown the four ultimate realities through six chapters, he now spoke the opening verse while demonstrating their collective aggregation (*samuccaya*), which consists of various respective groups:
"Those seventy-two kinds of entities (*vatthu-dhamma*) with their own specific characteristics that have been [explained] by me..."
[They] have been stated. Now, the construction [of the sentence] is: "I shall explain their synthesis as appropriate.
In that context, by the words "dhammas possessing their own characteristics and bases" (*salakkhaṇāvatthudhammā*), he rejects the ten kinds of unconditioned matter (*anipphannarūpa*).

For these do not possess their own characteristics (*salakkhaṇā*) by way of a specific individual nature (*sabhāva-lakkhaṇa*) nor by way of general characteristics such as impermanence (*aniccatādi-sāmañña-lakkhaṇa*), because they are exclusively ultimate reality (*ekantaparamatthatāya*).

Because of its non-existence. For that very reason, it does not become a "thing" (vatthu) or a "dhamma. This is because it is not apprehended as having a specific form (sarūpa). For here, the word *vatthu* denotes a substance (*dabba*).
And what is called a "substance" here is simply an intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) that is obtainable as a specific form.

By this, it is stated that even for Nibbāna, there is an intrinsic nature obtainable as a specific form within the knowledges of reviewing the Path and the Fruit. [This applies] to unconditioned forms (*anipphanna-rūpa*).
It should be understood that [this] prevents either (1) a mere state of being visible by depending on a substantial dhamma (*vatthudhamma*), like a reflection;

or (2) a mere state of being a conceptualized mode of appearance, like conceptual dhammas (*paññattidhamma*); or (3) a state of being entirely non-existent and merely conceptualized, like a hare's horn, a tortoise's hair, and so forth.
And herein, "the seventy-two kinds of substantial dhammas possessing characteristics" refers to...
There will be no purpose in stating it [again]. For among those seventy-two kinds [of phenomena], only certain factors have already been included in the three preceding groupings.
Furthermore, in the final "all-inclusive" grouping, even unconditioned material phenomena (*anipphanna-rūpa*) are intended.
And here, by the words "the characteristic of the basis-phenomena," the possession of a characteristic for unconditioned material phenomena is rejected.

What ought to be said has already been stated in the *Rūpasamuddesadīpanī*. The "unwholesome compendium" (*akusalasaṅgaha*) is the inclusion of the fourfold sets of taints (*āsava*) and so forth, which belong to the category of exclusively unwholesome states;
it is not merely the inclusion of those things that have become unwholesome through association with the unwholesome, such as consciousness, contact, and the rest.
The "mixed compendium" (*missakasaṅgaha*) is the inclusion of those states that are wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate combined.
"Bodhi" is said to be the knowledge in the four paths, because one awakens by means of it. "Wings of enlightenment" (bodhipakkhā) means the factors of enlightenment;
the meaning is "requisites for enlightenment. Those which exist within the wings of enlightenment—that is, are included therein—are "conducive to enlightenment" (bodhipakkhiyā).
Their compendium is the "Compendium of Factors Conducive to Enlightenment" (bodhipakkhiyasaṅgaho). A compendium of all things without exception is the "Universal Compendium" (sabbasaṅgaho).
They are called *āsava* (taints) because they resemble [fermented] liquors (*āsava*) in the sense of having been stored for a long time and in the sense of being intoxicating.

If they were to be called *āsava* on account of both these characteristics, then only these [defilements] such as greed (*lobha*) and so forth would be called *āsava*. For in the world, the six kinds of flower-liquor and so forth themselves undergo fermentation in jars for about five or seven nights. And in the jar...

They cause [others] to undergo the probationary period (*parivāsa*). Yet these [defilements], within the beginningless cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), themselves undergo the probationary period within the continuum of sentient beings (*sattasantāna*), and they cause the continuum of sentient beings to undergo that probationary period.
The entire continuum of sentient beings is always filled with the taints (*āsava*). As it is said:
"The eye in the world is a form of endearment, a form of gratification; herein this craving, when arising, arises. Herein..."
"Settling down, it settles down," and so forth. In this context, when this craving arises by way of an active obsession (*pariyuṭṭhāna*), it arises right here.
Having arisen, and having again made its dwelling through the state of a latent tendency (*anusaya*), it settles down right here;
such is the meaning. And as long as the cleansing of the Noble Path is not obtained, the continuum [of existence] is like a well filled with excrement.
Having been difficult to purify, they continue to flow. While fermented liquors such as flower-essences produce intoxication, they do so for only a brief moment.
These [defilements], however, produce constant intoxication for as long as one does not attain the Noble Path.
Therefore, it is these alone that, by virtue of being long-fermented and by virtue of being intoxicants, truly deserve to be called "āsava" (taints).
Alternatively, they are called *āsava* (taints) because they leak out, being similar to [the word] *āsava* in the sense of leaking.

For just as the pus known as *āsava* from the openings of a leper’s large sores leaks out and spoils pieces of cloth, so too do these [taints], having leaked out through the six doors, spoil the six objects.
Or, they are called *āsava* because they flow forth, pour out, and increase long-lasting suffering in *saṃsāra*.

Alternatively, they are called *āsava* because they flow (*savanti*) from the state of existence up to the peak of existence (*ābhavagga*), according to their nature, from the beginningless lineage (*āgotrataṃ*), by way of making an object;

this is due to the prefix *ā-* indicating the sense of a limit (*avadhi*). That limit is twofold: having the sense of a boundary (*mariyādavisaya*) and having the sense of pervasion (*abhividhivisaya*).
Among these, that [limit] where the action related to it proceeds by excluding itself, which has become the limit, is the one having the sense of a boundary.

[This is] called [the limit-inclusive]. For example: "The rain has fallen as far as Pāṭaliputta. That whose related action occurs by pervading its own self—which serves as the limit—and including it within, is called the domain of the limit-inclusive (*abhividhi-visaya*).
For example: "The fame of the Blessed One has spread as far as the Brahma-world.
Here, however, it should be understood as the domain of the limit-inclusive. Therefore, [it includes] both the peak of existence (*bhavagga*) and the change-of-lineage (*gotrabhu*).
The meaning should be understood as "flowing while encompassing and making it its interior.

However, in the *Vibhāvani*, after stating that [the prefix *pari-*, etc. is twofold—by way of limit (*avadhi*) and boundary (*mariyādā*), and by way of pervasion (*abhividhi*)—it explains this further: "In that regard, from Pāṭaliputta..."
He says: "In cases such as *devo vuṭṭho* ('the god has rained'), it is a limit (*mariyāda*) that functions by setting aside the action;

whereas in cases such as *ābhavaggā saddo abbhuggato* ('the sound has risen up to the peak of existence'), it is an inclusive extension (*abhividhi*) that functions by pervading the action. This is not tenable.
For the range of existence (*bhavagga*), which is the object of the inclusive extension (*abhividhi*), does not [itself] possess the action of the sound's rising up that pervades the three worlds.
It proceeds by pervading. And it is not logical that the object serving as the limit (avadhi) should proceed by placing the action either outside or inside itself;
rather, it is logical that the action itself proceeds by placing that [object] either outside or inside. And having established this, the *Mūlaṭīkā* states: "For the limit is of two kinds:
that which has the scope of inclusion (*abhividhi*) and that which does not have the scope of inclusion. That which has the scope of inclusion proceeds by pervading the action..."
"The fame of the Blessed One has reached as far as the peak of existence. Setting aside the other [meaning], it says:

"The King has emerged from Pāṭaliputta. It desires or seeks, thus it is *kāma*. That itself is a *āsava* (taint), hence *kāmāsava*. Or, it is desired—that is, sought—by way of coarse sensual pleasure, thus it is *kāma*.

All phenomena belonging to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) are taught by way of the five strands of sensual pleasure (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*). However, here, by that name, those [phenomena] which have that as their object...
Craving itself is intended [here], and "outflow" (āsava) refers specifically to sensual desire; thus, it is the "sensual outflow" (kāmāsava).
It is sensual lust that proceeds by way of relishing and delighting in phenomena belonging to the sense-sphere. However, this is precisely the meaning intended by the Elder.
For he will state later: "By the term 'sensual existence' (kāmabhava), craving which has that as its basis is intended."
In the *Vibhāvani*, however, the same meaning as before was stated. That is incorrect, because it fails to state the intended meaning here, which follows the opinion of the Elder (Thera).

Regarding the term "taint of existence" (*bhavāsava*), there are two kinds of existence: existence as kamma (*kammabhava*) and existence as rebirth (*upapattibhava*). Among these, the sublime wholesome states (*mahaggata-kusala-dhammā*)...

Kamma-bhava (kamma-existence). The resultant states produced by that are upapatti-bhava (rebirth-existence). Here too, by the word "existence" (bhava), craving which has that as its object is intended.
Craving for existence itself is "the taint of existence" (bhavāsava). It is lust for the fine-material and immaterial realms, proceeding by way of attachment toward those two kinds of existence.
[206] However, as for what is stated in the *Vibhāvani*:
“The lust accompanied by the eternalist view (*sassatadiṭṭhi*) is included right here,” that is not correct.
For the taint of existence (*bhavāsava*) arises in those mental occurrences that are dissociated from the four types of views and accompanied by greed (*lobha*).

This is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathākaṇḍa*. However, where it is said: "craving for sense-pleasures (*kāmataṇhā*), craving for existence (*bhavataṇhā*), and craving for non-existence (*vibhavataṇhā*)," it is logical that there too all lust accompanied by the eternalist view (*sassatadiṭṭhi*), any attachment to the process of becoming through wholesome or unwholesome kamma, and any aspiration for rebirth-existence (*upapattibhava*)—all these are included within craving for existence.
But here, having set aside the aforementioned taint of existence (*bhavāsava*), [only the other two are considered].
It is logical that all greed is included within the taint of sensual desire (*kāmāsava*) alone.
By this very fact, that which was stated there—
namely, "the third [craving] is accompanied by views" (*diṭṭhisahagata*)— is also refuted.
Whatever view there is, that is the taint of views (*diṭṭhāsava*). Whatever delusion there is, that is the taint of ignorance (*avijjāsava*).
Here one might ask: why are only these called "taints"? Are not others, such as conceit and so forth, also characterized by long-term fermentation and so on? True.
