However, when the taint of sensual desire (*kāmāsava*) has fermented, all states such as conceit that have sensual objects as their domain have necessarily fermented as well. In that [regard]...
When liberation has occurred, there is only the state of being liberated; likewise, when the taint of existence (*bhavāsava*) has been exhausted, there is only the sphere of existence;
and when the taint of views (*diṭṭhāsava*) has been exhausted, there is only the sphere of views. Furthermore, ignorance is the root of all three of these.
Thus, these [three] alone are predominant in such states as "dwelling in seclusion" (*pārivāsiya-ṭṭhā*), while the others merely follow along with them and do not constitute separate taints.
"They deserve to be spoken of" means: it is called a *ogha* (flood) because it falls upon people, leaves them without comfort, overwhelms them, and strikes—that is, kills—them.

It is the natural great flood (*pakati-mahogha*). Likewise, they are called *oghā* (floods) because they are similar to a flood in the sense of carrying away and in the sense of being difficult to cross.

Furthermore, there is the contingency that if they were called floods merely in the sense of carrying away and being difficult to cross, then [the term] would also apply to pride (*māna*) and the rest.
The avoidance of the state of being a flood (oghā) should be understood according to the method already stated.
They are called *yogas* because they yoke beings to the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*) or to the root of existence (*bhava*).

They are called *ganthas* because, together with death in one existence, they lead beings to and join them with rebirth-linking in another existence. "Covetousness" (*abhijjhā*) is a name for all lust; therefore, [it applies to] form and the formless...
It should be understood that attachment (*rāga*) is also included here. Ill-will (*byāpāda*) likewise refers to all forms of hatred (*dosa*).
"Adherence to the view 'this alone is the truth, everything else is vain'" is the adherence to wrong views (*micchābhinivesa*) that proceeds in such a manner.

"Adherence to rules and observances" (*sīlabbataparāmāsa*) is the grasping of things such as cow-vows and cow-observances—which are not actually the path to liberation from the suffering of the round of existence—after having conceptualized them in various ways.

And here, "the other" (*parato*) means that which is contrary to the true nature of things (*bhūtasabhāva*). Furthermore, the word *kāya* occurs everywhere in reference to both the material body (*rūpakāya*) and the mental body (*nāmakāya*).
Thus, because it binds (*ganthati*)—that is, connects—the present body with the past body and the future body with the present body, it is called a "body-fetter" (*kāyagantha*).
Alternatively, it is a "body-fetter" (*kāyagantha*) because it is a knot (*gaṇṭhi*) upon the body. It is an "internal knot" (*ajjhatta-gaṇṭhi*).
The meaning is as follows: In such terms as *nigaṇṭho nāṭaputto* (the Nigaṇṭha son of Nāṭa), the word *gaṇṭha* is used in the sense of a "knot.

They are called *upādānāni* because they seize intensely, taking hold with a grip that refuses to let go. Sensual desire (*kāma*) itself, being a defilement, is sensual clinging (*kāmupādāna*). Alternatively, it is called sensual clinging because one clings to sensual desire as its objective basis (*vatthu*).
The sixty-two views, the three great views, and whatever other views—whether appearing in the teaching or in the world—that consist of a perverted grasp, are the clinging to views (*diṭṭhupādāna*).
Alternatively, it is called clinging to views because one clings to a previously held view, thinking, "This alone is the truth; all else is false.
The specific conduct of cattle, dogs, and so forth is called virtue (*sīla*); clinging to that very [conduct]...

"Vow" (*vata*) refers to that which has been well undertaken. The firm grasping of both of these as "the path to liberation from *saṃsāra*" is called the clinging to rules and observances (*sīlabbatupādāna*).

Regarding "clinging to a doctrine of self" (*attavādupādāna*): here, "self" (*attā*) refers to the primary lord within each individual continuum of a sentient being, who is apprehended through conceptual construction; that which worldly people call a "sentient being," a "person," a "living soul," or a "Tathāgata."

They perceive [it] as transcending the world. And that which various sectarians proclaim—whether as created by a Lord (issaranimmāna), or as arisen by chance (adhiccasamuppanna), or as eternalism in its entirety, or as partial eternalism, or as annihilationism—that is called "clinging to a doctrine of self" (attavādupādāna) because beings thereby affirm and cling to a self.
This consists of twenty types of personality-belief (sakkāyadiṭṭhi). In this context, "they affirm" means they regard it as distinguished [from others].
They speak having made an effort. "They cling" means they grasp firmly. As it is said:
"In this regard, what is the view of a personal body (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*)?
Here, an uninstructed worldling regards form as self, or self as possessing form, or form as in self, or self as in form. He regards feeling as self... [and so forth].
Or the self as possessing feeling; or feeling as belonging to the self; or the self as existing within feeling. [The same applies to] perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
In this context, "one regards form as the self" means one grasps at form itself as the self.
"Or the self as possessing form" means one grasps at the thought, "Form belongs to my self. "Or form in the self" means one grasps at the thought that form exists dependent upon the self.
"Self in form" means one grasps that "self exists dependent upon form. How so?
When one says, "Today my body is stiff," or "Today my body is soft," one regards the form known as earth as self.
Or when one says, "Today my body is stiff" or "soft," [one regards] the remaining phenomena as self.
Or, having grasped the self as something apart from the Dhamma, one indeed regards that self as possessing earth.
One indeed regards earth within oneself when saying, "Today hardness or softness has arisen in me.
One indeed regards the self within earth when saying, "Today I am established in hardness; I am established in softness."
This is the mode of occurrence of the speculative view of identity (*saṅkhāyadiṭṭhi*) regarding the fourfold earth element.
It should be stated as applicable for the remaining twenty-seven material phenomena (*rūpa*). For even with regard to impermanence, this same view occurs in such ways as "I am dying" or "I shall die.
Regarding the remaining material phenomena, there is nothing further to be said. [One thinks: "This very thing I ate together with in the past, I eat together with today; in the future..."
Or he regards feeling as the self, thinking, "I shall enjoy," or "I am happy," or "I am suffering.
Or he regards the self as possessing feeling, thinking, "Today my body is happy or suffering," or "My mind is happy or suffering.
Or he regards feeling within himself, thinking, "Today happiness or suffering has arisen in me. Today I...
"One regards self in feeling thus: 'I am established in a state of happiness,' or 'I am established in a state of suffering.
This should be stated by expanding it individually for all fifty types of perceptions and formations.
"I see" is the regarding of eye-consciousness as self. "Seeing is mine" is the regarding of self as possessing consciousness.
He regards it thus: "I have what is called seeing"—thus he regards consciousness as the self within himself;
"I am capable of seeing"—thus he regards the self as being within consciousness. This same method applies to the remaining five types of consciousness.
"I am," "I am one," "I am a being," "I am an individual," "I am a soul," "I am the world," "I am a man," "I am a human," "I am a god," "I am Sakka."

Or it may be said that the five aggregates, or each individual aggregate taken as a whole, proceed [with the thought]: "I am Brahmā," "I go," "I stand," "I sit," "I lie down," "I bend," or "I stretch," and so forth.
For those who have not fully understood the basis [of the self], even for a mere moment, whatever [they do]—whether for themselves or for another—[is done with such a conceit].
When those speaking words associated with a self, their mind or speech proceeds by sometimes grasping the aforementioned material and immaterial phenomena as a self;
sometimes by way of being the self’s retinue; sometimes by way of being dependent on the self; sometimes by way of being supported by the self;
sometimes by way of individual phenomena; and sometimes by way of phenomena as a collective mass.
However, since what is called "the sign of self" (attanimitta) appears dependent upon the mode of exercising mastery,
and that mode of exercising mastery does not exist for those who clearly see that the occurrence of material and immaterial phenomena is dependent on conditions and momentary,
therefore— even when those who desire to fully understand speak words associated with a self— their mind [remains] like [a drop of water on] a lotus leaf.
It should be understood that [the mind] proceeds without adhering to those phenomena, just like a drop of water.
They are called "hindrances" (*nīvaraṇa*) because they prevent wholesome states from arising in the mental continuum of beings, or they obstruct them even when they have already arisen.
It is "sensual desire" (*kāmacchanda*) in the sense of desiring (*kāmana*) and in the sense of longing (*chandana*); it is intense lust. That itself is a hindrance.

Regarding the hindrance of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa*): because it is stated in the *Paṭṭhāna* that "depending on the hindrance of sensual desire, there is the hindrance of restlessness," with the exception of attachment to the fine-material and immaterial realms, there is no remaining greed whatsoever that is not included within the hindrance of sensual desire.

Furthermore, it should be understood that the state of being an opponent to jhāna belongs specifically to the lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure (*pañca-kāmaguṇika-rāga*). Malice (*byāpajjana*)...
Ill-will (*byāpāda*). Its meaning is the state of putrefaction of the mind; it is that which is called hatred.
But why, in this context, are two pairs of phenomena—the hindrance of sloth-and-torpor and the hindrance of restlessness-and-worry—spoken of as single hindrances?
Because they are similar in terms of their function (*kicca*), their condition (*paccaya*), and their opposite (*paṭipakkha*). For, first, in terms of function, the pair of sloth and torpor...

The function of the first two [hindrances] is to produce a state of lethargy in states of consciousness; the function of the pair consisting of restlessness and worry is to produce a state of non-tranquility.
In terms of their conditions: the first pair is conditioned by drowsiness and yawning; the latter pair is conditioned by thoughts concerning misfortune to kinsmen and so forth.
In terms of their opposites: the first pair is the opposite of energy; the latter pair is the opposite of serenity.
They are called *anusayas* because they "lie along" (*anu-senti*). The meaning is that they arise upon obtaining a corresponding cause.

Alternatively, they are called *anusayas* because they "lie down repeatedly" (*anu-anu senti*). The meaning is that as long as one has not yet attained the Path, they remain unexamined in the interim and arise again and again when a cause is obtained.
And here, "arising" refers to the state of being prone to arising in the sense of not having been abandoned.
It must be understood [in this way]. If it is asked how its arising is to be known from its own nature:

because it is stated that "for whom the underlying tendency to sensual lust arises, for that same person the underlying tendency to aversion arises. And having established it thus, in the Pāḷi, regarding the ordinary person (*puthujjana*), it is said in the section on underlying tendencies (*anusaya-vāra*) that "all seven underlying tendencies underlie together," and in the section on arising (*uppajjana-vāra*) that they "arise together."

As it is said: "In an ordinary person (*puthujjana*), the underlying tendency to ignorance (*avijjānusaya*) underlies [the mind], as do the underlying tendencies to sensual lust (*kāmarāga*), aversion (*paṭigha*), conceit (*māna*), views (*diṭṭhi*), doubt (*vicikicchā*), and the underlying tendency to lust for existence (*bhavarāgānusaya*). It is the same in the section on their arising.

Furthermore, while not yet having reached the state of full-blown obsession (*pariyuṭṭhāna*), [these tendencies exist] through wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate mental states occurring within the continuum (*santāna*).
They lie together, being concordant and non-opposed. They are called *anusayas* because they lie down (*senti*) without having arisen as separate associated mental states (*sampayutta-dhamma*).
Alternatively, they are called *anusayas* because they lie down repeatedly (*anu anu senti*).

By their very nature, they lie down again and again—doubling, tripling, and so forth—in the form of sensual lust and the other [defilements] exactly as they have previously lain dormant. They lie down in successive layers by way of their mode of lying down.
The meaning is "enveloping.
This is a designation for sensual lust and the other [defilements] when they abide in the first of the three states of lust and so forth.

For there are three states: the state of latent tendency (*anusaya*), the state of obsession (*pariyuṭṭhāna*), and the state of transgression (*vītikkama*). Among these, those sensual lusts and so forth—
Having arisen, they cause the limbs of the body and the limbs of speech to move; the state of their proceeding in such a manner is called the "state of transgression" (*vītikkamāvatthā*).

Those that proceed having arisen together with impulsion-consciousness (*javana-citta*) in the mind alone—the state of their proceeding in such a manner is called the "state of obsession" (*pariyuṭṭhānāvatthā*).
However, those which do not even reach the state of being co-nascent with impulsion, like the latent dispositions (*vāsanā-dhātu*), [are different].
Having become latent within the continuum, they persist as seeds for the attainment of active outbursts (*pariyuṭṭhāna*).

When objects such as the sign of beauty (*subhanimitta*) enter the field of perception, it is through the power of these [latent tendencies] that the adverting consciousness (*āvajjana*) turns back toward the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) in an improper manner for the sake of the manifestation of lust and so forth;
and it is through their power that the untrained mind does not attain mastery. Such is the state of those [latent tendencies] as they thus proceed.
The state of the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) is as follows: the lust for sensual pleasure (*kāmarāga*) and so forth, which exist in that state, are called "underlying tendencies.

However, they are not non-existent as ultimate realities (*paramattha*), because they are of the nature of absolute ultimate reality. Nor are they of the nature of the wholesome or the indeterminate, because they are of the nature of absolute unwholesomeness.
Nor are they opposed to the wholesome and the indeterminate, because they are not perceived as separate associated states (*sampayutta-dhamma*). Nor are they exempt from the three periods of time.

Because they proceed by depending upon the concomitant states that arise simultaneously with them. However, when those [latent dispositions] emerge and attain the state of active obsession (*pariyuṭṭhāna*), they then attain the status of distinct associated states;
their nature as having an object (*sārammaṇa*) and so forth also becomes fully manifest.

It is with reference to this meaning that, in the *Kathāvatthu*, their status as states possessing objects and their inclusion within the aggregate of mental formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*) are discussed.
"It has been established" means as follows:
just as when a poison-thorn is inserted into a fruit-bearing tree, the sap that depends on the tree and serves as the condition for the production of fruit goes to exhaustion;
consequently, the fruits that would have arisen at the proper time do not arise.

Thus, in a mental continuum that still possesses latent tendencies (*anusaya*), at the very moment the Path (*magga*) becomes manifest, each respective latent tendency goes to its destruction simultaneously with the arising of the Path.
Once destroyed, there is no further manifestation (*pariyuṭṭhāna*) of it; how then could there be transgression?
It is with reference to this meaning that it is said: "The Path abandons the class of defilements by way of future non-arising."
It is stated here and there. In that context, "the generality of the future" means what is considered to be future, not that which is exclusively future.
For this very reason, it is said in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "The path abandons certain defilements;

as for those [defilements], they should not be described as past, or future, or present. And by this, through the gateway of the defilements, [the path] also [abandons] whatever wholesome and unwholesome kamma and the five aggregates of clinging (upādinnaka-khandha-pañcaka).
He demonstrates that those [phenomena] which one abandons—whether past, future, or present—are not to be described [as existing].
If this were so, then all those phenomena of the three planes abandoned by the Path would be called "timeless," "unconditioned," and "without conditions. This is not so;
for they possess the nature of being born across the three times, and they possess the nature of being conditioned and having conditions. For when the Path has not yet arisen, they...

Because these named phenomena are grasped by knowledge striking at the characteristic of the conditioned— namely, that "these will arise" and "these will cease"— they partake of the state of belonging to the three planes and so forth by way of their characteristics.
And having done so, even for those [latent tendencies] that have not yet reached the status of associated states,

there exist the states of the underlying tendency (*anusaya*), the state of the latent impression (*vāsanā*), the state of being possessed of karma (*kamma-samaṅgitā*), and the dispositions and inclinations (*āsaya-ajjhāsaya*).

In the cases of those established in the bases for conduct such as that of the *dhimutta*, the ultimate nature (*paramattha-dhammatā*) and the state of being unwholesome and so forth must be understood by way of their intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).
However, in the *Vibhāvanī*, it is said:

"For defilements that have not been abandoned, when they encounter their appropriate conditions, are ready to arise; they remain as if persisting as latent tendencies (*anusaya*) within the continuum."
"Those states existing in that condition are called *anusayas*. Furthermore, they are, in the primary sense (*nippariyāyato*), future defilements;
however, because past and present [defilements] possess that same nature, they are likewise so called. This has been said.

In this context, it is stated that *anusayas* are exclusively future defilements that have never previously arisen in the continuum, and thus they "lie latent" (*anusayitā*) within the continuum as it were. That is not tenable.
For they do not exist as if merely latent; rather, they exist exclusively as actualized latencies.
Furthermore, that which was stated there—"But those, in the ultimate sense, are future defilements"—is also not tenable.

For latent dispositions (*anusaya*) that have not been abandoned by the Path do not belong to the future. Furthermore, it cannot be said in an absolute sense (*nippariyāyato*) that even those [dispositions] already abandoned belong to the future.

This is because the common characteristic of being "future" is what is intended here. By this, the claim that past and present [dispositions] are also called such [i.e., "future"] because they possess that same nature is refuted.
Moreover, only those [phenomena] that have reached arising, presence, and dissolution are exclusively...

The statement that “there is simultaneity” (tekālikatā) is appropriate only as a figurative way of speaking regarding the present state of those underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) that have not yet been abandoned.

And this being the case, in the Pāḷi it is stated only the section on arising pertaining to the present time— such as, “In one for whom the underlying tendency to sensual lust arises, the underlying tendency to aversion also arises”—
and not the section on cessation, nor the sections on the past and the future.

However, as for what is stated in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*: "If one abandons defilements in the present, then surely one who is lustful abandons lust, one who is corrupt abandons hatred, and one who is deluded abandons delusion"—this should be understood as having been said with reference exclusively to the moment when [defilements] have reached the state of active obsession (*pariyuṭṭhāna*).
For it is precisely for this reason that the *Aṭṭhakathā* speaks of "presently arising" (*vattamānuppanna*) and "arising after having existed and then vanished" (*bhutvā vigatuppanna*).
It is stated that there are four kinds of "arisen" (*uppanna*) that are not to be abandoned by the Path: arisen as having gained an opportunity, and arisen as manifest activity (*samudācāra*).

There are also four kinds of "arisen" that are to be abandoned by the Path: arisen as having attained the plane, arisen as apprehending an object, arisen as un-suppressed, and arisen as un-eradicated.
Among these, the pair consisting of "arisen as occurring" and "arisen as manifest activity" refers exclusively to the momentary present (*khaṇapaccuppanna*).
That which has arisen and passed away is simply the past. That which has arisen by way of having made room [for its manifestation] is simply the future.
However, both of these are called "arisen" because they are in proximity to the present; what is meant is that they are the "near-present.

That which is called "arisen by way of having acquired a basis" refers specifically to those underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) that reside within one's own aggregates and have not yet been abandoned by the Path.

The term *nāma* refers to those very same [defilements] that have reached an excessive state of intensity (*adhimatta-thāmagata*) after having impelled once upon an object such as a beautiful sign (*subha-nimitta*),
and which remain so until the force of the obsession (*pariyuṭṭhāna-vega*) rooted therein has subsided.
For what are called latent tendencies (*anusaya*) are those which, throughout the beginningless cycle of existence (*anamatagga-saṃsāra*), have repeatedly attained the state of active obsession.
By way of the defilements (kilesa), through attaining progressively firmer and more solid states, they become firmly rooted by their very nature;

thus, they cannot be abandoned by any means whatsoever. Even so, whenever a particular underlying tendency (anusaya) becomes abundant in its manifestation (pariyuṭṭhāna) due to the acquisition of conditions, then that specific tendency reaches a state of particularly intense firmness.

Having reached that state, it remains. Whenever whichever opposing state (paṭipakkhadhamma) has been suppressed by the undertaking of its antidote, then each of those, having reached a state of diminished strength, remains.
That which is called "arisen but not suppressed" refers specifically to those states that have not been properly restrained by serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā).
That which is called "arisen but not eradicated" refers to [those states] by means of the Path (magga).
The name applies to those very same [defilements] that have not been abandoned but have already gained a footing on the plane.

However, because supramundane states are the absolute antidotes to the defilements, the trainees (sekkhā) dwelling in the lower paths and fruits—during the moments of their own respective paths and fruits—are neither said to "possess latent tendencies" (*sānusaya*) nor "be free from latent tendencies" (*nirānusaya*) with respect to the higher paths and the intermediate stages; nor are they said to be "powerful" or "weak."

They are not to be so described. Therefore, even though the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) exist in such a present state, if one abandons the defilements (*kilesa*) in the present, it should be understood that there is no fault in saying that one abandons the underlying tendency when it has become firmly established.
*Kāmarāgānusaya* is simply the underlying tendency of sensual lust (*kāmarāga*).

They are called "fetters" (*saṃyojana*) because they yoke and bind. These consist of five lower fetters: personality-belief (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*), doubt (*vicikicchā*), adherence to rules and observances (*sīlabbataparāmāsa*), sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*), and ill will (*byāpāda*).
Then there are five higher fetters: lust for the fine-material realm (*rūparāga*), lust for the immaterial realm (*arūparāga*), conceit (*māna*), restlessness (*uddhacca*), and ignorance (*avijjā*).
Thus, ten fetters are mentioned in both the Suttantas and the Abhidhamma. As for the others...

Since these [topics] have already been included in the Abhidhamma itself, the term "Suttanta" is used here for the purpose of distinguishing them from that. Furthermore, the sequence of the two does not accord with the order of the Pāḷi;
however, because of the inclusion of similar phenomena (*sabhāga-dhamma*), the sequence may have been stated differently here.
They are called *kilesas* (defilements) because they defile, afflict, and torment the mind. Alternatively, they are so called because they cause the mind to become stained (*malīna*) and debased.
They are called *kilesas* (defilements) because beings go (*gacchanti*) by means of them.

By the term "desire" (*kāma*) is meant that which indicates the desire for sense-objects (*vatthukāma*), and by the term "existence" (*bhava*) is meant that which indicates existence in the realms of form and formlessness. That which has as its basis (*tabbatthukā*) such things designated as desire and existence, being the objective support (*ārammaṇa*), is so called.
In this manner do the rules and observances (*sīlabbata*) proceed: by way of grasping from others in the manner of "this is truth, the other is vain," and by way of dogmatic adherence (*abhinivesa*).
And it occurs in the mode of adherence to a self regarding the aggregates (*khandha*). "As a basis" means as a phenomenon possessing intrinsic nature (*sabhāva-dhamma*).
The construction is: "This compendium of evil, the compendium of the unwholesome, is stated in nine ways. [The Compendium of the Unwholesome] 163.

In the *Missaka-saṅgaha* (Compendium of Miscellaneous Items), even for those performing evil deeds such as killing living beings, there is what is called the straightening of the mind upon its object.
It is said that without *jhāna* nothing is accomplished; thus, there are "seven factors of *jhāna*. The meaning is:

they are the factors for the function of "close contemplation" (*upanijjhāyana*), which consists in directing the mind straight toward an object, whether it be beautiful or foul. Among them, mental distress (*domanassa*) is an unwholesome factor of *jhāna*;
the remaining ones are wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate. [This applies] to those things designated as wholesome and unwholesome kamma...

Whether in good destinations, bad destinations, or those reckoned as the cycle of existence (*vivaṭṭa*), in various directions—that is, in whatever direction the manifestation [of consciousness] occurs—the "course" (*gati*) of the mind is accomplished precisely through the activities of seeing and so forth, whether they proceed rightly or wrongly; thus it is said that there are twelve path-factors (*dvādasamaggaṅgāni*).
Whether the course of the mind is straight or crooked, these are the factors of the path for its movement, meaning they are the factors of the means (*upāyaṅgāni*). In this regard:

Wrong view, wrong intention, wrong effort, and wrong concentration are the factors that serve as the means for the mind’s crooked course toward the unwholesome directions, which consist of evil deeds and rebirths in the miserable states (*duggati*).

The others [right view, intention, effort, and concentration] should be understood as the straight course toward the wholesome directions, which consist of beautiful deeds, rebirths in happy states, and the phenomena of turning away from the cycle of existence (*vivaṭṭadhamma*). In this regard, concerning the deed of taking life:

The four-factored jhāna, consisting of applied thought (vitakka), sustained thought (vicāra), mental distress (domanassa), and one-pointedness (ekaggatā), as well as the three-factored path, consisting of wrong intention (micchā-saṅkappa), wrong effort (micchā-vāyāma), and wrong concentration (micchā-samādhi), should be understood.
In this same way, the jhānas and paths should be extracted from the remaining good and bad courses of action (sucarita-duccarita-kamma).
However, in the Vibhaṅga and in the Suttantas, wrong speech (micchā-vācā), wrong action (micchā-kammanta), and wrong livelihood (micchā-ājīva) [are also included].
"Wrong mindfulness"—these four are also included here. However, these are not separate mental factors (*cetasika-dhamma*).
Since they are merely designations for the four aggregates (*khandha*) as they occur in various ways, they are not taken up separately here.
As for what is stated in the *Vibhāvani*:
"It is said: 'Because they lead toward a good destination, a bad destination, and Nibbāna, they are paths; their factors, being constituent parts of those paths, are "limbs" (maṅga).
That is not correct; for the factors are not called "paths" themselves. In the commentaries, it is the word *magga* alone that is used as a synonym for "path," not the word *aṅga*.
And as for what is stated therein...
It has been said: "The factors of the eightfold path are the path-factors. That too is untenable;
for here, various paths are intended, such as a threefold path in some instances of consciousness and a fourfold path in others.

They are called faculties (indriya) in the sense of dominance (ādhipacca). And what is this dominance? It is [the state] of one's own course regarding those phenomena that proceed under one's own control.

The state of being capable of exercising complete control. Thus, they are called *indriyas* because they exercise (*karonti*) and accomplish (*sādhenti*) the lordship (*indaṭṭha*) known as sovereignty (*ādhipacca*) over their respective functions.
Alternatively, they are called *indriyas* because they exercise lordship (*indaṭṭha*). What is meant is that they are lords (*issara*) or masters (*adhipati*).
In this context, the five [faculties] beginning with the eye are the lords of eye-consciousness and so forth in their respective functions such as seeing.
Because it causes the conformity of one's own form (*attākāra*) to those that are strong, weak, dull, sharp, and so forth.

The two [mental] states (*bhāva*) are the master of material phenomena arising from the four origins (*catusamuṭṭhānika-rūpa*) during their occurrence by way of female form and so on, or indeed of the entire five aggregates (*pañcakkhandha*), because they do not occur otherwise.
For instance, in whatever continuum (*santāna*) the female state (*itthibhāva*) occurs at rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), in that [continuum] all...
When conditions such as kamma arouse a continuity of material phenomena (rūpa-santati) arising from the four causes, they do so only with the female form, and not otherwise.
Even when desire and consciousness are predominant, they proceed only with that dull form.

The male continuum should be understood as the opposite of this. The two types of life-faculty (jīvita) sustain the continuities of material phenomena through the succession of nights, days, months, and years.
In the pervading of the course of existence, it is the master of the co-nascent states; it is their agent, for their functioning is dependent upon it. The mind is so in the function of cognizing.

The pentad of feeling is so in the experiencing of the flavor of the object in its various ways. Faith is so in the unshackling from the object. Energy is so in the state of non-sluggishness in activity.
Mindfulness is so in the establishing of the object. Concentration is so in the steadiness of the mind upon the object.
Wisdom is sovereign over its associated states in the function of non-delusion, because it proceeds in a manner that cannot be overcome by anything else.
Just as earth in a stone is not overcome by its co-nascent elements, so wisdom proceeds having itself overcome them, making them as if they were no longer individually apparent.
And just as water in water, fire in fire, or wind in wind [is not overcome by other elements].
This should be understood in this way:
"It was known, it was penetrated" is *aññāta*. That which is not unknown is *anaññāta*—namely, the Dhamma of the Four Truths or the Deathless State (*amataṃ padaṃ*).
"I shall know what is not yet known" is *anaññātaññassāmi*. For even a verbal noun may function as a technical term (*saññā-sadda*).
It stands in its own place; it remains as it is. Just as Makkhali Gosāla said, "Come and see for yourself.

For if this were the case, there would be no contradiction in its being a compound together with the following word. "The faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown'" (anaññātaññassāmītindriya) is the faculty of one who has practiced in such a manner.
From the very beginning of the application of the mind, it is accompanied by such an effort.
For one who has begun insight (vipassanā) and, while that effort has not yet subsided, attains the path at the mere moment of the stream-entry, it is called a "faculty" (indriya).
"He understands" means "higher knowledge" (añña). That very faculty is the "faculty of higher knowledge" (aññindriya);
for even though one has known what was previously unknown by means of the first path, because the task of abandoning the defilements is not yet completed, the function of knowing remains unfinished.

It is said that "faculty" (*indriya*) refers to those engaged in the task of knowing again and again that very Dhamma of the Four Truths, which is the state of the Deathless (*amatapada*), once it has been seen.

"The faculty of one who has already known" (*aññātāvindriya*) means the faculty of one who has already known—that is, of one whose task of full comprehension is finished and whose taints are destroyed;
thus it is the faculty of one who has already known. All three of these are associated with such a mode of knowing.
It should be understood that he is the lord of phenomena.

In this context, the five faculties of clarity are mentioned first in order to illustrate how the intensity of the grasping at a self within the manifest material body of these beings—and their liberation from it—occurs through non-comprehension and comprehension, respectively. Of that self, [the faculties of] femininity and masculinity...

The non-distinction between these two occurs by way of these [two faculties]. Furthermore, in order to demonstrate that the apprehension of "woman" or "man," as well as the absence thereof, arises from the lack of full understanding (*apariññā*) and the presence of full understanding (*pariññā*) regarding these two, the pair of faculties pertaining to existence (*bhavindriya*) was stated immediately after them.
And it is by way of this [body] that the self acquires the notion of a "living being" (*jīva*).
Moreover, the apprehension of a "living being" and its absence occur through the lack of full understanding and the presence of full understanding regarding this [body].

The life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) is mentioned immediately after that to illuminate how [the body] comes to be. However, it should be understood that although this [life-faculty] ought to have been mentioned prior to the faculties of existence (*bhāvindriya*), it is mentioned here because of the mixture of the material and the immaterial.

Among the mental faculties (*nāmindriya*), the mind-faculty (*manindriya*) is mentioned first to illustrate how there is a firm grasping at a self within the mental body and its liberation, respectively, through the non-comprehension and comprehension of this [mind-faculty].

Furthermore, the immaterial self becomes defiled and agitated by means of these [five aggregates]. Or else, the grasping at that [self] as happy or suffering, and its liberation therefrom, occurs through the non-comprehension and comprehension of these [aggregates].
To illustrate this, the pentad of faculties beginning with faith is stated immediately thereafter.
This is for the purpose of showing the practice for the purification of that defiled [self], or for liberation from those respective graspings.
Immediately after that, the five faculties beginning with faith (*saddhā*) were stated.

Then, at the end, the three supramundane faculties (*lokuttarindriya*) were stated in order to show the beginning, middle, and conclusion of the attainment of purification (*vodāna*) through that practice.
However, in the *Vibhāvanī*:
It has been stated: "Because the intended meaning is established by this much, others are not included. This is not tenable.

For even though other phenomena exist that are capable of being faculties (*indriya*), it is not reasonable to say that because the intended meaning is established by this much, those others are not included by the Blessed One and the Elder. [This is so] regarding that which is capable of being a faculty...
Because another is impossible. For if it were possible, he would indeed take even a hundred or a thousand.
They are called "powers" (*balāni*) because they prevail, endure, and crush opposing states as they arise. Just as those who are weak are overpowered by the strong.
"Crushing these dangers" (*maddantenaṃ parissayā*): here, "weak" (*abalā*) means feeble; "them" (*naṃ*) refers to people of inferior energy; "they prevail" (*baliyanti*) means...

They act with force and overwhelm. "Dangers" (*parissaya*) means dangers such as lust (*rāga*) and so forth, which are weak. Furthermore, in the sense of being unshakable by opposing states, it is called "chariot" (*akkha*);

in the sense of being powerful, it is called "strength" (*bala*). Therefore, the power of faith (*saddhā-bala*) is the state of being incapable of being shaken by the opposing state known as lack of faith (*assaddhiya*).
[The power of energy] is the state of being incapable of being shaken by what is known as laziness (*kosajja*).

The state of being impossible to shake by negligence is called the power of energy (*vīriya-bala*). The state of being impossible to shake by forgetfulness is called the power of mindfulness (*sati-bala*).
The state of being impossible to shake by restlessness is called the power of concentration (*samādhi-bala*).
The state of being impossible to shake by ignorance is called the power of wisdom (*paññā-bala*). As for the remaining two pairs of factors, they should be applied to one another as mutual opposites.

In the *Vibhāvani*, however, because it was deemed that the dyad of the power of evil (*pāpabala-duka*) could not be applied by way of its opposite, it was stated: "But the pair of shamelessness (*ahirika*) and lack of moral dread (*anottappa*) are 'neither' in terms of their stability among associated states.
That is not correct. For "stability among associated states" and "unshakability by opposites" do not differ in meaning.
The powers of energy and concentration are wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate. Shamelessness (*ahirika*) and lack of moral dread (*anottappa*) are unwholesome powers.

The remaining ones are wholesome or indeterminate. Regarding the term "predominant" (*adhipati*): here *pati* means master or lord. That [lordship] is twofold: partial lordship and universal lordship.

Among these, the faculties (*indriya*), having themselves operated over the objects of others while they were under the control of others, [exercise sovereignty] only over their own respective objects.
Those who cause others to act under their own control are called "limited lords" (*padesissara*).

However, once one has reached the state of sovereignty that occurs as distinguished by its priority—either by way of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) or by way of being first in arrival—there is no other second lord.

Therefore, it is a "lord" (*pati*) who is superior; thus, he is an "overlord" (*adhipati*). Furthermore, they say that he is an "overlord" because he is the lord of those whose conduct is inferior (*dhīnavutti*).
"Chanda-adhipati" means one who has desire as the dominant influence (*adhipati*). For one possessed of desire, what action indeed would not succeed?

Thus, by way of previous volitional formations (*pubbābhisaṅkhāra*), or by way of having thoroughly cultivated the inclination toward desire in past lives, among those various wholesome and unwholesome karmas, the associated states—like a great flood upon a heap of grass and leaves—are constantly held with effort, being dependent on oneself and under one's own control.
The desire for action (*kattukamyatā-chanda*) is that which proceeds having performed [the preliminary work]. This same method applies to the remaining factors as well. Now, one might object:

"In this context, do not the last three states, when assuming the status of predominance (*adhipati*), do so without abandoning their status as faculties (*indriya*); thus, while being predominant, they still function under the control of others by way of the function of a faculty"?
True; however, the function of predominance is one thing, and the function of a faculty is another.

"Regarding the function of the faculties (*indriyakicca*), there is no fault here. For example, a Wheel-turning Monarch (*cakkavatti-rāja*) might receive a single divine science (*dibba-vijjā*) from one of his own chaplains.
Yet, he does not cease to be called a Wheel-turning Monarch on that account, nor does he come under the control of another because of that science.
For the duties of a Wheel-turning Monarch as a ruler are one thing, and the duty of receiving a science is another."

This should be understood in exactly this way. In this context, "sovereign function" (*adhipatikicca*) refers to the carrying of the burden by overcoming co-nascent phenomena with unequal strength, without regard for their respective specific functions, and ensuring they do not turn back from their own tasks.
However, "faculty function" (*indriyakicca*) is spoken of with reference to functions such as cognizing and so forth.
They are called *āhāras* because they "bring" (*āharanti*)— that is, they carry and maintain [their effects] by means of their general status as conditions such as co-nascence,

but with an additional, specific power of a condition not shared [by others]. Alternatively, they are called *āhāras* because those various conditioning states produced within and the conditioned states produced by them "well bring" (*suṭṭhu haranti*) and "convey" (*vahanti*) both themselves and their respective functions as conditions and their functions as conditioned states.
"By these" refers to the nutriments (*āhāra*). As it is said: "All beings subsist by means of nutriment.

Here, by the phrase "all beings," all internal phenomena consisting of conditions and conditionally arisen states are expressed. "Subsisting by means of nutriment" means subsisting by means of conditions.
The meaning is that they have the nature of subsistence through the twenty-four conditions as appropriate. But is it not the case that here only the nutriment-as-condition is mentioned?

It is not the nutriment-condition (*āhāra-paccaya*). However, here it is stated that only the twenty-four dhammas which possess the characteristic of being a nutriment-condition are meant. This is true;
yet, among all twenty-four dhammas termed "nutriments" in the sense of being conditions, those specifically designated as the "four nutriments" are distinguished.
Thus, it is established that these [four] are indeed nutriments even for those other dhammas that serve as their conditions. In this sense:
The great magnitude of the four nutriments becomes manifest.
In this regard, just as the potency of barley seeds or rice seeds is the primary factor for the arising of the sprout and the stalk,
thereafter, once they have attained the state of a crop, for five or six months, it is the earth that provides either their growth or their maintenance.

Just as among the flavors, the flavor of water is predominant, even so, for those beings attached to sensual pleasures who subsist on edible food, the power of karma is indeed predominant in the production of rebirth-form.
Thereafter, however, for as long as the life-span lasts—whether it be for growth or for maintenance—the power of temperature and nutriment is predominant.
For the material qualities born of karma persist until the approach of death.
Even when they are occurring, they occur only when assisted by temperature and nutriment.

Temperature and nutriment perform their respective functions only when they have provided support. Therefore, the fourfold continuity-form (*catusantatirūpa*) of those beings does not persist for long if it is not supported by physical nutriment (*kabaḷīkārāhāra*).
Only when being supported does it continue to exist for the duration of its life-span. And just as a bird...
Just as gadflies, mosquitoes, and the like sustain their own bodies by taking food with their proboscis,
and die if they lack a proboscis and thus fail to obtain food; even so, these beings take up flavor in objects through contact,
accomplish enjoyment and utilization known as feeling, reach an abundance of craving, fulfill the threefold round of existence, and continue on until the end of time.
They proceed by revolving in a cycle.

For if there were no such thing as contact (phassa), feeling (vedanā) would not obtain the flavor of the object; and without the enjoyment [of that flavor], there would be no occasion for the arising of craving (taṇhā).
Thus, the threefold cycle itself would not exist. And just as those birds and others, having spread their wings...
Falling from one tree to another, from one forest to another, they wander about and sustain themselves.
But when their wings are gone, unable to achieve flight, they fall and die.

In the same way, these beings, having willed with volition characterized by exertion, having accomplished the possession of kamma, and having wandered from existence to existence, [sustain themselves] until this present life.

They wander in the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*). For if there were no such thing as volition (*cetanā*), there would be an absence of the cycle of kamma. In the absence of that, there would be an absence of the cycle of result (*vipāka*).
And in the absence of that, there would be an absence of the cycle of defilements (*kilesa*) which underlie it; thus, what is called the "cycle" would not exist.
And just as those birds and others, having discerned their field of vision or their respective directions with the eye, [remain] for as long as they live...
They sustain themselves. When the eye is absent, having found no object to grasp nor any place to go, they die right there.

In the same way, the associated mental states (dhammas), having obtained their respective objects through consciousness—which has the characteristic of cognizing an object—give rise to contact and the other factors therein, and thus cause the threefold round of existence to revolve. For if consciousness...
It would not exist; since there would be no acquisition of objects for contact and the other factors, the round of existence itself would not exist. Therefore he said: "The four nutriments...
consciousness is the fourth. And in the *Saṃyutta Nikāya*:
"Monks, these four nutriments are for the maintenance of beings who have come to be, or for the assistance of beings who are seeking existence."
It is said: "Edible food, whether gross or subtle; contact is the second; mental volition is the third; and consciousness is the fourth.

In this context, "of beings" (bhūtānaṃ) refers to those who have reached growth; "of those seeking existence" (sambhavesīnaṃ) refers to those existing at the stage of the embryo (*kalala*) and so forth.
Furthermore, these four nutriments, as they occur, serve for the maintenance of beings either throughout the beginningless cycle of existence (*saṃsāravaṭṭa*) or within this or that particular birth.
The mode of occurrence through assistance should be understood in the manner already stated. However, in the Commentary it is asked: "What is nutriment here? What does it nourish? It is said:
"Edible nutriment nourishes the eight kinds of material phenomena consisting of nutritive essence;

contact-nutriment [nourishes] the three feelings; mental volition-nutriment [nourishes] the three realms of existence; consciousness-nutriment [nourishes] the mind-and-matter of rebirth-linking. This is stated by way of the manifest fruit.

It should be understood that this is what was stated. However, the production of the eight types of materiality consisting of nutritive essence (*ojā*) is not the great function of edible food (*kabaḷīkārāhāra*);

rather, the support of the fourfold continuity of matter (*catusantatirūpa*) alone is the great function. For this very reason, it is said in the Pāḷi: "for the sake of maintenance" and "for the sake of assistance.
Furthermore, just as the conditions of decisive support (*upanissaya*) and repetition (*āsevana*) are twofold according to the Sutta method and the Abhidhamma method respectively;

Thus it is. Likewise, the nutriment-condition (*āhāra-paccaya*) is also twofold. In that regard, what was stated—that "mental volition-nutriment (*manosañcetanāhāra*) is for the production of existence"—was said with reference to the method of the Suttanta.
For in the *Paṭṭhāna*, immaterial nutriments do not become conditions in the sense of being a nutriment for states that are not co-nascent.
Furthermore, the factors of absorption (*jhānaṅga*) are not found in the fivefold sense-consciousnesses; for those [consciousnesses] possess weak functions, objects, and bases.
Since they are merely directed toward visible forms and so forth, the concentration (*ekaggatā*) present within them does not accomplish the function of jhāna.
It is said that jhāna has "applied thought" (*vitakka*) as its final member;

since applied thought, which acts as the leader of the jhāna factors, is absent in those [states], the concentration present therein does not accomplish that [function]. [They are] devoid of the support of energy (*vīriya*).
Since states do not attain stability among associated states, the function of concentration-power is not accomplished in the sixteen rootless consciousnesses that lack energy (*vīriya*).
For it is said, "Energy is the last of the powers"; thus he says that the powers are not found in those lacking energy.
Furthermore, states devoid of a cause serve as the path for the attainment of both saṃsāra (*vaṭṭa*) and *nibbāna* (*vivaṭṭa*).
They do not proceed. For it has been stated that "the path is the last of its causes"; thus he said that the path-factors are not found among the rootless states.

In a consciousness associated with doubt, one-pointedness is devoid of resolve, and because it is overwhelmed by doubt—which is by nature exclusively a state of vacillation—it is not powerful enough to function as a faculty or a power of the path; hence it was said [that] doubt...
"One-pointedness of mind does not attain the state of being a path-factor, faculty, or power.

Regarding the phrase "only in two-rooted and three-rooted impulsions," here the terms "two-rooted" and "three-rooted" exclude the impulsions of extreme delusion (*momūha*), the two types of laughter, and the functional impulsions.
The term "impulsion" excludes the resultant states of the three planes, whether they be two-rooted or three-rooted.
In the *Vibhāvani*, however, it is stated:

"By the mention of the two-rooted and three-rooted [consciousnesses], the absence of predominance-factors (*adhipati*) among those with a single root is shown. Yet, because of their commonality as states of impulsion (*javana*), their absence must indeed be shown even in the consciousness of laughter.
The phrase "as far as possible" (*yathāsambhava*) refers to those factors that have been previously obtained for each individual formation (*saṅkhāra*) and for the traditional lineage (*āgama*).
Only one [adhipati condition] is obtained according to its possibility; there is no second. Otherwise, it would not even exist as a predominance condition (*adhipati-paccaya*).

And having established this, it is not stated in the analysis of the predominance condition (*adhipati-paccaya-vibhaṅga*) in the *Paṭṭhāna* in the same way as it is stated in the analysis of the faculty condition (*indriya-paccaya-vibhaṅga*), where "the immaterial faculties are a condition by way of the faculty condition for associated states and for the material phenomena originated by them."

In that context, however, it is stated according to the classification of each individual predominance (adhipati), beginning with "the predominance of desire for those associated with desire," and so forth.
For when this is the case, the distinction between the predominances and the faculties (indriya) becomes manifest. "Nine are impelled" means nine are impelled, i.e., explained.
"Interspersed with the wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate" means interspersed with the wholesome and so forth. [The Summary of the Mixed.]
164. It is called *bodhi* because one awakens (*bujjhati*) to the four truths; or, it is *bodhi* because those [truths] are awakened to by means of this [wisdom] belonging to one who possesses it.
It is the knowledge of the four paths. For this has been said in the *Mahāniddesa*: "Bodhi is said to be the knowledge in the four paths. A "side" (*pakkha*) means a portion or constituent factor.
They are "factors conducive to enlightenment" (*bodhipakkhiya*) because they exist on the side of enlightenment. These are the higher virtue, higher mind, and higher wisdom.
This is the name for those teachings of the Teacher’s dispensation that are included within the three trainings as they have been analyzed.
Furthermore, since they consist of seven types by way of their divisions, he says: "the four foundations of mindfulness," and so forth.
Being preeminent and principal among associated states, they abide upon objects such as the body, having turned back the mind from wandering toward various objects.

They are called *paṭṭhānāni* (foundations) because they proceed by way of binding the mind to those very [objects] such as the body. Since mindfulness itself is the foundations, they are "foundations of mindfulness" (*sati-paṭṭhānāni*).

Although one should say "four foundations of mindfulness," it should be understood that they are called "the four foundations of mindfulness" with reference to their nature as phenomena (*dhamma-bhāva*).

"Contemplation of the body" (*kāyānupassanā*) means contemplation upon the body. Regarding the physical body, which is a collection of material form, [there is the contemplation] of inhalation, exhalation, and so forth...

The meaning is: the repeated, continuous contemplation until delusion regarding each respective part of the body—as being that particular part of the body, or as being impermanent and so forth—is abandoned in relation to each such part.

Furthermore, among the ninefold divisions of feeling, there is the contemplation of pleasant feeling and the others as being specific feelings of bodily parts, by way of their arising and passing away.

Contemplation of feelings (*vedanānupassanā*). Contemplation of the mind (*cittānupassanā*) is the contemplation, by way of its specific mental state and by way of its arising and passing away, of a particular constituent mind—such as a mind with lust (*sarāga*) among the sixteenfold classification—within minds that possess lust and so forth.

Contemplation of phenomena (*dhammānupassanā*) is the contemplation, by way of their specific nature and by way of their arising and passing away, of a particular constituent phenomenon—such as sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) among the fivefold classification of phenomena beginning with the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*).
Contemplation is the contemplation of phenomena (*dhammānupassanā*).

As for what is stated in the *Vibhāvani*: "The body (*kāya*) is the origin (*āya*) of the loathsome things such as head-hairs and so forth; or else, the body is the collection of inhalations and exhalations"—that is not at all satisfactory.
[216] And as for what was stated there, "Contemplation of the body is 'body-contemplation' (*kāyānupassanā*)," that too is not correct.
For it is said, "He dwells contemplating the body in the body. By this, the meaning "contemplation in the body is body-contemplation" is shown as the primary sense.

[217] Furthermore, as for what was stated there—"contemplation by way of feelings"—that too is not correct. For it is said, "one who contemplates feelings in feelings. The same applies to the section on contemplation of the mind.
[218] As for what was also stated there...

It has been stated: “The contemplation of phenomena that have distinct characteristics, such as perception and mental formations, is ‘contemplation of phenomena’ (dhammānupassanā). This too is not entirely correct.
For nowhere in the Canon (Pāḷi) are perception and mental formations specifically singled out and called “phenomena.
Indeed, in the Canon, first the six hindrances are called “phenomena”; after that, the five aggregates of clinging; and after that, the twelve sense bases.

Then there are the seven factors of enlightenment; then the four truths. If this is so, since the others are established when one single contemplation of phenomena has been taught, then only a single foundation of mindfulness should be mentioned, not four.

This is not so. For that aggregate of form which was mentioned in the context of the contemplation of phenomena was mentioned by way of contemplating its characteristic of being afflicted (*ruppana*). Indeed, the characteristic of being afflicted belongs to that which is produced...
It is the ultimate reality (*paramattha-dhamma*). And for one who contemplates in that manner, it serves specifically for the abandoning of the subtle perversion regarding self (*attavipallāsa*).

Furthermore, "body" (*kāya*) should be understood by way of the various material phenomena (*rūpa-dhamma*) that constitute a particular collection, and not by way of the characteristic of non-arising.
Nor is that collection of material phenomena, when apprehended as a particular body, called an "ultimate reality."

It exists because it is mixed with conceptual designation (*paññatti*). And for one who contemplates in that manner, it serves specifically for the abandoning of the gross perversion of beauty and so forth.
Likewise, in the case of feeling and consciousness as well, there are two types of perversions each:
the gross perversion and the subtle perversion. Among these, the perversions of permanence and pleasure associated with the self are gross; the perversion of self [is subtle].
It is subtle. Therein, the contemplation of feelings and the mind are stated separately for the abandoning of gross perversion.
Among the phenomena, the aggregates of feeling and consciousness are for the abandoning of subtle perversion. Therefore, only four foundations of mindfulness should be mentioned.
They are called "right endeavors" (sammappadhāna) because one exerts oneself rightly by means of them. Granted, even skin and sinews—
"Let only the bones remain; let the flesh and blood in my body dry up.
Whatever is to be attained by human strength and human exertion—that shall not be left unattained before my energy falters.

This is the name for right effort (*sammāvāyāma*) as it proceeds with such an irreversible application. Furthermore, although it proceeds in that single manner, by way of the accomplishment of its task—
"It becomes fourfold" refers to what was stated beginning with "of those arisen," and so forth.
Therein, "of evil things arisen" means: "At such a time, in such a place, or at such a spot, I committed this and that evil;
this and that indeed has arisen in me"—thus, they are known by way of their having arisen within one's own continuum.

"Of the unwholesome states": for the purpose of their abandonment—that is, for the sake of bringing about the state of non-arising again from this day forward until final Nibbāna within one's own continuum.
"Exertion" (*vāyāma*) means firm effort in the tasks of fulfilling virtue (*sīla*), and in the cultivation of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*).

"Unarisen" refers to those [unwholesome states] that have not previously arisen in one's own continuum, or which are unknown in the continua of others, or which are seen or heard in the discourses (*suttanta*).

"Of those known": "for their non-arising" means that those unwholesome roots, by whose existence such kinds of defilements or evil karmas arise in these beings, exist within me as well; I too am indeed not liberated from those defilements or karmas.
I too shall produce them within my own continuum either tomorrow, or the day after, or in future lives.
"Thinking, 'I am indeed a human being,'" one reflects in this way in order to sever the conditions for the arising of those unwholesome roots within one's own continuum.

Regarding "of wholesome states not yet arisen": among the wholesome phenomena belonging to the four planes of existence, which are divided into the seven purifications (*visuddhi*), one realizes, "These purified states have not yet been reached or attained by me," and thus, without transgressing the proper time, [one applies oneself].
For the sake of attaining those states of purification not yet reached or attained.
"For the further development of wholesome qualities that have arisen" means:

those wholesome qualities such as virtue (*sīla*) and so forth that have arisen in me—so long as they have not entered the path of certainty (*niyāma*), it is not appropriate to say, "These belong to me. Whether tomorrow or the day after tomorrow...

"Even after passing to another existence, they will surely break apart. Having reflected thus, [the effort] is for the sake of further increasing those [factors] that have arisen in one's own continuum by way of bringing about their state of being entirely unshakable.
Furthermore, it should be understood that the effort arising through any one of these four doors accomplishes all four functions.
In the *Aṭṭhakathā*, however, it is stated that at the very moment of the path (*magga-khaṇa*), one [supernormal power] accomplishes its four functions.
"Success" (*iddhi*) means succeeding; the meaning is the accomplishment, the fulfillment, and the production of each respective application of effort (*yogakamma*).

Briefly, this consists of: the accomplishment of direct knowledge (*abhiññā*) regarding phenomena to be directly known; the accomplishment of full understanding (*pariññā*) regarding phenomena to be fully understood; and the accomplishment of abandoning (*pahāna*) regarding phenomena to be abandoned.
It is fivefold: the accomplishment of abandoning, the accomplishment of realizing those things to be realized, and the accomplishment of developing those things to be developed.
Or, "success" (*iddhi*) means that it succeeds; it is the name for all sublime and supramundane states that succeed through the practice of yoga in the Teacher’s dispensation.
It is called a "foot" (*pāda*) because one goes by means of it. Thus, "the foot of success" is *iddhipāda*.
It is said that the means for attaining success (*iddhi*) is the powerful method and the cause of striving.
Furthermore, since it occurs in four ways by virtue of the four dominant factors (*adhipati-dhamma*), it is stated: "The four bases of success" (*cattāro iddhipādā*), and so forth.

The base of success that consists of desire itself is the "base of success consisting of desire" (*chandiddhipāda*). This same method applies to the remaining ones as well. And herein, all those states that are exalted and unsurpassed—those beyond the human state—...
These states are not to be attained by ordinary desire, energy, consciousness, or wisdom.
They are to be attained only by desire and the rest when they have reached the state of predominance (adhipati), being incapable of being obstructed by any impediment whatsoever.
Therefore, it should be understood that these four states are intended here precisely as predominant factors.
[219] Furthermore, regarding what is stated in the *Vibhāvanī*:
“It is called *iddhi* because one succeeds (*ijjhati*) by means of it, such as through resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna*) and so forth;

thus it is the knowledge of the various kinds of success (*iddhividha-ñāṇa*). A basis for success is a ‘basis of success’ (*iddhipāda*)”—that is explained in the *Saṃyutta Nikāya*: “And what, monks, is success? Here, monks, a monk [performs] manifoldly...”
"He experiences the various kinds of psychic power (*iddhividha*): being one, he becomes many... [and so on] up to: he exercises mastery with his body as far as the Brahma-world.

This accords with the scriptural passage: "This, monks, is called psychic power. Nevertheless, even though this is so, it does not fit here, because what is intended here is specifically the Abhidhamma method.
In the *Vibhaṅga*, however, in the first section, the aggregates of consciousness and mental factors—both mundane and supramundane—are stated to be the "bases of psychic power" (*iddhipāda*).
And in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "The preliminary work for the first jhāna is called a 'base of psychic power'; the first jhāna itself is called 'psychic power'... [and so on]...

The preliminary work for the jhāna of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is called a 'base of psychic power'; the jhāna of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is [psychic power]."
Regarding "success" (iddhi): insight into the path of stream-entry is called the basis of success; the path of stream-entry itself is called success. ...
Insight into the path of arahantship is called the basis of success; the path of arahantship itself is called success.
Furthermore, the first jhāna is called the basis of success; the second jhāna is called success. ... The jhāna of the base of nothingness is called the basis of success.
The base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is called "supernormal power" (*iddhi*). The path of stream-entry is called "basis of supernormal power" (*iddhipāda*).
The path of once-returning is called "supernormal power," and so on, up to the path of arahantship, which is also called "supernormal power.

It is also appropriate to say that each respective meditative absorption (*jhāna*) serving as a foundation is called "basis of supernormal power," and the path generated after emerging from each of those is called "supernormal power. However, in this context, within the *Uttaracūḷabhājaniya*...
According to the method already explained, the four dominant states (*adhipatidhamma*) themselves are called the bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*).
However, in that context, only those that are supramundane (*lokuttara*) were intended; here, they are both mundane and supramundane.

As for the faculties (*indriya*) and powers (*bala*), their meaning has already been explained below. From the perspective of their prominent positions, however, the strength of faith among the four factors of stream-entry (*sotāpattiyaṅga*) is [to be understood].
It should be understood as follows. As it was said: "Bhikkhus, where is the faculty of faith to be seen? It is to be seen in the four factors of stream-entry.
And regarding energy among the four right efforts: as it was said, "Bhikkhus, where is the faculty of energy to be seen? It is to be seen in the four right efforts."
Of mindfulness, in the four foundations of mindfulness. As it is said: "Bhikkhus, where is the faculty of mindfulness to be seen?
Bhikkhus, the faculty of mindfulness is to be seen here in the four foundations of mindfulness. Of concentration, in the four jhānas. As it is said:
"Bhikkhus, where is the faculty of concentration to be seen? Bhikkhus, the faculty of concentration is to be seen here in the four jhānas."
The strength of wisdom regarding the four noble truths is to be understood. As it has been said: "Bhikkhus, where is the faculty of wisdom to be seen? It is to be seen here, in the four noble truths.
Perfect enlightenment (*sambodhi*) is called the knowledge in the four paths; for it is so termed because one awakens thoroughly, penetrates thoroughly, or because by means of it they awaken.
For she, while awakening to the Dhamma of the Four Truths, awakens all around simultaneously with sixteen meanings, rather than in part;
thus, in the sense of being the originator of that awakening, it is a factor of awakening (*sambojjhaṅga*)—that is, a cooperative condition providing strength for awakening.
Mindfulness itself is the awakening-factor of mindfulness (*satisambojjhaṅga*). For it [is established] upon the four [objects], such as the body, within itself...

Through the process of cultivation within the spheres of activity, these [faculties] grow well and, in due course, having dispelled the entire side of negligence and fulfilled the entire side of diligence,
they give rise to full enlightenment (sambodhi), which is comprised of the knowledge of the four paths.

One investigates internal and external phenomena— which serve as the ground for insight— by means of their hardness, contact, and so forth, as well as by means of their impermanence and other characteristics.
Investigation of phenomena (*dhammavicaya*) is so called because, as if pulverizing them into various forms, it thoroughly examines every aspect of those things that are to be seen therein.
That very [factor] is a factor of enlightenment; thus, it is the "enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena.
For when it is well-cultivated through the process of development regarding those phenomena which constitute its own domain, it gradually overcomes the entire side of delusion.

Having dispelled everything belonging to the side of delusion and having fulfilled [the factors] on its own side, it arises having itself become the enlightenment consisting of the knowledge of the four paths.
Thus, right effort (*sammappadhāna*) as energy is the energy factor of enlightenment (*vīriya-sambojjhaṅga*).
For that too, when it is well-developed by way of cultivation within its own fourfold objective domains, gradually [leads to] all wholesome states.

Having dispelled the entire mass of defilements belonging to the side of lethargy, contraction, and indolence, and having fulfilled every aspect of the side of exertion, one brings forth the aforementioned enlightenment.
Thus, rapture itself is the enlightenment factor;
it is "rapture as an enlightenment factor. For that too, when it is well-nourished upon the aforementioned objects, [leads to enlightenment].

Having dispelled every aspect of mental aversion and restlessness regarding wholesome states, and having fulfilled every aspect of delight in the Dhamma, joy in the Dhamma, and delighting in the Dhamma, one brings forth the aforementioned enlightenment.
Because it is enlightenment through tranquility, it is the "tranquility factor of enlightenment. For that [tranquility] also, by way of cultivation, occurs within the aforementioned objects.

When fully developed, it dispels every part of the mind’s agitation and distress, fulfills every part of the side of total tranquility and coolness, and gives rise to the aforementioned enlightenment.
Thus, concentration itself is a factor of enlightenment; concentration is a factor of enlightenment. Its quality of giving rise to enlightenment is evident.
Equanimity, which is reckoned as "neither-pleasure-nor-pain," is itself a factor of enlightenment.
The enlightenment factor of equanimity (*upekkhā-sambojjhaṅga*).

For this too, when it is well-cultivated through the method of development upon the objects of mindfulness and the other factors already mentioned, it dispels all tendencies toward mental sluggishness and agitation, fulfills the side of evenness, and gives rise to the aforementioned full awakening.
Right view (*sammā-diṭṭhi*) is seeing correctly, without error. It...

Furthermore, knowledge is fourfold: knowledge of suffering, knowledge of the origin of suffering, knowledge of the cessation of suffering, and knowledge of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.

Right intention (*sammāsaṅkappo*) is the correct, non-erroneous forming of an intention. The meaning is that it functions as the preparation for right view, just as right view proceeds by pervading the essential natures of things as they are to be seen. For it is by that very [intention] that—
Thus, it is included within the aggregate of wisdom (*paññākkhandha*). As it has been said: "Friend Visākha, right view and right intention—these states are included within the aggregate of wisdom.
Right speech and the others have their meanings already explained above. One exerts oneself rightly in one way, thus it is right effort (*sammāvāyāma*).

It is the energy of the four right strivings (*sammappadhāna*) that accomplishes the four tasks. The two kinds of tranquility (*passaddhi*) are [treated] by way of the common characteristic of tranquility.
It is said that these fourteen [factors] are one by way of their intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).

"Sevenfold" means by way of the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right endeavors, and so forth, as previously described. Now, in order to show the classification of the bases for those fourteen functions, he says: "Intention, tranquility," and so on.
[220] Furthermore, as for what is stated in the *Vibhāvanī*:
“Having said that there is a sevenfold inclusion therein, it was further said ‘intention and tranquility,’ etc., in order to demonstrate that”; this is not tenable.
For the sevenfold nature is not found there in its own form. Intention and the three abstinences constitute a single factor of the Path.
[One] attains [it]. Tranquility, rapture, and equanimity share one station as enlightenment factors (*bojjhaṅga*).
Desire and consciousness share one station as bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*). Thus, nine states share one station.

Single energy (*vīriya*), by way of the four right strivings (*sammappadhāna*), bases of psychic power, faculties (*indriya*), powers (*bala*), enlightenment factors, and path factors (*maggaṅga*), has nine stations. Single mindfulness (*sati*) [is shared by] the four foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*).

By way of the faculties (*indriya*), powers (*bala*), factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*), and path-factors (*maggaṅga*), [wisdom] consists of eight bases. One concentration (*samādhi*) consists of four bases by way of the faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, and path-factors.
One wisdom (*paññā*) consists of five bases by way of the bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*), faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, and path-factors.
One faith (*saddhā*) consists of two bases by way of the faculties and powers. These, moreover, are the thirty-seven divisions.
In the preliminary stage, mental states have various objects and occur at various moments.
However, in the paths and fruits, the energy (viriya) consisting of nine factors takes Nibbāna as its sole object;

it proceeds as a single unity, accomplishing nine functions by way of uprooting the opposing evil states within those nine positions. This same method applies to the energy consisting of eight factors and so forth.
Therefore, it is said that "all are present in the supramundane" because they are all apprehended together within a single moment and a single consciousness.

Regarding the phrase "nine types of applied thought and rapture," here the word *vā* has the sense of "in some cases. The meaning is: in some cases there are applied thoughts belonging to the second jhāna and so on;
however, in some cases—namely, in the supramundane—they do not exist for those beginning with the fourth jhāna.

"Even in the worldly" refers even to the arising of worldly wholesome functional consciousnesses, such as those of sense-sphere wholesomeness, which proceed by way of the purification of virtue and so forth.

"According to what is suitable" means in accordance with the three types of abstinence and other factors that are to be applied in the tasks of purifying virtue, the task of serenity, and the discernment of name-and-form.
"In the proceeding of the sixfold purification" refers to the six purifications beginning with the purification of virtue.

In due course, during the time of its occurrence. By this, it is shown that even within the fourfold purification of virtue (catupārisuddhi-sīla) fulfilled for the sake of being established in the path and fruit in this very life, faith, mindfulness, and so forth are indeed included among the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya).

Likewise, it shows that joy is included in the sublime meditative absorptions (mahaggata-jjhāna) produced for the purpose of providing a basis for the path. For thus it is said in the Bojjhaṅga-Saṃyutta:
"Thus, Kuṇḍaliya, when the restraint of the sense faculties is developed, it fulfills the three types of good conduct.
When the three types of good conduct are developed in this way, they fulfill the four foundations of mindfulness.

When the four foundations of mindfulness are developed in this way, they fulfill the seven factors of enlightenment. When the seven factors of enlightenment are developed in this way, they fulfill true knowledge and liberation—so it has been said."
In the *Aṭṭhakathā* as well, it is stated that the factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*) are not extracted only in the case of powerful insight (*vipassanā*), the paths, and the fruits;

they are also extracted in the case of the jhānas based on insight, the kasiṇa-jhānas, the mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpāṇa*), and the sublime abodes (*brahmavihāra*). [Summary of the Requisites of Enlightenment] 165.

In the *Sabbasaṅgaha*, "five aggregates" (*pañcakkhandha*) refers to five heaps. An aggregate (*khandha*) is a collection of material phenomena (*rūpa*) divided according to categories such as the past and so forth.

"Rāsi" means the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*). It refers precisely to those phenomena of form that have been grouped together into a heap by way of the single characteristic of being "formed" (*ruppana-lakkhaṇa*) and apprehended by wisdom.

Likewise, those feelings and perceptions—distinguished by such divisions as past and so forth—that have been grouped into heaps by way of the single characteristic of "being felt" (*vedayita-lakkhaṇa*) and the characteristic of "perceiving" (*sañjānana-lakkhaṇa*) and apprehended [by wisdom], are called the aggregate of feeling (*vedanākkhandha*) and the aggregate of perception (*saññākkhandha*).
