They are called "formations" (*saṅkhārā*) because they "construct" (*saṅkharonti*). Contact (*phassa*)...
Volition and the rest: by these, whether at the six doors of rebirth or at the three doors of action, having come together and assembled,
they perform all their respective functions— such as touching and intending— or their common functions such as seeing and hearing,
or bodily, verbal, and mental actions such as lying down, sitting, standing, going, speaking, and thinking.
"They perform and fashion. For this has been said in the *Saṃyutta Nikāya*:
"And what, monks, do you call 'formations' (*saṅkhāra*)? Because they construct the constructed (*saṅkhata*), monks, they are therefore called 'formations.
And what do they construct as the constructed? They construct form for the sake of form; [they construct feeling for the sake of feeling...]"
They construct. They construct the conditioned for the sake of feeling. They construct the conditioned for the sake of perception.
They construct the conditioned for the sake of volitional formations. They construct the conditioned for the sake of consciousness.
"They construct the conditioned," monks—this is what it means.
Therefore they are called "formations" (*saṅkhārā*).
In this context, "they construct the formed for the sake of form" means that at whatever time a particular modification of form is desired—
whether occurring through lying down, sitting, or other such postures— at that very time, for the sake of the arising of that specific modification of form...
The meaning is that they construct various conditioned material transformations by means of changing postures and so forth.

It is entirely appropriate to include and apply all external matter—such as food and drink, clothing and ornaments, beds, chairs, houses, chariots, and the like—which serves as objects of enjoyment and utility. "Feeling" refers to that pertaining to the present life (*diṭṭhadhammika*).

And all feeling pertaining to future lives (*samparāyika*). Therein, while constructing conditioned things (*saṅkhata*) that pertain to the present life (*diṭṭhadhammika*), such as mental acts, dancing, singing, and so forth, by way of accomplishing the various requisites for feeling;
and while constructing those pertaining to future lives, one accomplishes giving, virtue, and so forth, having aspired to this or that feeling, whether human or divine.

They construct [them] by way of these [cravings]. This method applies to the remaining [aggregates] as well. Regarding volitional formations (*saṅkhārā*), however, one should expand upon them by understanding the entire course of worldly existence—such as "contact for the sake of contact," "volition for the sake of volition," and so forth;
or alternatively, "giving for the sake of giving," "virtue for the sake of virtue," "killing for the sake of killing," and so on.
Here it may be asked: why are they manifest among volitional formations?
Volition and the rest, applied thought and the rest, greed and the rest, and faith, mindfulness, wisdom, and the rest—these states are not mentioned individually as being distinct aggregates;
rather, only feeling and perception are mentioned. To this it is said:
Just as a skilled great physician, having taken the roots of medicinal herbs and grinding them into powder, [identifies] those roots as follows...
Even the large pieces become soft. Knowing that these small ones are hard, he first extracts the hard ones separately, grinds them well, and makes them into powder.
Then, having gathered all the remaining soft pieces together, he grinds them and makes them into powder.
Afterward, having mixed both together and ground them on a stone, for the medicinal preparation—
He brings them near. Acting in this way, he does not grow weary.

In the same manner, the Blessed One, having applied the three characteristics to the phenomena of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), and knowing that gods and humans who strive for the sake of abandoning the perversions of permanence, pleasure, and self would become exhausted regarding the three phenomena if no distinction were made, [he taught] the three [phenomena] designated as feeling, perception, and consciousness among the phenomena of name.
Having extracted the Dhamma from its various parts and designated each as a "khandha," he taught it.
For instance, just as fish have no such thing as weariness so long as there is water, but become utterly weary when it is absent;
or just as honey-bees or bumblebees have no weariness in whatever forest they find the nectar of flowers or the juice of fruits.

There is none. But failing to obtain them, beings become utterly despondent. In the very same way, among the refuges designated as "happiness" for these sentient beings, there is no refuge equal to feeling (*vedanā*).

Even when enjoying the attainments of humans, devas, and brahmās, they enjoy them solely for the sake of pleasant feeling. And if, without those [attainments], one were to obtain pleasant feeling according to one's desire...
[They] would obtain [it]. Who indeed would consent to that?

Likewise, even while constructing any conditioned thing—whether pertaining to this life or the future life—by means of the mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha) such as contact, volition, and so forth; applied thought, sustained thought, energy, and so forth;
and greed, hatred, and so forth; as well as faith, mindfulness, wisdom, and so forth, they construct it solely for the sake of pleasant feeling. And if...
"Even without such volitional formations, they could obtain whatever pleasure they desire;
therefore, there is no need for those phenomena—so who indeed would form them?
Thus, among those phenomena designated as "pleasure," feeling (*vedanā*) is the state that represents the ultimate pinnacle of what is designated as pleasure for these beings.
Therefore, the Blessed One, having made that a separate single aggregate, teaches the exposition of the aggregates.
Likewise, among the things designated as "self" which serve as refuges for these beings, there is no refuge equal to perception.
For in each respective class of beings, those various beings [rely] upon everything within their own respective domains.
Having perceived through perception, they attain discernment (*viññutta*). Attaining such discernment, they think:
"As much as others know, so much do we also know. Who is superior to us?
Thus, having made perception—the supreme conceit of knowledge in the world—their self, they wander about. Such is the nature of these phenomena designated as "self," namely, perception.
It is the supreme refuge for beings, the place designated as "self. Therefore, the Blessed One also teaches the exposition of the aggregates by making it one distinct aggregate.
Likewise, among the things regarded as permanent refuges by these beings, there is no refuge equal to the mind.
For indeed, what is called pleasure and pain is impermanent.
For those who have attained happiness, there is no suffering; for those who have fallen into suffering, there is no happiness. Perception (saññā) is impermanent:
sometimes it is forgotten, sometimes it is not forgotten. Energy (vīriya) is impermanent:
sometimes one exerts it, sometimes one does not exert it. Greed (lobha) is impermanent: sometimes it arises, sometimes it does not arise. Hatred (dosa) is...
It is impermanent. Sometimes it arises, sometimes it does not arise. That which is called faith is impermanent;
sometimes one has a confident mind, sometimes one has a lack of confidence. That which is called wisdom is impermanent; sometimes one knows what ought to be known, sometimes one does not know it.
Thus, the impermanent nature of mental phenomena is understood even by some worldly people.
It is evident [to them], but not as it truly is regarding the mind. For beings do not grasp that what is called "mind" is impermanent;

they think, "Sometimes it arises, sometimes it does not arise. Yet, while the mind itself is proceeding constantly, they conceive of it as permanent, thinking such things as, "Sometimes it is associated with pleasure, sometimes with pain," and so forth. Thus, as for what is called "mind":
Among phenomena regarded as permanent, there is a state regarded as permanent that has reached the highest point.
Therefore, the Blessed One, having made even that a separate aggregate (*khandha*), teaches the exposition of the aggregates.
[221] As for what is stated in the *Vibhāvani*:

“Only five [aggregates] are mentioned according to the analogy of the vessel, the food, the condiment, the cook, the eater, and the disposer,” it is said; and in order to explain this, [it is stated]:
“For form (rūpa) is like a vessel because it is the support for feeling (vedanā). Feeling is like food because it is what is to be consumed.
Perception (saññā) is like a condiment because it is the cause for obtaining the relish of feeling. Volitional formations (saṅkhārā) [are like a cook] because of their fashioning.”
“Consciousness, being the experiencer, stands in the place of the eater.
It is for this reason that only five [aggregates] are mentioned, since the intended meaning is established by this much. This should not be taken as authoritative.
For that [explanation] does not appear in the *Aṭṭhakathā* as a definitive analysis limited to this extent; it appears merely as an illustration through a simile. Nor...
It can be said that the Blessed One spoke of only the five aggregates with the aim of establishing the mere conceptualization of the "vessel" and so forth;
for there would be no purpose in establishing such a thing as it actually exists.
And as for what is therein...

“It is for this very reason that [the order] is thus in the sequence of the teaching: because he wishes to show, in their proper order, where one eats, what one eats, by means of what one eats, who the eater is, and who the one who causes eating is. This too is without substance.
The aggregates that are the objective sphere of the four kinds of clinging are the “aggregates subject to clinging” (*upādānakkhandha*).

All phenomena belonging to the same class, both with taints (*sāsava*) and without taints (*anāsava*), are stated to be the five aggregates by way of exhausting all such phenomena; however, they are only those with taints when considered by way of encompassing the plane of insight (*vipassanā*).

The five aggregates of clinging (*pañcupādānakkhandhā*) have been mentioned. They are called "bases" (*āyatanāni*) because they exert themselves intensely (*āyatanti*), as it were, toward the production of their own results.
Now, when the term "base" (*āyatana*) applies to the six internal door-phenomena, it is used in the sense of a place of origin, a dwelling place, or a source;
whereas regarding the six external object-phenomena, [it is used in the sense of being the field of experience].
In the sense of a coming together (*samosaraṇa*), it occurs; in both cases, it occurs in the sense of a cause (*kāraṇa*).

Therein, the mental states (*citta*) and mental factors (*cetasika dhammā*)—arising again and again, either in a single existence or in the beginningless cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*)—arise only at the six locations of the sense-doors, such as the eye, and nowhere else.
Even while persisting by way of a continuous succession (*santānānubandha*), they abide only in those very places.
They dwell there and not elsewhere. Even while functioning, they proceed only in those very places, as if scattered and established there, and not elsewhere.

Therefore, the eye and the other [senses] are called "bases" (āyatana) in the sense of being the place of birth for the six [consciousnesses], in the sense of being their dwelling place, and in the sense of being their source.
It is also appropriate to say that they are so called in the sense of being a foundation, like a deity’s shrine (devāyatana).

Just as birds constantly gather from here and there at trees that are secure and abound with flowers and fruit, for the sake of shelter and food, so too do consciousness and mental factors constantly gather from here and there at the six bases, beginning with visible form, for the purpose of making them their object.
Therefore, visible form and the rest are called "bases" (*āyatana*) in the sense of being meeting places. Both of these [the bases and the elements]...
Furthermore, these [bases] are called *āyatanas* in the sense of being the causes for those minds and mental factors.
It is the eye and it is a base (*āyatana*), thus it is the "eye-base" (*cakkhāyatana*). The others are to be understood in the same way.

Among them, the eye and the ear are mentioned first because they are of great assistance in beings' performance of beneficial actions, because they pervade both the desire and fine-material realms, and because they are prominent. Because it is proximate to them, the nose follows immediately after.
Then there is the tongue—these four are called the sense-bases of the physical locations (*padesāyatana*). Then there is the body, which pervades the entire physical frame.

Then there is the mind (*mano*), which grasps the objective spheres and domains of all those [senses]. As for the remaining [objects], they are mentioned in that same sequence because they constitute the respective objects of those [faculties].
However, this does not occur under the sway of any particular individual, being, human, deity, or Brahmā.

They are called *dhātus* because they bear their own individual nature (*sabhāva*). Alternatively, they are called *dhātus* because, owing to their being established in distinct individual natures, they are borne, characterized, and defined according to their respective natures.
Furthermore, they are *dhātus* in the sense of being devoid of a sentient being (*nissatta*) and devoid of a living soul (*nijjīva*).

In this context, "in the sense of being devoid of a sentient being" means in the sense of the absence of the mode of a being, in the sense of the absence of the state of a being, and in the sense of the absence of the function of a being. What...

In this context, what is the mode of being a sentient being (*sattākāra*), and what is the function of a sentient being (*sattakicca*)? The mode of being a sentient being is the association with life-force (*jīvayoga*). The function of a sentient being consists of striving (*īhā*) and activity (*byāpāra*). "In the sense of being devoid of a soul" (*nijjīvaṭṭhena*) means:

as long as one does not die within a single existence, or as long as the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) does not cease throughout the succession of existences, it continues on as one and the same, unbroken and uninterrupted;
thus, it is in the sense of the non-existence of a "life-force" (*jīva*) conceived in such a manner.

The elements beginning with the eye are entirely devoid of the mode of a sentient being and devoid of the functions of a sentient being. They are not themselves called "living beings," nor are they associated with a living being.
Thus, in the sense of being without a sentient being and in the sense of being without a life-principle, these are called the four elements.
Furthermore, their manner of appearance is described in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā), as it says: "The eye-element is like the surface of a drum."

They are to be seen as follows: the visible-object element (*rūpadhātu*) is like a stick; the eye-consciousness element (*cakkhuviññāṇadhātu*) is like the sound [produced by it]. Likewise, the eye-element (*cakkhudhātu*) is like the surface of a mirror;
the visible-object element is like the face; the eye-consciousness element is like the reflection of the face.
Alternatively, the eye-element is like a sugarcane-pressing machine; the visible-object element is like the axle and wheel of that machine; the sugarcane juice...
The eye-consciousness element is like the oil. Likewise, the eye element is like the lower fire-drill;
the visible-form element is like the upper fire-drill; and the eye-consciousness element is like the fire. This same method applies to the ear-consciousness element and the others.
As for the mind element, however, it should be regarded as preceding and following the eye-consciousness element and the rest, according to their occurrence.

Within the element of phenomena (dhammadhātu), the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha) should be regarded as like a dart and like a stake. Perception (saññā) and the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha), being joined with the dart and stake of feeling, should be regarded as like those who are afflicted.

Alternatively, for worldlings (puthujjana), perception is like an empty fist because it generates longing and because it grasps signs that are not according to reality, like a forest deer. Mental formations [are so called] because they cast one into rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi).
Form should be viewed as being like men throwing glowing embers; like a thief pursued by royal guards because he is bound to suffering through birth;

like seeds of a poison tree because they are the cause of the continuity of the aggregates which bring about all manner of harm; and like a razor-wheel because it is the sign of various kinds of calamities.
The unconditioned element should be viewed as the deathless, the peaceful, and the secure.

Why? Because it is the opposite of all that is harmful. Mental-consciousness-element (manoviññāṇadhātu) is like a monkey in the forest because it proceeds by letting go of one grasped object and seizing another; it is like a wild colt because it is difficult to tame;
it is like a staff thrown into the air and falling wherever it may; and it is like an actor because of its association with various kinds of defilements such as greed, hatred, and so forth.
"They are to be seen as if [they were]... Regarding the term "Noble Truths" (*ariyasaccāni*): here, the state of a phenomenon that is real is "truth" (*sacca*).
"Of that which is real" means of that which is existent, such, non-perverted. Furthermore, in what sense is it "truth"?

In the sense of being such (*tatha*), in the sense of being non-false (*avitatha*), and in the sense of being non-otherwise (*anaññatha*). For that which is the suffering-nature of the eye is such, non-false, and non-otherwise.

It is so called because it constantly oppresses the person endowed with it by means of the three types of suffering known as the suffering of pain (*dukkhadukkha*), the suffering of formations (*saṅkhāradukkha*), and the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmadukkha*).
Among these, "suffering of formations" refers to the suffering involved in the performance of various kamma-formations, let alone the suffering at the time of the arising of what is born of kamma.

Likewise, it refers to the suffering involved in the performance of various seasonal, mental, and nutriment-born formations, let alone the suffering at the time of the arising of what is born of the seasons and so forth.
For the eye indeed arises only for those material-brahmās who, in a previous existence, experienced the great suffering of volitional formations consisting of the cultivation of jhāna;

it does not arise otherwise. But even for those attached to sense pleasures, although the eye may have arisen after they experienced the suffering of karmic formations in a previous existence, there is still the suffering of the formations of food and so forth during its continued activity throughout life, as well as the suffering of maintenance.

It proceeds only while being experienced, and not otherwise. While it is proceeding, it breaks up at some time or other—either due to a deficiency of conditions, or because of birth, or because of an obstacle that has arisen.
But when the time of death is reached, it necessarily breaks up.
Therefore, for those who, relishing it, perform karma for its sake, or prepare food and other requisites, or provide maintenance, there is no end in sight.

In *saṃsāra*, there is indeed no end to the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṅkhāradukkha*). Thus, the entire eye constantly oppresses the person with this boundless suffering of conditioned formations.

This is its suffering of conditioned formations. Furthermore, this thing called the "eye" is by nature subject to breaking at any time—whether it arises due to a deficiency of conditions or when an obstacle has arrived.
Therefore, out of fear that it might break, one should [act] beforehand...

The suffering of procuring conditions, the suffering of providing for protection, defense, and security, and the suffering of sorrowing and lamenting upon seeing signs of decay, while it is decaying, or when it has decayed—this is called the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmadukkha*).
Thus, the eye constantly afflicts the person with this boundless suffering of change. This is its [nature].
There is the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmadukkha*). Furthermore, the suffering of suffering (*dukkhadukkha*) is established together with both of those types of suffering.

Thus, the eye—by means of these three sufferings known as the suffering of suffering, the suffering of formations (*saṅkhāradukkha*), and the suffering of change—constantly afflicts the person who possesses it.
And that affliction of it is true; it is not false.
There is no other way. Therefore, the eye is called the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*).
This same method applies to the ear and so forth, as well as to all phenomena belonging to the three planes of existence.

Regarding the remaining truths, one should explain how it is that greed alone is the origin of suffering, why Nibbāna alone is the cessation of suffering, and why the Eightfold Path alone is the path leading to the cessation of suffering, and so on.
As long as greed is not abandoned, one continues to relish the eye and the other [senses].

As long as one relishes them, one continues to form volitional formations (saṅkhāra) such as karma for their continued occurrence. As long as one forms such volitional formations, the eye and the others continue to occur.
As long as they occur, they are subject to the aforementioned kinds of suffering and other [defilements] inherent in those formations.
It is indeed abandoned. Therefore, the fact that greed is the origin of suffering is true.
Furthermore, while the eye and the other [senses] are active, all the aforementioned suffering indeed arises; when they are not active, it does not arise.
Therefore, the fact that Nibbāna—which is the cessation of their activity—is the cessation of suffering is true. Likewise, because of the abandoning of greed...
There is no other path for the cessation of suffering; and when the Eightfold Path arises, it abandons that [suffering] absolutely.
Therefore, it is only the Eightfold Path that is truly the "path leading to the cessation of suffering"—it is suchness, not otherwise, and not different.
Even so, because the word *sacca* (truth) also applies to truths in a figurative sense, it is said: "the Four Noble Truths."
In that regard, concerning the truth of suffering (*dukkha-sacca*), those internal phenomena designated as "personality" (*sakkāya*) are indeed called a noble truth (*ariyasacca*).
For it is precisely these [phenomena] that, having become the basis for the conceit "I am" (*asmimāna*), cause suffering to persist as long as they do not eradicate that conceit.
Furthermore, the full comprehension of suffering (*dukkha-pariññā*) occurs only through the uprooting of this conceit "I am. And that conceit "I am" resides in those very [phenomena].
"It settles upon internal phenomena" means that when those [phenomena] have been fully understood (*pariññāta*), the task of full understanding is already accomplished.

Conversely, however, those phenomena not bound by the faculties (*anindriya-baddha-dhammā*)—namely, the path and fruit states, excluding the eight factors [of the noble path]—are called the truth of suffering (*dukkha-sacca*) because they are not yet liberated from the suffering of formations (*saṅkhāra-dukkha*) and the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-dukkha*) due to their arising and passing away and their state of oppression. Regarding the truth of origin (*samudaya-sacca*):

Greed alone is what is called a Noble Truth (ariyasacca). For it, by producing a sense of gratification in beings who possess a self, as well as in the self itself and in the phenomena that serve as its objects, causes them to never feel weary of the suffering of the round of existence (vaṭṭadukkha).
Therefore, there appears to be no other—whether kinsman, friend, companion, self, or anything belonging to a self—that is like this greed. Thus, it is similar to that.

There is no other thing whatsoever that provides the suffering of the round of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*). And for one capable of abandoning that [ignorance], there is nothing else that is difficult to abandon.
Furthermore, all remaining defiled (*sāsrava*) states—both wholesome and unwholesome—are called the truth of the origin (*samudayasatya*).
Here it might be asked: "Is not ignorance also said to be the root of all the suffering of the round? Therefore, should it not also be included in the origin?"

"It should be said that they are indeed the Noble Truths. It is replied: For instance, a certain clever park-keeper, having obtained a plot of land endowed with favorable conditions, by the power of his own knowledge prepared both the ground and various seeds, and constructed a garden resembling the Nandana grove.
In that case, the function of the ground is to serve as the foundation for the park-keeper, the seeds, and the trees.
It accomplishes [its purpose]. Just as seeds accomplish the function of producing a sprout, yet it is the gardener alone who accomplishes all the tasks;
for he performs whatever must be done regarding the soil, the seeds, and the trees.
He takes possession of them as "mine," guards them, and then enjoys the wealth produced from them. Therefore, who was it that laid this out?
When it is asked, "Whose park is this?", if it is said that the park-keeper himself laid it out, then it is called "his park.
One does not lay out the ground; rather, they sow the seeds. When it is asked, "Whose park is this?", it is called "their park.
Furthermore, when it is asked what the succession of conditions for the excellence of a park is, first the ground itself must be mentioned, and not the park-keeper, nor the seeds.

This should be understood in this very way. For when one has reached the method of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*), in the exposition of the occurrence and cessation of suffering phenomena by way of the succession of conditions, it is ignorance (*avijjā*) alone that is the primary source and the principal factor, not craving (*taṇhā*).
However, in the teaching on the Truths (*sacca-desanā*), in the exposition of the factors that produce them, it is craving alone that is the sovereign lord and the principal factor.
It exists. "There is no ignorance" should be understood as meaning that there is no opportunity for ignorance to exist within the state of the Noble Truth of Origination.

The cessation of defilements through their partial cessation (*tadaṅga-nirodha*), suppression (*vikkhambhana-nirodha*), and eradication (*samuccheda-nirodha*) is called the Noble Truth of Cessation. Nibbāna is called the Noble Truth of Cessation.
Within the six mundane purifications, the factors of the path (*maggaṅgāni*) are called the Noble Truth of the Path. It is precisely the supramundane Eightfold Path [that constitutes this].
"Regarding the term 'the Noble Truth of the Path':
here, the word *ariya* (noble) signifies the supreme state because it is, in some respects, for some people, from some source, and in some manner, non-false (*avitatha*).
Furthermore, the meaning of the word *sacca* (truth) has been elucidated in the *Vibhāvanī-ṭīkā* according to the method stated in the commentary [beginning with] 'Suffering is noble...'"

Regarding "truth" (*sacca*), the fact that each individual phenomenon of the three planes—beginning with the eye—is the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*) should be understood through these four meanings: the meaning of oppression, the meaning of being conditioned, the meaning of burning, and the meaning of changeability.

Among these, the meaning of being conditioned and the meaning of changeability are exactly as previously explained in the context of the suffering of formations (*saṅkhāradukkha*) and the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmadukkha*).
That which is conditioned by conditions as they are established in their respective positions is "conditioned" (*saṅkhata*).

This implies that it does not arise or proceed even without the suffering produced by the conditioning of kamma and other such conditions. "Transformation" (*vipariṇāma*) means changing into a different state;

it is both decay and disintegration. Regarding the sense of "affliction" (*pīḷanaṭṭha*): here, "affliction" (*pīḷana*) refers to that which is to be afflicted, or it is so called because it afflicts, or it is being afflicted.
"Pīḷanaṃ" means "the state of being oppressed. "Attha" means "essential nature. The analysis of the compound is: "that whose essential nature is oppression.

In this context, it is just as when a son is born from the womb of a certain woman of ill-repute; he, being himself constantly oppressed by various diseases, in turn constantly oppresses his mother with the hardships of nursing him. And that which is the birth of such a son from her womb—

And that [suffering] is merely the function of oppression for that woman. In the same way, those phenomena such as the eye and so forth, which are constantly oppressed by aging and death, constantly oppress the person endowed with them through the sufferings of their maintenance.
And their arising within his continuum is merely their function of oppressing him. As it has been said: "O monks, just as..."
The arising, the persistence, the manifestation, and the appearance of the eye; this is the arising of suffering, the persistence of diseases, and the manifestation of aging and death.
"Monks, whatever is the arising of the ear, the nose, the tongue, the body, and the mind," and so forth.
The "state of burning" means the state of being intensely scorched by the eleven fires, such as the fire of lust and the rest. As it is said:
"The eye is ablaze. By what is it ablaze? It is ablaze with the fire of lust, the fire of hatred, and the fire of delusion;
it is ablaze with birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair—thus I say.
The ear is ablaze... the nose is ablaze... the tongue is ablaze... the body is ablaze... the mind is ablaze."
"Kindling, burning, and blazing" are identical here in meaning. Here it might be argued:

"The Noble Path (ariyamagga) also indeed afflicts the person thoroughly with the suffering of the volitional formations of the perfections (pāramitā) over a long period of time, and with the suffering of the volitional formations of the cultivation of purification such as virtue (sīla) in the final existence;
likewise, it is subject to the nature of change. Therefore, it too would be included within the Truth of Suffering (dukkhasacca) in the sense of affliction and so forth."
It cannot be said that it "might be. Because it is the pacification of all suffering.
For when it arises once in a person who has fully experienced the aforementioned suffering of volitional formations (*abhisaṅkhāradukkha*), it arises expelling the entire mass of defilements.
And when it ceases, it ceases pacifying the round of suffering in the beginningless cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) for all time to come. And when it has been pacified—
Compared to future suffering, the aforementioned suffering of volitional formation (*abhisaṅkharaṇa-dukkha*) does not even approach its magnitude.
Furthermore, when it dissolves, it does so only after bestowing the unsurpassed bliss of liberation (*anuttara-vimutti-sukha*).

Therefore, because there is no loss whatsoever for the person resulting from the condition of its change, it is not included within the Truth of Suffering (*dukkha-sacca*). However, as for mundane phenomena (*lokiya-dhammā*) arising...
When they arise, they do so having intensely oppressed [the person] with the aforementioned types of suffering inherent in formations;

and when they cease, they do so having generated great suffering of fever and binding the individual to the wheel of the round of existence—which is like a razor-edged wheel and has no end—while they themselves cease.
Therefore, by way of these meanings such as oppression and so forth, they are exclusively suffering.

"They exist. By this, the undesirable consequence that even *nibbāna* would fall under the category of the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*)—on account of its being affected by even a trace of the formative activity (*abhisankhāra*) of conditions that bring about [existence]—is averted.
Regarding "the noble truth of the origin of suffering" (*dukkhasamudaya ariyasacca*): here, the mass of suffering known as becoming and non-becoming (*bhavābhava*) originates.

It is called the "origin of suffering" because it arises (*samudeti*), rises up again and again without interruption (*abbocchinnaṃ katvā udayati*), brings it forth, and increases it; thus, its meaning is that of accumulation (*āyūhana*).
The fact that greed is the origin of suffering should be understood through four meanings: the meaning of accumulation, the meaning of bondage, the meaning of impediment, and the meaning of source.

Therein, the "meaning of accumulation" refers to the sense of furthering and heaping up—that is, the sense of being a source—the mass of suffering associated with sensual objects pertaining to each individual existence within the cycle of becoming and non-becoming; it is that very [suffering] occurring without interruption.
"Having made [it], the sense of bestowing" means the sense of handing over. "The sense of bondage" means the sense of a firm fetter within the very mass of suffering (*dukkhakkhandha*).
"The sense of impediment" means the sense of being bound by way of obstructing the respective means for liberation from that [suffering];
the meaning is the sense of confinement. Regarding "the noble truth of the cessation of suffering," here [is the cessation] of the suffering of the round of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*).

The cessation of suffering is the cessation of those things that are wasting away by way of their ceasing and the attainment of the nature of non-arising. Or, it is "the cessation of suffering" because suffering ceases and does not proceed further within it.

The meaning of Nibbāna as the cessation of suffering should be understood through four meanings: the meaning of escape, the meaning of seclusion, the meaning of the unconditioned, and the meaning of the deathless. Therein, the meaning of escape refers to escape.
The meaning of liberation is the act of being liberated. The meaning of seclusion (*viveka*) is the act of being secluded from the obstacles of the suffering of the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*).
The meaning of the unconditioned (*asaṅkhata*) is the absence of the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṅkhāra*). The meaning of the deathless (*amata*) is the absence of the suffering of death.
Regarding the phrase "the practice leading to the cessation of suffering": here, it leads to, that is, brings about, the cessation of suffering; thus, it is "leading to the cessation of suffering."
It is called *paṭipadā* because it is to be practiced as the means for obtaining [the goal] within one's own continuum. The analysis of the compound is:

"it is both the path leading to the cessation of suffering (*dukkhanirodhagāminī*) and the path itself (*paṭipadā*). The fact that the Eightfold Path is the path to the cessation of suffering should be understood through four meanings: the meaning of deliverance (*niyyāna*), the meaning of cause (*hetu*), the meaning of seeing (*dassana*), and the meaning of predominance (*adhipateyya*). Among these, the meaning of deliverance is:

The sense of turning away is the meaning of emerging by reversing the stream of the round of existence—beginning with "with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise"—and facing the counter-stream of the round, beginning with "from the cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of volitional formations.
The sense of cause is the meaning of establishing all noble qualities in a well-founded state.
The sense of seeing is [the meaning] of the Dhamma of the Four Truths by way of abandoning delusion, which consists of unknowing and non-seeing.

The sense of penetration (*paṭivijjhanaṭṭha*). The sense of sovereignty (*adhipateyyaṭṭha*) means the sense of shining forth by being oneself one's own master through the attainment of the state of a true free person, liberated from the slavery of craving (*taṇhā*).
For mundane paths, remaining as objects for craving, do not transcend the slavery of craving. And herein, these so-called beings are absolutely repulsive as suffering.
They are afraid of suffering. Yet, they perceive as enemies those very beings who produce suffering within themselves.
However, they do not recognize that which is exclusively suffering, or that which produces exclusively suffering, for themselves.

Therefore, whatever action they undertake for the sake of their own liberation from suffering, each such act results only in the increase of their own suffering. But what, indeed, is exclusively suffering?

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "producing absolute suffering": the very phenomena belonging to the three planes (*tebhūmakadhammā*), which have existed in the past, future, and present, and which are included within one's own selfhood (*attahāva*), are themselves called "absolute suffering" for each respective individual.
Why? Because when one is separated from them, one is liberated from all sufferings, whereas when one is not separated from them, one is not liberated.
One's own craving (*taṇhā*) alone is what is called "the producer of absolute suffering" for oneself.
Why? Because when that [craving] is abandoned, one is liberated from exclusively painful states, whereas when it is not abandoned, one is not liberated.
Likewise, these beings desire happiness exclusively and delight in happiness; they conceive the perception of "dear friend" toward those who produce happiness for them.
Yet, they do not know either absolute happiness or the path to absolute happiness for themselves.
Therefore, whatever action they exert for the sake of increasing their own happiness results only in the increase of their own suffering.
But what is absolute happiness, and what is the path to absolute happiness? The very absence of the nature of absolute suffering is called one's own absolute happiness.
And the path that abandons that which produces absolute suffering is indeed the path to one's own absolute happiness.
It should be understood that these four terms for the Truths were spoken by him in order to demonstrate this meaning:
"The path to happiness. Furthermore, regarding what is stated in the *Vibhāvani*:
"The non-arising and cessation of suffering—either through this [path] or here [in this state]—is the cessation of suffering," the phrase "through this" (*etenā*) is not appropriate in that context.
For Nibbāna is not a cooperative cause for the production of suffering in the process of its non-arising and cessation.
"The remaining mental factors" refers to the fifty mental factors other than feeling and perception.

[They are so called] in the sense of being a collection (*rāsa*) of phenomena that are divided into three types by way of the past and so forth, and into two types by way of internal and so forth, gross and so forth, inferior and so forth, and distant and so forth.
There is conventional designation for the aggregates (*khandha*). However, for Nibbāna, there is no such differentiation; thus it is said, "by the absence of differentiation," and so forth.
For that [Nibbāna] does not exist even as one among the threefold divisions of past and so on. Why? Because its nature is indefinable.
For it is precisely the signless (*animitta*) phenomenon, consisting in the destruction, fading away, and cessation of phenomena belonging to the three times. Therefore, regarding the past...
It cannot be demonstrated by way of distinctions of time, such as: "Nirvana occurred during the time of such-and-such a Buddha," "this will occur in the future," or "this occurs at present.
Likewise, it cannot be shown by distinctions of direction, country, or location, nor by distinctions between individuals who have attained final Nibbana.
Rather, it is only by means of the qualities established as the opposites of whatever unwholesome states (*anattha*) are seen throughout the beginningless cycle of existence (*saṃsāra-vatta*).
"It should be explained as follows. Regarding the dyads, however, upon reaching the internal dyad, it is only external;
it is not internal. Upon reaching the gross dyad, it is only subtle; it is not gross. Upon reaching the inferior dyad, it is only sublime; it is not inferior.
Upon reaching the distant dyad, it is only distant; it is not near. "Released from inclusion within the aggregates" means liberated from inclusion within the aggregates.
"By way of the distinction between doors and objects" means by way of the distinction between the six doors and the six objects. The construction is: "there are twelve bases.

In this context, it should be understood that the "six doors" have only the mental object (dhamma) as their object; therefore, the "six objects" are stated with reference to the remaining objects of the other [five] factors.
"By way of the doors... etc., by way of the sequence" refers to the six doors and the six objects.
The construction is as follows: "The eighteen elements arise in sequence from those doors, objects, and consciousnesses that have arisen.

Here too, within the sixfold set of doors, the mind-door (*manodvāra*) is merely a portion of consciousness. And the sixfold set of doors and the sevenfold set of consciousnesses are merely a portion of mental phenomena (*dhammā*) as objects.
The construction is: "The supramundane path is what is called 'the path' (*magga*). The twenty-nine factors associated with the path [are as follows]:...
And the thirty-seven states that have become the fruit are dissociated from the Four Truths; they are dissociated and liberated from the four Noble Truths.
Whatever needs to be said regarding this has already been stated above.
Thus ends [the commentary on] the *Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha*, titled *Paramatthadīpanī*.
The Elucidation of the Ultimate Meaning (*Paramatthadīpanī*) for the Compendium of Categories (*Saṅgaha*),
within the Fourth Commentary, is finished.
[Now begins] the Elucidation of the Ultimate Meaning of the Compendium of Conditions (*Paccayasaṅgaha*).

166. Having thus shown the method for the first knowledge, the delimitation of mind-and-matter (*nāmarūpa-pariccheda-ñāṇa*), by means of seven sections, he now spoke the passage beginning with "Of those conditioned phenomena...
in order to show the method for the second knowledge, the discernment of conditions (*paccaya-pariggaha-ñāṇa*).
Now, [he explains] which conditioned phenomena, which phenomena that are both conditioned and unconditioned, in what manner, and by which causes and so forth...
Conditions are supportive by way of their modes of conditionality (*paccayākāra*). The construction [of the sentence] is as follows:

"I shall explain, as appropriate, the classification of those conditioned phenomena that have arisen through conditions, the classification of those conditioning phenomena themselves, and the classification of these modes of conditionality, within this compendium of conditions (*paccayasaṅgaha*) now being spoken."
[224] However, in the *Vibhāvanī*, it is stated:
"In order to show the conditions. This does not accord with the phrase "according to their respective divisions" (*taṃ taṃ vibhāgaṃ*).
[225] And as for that which is therein...
The explanation of the meaning of the word *iha* (here) as “in this place immediately following the *Samuccaya-saṅgaha*” is stated; however, that too is not tenable.
For if that were the meaning, the word *idāni* (now) would be redundant. [Rather,] *paṭiccasamuppāda* means that from this [condition], the fruit arises dependently (*paṭicca*).
In that context, *paṭicca* means "not without" (*avinā*), that is to say, "not having abandoned. It refers to a conditioning phenomenon (*paccayadhamma*) such as ignorance (*avijjā*), etc.

They praise [it]. Alternatively, *samuppāda* means "arising together" (*samuppajjana*). The meaning is the manifestation and production by way of a single group (*kalāpa*) together with the co-nascent phenomena.
Dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) is the arising together (*samuppāda*) in dependence upon its respective conditions, being inseparable from them.
In terms of actual meaning, however, it refers to all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhata-dhamma*) consisting of both conditions and the things arisen from conditions.
There is one universal characteristic common to all conditioned things, known as "existence dependent on conditions.
This is what is called "specific conditionality" (*idappaccayatā*). In this context, "specific conditionality" is to be demonstrated thus:

"this is a condition for this," and "this is a condition for this. Those for whom these are the conditions are "those having specific conditions," namely, conditioned phenomena. The state of being those having specific conditions is "specific conditionality."

"Conditionality by way of this" (idappaccayatā). The meaning should be understood as precisely the aforementioned general characteristic (sāmaññalakkhaṇa); it is not that "dependent origination" (paṭiccasamuppāda) means "that from which a fruit arises dependently.
Furthermore, ignorance and the other factors are the conditioning states (paccayadhammā), and these conditions are "conditions by way of this" (idappaccayā).

The state of being these conditions-by-way-of-this is "conditionality by way of this" (idappaccayatā). In the *Visuddhimagga*, however, it is stated that "arising together" (samuppajjana) is "origination" (samuppāda).
This meaning is rejected; however, in the Pāḷi, this very [meaning] appears as if intended.
As it is said: "And what, monks, is dependent origination? With birth as condition, monks, there is aging and death.
Whether Tathāgatas arise or whether Tathāgatas do not arise, this element remains fixed: the stability of phenomena, the regularity of phenomena."
"Specific conditionality": [the formula] "with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise," and so forth, up to "specific conditionality.
Thus, monks, herein there is suchness, non-falsity, non-alterability, and specific conditionality. This, monks, is called dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*).

For it is by means of the phrases "that element remains established therein" and so forth, and "therein there is suchness, non-falsity" and so forth, that this aforementioned specific conditionality is demonstrated.
This shows that the very characteristic of the state of being a recluse (*sāmañña-lakkhaṇa*) is what is designated by the term "dependent origination" (*paṭiccasamuppāda*).

Furthermore, there is no contradiction regarding the grammatical compatibility of the expression, such as the objection that when the term is formed as an abstract noun (*bhāvasādhana*), the word *samuppāda* cannot share the same agent with the word *paṭicca*.
This is because it is possible for the very same one who is the agent of the action of "depending" (*paṭicca*) to also be the agent of the action of "arising together" (*samuppāda*). It is not...

For indeed, an action called "doing" is impossible without an agent. Furthermore, since conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhata-dhammā*) are profound, this characteristic of the conditioned (*saṅkhata-lakkhaṇa*)—just like the characteristics of impermanence and so forth—is also profoundly deep; thus, no contradiction with the term "profound" arises here.
On the contrary, the characteristic of the conditioned itself is even more profound than the conditioned phenomena. However, by such [a characteristic]...

The conditioned phenomena mentioned above, beginning with ignorance (*avijjā*), which are endowed with the common characteristic (*sāmaññalakkhaṇa*) [of being impermanent, suffering, and non-self], are called "dependently arisen" (*paṭiccasamuppanna*).
As it is said: "And what, monks, are dependently arisen phenomena? Aging-and-death, monks, is dependently arisen...
Ignorance, monks, is dependently arisen. Thus, for all things that have become conditions and conditionally arisen, [the term applies].

The conditioned phenomena have conditions; and that dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda), being designated as "sevenfold occurrence," is led, known, and penetrated—thus it is called a "method" (naya).
It is called *Paṭṭhāna* because it establishes (*paṭṭhapeti*) conditioned phenomena, causes them to proceed, and teaches them through various modes of conditions.
It is the Great Treatise (*Mahāpakaraṇa*). The method taught in the *Paṭṭhāna* is the *Paṭṭhāna-naya*.

When each respective conditioning state (paccayadhamma) exists, those [consequent states] come to be by virtue of that; thus they are "occurring through the existence of that" (tabbhāvabhāvino). These are conditioned phenomena (saṅkhata-dhammā).

Their state is "the state of occurring through the existence of that" (tabbhāvabhāvibhāva), which is the fixed order of conditioned phenomena (saṅkhata-dhamma-niyāma) proceeding in this way: "When this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises.
The very mode (ākāra) of that state of occurring through the existence of that is the "mode of the state of occurring through the existence of that" (tabbhāvabhāvibhāvākāra).

Thus, it is merely the state of occurring when that [other] exists (*tad-bhāva-bhāvitva*). By the word "merely" (*matta*), he excludes the restriction of the causal relation (*hetu*) and other conditions.
The method characterized by this is the method of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda-naya*). Regarding the phrase "starting from the establishment of the specific condition":

here, the specific power of the condition (*paccaya-satti-visesa*), consisting of the various ways of being helpful according to the respective causes and objects (*hetu-ārammaṇa*-ādi), is called the "establishment of the specific condition."

For this is called "establishment by direct impact" (*āhacca-paccaya-ṭhiti*), because it is taught not merely as the extraction of the conditioning state— as in such passages as "with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise"—
but rather by reaching the very pinnacle through the extraction of the specific power of the conditions,

such as "the root-condition" (*hetu-paccaya*) and "the object-condition" (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*). The conditioning states thus stand, performing their own function of producing the conditioned formations.
It is so called because by means of it [the mind] proceeds without shrinking back when it encounters what is to be done. "Ārabbhā" means "dependent upon.
"Vuccati" means "is spoken by the Blessed One.
However, the phrase "the teachers proliferate by mixing both together" refers to their proliferating with respect to dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*).
It has been said: "By means of those [concepts], they proliferate; bringing even the method of the *Paṭṭhāna* (Conditional Relations), they proliferate.

Just as the rising sun, having dispelled the darkness, makes the various objects and materials manifest to the great multitude, even so, the knowledge of the Four Truths that has arisen, having dispelled the darkness of ignorance, finds and makes manifest the Dhamma of the Four Truths.

Knowledge (*vijjā*). Its opposite is delusion (*moha*), which is called ignorance (*avijjā*). For when it arises, it arises only by producing a darkness characterized as non-knowing and non-seeing regarding phenomena.
That from which a fruit comes or arrives, or by means of which it does so, is a condition (*paccaya*).
Ignorance that is a condition is "ignorance-condition" (*avijjāpaccaya*). Therefore: "With ignorance as condition, volitional formations [arise]."
The connection is that they "arise. They are called *saṅkhārā* because beings construct (*abhisaṅkharonti*) conditioned bodily, verbal, and mental actions by means of them.
It is called *viññāṇa* because it cognizes; or alternatively, it is *viññāṇa* because beings cognize by means of it. It is called *nāma* because it bends (*namati*) toward its object.
It is called *rūpa* because it is affected (*ruppati*), that is, it undergoes change. It is called an *āyatana* in the sense of a basis, like a dwelling place for deities.
It touches (*phusati*), thus it is contact (*phassa*). Or, contact is so called because associated mental states touch by means of it.

It feels (*vedayati*), thus it is feeling (*vedanā*). Or, feeling is so called because beings feel and experience by means of it. One thirsts (*tassati*) and is agitated (*paritassati*), thus it is craving (*taṇhā*).
The meaning is that, due to the cause of the object, one constantly trembles and yearns on account of constant thirst. One thirsts, is agitated, and trembles.
Or, craving (*taṇhā*) is so called because beings (*sattā*) run toward it. It is "clinging" (*upādāna*) because one clings; the meaning is that one grasps with a firm grip.
Or, clinging is so called because by means of it beings cling.
It is "existence" (*bhava*) because it comes into being or increases. Or, existence is so called because by means of it pleasure and pain come into being, arise, and increase.
Birth (*janana*) is birth (*jāti*). Or, it is called birth because conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhata-dhammā*) are born—that is, they manifest—by means of it.
Aging (*jīraṇa*) is old age (*jarā*). Or, it is called old age because things age—that is, they reach a state of decay—by means of it. Sorrowing (*socana*) is sorrow (*soka*).

Or, it is called sorrow because by means of it one sorrows—that is, one undergoes mental fever (*citta-pariḷāha*). Lamentation (*paridevana*) is lamenting (*parideva*). One laments by recounting various occurrences.
*Parideva* (lamentation) is so called because one laments by means of it. *Dukkha* (suffering) is that which is difficult to endure or bear.

*Domanassa* (mental distress) is the state of one who is dejected and whose mind is disfigured. *Upāyāsa* (despair) is intense exhaustion; "exhaustion" (*āyāsana*) means a lack of relief, the sense of being despondent.

"Thus" (*evaṃ*) refers to what has been stated above. By way of the sequence of conditions and conditionally arisen states, beginning with ignorance and the formative forces (*avijjādi-saṅkhārādi-paccaya-paccayuppanna-parampara-vidhinā*).

The connection is: "there is an arising. "Of this entire mass of suffering" means that there is the manifestation of this whole heap of suffering—consisting of ignorance and so forth—or of this heap of suffering unmixed with any pleasure.
And herein, the method of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) is twofold: the Sutta method and the Abhidhamma method.
In this regard, according to the method of the Suttanta, ignorance is fourfold:
that which conceals suffering, that which conceals its origin, that which conceals its cessation, and that which conceals the path. According to the method of the Abhidhamma, however, it is:
that which conceals the past, that which conceals the future, that which conceals both the past and the future, and that which conceals dependent origination.
It should be understood that there are eight types together with the four.

According to the method of the Suttantas, volitional formations (*saṅkhārā*)—which are tainted (*sāsavā*) wholesome and unwholesome intentions (*cetanā*)—are threefold: the formation of demerit (*apuññābhisaṅkhāra*), the formation of merit (*puññābhisaṅkhāra*), and the formation of the imperturbable (*āneñjābhisaṅkhāra*).
Among these, the twelve unwholesome intentions are called "demeritorious formations."

Volition associated with the fine-material sphere and wholesome volition are called the meritorious formation (*puññābhisankhāra*). Volition associated with the immaterial sphere is called the imperturbable formation (*āneñjābhisankhāra*).
However, according to the method of the Abhidhamma, all wholesome and unwholesome volitions, whether mundane or supramundane, are called formations (*saṅkhāra*).
Furthermore, all functional volitions (*kiriyacetanā*) are not included in the *Vibhaṅga*. And in the Commentary, regarding functional states (*kiriyadhammānaṃ*),...

Because neither ignorance nor the wholesome roots obtain the status of a decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*) for wholesome states, it is said that the mode of conditions (*paccayākāra*) is not stated by way of functional states (*kiriya*). Furthermore, ignorance and the wholesome and unwholesome roots are never decisive support conditions for functional phenomena.
Therefore, it is said that functional phenomena are not included in the teaching on dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*).

It exists. In the *Saṃyutta Nikāya* as well, it is said: "Bhikkhus, when ignorance has been abandoned by a bhikkhu and true knowledge has arisen, through the fading away of ignorance and the arising of true knowledge, he does not form a volitional formation of merit, nor a volitional formation of demerit, nor a volitional formation of the imperturbable.
However, according to their respective appropriate conditions, even for them...
Dependent origination (paṭicca-samuppāda) is indeed unobstructed; for there is no conditioned phenomenon whatsoever that is devoid of dependent origination.

This same principle applies to consciousness (viññāṇa) and the other factors as well. According to the method of the Suttas, "consciousness" refers to the thirty-two types of mundane resultant consciousness.
However, according to the method of the Abhidhamma, it refers to the sixty-nine types of mundane and supramundane consciousness, excluding the functional (kiriyā) consciousnesses.

"Name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*) refers, according to the method of the Suttas, to the three aggregates beginning with feeling that arise simultaneously with mundane consciousness, as well as to the matter born of kamma at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) and the matter born of mind during the course of existence (*pavatti*).
According to the method of the Abhidhamma, however, it refers to all three aggregates associated with wholesome, unwholesome, and resultant states, along with the aforementioned types of matter.
In the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), moreover, it includes that which has obtained the condition of post-nascence (*pacchājāta-paccaya*).
All matter arising from the four origins is indeed included.
However, in the *Vibhāvanī*, it is stated:
“Both of these are here accompanied by rebirth-linking consciousness. That is untenable.
The "six bases" (saḷāyatana) are explained everywhere in the Canon as being exclusively the six internal bases.
However, some teachers, considering that the external bases also serve as conditions for contact, include them here as well.
This too is indeed consistent with the text of the Nidāna-vagga, as it says:
And what, monks, is the origin of the world? Dependent upon the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises.
The meeting of the three is contact. With contact as condition, feeling arises; with feeling as condition, craving arises... [and so on] ...grief and despair come into being.
This is the origin of the world. Dependent upon the ear... [and so on] ...dependent upon the mind and mental phenomena, mind-consciousness arises.
Mind-consciousness. The meeting of the three is contact (*phassa*). ... "The origin of the world" [is explained].

Contact, feeling, and so forth should also be understood as being associated with their respective consciousnesses within the two methods [of exposition]. Craving (*taṇhā*) and clinging (*upādāna*) are evident.
Existence (*bhava*) is twofold: kamma-existence and rebirth-existence. It is also the volition (*cetanā*) consisting of mundane wholesome and unwholesome states. [It is] associated with volition...
Covetousness and so forth, as well as non-covetousness and so forth, constitute *kammabhava* (the existence consisting of karma). As it is said: "All karma leading to existence is *kammabhava*.
Furthermore, according to the method of the Suttantas, all mundane resultant aggregates produced by karma and all material forms born of karma constitute *upapattibhava* (rebirth-existence).
However, according to the method of the Abhidhamma, even supramundane aggregates are included in the *Vibhaṅga*. Birth, aging, and death [constitute *jātibhava*].
These are the characteristics of all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhata-dhamma*).

Among these, sorrow (*soka*) is the feeling of mental distress (*domanassa-vedanā*) that arises in one who is afflicted by the loss of relatives and so forth, manifesting in the mode of grieving. Lamentation (*parideva*) is the undesirable sound born of the mind that arises in the mode of weeping.
Physical painful feeling is called suffering (*dukkha*), while mental painful feeling is called distress (*domanassa*).
The term *upāyāsa* refers to the state of dejection and despondency that arises with the loss of relatives and so forth as its cause; this is the distinction here.
Furthermore, for those in whom ignorance regarding the suffering inherent in the aggregates has not been abandoned, that ignorance remains unabandoned even with respect to the other truths.
Consequently, they perceive pleasure only in the occurrence of the aggregates, and perceive suffering in the cessation of the aggregates.
They perceive the path of the arising of the aggregates as a path to happiness, and the path of the cessation of the aggregates as a path to suffering.
Therefore, for those beings who are shrouded by ignorance, who desire happiness, and who are averse to suffering,

it is said that "volitional formations conditioned by ignorance" are their refuge— namely, the phenomena of meritorious, demeritorious, and imperturbable volitional formations which serve as the conditions for the arising of the aggregates.
And herein, specifically, it should be understood that through ignorance which conceals the present aggregates, unwholesome volitional formations consisting of misconduct arise;
and through ignorance which conceals future aggregates, wholesome and imperturbable volitional formations consisting of good conduct arise.
When these volitional formations exist, for beings whose craving for existence has not been abandoned, immediately after death—

There is no obstacle whatsoever to the production of renewed existence. Therefore, conditioned by volitional formations, consciousness, mentality-materiality, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling—these five factors known as the personal identity—manifest in another becoming.
Among these, however, it is stated that consciousness alone is the primary and the foremost; thus it is said: "Conditioned by volitional formations, consciousness."

It is said that when consciousness exists, there is no obstruction whatsoever to the arising of name-and-form (nāmarūpa), which are its products. Thus: "With consciousness as condition, name-and-form.
Up to this point, the body has been described in its general sense, both as the complete whole and specifically as the material body (rūpakāya).
Nevertheless, among these two bodies, those factors which serve as the primary constituent parts for the designation of a "being" [are now to be discussed].

These contacts and so forth are included among the subsequent factors. However, because beings grasp at a self more firmly in relation to these [specific factors], they have been extracted separately and shown by the statement:
"With name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases. When name-and-form exists, there is no obstruction whatsoever to their arising.
Furthermore, contact that originates from the six sense bases occurs within the six sense bases.

Because contact necessarily arises when the six sense bases exist, it is said: "With the six sense bases as condition, there is contact. And because feeling, which is produced by contact, necessarily arises only when contact exists, it is said: "With contact as condition, there is feeling.
Since there is no support for craving comparable to pleasant feeling, it is said: "With feeling as condition, there is craving. Furthermore, as for the clinging to sensual pleasures... [in one...]

Craving itself, having repeatedly manifested toward an object and reached a state of firmness, as well as views and the self—these attain firmness by way of craving, which consists of relishing, acceptance, and approval toward their respective objects; thus it is said:
"With craving as condition, clinging arises. And while clinging, one perceives benefit and growth in each respective thing that is subject to clinging.

"They indeed accumulate this or that kamma-existence," thus it is said: "With clinging as condition, existence. Here, the word *bhava* (existence) is used in the sense of increase (*vaḍḍhi*). As it is said:
"Existence is easy to understand; decline is difficult to understand."
Since, when there is kamma-existence (*kamma-bhava*), rebirth (*punabbhava*) necessarily occurs, it is said: "With existence as condition, birth.

And since, when there is birth, aging and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) necessarily follow, it is said: "With birth as condition, aging and death. This is the method of the principle of "the occurrence of this being due to the occurrence of that" (*tabbhāvabhāvibhāva-vidhi*) in this context.

Furthermore, the mention of sorrow and the rest here refers to the entirety of the phenomena of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭadhamma*) which proceeds by means of such a principle of "the occurrence of this being due to the occurrence of that."

"It is said that there is no destruction for one who has seen the sword of danger. "In this" means in this compendium of conditions (*paccaya-saṅgaha*). "Therein" means in that method of dependent origination (*paṭicca-samuppāda-naya*).
It is called *addhā* because it firmly holds (*dhāreti*) phenomena over a duration (*addhāna*). It is time (*kāla*).

For it [time] holds together phenomena belonging to the three periods through the continuous succession of a stream, as well as the successions of eons, years, seasons, months, fortnights, nights, and days.

"Having offered [the sacrifice], it remains as if supporting those who have not yet fallen. Alternatively, *addhā* is that wherein temporal phenomena (*tekālikā dhammā*) burn intensely, persist, and proceed;

thus it is "time" itself. Although time is inherently indivisible, it is appropriate to treat it as if divided by way of the phenomena that possess division; hence it is said, "three times" (*tayo addhā*).
[227] As for what is stated in the *Vibhāvanī*:
"It is called *addhā* because it moves (*atati*), goes constantly (*satataṃ gacchati*), and proceeds (*pavattati*)," that is not correct.

For if that were the case, the term *addhāna* would not be established, as in the expression "one who has set out on the path of travel" (*addhānamaggapaṭipanno*). "Limbs" (*aṅgāni*) refers to the limbs that are primary constituent parts.
"Requisites for striving" is what is meant. "Factors" (*ākāra*) refers to constituent parts; here the word *ākāra* has the sense of a division, as in the expression "the thirty-two factors.
Others also say they are called "factors" because they are placed there, as if scattered and established in various places.
"Junctions" (*sandhi*) refers to the points of connection between each pair of summaries. "Summaries" (*saṅkhepa*) are the groupings of the primary phenomena of striving.
They are called *vaṭṭāni* because they roll (*vaṭṭanti*) and turn around again and again.

They are called *mūlāni* because all phenomena of the round (*vaṭṭadhammā*) take root (*mūlayanti*) there, since their existence is dependent upon it; thus, the meaning is "foundations" (*patiṭṭhā*) or "sources" (*pabhava*).
For a single person cannot, with a single finger, take up the water of the ocean and pour it into the mouths of the multitude, [let alone] the water of the four great oceans...

Just as one making known the state of saltiness [makes it known through its taste], the Blessed One also, by teaching a single present existence in its entirety through such statements as "with ignorance as condition,
volitional formations arise," made known the process of the entire cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) that has no beginning or end.
And when teaching something in its entirety, both the cause of that single existence must be taught, as well as its fruit.
It exists. In this context, "causes" (*hetu*) refers to ignorance (*avijjā*) and volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*) established in a previous existence;

"fruit" (*phala*) refers to birth (*jāti*) in a future existence. Thus, although this teaching concerns a single existence, it is said—by way of a partial illustration—to be common to both the past and the future, as in the passage beginning, "Ignorance and volitional formations are the past time," and so forth.
And here, having treated the time-period (*addhā*) and those who traverse the time-period (*addhāvanta*) as if they were non-different:
The statement [that time is] distinct from the Dhamma shows the non-existence of time reckoned as a duration.

It also precludes the false doctrine that "time alone causes the world to proceed and withdraw," for it is not logical that time, being itself non-existent, could be the cause of the proceeding or the withdrawal of anything.
Why, then, is each individual present [moment] mentioned here?
In demonstrating the process of the personal existence (*attabhāva*), the Blessed One shows both the cause in the past life and the fruit in the future life.

It should be understood that the demonstration of the past cause is for the purpose of warding off the views of no-cause (*ahetu*) and irregular cause (*visamahetu*); the demonstration of the future fruit is for the purpose of warding off the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadiṭṭhi*);
and the demonstration of both is for the purpose of warding off the view of eternalism (*sassatadiṭṭhi*). In this regard:
The view that beings proceed, cease, become defiled, and become purified without cause or condition is called the "view of no-cause" (*ahetu-diṭṭhi*).
The perception of a false cause by means of [theories such as] Brahmā, Pajāpati, or the creation of a Supreme Lord is called the "view of an improper cause" (*visama-hetu-diṭṭhi*).
The view that beings are annihilated at death and that there is no such thing as future birth is called the "view of annihilationism" (*uccheda-diṭṭhi*).
The view that "the self is eternal and stable, and it runs on and wanders from one state of existence to another" is called the eternalist view (*sassataditthi*) regarding the process of existence.
However, even if it were eternal in this way, its running on could not be accomplished by ignorance (*avijjā*) and the other factors.
Therefore, by stating that consciousness arises again in another existence through ignorance and volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*), the eternalist view is indeed refuted.

But why are sorrow and the rest not included among the factors here? Because, while sorrow and the rest invariably arise when birth exists, they lack the characteristic of being present whenever that [birth] is present.
For even when birth exists, these do not arise in the world of form (*rūpaloka*) or the formless world (*arūpaloka*).
Even in the sense-sphere world (*kāmaloka*), they certainly do not arise for some individuals. If this is so, for what purpose are they [included]?

Regarding the term "vacana" (statements): it is said that the mention of sorrow and so forth here is intended to demonstrate the outflow-result (*nissanda-phala*), in order to show the purpose of pointing out the entire mass of great dangers inherent in the process of the round of existence (*vaṭṭa-pavatta*)—whether it be birth itself or the whole cycle beginning with ignorance as previously described.
In this context, "demonstrating the outflow-result" means demonstrating the arising-result (*udaya-phala*) characterized by the mass of great dangers belonging to birth. But why is this [stated]?
Regarding the present existence, only two factors—ignorance and volitional formations—are stated in the text as conditions for the past.
But do only those two serve as its conditions? Indeed, there are others as well. If so, why are they not mentioned in the text?

Because even though they are not explicitly mentioned, they are obtained by implication. And how are they obtained even though unstated? By the characteristic of their presence being contingent upon the presence of those [two].
Showing that [the factors] are obtained by way of their characteristic of being inseparable from that [ignorance], he said: "By the mention of ignorance and formations," and so forth.

This same method applies to the subsequent cases as well. Therein, "by the mention of ignorance and formations" refers to the expression "ignorance and formations" stated at the beginning of the text.
Craving, clinging, and becoming are also included because they exist when ignorance exists and do not exist when it does not.
By the mention of ignorance (*avijjā*), craving (*taṇhā*) and clinging (*upādāna*) are also included.

Furthermore, the meaning is that by the mention of volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*), kamma-existence (*kammabhava*) is also included, because [volitional formations] exist when existence exists, and do not exist when existence does not exist.
In the *Vibhāvani*, however...

Because of their commonality as defilements (*kilesa*), craving (*taṇhā*) and clinging (*upādāna*) are included by the mention of ignorance (*avijjā*). Because of their commonality as kamma, the existence of kamma (*kammabhava*) is said to be included by the mention of volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*).
That too is logical. Thus, the connection is that ignorance and volitional formations are included.

The meaning is that because they exist inseparably, ignorance is included by the mention of craving and clinging, and volitional formations are included by the mention of existence. [This is] in the same way that characteristic phenomena are [included] by the phenomena characterized.
It is said that because of the state of inseparable connection (*avinābhāvibhāva*), birth, aging, and so forth are grasped by way of their inseparable connection with that [conditioned phenomenon].
"By this reason" means by this cause. The connection is: "there are twenty aspects. The first pentad of causes is one summary;
the second pentad of results is one; the third pentad of causes is one; and the fourth pentad of results is one.
"Summary" means there are four summaries; the sense is that there are four compendia.

Furthermore, when the four summaries are established, the three junctions are likewise established: by the first [summary] the second is established, by the second the third, and by the third the fourth.
Thus it is said, "there are three junctions and four summaries. And herein, the fivefold cause—
The term "fivefold fruit" (*phalapañcaka*) is stated here according to common worldly usage.

However, since the terms "cause" (*hetu*) and "fruit" (*phala*) are indeed synonymous with "condition" (*paccaya*) and "that which has arisen from conditions" (*paccayuppanna*), it is entirely possible for the first pentad to be considered a "fivefold fruit" in relation to the second pentad, and a "fivefold cause" (*hetupañcaka*) in relation to the third.
Likewise, the third pentad may be considered a "fivefold cause" in relation to the fourth, and [a fivefold fruit] in relation to the second.
"And because of the fivefold nature of the fruit. For if this were so, there would be only fruit from the cause; there would be no cause from the fruit—thus, the objection finds no footing at all.
However, regarding the two sets of five causes, the distinction between *saṅkhāra*, *kamma*, and *bhava* has already been stated in the Commentary.
As it says: "For one who, having generated the thought 'I shall give a gift,' prepares the requisites for giving for a month or even a year..."

The volitions that have arisen previously are called "formations of accumulation" (*āyūhana-saṅkhāra*). However, the volition that arises when one places the offering into the hands of the recipients is called "existence" (*bhava*).

Alternatively, among the six impulsive moments (*javana*) of a single thought-moment, the volitions are called "formations of accumulation," while the volition of the seventh impulsion is "existence. Or, whatever volition constitutes existence, the [factors] associated with it—

"Accumulation of volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*). It is stated that the two types of existence—the kamma-existence (*kammabhava*) and the rebirth-existence (*upapattibhava*)—are constituent parts of the single "existence" member (*bhava-aṅga*) among the twelve factors;
thus it is said, "a portion of the existence termed kamma-existence," and so forth.
Furthermore, the distinction between volitional formations and kamma-existence should be understood according to the method already explained.
[228] Furthermore, as for what is stated in the *Vibhāvani*:

“In the phrase ‘a portion of existence consisting of kamma-existence,’ it should be understood that the volition which is the condition for rebirth-linking in the future is ‘formations’ (saṅkhāra),” this does not fit here.
This is because both of those two are included within the two sets of five causes (*hetupañcaka*). Or perhaps this was stated according to the method of the literal text (*rutapāḷi*).
It should be understood. The phrase "the remainder" is stated with reference to the pentad of results beginning with consciousness, together with birth, aging, and death.

And herein, that pentad of results beginning with consciousness which was previously included under the mention of birth, aging, and death is, in actual fact, nothing other than rebirth-existence (*upapatti-bhava*).
For there is no such thing as rebirth-existence apart from this pentad of results.

Even though this is so, it is appropriate to hold that the fourth pentad is included by the term *upapattibhava* (rebirth-existence) for the purpose of preserving the classification of the factors (*dhammavibhāga*).
Among the twelve factors, ignorance (*avijjā*) is delusion (*moha*), and it is an unwholesome root (*akusalamūla*). Craving (*taṇhā*) is greed (*lobha*), and it too is an unwholesome root.
Thus it is said: "By way of ignorance and craving, there are two roots. Alternatively, "root" (*mūla*) means "head" (*sīsa*). There are two...

The meaning is "having rounded tops. In the Commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), however, having treated the first pair of pentads as one wheel of existence (*bhavacakra*) and the latter pair of pentads as another wheel of existence, it states that the former has ignorance as its root;
