and that is the wheel for those of speculative temperament (*diṭṭhicarita*) or those bound for the states of misery (*apāya*). The latter has craving as its root; and that is [the wheel] for those of lustful temperament (*rāgacarita*) or those bound for the happy destinies (*sugati*).
The term "wheel" (cakkam) has been shown. However, that from which the continuity of the round (vaṭṭa-santāna) begins is called a wheel only when it returns again to that same point.
Therefore, it is appropriate here that the entire cycle, together with the second pair of cause and fruit, constitutes a single wheel.
But why, in this context, is ignorance alone stated as the head among the factors of coming (āgamana-sambhāra), and craving alone among the factors of going (gamana-sambhāra)?
Should it not be said that both are the heads in both cases? It is replied:

there is indeed no nutriment for craving comparable to pleasant feeling. Therefore, when connecting the factor of the cycle of existence (vaṭṭaṅga) subsequent to the factor of feeling, [ignorance is placed first].
It must be said that it is craving for form alone [that is the cause]. Ignorance has no place among the requisites for going;
for, at the very beginning when one first undertakes [the journey], ignorance is what must be called the most predominant factor.
And since it is the factor that does not fail in the production of the formations, there is nothing further to be said regarding any other single factor in between them.
"There is no room for craving among the requisites for arrival.
For this teaching on dependent origination proceeds by way of grasping the primary factors, not by way of grasping every phenomenon that exists.
As for what was stated in the *Vibhāvani*:
It is said that ignorance is the root of the past and craving is the root of the future.

In this context, "of the past" means of the prior portion consisting of causes and fruits; "of the future" means of the subsequent portion consisting of causes and fruits—this is the meaning. But why are these called the two roots? He says:
"And by the cessation of those very roots, [the cycle] ceases."
Through their arising, the entire cycle of existence (vaṭṭa) arises; through their cessation, it ceases. Therefore, it is said that these two are called the "roots.
Some, however, say that this is the vision of dependent origination in reverse order. Dependent origination in reverse order begins:
"With the cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of volitional formations; with the cessation of volitional formations comes the cessation of consciousness," and so forth.
The section on cessation. Now, the mention of sorrow and so forth is not intended merely to illustrate the outflow-result (*nissandaphala*);

rather, it is also intended to show that, together with aging-and-death, they constitute a single factor that serves as an illustration of the states of suffering which establish the fundamental phenomena of the round of existence (*vaṭṭamūla*). Demonstrating this, he said: "With aging-and-death as the root," and so forth. In that regard:
By the term "infatuation" (*mucchā*), grief and the rest are included. For these too, having themselves arisen from the taints (*āsava*), become conditions for the further arising of taints;
by this, their inclusion within the factor of aging-and-death (*jarāmaraṇa*) is established.
For fools who are constantly oppressed by infatuation with aging-and-death, the taints arise repeatedly. And from the repeated arising of the taints, ignorance (*avijjā*) [arises].

It increases. For it has been said: "With the arising of the taints (āsava), there is the arising of ignorance. This being so, the meaning is that "with ignorance as condition, volitional formations (saṅkhāra) [arise]" thus continues the cycle once again. And herein:
Because of the occurrence of sorrow and the rest in one who is touched by various calamities;
It should also be stated: "Ignorance and craving increase, from which the round of existence proceeds.
As it has been said: "And what, monks, is the ripening of suffering? Monks, I declare that suffering has delusion as its ripening, or it has seeking as its ripening.
In this context, delusion is ignorance (*avijjā*), and seeking is craving (*taṇhā*). Both of these—

Because it has maturation (*vipāka*) as its result, the suffering consisting of aging, death, sorrow, and so forth—which is the ripening of delusion (*sammoha*) and the ripening of seeking (*pariyiṭṭhi*)—is so called.
In this context, "delusion" refers to that which is described as follows: one who is touched by the loss of relatives and the like sorrows, laments, beats one's breast, and wails;
thus it is "delusion" because one falls into confusion. "Seeking" refers to being oppressed, for example, by hunger, [and seeking] food.
Afflicted by thirst, one desires and seeks water; likewise, when touched by any suffering, one desires and seeks happiness—thus occurs the craving for seeking (*pariyiṭṭhitataṇhā*).
Furthermore, in this context, there is no place of suffering in this world that is as great, pervasive, and certain as aging and death.
And the Teacher’s dispensation is for the purpose of escaping suffering. Therefore, this teaching on dependent origination has aging-and-death as its source.
As it is said: "Alas, this world has fallen into hardship; it is born, it grows old, it dies, it passes away, and it is reborn.
And yet, it does not understand the escape from this suffering, namely, from aging-and-death," and so forth. Now, regarding those [factors]...
Having first understood the factors beginning from the beginning, one is able to uproot aging and death and thereby liberate oneself from them.

To demonstrate those [factors], the preceding members beginning with birth were taught. Furthermore, by remaining within a single existence, and by means of both the requisites for coming and the requisites for going, the production of the personal entity (attabhāva) was shown together with its arrival and departure in the past.
Furthermore, the arising of this or that individual existence within this or that state throughout the entirety of future saṃsāra is precisely demonstrated [by this].
All speculative views are thereby turned back, yet the wheel of existence continues to bind, being without beginning.

Therefore, whether by means of the terms "aging and death" or "sorrow and so forth," it is not ignorance that is being considered; rather, it is the demonstration of the great danger inherent in the process of the cycle of existence.

"It is to be understood" (*paccetabbaṃ*). "In this very way," and so forth, is the conclusion. The connection is: "In this very way, he set it rolling by means of the method beginning with 'with ignorance as condition, volitional formations [arise],' etc.
They also apply the term "the cycle" (*vaṭṭa*) to this very binding, which is beginningless and belongs to the three planes of existence.
Therein, "binding in this very way" refers to the repeated binding described by the method stated in the passage beginning with "the intoxication of aging and death," and so forth.
Why is it said “beginningless”? Is it not the case that ignorance (*avijjā*) was mentioned at the beginning? It is replied:

Ignorance was not mentioned at the beginning because it is the very beginning of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*). It was mentioned at the beginning precisely because it constitutes the head of the discourse on the cycle of existence.

Furthermore, by its being so mentioned, the beginninglessness of the cycle of existence is also demonstrated. For what is called ignorance is not found outside; it exists within the continuum of sentient beings (*sattasantāna*).

That this is indeed obtained is established by direct experience itself. Therefore, since ignorance (*avijjā*) was established in the past existence, the personal identity (*attabhāva*) which serves as its basis is likewise established in that existence.
And in being established, it is established through that very same ignorance according to the method described above, and not otherwise. And thus, once again—
Since even his personal existence (*attabhāva*), which serves as the basis for that [ignorance], is established, both ignorance and personal existence are thus unstable and indeed beginningless.
Furthermore, because it is the primary condition for all three types of the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*), it constitutes the head of the discourse on the round.
If it were not the beginning of the round, then there would have to be a condition for it as well.
"It should be stated": this is true. However, even when its condition has been stated, it follows that the condition for that condition must also be stated.
This being the case, there would be no finality at all; one would never reach a conclusion. But elsewhere it has indeed been stated, as when it was said:
"With the arising of the taints (āsava), there is the arising of ignorance (avijjā). And as it was also said: "Bhikkhus, I say that ignorance..."
I say it has nutriment, it has a source. What is its nutriment? It should be said: "The five hindrances. As it is said: "Ignorance is the condition;
volitional formations are the conditionally arisen. Both of these have arisen dependently.
"He set forth" means he established, he taught. [The Method of Dependent Origination.]
167. Now, in order to show the method of the *Paṭṭhāna*, the section beginning with "the root condition" (*hetupaccaya*) is commenced.

Therein, it is a "root condition" because it is both a root and a condition; having become a root, it is a condition, meaning it is a condition by way of its nature as a root. In this context, in what sense is it a "root"?

It is in the sense of being a foundation (*mūla*). And what is the sense of being a foundation? Just as the root of a tree is for trees, so too is it for co-nascent phenomena in relation to the ground.
The meaning of "root" (*mūla*) is the state of being well-established among objects;
it is also said that the meaning of "root" is the state of establishing the co-nascent phenomena as wholesome and so forth. Whatever else needs to be said here has already been stated above.
As for the etymological meaning: co-nascent phenomena "stand well" (*suppatiṭṭhahanti*) by way of attaining growth, increase, expansion, and abundance.

In this context, the cause (*hetu*) is that which falls firmly upon the object (*ārammaṇa*), being endowed with power and strength. The word "condition" (*paccaya*), however, has the sense of being "an auxiliary" (*upakāraka*).

And as for being an auxiliary: when phenomena are being perceived through their own respective intrinsic natures—whether they have not yet arisen, have already arisen and persist, or have persisted and are undergoing successive growth and development—it is by becoming a condition for these that it acts as an auxiliary.

It is simply through the perception of suchness by way of its own intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*). For among phenomena that possess an intrinsic nature, neither striving (*īhā*) nor activity (*vyāpāra*) is perceived, by which [a self] might be perceived as an agent or a causer.

But when there is such perception, because corresponding conditionally arisen phenomena arise if they have not yet arisen, or attain a state of stability if they have already arisen, or reach successive growth and increase if they are already stable; [it is through this process that things are known].
Because it thoroughly accomplishes its task as if making it well-done by way of abandoning the state of being a condition, it is called "beneficial" (*upakāraka*).
Thus, the six causal phenomena that are beneficial by way of their root-nature— which consists in the accomplishment of the growth and increase of stability regarding the object—
are called the "root-condition" (*hetu-paccaya*).
It is called an *ārammaṇa* because the mental states (*citta-cetasika-dhammā*) rest upon it, proceeding as if experiencing intense delight while hanging down over it.
The six types of objects that are helpful by virtue of their very nature as objects are the object-condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*).
The meaning of the word *adhipati* has already been explained above. A phenomenon that is helpful by virtue of its being predominant is the predominance-condition (*adhipati-paccaya*).

Thus, objective predominance (*ārammaṇādhipati*) is twofold by way of co-nascent predominance (*sahājātādhipati*). For certain objective phenomena (*ārammaṇadhammā*), when they are treated with reverence, exercise control over their own subjective phenomena as masters do over slaves;
they cause [the latter] to be constantly inclined, sloping, and leaning toward themselves.
That which has no interval between it is "immediate" (*anantara*); an immediate condition (*anantarapaccaya*) is a phenomenon that assists by way of its immediacy.

A phenomenon that assists by way of immediate succession is the *samanantara-paccaya* (contiguity condition). Between these two conditions, there is no difference in terms of their essential nature (*dhamma*).
However, in terms of their functional meaning (*attha*), even though the preceding consciousness has ceased, it does not allow the subsequent continuity to be cut off;
rather, by means of the linking of the continuity, it serves as a phenomenon with an object (*sārammaṇa-dhamma*) for another phenomenon that is similar to itself.
The production [of a state] is immediate conditionality (*anantarapaccayatā*).

Even when one state is being produced after another, the production of a subsequent state that is appropriate only after having established the fixed order of consciousness—namely, the sequence of the functional positions such as rebirth-linking and so forth, without producing just any random state—is "proximate conditionality" (*samanantarapaccayatā*). For it being thus, for one emerging from cessation...

In the case of a being passing away from the realm of non-percipient beings (*asaññasatta*), the state of immediate succession (*anantarata*) and the state of contiguous succession (*samanantarata*) are established even for the mental states occurring at the preceding and succeeding moments [of that existence].
For it is not the case that an interval of time, which is a non-entity, creates a gap between them;
nor is there a material phenomenon (*rūpadhamma*) belonging to another continuum that intervenes. Indeed, the material continuum is one thing, and the immaterial continuum is another.
In the *Aṭṭhakathā*, however, having rejected the view that "immediate succession" (*kālānantaratā*) constitutes the "proximate condition" (*samanantara-paccaya*), it is stated:
"Because they lack shape, they are perfectly immediate; thus they are called 'proximate' (*samanantara*).

By this, it is shown that while for material phenomena (*rūpa-dhamma*) which possess shape, their "immediacy" consists in being delimited by an interval in between, such is not the case for immaterial phenomena (*arūpa-dhamma*), which are devoid of shape.
Therefore, it is called "immediate succession" (samanantaratā) because of the state of those preceding and succeeding factors occurring as if they were one.
Thus, he shows that the capacity for such occurrence is the "condition of immediate succession" (samanantara-paccaya).

Furthermore, those phenomena which arise only when [the preceding factor] has already arisen, and not when it has not yet arisen; and which arise together with it, and not before—[these constitute this condition].
Furthermore, a *sahajāta-paccaya* (simultaneous condition) is a phenomenon that assists by being born together with those [other phenomena], as if for their sake;
it is like a lamp for illumination. For the flame of a lamp arises simultaneously with the light known as illumination.
It functions by way of mutual support, like a tripod of three staffs leaning against one another.
A supporting phenomenon is a mutuality condition (*aññamañña-paccaya*). This being the case, the distinction between this condition and the preceding one becomes evident;
for the term "co-arisen" (*saha-jāta*) does not convey such mutual reinforcement.

That which is depended upon is a support (*nissaya*); a phenomenon that assists by way of being a support is a support condition (*nissaya-paccaya*). Furthermore, that is the co-arisen support (*sahajāta-nissaya*).

The object-prenascence support (vatthupurejāta-nissaya) is twofold. Therein, a state that is co-nascent and assists by way of being a foundation—like a plastered wall for paintings—is the co-nascent support (sahajāta-nissaya).
A state that has arisen previously and assists by way of being a basis—like the earth for grass, trees, and so forth—is the object-prenascence support. However, the latter is stronger.

The support (nissaya) and the decisive support (upanissaya). For just as, in the production of rice porridge, the cook, the mortar, the firewood, or the fire are merely supports (nissaya) and not decisive supports (upanissaya);

whereas the rain showers upon the rice field are indeed the decisive support—for if those are absent, there is no such thing as stability even for the cook and the others regarding the production of the porridge—so too, in the absence of a certain condition, even the supported phenomena...
There is none. How could there be supported phenomena? That condition is called "decisive support" (*upanissaya*) in the sense that it is even stronger than a support (*nissaya*).
Furthermore, that [decisive support] is threefold: object-decisive support (*ārammaṇūpanissaya*), proximity-decisive support (*anantarūpanissaya*), and natural-decisive support (*pakatūpanissaya*).
Among these, objects that have been made much of (*garukata*) become dominant (*adhipati*) precisely because they have been made much of, and they also become powerful supports.
The states that function as proximity-condition (*anantara-paccaya*) are indeed powerful supports, because without them there would be no occurrence of the mental continuum at all.
Regarding the term "natural decisive support" (*pakatūpanissaya*): here, it is called "natural decisive support" because it is a decisive support (*upanissaya*) that is natural (*pakata*).
And it is "natural" in the sense that, when it has been performed, the conditionally arisen phenomena necessarily manifest within that same continuum at the appropriate time.

The meaning is "well done" (*suṭṭhu kata*). Here, "doing" (*karaṇa*) refers to the thorough production within one's own continuum, in the manner previously described, of the following factors: faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom; as well as lust, hatred, delusion, conceit, views, and aspiration.
Furthermore, it includes bodily pleasure, bodily pain, the person, the season, food, and lodging.
The thorough cultivation of these aforementioned phenomena should also be understood.
A phenomenon that arises earlier and assists by way of its continued presence is the *purejāta-paccaya* (pre-arising condition).

It is twofold, by way of object-pre-arising (*ārammaṇa-purejāta*) and support-pre-arising (*nissaya-purejāta*). For indeed, certain phenomena that serve as supports or objects are themselves pre-arisen.
It is said that the pre-arising condition (*purejāta-paccaya*) is distinguished from that [nutriment condition] by its priority.
However, the Elder Ācariya Ānanda has stated that the pre-arising condition is the state of being an assistance in the mode of pre-arising, distinguished by its dependence, object, and aspect.
Even so, apart from the specific powers of dependence and object distinguished by their priority, no separate, distinct power of pre-arising will ever be seen.
Just as water poured later upon young trees that have been planted and grown, a postnascent non-material dhamma (arūpadhamma) is an assistant by way of support;
it brings about both the growth and flourishing of the material phenomena (rūpadhamma) arising from the four origins that were produced earlier,
and serves as a condition for the continued occurrence of a stream of matter similar to itself even after its own arising.
The postnascent condition (*pacchājāta-paccaya*). However, in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated that the intention (*cetanā*) for the food of the bodies of young vultures is [the condition].

And in the *Mūlaṭīkā*, by this [statement], it shows that the material body is supported by immaterial phenomena (*arūpa-dhamma*) occurring through the nutriment of mental volition (*manosañcetanāhāra*);
for that very reason, instead of saying "like the desire for food," it uses the term "volition" (*cetanā*).

It is said that it "does. That volition (cetanā), which is a nutriment-desire (āhārāsā) arising subsequently together with its associated states, acts as a support by establishing the condition for those previously arisen bodily forms of the vulture to remain unfaded even in the absence of physical food for a long time, and for the continuous production of a series of bodily forms that grow and increase further and further. This is because [it is] clearly evident...
This simile appears here as if stated for the purpose of establishing the entire post-nascence condition (*pacchājātapaccaya*) by means of a portion of it.

It can certainly be said that volition (*cetanā*) and grasping (*gahaṇa*) are included here in order to show that even when they have reached the post-nascence condition, volition alone remains predominant. For if this were so, [the function] of the post-nascent object...
The establishment by means of an analogy arising later is thus appropriate. This very meaning is indeed obtainable even from the reading of the aforementioned commentary (*ṭīkā*):

"They cultivate" (*āsevanti*) means they thoroughly associate with it; phenomena arising one after another, as if thoroughly serving and associating, proceed again and again having grasped the entirely complete mode of that preceding [phenomenon]. Thus, it is "cultivation" (*āsevana*).
"Āsevati" means he causes those states to thoroughly take up his own dwelling (parivāsa). Or, "āsevana" means increasing.

Furthermore, according to the *Mūlaṭīkā*, the meaning of "cultivation" (*āsevana*) is the repeated performance and occurrence of a subsequent state that is to be done through an application similar to oneself by way of being wholesome and so forth; or it is the perfuming (*vāsana*), which is the bringing about of a state similar to oneself in one who is like oneself.

It has been stated. In that context, by the phrase "to be performed by means of an effort" (*payogena karaṇīya*), two types of adverting consciousness (*āvajjana*) and all resultant states (*vipāka-dhamma*) are excluded.
For even though the two types of adverting consciousness may occur two or three times, they possess no quality of being "to be performed by an effort," because they are extremely weak.
Furthermore, among the resultants, the noble fruits (*ariya-phala*) are not [performed] by preparatory effort.
Even those things that ought to be done cannot be accomplished by that practice alone, without the power of the volition of the Path.
It is simply because there is nothing at all to be said regarding the mundane results (vipāka) cast into the continuum by the force of karma.
"Practice" (pavattaṇa) means repeated performance; it refers to the continued engagement [of the practice] along with the attainment of a state of greater proficiency and strength.

Thus it has been said. For this being so, it is established that the condition called "repetition" (āsevanapaccaya) is a state that assists those states of the same kind occurring in the immediately succeeding moment to become proficient and strong by way of repetition, just as prior application is to the acquisition of the Dhamma of the scriptures, sciences, and crafts.

The kamma-condition is a phenomenon that assists by way of the state of activity known as mental volition (cittappayoga), which consists in the formative activity of the body, speech, and mind. It is twofold, according to the distinction between the co-nascent (sahajāta) and the asynchronous (nānākkhaṇika).
Among these, all co-nascent volitions (sahajātacetanā) function by accomplishing both their own function and the functions of others, like the master carpenter and his apprentices.

The conascence condition (*sahajāta-paccaya*). Just as the simultaneous union of a man and a woman accomplishes both the function of experiencing sensual pleasure and the function of depositing the seed in the womb for the sake of the manifestation of a child at a later time;

even so, the aforementioned function of volitional formation (*abhisaṅkharaṇa-kicca*) and the momentum generated by that volitional formation accomplish the functions of resultant and kamma-produced matter at a later time.

Wholesome or unwholesome volition (cetanā) that has ceased after performing its function as a specific deposit within the continuum for the sake of manifestation is called the asynchronous kamma-condition (nānākkhaṇika-kamma-paccaya).
A phenomenon that assists by way of the state of ripening is the resultant condition (vipāka-paccaya).
And this state of ripening is, in the world, the time when all flowers, fruits, and so forth have reached full maturity.
In every respect, there is a state of dullness. Thus, there is a manifestation in the continuum in a very slow manner, characterized by a tranquil state devoid of effort.
For that very reason, the occurrence of resultant consciousnesses is indistinct.

Even though those [resultants] occur with respect to objects such as karma established in a previous existence for one who has been asleep all night, at the time of waking, they are merely a consciousness that knows something slightly.

It is not that they serve as conditions for the occurrence [of consciousness]. However, although the fivefold sense-consciousnesses and so forth do indeed serve as conditions for the occurrence of the subsequently arising cognitive mind,

it should be understood that they exist simultaneously through the power of the impact between the physical basis (*vatthu*) and the object (*ārammaṇa*), and not merely by virtue of their own effort or activity.
The three immaterial nutriments are nutriment-conditions for co-nascent phenomena by way of producing them and by way of supporting them;
however, edible food is a nutriment-condition for this body—which arises from the four [great] primaries—solely by way of supporting it.
Furthermore, the meaning of "nutriment" (āhāra) is primarily that of support. For this very reason, in the Canon, edible food...

Instead of saying that "nutriments are a condition for nutriment-originated matter by way of the nutriment-condition," it is simply stated that "[they are] a condition for this body by way of the nutriment-condition.
Therefore, the function of even immaterial nutriments should be understood as providing support (*upatthambhana*) alone.
For even while producing [matter], nutriments act as conditions for the maintenance of the continuity of what they themselves have produced, as well as for other [factors] within that same continuum.
"Producing [the effect] together with support.
A phenomenon that is helpful in the sense of lordship (*issariyattha*) is the faculty-condition (*indriyapaccaya*). It is threefold by way of being co-nascent (*sahajāta*), and so forth.
Among these, immaterial phenomena that have become lords over their respective functions among co-nascent phenomena are the co-nascent faculty-condition.

The five types of sensitive faculties (*pasādindriya*) that have arisen earlier are the "pre-arisen faculty condition" (*purejāta-indriya-paccaya*) because they act as the sovereign factor for the five types of consciousness that arise later in their functions such as seeing and so forth.

The material life-faculty (*rūpa-jīvitindriya*), which acts as the sovereign factor for the maintenance of the long-term existence of co-nascent *kaṭattā*-derived matter, is the "material life-faculty condition.
Why, however, are the two mental faculties (*bhāvindriya*) not included here?

It is said: that which possesses the quality of being a producer (*janakatta*), a supporter (*upatthambhakatta*), or a preserver (*anupālakatta*) is called a "conditioned phenomenon" (*paccayadhamma*).
However, for the sake of the two states of co-nascent phenomena (*sahajāta-dhammā*), these three [qualities] do not exist.

Rather, it refers to the phenomena arising from the four bases (*catusamuṭṭhānika*) within a continuum associated with those [states], proceeding by means of their respective conditions such as karma and so forth.
The fixed order of occurrence that exists by way of their respective modes (ākāra) and so forth is established through the influence of their intrinsic nature (bhāva-rūpa).
Therefore, because they possess sovereignty over such a regulating function regarding those phenomena, both are called "faculties" (indriya).

It should be understood that this is not included here [in the list of conditions] because it does not constitute the conditionality of a faculty (indriya-paccayatā). Having approached the object and having fallen firmly and intensely upon it—

A dhamma that is beneficial in the sense of meditating (*jhāyana*) and in the sense of looking upon (*olokana*) is the condition of jhāna (*jhānapaccaya*). A dhamma that is beneficial in the sense of leading to an unhappy destination, a happy destination, or Nibbāna is the condition of the path (*maggapaccaya*).

And herein, because they are endowed with specific characteristics such as right seeing (*sammādassana*) and so forth, the wholesome factors beginning with right view (*sammādiṭṭhi*) lead to a happy destination and Nibbāna.
They are indeed path-conditions. Although they are indeterminate (abyākata), each possesses its own specific characteristic;
therefore, it should be understood that for them too, the state of being a path-condition is stated in that very sense.
Even though the path-factors (maggaṅga) are helpful in the sense of bringing about their respective results, that purpose is not attained by the material phenomena (rūpadhamma) arising from them.
Furthermore, their status as "arisen by way of path condition" (maggapaccayuppanna) is to be understood precisely because they have arisen from those very phenomena that serve as path conditions.
This same method applies to the conditions of root (hetu), kamma, faculty (indriya), and jhāna.
That which assists by way of mutual association—having become, as it were, unified and equal through such modes as simultaneous arising (ekuppādatā)—is [the path condition].

Dhamma as an associated condition (*sampayutta-paccaya*). Even though there is equality in terms of being co-nascent (*sahajāta*) and being supported and supporting (*nissaya-nissita*), a dhamma that assists by way of dissociation (*vippayutta*)—due to the absence of the characteristics of association such as simultaneous arising (*ekuppāda*)—is the dissociated condition (*vippayutta-paccaya*).
Wherever a suspicion of association might arise, it is precisely there that this [condition] is taught for the purpose of removing that suspicion.
Since this is called the "dissociation condition" (vippayutta-paccaya), it should be understood that there is no occasion for the application of the dissociation condition to objects,

immediate antecedents, and so forth, which are devoid of such [mental] formations. Among the types of conditioning states mentioned above, whichever [state] exists by way of its presence as a momentary present concomitant,
[acts as a condition] for another state of the same kind that is likewise a momentary present concomitant.
That which is beneficial by way of being co-nascent and so forth is the presence-condition (*atthipaccaya*).

That phenomenon which, when present and existing, does not allow another to arise because it occupies its place, is the absence-condition (*natthipaccaya*), being beneficial through its own state of having disappeared, which is termed "yielding room" for that other.
This too does not possess a separate specific efficacy. For this very reason, one goes or sits down with that same consciousness.
By the statement beginning with "it stands," there arises in the world the conceit that even for those things situated in the final consciousness, the preceding consciousness still persists.
Therefore, it should be understood that this condition is stated in order to eliminate that very misconception wherever a doubt regarding existence might arise.

"Passed away" means gone. That phenomenon which, by its own state of having passed away—counted as the giving of space—is the benefactor for another [phenomenon] that cannot arise while it has not yet passed away, is the *vigata-paccaya* (passed-away condition).

A phenomenon which, by its state of not having passed away—counted as the state of being present—is the benefactor for a similar phenomenon, is the *avigata-paccaya* (not-passed-away condition). And here, it is precisely the same pair of conditions as the preceding ones.

It should be understood that this was taught by using a different synonym for "vigata-duka" (the pair-free) in order to avoid the contingency of various other meanings and to clarify the knowledge [of the teaching].

For indeed, the words *atthi* (is) and *natthi* (is not), which illuminate various meanings, are seen both in the Dispensation and in the world, as in: "‘It is,’ Kaccāna, is one extreme; ‘it is not’ is the second extreme," and so forth. Previously...
Furthermore, stating again in another way the very same meaning already expressed serves to clarify the knowledge of the listeners.
However, the commentators merely describe the many possible variations in meaning for those pairs of conditions (*paccaya-duka*). [Enumeration of Conditions] 168.
Now, regarding the twenty-four conditions as they have been enumerated, first grouping them into six sets, and then...
Showing the exposition of those conditions in their respective order for those who are seated, he spoke the two verses beginning with “Nāmaṃ nāmassa chadhā.
Name is a condition for name in six ways, that is, by way of six kinds of conditions. Name is a condition for name-and-form in five ways.
Furthermore, name is a condition for form in one way; and form is a condition for name in exactly one way. [The same applies to] designation, name, and form.
"Name is twofold; the pair is name-and-form; for that same pair, name-and-form, there are nine"—thus, by way of the sixfold and fivefold sets and so forth, the conditions are sixfold.
The construction is: "How do they come to be?
[229] Furthermore, as for what is stated in the *Vibhāvani*:
“It has been stated that ‘the concepts and name-and-form are conditions for the mental process (nāma) in two ways and of two kinds. That is not correct.
For a discussion of conditions is well-stated only when it is presented in three modes: as the condition itself, as the conditioned product, and as the conditioning capacity.
However, since the conditions such as the immediate (anantara) and so forth serve to ensure the non-interruption of the mental continuum and to establish the sequence of functions and stages...”

And such indeed they are. Therefore, among the immaterial phenomena (arūpadhamma) such as the wholesome (kusala) and so forth, there is no single phenomenon that does not serve as a condition for some other non-opposing phenomenon;
thus it was said: "the immediately preceding ceased mind and mental factors," and so on.
In this context, by the phrase "for a non-opposing [phenomenon]," those wholesome and unwholesome states that are mutually opposed, as well as joy (somanassa) and grief (domanassa), are excluded.
The negation of the mutual and immediate conditions (*aññamañña* and *anantara-paccaya*) should be understood [here].

Regarding the term "present" (*paṭuppannānaṃ*), it means those that have arisen again or those that have arisen in succession. The condition called "repetition" (*āsevana-paccaya*) is so named because it occurs by way of repeatedly perfuming the mental continuum;

it is stated that this is found only in instances of consciousness-moments accompanied by the speed and force of impulsions (*javana*) which are accomplished through effort, as indicated by the phrase "the preceding impulsions," and so forth.

In this context, "impulsions" (*javana*) refers to the mundane wholesome and unwholesome functional impulsions, excluding the impulsions of the Path and Fruition, [which serve as] the "preceding impulsions" for subsequent impulsions—namely, for the wholesome, unwholesome, and functional impulsions, excluding the fruition-impulsions.

For phenomena of different classes are unable either to receive or to cause one another to receive a "retinue" that is complete in every respect. If they were able to do so, [the result would be impossible].
It might be thought that even by virtue of being of the same genus (*jāti*), mental states (*dhamma*) would be indistinguishable as preceding or succeeding one another.
Therefore, a resultant impulsion (*phala-javana*) of a different genus cannot take the "retinue" (*parivāra*) from the Path (*magga*). Nor can the Path give its own retinue to the Resultant.
Furthermore, the resultant consciousnesses perform the function of impulsion through the power of the preliminary work (*parikamma*) and the application (*payoga*), and not through mutual influence.

"By the power of receiving and taking the probationary period (parivāsa)": because the attainment of the sublime and unsurpassed states from the sense-sphere state occurs through the power of repetition (āsevana-bala), therefore the distinction of the planes of the change-of-lineage (gotrabhu), jhāna, and path should be understood here as immeasurable. Regarding "of the causes...
of name-and-form": herein, the path-factors are for those [consciousnesses] excluding the rootless (ahetuka); the jhāna-factors are for those excluding the fivefold sensory consciousnesses.
Of co-nascent mind-and-matter. As for the characteristic of co-nascent matter, he will explain it himself.

Volition, while occurring, accomplishes two functions: the arrangement of co-nascent factors for the sake of the future ripening of their result within that continuum, and the depositing of its own seed, known as the mode of occurrence, in that same continuum. Therein, the function of arrangement—
All volition is common [to all formations]. However, the function of depositing a seed belongs only to that volition which has attained the state of being either wholesome or unwholesome;
thus it is said, "volition conascent," and so forth. In this context, "conascent volition" includes even volition conascent with the fivefold sensory consciousness (*pañcaviññāṇa*).
For that too proceeds by way of the nature of kamma, which is defined as the coordinating of those factors that have arisen together.
"It is indeed called *kamma*. Because it is the depositing of the seed of fruition—which consists of its own mode of occurrence—it does not fulfill the function of a seed immediately.
Like mango seeds and the like, it fulfills that function only after reaching a state of ripeness at a subsequent moment;
thus it is said, "volition belonging to a different time," and so forth. In this context, "volition belonging to a different time" refers to the phenomenon arisen from its own conditions...

Wholesome wholesome volitions are established in the past time, which is distinct from the moment of their occurrence (*pavattikkhaṇa*). Alternatively, the reading may be *kusalākusalacetanā* (wholesome and unwholesome volitions).

Regarding the phrase "the resultant aggregates and the mutually co-nascent material phenomena" (*vipākakkhandhā aññamaññaṃ sahajātānaṃ rūpānaṃ*), the meaning here is "and for the mutual [aggregates] and for the co-nascent material phenomena.
This is just as, for example, young *sāla* tree saplings born previously [are nourished] by the showers of rain falling subsequently year after year.
Having attained growth, increase, and abundance by means of that [nutriment],

they serve as conditions for the continued existence of a vast grove of *sāla* trees in that place until the end of the eon. In the same way, from the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) onwards,

all the body-born elements (*kāya*) produced in the preceding moments throughout the entire body— namely, the karma-born body, the mind-born body, the temperature-born body, and the nutriment-born body— reside within the whole body.

Material phenomena arising from the four causes, having attained growth, increase, and abundance by way of the mind and mental factors of the first bhavaṅga and so forth that are born subsequent to them, become conditions for the successive occurrence of a series of material phenomena arising from the four causes;
thus it is said: "the mind and mental factors that are born subsequently," and so on. In this context, "of that which is born prior" means:
They say that [the nutriment] arises in the consciousness immediately preceding the past one. This lasts up to the eighth consciousness for that which is pre-arisen.
For this much time is called the period of growth for material phenomena; beyond that, during the period of decline, there is no need for the post-arisen nutriment.
Or else, it lasts up to the sixteenth consciousness for the pre-arisen. For at the point when, at the time near death, the physical basis (vatthurūpa) [is affected] by the death-consciousness—

It enters into the state of being a prenascence condition (*purejāta-paccaya*). For that very reason, it cannot be said that the death-consciousness (*cuti-citta*) is not a postnascence condition (*pacchājāta-paccaya*) for that bodily basis (*vatthu-rūpa*), nor so for the remaining types of matter.

For just as nutriment, while supporting, supports only that which is situated on the side of growth; there is no case where it does not support that which is situated on the side of decline—even then, it conforms to that [state].
Because support is required. Thus it is said. The power of immaterial phenomena (*arūpadhamma*) is indeed a great expansion;
therefore, even though they arise in a specific location within the body as their basis, they are certainly able to support this entire four-element body.
Hence it is said: "of this body. [The same applies to] the eye and so forth.
The bases of confidence (pasādavatthu), through their simultaneous acquisition of impact with visible forms and so forth, become the support for consciousness.

Since this impact occurs precisely at the moment they reach stability, it is established that these [bases] serve as a pre-arising condition (purejāta-paccaya) for their own consciousness at all times.
Furthermore, in the five-aggregate existence (pañcavokāra-bhava), consciousness is unable to arise without a physical basis (vatthu) as its support.
When one does not obtain a pre-nascent or a growing basis, then at the moment of rebirth-linking or at the time near death, it arises supported by whatever [basis] one happens to obtain.
But when one obtains a pre-nascent basis that is very strong, then it proceeds supported by that alone; and this is a rule.

It is obtained only during the course of existence (*pavatti*), not at the time of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*). For it is impossible for the base-prenascence (*vatthu-purejāta*) to have arisen by way of consciousness as a condition at that time;
thus it is said: "The six bases [occur] in the course of existence.
And the five objects [occur] in the fivefold cognitive process (*pañcaviññāṇa-vīthi*); this is stated by way of grasping the establishment of the rule. All [of these].

However, present elements that are produced material phenomena (*nipphanna-rūpa*) certainly serve as the prenascence condition (*purejāta-paccaya*) for the mental-consciousness process (*manoviññāṇa-vīthi*).
Having established this, the *Paṭṭhāna* states: "A present state is a condition for a present state by way of the prenascence condition.
As object-prenascence (*ārammaṇa-purejāta*), one contemplates the eye as impermanent, suffering, and non-self; [likewise] the ear, the nose..."

It is stated: "One contemplates the tongue, the body, visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, the physical base, and the present aggregates as impermanent, suffering, and non-self; one relishes and delights in the present eye," and so forth.
Furthermore, in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, it is said that after the moment of arising has passed, it is precisely the eighteenfold materiality that has reached the stage of presence (*ṭhiti*).

It is said that there is the "pre-arisen condition" (*purejāta-paccaya*). Herein, although in the *Paṭṭhāna* it is stated that "the rebirth-linking consciousness with a present object is a condition for the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) with a present object by way of the proximity condition," and thus the rebirth-linking and life-continuum are also described as having present objects,
[it refers to] taking as objects the signs of kamma and the signs of destiny which have become present.

At the time of the process of existence (*pavatti*), even for rebirth-linking consciousnesses (*paṭisandhicitta*), it appears as if an object-prenascence condition (*ārammaṇapurejāta*) is being obtained.

Nevertheless, regarding the opposite case of the prenascence condition, that [possibility] is rejected in the Canon itself by such passages as: "At the moment of rebirth-linking, there is one resultant indeterminate aggregate," and so forth.
And here, as in the formless realm (*ārūpa*), because of the absence of a base-prenascence (*vatthupurejāta*) at the moment of rebirth-linking, [it does not apply].
They state the reason for its rejection as follows: because that object is indistinct, it remains merely as an object [without being clearly apprehended].
"The object itself is made weighty" refers to a desirable object that has been made weighty by way of reflection (*paccavekkhaṇa*) and by way of relishing (*assādana*), and so forth;
this, moreover, should be understood according to the inclination of that particular individual. Even excrement, corpses, and the like [can become such objects].
For indeed, for those who delight in such things, do objects that are heavy only to flies, dogs, vultures, crows,
and the like become [objects of] attention?
As for what was stated in the *Vibhāvani*— "‘Making it heavy’ means reflecting upon it after making it heavy," and so forth— that is untenable.
The exposition of "his" (assa) occurs by way of gratification and so forth, as in the passage beginning, "Having made the eye heavy [with craving], he relishes it, he delights in it. Furthermore,

by the phrase "but the states such as lust," the ten unwholesome courses of action and the five deeds of immediate retribution are included, along with those states mentioned as lust, hatred, delusion, conceit, wrong view, and longing.

They exist. Among them, those [factors] excluding the immediate offenses (ānantariya-vajja) serve as powerful supports for the arising of all wholesome states belonging to the four planes within oneself, by way of transcending them as appropriate.
However, the immediate karmas are powerful supports specifically for the arising of wholesome states of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara).
And all of these, as appropriate, [serve as supports] both internally and externally for lust and so forth, as well as for killing and so forth.
They are powerful supports for the arising of all unwholesome states, as well as bodily pleasure, pain, and so forth, and indeterminate phenomena.

By the phrase "faith and the rest," it is meant that together with the qualities mentioned— namely faith (*saddhā*), virtue (*sīla*), learning (*suta*), generosity (*cāga*), and wisdom (*paññā*)— all acts of giving, morality, and so on,
as well as all wholesome states of the four planes, unwholesome states such as lust (*rāga*) and the like, and pleasure, pain, and so forth of the four planes [are supported].

"Undetermined [states] are also strong supports for the arising of [other states]" means that by the terms "pleasure," "pain," "person," "food," and "lodging," all determined (byākata) states of the four planes—excluding Nibbāna—are included.

For these too, as appropriate, serve as strong supports for the arising of wholesome, unwholesome, and determined states both internally and externally. "Of kamma and its resultants... [is the phrase].
Here, it is strong karma that is intended, not weak. But why are material phenomena (*rūpadhammā*) not included among the conditionally arisen?

Is it not the case that for the growth, sprouting, and expansion of external things such as trees and grasses, and for internal purposes such as health and so forth, there are powerful supports like the essence of earth, the essence of water, rainwater, seeds, roots, and medicinal herbs?
"Exist" (honti). This meaning has already been explained in the *Mūlaṭīkā*. For it is said there:

"A material indeterminate state does not obtain natural strong-dependence (*pakatūpanissaya*), because in the case of a non-conscious material continuity, there is an absence of anything that could act as a 'natural' [condition].
Just as faith and so forth are produced by a non-material continuity acting as an agent, and weather, food, and so forth are utilized [by it]."

It is not by means of such a continuity of matter. When matter proceeds due to the presence of seasonal conditions, seeds, and so forth, as well as karma and so forth, that matter is not produced by that [volition].

For it is only through the power of the arising, cultivation, and application of volition in one who possesses consciousness that there is the fashioning, planning, and performing of volition; and matter is devoid of consciousness.
This is what is meant: there are two kinds of continuity, namely, material continuity (*rūpa-santāna*) and immaterial continuity (*arūpa-santāna*).

In that regard, whatever state was previously well-produced or cultivated by means of a particular continuity, those very states produced or cultivated by oneself in the past become, at a later time, the decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*) for oneself. And such production and cultivation is termed "preparation" (*pakarana*).

It is obtained only within a conscious continuum of form (rūpa-santāna), not within an unconscious one. Therefore, material phenomena (rūpa-dhammā) do not possess what is called a decisive support (upanissaya).
However, according to the method of the Suttanta expressed as "when this exists, that comes to be;
when this does not exist, that does not come to be," a decisive support must indeed be predicated even among material phenomena.
In the *Vibhāvani*, however, it is stated:

"Having analyzed 'lust and so forth internally and externally... and the lodging' as appropriate, [it is said]: 'For lust and so forth are productive internally; persons and so forth are cultivated externally. This is not correct.
For lust and so forth that have arisen in oneself and another do not serve as powerful supports for lust and so forth within the mental continuum of another or of oneself.
They do not exist. In this context, women and men who share the same inclinations, as well as the gods and others afflicted by mental corruption, serve as examples for lust and the other defilements.
Furthermore, the exposition of the meaning provided there—by applying the principle of "according to how they stand" and stating "for oneself, lust and so forth"—is likewise untenable.

For by that [passage], one’s own lust and so forth, as well as one’s own faith and so forth, are shown to be internal; however, the faith and so forth of others, as well as the wholesome [states] of others, are shown to be external. Thus, the meaning is explained as being incomplete.

Furthermore, that which was stated by the words “In that case” (*tattha*) and so forth—namely, the manner in which the arising of only wholesome and unwholesome states occurs internally in dependence on one’s own lust and so forth—that too is simply untenable.
For even a commentary, which consists merely of a method and insight, must be spoken by completing the "door of method" (*nayamukha*).
Regarding the phrase "the object is treated with respect":

here, all mundane wholesome states, the lower paths and fruits, and Nibbāna are the objects for sense-sphere wholesome consciousness; likewise, the Arahant path and fruit, and Nibbāna are the objects for the four great functional javanas associated with knowledge.
With the exception of Nibbāna and the eight types of supramundane consciousness, as well as the two types of consciousness accompanied by aversion,

the two types accompanied by delusion, and body-consciousness accompanied by pain, all remaining mundane states— whether wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate— arise for a consciousness accompanied by greed;
thus should the distinction between conditions and conditionally arisen phenomena be understood.
[234] Furthermore, regarding what is stated in the *Vibhāvani*:

“That object is ‘weighty’ means an object that has been made weighty by way of the relish of reflective contemplation (*paccavekkhaṇa-assāda*) and so forth. Having said this, in order to explain it, [it says]:

“For that [object] consists of the various factors such as the jhānas, the paths, the fruits, insight (*vipassanā*), and Nibbāna; [and it is weighty] by way of the relish of reflective contemplation upon the phenomena such as the paths and fruits.”
"It makes [the mind] dependent on itself; thus it is called 'object-predominance' (ārammaṇādhipati). This is not correct.

Rather, one should say that giving, virtue, the observance-day rites, previously performed deeds, the lineage (gotrabhu), purification (vodāna), the path, the fruit, and Nibbāna—as well as lust, views, the eye, the ear, and so forth—are [predominant].
Furthermore, the mention of "insight" (vipassanā) here may have been stated with reference specifically to the lineage and purification stages. And yet...
These are called insight (vipassanā) because they have Nibbāna as their object. "Of the co-nascent mind and matter" means of those co-nascent with a double-rooted or triple-rooted impulsion (javana);

this is the intended meaning. "And of each other and of the co-nascent material phenomena" refers to the mutual relation between the consciousness-originated matter during the course of existence and the kamma-originated matter at the moment of rebirth-linking; the same principle applies elsewhere as well.
At the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) in the five-aggregate existence (*pañcavokārabhava*), consciousness does not find a footing without a physical basis (*vatthu*).
It is said that at the moment of rebirth-linking, the physical basis and the resultant [consciousness] are mutually dependent.
In the relation of mutuality (*aññamañña-paccaya*), that which supports its own supporting condition likewise becomes the state of the conditioned. Mind-originated...

Furthermore, material phenomena (rūpa) are unable to support the mind (citta). Likewise, it is stated that derived material phenomena (upādārūpa) and the primary elements (mahābhūta) [do not support one another], as well as mental states and mental concomitants (cittacetasika-dhamma) [do not support] each other, and so forth.
However, in the *Vibhāvanī*:
"However, because mutual conditionality exists only by way of mutual support—and not merely through co-nascence—matter is not a mutual condition for mentality during its course of occurrence.
Therefore it was said: 'Mental states and mental concomitants are mutual [conditions].
In this context, the phrase 'not merely through co-nascence' implies that if mutual conditionality were to exist merely through co-nascence..."
If this were so, it would be admitted that during the course of existence (pavatti), material phenomena (rūpa) could be a mutual condition for mental phenomena (nāma).

However, even in the case of the co-nascent condition (sahajāta-paccaya), material phenomena are not at all a condition for mental phenomena during the course of existence. Therefore, this [view] is not correct.

Regarding the statement, "The six bases are the conditions for the seven elements of consciousness," here [we refer to] the co-nascent support of the base (vatthusahajāta-nissaya) and the pre-nascent support of the base (vatthupurejāta-nissaya).
The basis-depending condition (*vatthu-nissaya*) is threefold: the object-basis, the pre-arisen basis, and the support-basis.
Among these, at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), the physical basis (*vatthu*) is the co-arisen support-basis for the resultant aggregates (*vipāka-khandha*).

Furthermore, that which is pre-arisen during the course of existence (*pavatti*) and upon which consciousness arises is called the pre-arisen basis-support for that consciousness. Moreover, that which...

A pre-arisen physical basis (*vatthu*) which serves as both the support (*nissaya*) and the object (*ārammaṇa*) for a particular consciousness is called its "pre-arisen basis-object support" (*vatthārammaṇa-purejāta-nissaya*).
For this is stated in the *Paṭṭhāna*: "Object, support, pre-arisen, dissociated, presence, and non-disappearance—these are three.
And how does that [basis] serve as both the support and the object for consciousness? It is by way of the present physical basis.

Whether consciousness arises by way of comprehension through an object, or by way of relishing it and so forth, or by way of the resolve for the exercise of supernormal powers, in that manner it becomes both the support and the object of that consciousness. For this has been stated in the *Paṭṭhāna*:
"One contemplates an internal basis as impermanent, suffering, and subject to change; one relishes it, one delights in it. Taking that as an object, lust arises."
Wrong view arises, doubt arises, restlessness arises, and mental distress arises.
Now, regarding this, the teachers introduced this so-called "base-object-prenascence-support" (vatthārammaṇa-purejāta-nissaya) into the path of recitation specifically at the time of death.
This is their intention here: first, in the Commentary, it is stated that when an undesirable object is adverted to by the mind-door...
The occurrence of consciousnesses outside of the cognitive process (vīthi) is thereby precluded.
Likewise, the commentators maintain that for a single-adverting process, the object of the consciousnesses is indeed identical in both nature and time.
Furthermore, in their natural state, consciousnesses each have their own respective bases as support. Therefore, when an internal present base—
When they comprehend [the object] by way of its impermanence and so forth, or when they relish it as "this is mine," then this base has been adverted to.
The impulsion moments (*javana*) also seize that very same [object]. They do not seize their own respective supporting bases.
For if they were to seize those or any other object, the impulsion moments would be called "without adverting" (*nirāvajjana*). Why? Because of the adverting consciousness (*āvajjana*).
Because it proceeds by taking another [object] instead of the one adverted to; thus they are called "divided objects.
Or because it proceeds by taking either subsequent individual bases (*paccekavatthu*) or something else; yet it cannot be so, due to contradiction with the *Aṭṭhakathā*.
Therefore, that base-and-object pre-arising condition (*vatthārammaṇa-purejāta-paccaya*) cannot exist at the time of its natural occurrence.
"Obtained. However, at the time near death, all the mental states beginning with adverting (āvajjana) proceed by depending upon one and the same physical basis;

therefore, for those [mental states] such as adverting that proceed taking that [basis] as their object, that very basis becomes both their physical support (vatthu) and their objective field (ārammaṇa).
For this being so, there is neither a lack of adverting nor a difference in the objective field for them—this is their intended meaning.

In that regard, it would first be illogical to say that if the mental objects were grasped by the impulsions without being presented by the adverting consciousness, those impulsions would be "without adverting.
This is because they grasp only that which has been presented by the adverting consciousness; for just as the adverting consciousness adverts to an object, so too do they.
The impulsions (javana) impel only toward their own object; they do not do so otherwise. Thus, there is no absence of adverting for the impulsions.
And just as there is no absence of adverting, likewise there is also no difference of object for them.

Why? Because a distinction is impossible. For when many [moments] proceed in succession, appearing as if unified by way of the density of the mental continuum (santati), [a distinction of object cannot be discerned].
Regarding the bases, they are able to apprehend each individual base separately, distinguishing it as "this is that very one," whether by way of adverting or non-adverting.

However, in those cases where such separation is impossible, it is absolutely not possible to find a distinctness of object—whether by way of the nature of the phenomenon (*dhamma*) or by way of time;
thus, for them, there is no distinctness of object at all. To this extent, [the relationship] of this [consciousness] to its base and object is a pre-arising support (*purejāta-nissaya*).
Thus, it is established that the method is available even at its natural time.
Furthermore, for those who, regarding their own present material body,
contemplate it as "my form is impermanent" or "this is mine," this name-and-form within their internal forms does not become the object of that consciousness.

It is not to be stated [in that way]. However, among those things that have become objects, it can be said that some are merely objects (*ārammaṇamatta*), some are object-prenascence (*ārammaṇapurejāta*), and some are both base-and-object-prenascence (*vatthārammaṇapurejāta*).

"Edible food" (*kabaḷīkāra-āhāra*) refers to the material nutriment produced by the fourfold origination from the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) onwards for beings in the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara*), as well as external food. For those born from a womb...
As long as the mother’s intake of food is not yet available, during the stages of the *kalala* and so forth, internal nutriment alone—arising from three sources—fulfills the function of support.

For this is stated in the *Paṭṭhāna*: "At the moment of rebirth-linking, edible nutriment is a condition for this body by way of the nutriment-condition. However, its support by external nutriment consists in the production of the eightfold materiality consisting of nutritive essence (*ojā*).
"It should be understood as 'only when it has been obtained.
If this is so, why was it said: 'Whatever food, drink, and sustenance his mother eats, by that he is sustained there, though enclosed within the mother's womb'?
It was said for the purpose of making known to that *yakkha* [the fetus] the food that is manifest [to the mother]. "Of this body" refers to those dwelling in the womb.
At the moment of arising of the rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhicitta), there is a body produced by one [nutriment]; at the moments of its presence and dissolution, it is produced by two;
thereafter, during the time of the pervasion of nutritive essence (ojā), it is produced by three; and at the time of the [full] diffusion of nutritive essence, it is produced by four.

This should be stated accordingly for the others as well. However, in the realm of form (rūpaloka), even without the twofold function of the nutriment of nutritive essence, [the body] reaches absorption (appanā).
By means of the material life-faculty (*rūpa-jīvitindriya*)— which is established through a specific type of kamma and capable of persisting for an extremely long duration—

and by means of such immaterial nutrients (*arūpāhāra*) included within the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*), the persistence of one’s personal existence (*attabhāva*) for even many eons (*anekakappa*) is to be understood.
By this method, [this applies] even for very long periods among the gods, who possess many bodies born of kamma, as well as among the hungry ghosts (*peta*) and those in hell.
It should be stated that at times the continuity of the personal existence (attabhāva) occurs even without external nutriment;

however, since internal nutriment is indeed obtainable in those cases, although the resultant aggregates (vipākakkhandhā) are also conditions dissociated from the physical basis (vatthu) at the moment of descent into the womb, they will nevertheless be included here under the category of "mental states and mental factors (cittacetasikadhammā) together with the co-nascent material phenomena (sahajātarūpa). This being so—
It is said: "of the resultants [arising] at the very moment of descent [into the womb].

The word "all" (*sabbathā*) should be construed with "in every way," such as "co-nascent" (*sahajāta*), and so forth. Furthermore, this "way" (*pakāra*) is to be understood as threefold, by way of "co-nascence condition" (*sahajāta-paccaya*) and so on.
Thus it was stated by the ancients: "and material life-force"—this is the presence condition (*atthi-paccaya*) and the non-disappearance condition (*avigata-paccaya*).
It should be applied. [Objection: Is it not the case that edible food (*kabaḷīkārāhāra*) and the material life-faculty (*rūpa-jīvitindriya*) should be included under "conascent" (*sahajāta*)?
For if that were so, the presence-condition (*atthi-paccaya*) would be only threefold. [Reply: No.

Because the characteristic of simultaneous arising, which is defined as "arising together," is absent. For the conascent condition is characterized by simultaneous arising. And edible food [consists of] the eight types of material phenomena beginning with nutritive essence (*oja*).
Even when producing [materiality], it produces it only at the moment of its own subsistence, not at the moment of its arising.
And just as the great elements, while supporting co-nascent material phenomena, support them only by having previously arisen together with them, that nutriment does not do so.
Rather, even without the function of simultaneous arising, it supports both co-nascent and non-co-nascent [phenomena]; thus, it is also the life-faculty of materiality (*rūpa-jīvita*).
Even without the function of arising together, it protects the co-nascent material qualities.

Thus, these two states are not included in the co-nascence condition precisely because they lack the characteristic of being co-nascent. Now, in order to show that all twenty-four conditions, when subsumed, result in four conditions, it is said: "The object, decisive support... [etc. ...come together."

In this regard, the method of synthesis is as follows: among the twenty-four conditions, the predominance condition (adhipati-paccaya) is first of two kinds, by way of object (ārammaṇa) and conascence (sahajāta).
Among these, objective predominance (ārammaṇādhipati) is included within the three [types of] conditions excluding kamma.
For even the mere object does not enter into synthesis with kamma; how much less so that which has become a predominance?
Here it might be asked: why is it said that [the mind] does not go even to the mere object?
Is it not the case that rebirth-linking, the life-continuum, and death are indeed conditioned by kamma as their object? True;

however, in this context, according to the *Mūlaṭīkā*, kamma becomes a condition for those states occurring at that time by virtue of its having been performed and accumulated, and not by way of being an objective mode (*ārammaṇākāra*). This is because [kamma] is the domain (*visaya*).

And it is by way of its state of being intoxicated (*mattatā*) that it serves as an object-condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*), not by way of the mode of the kamma-condition (*kammapaccayākāra*), which is defined as the production of a fruit through a specific modification of the mental continuity (*santānavisesana*).
Therefore, because they belong to different classes of conditional modes (*paccayākāravisabhāga*), they do not combine together; thus, they have been rejected [as such].
However, co-nascent predominance (*sahajātādhipati*) is included within the presence-condition (*atthipaccaya*). The support-condition (*nissayapaccaya*) is threefold: co-nascent...

The pre-arising condition (*purejāta-paccaya*) is threefold: object-pre-arising, basis-pre-arising, and basis-and-object-pre-arising. Among these, the first two are "existence" conditions (*atthi-paccaya*), while the last one is an "object-existence" condition (*ārammaṇa-atthi-paccaya*) among the two types of object-conditions; if it is highly esteemed, it is also a "decisive support" condition (*upanissaya*).
Thus, the pre-arising condition is threefold: object-pre-arising, basis-pre-arising, and basis-and-object-pre-arising. Among these, the basis-pre-arising...

Regarding the presence condition (*atthipaccaya*): the other two [conditions] are included within the two types of presence conditions, namely the object-predominance and the presence conditions. These three [types] become predominant. Regarding the decisive support condition (*upanissaya*):
the kamma condition is twofold, namely co-nascent (*sahajāta*) and asynchronous (*nānākkhaṇika*). Among these, the co-nascent is included in the presence condition.
The asynchronous, however, is twofold: powerful and weak. Furthermore, the powerful is twofold: immediate (*akālika*) and delayed (*kālika*). Both of these...

In the case of decisive support (upanissaya). However, the weak [decisive support] is simply a condition by way of kamma. All nutriment conditions and all faculty conditions are included in the presence condition (atthipaccaya).
The dissociation condition (vippayuttapaccaya) is fourfold: conascent, base-prenascence, base-object-prenascence, and postnascence.
Among these, the first two and the last are included in the presence condition; the third, however, is included in two types of object-presence conditions.

If it is "venerated," it is also a decisive support (upanissaya). As for the remaining seventeen conditions, eight conditions—namely, root (hetu), conascence (sahajāta), mutuality (aññamañña), result (vipāka), jhāna, path (magga), association (sampayutta), and non-disappearance (avigata)—are included in the presence condition (atthipaccaya), as is the postnascent (pacchājāta).
Five conditions—namely, proximity (anantara), contiguity (samanantara), repetition (āsevana), absence (natthi), and disappearance (vigata)—are included in the decisive support condition (upanissaya).
Thus, all twenty-four conditions, when condensed by way of their inclusion into similar classes, converge within the four conditions beginning with the object-condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*).
However, in the *Vibhāvanī*...

Regarding those four [types of objects], all twenty-four conditions converge within each one. With this intention, it was stated: “There is no such condition as that,” and so forth. All of that, however, is merely the opinion of the teacher.
For, as to what was said therein:
“There is no such condition whatsoever that would not become an object for consciousness and mental factors.”

That, first of all, is not tenable. For here, a mere convergence by way of the intrinsic nature of phenomena (dhammasarūpamatta) is not intended; rather, it is intended precisely by way of their conditionality (paccayaṭṭha).
And the sense of a condition such as "cause" (hetu-paccaya) is not the same as the sense of a condition such as "object" (ārammaṇa-paccaya). This same method applies here as well to the statement:
"Each [condition] does not become a decisive support (upanissaya) for that which has arisen from its own respective condition."

In this context, however, the construction is as follows: there is no condition whatsoever that does not function as a decisive support (*upanissaya*) for that which has arisen from its own respective conditions.
Furthermore, regarding what was stated there:
"Because the occurrence of the world is caused by karma, all things, by way of the metaphorical designation of 'cause' applied to the fruit, do not transcend the nature of karma."

[239] And as for what was stated, that "those [factors] exist both in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*) and by way of worldly convention (*lokasammuti*)," both of these points are entirely contrary to the logic of the Teaching (*sāsanayutti*). "In this" refers to this system of the *Paṭṭhāna*.
"In all cases" refers to all conditions (*paccaya*) that possess the characteristic of arising together (*sahajāta-sabhāga*).

For the rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhi-viññāṇa) is that which, in the mutual dependence of name-and-form (nāmarūpa), constitutes the head and the seed of each respective existence (bhava) delimited by death;
from it arises the entire continuum of various material and immaterial phenomena comprising the whole body, just as a great tree arises from a seed. As it has been said:
"For if consciousness, Ānanda, were not to descend into the mother’s womb, would name-and-form coagulate there?"—"No indeed, Bhante.
"And if consciousness, having descended into the mother’s womb, were to depart, would name-and-form come to birth in this state of being?"—"No indeed, Bhante. "And if consciousness..."
"Ānanda, if they were to cease while still young—whether as a boy or a girl—would name-and-form reach growth, increase, and fullness?
"No indeed, Bhante. "Therefore, Ānanda, this is the cause, this is the source, this is the origin, this is the condition for name-and-form: namely, consciousness."
In this context, "you will accumulate" means you will increase. For name-and-form is indeed the increase of consciousness. "You will deviate" means you will break apart.
"For the sake of this state" means for the sake of such a personal existence (*attabhāva*); this is the meaning. "Growth, development, and abundance":
growth by way of the first stage of life; development by way of the middle stage of life; and abundance by way of the final stage of life.

"Vepulla" (abundance) is what is stated in the Aṭṭhakathā. Therefore, it should be understood that at the moment of rebirth-linking, consciousness is an absolute condition for the arising of material phenomena.

Furthermore, once this rebirth-linking materiality has arisen, it remains throughout that existence until death as the support and the seed for all successions of material phenomena produced by the four causes as they proceed.
For even a mind that is exceedingly powerful is unable to produce matter if there is no prior succession of matter (rūpapaveṇī).

The same applies to temperature and nutriment. For this very reason, in the formless realm (arūpabhava), even those sense-sphere and other types of consciousness capable of producing matter do not produce matter there.
Likewise, in the case of non-percipient beings (asaññasatta), the successions of matter originated by temperature cannot arise because of the previously arisen succession of matter born of kamma.
"Knowledge arises precisely from the state of probation (mānatta). For it is said in the *Vibhaṅga-ṭīkā*: "But the immaterial (arūpa) is not the locus (okāsa) for the material;
that is to say, when a certain material exists, the mind would produce another material, yet that very [locus] is absent there—this is the meaning.
For even the preceding material possesses the status of a condition, as shown by the analogy of the joy felt toward a son. And here, regarding the son...
"By showing the similarity to joy": by this he shows the following point.
Just as grasses and trees possess a specific form called "determining-form" (*niyāmarūpa*), which is their seed-state;

through the power of which, the grasses and trees produced from it, while growing, do not grow in just any way, but rather, taking on a form entirely identical to other grasses and trees that have the same seed as themselves, they continue to grow.
In the same way, for beings born from a womb, there exists a source called "the determination of existence" (bhāvasaṅkhāto niyāmo rūpanāma).
By the power of which they become exactly similar in appearance and shape to those of a like kind, and especially to their own parents.
Thus, just as there is a determination of the seed, there is also a determination of the womb. And this should be understood as the specific efficacy of the rebirth-linking matter itself.

Furthermore, this so-called "determination of the womb" (*yoniniyāma*) is simply the continuity of temperature-born material form (*utujarūpa-santāna*) produced by the mother and father within the bodies of children during the stages of the embryo (*kalala*) and so forth.
By its power, that continuity becomes similar in shape to beings of the same species and similar to one's own family lineage.
For example, just as the physical form such as femininity and so forth [produces] the female sex-marks and other characteristics of beings, and the seed-form [produces] the sprout.

It determines the respective colors, shapes, and so forth of grasses and trees. Thus, the materiality of the womb (yonirūpa) acts as the regulator and determiner of beings according to their various species.

Up to this point, with the exception of mind-born materiality (cittajarūpa), all materiality produced by the three [other] origins is independent of the mind for its arising and is dependent upon the continuity of previously arisen materiality.

It has been established. For that very reason, their arising occurs even at the moments of the mind's stability and dissolution, and even during the time of the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), which is devoid of mind.
Therefore it was said: "But here, 'co-nascent matter'... and so forth. The words "Thus," etc., constitute the conclusion.
In that context, *sambhavam* means "according to how they arise"; or alternatively, *sambhavā* means "arisen. *Ajjhattañca* means "and those that have become internal."

"External" (*bahiddhā*) means those that have become external. "Conditioned" (*saṅkhata*) means those that have become conditioned. "Unconditioned" (*asaṅkhata*) means those that have become unconditioned.

Thus, there are those belonging to the three times and those transcending time, as well as those arisen internally and externally. Likewise, there are those that have become conditioned and unconditioned.
By way of the classification of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), these phenomena (*dhammā*) established in the *Paṭṭhāna* are of three kinds; in every respect, they are called the twenty-four conditions.

The construction is: "they exist. And herein, when the threefold states that have been established possess the temporal distinctions of being past, present, or future, the twenty-four conditions also become established as having the respective divisions of being past, present, or future, according to their possibility. Among these, the object-condition (*ārammaṇa*), the predominance-condition (*adhipati*), and the decisive-support-condition (*upanissaya*) are of all three times and also timeless.
In the *Vibhāvani*, however, it is stated:
“The object, predominance, and decisive-support conditions are of all three times.
