That is not tenable, because even designations (*paññatti*) and Nibbāna—which are timeless—are included among them. In this context, regarding those that are newly arisen in this existence...

The status of future [states] as decisive support conditions (*upanissaya-paccaya*) should be understood for one who performs prior practice (*pubbayoga*) for the sake of obtaining wealth, grain, and enjoyments; or learning, crafts, and proficiency in the sciences; or virtue, concentration, and wisdom;
or the attainment of excellence in existence, excellence in enjoyments, and the attainment of the paths and fruits in a future life. However, in the *Paṭṭhāna*, future possession of the eye...
By stating, "Aspiring for excellence of the ear, nose, tongue, and body; aspiring for excellence of beauty, sound, smell, taste, and touch;
aspiring for future aggregates, one gives gifts and undertakes virtue," etc., it is the excellences included within other existences that are described.
These, moreover, arise according to the nature of the kamma such as giving and so forth.
They are to be understood as "stated. The kamma condition, however, belongs to two periods of time by way of the present and the past.
The conditions of proximity, contiguity, repetition, absence, and disappearance belong to the past period. The remaining fifteen conditions belong to the present period.
In the dyads of internal and external, the object, predominance, conascence, mutuality, support, decisive support, and prenascence [conditions are to be understood].
Nutriment exists as both internal and external. The remaining fourteen conditions are exclusively internal.
Object, predominance, and decisive support may be either conditioned or unconditioned; the rest are conditioned.
It is called "the fivefold immaterial" because it never attains the state of shape known as "form," and it is also called "name."
Why? Because it is that which must be grasped by those who hear it, by way of being designated through names, designations, and expressions.
(169) It is "conceptualization" (*paññatti*) because it is made known (*paññapīyati*). This too is one meaning of the word: it is established by the common people of the world;
the sense is that it is both expressed in conventional usage and accepted. It is any meaning of the phrasing that constitutes conventional truth (*sammutisacca*).
"Paññatti" is so called because meanings are made known (paññāpetabbā) by it. The word "paññatti" signifies that which illuminates both the phrasing and the meaning;

thus it is said that there are two kinds of *paññatti*. As for the phrase "the remainder... becomes twofold": therein, it is called "meaning-paññatti" (*attha-paññatti*) because it is that which is made known;
it is called "word-paññatti" (*sadda-paññatti*) because it is the act of making known. [It refers to] the mode of the transformation of each respective reality.
The mode of transformation of those respective great elements, such as earth and so forth, characterized by their specific states and modes of predominance;
this is the meaning of "the mode of particularity in the process [of existence]. "Dependent upon" (upādāya) means relying upon;
it means having first grasped [them] with the mind. "Designated in such and such a way" means: "this is called 'earth,' this is called 'mountain,'" and so on.
The meaning is that it is designated, spoken of, and expressed by the multitude of people in this manner and so forth.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "earth, mountains, and so forth," rivers, oceans, and the like are included. This is called collective designation (*samūha-paññatti*).
However, in the *Vibhāvani*:
“It is called a ‘description by shape’ (saṇṭhānapaññatti). It will appear as if it were appropriate [to say this], for here shape is not the primary factor.
“The mode of arrangement of the constituent parts” means the mode of arrangement of the constituent parts such as wood and so forth.
Here too, by the word “etc. (ādi), boats and other such things are included. This is shape...

Conceptual designation (*paññatti*). For it is firewood and so forth, when arranged in the form of a house, that are called a "house," and when arranged in the form of a chariot, that are called a "chariot.
However, in the *Vibhāvanī*, it is stated: "It is a collective conceptual designation (*samūha-paññatti*). That is not tenable.
For here, the aggregate is not the primary factor. The designation of a "being," such as a person or individual, is also called a "dependent designation" (*upādāpaññatti*).
"The revolving of the moon and so forth" refers to the moon, sun, and other celestial bodies revolving clockwise around Mount Sineru.
That direction from which the moon and sun rise is called the "eastern direction" (*pubbadisā*), because it is the first to receive illumination. However, where...
They go toward their setting; that is called the western direction (*pacchimadisā*), because its light has been received last.

The direction on their right side is called the southern direction (*dakkhiṇadisā*) in the sense of increase. The other, however, is called the northern direction (*uttarādisā*) in the sense of being higher.
When the sun rises, it is called "forenoon" (*pubbanha*) because it constitutes the prior portion of the entire day. Such are these [terms].
These are known as the designation of direction and the designation of time. By the word "etcetera," the designation of place—such as land, low ground, and so forth—is included.
The "mode of non-contact" refers to the mode in which the great elements do not touch one another; this is called the designation of space.
The "signs of the respective elements" refer to the signs of the elements such as the earth-kasina and so forth, as well as the bloated corpse and so forth. [Also] the blue-kasina and so forth.
And the sign of color (*vaṇṇanimitta*) is included right here. "The distinction of development" refers to the specific types of development such as the preliminary stage (*parikamma*) and so forth.

By this, he states the established cause for the preliminary sign (*parikammanimitta*), the learning sign (*uggahanimitta*), and the counterpart sign (*paṭibhāganimitta*). This is called the "description by means of signs" (*nimittapaññatti*).

Regarding the phrase "such distinctions as these," the word "etc. includes the designations of "derived" (*upādā-paññatti*), "relative" (*upanidhā-paññatti*), and so forth, as they appear in the *Aṭṭhakathā*.
By the phrase "though non-existent in the ultimate sense" (*paramatthato avijjamānāpi*), he shows that they possess existence from the standpoint of conventional designation (*sammuti*).
For it is precisely because of this that there is no charge of false speech for those who employ various expressions while apprehending the existence of these [designations].

"By way of the shadow-form of the meaning" means by way of the shadow-form consisting of the collection, configuration, and so forth, of those ultimate realities such as the primary elements (*bhūta*).

Alternatively, "by way of the shadow-form of the meaning" means by way of a form resembling a substance, which is designated by the term "shadow-form of the meaning" and possesses a tangible appearance;

this is the sense. "Depending upon each respective [factor]" means depending upon the specific mode of occurrence of each respective ultimate phenomenon (*paramattha-dhamma*). "In comparison with" (*upanidhāya*)...

*Olumpiya*. "Being conceptualized" (*parikappiyamānā*) means being grasped after having been conceptualized by a conceptualizing consciousness (*parikappa-buddhi*). Here, however, the construction is as follows:

all designations (*paññatti*), which serve as objects and are being conceptualized through such various distinctions as "thus" (*evaṃ*) and so forth, are called "designations" (*paññatti*) in the sense that they are "made known" (*paññāpīyati*).
"Is reckoned" (*saṅkhāyati*) means it is counted. The meaning is that it is established after having been brought into the sphere of calculation (*gaṇanūpaga*). "Is designated" (*samaññāyati*)...
It is authorized. Name (*nāma*), naming-act (*nāmakamma*), designation (*nāmadheyya*), etymological expression (*nirutti*), phoneme (*byañjana*), and utterance (*abhilāpa*):
these six are the names and naming-acts. Therein, it is called "name" (*nāma*) because it inclines toward the meaning (*atthe namati*).

It is called "meaning" (*attha*) because it proceeds having the meaning as its very object. And it is called "name" because it inclines itself toward the meaning. For when the "names" comprised within the Three Pitakas exist, for those who grasp them...
All of these meanings come forth at every step and in every sentence.
Furthermore, because it directs the knowledge of those who hear it toward this or that specific meaning, it is called *nāma*.

Since it is to be performed by way of grasping a name, it is the "name-action" (*nāmakamma*). It is called *dheyya* because it is held or maintained; thus, a name which is itself the object to be held is a "name-object" (*nāmadheyya*).
*Nirutti* (etymology) is so called because meaning (*attha*), which resides on the side of the unknown, is drawn out from that [meaning] by means of this [language] and spoken—that is, explained.

*Byañjana* (the phrasing) is so called because it makes the meaning manifest (*byañjana*) through its expression. *Abhilāpa* (utterance) is so called because the meaning is spoken (*lapīyati*) or explained by means of it, having been made clearly evident (*abhibyatta*).

Furthermore, herein there are: designation by phonemes (*vaṇṇa*), designation by syllables (*akkhara*), designation by vowels (*sara*), designation by long [vowels], and designation by short [vowels].
Designation (*paññatti*). There are designations of phonemes, groups, vowels, and consonants; designation of gender; designation of words;

and designations of sentences should be understood as subdivisions of this very [designation]. Designation that occurs with respect to meanings existing in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*) is called "designation of the existent" (*vijjamāna-paññatti*).
Designation that occurs with respect to things not existing in the ultimate sense, such as the earth or mountains, is called "designation of the non-existent" (*avijjamāna-paññatti*). These...

Having thus reached the place of the compound, the phrase beginning with "therein" (*tattha*) is stated in order to show that the other four [types of designation] also exist by way of the conjunction of two words.
By the expression "they designate by means of this," he states the meaning: "those by which they designate an existing object are 'designations of the existent' (*vijjamānapaññatti*).

This same method applies elsewhere as well. Having formed the term *chaḷabhiñño* (one possessing the six direct knowledges) from the sense of "one who has six direct knowledges," [the word refers to] those things which function as qualifiers...

Because the six higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) exist while the person (*puggala*) who possesses them does not exist, "one possessing the six higher knowledges" (*chaḷabhiñño*) is called a designation of the non-existent by means of the existent.
"Woman" (*itthī*) does not exist, whereas "sound" (*saddo*) does exist;
thus, "the sound of a woman" (*itthisaddo*) is called a designation of the existent by means of the non-existent. Both the eye and eye-consciousness (*cakkhuviññāṇa*) are likewise [existent].
"Existing consciousness in the eye is 'eye-consciousness'"—this is called a designation of the non-existent by means of the existent.
"Both the king and the son are non-existent," yet "the king's son" is "rājaputta"—this is called a designation of the non-existent by means of the non-existent.
Demonstrating this meaning, he said, "Of both," and so forth.

In this context, however, some say that there is no such thing as a "conceptual designation" (*nāmapaññatti*) existing separately from the word itself and its literal meaning, apart from the inherent nature of sound.
This is not tenable, because it is established as distinct by virtue of its function of illuminating the meaning.
For a so-called "word" is only capable of illuminating meaning when it has assumed the form of syllables, phrases, and phonemes. And the term "ultimate reality" (*paramattha-sadda*)...
"Momentsary, reduced to dust and powder, it does not exist once it has entered into that state. Therefore, the designation (*paññatti*) of the nature of sounds exists as something distinct.

Showing that its existence is evident through the occurrence of a mind directed toward the letters, words, and phonemes immediately after hearing the sound of the speech, and of a mind cognizing that meaning immediately thereafter, he spoke two verses.

In this context, the connection is as follows: "by way of the sequence of the vocal sound" means that this designation (*paññatti*) becomes the object-sphere of the mind-door (*manodvāra*) arising immediately after the occurrence of the ear-consciousness process (*sotaviññāṇavīthi*), which itself arises by way of taking as its object the "vocal sound"—that is, the sound consisting of articulated speech.
But what kind of designation is it? To this he says: "for the purpose of which... and so forth.
"Beyond that" (tato paraṃ): here, the connection is that "beyond the arising of the mind-door which has the designation of names as its object, meanings are cognized. The construction is:
"That this designation, by means of which meanings existing as designations of ultimate reality are cognized, is fashioned by worldly convention—this is how it should be understood."

And here, by the phrase "the cognitive process of ear-consciousness," it should be understood that the cognitive process of mind-consciousness (*manoviññāṇavīthi*) which follows upon that—having as its object the mere past sound—is also included. For it is said in the *Sāratthadīpanī*:

"In the words spoken by him, however many syllables there are, taking each one of them both as present and as past, [they are grasped] by the cognitive process of ear-consciousness and by the cognitive process of mind-consciousness."

Once that [mental process] has arisen and ceased, at its conclusion, those syllables are combined; having grasped the collection of syllables, a single cognitive series of mind-consciousness arises and ceases.

Immediately following that, once another cognitive series of mind-consciousness has arisen and ceased by way of grasping the designation of a name—thinking "this collection of syllables is the name for this"—immediately thereafter...
When a cognitive process of mind-consciousness has arisen, the natural discernment of its meaning as "this is its significance" becomes possible.

However, in the *Maṇisāramañjūsā*, it states that after the process which follows that [process], there is one process of determination (*vinicchaya-vīthi*) and a process of grasping the intimation (*viññatti-gahaṇa-vīthi*).
Following that, when a sound consisting of a single syllable occurs, there is the grasping of the designation of a name (*nāma-paññatti*) which illuminates a single meaning. As for that...
When one speaks, that which was previously determined by the mind is called the "conceptual sound" (*paññatti-sadda*). Thereafter, there is the grasping of its meaning.

However, in such instances, the sequential description of the various stages of the impulsion process (*javana-vīthi*) should be understood as being stated by way of grasping what is primary and prominent.
For it has been said that within a single moment, many hundreds of thousands of millions of consciousnesses arise. Likewise—
That which consists of one *matta* is called short (*rassa*); that of two *mattas* is called long (*dīgha*);
that of three *mattas* should be known as protracted (*pluta*); and a consonant (*byañjana*) is considered to be half a *matta*.
Furthermore, even a hundred thousand combinations of ultimate words (*paramattha-sadda*) cannot constitute a single syllable (*ekakkhara*). Therefore, we have not engaged in extensive analysis here.
Thus ends the Elucidation of Ultimate Meaning (*Paramatthadīpanā*) for the eighth section,
the Compendium of Conditions (*Paccayasaṅgaha*), within the fourth commentary on the *Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha*,
titled the Elucidation of Ultimate Meaning.
170. Having thus shown the analysis of mind-and-matter (*nāmarūpa*) together with its specific conditions through eight chapters,

he now spoke the passage beginning with "The method of serenity and insight" in order to show the procedure for the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) for one who has understood the analysis of mind-and-matter.

The construction of the sentence is as follows: "After this summary of conditions, I shall explain in due order both types of meditation subjects (*kammaṭṭhāna*) for the development of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*).
In that context, *samatha* is so called because it calms (*sameti*) defilements or other gross phenomena such as applied thought (*vitakka*).
It is the concentration (*samādhi*) characterized by one-pointedness (*ekaggatā*) proceeding in that manner. [As for *vipassanā*: they see specifically (*visesena*) by means of this.
Vipassanā is the wisdom of meditation consisting of the contemplation of impermanence and so forth.

For by means of this, the practitioner, transcending what is seen by the worldly masses in the aggregates—such as "woman" or "man," or "permanence" and "pleasure"—sees specifically only impermanence and the rest. They are called *bhāvanā* because they are to be cultivated (*bhāvetabbā*);
or else, they are called *bhāvanā* because one cultivates the continuum of consciousness by means of them. It is an action, a deed; it persists.
"Herein" (*ettha*) means a place. "The place of action" (*kammatthāna*) means a subject for meditation (*kammaṭṭhāna*).

The meaning is: the locus for the occurrence of the work of yoga, which is designated as the exertion of energy (*vīriyārabbha*). This refers to the disk of the *kasiṇa* and so forth, as well as the cultivation of the *kasiṇas* and so forth.
For this single work of cultivation—such as the cultivation of the earth-*kasiṇa*—which constitutes the whole consisting of the beginning, middle, and end, [serves] for its own constituent parts...
"The basis for the occurrence of the work of yoga is possible.
However, in the *Vibhāvanī*, it is also stated:

"It is the method of cultivation that constitutes the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna), by virtue of being the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) for each successive stage of the work of yoga. That too is indeed appropriate.
Or, the work of yoga (*yogakamma*) itself is called *kammaṭṭhāna* in the sense of being the basis (*adhiṭṭhāna*) for specific kinds of happiness.
"Therein" means in both these two types of *kammaṭṭhāna*. "Included under serenity" means included under the *kammaṭṭhānas* of serenity (*samatha*).
"The ten kasinas" refers to the ten circles of the kasina and the jhānas of the kasina; for both of these are [included] under serenity, which is defined as the practice of yoga.
Because they are the bases for the occurrence of karma, they are called "subjects of meditation" (*kammaṭṭhāna*).

"The ten foul things" (*dasāsubha*) refers both to the ten bases of foulness (*asubhavatthu*) and to the meditative absorptions on foulness (*asubhajjhāna*). "The ten recollections" (*dasaanussatiyo*) refers to the ten bases of recollection, such as the qualities of the Buddha, and to the mindfulness (*anussaraṇasati*) that recollects them.
The remaining [terms] should also be explained accordingly. "Caraṇa" means conduct (*cariyā*); the sense is "practice" (*samudācaraṇa*).
"What is meant is 'abundance of occurrence. 'Rāgacariyā' means the conduct of lust. The reading 'rāgacaritā' does not exist in the Aṭṭhakathā;
it is appropriate only in the context of the 'person' (puggala). This same method applies to the others as well. As for what is in the *Vibhāvanī*:
The classification of temperaments (*cariyā*) according to their combinations has been mentioned;
however, that is not intended here. For it is not the case that two or three meditation subjects (*kammaṭṭhāna*) should be given even to one person of a combined temperament.

That is precisely why such a classification is not taken into account in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*). All [states] occurring prior to absorption (*appanā*) belong to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*).
"Meditative development" (bhāvanā) refers to preliminary development (parikamma-bhāvanā). That, moreover, is twofold: proximate and remote in relation to absorption (appanā).
Of these, that which is proximate is called "access development" (upacāra-bhāvanā) because it proceeds having approached and remained near to absorption.

The other, however, is simply named "preliminary development. Thus, although it is the same as preliminary development, [it is distinguished] for the purpose of making clear the specific differences between what precedes and what follows.
It is stated in the commentaries that [this meditation] is taken under two names: "development as preliminary work" (*parikamma-bhāvanā*) and "Tissa’s development" (*tisso-bhāvanā*).

However, the distinction between these two will be explained later. The "sign of the preliminary work" (*parikamma-nimitta*) refers to the sign such as the disk of the *kasiṇa* which serves as the object for the development as preliminary work.
Although it is one and the same in its status as the object of that [development], it is mentioned [separately] for the purpose of making clear the distinction between its earlier and later stages.
It is stated by dividing it into two types: the preliminary sign (*parikamma-nimitta*) and the learning sign (*uggaha-nimitta*). The distinction between these two will also be explained later.

Whether made or unmade, the surface of the earth-circle—measured either by the small dimension of one span and four fingers, or by the large dimension of a threshing-floor circle and so forth—is called the "earth-kasina" (*pathavī-kasina*) in the sense that it completely pervades everything without exception.
For the word *kasiṇa* is a term signifying "entirety," as in the expression "the whole of Jambudīpa by means of the *kasiṇa*.

Therefore, to whatever extent one grasps the sign upon the surface of the earth, it must be grasped after having pervaded that entire area with the mind without exception—not by standing in only one part of it. For this reason, it is said that the surface of the earth-circle itself must be pervaded without remainder.

"Kasiṇa" means earth-kasiṇa (*pathavīkasiṇa*). This same method applies to the remaining kasiṇas as well. Herein, the "earth-kasiṇa" refers to the designation of the shape of earth that has not manifested its color, arranged as a single level surface. The same applies to the water-kasiṇa and the fire-kasiṇa.
A column of air, grasped by forming a shape with the mind at the point where it is touched, is called the air-kasiṇa (*vāyokasiṇa*).
A specific shape-designation distinguished by the color blue is called the blue kasiṇa (nīlakasiṇa). Likewise there are the yellow, red, and white kasiṇas.
A shape-designation seen somewhere, distinguished by the light of the moon, sun, fire, or a lamp, is called the light kasiṇa (ālokakasiṇa).
A shape-designation seen through the openings of windows, air-holes, and so forth, distinguished by space, is called the space kasiṇa (ākāsakasiṇa).
"Uddhumātaka" refers to that which has become excessively bloated and has reached a state of inflation. Because it is loathsome, it is called "uddhumātaka.

This is the name for a corpse in such a state. When that very same [corpse] reaches a state of putrefaction, having abandoned its previous color and attained a bluish state once more, it is "vinīlaka. That very same [corpse], having further decomposed and begun to ooze pus from here and there, is [called "vipubbaka"].
*Vipubbakaṃ*: [The bloated]. *Vicchinnakaṃ*: That which has been placed on battlefields and the like with the body cut through the middle by a weapon, resulting in a disfigured severed form.
*Vikkhāyitakaṃ*: A body associated with places where it has been eaten in various ways by dogs, jackals, and so forth.
[A body] associated with limbs and members that have been torn apart piece by piece by dogs, jackals, and the like, dragged away, and scattered here and there.

A body that has been cut up with a knife and scattered here and there, with its limbs and members separated from one another, is called "cut and scattered" (*hatavikkhittaka*). A body from which blood is trickling is called "bloody" (*lohitaka*).
A body completely covered with maggots is called "maggoty" (*puḷuvaka*). Or [it refers to] a whole skeleton, or even a single bone.
"Bone" means a skeleton. "Recollection" (*anussati*) is the act of remembering again and again without interruption.

"Recollection of the Buddha's qualities" (*buddhānussati*) is the recollection of the Buddha’s virtues. This same method applies to the others as well. In this context, the qualities such as being an *arahant* are called the "qualities of the Buddha.

The qualities such as being well-expounded are called the "qualities of the Dhamma. The qualities such as being well-practiced are called the "qualities of the Saṅgha. [The qualities] of one's own virtue, such as its being unbroken...

"Virtue" (*guṇa*) refers to the virtue of moral discipline (*sīlaguṇa*). The virtue of one's own generosity, characterized by the absence of the stain of stinginess and so forth, is called the "virtue of relinquishment" (*cāgaguṇa*).
The virtues of one's own faith and so forth, which are capable of carrying oneself to the state of a deva, a Sakka, or a Brahmā, are called the "virtues of a deity" (*devatāguṇa*).

[These may be developed] either by way of fulfilling duties, by way of undertaking the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*), by way of meditative attainments (*jhānasamāpatti*), or by way of insight (*vipassanā*).

The subsiding of sensual lust and other defilements that have been suppressed for a long time within one’s own continuum, as well as the Nibbāna attained by oneself, is called "subsiding" (*upasama*).
The dissolution of one’s own continuum of aggregates (*khandha-santāna*) comprised within a single existence is called "death" (*maraṇa*).
This body, which is a collection consisting of various parts such as hair and the physical frame, is called "body" (*kāya*). [The defilements] occurring without interruption within oneself...
In-and-out breathing is called *ānāpāna*. It is called *mettā* because it sprinkles and moistens.

The meaning is that, taking something as its object, it brings about well-being and happiness for that [object] and holds it together without letting it fall apart. Alternatively, it is *mettā* because it belongs to a friend (*mittassa*) or exists among friends (*mitteṣu*).
In terms of its essential nature, however, it is simply non-hatred (*adosa*) manifested through the promotion of welfare toward other beings. Toward other beings...

Equanimity (*upekkhā*) is so called because it looks upon beings from the perspective of their arising through the reinforcement of their own kamma, having abandoned the threefold activity consisting of bestowing benefit, conferring pleasure, and removing harm.
It is precisely that state of neutrality (*tatramajjhattatā*) occurring in such a manner.

It is called "immeasurable" (*appamaññā*) because it extends toward immeasurable beings; for these should not be practiced toward only this many beings, nor should one think, "It is not toward others."
Thus, it is said that these [meditations] have a delimitation of their respective objects.
Even so, a beginner, having first attained mastery and distinction in the development of his own mind toward a single individual, should subsequently expand it to two, three, and so forth;

and the breaking down of boundaries (*sīmasambheda*) should be performed just like the limited pervasion (*odhisopharaṇa*), the unlimited pervasion (*anodhisopharaṇa*), and the pervasion of the directions (*disāpharaṇa*).

As for the method of loving-kindness (mettā) described in the Vibhaṅga as "dwelling having pervaded one direction with a mind imbued with loving-kindness," and in the Paṭisambhidāmagga as "may all beings be free from enmity," and so forth—
that should be understood as being taught with reference to those who have attained mastery over the jhāna of loving-kindness.
These, moreover, are specifically the direct antidotes to the defilements belonging to the side of hatred.
"Beings" (*bhonto*) refers to those who possess that [state]; because they constantly exist with a heart full of sublime love, they are called "Brahmās.
Their "abiding" (*vihāro*) is thus "the divine abode" (*brahmavihāro*). Alternatively, it is the "divine abode" because it is the abiding of the supreme ones, or the abiding that itself is supreme.
"Food" (*āhāra*) refers to the fourfold ingested food consisting of what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted. "Perception of repulsiveness" (*paṭikūlasaññā*) [is practiced] on account of food.
The perception of abandoning attachment to that [body] occurs by way of reflecting on the inherent repulsiveness of painful phenomena that must be experienced,
by way of reflecting on the receptacle and its contents, and by way of reflecting on the ripened and unripened fruits and their outflows.
"Analysis of the four elements" refers to the specific characteristics of the four great elements— earth and so forth— contained within the body.

It is the contemplation by way of delimiting each [element] individually day by day. For it is called "the definition of the four elements" (*catudhātuvavatthāna*) because by means of it the four elements are defined, determined, and observed.

Because of the statement, "The perception of foulness (*asubhasaññā*) should be developed for the abandoning of lust," it is said that the ten kinds of foulness are suitable for one whose temperament is characterized by lust.
In this context, "one who acts with lust" is one whose temperament is dominated by lust (*rāgacarita*).

For although such a person may occasionally act out of hatred or delusion, or even occasionally through any one of the qualities beginning with faith, it is lust that is predominant in them. Therefore, because of that predominant lust, they are designated as "one of lustful temperament.
This same method applies to the others as well. As it is said: "Loving-kindness should be developed for the abandoning of ill-will."

The four immeasurables (appamaññā) are mentioned because the three divine abodes beginning with loving-kindness (mettā) are stated to be the escape from ill-will, cruelty, and discontent respectively, and because the color-kasinas (vaṇṇakasiṇa), when perfectly purified, lack the basis for aversion (dosa).

It is said, "for one of an aversive temperament" (dosacarita); however, this classification of temperament applies only to a beginner. Furthermore, equanimity (upekkhā) is not possible for a beginner.

It will be said that [the fourth jhāna] has equanimity as its fifth factor. Therefore, it should be understood that for one for whom the first three [immeasurables] are suitable, the equanimity that follows them is also called "suitable"; thus, it is stated that there are "four immeasurables.
Otherwise, since it is said, "This equanimity, which is the liberation of mind, is the escape from lust," equanimity would not be [suitable] for one of a lustful temperament.
"It may be said": the statement "the four kasiṇas beginning with blue" is made with reference to those pleasing forms such as blue;

however, those same [forms], when unpleasing, are suitable only for one of lustful temperament (*rāgacarita*). Because of the statement, "Mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasati*) should be developed for the cutting off of applied thought (*vitakka*)," it is said that [this] is for one of a thinking temperament (*vitakkacarita*). But as for one of deluded temperament (*mohacarita*), by nature...

He becomes full of negligence and his mind is distracted. Since the breath (ānāpāna), as it proceeds continuously, acts as if it were generating mindfulness for him, it may be said that this is suitable for one of deluded temperament (mohacarita).
However, in the *Vibhāvani*:
The reason given—that it is the antidote to delusion by way of being an object of the intellect (*buddhi*)—does not appear to be appropriate.
For if that were the case, it would have to be discussed together with the practice of the intellect (*buddhicarita*).

Granted, the qualities of the Buddha and so forth are exclusively objects of the intellect; however, because they specifically nourish faith (*saddhā*), it is called "recollection of the Buddha" (*buddhānussati*).
"Of one whose temperament is faith": death and so forth are, in the ultimate sense, more subtle and are objects only for those of vast intelligence;
thus it is said, "death... [and so on]... of one whose temperament is wisdom. As for "of one whose temperament is the Buddha":
all the remaining ones as well—namely, the tenfold meditation subjects consisting of the four primary *kasiṇas*, the two *kasiṇas* of light and space, and the four formless attainments (*āruppa*).
"In those too" means among those ten remaining meditation subjects. A broad one, the size of a threshing floor and so forth, is suitable for one of deluded temperament (*mohacarita*).
For in a cramped space, the mind falls into even greater confusion. A small one, the size of a span or four finger-breadths, is suitable only for one of discursive temperament (*vitakkacarita*).
For a large one is a condition for the running of discursive thoughts. And therein:
Regarding the phrase "only for one of discursive-thought temperament" (*vitakkacaritasseva*), here the word *eva* (only) is appropriate in connection with the word *khuddaka* (small).
For one of discursive-thought temperament, only what is small is suitable; not what is extensive. All of this is stated by way of direct opposition and also by way of extreme suitability.
Furthermore, there is no such thing as a wholesome development that does not suppress lust and the other [defilements], nor one that does not assist faith and the other [wholesome qualities].
This is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*. "In all cases" means in all forty meditation subjects (*kammaṭṭhāna*).

Preparatory development (*parikamma-bhāvanā*) is indeed found [in all], because not a single meditation subject can be accomplished without preparatory development. In ten meditation subjects, only access development (*upacāra-bhāvanā*) is accomplished;

there is no absorption (*appanā*). If one asks why, it is because of the [meditation subjects on] the Buddha, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, virtue (*sīla*), generosity (*cāga*), deities (*devatā*), and tranquility (*upasama*).
Regarding this, it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "Because of the profundity of the qualities, and because of being intent upon recollecting the various kinds of qualities.

Herein, by the phrase "because of the profundity," it is meant that since each individual quality-word is profound, the concentration (samādhi) having that as its object is unable to reach absorption (appanā) and remain steady there, like a hare in the great ocean.
This shows that because one is intent on recollecting their manifold qualities, one cannot even maintain one’s own mind with the thought,
“I shall reach absorption by remaining fixed upon just this many quality-terms,” since those qualities are by nature inexhaustible.

As for the remaining foundations of mindfulness, first, death— because it is a phenomenon according to its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva-dhamma*) and because it is a phenomenon that inspires urgency (*saṃvejanīya-dhamma*)— is [to be developed].
The other two [formless attainments] do not reach absorption because their intrinsic nature (*sabhāvadhamma*) is profound.

If this is so, why do supramundane jhānas reach absorption in the extremely profound intrinsic nature known as Nibbāna, and why do the second and fourth formless jhānas reach absorption in the intrinsic natures known as the first and third formless states? It is said in reply:
First, as for the supramundane jhānas, starting from the knowledge of comprehension (sammasana-ñāṇa) and proceeding through purification,
they are able— by the power of the successively higher stages of purified development— to become established in absorption (appanā) even upon the extremely profound phenomenon known as Nibbāna.
The formless (āruppa) jhānas, moreover, are merely the arising of the fifth jhāna concentration once it has reached absorption.

"They exist" means that by merely transcending the object, they are able to become established in the state of absorption (appanā) even with respect to an object that is a dhamma possessing intrinsic nature (sabhāva).
"Among those" refers to among those thirty types of meditation subjects for absorption.
"Associated with the fivefold jhāna" means belonging to the fivefold jhāna; it is said that they are suitable to serve as the objects of the fivefold jhāna.
Objects that are repulsive are exceedingly undesirable, coarse, and very weak in producing mental delight;
therefore, they cannot cause the mind to take pleasure in them and remain fixed there. Consequently, without the power of applied thought (*vitakka*), the mind does not abide one-pointedly upon them.
It is for this reason that it is said: "The ten foulness meditations (*asubha*), etc., belong to the first jhāna."
If this is so, how can there be a jhāna of mental joy (*somanassajjhāna*) in those [meditative states]?
It occurs through the power of abandoning the torment of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) and through the power of the knowledge that perceives their respective benefits (*ānisaṃsa*).

This is like the case of a sick person afflicted by the pain of disease who, during the process of emesis and purgation, perceives the benefit, thinking, "Now I shall receive a large fee," just as a flower-gatherer perceiving the benefit sees a heap of dung.

And it should be understood as "just like. Since the three sublime abidings beginning with loving-kindness (mettā) serve as the escape from ill-will, cruelty, and aversion—which arise from mental distress—they never reach absorption (appanā) without joy;
thus it is said that the three beginning with loving-kindness possess four jhānas. Equanimity (upekkhā), however, is entirely on the side of indifference toward sentient beings...
Because it must be developed while standing [on that basis], it never reaches absorption (appanā) without the feeling of equanimity; thus it is said to be "the fifth jhāna with equanimity.
Regarding "the four immaterial states" (āruppa): these are the four objects of the immaterial states, beginning with the space derived from the removal of the kasiṇa.
"In all cases" means in all forty meditation subjects (kammaṭṭhāna). "As appropriate" means in accordance with each respective object. By means of the object...

Without preliminary work (*parikamma*), nothing is accomplished. Without the "learning sign" (*uggaha*), which is defined as the firm and clear apprehension of the object, there is no attainment of the object.
And if there is no attainment of the object, even access concentration (*upacāra-jhāna*) is not achieved;
how much less absorption concentration (*appanā-jhāna*)? Thus it is said regarding the preliminary sign (*parikamma-nimitta*). ... "It is indeed obtained."
In this context, "in all cases" means in all forty meditation subjects (*kammaṭṭhāna*). "As appropriate" means according to the suitability of each respective meditation subject.
"By way of method," however, is said because for some objects, even while one is looking at them with the eye, they are not fully manifest.

But in those cases where, having first apprehended the phenomenon as a specific individual essence (*sabhāvadhamma*), one subsequently [apprehends] its corresponding aspect (*tadākāra*) or its configuration (*tasaṇṭhāna*)...
Access concentration or absorption occurs with a concept as its object.

It is said that it is precisely there that what is called the "counterpart sign" (paṭibhāga-nimitta) is obtained; thus he says, "And the counterpart sign," and so forth. To strengthen this very point, he says, "For there," and so on.
Having thus shown the skill in learning for the work of serenity, he now [explains] the method of development starting from the beginning.

"He shows how," and so forth, he said. "Of one who grasps the sign" means of one who grasps and contemplates the mode of appearance of the object as it exists, making it increasingly clear in the mind.
"And that cultivation" refers to that mental cultivation consisting of a succession of impulsion-moments (*javana-vīthi*) proceeding by way of the mode of grasping;
this is called preliminary cultivation (*parikamma-bhāvanā*). Again and again...

Because it is established in the mode of increasing by way of its instrument. Having stated "it is well-apprehended" (*samuggahitaṃ*), in order to show how it is called "well-apprehended" (*samuggahitaṃ*) when it is thoroughly apprehended, it is said:
"it has come into the range of the mind-door for one who is seeing with the eye.
In that context, "it has come into the range of the mind-door" means whether one has closed one's eyes or is standing in another place.
As he adverts [to it], it appears at the mind-door as if seen with the eye.
This is called the "learning sign" (*uggahanimitta*), because it was grasped having been made very firm and imperishable. And that meditation becomes concentrated.

The intention is that it has not yet reached the state of "access" (*anantarabhāva*). "Of one thus concentrated" means by means of that preliminary concentration (*parikammasamādhi*) which has reached its culmination.
"For this meditator who is concentrated. "Beyond that" means after the arising of the learning sign (*uggahanimitta*).
The connection is: "settled in the mind of one who is devoted to cultivation. In that context, "of one who is devoted" means of one who exerts effort continuously.
"Resembling that" means similar to that learning sign which has become a phenomenon of intrinsic nature (*sabhāvadhamma*). "Released from the objective phenomenon" means...
Like the lunar disk emerging from behind a cloud or from the mouth of Rāhu, it stands distinct, having been released from the learning sign which was its natural state.
For that very reason, it is called the "sign of description" (*nimitta-paññatti*), being reckoned as a conceptual construct.
"Produced by meditation" means established solely through the power of the meditative mind. "Object" (*ālambana*) refers to that very same thing.

"Grasped, having the sign as its object, settled in the mind, and well-fixed" means that it has become well-established in the mental continuum of the mind-door, remaining motionless and being thoroughly fixed or introduced. "That is called the sign as the object"—this is the grammatical connection.
Because of the state of being perfectly pure and radiant of that sign as the object, like [the reflection of] the lunar disc and so forth...
What is called "establishment" occurs solely by virtue of the mind having become radiant and purified through the suppression of the stains of the defilements;
it does not occur by virtue of that object. For such a quality is not found within the conceptually designated phenomena themselves.
Therefore, when the counterpart sign has arisen, [there is the overcoming] of those obstructing states known as the hindrances.

"It is established as being suppressed" refers to the passage beginning with "from that time onwards," and so forth. They are called *paṭibandhā* because they obstruct, hinder, and cause the mind—which tends toward the side of escape—to fall back;
thus, they are the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa-dhammā*). That by which the obstructions are specifically abandoned is "that by which the obstructions are thoroughly relinquished" (*paṭibandhavippahīnā*).
"For one who is practicing well" (*samāsevantassa*) means for one who is cultivating it thoroughly. This is the sevenfold method for guarding the sign (*nimitta*).
The meaning is: having accomplished [the practice] and protected it well—like the embryo of a wheel-turning monarch—one should cultivate it repeatedly by way of meditation.
One should avoid these seven things that are unsuitable: dwelling, resort, speech, person, food, climate, and posture.
"One should cultivate the seven things that are conducive;
for one who practices in this way, absorption (appanā) will indeed arise before long. Thus it is said.
"It enters the first jhāna of the fine-material sphere" means that, having transcended the state of being an object for sensual craving, it has attained an exceedingly subtle and refined condition.

The meaning is that the first jhāna of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara), which is endowed with jhāna factors more stable by a hundredfold or a thousandfold than access concentration (upacāra-jjhāna), proceeds as if it has entered into that sign.
The connection is: "having made that very first jhāna masterful. Regarding the five kinds of mastery, however, from the first jhāna...
Having emerged [from the attainment], he first adverts to the initial application (vitakka); then to sustained application (vicāra); then to rapture (pīti); then to pleasure (sukha);

then to concentration (samādhi); then again to initial application; then to sustained application—and thus, as he adverts repeatedly to the factors of jhāna, when the series of consciousnesses having those respective jhāna-factors as their object becomes interspersed from time to time by several moments of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), [the attainment is considered lost].
They proceed as if they were continuous. At that time, adverting, reviewing, and mastery become fully mastered.

These, however, reach their pinnacle in the case of the Omniscient Buddhas. For when they desire a rapid occurrence during such occasions as the Twin Miracle, even a series of consciousnesses consisting of the factors of those respective jhānas and the object lasts for only four or five impulsion-moments (*javana*).

The life-continuum (bhavaṅga) and the two types of transition-moments (antarābhavaṅga), which serve as the preliminary to the final stage and are termed "vibrations of the life-continuum," also proceed.
This occurs where another jhāna-factor enters the field of perception;
for the life-continuum does not vibrate until the object has entered its range, nor is there such a thing as the arising of adverting (āvajjana) without the vibration of the life-continuum.

It is stated in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga-aṭṭhakathā* that, with the exception of the Omniscient Buddhas, there is no counting even for those who have attained mastery (*vasibhāva*) when they occasionally lapse into the flow of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*). However, in the *Visuddhimagga*, it is said:
"This mastery, having reached its pinnacle, is found in the Blessed One at the time of the Twin Miracle (*yamakapāṭihāriya*); or, for others, at such a time. Regarding jhāna:
The capacity to enter [jhāna] even more swiftly is called mastery in entering (samāpajjana-vasī). For it is for this very reason that it is stated in the Pāḷi:

"There is no delay in entering. This same method applies to the remaining types of mastery as well. Likewise, the capacity to maintain the jhāna already entered for an extremely brief duration, such as the time of a finger-snap, is called mastery in resolving (adhiṭṭhāna-vasī). From the jhāna thus entered...

The capacity to emerge [from concentration] very quickly is called mastery of emergence (*vuṭṭhāna-vasī*). As for mastery of review (*paccavekkhaṇa-vasī*), it is established as soon as mastery of adverting (*āvajjana-vasī*) is established.
However, in the *Vibhāvanī*, it is said:
The ability to maintain a jhāna for as long as one desires—that is, for a longer duration—is called "mastery over resolution" (adhiṭṭhāna-vasitā).

Likewise, the ability to emerge from that jhāna at the very end of the predetermined time without emerging earlier than the limit set is called "mastery over emergence" (vuṭṭhāna-vasitā). This too is indeed logical.
For in the Pāḷi it is said: "One resolves upon the first jhāna wherever one wishes, whenever one wishes, and for as long as one wishes.

There is no sluggishness in resolving. Thus, whether it be more quickly or more slowly, for whatever length of time one wishes to maintain the jhāna, or for whatever length of time one wishes to emerge from it—for that much time, neither less nor more.
The capacity to resolve (*adhiṭṭhātuṃ*) or to emerge (*vuṭṭhātuṃ*) is likewise shown to be [inherent].

This being so, since the mastery of emergence (*vuṭṭhānavasitā*) is established once the mastery of resolution (*adhiṭṭhānavasitā*) is established, it should be understood that even the attempt to establish a distinction between these two is purposeless.
Mastery (*vasī*) means dwelling (*vasana*). The meaning is "capacity" (*samatthatā*); what is meant is "the state of lordship" (*issarabhāva*). It is simply mastery (*vasī*).
Mastery. Just as "the deity is indeed a god. The connection is with the words "having made" and "having struck the path.

Regarding the phrase "for the abandoning of the gross factor such as applied thought (vitakka)," etc.: first, for one who remains having attained mastery over the first jhāna, applied thought appears as gross.
At that time, his aspiration becomes fixed thus: "Oh, may there be this jhāna without applied thought! At that time...

For one who again performs the preliminary work on that counterpart sign with the thought, "I shall attain the meditative absorption (jhāna) without applied thought," that cultivation is called the cultivation of the fading away of applied thought (*vitakkavirāga-bhāvanā*).
As long as the attachment to applied thought has not been fully exhausted, it is still called preliminary cultivation (*parikamma-bhāvanā*);
however, once the attachment to applied thought is exhausted, it is called access cultivation (*upacāra-bhāvanā*).
This is the method for the remaining jhānas and access concentrations as well.

Thus, by the power of the development of dispassion toward each respective jhāna-factor, for the purpose of abandoning each coarse factor such as applied thought (*vitakka*), there arises the subtle factor such as sustained thought (*vicāra*).
That is to say, there arises one of the four, three, two, or again two subtle jhāna-factors—sustained thought and so forth—in place of each respective applied thought and the rest.
"Without a gross factor" means without the further arising [of that factor]. "Pāhato" means for one who exerts;
the meaning is: for one performing the ardor and energy known as *padhāna*. "The second jhāna and so forth" refers to the second jhāna and the remaining fine-material-sphere jhānas.
"As appropriate" is said with reference to the kasiṇas and breath-meditation (*ānāpāna*) which are suitable for the second jhāna and so forth among the twenty-two meditation subjects (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
Regarding the remaining eighteen meditation subjects, since the immaterial jhānas proceed only by way of transcending their objects,
and because the "removal of the kasiṇa" exists for the purpose of that transcendence,
it is said "among the kasiṇas excluding space" in order to show only those kasiṇas in which such removal is possible. For as for the space kasiṇa...
Even when it is opened up, it is simply space; thus, there is no possibility of transcending that [space].

"Having opened up" means that when one does not attend to the perception of the *kasiṇa*-sign in the *kasiṇa*-sign as it was previously seen, but instead causes the perception of space—thinking "space, infinite space"—to proceed toward it, that *kasiṇa*-sign disappears from the mind. It diminishes accordingly.
Only space appears. Thus, by the dispersal of the perception of the kasiṇa and the occurrence of the perception of space, the meaning is:
having removed and separated whatever kasiṇa there was. The connection is made by supplying the words "having taken as an object the space thus obtained.
This same method applies to the phrases "the first consciousness of form," and so forth. "By way of its infinity" means by way of the attention occurring thus: "space is infinite."
"Performing the preliminary work [with the thought] 'This is peaceful, this is sublime'":

here, even for one performing the preliminary work after having thus reflected, the higher jhāna certainly arises because the object has been transcended; therefore it is said, "he enters the fourth immaterial attainment.
"Having performed the preliminary work": that Blessed One, having performed the preliminary work of recollecting [him] with such phrases as "He is indeed an Arahant," etc. In him...
"In that object" (*tasmiṃ ālambane*) refers to the object consisting of the qualities of the Buddha and so forth; this locative case (*bhummavacana*) is used in the sense of location (*bhūmatthe*).
"In the sign" (*nimitteti*) means in the sign which is reckoned as the mode (*ākāra*) of that object; this locative case is used in the sense of a characteristic of a state (*bhāvalakkhaṇe*).

"Well apprehended" (*sādhukaṃ uggahite*) means well grasped either by way of the extreme clarity of the object or by way of the mind’s inclination, leaning, and tendency toward it. And "access" (*upacāro*)...
The intention is that this succeeds for noble disciples who have seen the Truths. Or, it may be for others as well, in the establishing of the perception of death.
And here, the accomplishment of the access [attainment] should be understood through the suppression of the hindrances and the manifestation of the jhāna factors.
Having thus shown the occurrence of serenity-jhānas as appropriate among the forty meditation subjects, [the author now discusses] the kasiṇa-jhānas within those serenity-jhānas.
In order to show the occurrence [of supernormal powers] as the result (*nisanda*) [of meditation], it was said:

"occurring by way of supernormal power," and so forth. In that regard, there is one who has performed the preliminary work; or one who has applied himself to the *samatha*-meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) in a previous existence;
or a Great Being who has fulfilled the requisites for enlightenment (*bodhisambhāra*). When the eightfold or ninefold *samatha*-absorptions are being mastered by such a person:

The direct knowledges (*abhiññā*) are indeed accomplished. Some say that they are accomplished even when only the fine-material jhānas (*rūpajjhāna*) are accomplished. For this very reason, in the *Aṭṭhasālinī* and the *Visuddhimagga*, it is stated that the possibility of the space-kasiṇa jhāna serving as a basis for the direct knowledges exists even for one who has not attained the immaterial jhānas (*ārūppajjhāna*). However, in the *Dīghanikāya-aṭṭhakathā*, regarding the eight attainments (*samāpatti*), it is said: [omitted]... "Indeed, among the eight attainments... [omitted]... "In the case of the first jhāna, the five direct knowledges are accomplished. [omitted]... "In the case of the second jhāna, four direct knowledges are accomplished, excluding the supernormal power of transformation (*iddhividha-ādesanā-pāṭihāriya*). [omitted]... "In the case of the third jhāna, three direct knowledges are accomplished, excluding the supernormal power of transformation and the supernormal power of the divine ear (*dibbasota*). [omitted]... It is stated that the attainment of higher direct knowledge occurs without having mastered these fourteen modes.
However, it is appropriate to say that this was stated as a general rule for the many beginner noble sons, setting aside exceptional individuals.
For it is said in the *Visuddhimagga*: "But without having fully tamed the mind by means of these fourteen modes..."
It has been said that it is impossible for a beginner practitioner who has not previously developed meditation to achieve the transformation of psychic power (*iddhi-vikubbana*).
Therefore, for those noble sons who have mastered the eight attainments (*samāpatti*) and are beginners in the work of direct knowledge (*abhiññā*),
[the method] is stated by way of fourteen modes, such as "from the kasiṇa in forward order" and "from the kasiṇa in reverse order."

The construction is as follows: having disciplined one’s own mind through the fivefold jhāna of form by means of its modes (ākāra), making it sharp, keen, and capable of directed application (abhinīhāra), those who begin with the thought, "Now I shall perform a supernormal transformation," [experience] the five fine-material-sphere jhānas occurring by way of direct knowledge (abhiññā);
these jhānas then become absorbed (appeti) respectively upon the six objects, beginning with visible forms.

It should be understood thus: "Having emerged from the fifth jhāna that serves as the basis for direct knowledge" means that one first enters whichever type of fine-material-sphere fifth jhāna is appropriate as the foundation for direct knowledge.
Then, having emerged by way of the occurrence of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), one should resolve:
"Let there be a thousand forms with their respective bases," such as a hundred forms and so forth.

"Created form" (*nimmitarūpa*): that which has "resolution" (*adhiṭṭheyya*) and so forth as its basis, such as the acts of appearing and disappearing, is called "resolution and so forth" (*adhiṭṭheyyādika*).
Regarding the phrase "for one performing the preliminary work after having adverted":

here, in the case of the supernormal powers (*iddhividha*), whatever created form—such as a head and so forth—or whatever created act—such as appearing and so forth—one desires to accomplish, one adverts to each of those.

For one performing the preliminary exercise by observing, "May I be a hundred," or "May I be a thousand," or "May there be a hundred," or "May there be a thousand," or "May this and that come to be," or "May it be thus and so"—
and likewise, regarding the divine ear and so forth, whatever object one desires to hear, see, know, or recollect, having observed that very thing, [one directs it] toward such-and-such a person...
For one performing the preliminary work (*parikamma*) by thinking, "I hear the sound of such-and-such people," and so forth;
however, in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated that after performing the preliminary work, one must again attain the foundational absorption (*pādakajjhāna*). As it is said:

"Having attained the absorption that is the basis for direct knowledge (*abhiññāpādakajjhāna*) and emerged from it, if one wishes to become a hundred, one performs the preliminary work by thinking, 'May I be a hundred,' and then [attains] the absorption that is the basis for direct knowledge once more."
Having entered [the attainment] and emerged, one resolves. Together with the mind of resolution, there is mindfulness.
In this context, first of all, the entry into the foundational jhāna is for the purpose of securing the preliminary-work consciousness (*parikamma-citta*).
The latter, however, is for the purpose of providing strength to the direct knowledge (*abhiññā*). For it is by the power of the foundational jhāna that [the mind] is well-concentrated.
The preliminary consciousness (parikamma-citta) is of the same nature as the direct-knowledge consciousness (abhiññā-citta) regarding its own object.
At the time of recollecting past lives, by means of that very consciousness, one knows the categories of phenomena belonging to that past existence back to the moment of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi).

For this reason, it is stated in the Commentary that the knowledge associated with it is "preliminary concentration-knowledge" (parikamma-samādhi-ñāṇa); it is also called "knowledge of the past" (atītaṃsa-ñāṇa).
"It is so called. Regarding the remaining direct knowledges (*abhiññā*), the specific range of that knowledge should be stated accordingly for each.
However, it should be understood that the Elder did not include the final entry into the foundational jhāna (*pādakajjhāna*) because it does not apply to everyone;

for those who have attained mastery over the direct knowledges, there is no further need for the foundational jhāna. It "enters" into objects such as visible forms (*rūpa*) and so forth, as appropriate.
Herein, first of all, the knowledge of the various supernormal powers (*iddhividhañāṇa*) operates upon the six objects belonging to the three periods of time.
For that [knowledge] proceeds by taking as its object whichever among the six objective phenomena—visible forms and so forth—it brings about.

However, when one travels through the air with a visible body by resolving upon the mind of the foundational jhāna (*pādakajjhānacitta*) as being of the nature of the body, the past foundational jhāna-mind [is the basis].
It proceeds by taking something as its object. When one resolves that the body shall follow the mind and travels with an invisible body, it proceeds by taking the present material body as its object.
However, for that knowledge proceeding in such a manner, some material form is merely an object, some is an object-prenascence condition, and some is both a basis and an object-prenascence condition.

It should be understood that [the mind] occurs [thus]. At the time of resolving, "In the future, let this be such-and-such," it proceeds by taking as its object that respective material phenomenon (rūpadhamma) in the future.
A present sound becomes the object of the divine ear (dibbasota).
Within the interval of seven days in the past and seven days in the future, the mind of another (parassacitta), which exists as past, future, or present, [is apprehended].

Or, there are four aggregates for the knowledge of penetration of minds (*cetopariya-ñāṇa*). For one who knows the mind, if he so desires, he will certainly know the mental states associated with it as well.

And having established this, in the *Paṭṭhāna* it is stated—combining the two types of knowledge together—that "wholesome aggregates are a condition by way of object-condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*) for the knowledge of penetration of minds and for the knowledge of destiny according to deeds (*yathākammūpaga-ñāṇa*). And here, in the Commentary...
Thus far, the fact that the consciousness of another has a present object has been explained either by way of continuity (*santati*) or by way of duration (*addhā*).
For if one were to explain it by way of the moment (*khaṇa*), then after having adverted to any single present mind, once that [advertence] has ceased,
the impulsion moments (*javana*) would also take as their object that very same [mind] which has ceased together with the adverting— thus they would be past in terms of time.
Together with the adverting consciousness (āvajjana), they are said to have different objects.

However, the commentators (Aṭṭhakathācariyas) do not approve of their having different objects even for a mere moment at any place other than the path and fruit moments within the cognitive process (vīthi) when directed toward the unwholesome.
Therefore, in such instances, it is appropriate to understand "the present" by way of continuity (santati) and by way of duration (addhā).

In the *Mūlaṭīkā*, however, it is applied solely by way of the momentary present (*khaṇika-paccuppanna*). For it cannot be said that in the Abhidhamma, the "Triplet of Past Objects" (*atītārammaṇattika*) is stated only by way of continuity (*santati*) and duration (*addhāna*);

otherwise, one would have to say that a present state (*dhamma*) is a condition for a present state by way of the proximity-condition (*anantara-paccaya*) and the repetition-condition (*āsevana-paccaya*). But this is not [the case].
However, it is stated that a past state (dhamma) is a condition for a present state by way of proximity-condition (anantara-paccaya) and repetition-condition (āsevana-paccaya).

Therefore, it is logical that all consciousnesses, beginning with adverting (āvajjana), each grasp subsequent states of consciousness as they arise simultaneously according to their own momentary nature;
yet, these are not distinct entities apart from the phenomena themselves, nor do they have separate objects.
They are [cognitions]. Because there is no difference between the act of grasping and the agent, for even the adverting (āvajjana) adverts as a cognition itself;
and the impulsive moments (javana) impel as a cognition itself. And all these are indeed cognitions.

However, starting from the death-consciousness (cuti-citta) that has just passed away, the past aggregates (khandhas) are called "aggregates following upon aggregates," as well as designations (paññatti) such as the lineage, the kasiṇa, the sign, and so forth.
Nibbāna is the object of the knowledge of past lives, and present visible form is the object of the divine eye;

thus, it applies appropriately to each of the six objects beginning with visible form. Now, in order to show the classification of that fifth jhāna—which will be explained by way of the direct knowledges (*abhiññā*)—according to its different functions, he spoke the verse beginning with "the modes of psychic power" (*iddhividha*).

In this context, *iddhividha* means that which has as its variety (*vidha*), portion (*koṭṭhāsa*), or mode (*pakāra*) the success (*ijjhana*) of whatever one resolves upon, and in whatever manner one resolves it. That, moreover, is threefold by way of:

resolve-mastery (*adhiṭṭhāna-iddhi*), transformation-mastery (*vikubbanā-iddhi*), and mind-made-mastery (*manomaya-iddhi*). Among these, [the first] is that which does not abandon one's own natural form...
The supernormal power that proceeds by way of making many from one— such as hundreds of thousands— or by way of traveling through the air,
or by way of displaying various external miracles, is called "supernormal power of resolve" (*adhiṭṭhāna-iddhi*). However,
the supernormal power that proceeds by abandoning one's natural appearance and manifesting oneself in the form of a youth, an elephant, or the like, is [called "supernormal power of transformation"].

The supernormal power (iddhi) known as transformation (vikubbanā). Having fashioned another body within one’s own body that is in every respect identical to oneself, and having brought it forth, the supernormal power that functions by way of displaying it is called mind-made supernormal power (manomaya-iddhi). That which exists in the heavens is "divine" (dibba);

the meaning is that it is born in the world of the gods (devaloka). It is divine and it is hearing, thus it is the divine ear (dibbasota). [It is] produced by the sublime karma of the gods, even from afar...
Even when it is concealed, it is the translucent ear-faculty capable of receiving objects.
However, because it resembles the divine ear, this knowledge of direct higher power (*abhiññā-ñāṇa*) is also called the "divine ear.

Alternatively, it is the "divine ear" because it is obtained through the "divine abode" (*dibbavihāra*), which is designated as the meditative absorption on the kasiṇas, and because it itself is included within that divine abode; thus, it is both divine and an ear.
"Knowledge of others' minds" (*paracittavijānana*) means that by means of this, one discerns the mind of another.
Because one discerns [the mind] precisely by means of this, it is also called "knowledge of the penetration of minds" (*cetopariyañāṇa*).

"Past abodes" (*pubbenivāsa*) refers to the phenomena that have clearly been known as they entered through the six sense-doors of oneself in past existences. Their "range" (*gocara*) refers to past births.
They "dwelt" by way of dwelling because their own sixfold doors of consciousness dwelt therein.
However, for the Omniscient Buddhas, even phenomena apprehended through the six doors of others constitute a former dwelling; the recollection of that former dwelling is *pubbenivāsānussati*.
Here, however, it is the knowledge associated with that [recollection] which is intended. And the divine [eye], in the manner previously stated...
That which is called "the eye" is the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*). Because it is similar to that, this knowledge of direct higher power (*abhiññāñāṇa*) is also called the "divine eye.
It is the "divine eye" because it is obtained by means of the divine abodes (*dibbavihāra*), and because it itself is supported by the divine abodes.

The two knowledges—the knowledge of the destiny according to deeds (*yathākammupagañāṇa*) and the knowledge of future states (*anāgataṃsañāṇa*)—are known as the "adjunct knowledges" (*paribhaṇḍañāṇa*) of this very [divine eye].
For them, there is no separate preparatory work consisting of the taming of the mind for the sake of attaining it;

rather, when the knowledge of the divine eye is attained, theirs is also attained. In that regard, for one who performs the preparatory work with the thought, "Having seen beings experiencing suffering in the hells or happiness among the devas with the divine eye, I shall know their past karma," [the divine ear-knowledge arises].
The knowledge that goes according to karma (*yathākammūpaga-ñāṇa*) occurs with that kamma as its object.

Then, for one who performs the preliminary work thinking, "Having passed away from there, where will they be? I shall see their future course," the knowledge of the future (*anāgataṃsa-ñāṇa*) occurs with their future aggregates as its object.
And just like the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pubbenivāsānussati-ñāṇa*), all categories of future phenomena are likewise [perceived].
This indeed becomes its object. For it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* that "this is the range of the knowledge of omniscience within its own domain.

However, in the *Vibhāvanī*, it is intended that "from the seventh day into the future, any mental state or mental factor, and from the second day onwards, any object whatsoever, is the domain of this [knowledge]. That too appears to be reasonable.
It cannot be said that because this [knowledge] is unable to know future phenomena even in another existence, it is therefore incapable of knowing future phenomena in this very life.
And just as this is so, the same applies to the knowledge of past lives (*pubbenivāsañāṇa*), which concerns past phenomena belonging to the mental continuum of others in this very life.
However, in the Canon and the Commentaries, these two types of knowledge are described only in relation to phenomena pertaining to other existences.
It has been included. However, it may be appropriate that it was included for the purpose of making its specific power evident by way of its unique temporal factor.
"Difference in objective field" refers to the difference in the occurrence of serenity jhānas within objective fields such as the ten kasiṇas and so forth.
This is the method for the meditation subject of serenity.

171. *Vipassanā* is so called because by means of it one sees specifically, having transcended what is seen by the great masses of worldly people—namely, [the notions of] a person (*puggala*), a being (*satta*), a woman (*itthī*), a man (*purisa*), and so forth, as well as permanence (*nicca*), stability (*dhuvam*), pleasure (*sukha*), a self (*atta*), and signs (*nimitta*).

It is an action (*kiriyā*), a deed (*kamma*), an application of development (*bhāvanā-payoga*). It is the work of insight, thus "insight-work" (*vipassanā-kamma*); or, insight itself is the work, thus "insight" (*vipassanā*).

It is action (*kamma*). Because it is the place, the foundation, and the ground for the action of insight, it is called "the subject of meditation for insight" (*vipassanā-kammaṭṭhāna*). It refers to the collection of phenomena such as the aggregates.

Alternatively, insight itself is the "subject of meditation for insight" because it is the place—the proximate cause—for the successive excellence of development or the successive excellence of benefits.
Regarding that subject of meditation for insight, there is purification in seven ways.
The connection [of the text] is by way of the passage beginning with "Inclusion consists of the three characteristics," and so forth.

"Purification of virtue" (sīlavisuddhi) means that constant virtue itself is purification because it is purified of the stain of immorality, and because it purifies both body and speech from that [stain].

"Purification of mind" (cittavisuddhi) means that the well-developed continuum of consciousness itself is purification because it is purified of the stain of the hindrances (nīvaraṇa), and because it purifies the person possessing it from that [stain].
Purification of mind (*cittavisuddhi*). Here, by the term "mind," concentration (*samādhi*) is intended.

It is called purification of view (*diṭṭhivisuddhi*) because it purifies the person endowed with it from the stain of the view of individuality (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*) by means of the knowledge termed "discernment of phenomena" (*dhammavavatthānañāṇa*).

It is called "crossing over doubt" (*kaṅkhāvitaraṇā*) because by means of it one crosses over—that is, transcends—the sixteen kinds of doubt (or the eight kinds). It is the knowledge of the discernment of conditions (*paccayapariggahañāṇa*).

That very [insight], because it purifies the person possessing it from the two kinds of doubt already mentioned—namely, the view of no-cause and the view of wrong causes—is called "purification by overcoming doubt" (*kaṅkhāvitaraṇavisuddhi*).

"Path and non-path" refers to the path and what is not the path. In this context, either the method of attention (*manasikāra-vidhi*) which serves as the means for attaining purification by knowledge and vision, or the Noble Path itself, is intended.
The "path" (magga) is as follows: attention that is not a means for it, or the bases for overestimation, are called the "non-path.
Knowing and seeing the path as the path and the non-path as the non-path is the "knowledge and vision of the path and non-path" (maggāmagga-ñāṇadassana).

Because it purifies that very person who possesses it from the perception of a path where there is no path, it is called "purification" (visuddhi); thus, it is named "purification by knowledge and vision of the path and non-path. Above—
It is called *paṭipadā* because by means of it they proceed toward distinction (*visesa*). It is the preliminary path, consisting of a succession of insights (*vipassanā*).

"Knowledge and vision as the way" (*paṭipadā-ñāṇadassana*) refers to knowledge that constitutes the way. Because it is purified of the perception of permanence and so forth, it is called "purification";
thus, it is named "purification by knowledge and vision of the way," which is precisely the knowledge and vision known as the noble path (*ariyamagga*).
Because it is purified from the stain of delusion, it is called "purity" (*visuddhi*); its name is "purification by knowledge and vision" (*ñāṇadassanavisuddhi*).

Here, one should understand that the inclusion of the term "vision" (*dassana*) in every instance is intended to exclude inferential knowledge (*anumāṇañāṇa*), which—though established through means such as learning—is merely "knowledge" (*ñāṇa*) alone, and to include only the direct experiential knowledge of the object (*atthapaccakkhañāṇa*). These [phenomena] are characterized and discerned thus: "These are indeed impermanent."

"Characteristic" (*lakkhaṇa*) means that by means of this, phenomena (*dhammā*) are definitively determined. Impermanence itself is the characteristic; thus it is the "characteristic of impermanence" (*anicca-lakkhaṇa*).
In the first word [of the compound], there is an elision of the abstract suffix (*bhāva-paccaya*). For impermanence is one thing, and impermanence-ness (*aniccatā*) is another.

In this regard, just as a person is said to be "gone" due to their connection with the action of going, yet the action of going is not the person, nor is the person the action of going; they are distinct.
For the action is one thing, and the person is another. Likewise, by way of its association with impermanence, every conditioned phenomenon (*saṅkhata-dhamma*) is said to be "impermanent.
However, impermanence is not that phenomenon, nor is that phenomenon impermanence; for impermanence is one thing, and that phenomenon is another.
But what is this impermanence? It is the mode of change (*vipariṇāma-ākāra*); it is the mode of aging and the mode of dissolution—this is what is meant.
Having seen that aspect, knowledge proceeds toward the phenomena possessing that aspect, [realizing]: "This phenomenon is impermanent.
Therefore, it is precisely that impermanence which is also called the "characteristic" (*lakkhaṇa*) here. This same method applies to the other two as well.

In that context, however, the aspect of being repeatedly oppressed is called "suffering-ness" (*dukkhatā*), and the aspect of not being subject to mastery is called "selflessness-ness" (*anattatā*). According to what has been stated...

Furthermore, "contemplation of impermanence" (*aniccānupassanā*) is the continuous contemplation of the state of impermanence together with an impermanent phenomenon, or of impermanence together with an impermanent phenomenon.

This same method applies to the other two [contemplations] as well. As long as the fact that phenomena within the body are endowed with the three characteristics becomes apparent through one's own knowledge, so long is there repeated rubbing [of the mind] by way of clarifying those three characteristics in them.
Pressing (āmasana) is full comprehension (sammasana). Knowledge that occurs in the mode of full comprehension is "knowledge of comprehension" (sammasanañāṇa).
"Arising" (udaya) is said to be the manifestation of ever-new phenomena, corresponding to their respective moments and their respective conditions, as well as their progressive increase.
"Passing away" (vaya) is said to be [the cessation] wherever ever-new phenomena, having obtained conditions, manifest.
And they increase. Therein, the disappearance of old phenomena that have not obtained conditions here and there is [the knowledge of passing away].

However, the knowledge that contemplates either the side of arising or the side of falling away by way of the continuity of the aggregate-series is the knowledge of arising and passing away (*udayabbaya-ñāṇa*).
Of those two sides, the portion of arising becomes increasingly manifest as it proceeds. The portion of falling away...
But it is not manifest. And because that very [moment] is the ultimate limit of impermanence, the knowledge that clearly contemplates that very thing is the knowledge of dissolution (*bhaṅga-ñāṇa*).

When dissolution has been seen, the knowledge that contemplates in various ways the manner in which phenomena—which have the nature of breaking up—are to be feared as being the basis for many thousands of sorrows and sufferings, is called the knowledge of fear (*bhaya-ñāṇa*). However, in the world, there is no object of fear whatsoever...
Even when passing by nearby, people do not fear if there is another refuge; they fear only when there is none.
Thus, the knowledge that discerns the total absence of any other refuge for those things that ought to be feared is called "knowledge of danger" (*ādīnavañāṇa*).
