The insight-knowledge (*vipassanāñāṇa*) accompanied by a sense of weariness arising from the absence of any refuge whatsoever is called "knowledge of disenchantment" (*nibbidāñāṇa*). By those who are becoming disenchanted...

The insight-knowledge accompanied by the aspiration to liberate oneself from those [defilements] is called the knowledge of the desire for deliverance (*muñcitukamyatā-ñāṇa*). For one who intensely desires to be liberated,

the insight that proceeds with even greater expansion through the contemplation of the mass of manifold disadvantages in those phenomena by way of forty aspects, for the sake of swift liberation— this is [the knowledge of the desire for deliverance].

Knowledge is called "knowledge of reflective contemplation" (*paṭisaṅkhā-ñāṇa*). When, however, the multitude of their many dangers has been clearly seen and attachment to formations has been exhausted, one thinks:

"Now the means of liberation has been found. Without exerting excessive effort, but grasping formations with balanced energy, for one who thus comprehends formations, there arises—either toward the formations themselves or in the act of comprehending them—a state accompanied by equanimity.
Having abandoned both fear and delight, the knowledge of insight accompanied by a state of equanimity is called the knowledge of equanimity towards formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā-ñāṇa*).

The knowledge of insight that is endowed with the strength and power of the conformities (*anuloma*) for the arising of the path—being capable of carrying the progression of the path further upward—is called the knowledge of conformity (*anuloma-ñāṇa*). Or rather, it is the conformity to the preceding knowledges.

It is called "adaptation knowledge" (*anuloma-ñāṇa*) because it more thoroughly clarifies the three characteristics, or because it is the preliminary stage (*parikamma*) for the subsequent path, and also because it serves as its proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*).

The path that is being liberated from the fetters of the defilements within the aggregates by the power of seeing the emptiness of self and soul is called the "emptiness liberation" (*suññatā-vimokkha*). As for the signs (*nimitta*) of conditioned phenomena...

It becomes a refuge for the defilements. Having dispelled those [defilements], the path that is liberated by the power of seeing the state of all phenomena as being entirely without a protector is called the signless liberation (*animitta-vimokkha*).
The path that is liberated by the power of seeing the total absence of consolation regarding conditioned phenomena is called the desireless liberation (*appaṇihita-vimokkha*).
"Contemplation of emptiness" is contemplation of non-self. That...

Because it proceeds by way of resolving each respective "mass"—namely, the mass of the collection of phenomena (*samūhaghana*), the mass of continuity (*santatighana*), the mass of function (*kiccaghana*), and the mass of the object (*ārammaṇaghana*)—and because it contemplates the absence of any core substance that could be grasped as a "self," it is called the "contemplation of emptiness" (*suññatānupassanā*).
The "signless contemplation" (*animittānupassanā*) is the contemplation of impermanence (*aniccānupassanā*); for that too proceeds by way of the interruption of the continuity [of formations].
It is called "contemplation of the signless" (*animittānupassanā*) because it dispels the sign grasped as "I" due to its occurrence [as such].

"Contemplation of the desireless" (*appaṇihitānupassanā*) is contemplation of suffering. For that too, by way of manifesting the state of being a great mass of danger, occurs as the contemplation of the absence of any quality of desirability (*paṇihita-guṇa*) to be grasped as "this is mine" or "this is for me"; thus it is called "contemplation of the desireless."
It is called "pātimokkhasaṃvarasīla. *Pātimokkhasaṃvarasīla* is the virtue of the Vinaya formulation.

For it is the eldest among all mundane virtues, and thus it is their "foremost" (*pati*). And because it is the primary source for the wholesome states of the four planes, it is their "mouth" (*mukha*).
Thus, in the sense of being foremost, it is called *pātimokkha*. And because it restrains and shuts off the path of misconduct, it is a "restraint" (*saṃvara*).

It is said: "Of those phenomena whose arising causes the faculties such as the eye to quiver, makes them restless, and gives rise to unwholesome states that follow upon them—the mindfulness that functions by way of restraining their arising is called 'restraint of the faculties' (*indriya-saṃvara*).
That itself is virtue; thus it is the virtue of restraint of the faculties (*indriya-saṃvara-sīla*). Regarding livelihood (*ājīva*):
"Ājīva" (livelihood) is so called because they maintain their life by means of it; it is the effort involved in seeking the requisites.

That very [effort] is called "purity of livelihood" (*ājīvapārisuddhi*) because it is completely pure, being free from improper applications such as giving flowers—which are censured by the Buddha—and the three grounds for hypocrisy.
This itself is the "virtue" (*sīla*); such is the compound. [It refers to] those things obtained through such a completely pure application, such as the practice of alms-gathering.
The knowledge of reflection regarding the use of requisites (*paccaya-sevana-patisankhā-ñāṇa*), which operates by way of discerning and reviewing the specific purpose,
the proper limits, the characteristic of repulsiveness, or the characteristic of being merely elements for the sake of abandoning delusion,
greed, intoxication, and negligence at the times of receiving and using requisites, is called virtue dependent on requisites (*paccaya-sannissita-sīla*).

"Purification" (*pārisuddhi*) means it is thoroughly purified (*parisujjhati*). "Purification" (*pārisuddhi*) is simply purification (*parisuddhi*). The compound is: "that itself is virtue" (*sīla*). "The fourfold virtue of purification" (*catupārisuddhisīla*) refers to the four types of virtue consisting of purification.
Regarding "purification of mind" (*cittavisuddhi*), it is stated here that by the word "mind" (*citta*), concentration (*samādhi*) is indicated;
thus, both kinds of concentration are called "purification of mind. [The following concerns] its characteristic, function, manifestation, and proximate cause.
"By way of" (*vasena*): here, the specific individual essence (*paccatta-sabhāva*) of phenomena is called their "characteristic" (*lakkhaṇa*), just as heat is for fire.

The function to be accomplished by that essence, or the excellence (*sampatti*) consisting of the qualities acquired through the instrumental conditions (*sādhanapaccaya*), is called its "flavor" (*rasa*), just as the burning and illuminating [powers] are for fire.
That same excellence, or the fruit (*phala*) termed the "resultant effect" (*kāriya*), is called its "manifestation" (*paccupaṭṭhāna*).
Like smoke to fire. The proximate cause, which is reckoned as the specific condition for its own arising, is called the "proximate basis" (*padatthāna*).

By means of these, the discernment of mind and matter—the grasping after delimiting them with knowledge—is called the "definition of mind-and-matter" (*nāmarūpa-vavatthāna*) and "purification of view" (*diṭṭhi-visuddhi*).
Herein, discernment is twofold: concise discernment and detailed discernment.
In this context, having divided internal phenomena into two— namely, "this is name only, not form" and "this is form only, not name"—
and having clearly seen through direct experience that name is one thing and form is another, and that apart from both of these there is no self,
life-principle, being, person, human, deity, or Brahma, the act of grasping [this] is called "grasping by way of summary."

A person who possesses supreme knowledge is able, by this much alone, to suppress the view of a self-existent body (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*) along with the perversion of perception and the perversion of mind.
For there are three perversions, as it is said: "The perversion of perception, the perversion of mind, and the perversion of view regarding what is non-self as self.
In that regard, even by means of mere faith well-established in the Dhamma of the Teacher’s instruction—
The perversion of views has been suppressed; however, the others are suppressed only when the comprehension of mind-and-body (nāmarūpa) has been accomplished.

As long as these two remain unsuppressed, the comprehension of mind-and-body remains impure, and furthermore, the defilements rooted therein remain unsuppressed as well. This is because of the four nutriments...

Name-and-form (nāmarūpa) should be comprehended by way of such methods as fourfold according to the [four] aggregates, fivefold according to the five aggregates, sixfold according to the six elements, and so forth.

Therein, the "six elements" are the earth element, the water element, the fire element, the air element, the space element, and the consciousness element. For the clansman Pakkusāti [spoke of] these six elements.
Having comprehended [the aggregates], attained the fruit of non-returning, and cast off [the defilements], he is reborn in the Suddhāvāsa [Pure Abodes].

Alternatively, however many phenomena one comprehends that enable one to suppress the perversion of perception, mind, and view which occur as "this is my self"—just those many should indeed be comprehended. In this manual of compendium (*Saṅgahapakaraṇa*), whichever [states] of consciousness and mental factors...
The analysis of the elements and the analysis of matter have already been explained below.
The comprehensive grasping of name-and-form by means of all these [analyses] is called "detailed comprehension. This, however, is not within the scope of beginners;
it should be understood as being within the scope only of those Abhidhamma masters who have penetrated the Four Noble Truths. Furthermore, for one who is comprehending name-and-form, name-and-form...
Furthermore, by demonstrating the non-existence of anything other than [the aggregates] themselves, the view that there exists within the body a self designated as "life" (jīva)—
one who acts, one who experiences, one who transmigrates, and one who wanders— is abandoned.
This occurs because of the complete vision of the total absence of any such striving or activity designated as "name," "person," "being," or "action."
By seeing that these two are obtained only through their conjunction, the view that occurs with reference to both together— or either one individually—
asserting "this is the self" (attā), is abandoned. Furthermore, regarding conventional expressions such as "self," "living being" (jīva), "sentient being" (satta), "person" (puggala),

"human," "deity," or "Brahmā," instead of remaining at the mere level of conventional usage, [one abandons the view] by thinking, "there definitely exists what is called a self," or "there definitely exists what is called a living being," and so forth.
It should be understood that by means of this adherence to its meaning, "over-reaching" (atidhāvana) is abandoned.

"Adherence to its meaning" refers to a firm conviction such as "there is a self," "there is a life-principle," and so forth. "Over-reaching" refers to the grasping of name-and-form as a self, and so forth.
Regarding "the discernment of conditions" (paccayapariggaha), here too the discernment of conditions is twofold in brief.

"And in detail": herein, one who discerns the condition for name by way of its basis and object, for form by way of consciousness, temperature, and nutriment, and for both together by way of ignorance, craving, clinging, and kamma, is said to "discern in brief.
One who discerns by means of the methods of dependent arising and the *Paṭṭhāna* (Conditional Relations) as analyzed in the preceding Compendium of Conditions is said to "discern in detail."
In this context as well, the analysis according to the method of the *Paṭṭhāna* is entirely beyond the scope of beginners.

Furthermore, for one who discerns conditions, the view of causelessness (*ahetuka-diṭṭhi*) is abandoned by seeing that all name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), as it has been defined, exists in every respect dependent upon conditions.
The view of creation by a Supreme Lord (*issara-nimmāna*) is abandoned because no occurrence is seen other than through the assembly of conditions appropriate to itself.
The view of false causes, such as time, destiny, and so forth, is abandoned.

Through the understanding that there is no agent other than the causal equipment and conditions for the occurrence of karma, nor any experiencer of the result other than the occurrence of the ripening [of that karma], the view of an agent and an experiencer is abandoned.
And throughout the beginningless cycle of existence, by way of the succession of cause and effect across the three periods of time...
Because one sees the occurrence of mere name-and-form alone, there comes to be the transcendence of the sixteenfold doubt concerning the person and the being—
such as, "Did I exist in the past?"— and because one has clearly seen the occurrence of phenomena according to their intrinsic nature,
one perceives the excellence of the Dhamma taught and, having seen the Buddha’s perfect Buddhahood, [one gains confidence] in the Teacher.
The eightfold doubt—beginning with "he doubts the Dhamma," "he doubts" (kaṅkhati), and so forth—is abandoned.
Because even though supramundane states are conditioned, they do not come within the scope of reflective contemplation (*asammasanupagattā*), it is said:

"among the conditioned phenomena of the three planes. And because contemplation is for the purpose of uprooting the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*), those very phenomena in which the underlying tendencies such as sensual lust reside are the objects worthy of contemplation.
"It is said that they exist among the formations of the three planes. This phrase is connected with the words "for one who comprehends the three characteristics of this [state].
"Divided by the distinctions of past and so forth" means divided by the eleven distinctions, such as past, future, present, internal, external, and so on.
"Taking up the method of the aggregates and so forth" refers to the fivefold aggregate system analyzed in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*.

The meaning is: having followed the method for classifying the planes of comprehension—beginning with the six doors, the six objects, the six consciousnesses, the six contacts, the six feelings, the six perceptions, and so forth—in accordance with that method.
Therein, whichever of the twenty-three categories of phenomena is clear to one, one should take that [category] and...
Comprehension should be undertaken. However, one who is able should undertake it by taking everything together.

"Having condensed by way of groups" means that first, with respect to the five aggregates, all matter—even though it is divided into such categories as past, future, and present—is condensed into a single lump of matter;
this same method applies to feeling and the other aggregates as well. In this regard, the method is as follows: whatever...
Form—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior;

far or near—all form is impermanent in the sense of destruction, suffering in the sense of terror, and non-self in the sense of corelessness. Whatever feeling... Whatever perception... Whatever formations...

Whatever consciousness—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—all consciousness is impermanent in the sense of destruction, suffering in the sense of terror, and non-self in the sense of corelessness.
Consciousness... All consciousness is impermanent in the sense of destruction; it is suffering in the sense of terror; it is non-self in the sense of being coreless.
And here, the inclusion of "all form" up to "all consciousness" should be understood as a condensation by way of aggregates (*kalāpa*).
Regarding the phrase "impermanent in the sense of destruction": herein, form is impermanent in the sense of destruction; feeling is impermanent.

"Perception is impermanent; formations are impermanent; consciousness is impermanent in the sense of destruction"—in such a manner, the contemplation must be performed together with the discernment of the phenomena to be contemplated.

Otherwise, the contemplation does not succeed. However, because that meaning is already evident, it should be understood that here the Elder has taken up only the words of the contemplation itself, beginning with "impermanent in the sense of destruction. In this regard:
"Form is impermanent in the sense of destruction": having firmly grasped each respective form with knowledge, one should perform the contemplation (*sammasana*) in such a manner as:
"This earth element is impermanent in the sense of destruction; this water element is impermanent in the sense of destruction," and so forth.
In that regard, within this body, everything that consists merely of the function of hardness is called "earth. And that function [is characterized] by the alternation of cold and heat.

It changes. It changes either through the change of various nutriments, or through the change of various states of consciousness, or through the change of various postures, or through the change of various bodily activities.
The meaning is that there is a transition of various successions.
In this regard, as ever-new successions of activity manifest, the previous successions of activity perish. And because—
What is called "continuity" does not exist as something separate from the phenomena themselves;

therefore, the manifestation of ever-new continuities is simply the arising of ever-new activities. Likewise, the disappearance of preceding continuities is simply the breaking up of preceding activities.
Thus, observing the transformation of various stiffening activities within one's own body, one perceives the waning and passing away of the earth element.
He sees it. And seeing that, he sees precisely the exhaustion and passing away of the material forms co-nascent with it. What is called "water" is merely the function of cohesion.
What is called "fire" is merely the function of coldness and the function of heat.
What is called "air" is merely the function of distension. And these functions change from moment to moment. Seeing the continuous change of each of these individually—
He sees the destruction and passing away of the feet and those material qualities co-nascent with them.
However, he knows the transformation of the continuity by seeing it externally with the eye; internally, within the body, he knows it through tactile contact.
But the destruction and passing away of the elements constituting the continuity and the body, he sees through knowledge alone. Therefore, within his own body, that particular continuity—

Having understood the transformation, or having adjusted [the meditation] accordingly, one should make the impermanence of the material elements well-seen by means of knowledge and contemplate it again and again.

Regarding the remaining aggregates as well, having understood the diversity of their respective continuities and made the destruction and fall of feeling and the other aggregates well-seen, contemplation should be performed. "In the sense of fear" means in the sense of that which is to be feared.
For whatever is impermanent and subject to change even in a mere moment must certainly be feared. Why?
Because he who does not fear it places his trust in it, treats it as his own limb, and preserves it;
yet that [thing] constantly [afflicts him] with countless thousands of limitless sufferings of volitional formations or sufferings of transformation.

It oppresses; it afflicts. Thus, because its nature is to constantly and repeatedly oppress with various states of suffering, it is called "suffering" (dukkha) in the sense of being absolutely terrifying.
It is "non-self" (anattā) because it is the opposite of a self.
For that which is apprehended as having the state of being the ultimate innermost—thinking, "Beyond this, there is nothing more internal to me"—is what is called "self."
It is said [thus]. But what is it that should be grasped in such a way? That which functions entirely under one's own control.

Without the aforementioned activities of volitional formation, it proceeds constantly and unfailingly by mere desire, or by power, or by inclination, or by the issuing of a command. That is what should be grasped in such a way. Such a thing...
For indeed, this Dhamma constantly performs its own function for those beings who desire constant happiness and are averse to suffering.
But that which destroys and scatters the happiness as it occurs for those who desire constant happiness,

and which produces and increases the various sufferings rooted in volitional formations (*abhisaṅkhāra*) and so forth for those who are averse to suffering— that is precisely the opposite of one's own welfare (*attapaṭipakkho*).
And this material form is exactly like that. Thus, because it does not perform its own function and because it performs a function contrary to itself, material form is called "non-self" (anattā).
But why does it not come under the control of a self, why does it not perform its own function, and why does it perform a function contrary to itself?
To this he says: "in the sense of being coreless" (*asārakaṭṭhena*). In this context, "core" (*sāra*) refers to the completeness of conditions.

It is called a specific excellence of strength (*thāmabala*) characterized by the capacity to arise solely through mere intention, or, having arisen, to remain established at will without the support of conditions.
However, matter itself is not such a "sāra" (essence), nor is it endowed with such an essence; for [matter] does not [possess this] through the completeness of its conditions.
There is no stability or strength in them to arise without [conditions], nor, even having arisen, to remain established for even a moment without the support of conditions.
And that which arises solely through the power of the completeness of conditions, without its own inherent strength or power,
and remains established only through the support of conditions— that involves thousands upon thousands of sufferings of conditioning the conditions.
Having arisen, it invariably performs the function of being the opposite of the self; it oppresses and indeed afflicts [it].

This is the method [of analysis] regarding such passages as "feeling is impermanent in the sense of destruction," and so forth. Thus, the connection is: "the three characteristics are well established.
"By way of duration" means by way of the period of occurrence delimited by each individual existence (*bhava*). For that which has arisen in another existence...
The pentad of aggregates goes to another state of existence; it ceases without remainder right there in each respective state of existence.

Furthermore, even within a single state of existence, the division of time should be applied according to the three stages of life (youth, etc.), the ten decades beginning with infancy, and the years, seasons, months, fortnights, lunar days, days and nights, watches, and periods. This is by way of continuity (*santati*).
By way of a homogeneous continuity means by way of a material continuity or an immaterial continuity that proceeds as a homogeneous stream.
By way of moment means by way of the moment reckoned as the measure of the lifespan of material and immaterial phenomena.
And herein, comprehension by way of moment would be the domain of the Omniscient Buddhas alone, not of the disciples; for they do not [perceive] the arising within such a brief moment.

"Or they are able to attain cessation. Therefore, it should be understood that here "comprehension" (*sammasana*) is intended specifically in the sense of the continuity of the course of existence (*addhā-santati*).

"Comprehending the three characteristics" means applying the three characteristics to those phenomena consisting of the conditioned states of the three planes, and repeatedly touching and rubbing them. Of those phenomena, impermanence...
The meaning is: "making clearly manifest in knowledge that which is produced by birth, produced by suffering, or produced by non-self.
Specifically, however, in this knowledge, the observation of the characteristic of impermanence alone is primary.
When that has been seen, the others are seen in due course; when it has not been seen, they remain unseen. Therefore, first of all, [one should observe] the characteristic of impermanence itself.
The intended meaning is that the state of being clearly manifest is meant. "In those very [formations]" means in the formations of the three planes (*tebhūmaka-saṅkhāresu*) alone.

"By way of conditions" refers, first, in the case of the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*), to the conditions consisting of ignorance (*avijjā*), craving (*taṇhā*), clinging (*upādāna*), kamma, and nutriment (*āhāra*).

However, in the case of feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saññā*), and formations (*saṅkhārā*), contact (*phassa*) should be stated in the place of nutriment; and consciousness (*viññāṇa*) is name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). Herein, this is the method: in the immediately preceding past existence...

When ignorance, craving, clinging, and kamma have arisen through their non-abandonment, the continuities of form, as well as the continuities of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, arise from the moment of rebirth-linking in this existence.
Until the time of death, they arise and produce themselves at every moment by way of various aggregates. However, among those [factors], through their abandonment within that very existence—
When those continuities of form and formless states have ceased, they reach a cessation known as non-arising in another existence.
In this regard, just as fish exist when there is water and do not exist when there is none, so too, when the name-and-form born of kamma exists, the other name-and-forms exist;
when they do not exist, the others do not exist. Thus, all the others [depend] upon those born of kamma.
It should be understood that the manifestation of arising and passing away has been grasped by way of the cause of kamma.
Thus, through the conditions of ignorance, craving, clinging, and kamma, there occurs the process of the arising and passing away of the five aggregates.
Furthermore, those [aggregates] which arise in this existence by way of kamma, from the moment of rebirth-linking onwards, receive support from physical nutriment at every moment.
In this way, as the successions of materiality proceed, new successions of materiality arise continuously;

yet, failing to obtain further conditions, they cease. Within that succession, they reach the cessation of a single existence, which is termed non-arising, such that the proceeding successions are cut off, broken, and disappear.

Feeling, perception, and mental formations, however, arise as the sixfold doors—consisting of wholesome, unwholesome, resultant, and functional states—only after obtaining contact with external objects that have come into range. New successions (santati) manifest;
but when they do not obtain [contact], they cease and do not form a continuity. This applies to consciousness as well as its co-nascent name and the physical basis (vatthurūpa).

"It proceeds while proceeding; it ceases while ceasing. "By way of moments" means by way of the moment of the occurrence of name-and-form alone, without regard for the conditions of the kind already described.

And here, by the word "moment," both the continuity of form and the continuity of name mentioned in the context of comprehension-knowledge (*sammasana-ñāṇa*) should be understood. For the knowledge of disciples does not [penetrate] name-and-form by way of moments.
"He is able to attain either arising or passing away.

Just as, in the darkness of night within a cave, a great mass of gloom arises, yet for one who lights a lamp, the radiance of that lamp arises in a single moment pervading the entire interior of the cave—there is the arising of light and the passing away of the mass of gloom. Again...
When a lamp is being extinguished, there is the arising of a mass of darkness and the passing away of light. In the very same way,
for one who clearly sees and contemplates the various successions of arising and passing-away phases within the body— whether by way of various temperatures, various foods, various states of mind,
various postures, or various activities— as they arise as arising and pass away as passing away.

The meaning is as follows. For one who thus contemplates and has attained the state of one who has commenced insight (vipassanā), while the knowledge of arising and passing away (udayabbaya-ñāṇa) is proceeding keenly, powerfully, and vigorously, ten kinds of obstructive states known as the defilements of insight (vipassanupakkilesa) arise.
To demonstrate these, he spoke the verse beginning with "Light" (obhāsa). Therein, "light" (obhāsa) refers to the bodily radiance produced by the mind through insight.

*Pīti* (rapture) refers to the fivefold rapture associated with the mind of insight (*vipassanā*). *Passaddhi* (tranquility) refers to the two kinds of tranquility. *Adhimokkha* (resolution) is resolution through faith (*saddhā-adhimokkha*).
*Paggaha* (exertion) is energy (*vīriya*). *Sukha* (bliss) is mental joy (*somanassa*). *Ñāṇa* (knowledge) is the knowledge of insight. *Upaṭṭhāna* (establishment) is mindfulness (*sati*).
*Upekkhā* (equanimity) is both the equanimity of neutrality (*tatramajjhattupekkhā*) and the equanimity of adverting (*āvajjanupekkhā*). *Nikanti* (attachment) is...
Subtle craving is that which establishes a basis for insight together with the illumination and other such phenomena. This alone is exclusively an imperfection of insight;
however, the illumination and so forth are called "imperfections" because they serve as its objective bases.
For when these arise, one thinks: "Indeed, never before has such an illumination arisen for me," or "such rapture," and so on.

"Equanimity has arisen before; surely I have attained the path! Surely I have attained the fruit!"—thus, accompanied by gratification, a perception of a path arises where there is no path, and a perception of a fruit arises where there is no fruit.

At that time, some unskilled practitioner, having abandoned his meditation subject, wanders about distracted by way of overweening conceit (adhimāna). But the skilled one, at that very moment, regains his mindfulness.
Now, regarding these [signs] such as the illumination, there appears to my mind a mode of attachment, thinking: "This is mine, this am I, this is my self.
And the supramundane state (lokuttara-dhamma) is not the basis for such attachment. Surely some defiled state (saṃkilesa-dhamma) has arisen in me;
if it increases, it will cause me to fall from the gateway to deliverance (niyyāna-mukha) and join me to the gateway of the round of existence (vaṭṭa-mukha). Come now, upon those very [signs]...
Thinking, "Having applied the three characteristics and purified my attachment, I shall set [the mind] upon the course of insight as it occurs," he first grasps those very phenomena such as the aura.

The meaning is that he comprehends them thus: "This aura of mine is impermanent in the sense of destruction, suffering in the sense of fear, and non-self in the sense of being coreless," and so forth. In this way, those phenomena such as the aura, which have become defilements for insight—

The knowledge of discerning the characteristics of what is the path and what is not the path, which arises in one who has grasped the states that are obstacles and, by means of that grasping, has exhausted attachment to them, is called the purification by knowledge and vision of what is the path and what is not the path.

This is because it is purified from the stain of perceiving what is not the path—such as the [meditative] illumination and so forth—as being the path, and from the stain of attachment as previously described. For that knowledge, regarding those [states]:
Because the illumination and so forth are obstructed precisely when attachment has been suppressed, it is called "thoroughly purified.

However, in the *Vibhāvanī*, the discernment that obstructs the illumination and so forth by way of impermanence and the other characteristics is not mentioned separately; instead, it is stated that the purification of knowledge and vision of what constitutes the path and what does not constitute the path consists merely in knowing the path and the non-path. This does not accord with the *Aṭṭhakathā*.

"Likewise, for one who is freed from obstacles": having thus grasped [the object], for one who is freed from the obstacles consisting of the defilements of insight (*vipassanūpakkilesa*), "as far as conformity" means up to the knowledge of conformity (*anulomañāṇa*). The connection is with "having applied the three characteristics.

"Having reached the maturity of insight" means having attained the state of equanimity regarding formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā*) and, through the attainment of the state of the three doors of liberation, [having reached] the classification of the seven noble persons (*ariyapuggala*).
And because of the attainment of the state of being a condition, having reached the maturity of insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*), it is said: "Now absorption (*appanā*) will arise.
This is to be connected with the phrase "at the moment when it is to be spoken. "Absorption" refers here to the absorption of the stream-entry path (*sotāpatti-magga*).

"Two or three moments of insight-consciousness" means two moments of insight-consciousness for one of sharp wisdom (*tikkha-pañña*), and three moments of insight-consciousness for one of dull wisdom (*manda-pañña*). "Whatever" means...
"Any one of the three characteristics. "Equanimity regarding formations that has reached its peak and conforms to adaptation":

this refers to the equanimity regarding formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā*) which has attained its culmination and is accompanied by knowledge of adaptation (*anuloma-ñāṇa*). The construction is: "That is called 'insight leading to emergence' (*vuṭṭhānagāminī-vipassanā*).
Knowledge of equanimity regarding formations and knowledge of adaptation—these two knowledges are named "insight leading to emergence."
"It is said" means it has been stated. This, however, is a term for vision consisting of insight that has reached maturity. And here, "emergence" (*vuṭṭhāna*) refers to the Path (*magga*).
For that [Path] emerges from the sign of formations (*saṅkhāra-nimitta*), which serves as the object of insight-knowledge, or it emerges from being itself a basis for the fetters (*saṃyojana*).

Or, it causes the person possessing it to emerge from the state of an ordinary worldling (*puthujjana*) by way of the abandoning of the origin [of suffering], and from the turning of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa-pavatta*).
It causes one to emerge; therefore it is called "emergence" (*vuṭṭhāna*). Because by means of this [knowledge] they inevitably go to emergence, it is called "leading to emergence" (*vuṭṭhānagāminī*);
thus should the quality of leading to emergence of these two knowledges be understood.
"Beyond that" means beyond the occurrence of either two or three moments of insight-consciousness, having taken Nibbāna as its object—that is, in the place of adverting for the Path.
Having offered [the oblation], by acting as its precursor, one takes Nibbāna itself as the object. And for that very reason, it does not receive the name "insight" (vipassanā).
Regarding the phrase "overcoming the lineage of the worldling" (puthujjana-gotta): by this, it is called *gotrabhū* because it overcomes the lineage (*gotta*).
Here, "lineage" (*gotta*) refers to the class of worldlings (*puthujjanajāti*), which is characterized by the state of being ignoble due to the complete association with defilements.
"Is called" indicates this meaning. Regarding "attaining the noble lineage": by this it is shown that *gotrabhu* means one who reaches or arrives at the lineage (*gotta*).
Furthermore, "lineage" refers to the noble birth (*ariyajāti*), which is defined as the state of purification from various defilements;
this is the meaning indicated. The connection is: "the path descends into the stage of absorption. "One who fully understands the truth of suffering..."
He knows, having delimited the state of absolute suffering of phenomena belonging to the three planes.
Herein, "thoroughly understanding" (parijānana) should be regarded as precisely the abandoning of the delusion that conceals their state of suffering.

"Abandoning the truth of the origin" means abandoning, either partially or entirely, the truth of the origin—consisting of craving—which exists within the continuum of one's own mind in the form of underlying tendencies (anusaya).
Abandoning [the defilements] either without remainder or by way of non-recurrence; "realizing the truth of cessation" means that,
like one with vision beholding the lunar disk shining in the midst of the sky,

one brings about the state of being subject to non-arising again within one's own continuum— whether it be a portion or the entirety of the cycle of defilements, or the cycle of future results yet to come.
Making Nibbāna, which is characterized as cessation, directly manifest.

"By way of the cultivation of the truth of the path" means by way of the cultivation consisting in the arising of the eightfold path-truth that had never previously arisen throughout the beginningless cycle of existence prior to this.
However, because the volition of the path has immediate fruit (*ānantarika-phala*), at that very moment, in a place where the tip has been removed...

Then, as if sprinkling water to extinguish [the fire], two or three fruition-consciousnesses (phalacitta) proceed in accordance with the course of the path, performing the four functions beginning with the full understanding of suffering (dukkhapariññā).
To show that after this there is a lapse into the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), he says "after that," and so forth. Just as by means of the physical eye or the divine eye...
For one seeing a certain form, those eyes cease having made that form manifest to themselves and subsequently making it manifest as something directly perceived by that person.
At the very moment of their arising, that form does not yet become evident to him such that he thinks, "I am seeing this, which is called so-and-so.
However, it becomes so only when the stages of subsequent reflection are occurring.

That form and its concomitants appear to him in various ways. In the same way, here too, while the sections on reviewing are occurring, Nibbāna and its concomitants—the path, the fruit, and so forth—also become manifest;
thus it is said: "The life-continuum occurs again," and so on.
Now, in order to show the plane of reviewing knowledge, the verse beginning with "The path, the fruit, and Nibbāna" is stated.
"Māha. In this context, "the wise one" refers to one who possesses noble wisdom and has attained the fruit of the path. "Abandoned" means those defilements that have been relinquished.

"The rest" refers to those not yet abandoned, which are to be eliminated by the higher paths. However, it is said that these two types of reflection on the defilements abandoned and remaining are not possible for certain individuals whose lives are devoted solely to their livelihood, nor for those unskilled in the classification of defilements; hence the phrase "if he reflects."
In this *Visuddhimagga*, first of all, the reviewing of the path is stated; after that, the reviewing of the fruit;
after that, the reviewing of the defilements abandoned; after that, the reviewing of the remaining defilements; and at the very end, the reviewing of Nibbāna is stated.
However, in the commentary on the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*, the reviewing of the defilements is intended to come first of all.
For it is said there that among the reflections, first comes the reflection on the defilements, followed by the reflections on the Path, the Fruit, and Nibbāna.

However, that was stated because, prior to the exposition of the knowledge of reflection in the Pāḷi, the "knowledge of liberation through wisdom" (*paññāvimutti-ñāṇa*)—described as "the cutting off has been seen"—was presented separately as the "knowledge of liberation. In that context, "cutting off" (*chinna*)...

The meaning is: the mass of defilements eradicated by each respective path. However, when the text is explained according to its sequence, first there is the reviewing of the defilements abandoned; then, the reviewing of each of the path factors, enlightenment factors, and so forth;
then, the reviewing of Nibbāna, which is their object; and then, the reviewing of the qualities of the fruits.
Therefore, it should be said that there is a reviewing of Nibbāna, which has become their object.
For in the Pāḷi, in the exposition of reviewing-knowledge, Nibbāna appears twice—both in the section on the Path and in the section on the Fruit.
Thus, what is called "reviewing of Nibbāna" occurs either at the beginning, in the middle, or intermittently among the other types of reviewing.

It is established that [the mind] proceeds at any point whatsoever, even at the very end. Likewise, the reviewing of the defilements may occur either at the beginning or after the reviewing of the Path and the Fruit.
For this being the case, this verse—“The Path, the Fruit, and Nibbāna”—is also not contradicted.
And having done so, in the commentaries on the exposition of overestimation (*adhimāna*), it is said: “For he [sees] the Path, the Fruit, Nibbāna, and the defilements abandoned...”
It is said that one who has become joyful through the reviewing of the defilements destroyed by the Vasiṭṭha [path] is "free from doubt" regarding the penetration of the noble qualities.
In this context, there are five reviews for a stream-enterer; likewise, five for a once-returner; five for a non-returner;
and for an arahant, since there are no remaining defilements, there are four—thus, there are nineteen reviews in total.
"They exist. This was said with reference to what is obtained when [the factors] are complete.
However, they do indeed exist even when incomplete. For thus it is said in the commentary on the *Cūḷadukkhakkhandha-sutta*: "But that [reviewing knowledge] is not complete for everyone.
For one person reviews only the defilements already abandoned; another, only the remaining defilements; and another, only the path."
There is only one fruit; there is only one Nibbāna. However, it is said that among these five kinds of reviewing, it is not possible to obtain even one or two of them at a time.
Thus, the fourfold path that is to be developed by means of the sixfold purification is called "purification by knowledge and vision"—this is the connection.
And here, by the word "path," the fourfold knowledge of the path is intended by way of its occurrence in conformity with that [Nibbāna].
And it should be understood that the knowledge of the fruit (*phalañāṇa*) is also included. "Therein" means in the meditation subject of insight (*vipassanākammaṭṭhāna*).
"In those" refers to the paths and fruits among those [insight] contemplations. "Adherence" (*abhinivesa*) is the act of adhering.

The meaning is that it proceeds by grasping firmly at the internal aggregates, like the base of Mount Sineru which is fixed in the stone earth below. Adherence as "self" is self-adherence (*attābhinivesa*).

That adherence to a self (*attābhinivesa*). They "release" it by repeatedly contemplating [the aggregates] as "form is non-self, feeling is non-self," and so forth, having made those two well-seen; for that adherence occurs because one has not seen that internal phenomena exist solely dependent on conditions and because one has not seen their momentary dissolution.
Therefore, by making those two well-seen, they release that adherence through the process of repeated contemplation.
It is the meaning. It is a gateway to liberation because it serves as the entrance door to the path and the fruit known as the emptiness-liberation (*suññatā-vimokkha*).
"The sign of perversion" (*vipallāsa-nimitta*): perversion (*vipallāsa*) is the approaching, the resorting to, or the proceeding by way of inversion.

The meaning is: the approaching or the proceeding [of the mind] by taking what is impermanent to be permanent. That very thing, because it is the proximate cause for the arising of defilements, is so called.

"Sign" (*nimitta*) means the sign of perversion (*vipallāsa-nimitta*). "They release" means that because they have not seen the momentary dissolution (*khaṇabhaṅga*) of internal phenomena, that sign arises;

therefore, having clearly seen their momentary dissolution, the meaning is that they liberate themselves from that sign by repeatedly contemplating [them] in such ways as "form is impermanent," "feeling is impermanent," and so forth. "Craving and longing" (*taṇhā-panidhi*)...
Because craving itself fixes the mind firmly upon an object by way of attachment and directs it toward it, it is called "aspiration" (*paṇidhi*);
thus, it is "craving-aspiration. They "release" that craving-aspiration because they have not seen the great mass of danger inherent in internal phenomena;
therefore, having clearly seen the great mass of danger in those [phenomena], [they realize] "form is suffering."
The meaning is: by means of repeatedly contemplating [them] through such phrases as "feeling is suffering," one is liberating that aspiration.
"Therefore" means: because these three contemplations, which serve as gateways to liberation, possess such specific names; therefore.
Because, by way of seeing emptiness (*suññatā*) in formations (*saṅkhārā*), there is the accomplishment of the goal known as the mere relinquishing of the adherence to a self.
The power belongs to wisdom (*ñāṇa*) itself, which is the direct opposite of the grasping of views;

therefore, for one who is liberated by seeing in such a way, both insight (*vipassanā*) and the path (*magga*) receive the designation "conascent wisdom" (*sahajāta-ñāṇa*) by virtue of their function. Thus it is said:
"That which is emergence... the path called the void liberation. By means of the accomplishment of the goal through the vision of impermanence, [the sign] becomes the basis of attachment.

The power of faith also exists as the counteragent to the grasping of conceit. Therefore, for one who is liberated by viewing things in such a way, both insight and the path receive their respective names through the function of the co-nascent faith; thus it is said: "If [one views] from the perspective of impermanence...
[the liberation is] called the signless liberation. By means of seeing suffering, the purpose is accomplished through the counteraction of the grasping of craving known as "wish" (*paṇidhi*).

There is also the power of concentration. Therefore, it is said that for one who is liberated by viewing [the aggregates] in such a way, both insight and the path receive their name through the function of the co-nascent concentration.
If [one views them] as suffering... [and so on]... it is called the "wishless liberation. For this has been stated in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*:
"When one attends to [the aggregates] as impermanent, the faculty of faith becomes predominant."
When one attends to [the aggregates] as suffering, the faculty of concentration becomes predominant; when one attends to them as non-self, the faculty of wisdom becomes predominant.
It is said that the "Path" is established by way of the very process of arriving at insight (*vipassanā*), wherein there is a specific distinction in the function of the three factors.
Thus it receives its various names. In that regard, the noble disciple who is liberated by means of the emptiness liberation (*suññatā-vimokkha*)...

At the moment of the path of stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga), one is called a "follower by Dhamma" (dhammānusārī). In the middle six instances—the moments of the paths and fruits—one is called "one who has attained vision" (diṭṭhippatto).

At the moment of the fruit of arhatship (arahatta-phala), one is called "liberated by wisdom" (paññāvimutto). One liberated by the signless liberation (animitta-vimokkha) is called a "follower by faith" (saddhānusārī) at the moment of the path of stream-entry;
in the seven subsequent instances, one is called "liberated by faith" (saddhāvimutto). One liberated by the desireless liberation (apaṇihita-vimokkha) [is likewise so called].

However, in all eight instances, one is called a "body-witness" (kāyasakkhī). That same person, having made formless jhāna the basis and being liberated, established in the fruit of Arahantship, is called "liberated both ways" (ubhatobhāgavimutto).

Up to this point, what was stated below—namely, "having reached the maturity of insight"—refers to the attainment of the state of equanimity regarding formations (saṅkhārupekkhā) and the attainment of the state of the three doors to liberation, as well as the classification of the seven noble persons (ariyapuggala).
And by reaching the maturity of insight-knowledge through the attainment of the state of being a condition, it is said "dependent upon. Thus, it has been explained according to its own nature.
The construction is as follows: on the path-continuum, the fruit likewise receives three names by way of the arrival of the path.
"For those who are practicing insight in the manner already stated" means in the manner described by the passage beginning with "if one contemplates as non-self," and so forth.
For the four types of persons who are at the stage of fruition (*phalaṭṭha*) and are practicing insight (*vipassantānaṃ*), there is "their own respective fruit" (*yathāsakaṃphala*).

This refers to the fruit of stream-entry for a stream-enterer, the fruit of once-returning for a once-returner, and so forth, according to this method. Whatever fruit belongs to each individual is called the "voidness liberation" (*suññatā-vimokkha*) and so on, precisely by way of their arrival at insight (*vipassanāgamana-vasena*). It is not by way of their arrival at the path (*namaggāgamana-vasena*).

This is the intended meaning (*adhippāya*). Here, the attainment of the name "signless" (*animitta*) for the Path by way of the approach to insight (*vipassanā*) is stated according to the method of the Suttantas.
However, in the Abhidhamma, the Path is not called "signless.

For it is not signless in the primary sense (*nippariyāyato*), because the sign of formations (*saṅkhāra-nimitta*)—which is subject to classification as inferior, superior, and so forth—is still present. For this very reason...
A distinction between inferior, superior, and most superior [levels] is observed either by way of the painful practice and slow direct knowledge (*dukkha-paṭipadā-dandhābhiññā*),
or by way of the limited or great nature of the perfections (*pāramī-dhamma*). However, in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*),

it is stated that although the contemplation of impermanence (*aniccānupassanā*) is identical to the contemplation of the signless (*animittānupassanā*) because it proceeds by way of dispelling the sign of permanence among conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*), [it is nevertheless distinguished].
Because it is included within the sign of formations (*saṅkhāranimitta*), it is absolutely unable to give its own name to the Path.
Therefore, it is said that according to the Abhidhamma method, the Path does not receive the name "signless" (*animitta*).

However, according to the Suttanta method, just as a jhāna having the earth-kasiṇa as its object is called the "earth-kasiṇa," so too [the Path] receives the names "emptiness" (*suññatā*) and so forth.
The paths and fruits that arise having Nibbāna as their object also receive the names "emptiness" and so forth by way of their object.
However, because of the absence therein— by way of being an object, by way of association,
or by way of being a hindrance, a sign, or a basis for aspiration— of the defiled states such as lust and the rest, they have no other arrival, object, or [defilement].
In order to show that [the three names] receive their designations such as "emptiness" (suññatā) even by way of their own intrinsic nature (sabhāva), it was stated:
"by way of the object," and so forth. Therein, "by way of its own essence" (sarasavasena) means by way of its own intrinsic nature.

"The triad of names" refers to the triad of names beginning with emptiness. "In all instances" means in all paths of the supramundane path and in all paths of the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti). "Of all" means of all paths and fruits.
"Exactly the same" (*samameva*) means precisely the same; it means identical. "In these" (*ettha pana*) refers to those paths and fruits mentioned above.
This is because all views and the sixteen types of doubt are rooted in the view of self (*attadiṭṭhi*).
When the view of self ceases, they all cease. Furthermore, all those karmas leading to the states of misery ripen only when the view of self exists.
In the absence of ignorance, they do not ripen. And for those who have seen the Truths, that view is abandoned in every respect. Therefore, it is said: "The path of stream-entry...

[is] one who has abandoned going to the states of misery. They are called "going to the states of misery" (*apāyagamanāni*) because one goes to the miserable states by means of them—namely, unwholesome states dissociated from views and doubt, as well as kamma consisting of previously committed misconduct. One for whom the going to the states of misery has been abandoned is "one who has abandoned going to the states of misery."

For those who have penetrated the Four Noble Truths and abandoned the view of self, the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakkhiyadhammā) stand firmly on the side of absolute increase, whereas the defiled states (kilesadhammā) stand on the side of decline.

Therefore, as these [defilements] gradually diminish and pass away, they reach total exhaustion at the upper limit within seven more existences; thus, one is called a "Stream-enterer with seven births at most" (sattakkhattuparama sotāpanna).
Regarding the term "hotīti" (it occurs): therein, by the word *sattakkhattu* (seven times), the cycles of taking seven rebirths are meant. *Paramo* (supreme) signifies the upper limit.

Thus, one for whom seven times is the supreme [limit] is a *sattakkhattuparamo*. Furthermore, he is of three kinds: one who has seven times as the supreme limit among devas, one who has seven times as the supreme limit among humans, and one who has seven times as the supreme limit in both places. As it is said:
And what kind of person is one who has at most seven more births?

Here, a certain person, through the complete destruction of the three fetters, becomes a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, and destined for full enlightenment;
having wandered and transmigrated among gods and humans for seven more times, he makes an end of suffering. This is called the person who has at most seven more births.
For here, the word *ca* has the sense of non-restriction (*aniyama*). By this, it is shown that there are three kinds of those called "seven-times-at-most" (*sattakkhattuparama*):
one who transmigrates seven times among gods alone; one who transmigrates seven times among humans alone; and one who transmigrates seven times by way of mixed existences among both gods and humans.
However, in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), regarding the mixed existence...

The meaning of *vasena* has been stated. And here, because it disregards the power of both the sublime meditative absorptions (*mahaggata-jjhāna*) and the insight (*vipassanā*) of the higher paths, the name "seven-times-at-most" (*sattakkhattuparama*) is applied solely according to the capacity of this particular path’s own power. And that [capacity] is found in the Canon [in the passage]:
"Of which five [types of persons] is there finality here? Of the seven-times-at-most, the family-to-family... (*katamesaṃ pañcannaṃ idha niṭṭhā. Sattakkhattuparamassa kolaṃkollassa...*)?

Because it is stated that the kola-seeder, the single-seeder, the once-returner, and he who becomes an Arahant in this very life [are all included], one should understand that they are either dry-insight practitioners devoid of jhāna within the sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*), or those who have fallen away from jhāna. For this very reason, in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga-aṭṭhakathā*, it is said:
"These three types of stream-enterers are spoken of with reference to the sense-sphere existence; however, in the fine-material and immaterial existences, there are many [others]."
It is said that they take rebirths. And in the *Aṅguttara-aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated: "The eighth existence means the eighth rebirth in the sense-sphere realm (*kāmabhava*).

Therefore, for those who attain the higher path either within seven rounds in the sense-sphere realm itself or even in this very life (*diṭṭhadhamma*), such a distinction in their course of existence occurs by the power of the higher paths and insight (*vipassanā*).
He should be understood as "accomplished" (siddha). For it is stated in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) that insight (*vipassanā*) governs the three higher paths.

Furthermore, there are those who, like Sakka, Anāthapiṇḍika, Visākhā, and others, attain jhāna either in this very life or in any one of the seven existences and go to the Brahma-world; and those who [attain it] only in the Brahma-world.
Having attained the path of stream-entry, they attain final Nibbāna right there.

Such a distinction in their mode of existence is accomplished through the power of sublime jhāna. Furthermore, because the Pāḷi states "seven times among devas," this indicates seven rebirths by way of spontaneous birth (*opapātika*) within the sensual realm;
and because it says "seven times among humans," this indicates seven rebirths by way of conception in a womb.

"He shows" means that by both [methods], fourteen types of rebirth-linking are shown. Therefore, with reference to the fourteen existences obtainable by that method, it is said in the *Sakkapañha Sutta*:
"Seven from here, seven from there—fourteen rounds of wandering. Likewise, in the *Aṅguttara Nikāya*, in the *Tikanipāta*.
“If, Udāyin, Ānanda were to pass away while still not free from lust, by virtue of that confidence in his mind, he would exercise sovereignty among the devas seven times;
he would exercise great sovereignty seven times right here in Jambudīpa.
Moreover, Udāyin, it has been said: ‘Ānanda will attain final nibbāna in this very life. However, some [interpret] these words of the sutta...
They maintain that for a stream-enterer who has seven births at most, there are fourteen rebirths in the sense-sphere realm (*kāmabhava*).
In the *Mahāvagga-saṃyutta-ṭīkā*, it is stated: "Some, however, say that one is reborn in the sense-sphere realm exactly seven times and not beyond that; this should be investigated.
Furthermore, in the *Vibhaṅga* and in various instances of the *Aṭṭhāna-sutta*, it is said: "It is impossible, it is out of the question, that one who is endowed with right view..."
"A person might produce an eighth existence— this is impossible," as stated in the *Aṅguttara Nikāya*, Chakkanipāta;
and "a person perfected in vision is incapable of producing an eighth existence," as stated in the *Mahānidessa*, Ajita-pañha,
regarding the cessation of volitional consciousness through the knowledge of the path to the stream-entry fruit, which excludes [the possibility of] another [existence] among the seven existences.
"Whatever name-and-form (nāma-rūpa) might arise within this saṃsāra, herein they cease; they subside, they come to an end, they become tranquil.
Since this was stated with such firmness, the meaning of those scriptural passages should be understood precisely according to the method already described.
"Of lust, hatred, and delusion" refers to sensual lust (kāmarāga), hatred (dosa), and the delusion associated therewith.
"Thinned out" (*tanukaratta*) means that, just as [defilements] arise powerfully within the continuum of a stream-enterer regarding wholesome objects of sensual desire—
since even sexual intercourse occurs for them— they are made thin by way of refinement (*saṃlikhana*), rendering them incapable of arising in that same manner.
This is also due to their infrequency of occurrence and the weakness of their obsessions (*pariyuṭṭhāna*).
The meaning is: "by making the state of being slight a means of accomplishment. In that context, "by way of occasional arising" means by way of arising only sometimes, after a long interval.
"By way of the weakness of obsession" means by way of an even weaker obsession in those [states] which arise only after a long interval.
However, the Elder Mahāsīva maintains that even for them, sexual intercourse with the basis of sexual union is intended; this is rejected in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*. And as for that...
In the Migasālāvastu of the *Chakkanipāta*, the Blessed One also declared the state of a *sakadāgāmin* for the brahmin Isidatta, who was not a practitioner of the holy life (*abrahmacārī*).
This declaration should be understood as having been made on account of his attainment at the time when death was imminent.
The construction is: "He is called a *sakadāgāmin* because, having come to this world only once more, he will not return [from there]. As for what ought to be said here:
This has already been explained below in the first chapter. "Having developed arahantship" means having developed the path to arahantship.
One whose four taints (*āsava*) are exhausted is called "one whose taints are exhausted" (*khīṇāsava*).

"Sacrificial gift" (*dakkhiṇā*) refers to the act of giving performed with faith in both the deed and its fruit, for the sake of obtaining a result in the future; it is so called because by means of it, beings flourish (*dakkhanti*) and increase.

Because of the total absence of defilements that cause the failure of that offering, and because of the complete perfection of qualities such as the aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha) that bring about its success, he is the foremost and eldest among those worthy of offerings;

thus, being one who is worthy of receiving that offering, he is called "the foremost of those worthy of offerings" (aggadakkhiṇeyyo). "The classification of persons" refers to the four types of persons established in the fruits (phalaṭṭhapuggala).
This is the brief classification. The detailed classification, however, should be understood as follows:

in the *Aṭṭhakathās*, ninety-six types of those established in the fruits are mentioned—namely, twenty-four stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*), twelve once-returners (*sakadāgāmin*), forty-eight non-returners (*anāgāmin*), and twelve arahants.

Among these, there are two types of stream-enterers: those resolved through faith (*saddhādhimutta*) and those resolved through wisdom (*paññādhimutta*). These [two] consist of the "one-seeder" (*ekabījī*) and the "family-to-family" (*kolaṃkolo*).
"Seven times at most" (sattakkhattuparama), when multiplied by three, becomes six. When further multiplied by the four paths of practice (paṭipadā), they become twenty-four.
Through the division of the threefold liberation (vimokkha) and the four paths of practice, there are twelve types of once-returners (sakadāgāmin) and twelve types of arahants.

As for the non-returners (anāgāmin), first, among those in the Aviha heaven, there are three who attain parinibbāna in the interval (antarāparinibbāyin), and one who attains it upon reaching the intermediate state (upahacca).

There are five types: one who attains *parinibbāna* in the intermediate state, one who attains *parinibbāna* upon landing, one who attains *parinibbāna* with effort, one who attains *parinibbāna* without effort, and one who goes upstream to the Akaniṭṭha realm.

These same five, when multiplied by two—namely, those who attain *parinibbāna* with effort and those who attain *parinibbāna* without effort—make ten. Likewise, in the Atappa, Sudassa, and Sudassī realms, there are forty-three.
However, in the Akaniṭṭha realm, since there is no such thing as "one who goes upstream to the Akaniṭṭha," there are only four who attain *parinibbāna* with effort.
There are eight who attain *parinibbāna* without exertion (*asaṅkhāra-parinibbāyino*). All together, they amount to forty-eight. However, in the *Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā*, there are fifty-four:
twelve stream-enterers (*sotāpannas*), twelve once-returners (*sakadāgāmis*), twenty-four non-returners (*anāgāmis*), two arahants, and four established on the paths (*maggaṭṭhas*).
These same individuals, when categorized by way of the burden of faith (*saddhādhura*) and the burden of wisdom (*paññādhura*), become two [groups].
It is stated that when multiplied, there are one hundred and eight types of persons (*puggala*). "In this" means in this classification of persons.

"Of all" means common to all four who stand in the fruits (*phalaṭṭha*). The intention is that, unlike the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), which is common only to certain individuals, these [qualities] are common to all.
[This refers to] one's own mental continuum (*cittasantāna*) which has been excessively cherished, praised, and clung to.

It is said that what is called "the making of a turning-back" (apavattikaraṇa) is accomplished only by those who are free from abundant lust; thus it is not obtained by non-returners (anāgāmin) or Arahants.

Even for them, it should be understood that only those who have attained the eight meditative attainments (aṭṭhasamāpatti) and have gone to the realms of sense-sphere existence (kāma-bhava) or fine-material existence (rūpa-bhava) are included here. Why?
Because one must proceed by the power of successive cessation (anupubbanirodha) starting from the beginning. Therefore he said, "Therein," and so forth. In this regard, this [is the explanation]:
The method: having entered the first jhāna and emerged from it, he contemplates the formations present therein as impermanent, suffering, and non-self.
Then, having entered the second jhāna and emerged from it, he likewise contemplates the formations present therein. Then the third jhāna; then the fourth jhāna; then the fifth jhāna.
Then the base of infinite space. Then, having entered the base of infinite consciousness and emerged from it, he likewise contemplates the formations present therein.
Then, having entered the base of nothingness and emerged from it, he performs these four kinds of preliminary duties:
not disturbing those bound by various ties, honoring the Saṅgha, summoning the Teacher, and delimiting the duration of the journey.
He performs [this]. Then he enters the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Having passed over one or two mental moments, he becomes mindless and touches cessation (*nirodha*). "Right there, right there" means at the very moment of emerging from each respective jhāna.
"Vipassantō" (insighting) is said because cessation must be attained through the power of the union of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*).

By means of the power of insight (*vipassanā*) as well, for the purpose of inducing a state of extreme subtlety and refinement in the mental continuum, one contemplates this first jhāna according to the method beginning with "it is impermanent" and so forth.

"Having gone as far as the base of nothingness" means having gone by way of attaining, emerging from, and contemplating the jhāna of the base of nothingness. Herein, there are also the acts of adverting, resolving, and reviewing.
These indeed are to be desired. For it is for this very reason that five kinds of mastery are described in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga* regarding the preparations for cessation (*nirodha*).

"Beyond that" means immediately after the insight into formations (*saṅkhāra-vipassanā*) within the jhāna of the base of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatana*). "It should be resolved upon" (*adhiṭṭhātabbaṃ*) means one should resolve upon it.
Having set aside the requisites bound to one's own body, [one considers] the various bound requisites such as robes and so forth.

The function of formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna-kicca*) is as follows: thinking, "May I not be destroyed by dangers such as fire," or "When a formal act of the Saṅgha is being performed within a single boundary, the Saṅgha will summon me;
at that time, I shall emerge from this attainment," or "The Teacher will call for me for some reason;
at that time, I shall emerge. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), it includes such things as: "Will I indeed die within the very midst of cessation? and so forth.
The limitation of time is grasped as occurring in the thought, "It will happen for me. For two [persons]...
the continuity of consciousness is cut off because, from the very beginning, such a specific application has been thoroughly performed for that purpose. "Then" means at that time.
For a non-returner, the non-returning fruit-consciousness is without preliminary advertence (*anāvajjana*) and without preparation (*nipparikamma*); this is the intended meaning. For it is thus:
The preliminary work of insight (vipassanā-parikamma), which has been practiced repeatedly from the very beginning, remains as his preliminary meditation subject (parikamma-ṭṭhāna).
There is no separate "near-preliminary" (āsanna-parikamma) distinct from it. "Reviewing" (paccavekkhaṇa) refers to the reviewing of the fruit (phala-paccavekkhaṇa).
Having thus demonstrated the two-fold method of the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna-naya), he now [explains] the purpose for which it is demonstrated.
Instructing his followers, he spoke this verse beginning with "should be cultivated" (*bhāvetabba*). Therein, "practice" (*paṭipatti*) means that which is to be practiced;

or, it is practice because by means of it those who practice advance higher and higher. It refers to the phenomena such as virtue (*sīla*). "Flavor" (*rasa*) means that which is tasted, or experienced, by way of experiencing non-material happiness;
it refers to the dhamma of realization consisting of the jhānas, the path, and the fruit—or specifically, the fruit of arahantship itself.
Or rather, it is the joy and mental happiness that arise dependent upon both of those. The "flavor" (*rasa*) is the practice itself;
and since that very [practice] is to be relished in the sense of being something to be savored, it is called "the flavor of the practice" (*paṭipatti-rasa*).
The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: "A bhikkhu who aspires to the flavor of the practice within the Teaching should develop these two supreme forms of meditation thus described by me."
Thus ends the Elucidation of the Ultimate Meaning (*Paramatthadīpanā*) of the Compendium of Meditation Subjects (*Kammaṭṭhānasaṅgaha*),
which is the fourth commentary on the *Abhidhammattha-saṅgaha* entitled the Elucidation of the Ultimate Meaning (*Paramatthadīpanī*).
Nigama Paramatthadīpanī 172. *Cārittasobhitavisālakulodayo*:

one whose arising and growth (*udayo vaḍḍhi*) occurred in a noble family (*visālakule*) that was distinguished by conduct (*cārittena*), meaning family tradition (*kulācārena*), and expansive through the excellence of relatives, friends, wealth, and enjoyments;
[the compound refers] to him. [It refers to those] who have increased in faith and are utterly pure.

"In this [work] there is the arising and increase of one's own qualities such as virtue, learning, and generosity; thus it is 'the arising of pure qualities through the growth of faith' (*saddhātivuḍḍha-parisuddha-guṇodayo*).

By that. 'By him who is called Nampa' means by the lay follower (upāsaka) named Nampa. 'Having made a resolve' (*paṇidhāya*) means having placed it firmly in the heart, having taken it up, having relied upon it.
'Compassion for others' (*parānukampā*) means compassion for others—those of dull intellect and those belonging to later generations."
The connection is: “having directed compassion toward the non-arising [of suffering]. “Patthitaṃ” means requested.
“By that vast merit” means by that vast merit consisting in the composition of the *Abhidhammattha-saṅgaha* treatise.
“Tumūlasoma” refers to the monastery of that name. For it is said in the *Khuddasikkhā-ṭīkā*: “In the Saṅgha at the Tumūlasoma Monastery on the island of Sīhaḷa...”
Even the roofing shingles for the monastery were made by selling palm leaves; for there was no need for leaves there.
All the buildings, such as the palaces and so forth, were covered with bricks.

It is said that this monastery was originally built by Somadevī, who had been the chief queen of King Abhayagiri, and thus it was known even until the present day simply as the “Somavihāra. However, the tumultuous sound—
This is a synonym for a vast sound. Then there arose a tumultuous, terrifying,
and great clamor when the noble elephant was given away as a gift by the Sivi people, who increase their kingdom.
In these cases, like the word "as it were" (*viya*). That monastery was established with about sixty great courtyards; thus, it was exceedingly vast, great, and extensive.
Therefore, because of its vastness, greatness, and extensiveness, it is called "tumula-soma."
"Taṃ tumūlasomaṃ" means "that Mahāsoma Monastery. In terms of its meaning, it is said to be the monastery where [the Elder] dwelt.
By this, the Elder praises the dwelling place of his own lineage of teachers. His own specific residence, however, was praised in the *Nāmarūpapariccheda*.
"Dhaññādhivāsaṃ" means that monastery which had been inhabited by virtuous elders such as the Elder Mahinda, who were the original founders of that monastery.

Because he was born in the lineage of the Great Elder Mahinda, the illuminator of the island, the Great Elder who was the founder of that monastery is also called by the name Mahinda in the *Dhātuvaṃsa*.

"Exalted" (*uditodita*) means exceedingly exalted; the meaning is that he was pre-eminently prominent throughout the entire island of Siṃhala, like the orb of the full moon in the midst of the sky. By way of the wisdom of the Noble Path...

"Flowing with qualities purified by wisdom" means either by way of the confidence (*vesārajja*) regarding the scriptures (*pariyatti*) and so forth, or because they are "flowing" (*sotitā*) with qualities that are bright and radiant through wisdom;
thus it is "flowing with qualities purified by wisdom. They alone are modest and reproachful of evil. "May they remember" means may they recollect.

"For the sake of the auspiciousness consisting in the increase of abundant merit" means for the purpose of the auspiciousness known as the growth of vast merits. Herein, this is the construction: "By that abundant merit, [may there be] a dwelling in prosperity..."

May future generations consider that monastery—resplendent with the rising moon of Tumula, where the Elder Mahinda and others reside, monks who are pure in wisdom, adorned with virtues, and possessed of a sense of shame—as an auspicious source for the arising of merit and the desired longevity.
Alternatively, the construction may be understood as: "May others consider that monastery to be filled with monks who are pure in wisdom, adorned with virtues, and possessed of a sense of shame."

By this means, the Elder has set forth for future generations both a specific merit known as the "Recollection of the Unsurpassed" among the six unsurpassed qualities, and the method for exertion, thinking:
"May we too become partakers of such virtues. This concludes the *Paramatthadīpanī* commentary on the *Nigama-kathā*.
And to this extent:
"By me, who was born in the city of Dīparaṅga, in the village named Tiṇāmaka,
under the single [tree] of the two-fold eight-fold void, in Sāka."
While dwelling in the forest at Muṃrvā Village, in the monastery known as Laṅghati,
this commentary named *Paramatthadīpanī* was composed by the monk who acts for the benefit of a great community and perceives the essence.
For the benefit of those seeking the essence, who discern between the essential and the non-essential,
this commentary— fearless and free from calamity—
is well-concluded in the year nineteen hundred and twenty-one (1921), during the month of Kattika (Kumuda-sāra).
Likewise, may all those with noble intentions, which yield the fruit of immortality for the virtuous,
reach their ultimate goal— fearless and free from calamity—
just as both the moon and the sun shine throughout the world.
In the same way, this *Paramatthadīpanī* [is] among the ultimate meanings (*paramattha*).
This well-composed work, which elucidates the word-meanings (*sadda-nirutti*) regarding those things contained in the scriptures (*pāḷi*),
may both shine throughout the world as long as the True Dhamma (*saddhamma*) endures.
In that context, "in the city named Dīparaṅga" means in the city so named because it delights the great multitude of inhabitants of Dīpa.
"In the village named [so-and-so]" refers to a great village so named because it was established on ground that had been the dwelling place of red deer (rohitamiga).
"At Sāketa" refers to the Kali age. "That which by me" connects to the fact that the commentary named *Paramatthadīpanī* was composed by me.
"Laṅghatīti vissutālaye" means in the forest hermitage well-known by that name. "Sāresīnaṃ" means for those seeking the essence.
"Sārāsāravivekinaṃ" means for those capable of discerning and knowing the essence and the non-essence, thinking, "This is the essence; this is the non-essence.
"Sāke" refers to the Kali age. "Komudasāre" means during the autumn season associated with the *kumuda* flower, specifically in the months of Āśvina and Kārttika.
"Having the fruit of immortality" means having Nibbāna as its purpose. "Beautiful" means splendid due to the perfection of both meaning and phrasing.
"True Dhamma" refers to the threefold teaching of the Teacher.
Thus ends the fourth commentary on the *Abhidhammattha-saṅgaha*.
The commentary named *Bhūtā-paramatthadīpanī* has been completed in every respect.
